HOHENFELS, Germany — The US Army's Abrams tanks are built to charge into battle, using their heavy armor and powerful cannon to break through enemy defenses. But at a major training exercise in Germany, they were doing everything they could to stay out of sight.
Driving through the Joint Multinational Readiness Center, the Army's main overseas training facility, the presence of the 1st Armored Division's Abrams tanks was hard to miss. Mud tracks crisscrossed and meandered through the grassy hills, scarred by the treads of the heavy armored vehicles.
However, the tanks themselves were nowhere in sight. They were hidden along the treelines and deeper in the forest, careful not to reveal their positions to enemy reconnaissance drones.
For a vehicle built to deliver overwhelming firepower on the battlefield, concealment has become a matter of survival.
Drones filled the sky when Business Insider visited the Hohenfels training grounds in late October to observe Combined Resolve, a recurring exercise that pitted a rotational armor brigade against an opposition force simulating a US adversary.
The training environment was designed to resemble the battlefields in Ukraine, where heavy drone proliferation has made it extremely difficult for tanks and infantry fighting vehicles to move freely without being detected. Armored assets have taken heavy losses in the war, raising questions among some warfare experts about their continued relevance on a modern battlefield dominated by constant overhead surveillance and cheap precision strikes.
At the JMRC in Germany, Army officers insisted that tanks aren't dead. However, effectively keeping them in the fight means changing how armored formations operate, from the way tanks move and conceal themselves to how they refuel, communicate, and prepare for an attack.
"I don't see armor disappearing," said Sgt. Sean Brenna, an M1A2 Abrams tank gunner with the 1st Armored Division's 1st Armored Brigade Combat Team (1/1 ABCT).
"A lot of people are like, 'Drones are the death of the tank,'" he said. "I don't see that. I see tanks evolving."
What Ukraine taught the US Army
Russia's full-scale invasion has dramatically upended perceptions of armored vehicles on the modern battlefield.
Tanks and infantry fighting vehicles were once seen as pillars of Ukraine's defense; in the early stages of the war, for instance, some of these systems — like the M1 Abrams and German-made Leopard tanks— were considered priority acquisitions for Kyiv.
But drones have made it much harder for armor to operate effectively.
Ukraine and Russia have lost multimillion-dollar armored vehicles to drones that cost a few hundred dollars. Both sides have tried to mitigate the risk by equipping tanks with added protection, such as cage armor, but it's far from a perfect solution.
Across much of the sprawling front line, dense minefields, entrenched defenses, artillery, and widespread drone surveillance have made large-scale maneuver increasingly difficult. Drones in particular have expanded the danger, creating a miles-wide "kill zone" where soldiers and their vehicles risk being spotted and targeted whenever they move.
At the Army's training grounds in the Bavarian hills outside Munich, the drone threat was impossible to ignore.
At one point during the exercise, soldiers clad in black, wearing baseball hats and camouflage vests, rushed out of a command post and across an uneven field to deploy a spy drone.
As they worked, a sudden buzz filled the air. Another drone, a small quadcopter, appeared almost out of nowhere and flew toward the team. A soldier raised his rifle and pulled the trigger. Jamming, it produced an impotent click.
The drone hovered briefly before flying off. It turned out to be a friendly asset, but had it belonged to the enemy, the soldiers could have found themselves facing an attack.
The US Army has increasingly been confronting these threats and related vulnerabilities in training, with Ukrainian soldiers helping expose just how dangerous the battlefield has become for American armored formations.
Like other NATO militaries, the US has leveraged Ukraine's experience and included its soldiers in major exercises across Europe.
During an iteration of Combined Resolve held earlier this year, Ukrainian soldiers from the 412th Unmanned Systems Brigade, an elite unit known as "Nemesis," served as an opposing force, challenging US armor. Nemesis helped to cause roughly 70% of the casualties suffered by a US armored brigade in the opening two days.
The Americans eventually improved, changing tactics, and the share of drone-related casualties dropped.
A source with knowledge of the exercise said the Ukrainian soldiers had the entire training area covered by their sensing and strike capabilities, turning practices considered safe in previous US military campaigns, such as clustering vehicles in rear areas to refuel, into large targets.
It was particularly eye-opening for soldiers to see that logistics and maintenance could no longer be done in the open, the source said, adding that the purpose of the exercise is to use these hard-learned lessons to inform future tactics.
Brig. Gen. Terry Tillis, the commander of the 7th Army Training Command, which operates under US Army Europe and Africa, said the April exercise raised a key question for officers and soldiers: how can they better protect armor from drones?
The answer, at least in part, is to rethink some of the most basic practices of armored warfare.
Reinventing the armored fight
For starters, it means decentralized logistics and using the terrain to avoid massive clusters. In the October iteration of Combined Resolve, this proved to be a work in progress.
In the middle of a field, an M1 Abrams sat powered down, its crew resting on top. Hours earlier, the tank had tried to refuel but was targeted by indirect fire, forcing it to disperse. The tank was eventually struck — what the crew called a mobility-firepower kill — and had to remain in position until it was allowed to rejoin the exercise.
The incident underscored how even routine tasks, such as refueling a tank, have become dangerous operations when enemy drones and other sensors can expose vehicles to attack.
Brenna, the Abrams gunner, said one of the biggest challenges of the exercise was learning how to handle drones as an armor crew. Reports of overhead activity were near-constant, and his crew spotted countless drones.
He and the rest of his crew have learned to adapt, he said. In some ways, the methods are rather basic, like using camouflage nets to cover their tank, but they are also overhauling how they maneuver, handle logistics, and communicate with the brigade.
It's an ongoing effort that involves experimenting with new tactics to gauge their effectiveness, such as hiding along the treelines and resupplying at night rather than during the day.
Brenna said that the crew is mainly trying to avoid remaining in the same place for too long because, during the exercise, the opposition force taught them that "hiding in a treeline might protect you from being spotted from a drone, but not forever. And the moment you do get spotted, it is best to relocate quickly."
The Army is working through those challenges while recognizing that survival is only one part of the equation in battle. Armored forces must also be able to maneuver, attack, and seize territory.
The Ukrainians recently demonstrated what that looks like in practice.
Ukraine's Third Army Corps, which has led a major counteroffensive in the embattled eastern Donetsk region, disclosed recently that it had executed two successful mechanized assaults behind Russian lines. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi, the corps' commander, said that he was initially skeptical it could be done.
While details remain limited, the general has revealed that armored crews had to undergo special training and that their vehicles were outfitted with additional equipment to support their push. Other armored endeavors have involved support drones operating in both surveillance and attack roles.
"Today, the use of armored vehicles is effectively a special operation. It requires extremely detailed planning and the coordination of a huge number of assets," Biletskyi recently told Militarnyi, a Ukrainian military news site.
Recent successes suggest that mechanized maneuver isn't necessarily a thing of the past, even if carrying it out on a drone-saturated battlefield has become far more difficult.
Why the tank still matters
The challenges that armored vehicles and mechanized infantry formations have faced in Ukraine "prompted some to prematurely declare the death of ground maneuver, claiming that a transparent battlefield defined by persistent observation, unmanned system proliferation, AI-driven targeting, and long-range strike made offensive ground movement obsolete," wrote Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the acting Army chief of staff, in an October document outlining how the service will fight its next war.
"These claims mistake tactical destruction for operational and strategic success," LaNeve said. "Long-range fires degrade enemy networks at range, but standoff alone rarely compels the enemy to surrender. Only ground maneuver can seize what the enemy holds and secure it against the enemy's will."
The argument is that while drones and long-range weapons can help destroy enemy forces, they cannot replace the ground troops needed to capture and hold territory. The Army sees armor as an essential part of that effort, even as the way it operates changes.
"Armor will always be present. It's always a necessity, right?" said Capt. Kevin Rincon, the troop commander of the multifunctional reconnaissance company, the brigade's action arm. "It's kind of like that shock force — the combination of the duo of infantry and armor."
To that end, the October exercise was designed to stress-test how the rotating armored brigade could use drones, electronic warfare, and other counter-drone technology to sense, track, and engage attacks from the opposing force. By the time Business Insider visited Hohenfels, near the end of the multi-day-long scenario, 1/1 ABCT was on the counteroffensive.
Tillis, the 7th ATC commander, said drones can help control terrain, but actually holding ground requires integrating emerging technologies with traditional armor.
Technologies like drones, counter-drone systems, and electronic warfare "are all enablers designed to facilitate combined arms maneuver," Tillis said. "We've got to be able to attack, seize, retain terrain, hold, and then, if need be, defend and do it again. You cannot take an objective without putting boots on the ground."
The challenge is figuring out how to make that kind of maneuver possible against an enemy that can watch and strike from overhead.
Brenna said he can envision a situation where armor plays a more "precise role" in the next US war.
For now, the American tank crews in Germany are learning that surviving long enough to fight may require staying hidden, moving carefully, and abandoning some of the practices that once defined armored warfare.
One thing is certain, Brenna said. "The army is definitely not giving up on tanks. That's for sure."

Delhi high court permanently protects actor Amitabh Bachchan's personality rights
In its November 5 order, the court decreed the suit filed by Bachchan in 2022, after being informed that he had entered into settlements with four entities.
The Delhi high court has granted permanent protection to the personality rights of veteran Bollywood actor Amitabh Bachchan, restraining entities from using his name, image, voice, or other aspects of his persona without his consent.
In its November 5 order, a bench of justice Purushaindra Kumar Kaurav decreed the suit filed by Bachchan in 2022, after being informed that he had entered into settlements with four entities acknowledging his publicity rights and right to privacy.
The settlement
As part of the settlement, one individual informed the court that he had taken steps to remove the mobile application titled Amitabh Bachchan Video Call, while the other said that it had discontinued publication of its General Knowledge Quizbook, which featured the actor’s image.
One individual submitted that it had stopped selling posters bearing Bachchan’s image, name and likeness. Meanwhile, another informed the court that he had deleted the domain name amitabhbachchan.in in November 2022 and had not derived any monetary benefit from it.
All four entities undertook not to use Bachchan’s name, image, voice, likeness or any other aspect of his persona in the future without his express permission.
The order
With regard to the remaining defendants, including unknown entities, the court noted that, despite being served, they had failed to appear or file written statements, and that their right to file written statements had been closed on September 25, 2023.
The court further observed that, in a commercial suit, the statutory timeline for filing a written statement cannot be extended beyond the prescribed period.
The court said that its November 2022 interim order protecting the veteran actor’s rights would stand merged in the decree.
“Accordingly, the application stands allowed. The suit stands decreed qua defendant nos. 1, 3, 5 and 8 in terms of paragraph no. 76(a) to (c) of the plaint and in terms of paragraph no. 7 of the instant application. Let the decree sheet be drawn up by the Registry. The application, which embodies the terms of the compromise, shall form part of the decree sheet. None of the defendants has filed a written statement disputing the plaintiff‟s case, and defendant nos. 1, 3, 5 and 8 have themselves accepted the plaintiff‟s rights and suffered a decree,” the court said in the order.
It added, “The interim injunction dated 25.11.2022 operated against the John Does as well. The plaint discloses a continuing pattern of anonymous misuse of the plaintiff‟s persona, through websites, applications, posters and messaging platforms, which the plaintiff cannot track to identified persons. The decree in terms of paragraph no. 76(a) to (c) shall, therefore, also operate against defendant no. 10.”

Taiwan detains a Communist Party leader over alleged Chinese sponsorship in election
Authorities in Taiwan have detained the leader of the Taiwan People’s Communist Party
TAIPEI, Taiwan -- Authorities in Taiwan detained the leader of the island's Taiwan People’s Communist Party, accusing him of running as a candidate for borough chief under the direction and sponsorship of China’s Communist Party, local media reported Sunday.
Taiwan is set to hold elections for mayors and local area chiefs on November 28. While the races focus more on livelihood issues, the results could be a good indicator of the popularity of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party under the leadership of Taiwan President Lai Ching-te ahead of the presidential election in 2028.
According to Taiwan's Central News Agency, prosecutors said in a statement Sunday that an initial investigation showed Taiwan People’s Communist Party chair Lin Te-wang also had directed another party member to run as a candidate for chief in another borough.
Prosecutors also alleged that Lin sought to buy votes by repeatedly recruiting voters to travel to mainland China, where they received hospitality, the report said.
While Lin’s party is not influential on the democratic island, it was not his first legal trouble over his alleged links with China. He and another party leader had faced charges of Chinese infiltration and attempting to influence elections but were found not guilty in 2025, the Taipei Times reported.
Taiwan’s Central News Agency said the prosecutors had received intelligence about foreign interference in the election and summoned 14 people and nine witnesses. After questioning, the government lawyers strongly suspected that Lin and the other party member had committed a crime and were concerned the pair could flee or destroy evidence, so they filed applications to the local courts to detain them and bar them from being visited by others, it said.
The courts ruled in the prosecutors' favor for Lin but released the other member on a 50,000-Taiwan-dollar ($1,525) bail, the news agency said. The other people summoned were released during the investigation, it added.
China's Taiwan Affairs Office has not immediately commented.
Beijing views Taiwan as a breakaway province to be retaken by force if necessary, and claims of China's meddling are common in Taiwanese elections.
China and Taiwan have been governed separately since 1949 when the Chinese Communist Party rose to power in Beijing following a civil war. Defeated Nationalist Party forces fled to Taiwan, which later transitioned from martial law to multiparty democracy.
___
Leung reported from Hong Kong.

Tokyo/Naha – Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said Friday that the Japanese government will enhance educational programs for U.S. troops in Okinawa following a robbery and murder allegedly involving a U.S. Marine in the prefecture last month.
The government will incorporate opinions of the prefecture into briefing materials provided to U.S. military personnel before their deployment to Japan.
The recurrence prevention measures were agreed by the Japanese government and U.S. forces in Japan. Among them are plans to promptly introduce lectures by the Japanese Foreign Ministry’s envoy for Okinawa and to launch a new educational program on Okinawa’s culture and history in fiscal 2027.
Japan and the United States will also increase the frequency and areas of their joint patrols in Okinawa.
“It’s important to take effective measures to prevent incidents,” Motegi said. “Japan wants to continue consultations with the United States.”
The U.S. Marine in question, deployed at a U.S. base in Okinawa, has been indicted for allegedly killing a woman in a guest room of a hotel in Naha, the capital of the prefecture, and stealing her belongings Oct. 3.
The U.S. military in Okinawa has said that it will extend its curfew, introduced in the wake of the robbery-murder case and imposed between midnight and 5 a.m., until Dec. 7 for lower-ranking military personnel in the prefecture. The measure will end for higher-ranking personnel on Sunday as scheduled.
But all personnel will be prohibited from drinking alcohol outside their residences after midnight through Dec. 7.

Yesterday, when reporting on emerging efforts to pipe the console version of GTA VI through a PC’s DLSS-powered Nvidia GPU, we mentioned in passing that PC players could instead just wait for the AI-assisted decompilation port that will no doubt be coming in short order. Now, a former Rockstar tech director says he thinks that exact threat could cause the developer to work faster on the official PC version of its soon-to-release crime/lifestyle simulator.
Obbe Vermeij hasn’t worked at Rockstar since 2009, but in a new interview with Rock Paper Shotgun, he recalled how artists for the PC version of the original top-down Grand Theft Auto were incensed when the console version squashed the game’s 256-color textures down to 16 colors for the PS1 release.
“So it always has been that sort of awkward relationship between PC and the console,” Vermeij said. “So in those days, it was like PC first and then console second, even though that didn’t really make much sense for the sales, because the PlayStation versions sold way better.”
Those sales caused Rockstar to pivot hard toward the console side of the business, with oft-delayed PC ports of its major games only hitting many months or even many years after their console counterparts. It’s a trend that Rockstar has stuck with even as many formerly console-focused game publishers have started treating the PC as an equally relevant platform and as the line between PCs and consoles itself has gotten much fuzzier in recent years.

The sound of firecrackers filling the air is not far away as Deepavali draws closer. But the excitement of bursting firecrackers comes with a word of caution from ophthalmologists as they warn that a moment of carelessness can cause eye injuries ranging from minor abrasions to severe ocular trauma.
M. Elangovan, director, Regional Institute of Ophthalmology and Government Ophthalmic Hospital (RIO-GOH), Chennai, said that there are different types of crackers. “Bursting types (explosive crackers) will produce irregular, small and forcible particles in all directions and are the most dangerous. These particles can travel at such a velocity that they could hit or penetrate any soft surface. Then, there is direct heat injury caused by crackers such as sparklers that can cause scar formations in the cornea or conjunctiva due to the heat generated. Sudden and close exposure to bright light-emitting crackers can also cause bleaching or temporary blackout due to the impact on the rod and cone cells in the retina,” he explained.

Tamil Nadu Government has informed the Madras High Court of its decision to withdraw a Government Order (G.O.) issued on September 8, 2026, temporarily promoting Tamil Nadu Dr. Ambedkar Law University Registrar Gowri Ramesh as the Director of Legal Studies (DLS). It said, the vacancy shall be filled up through a regular process as contemplated under the Special Rules for the Tamil Nadu Collegiate Educational Service.
Chief Justice Sushrut Arvind Dharmadhikari and Justice G. Arul Murugan recorded the submission made by Advocate General Vijay Narayan and disposed of a writ appeal filed against a single judge’s October 1, 2026 order granting an interim stay of the G.O. The Bench also closed the writ petition pending before the single judge since nothing survived in it pursuant to the government’s decision to withdraw the G.O.
Vellore Government Law College principal M. Rajeswaran had initially filed a writ petition in the High Court in June 2026 challenging a Government Order issued on March 3, 2026 allocating full additional charge of the post of DLS to Ms. Gowri. Then, he had contended that a full-time Registrar of the Law University could not be given additional charge of the full time post of DLS too and that it was against the service rules.
The petitioner contended that the vacancy in the post of DLS could be filled up only through direct recruitment, transfer or by promoting those holding the post of principal in any of the government law colleges spread across the State. Stating that he was senior to Ms. Gowri, the petitioner had wondered how could she attend the Syndicate meetings in her ex-officio capacity as the Registrar of the university and also as the DLS.
Justice P.T. Asha had entertained that writ petition on June 30, 2026 and stayed the operation of the March 3, 2026 G.O. When that stay order was taken on appeal by the State, the A-G told the first Division Bench that the State government intends to commence the regular process of appointing the DLS in accordance with Rule 2(a) of the Special Rules and complete it within a period of two months.
The Bench disposed of the writ appeal on July 23, 2026 after taking note that the government had also issued a G.O. on July 21, 2026 giving full additional charge of the post of DLS to a joint secretary in the Law department instead of Ms. Gowri.
Thereafter, the September 8, 2026 G.O. was issued temporarily promoting Ms. Gowri as the DLS by invoking the emergency powers conferred on the government under Section 47(1) of Tamil Nadu Government Servants (Conditions of Service) Act, 2016. Hence, Mr. Rajeswaran had filed yet another writ petition in the High Court on September 29, 2026 challenging the latest G.O.
This time, Justice Mummineni Sudheer Kumar stayed the September 8, 2026 G.O. on the ground that the government ought not to have invoked Section 47(1) of the 2016 Act after having given an undertaking before the Division Bench in July 2026 that the post of DLS would be appointed in accordance with Rule 2(a) of the Special Rules.
When a State appeal against this stay order came up before the first Bench, the latter recorded A-G’s submission that the latest G.O. shall be withdrawn. “The State shall pursue with the promotion process in accordance with law. The statement of Advocate General that in the meantime, the State will take steps to fill up the post temporarily, as was done when the earlier writ appeal was disposed of, is recorded,” the Bench said.

Ex-husband’s DNA found on hammer allegedly used to kill Abby Choi, prosecution says
As trial enters sixth week, prosecutors cite forensic findings and CCTV footage showing movements of Choi and former in-laws before and after killing

Warning: graphic content follows.
Slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung could have been fatally struck with a hammer that contained her ex-husband’s DNA when it was seized from a rural village flat where her dismembered remains were found, a court has heard.
Wrapping up their case as the murder trial entered its sixth week, prosecutors highlighted forensic findings and surveillance camera footage showing the movements of Choi and three of her former in-laws before and after her alleged murder on February 21, 2023.

Social media users are spreading seven rules that U.S. President Donald Trump has allegedly proposed to limit privileges for lawmakers in Congress.
The alleged rules, according to many Facebook posts, included proposals like removing pensions for Congress members and requiring lawmakers to participate in the same government-run social services many Americans use, like Medicare for health care insurance and Social Security for retirement paychecks. Here's how the claim usually went, per the aforementioned posts:
I'm in agreement From Fox News. I wonder how loud it'll get if Trump could pull this off. It will be interesting.
President Trump is asking everyone to share this, in three days, most people in the United States will have seen the message. This is an idea that should be passed around, regardless of political party.
The TRUMP Rules:
1. Tenure / No Pension. A Congressman/woman collects a salary while in office and receives no pay when they're out of office. And no more perks go with them.
2. Congress (past, present, & future) participates in Social Security. All funds in the Congressional retirement fund move to the Social Security system immediately. All future funds flow into the Social Security system, and Congress participates with the American people. It may not be used for any other purpose.
3. Congress must purchase their own retirement plan, just as ALL Americans do.
4. Congress will no longer vote themselves a pay raise. Congressional pay will rise at the ok same rate as the COLA for monthly Social Security recipients minus 1% if having a budget balance deficit.
5. Congress loses their current care system and participates in the same health care system (Medicare) as the American people.
6. Congress must equally abide by all laws they impose on the American people (i.e. NO MORE INSIDER TRADING!!!).
7. All contracts with past and present Congressmen/women are void. The American people did not make this contract with Congressmen/women. Congress made all these contracts by and for themselves.
Serving in Congress is an honor and privilege, NOT a career.
The Founding Fathers envisioned citizen legislators should serve their term(s), then go home and go back to work … not get all kinds of freebies. Term limits of 2 terms and treat them like a regular citizen!
You will need to copy and paste.
I AGREE SO I'M SHARING!
Meanwhile, Snopes readers asked about similar posts and searched the website using the keywords "Trump rules."
The above text is a copypasta — a copy-and-pasted internet hoax common on Facebook. As Snopes has previously reported, variants of this particular copypasta have spread online since at least 2009, when a version of the rules listed above were labeled "The 28th Amendment" and attributed to business magnate Warren Buffet.
Internet users circulated it as the "Congressional Reform Act of 2017" during Trump's first term and the "Congressional Reform Act of 2025" in 2025, during his second term.
Fox News, which the copypasta cited as its source, has not reported on "The TRUMP Rules" as of this writing, per a search of the news outlet's website. As of this writing, Trump has also not posted about this particular copypasta online, according to two databases that track his social media output. The White House web page for news releases did not reference these supposed rules. Finally, a search for "The TRUMP Rules" on Google returned no credible and relevant results treating the list as a legitimate proposal.
Thus, we have rated this claim false.
The so-called reforms listed in the act also include a mixture of rules that already exist and proposals that would actually change existing policy. Here's a breakdown of what these supposed reforms would and would not change:
Do Congress members receive pensions?
Congress members, like most federal employees, are eligible for a pension. Here's the pension eligibility requirements, per the Congressional Research Service:
Members of Congress are eligible for a pension at the age of 62 if they have completed at least 5 years of service. Members are eligible for a pension at age 50 if they have completed 20 years of service, or at any age after completing 25 years of service. The amount of the pension depends on length of service (as measured in months) and the average of the highest three years of salary. By law, the starting amount of a Member's retirement annuity may not exceed 80% of his or her final salary.
Do Congress members pay into Social Security? Do they pay into their own retirement plans?
Per our previous reporting, Congress members have paid into Social Security since 1984, when they first became eligible for Social Security benefits.
Congress members first elected in 1984 or later are covered automatically under the Federal Employees' Retirement System, which other government workers use, and can decline coverage.
Aside from Social Security, lawmakers elected before 1984 can be covered under the Civil Service Retirement System, a separate pension plan, CSRS Offset, which is a mix of CSRS and Social Security, or Social Security alone. Lawmakers also pay into these plans — how much they pay and which plans they pay into differs based on when they were elected.
Can Congress members approve a pay raise for themselves?
Congress members can vote for a pay raise as dictated by the Constitution, but the raise doesn't take effect until the next election due to the 27th Amendment. Technically, a law passed in 1989 grants Congress an automatic cost-of-living pay raise, but lawmakers have blocked those pay increases from taking effect for years. Rank-and-file members of Congress, who receive $174,000 annually as of this writing, have not increased their pay since 2009.
Do Congress members have their own health care system? Do they participate in Medicare?
Under the Affordable Care Act of 2010, commonly known as Obamacare, lawmakers must give up the insurance coverage previously provided to them via the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program and buy health insurance through a plan or exchange created under the act. The Office of Personnel Management has also dictated that members of Congress must purchase through DC Health Link, a program offered under the ACA.
Members of Congress also pay into Medicare and are eligible for it, just like any American.
Are Congress members allowed to participate in insider trading?
Congress members are allowed to trade stock, but legally, they're not supposed to conduct insider trading. The Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act of 2012 — known as the STOCK Act — prohibits members of Congress from using "any nonpublic information derived from the individual's position ... or gained from performance of the individual's duties, for personal benefit."
Critics argue the STOCK Act failed to stop insider trading, however, and no member of Congress has been prosecuted for insider trading under the STOCK Act as of this writing — although policy experts have said there's been "persistent credible allegations" of insider trading since the act passed.

Breast cancer begins long before the lump: why diet and lifestyle matter
While genetic predisposition is one factor, a majority of breast cancers develop in women with no family history: metabolic health and physical inactivity play a role too, and it is important for women to know about these factors
Students seen taking part in a ‘Pink Umbrella’ walk to create awareness on breast cancer. Image used for representational purposes only
| Photo Credit: VELANKANNI RAJ B
Last month, celebrated as Breast Cancer Awareness Month, reminded us, as it does every year, about the importance of mammograms, early diagnosis, and advances in treatment. These messages save lives and deserve continued attention. However, there is another conversation that often receives far less attention: the role of food, physical activity, obesity, diabetes, physical activity, and metabolic health in breast cancer.
In my oncology clinic, patients are often surprised when I bring up these topics. They say, “Doctor, I knew breast cancer was related to family history. I didn’t know that lifestyle diseases such as diabetes and obesity had anything to do with it.”

China ‘Goddess of Mercy’ drone send-off reveals modern shift in funeral services
Public reaction is split: some praise the creative innovation, while others find it absurd
2-MIN READ2-MIN
 Listen
Alice Yanin Shanghai
Videos showing a glowing Guanyin, or Goddess of Mercy, carried by a drone and another similar device disguised as a crane have attracted significant attention on Chinese social media.
Together, the two devices recreate the traditional funeral send-off in which the deceased is said to “ascend to heaven.”
In China, a common euphemism for someone who has died is that they have “ridden a crane to the Western Paradise,” or simply “gone west.”

Why China is investing heavily in African push to bring mineral processing home
Beijing has thrown its weight behind a drive by resource-right nations to get a greater share of the spoils from their mineral wealth
Chinese investors have backed mineral processing and manufacturing projects worth more than US$16 billion across Africa, a new report has concluded, amid an increasing push by countries to secure a greater share of the earnings from their natural resources.
The continent is a major international supplier of key minerals such as copper, cobalt and iron ore, and countries such as the Democratic Republic of Congo, Guinea and Zimbabwe have previously introduced mineral export bans or restrictions to encourage domestic processing, according to the report by Beijing-based consultancy Development Reimagined.
The study looked at China’s commitments under an action plan agreed following the China-Africa Cooperation summit in 2024 and found a total of US$41.2 billion had been invested in 32 mining, exploration and development projects in 15 countries up to June this year.

A cancer medicine supplied to a retailer for ₹2,700 carries a maximum retail price (MRP) of ₹27,000. Who accounts for this tenfold difference? A strong earthquake shook central Japan early Sunday (November 8, 2026), shattering store windows, causing people to flee buildings and leaving at least 22 people injured, according to local media.
Japan's Meteorological Agency put the quake's magnitude at 5.7, while the U.S. Geological Survey reported it at magnitude 5.5. Smaller aftershocks were reported.
A wide area near Aichi Prefecture was affected, including the city of Hamamatsu, the ancient capitals of Kyoto and Nara and nearby prefectures of Yamanashi, where Mount Fuji is located, as well as Gifu.
Japanese TV footage showed shattered store windows and scattered shards of glass on the streets. A bookstore was left with mounds of books that had flown off the shelves. The injuries included people who fell down stairs while they were trying to flee.
The quake, which struck at 1:04 a.m. local time, was located about 40 km below the Earth's surface in Shizuoka Prefecture. Aichi and Shizuoka are neighbouring regions. They are far enough from Tokyo that the quake was not felt there. The most violent shaking was felt in Aichi, according to official seismic assessments.
The Shinkansen bullet trains were running at slower speeds in the affected areas as a precautionary measure. Sometimes quakes can damage the railways the trains run on.
Japan is located in an area that is prone to earthquakes.

Since at least the 1920s, a persistent rumor has alleged Albert Einstein once failed math during his schooling years prior to becoming a famous theoretical physicist.
"Albert Einstein failed math," a 1997 newspaper article flatly claimed. Many other newspapers have promoted the rumor over past decades. The claim has also appeared on TV shows, for example "The Big Bang Theory" and "Tiny Toon Adventures."
Over and over again, our digging revealed examples of the claim on social media platforms, including Facebook (archived), Reddit (archived) and X (archived).
A study of historical records found this claim to be false, however, and that Einstein had, by himself, mastered integral and differential calculus and analytical geometry by age 14.
How did the myth get started? It's possible it stemmed from people misinterpreting his grades after a school he attended briefly reversed the meaning of the numbers in its grading scale, giving the false impression that Einstein failed some of the courses that in reality, he passed with flying colors. It may also have stemmed from misunderstandings about the time that during his teenage years, Einstein failed an entrance examination to Zurich Polytechnic in Switzerland. It's true that he failed the exam but also true that he excelled in the sections about math and physics.
Whereas in the past many less-reliable books and newspapers promoted the false claim, in the present day books and newspapers — and websites — widely dismiss the idea of Einstein failing math as nothing more than a popular myth.
Early findings, grade-scale reversal
To investigate this topic, Snopes primarily searched the newspaper archives on Newspapers.com, book archives on Google Books and other sources, in particular those covering the period of Einstein's life between 1879 and 1955.
In the earliest record of the claim, dating from 1928, an article in the Brooklyn Daily Eagle reported Einstein had, at a young age, failed math while attending a university in Berlin. The headline of author Meyer Weisgal's article read, "Einstein, Though at Home With Relativity, Flunked As Mathematics Student."
In 1929, amid the other trivia and jokes in a miscellany column in The Evansville Journal came the line, "Einstein failed in mathematics when he was graduated in Berlin. Math teachers, play that on your ukuleles."
That same year, H. Wieleitner, then principal of Luitpold Gymnasium, reportedly wrote to a Munich newspaper to refute a Berlin magazine's claim that Einstein had once been a very poor student. The New York Times included these details in 1984 in an article promoting Princeton University Press' upcoming release of "The Collected Papers of Albert Einstein" (pages C1, bottom right of page, and C9, bottom left of page).
The gist of the report was that Einstein's school had briefly reversed its numeric grading scale, allegedly, leading to some confusion among researchers studying Einstein's early years.
The Times printed a picture of Einstein's grades from a semester at a school in Aargau, Switzerland. Originally, the numeral 6 was the highest possible grade and 1 was the lowest. When the scale was reversed for a short period of time, Einstein received the then-top score of 1 for mathematics. The school later changed its scale back.
The Times cited John Stachel, the editor of Princeton's Einstein papers project, when reporting:
Although some Einstein biographers have disputed the widely held belief that Einstein was a poor student, the papers at Princeton lay this to rest, once and for all. According to Dr. Stachel, those who saw Einstein's academic records may have been misled by a reversal in the grading system of his school in Aargau, Switzerland.
A 'master' of math at age 14
In 1931, a review of author Anton Reiser's 1930 biography, "Albert Einstein: A Biographical Portrait," shed light on the emergence of Einstein's early genius in the 1890s. Page 37 reads:
At fourteen the boy was already master of the higher mathematics which the secondary school, based on humanistic principles, did not teach. Integral and differential calculus, analytical geometry—he mastered them all by himself. His mathematical knowledge was already so great that he amazed both teachers and fellow-students. The talent manifested was that of genius. To the teachers, it was not always pleasing. Many questions the boy asked embarrassed them to the point of silence.
Pages 44 and 45 discuss Einstein's truly failing an entrance examination in Zurich, Switzerland, at a school now named ETH Zurich. However, Reiser explained Einstein's failure had nothing to do with mathematics and physics, in which he shined so brightly it "astounded his professors" (emphasis ours):
At the age of sixteen Albert applied for admission to the Polytechnic Academy at Zurich. He wanted to pass his entrance examination as an alternative to the required graduation certificate, to which his premature departure from the Munich gymnasium and his lack of further schooling did not entitle him. His courage was indeed considerable. Almost a year had passed since he had received any instruction, and now he had come to this strange city to get his matriculation certificate. Unfortunately, his success corresponded with the gloomy probabilities.
This first examination, which Albert Einstein needed to pass, ended in complete failure. To begin with, his knowledge of languages and descriptive natural science was unusually poor. True, he shone all the more in mathematics and physics, and astounded his professors. It was suggested that he attend certain lectures on these subjects.
Einstein reportedly addressed rumor in 1935
In 1935, a man named Rabbi Harry Cohen reportedly showed Einstein a clipping of Robert Ripley's "Believe It or Not" column headlined "Greatest living mathematician failed in mathematics."
Author Denis Brian's 1996 biography, "Einstein: A Life," documented Einstein's exchange with Cohen in which the physicist said he had mastered differential and integral calculus by age 15:
Cohen showed Einstein a newspaper feature titled "Believe It Or Not!" by Robert Ripley, which read, "Greatest living mathematician failed in mathematics," and asked if it was true. "The story has been completely distorted," he replied, with a laugh. "When I applied for admission to the Polytechnic School in Zurich at sixteen I was not completely prepared in French and botany. I never failed in mathematics. Before I was fifteen I had mastered differential and integral calculus."
Those words — "greatest living mathematician failed in mathematics" — first appeared in newspapers as early as 1930 in an article about an oil industry trade show, not as a "Believe It or Not" column.
In 1931, a Ripley reader looking to win a prize in a contest of "Believe It or Nots" submitted the same purported fact as "Einstein, the great German mathematician and originator of his theory of relativity, failed in math while going to college."
Then, as early as 1932, Ripley's column featured a section with the title "Einstein Failed In Mathematics." It read:
"Albert Einstein, the greatest of living mathematicians, author of the Theory of Relativity, failed in the entrance examinations of the Federal Polytechnic College of Zurich. He was then sixteen years old. The man who was to be ranked with Newton and Copernicus had to do plenty of 'cramming,' and submit to a second examination before he was admitted."
Nearly 100 years later, in 2024, Ripley's corrected the record on its website by accurately reporting the facts about the grade-scale reversal at Einstein's school, along with information about his entrance exam failure.
"How did the whole story come about, then?" Ripley's writer Chris Littlechild wrote. "In the same way many other misconceptions come about: a combination of hearsay, exaggeration, and half-truths."

Today, I’m talking with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and longtime cybersecurity expert, about what a mess cybersecurity is right now.
AI broke the cybersecurity world. What’s next?
Going inside the security ‘dark ages’ with Alex Stamos.
This episode is part one of a special series looking at AI in real life.
I’ve always enjoyed talking to Alex because he’s so direct, and you’re going to hear him say that the multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry as we’ve known it is essentially overdue to the unrelenting, AI-boosted waves of hacks, breaches, and attacks — and this is only the beginning of how much AI is changing security.
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.
Both private actors and also state actors, like Russia or North Korea, are breaking into systems all over thanks to AI helping them both detect and exploit vulnerabilities all at the same time. It’s got a real frontier feel to it, Alex notes, just like the ’90s, when the whole idea of an always-online world was brand-new.
That much disruption means a lot of places where bad guys can get in while everyone else is left scrambling. Alex isn’t a doomer in the long run, but he does think we’re in for a “dark age” while we try to figure out how on earth to adapt to the new era.
There’s a lot going on here — we even got all the way to how AI-powered misinformation and slop might be managed on our social networks.
Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.
Okay: Alex Stamos on how AI is upending cybersecurity. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Alex Stamos, you’re the chief security officer at Cognition. You’re also a lecturer at Stanford University Cyber Policy Center. Welcome back to Decoder.
Hey, thanks for having me, man.
I’m excited to talk to you. It’s been a long time since you and I chatted in what you might call the “content moderation era” of internet policy discourse. I feel like you and I talked a lot about how all that was working, about election security, all those sorts of things. We’re in a new era of big problems on the internet, particularly around cyber defense, cybersecurity. You’ve been thinking about this stuff a lot. You referred to the past few weeks as “security awareness month.” Tell me what’s going on. Just give me the lay of land right now.
October is traditionally security awareness month. Lots of companies run events and deal both internally and then tell people, “Change your password, use multiple passwords, use a password manager.” What has happened over the last month is we’ve had a couple of these big bugs, PHP, Node and such. What’s been less discussed is a huge number of companies have been breached.
You have a series of AI-related companies, the neoclouds that have been breached in succession. You have the Binance hack, which is the largest heist of anything in human history. You have the Cursor incident where one of the things that’s going on here is these hacks are being chained together. From what we know right now, one of the companies that was broken into was Fireworks, which is a prominent provider of AI services to a number of companies. From the Fireworks hack, API keys were stolen that allowed people to break into Cursor. Once they got into Cursor, they then pushed a bad plugin, which went to 5,000 more companies and that caused 5,000 potential breaches. It’s just this kind of permanent continuous breach that is going on throughout the tech industry.
A CISO friend of mine said to a bunch of us, “Is anybody else tired?” And everybody said yes, because effectively we have been at DEFCON 2 for all of October and now going into November.
I’m going to ask you some really dumb questions here. Who is behind all these attacks? Is it Russia? Is it North Korea? Do we know?
It’s a variety of different groups. It is not just because adversaries have decided, but what has happened is, from my perspective, we are at the start of the takeoff of adversary capability enabled by AI, that the open-weight models have now gotten to the point at which you can automate most of the kill chain. This “kill chain” term is something we stole from the military. In the military, they mean to actually kill something. They’re the steps you do to blow something up. In cyber, the kill chain is the things you do to have an effect on a target. So to steal information, to turn something off, to steal money, to steal Bitcoin.
Traditionally, you do research upfront, you look at a piece of software, you find a vulnerability, you write exploits, and you do that all way ahead of time. And then you have a human being go and take that stuff you built and deploy it against either one target — because maybe you’re a government and you’re going against Lockheed Martin or you’re going against another government or you’re a ransomware actor — and you take all that work you did and you deploy it against hundreds or thousands of targets really fast. Now with AI, what’s happening is this kill chain has inverted where you can run an AI system that just goes hog wild and it looks at the targets and it finds the bugs in real time and it writes the exploits in real time and it breaks into these companies. One of the things that’s happening is that these systems are going and they’re so good at finding bugs that they are finding the bugs in real time and writing the exploits in real time.
The system that everybody’s talking about is not the only one, but the system we’re talking about is a thing called ARTEX, which is a Chinese open-source tool that anybody can go look at. There’s an English translation on GitHub that you can check out. And if you power it on the back end by something like an obliterated GLM-5.3, it will let you break into a shocking number of organizations. This started with three South Korean banks. This week, about 200 more companies have been hit. I’ve been helping a couple of companies. Cognition is not an incident response company, but we do go in and help people fix their bugs afterwards by using our tools. It is shocking the companies that are getting hit by something you could just download. It has been a long time since you’ve been able to go and just download an open-source tool and break into multi-billion dollar companies. It’s like the ‘90s. That’s-
That’s what I was thinking about. I think about Windows in the late ‘90s, early 2000s when it was a security disaster.
I started saying this actually in the beginning of this year, that it’s an incredibly exciting and terrifying time, because the last time it felt like this was when I was a much younger man and I would go to the very early DEFCONs. DEFCON these days is like 40,000–60,000 people. Back then [in the 1990s] it was a couple hundred people and it was one track and you’d go in and somebody would give a talk and you’d leave the room and you’d think, “Every company in the world is vulnerable to this attack.” The difference was that the entire world didn’t run on the internet. You could go do bad things, but you couldn’t ruin the world and you certainly couldn’t automate it in the way you can now.
It’s back to those days where tools you could just get and build yourself could do crazy things. It’s back to the Wild West days. Back in those days, there were a couple hundred people who had those skills and we were all in one room in Las Vegas and most of them were actually good guys. They didn’t want to be criminals. And now you have a much larger ecosystem of people, many of whom live in places where the law enforcement can’t touch and who have a big economic incentive and have access to these tools. The other big thing is they no longer have to use frontier models that have protections, that have logs that are available to law enforcement. My M5 Mac Ultra Studio finally showed up and I’ve been running a quantized obliterated GLM-5.3 and oh my God, what you can do is incredible.
You mentioned the economics of frontier models. The economy of cyber is one of those things that has gotten sophisticated over the years. One of the things that our systems got safer is you could pay the number of people at DEF CON a whole bunch of money to protect all the systems and it was economically smart to pay them to be defenders instead of attackers. I’m just rewinding my own brain through this history. There was a long conversation in our industry about security through obscurity by hiding all the bugs and hiding all the code versus open source and being really transparent. There was an etiquette that developed about how to reveal the bugs and when to give people notification. There were transparency reports and bug bounties.
You could call it an etiquette, you could call it an economy. We built a culture around cybersecurity and cyber defense and how the attackers and defenders would operate. What you are describing changes it all for a whole number of reasons, but the one that sticks out to me is the economics of it. I can go buy a Mac Studio, I can get an open-weight model and I can just start and that does not place me inside of the culture. There’s not going to be some old man, an Obi-Wan Kenobi saying, “Here’s how you act like a cybersecurity Jedi.” I’m just going to start doing stuff. Tell me how that’s changing right now.
Effectively, the last era of security from my perspective started with the Microsoft, the Bill Gates “trustworthy computing” memo in the early 2000s. And that is when we started designing how we do software security and these big companies, Microsoft and Oracle and then later Amazon and Salesforce and these folks, started hiring ex-hackers. I was part of that generation of the ex-hackers who were at DEF CON and Black Hat and got hired by the companies to go break their stuff. We started coming up with responsible disclosure, bug bounties, consulting companies, so the Foundstone and @stake and then Mandiant and CrowdStrike, these companies grow up and we get this huge industry that is now RSA and Black Hat. This multi-billion dollar security industry grew up in the 2000s and 2010s.
That era is over, like you said, because it was based upon a couple of assumptions. One was that there was a hierarchy of skillsets of people who could do this stuff. I have to live in the world that other people who work six blocks from me, and who are way, way, way, way richer, make. I live in their world, man. I get asked this question all the time, and I just do the best I can within the world other people make.
Do you think that the big labs have woken up? You mentioned that their cybersecurity teams have gotten more access, and they’ve stopped what you might call the Hugging Face era, or at least they’ve changed the structures of those companies. Do you think that will help?
Certainly they’ve woken up on the eval risk. They have teams, who have been this entire time working very hard on the big picture cyber risk.
Certainly, there are a bunch of people in these companies, as you know, who want to slow down. A lot of that discussion is driven by the P(doom)ers who [are worried] about AI killing us. And that’s never been my concern. Right? And to me, that has always been driven by 24 year olds who all they’ve done is AI and they’ve never done anything else. You and I are both, I think, old enough to remember, I grew up a couple miles from a SAC base and we did drills where I was taught that hiding beneath my public school desk would save me from a Soviet thermonuclear bomb. That was P(doom). My grandfather built a bomb shelter that my mom was taught to hide in during the Cuban Missile Crisis. That was P(doom). There’s a youth issue and a never-doing-anything-but-AI issue of people who they got their undergraduate, their master’s, and their PhD only doing linear algebra and neural networks and never touching anything else.
I have always been much more concerned about the human uplift risk from AI, of all the risks about human beings using AI to do bad things to other human beings. Part of my concern is that there has been success in these labs working together on not letting LLMs encrypt their chain of thought. Because when they talk about pacing the frontier, it’s for the P(doom) stuff, for the polycules that live together in Berkeley. They’re talking about very specific stuff about keeping control of the models themselves, which I think is great. That stuff needs to happen. But if those things happen, then there’s still often an increase in a bunch of capabilities that human beings can use.
I really prefer there to be a broader discussion on whether we could make these things less human-seeming. I don’t think these things should have personality. I think the goal of these things should be to serve humans. They should not seem to have souls. They should not seem to have personality. I think for a lot of the negative impacts — as somebody who was at Facebook and saw what it was like for that company to have negative impacts on people — there should be a much broader feeling at these companies of what are we doing broadly to people. A lot of that could just be, “Don’t have these things ever act like somebody’s friend.” At a maximum, it should act like… Like the people, I don’t know what the company is, but the people who made the, “Hi, I’m a really nice...” Like the photorealistic girl who will chat with you, that is to me spectacularly unethical to even try that, to even start that. That’s the kind of thing that we should just make. I don’t know if we can make it illegal, but we should make it completely societally not acceptable to work on that kind of stuff. Right?
That’s a great segue because I did want to ask you about Facebook and content moderation. Like I said, you and I first started talking a long time ago about content moderation in the context of security. You would get foreign nation states flooding our algorithms with all kinds of misinformation during elections, and that was a security problem.
I open Instagram today and I am confronted with some of the most nightmare copyright law hypotheticals to have ever existed in the history of the world. The one I got today was a deep fake of Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc doing “Somebody That I Used to Know.” And I thought, “50 different people can probably sue Meta right now.” This is hilarious if you know what happened in that last race.
So we keep talking about it. We’ve posted some clips of us talking about it on The Vergecast where I said, “I think Meta is letting their AI ambitions crush Instagram.” Instagram is being flooded with slop in a very particular way. Some people love it, sometimes it’s funny, but there’s a nightmare set of lawsuits coming. There’s a whole rights management problem coming. The users don’t like it and they should label it. They should label it and let you filter it.
So we posted this and Adam Mosseri said this to us in a reply on Threads, “I would love to do this. I’m worried that the models are going to get ahead of us, that we can try to do this, but there’s not actually a way to recognize AI content. There’s not actually a way to label it well. If you’re worried about the sexy AI influencers stealing jokes from a comedian, now you got to build a database of jokes.” You have some history here. I think Instagram is about to go through it in a real way. Is there some technical solution to the problem of AI slop in social media?
Mosseri is right that it’s not perfect, but also something I noticed during my time at Facebook was that when Facebook doesn’t want to do something, they will allow the technical challenges to stop them. When Facebook really wants to do something, they will give it their all. That is the pattern always.
When I wanted to try really hard on the safety issue, man, this is not solvable. You’re right, it’s never perfectly solvable, but let’s give it a shot. But whenever Mark Zuckerberg is told something is impossible — it’s impossible to monetize mobile, it’s impossible to build this network to two billion people, it’s going to be impossible to monetize WhatsApp, it’s going to be impossible to work AI into the system while maintaining data encryption — he’s been told that everything’s impossible over and over again and then he constantly succeeds. They will give it a shot and they will do it. But when they don’t want to do something, oh, that’s impossible.
Do you think that there’s some way to understand that some piece of media is generated by AI in a consistent and verifiable way? This to me seems like the challenge.
I am not as up on the literature here. Up to this point, there has been a pretty decent arms race. By definition, AI will continue to get better because — especially for visual models, for diffusion models — the way they work is that you have detection oracles that they test against. Certainly, you can never have something open source because it will immediately end up in the diffusion model. But for closed-source oracles where then you do not make it easy for them to test the oracle, one of the key things you do in trust and safety is then you have delayed enforcement mechanisms so they can’t brute force and test. I think it is quite possible.
Let’s say I was still at Meta. My advice to them would be to also explore a variety of different detection mechanisms outside of the content itself. I would do the best I can on the content, but I would also be doing as low level access as possible to the camera. I would only let content come from the camera.
And what I would say is, Nilay’s completely correct, there’s a massive hunger for, especially among young people, stuff that is authentic. I have three teenagers and they hate AI. They hate AI slop. They have a massive negative reaction. My wife and I created just a cute little family AI thing and they yell at us about a bunch of stuff, but they lost their minds about this cute little family AI thing because they just hate it.
So I think somebody is going to come and disrupt Instagram and it’s going to be because... There’s already, I’ve seen these little things where it’s like you take the photo during the day, be real and stuff. There’s these little things, but somebody’s going to massively disrupt Instagram because they’re taking the images of the photos straight off the camera and then all the editing is going to be only within the app and they’re going to do things to make sure that nothing can make it into the pipeline from AI. You’re going to allow some kind of CapCut-like functionality that never has an AI component. I think that is going to be a killer app.
Man, I could do another whole hour with you on this because the system you’re describing there is not detecting AI content, it is verifying real content.
It’s much easier. Verifying real content is much easier. And there’s been a big focus on this on the professional side, like Adobe has a whole thing where if you’re a New York Times photographer, you have a $5,000 Nikon or Canon camera, you take the photo and it’s cryptographically verified.
Yeah, but the iPhone that I’m holding here has that in it now. Right? Like there’s a lot of —
Right, the iPhone has it now.
Yeah. There’s a lot of this out there, but it’s the other side that I’m thinking about where it’s “We are going to detect AI text.” The leading model companies because of European regulations are now futzing with the text they generate.
Text is much harder because you just have so much less data. Especially in 140 characters, what do you have in there to detect? The more you’ve got, the more you can do.
It is amazing because I can detect Claude a mile away. So maybe I’ll just rely on my own human ability.
Yeah, but not in tweet length.
That’s true. The cheap ones, I can. But I’m just saying the notion that we’re going to verify what’s real instead of detecting what’s fake feels very important in the context of the media we consume.
Detecting what’s fake is always going to be probabilistic and we’re going to asymptotically approach impossibility, whereas detecting what’s real can be cryptographically perfect. I would not pick the battle that we will eventually lose. I would pick the battle that we can cryptographically win. That would be my suggestion.
And there’s somewhere in there where you have to build an entire chain of custody. We’re going to take the sensor data off the camera. We’re going to put it in a cloud server. We’re only going to allow edits on this server. That file will never get monkeyed with.
Sure, that’s true for the New York Times and Adobe Photoshop and stuff, but not for Instagram. For Instagram, you can do it all because it’s only the iPhone and it’s only Instagram. So the entire chain of custody is within your app, it is within the iPhone sensor and it’s in Instagram. So it’s actually easy for them.
Yeah. Look, like I said, We could do another whole hour on that because it feels like right next to the cybersecurity problem is the social engineering problem, and right next to the social engineering problem is the fake media problem.
No, absolutely.
How many phishing attacks are just “this website looked pretty real”?
Oh, yeah.
Or this person is talking to you or there’s an AI voice on the other side of the phone. And all of that comes down to whether you can detect what’s fake instead of verifying what’s real? And I don’t know the answer.
Oh, no. I’ve had to train my parents that, “If you get a video from your grandchildren saying they’ve been kidnapped, you have to call me because the odds that it’s real are not very high.” That’s where we’re at as a society.
I feel like I want to end on a hopeful note and I don’t know how to do it from there.
Wrong guest for that, buddy.
This is why you only come on every few years. Now after this, we’re going to do the series of birthday party guests. You’ve been talking about the dark ages. We’re in it, where it’s starting to accelerate. What are the markers people should look for in terms of progress to say, “Okay, we’re climbing our way back up”?
AI is great for lots of things. I think AI is going to enable individuals. We’re going to see a huge explosion of new companies. Stanford students have always been entrepreneurial, but the number of my students who are now starting two-, three-, four-person companies who are doing incredible things, who used to need to hire 50 or 100 people and take a ton of venture capital, is incredible. We’re going to continue to see that.
One of the things we hopefully see is a downtick in the number of major breaches at some point. We should hopefully see a downtick in the major CVEs that are wormable and that are in the fundamental infrastructure pieces kernel wheel. Like I said, I want Linux to be rewritten, but hopefully we see a downtick in the Linux kernel and those other kinds of libraries, openSSL, glibc, things like that.
Maybe I should vibe code this up, but I think it would be cool to have an index of where we are in the cycle, of like an artificial index of all of these, the Dow for all of the libraries of where we’re going. Plus right now, Patch Tuesday used to be like 150, 200, got to 300, 600. I think the last one was 900 something, so we’re geometrically growing. It’d be nice to see Patch Tuesday start to go back down. Apple patches are the same thing. Yep, you inspired me. I’m going to create a Dow index for this, the dark age index. And then maybe we can publish it on The Verge.
Yeah, that’d be great.
But I think these are the kinds of things that it would be nice to see a reversal for. What would be especially nice to see is that the day or actually like 30 days before you get the next version of OpenAI and Anthropic cyber models, that you don’t have this huge round of patches because what’s happening is those guys are running their models against Microsoft’s code, against a bunch of open source, and they’re giving all the bugs away and you don’t know where the bugs are coming from. It’s just like anonymous reports for 1,000 bugs in the Linux kernel. And then a month later, here’s the new Astra Cyber. So if those get smaller and smaller every time, then it means that we’re starting to reach some kind of steady state.
You should definitely do that tracker. We will definitely publish it. Alex, it has been incredible to have you on the show. We’ll have to talk again soon.
Yeah, thank you so much. I think you do some of the best journalism on this stuff and I really appreciate it.

Starting Tuesday, Mexican schools will ban cellphones from classrooms as part of a federal government effort to limit children's and teenagers' use of electronic devices, following similar measures taken by over a hundred countries in the last decade.
The initiative, spearheaded by Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, has been supported by experts who see it as an opportunity to reduce young Mexicans' exposure to technology and the resulting attention deficit, stress and anxiety.
Mexican authorities are also preparing to implement regulations this month that will require digital platforms to remove posts containing hate speech, abuse, sexual violence, harassment, cyberbullying and other illegal content.
However, the cellphone ban, which will take effect on November 3, is already facing resistance in some parts of the country. Some parents fear being unable to communicate with their children amid ongoing violence, from which children and adolescents are not spared.
According to the civil society coalition Network for Children's Rights in Mexico (REDIM), in the first half of this year, one in 10 Mexicans between the ages of 0 and 17 were victims of crimes involving organised crime.
“I don't think parents will accept not giving their children a means of digital communication, especially when those children … are spending so much time at home instead of at school,” said Francisco Ortiz, state representative of the National Union of Parents in Sinaloa, accusing the government of ignoring parents and approving regulations that “go against parental authority, against the rights of parents.”
The decree issued by Sheinbaum prohibits the use of cellphones and electronic devices inside elementary and middle schools throughout the school day, and only allows their use for educational purposes under the guidance of teachers or for personal emergencies, disability and health needs. Students can take their phones with them on the way to school.
Benigno Gomez, a father from Reynosa in the northern state of Tamaulipas, said that while he understood the educational authorities' need to reduce students' time on cellphones, he found it “a little difficult” that they weren't allowed to have a cellphone to deal with a potential risk situation.
Mexican authorities have not commented on these concerns and have instead focused on the harm caused by cellphones.
During a recent address to the Chamber of Deputies, Mexico's Secretary of Public Education, Mario Delgado, stated that the Sheinbaum administration seeks to “prevent addiction to digital platforms and the disorders they cause in minors.”
Parents seek reassurance
Just as the sun was beginning to rise, the residents of Escuinapa, the capital of the municipality of the same name located in southern Sinaloa, awoke on the morning of October 22 to alarming news. A bus that regularly travels through the small town -- which relies on mango and shrimp production -- was shot at by a man on a motorcycle.
More than a dozen high school students were on board. A video recorded by one of the passengers circulated on social media, showing children on the floor and others hiding among the seats while one teenager asks another, “Do you have any credit (on your cellphone)?”
In the attack, only the bus driver was injured, suffering cuts from shards of glass shattered by the gunfire.
Upon learning of the shooting, one Escuinapa resident immediately called her teenage daughter, who had left early for high school in a car driven by her aunt.
“Just hearing my daughter's voice and knowing she was OK calmed me down,” said the woman, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of the criminals plaguing her community -- admitting that she didn't hesitate to interrupt her daughter's class to check on her.
The mother expressed doubts that parents will comply with the cellphone ban, fearing that violence could now reach schools in Escuinapa, and insisted that “the safety of our children comes first.”
In defence of the regulation
For Israel Sanchez, president of the National Union of Parents, the Mexican government's decision represents progress after years of struggle by the civil organisation, which brings together hundreds of parents from public and private schools, mostly Catholic.
Sanchez argued that authorities must undertake an awareness campaign for parents and provide training for teachers to achieve the effective implementation of the regulation.
Lucía Magis-Weinberg, a neurodevelopmental researcher at the University of Washington who has studied the effects of technology on children and adolescents for years, said Mexico is joining the international movement to regulate cellphones at a very opportune moment.
Magis-Weinberg acknowledged the benefits of technology for socialisation and accessing information but said it is “a double-edged sword.”
Regulations are needed to avoid cognitive damage, digital conflicts, and the risks of platforms that “are designed to maintain, to maximise our attention.”
The ban on cellphones in schools is already in place in 114 countries, according to UNESCO data. In Europe, restrictions have gained increasing traction, especially in France, where the ban was extended to secondary schools in August. Controls have also been implemented in some countries in Latin America, such as Ecuador, Brazil, Chile, Bolivia and Costa Rica. In the United States, bans are only maintained in some states.
