Lately a new kind of pitch has found its way into my inbox. “Not sure if you've heard,” writes someone named Nick, “but AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI are paying media companies such as Wired $350K to $1.8M as a one time fee for a copy of their old work records (documents, emails, slack messages, tickets, etc.) for training better models.”
Another email with a similar pitch (adding call transcripts to the list of desired information) raised the stakes to a possible $2 million. “Public data is exhausted, and the labs are spending over $45B on private data to build better models,” writes someone named Cora.
While I was aware that AI companies are buying expert data from various sources, there hasn’t been that much attention paid to it. But once I looked into it, I discovered that this business is way bigger than I suspected—and according to its practitioners, it could have as much impact on workers and society as the data centers that are dominating the news these days.
The companies that contacted me are part of an industry boom in data acquisition that’s been quietly buying the workflows of sizable companies and is still so hungry that it’s bleeding into our inboxes. A freelance writer recently wrote about her experience with a company called Handshake, which offered her $1,000 for her work on a single story. (She didn’t sell.) A representative from Handshake confirmed the offer to me: “We license professional documents across a lot of fields so the labs can test and train how models handle real knowledge work,” he said. “Journalism is one of those fields.” Handshake tells me that a big part of its business is buying graduate students’ papers and coursework.
An entrepreneur friend of mine tells me he’s been getting mail from multiple companies whose business is “helping startups wind down their companies," as one email from a company named Sunset explained it. “We handle the full process, scrubbing and anonymizing the data so the company people and any identifying details are stripped out, then brokering the deal with the labs.”
Those newer data acquisition startups are hoping to achieve the quick success of the dominant companies in the field, which themselves are only a few years old. Industry leaders Handshake, Micro1, and Mercor are snapping up databases as if it were a modern gold rush. The industry leader seems to be Mercor, founded in 2023; last year its three cofounders became billionaires at 22. Like all the companies, it claims to have partnerships with just about all the major AI labs. (The response from the companies themselves was more circumspect: Anthropic acknowledges that there’s a big market for data, but told me that it doesn’t buy workflow from live companies like WIRED. OpenAI didn’t come up with a response before publication.)
In an interview, Mercor CEO Brendan Foody told me that the market is poised to explode as the AI industry seeks dramatically more data. Mercor originally started as an AI recruiting company, but as the team got to know the players, it learned that the big labs were frustrated by the quality of the data. Generally, the industry had been hiring experts to simulate actual workflow, but that didn’t capture the messiness of an actual operating business. He urged me to consider that Big AI has two bottomless needs: compute and data. While the industry is very publicly making giant investments in the former, data gathering is just as important.
Foody is ready when I bring up privacy concerns. When a business streams the data to Mercor, the company strips out any personal identifying information, or PII. This de-identification can be verified, he says. Like all the people in data acquisition I spoke to, he felt that technology has solved the privacy issues of buying all that information.
Not surprisingly, Micro1 CEO Ali Ansari agrees that the data-buying market will soon approach that of AI’s compute infrastructure. He says that today, labs, enterprises, and robotics companies pay about $40 to $50 billion a year to get data. (I was unable to verify this.) “In the next two to four years, this is going to be over a trillion dollars a year,” says Ansari, who founded the company in 2022. Micro1 uses the information it buys largely to improve AI models it builds itself, but it also sells to big AI firms.
“Pretty much everybody’s trying to get into the data space now because there’s so much demand,” he says. “If you look at the YC startups, about half of them are data companies.” (Actually, it’s more—in the most recent YC batch, 40 of the 65 launched companies are classified as data startups.)
The Wild West aspect to this quest for fresh data got rare exposure when a bankrupt Spirit Airlines put its digital assets up for sale. The corpus included 80,000 email accounts, 500 million internal messages, 20.6 million Microsoft Sharepoint files, and a million time-card records. Google seemingly got the prize with a $10 million bid, but then Micro1 topped it by $2.5 million, setting off an argument over who the winner was. Presently the sale is on hold, for a reason that calls into question the entire practice of selling off human workflow: The flight attendants’ union has charged that the sale involved their private information.
The union’s objections cast a light on the dark side of this gold rush. Despite the claims of virtually all the data companies that no PII goes into AI models, critics feel that there is still danger of personal data leaking out. “It’s not clear that anonymizing can fully get rid of privacy issues,” says Mayu Tobin-Miyaji, general counsel of the Electronic Privacy Information Center, which has filed an amicus brief on behalf of the flight attendants. “Emails and Teams messages contain unstructured data, which is harder to root out. There may be messages where employees talk about doctor’s appointments or family issues.”
“We haven't set the norms and the standards for data acquisition, and it’s not being done appropriately ” says Gordon Ritter, a venture capitalist who has taken on the issue as a cause. “The AI industry is moving far faster than our ability to actually set the standards, and it's partially intentional.”
Probably the most troubling aspect of the data-gathering movement is that, in essence, it enlists workers, not always with explicit consent, to contribute to an effort where the ultimate goal is to replace or automate the human work that goes into all those documents, messages, and emails. When Mercor says that its motto is “Organizing human intelligence to power the AI economy,” the unspoken message is that the economy of flesh and blood workers will have less work to do. As the president of the flight attendant’s union told an interviewer: “This is really only data that became valuable in the age of AI in order to train models to replace jobs and commodify other portions of working in a work environment.”
When I ask Micro1’s Ansari whether one day the default for corporations will be selling their workflow data to big AI companies on an ongoing basis, he answers affirmatively. “I think it’s going to become more common than ads as a revenue line item for companies,” he says. I note that there is already considerable pushback to AI, and that people might not be happy with the idea that everything they do at work gets funneled into the maw of a big AI model.
“I think it’s a fair point,” says Ansari. But, in his view, such objections will be manageable. He suggests that workers will understand that the fruits of their labor will result in better AI models, which will make their lives easier. “You have to think of the upside, the abundance that AI can result in.” (I’ve found that the future abundance that AI will supposedly produce is a handy justification for all sorts of compromises.)
I did follow up on one of the cold pitches I got, from a woman whose email domain was gorexen.com. A “gorexen,” by the way, is a fusion of two Pokemon critters that “siphons the body fluids of prey through its thin, tubular mouth.” She set up a meeting with me with a two-year-old company called Tenkara (the name seems to be associated with a type of Japanese fly fishing). I found myself talking to “head of commercialization” Jonah Stillman, a young startup-looking dude sitting in an office in San Francisco.
I began peppering him with questions. Tenkara’s quest for data seems to be to boost the quality of its AI model to run office operations for manufacturing companies. (How WIRED’s archives would help is a mystery.) He confirmed that a big part of his job is doing calls like this to snap up data. I told him that the set of our meeting gave me a Glengarry Glen Ross vibe, but he wasn’t familiar with the reference.
I am, of course, not authorized to sell the documentation of WIRED’s editorial process to an AI company, and I did not risk my job by offering Jonah and his company the goods. I also wouldn’t be too pleased if my bosses made the sale.

Indonesian studio giant MD Entertainment will release a sequel to its 2025 horror smash “Pabrik Gula” in early 2028 and has three Imax films planned for 2027, Astrid Wienardi, the company’s head of content licensing and global business, said Sunday at Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei.
Wienardi delivered a presentation on how MD ties its film and series library to broadcast and streaming. The company took control of free-to-air channel NET TV in a deal worth up to $105 million and has brought in investment from Korea’s SBS.
“Pabrik Gula” sold more than 5 million tickets in Indonesia before traveling to Vietnam, Cambodia, Singapore, Malaysia, Brunei, the U.S. and Europe. Its hooks and popularity persuaded MD to commit to a second installment.
The Imax relationship started with “Badarawuhi,” the prequel to “KKN di Desa Penari” and the first Southeast Asian film shot for the format. One of the three 2027 Imax titles will draw on “Dhot Design,” a YouTube animated series about four friends that pulls between 8 million and 10 million views an episode. Lionsgate and CJ are also among MD’s strategic partners.
Active for more than two decades across film, series, animation, music publishing and talent management, MD has more than 200 features to its name and plans 12 to 13 releases in 2027, led by horror alongside comedy and drama. “KKN di Desa Penari” sold 10.7 million tickets at home, an Indonesian record at the time.
“Ivanna 2” is due early next year. The original is a spinoff from MD’s “Danur” horror universe about a headless Dutch woman.
“‘Ivanna’ was moderately accepted in Indonesia market, but it did fascinatingly well in Vietnam,” Wienardi said. “It actually broke records in the theatrical Vietnamese market.”
Feedback from platform partners, along with fan comments on social media, decides whether MD extends a series, spins off a title or grows a franchise. Netflix drama “Ipar Adalah Maut,” which Wienardi translated as “Brother-in-Law Is Death,” topped the streamer’s trending list in its first week and stayed in the top 10 for seven straight weeks. A second season is in the works and could launch on Netflix next year.
MD has eight titles on Netflix and three on WeTV, where seven of the platform’s top 20 titles were MD productions, including “Layangan Putus,” which trended in 25 countries. On Prime Video, mother-daughter series “Induk Gajah” (“Mother Elephant”) earned a Season 2 order soon after its 2023 debut and helped pull in new subscribers. A deal with iQIYI, unveiled in mid-October, will see two titles roll out by December and a third in the first quarter of 2027.
Music is part of the playbook too. Netflix series “Suara Hati,” whose two lead actresses are dangdut singers, generated 100,000 first-week downloads across Spotify and YouTube Music, while “Bakti,” a song from “Danyang: Mahar Tukar Nyawa,” which opened Nov. 5, has passed 200,000 downloads on Spotify.
“The golden rule for us is that the universal appeal should never mean stripping away local identity,” Wienardi said. “Local identity is very important for MD. Without local identity, we lose the soul of the story.”
She added that CEO Manoj Punjabi demands that soul at every greenlight meeting, and that MD wants folklore-rooted horror rather than “watered-down thrillers or any Hollywood-like thrillers.”
When an audience member asked how Indonesian films command around 65% of local moviegoing while Taiwanese films account for just 10%-12% at home, Wienardi cited Indonesia’s population of roughly 280 million and a deep well of haunting folklore that parents pass to their children.
“We are surrounded by a lot of mountainous areas where the spiritual taboos are actually discussed on family dinners,” she said.
Horror, MD’s specialty for more than 20 years, is the genre that crosses borders most easily, according to Wienardi, who said it has at times reached the U.S. and European markets. “When it comes to drama, it’s a bit different because then, you know, there’s a lot of sayings in Indonesia that probably are not translated or culturally translated well,” she said.
The traffic runs both ways. MD released adaptations of Thai and Korean properties this year, partnered with Korea’s Barunson on “Sorop” and has fielded co-production inquiries from U.S. and European producers. Wienardi said the studio sees strong potential in bringing Taiwanese and East Asian IP to Indonesia, and wants pitches that arrive with proof of concept, a clear fit for Indonesian viewers and a track record in their home market.
“When we’re talking about NET TV, data is number one,” Wienardi said. Free-to-air and pay-TV ratings land daily at 10 a.m. and determine whether a program is extended or changed, while MD series simulcast on the channel help widen its reach. The channel’s goal is a place in Indonesia’s top five.
Wienardi said she hopes MD will one day work with Taiwanese directors and producers and “share probably a common ground of storytelling.”

The 16 Best Subscription Boxes for Kids
Featured in this article
Rather than give your kid a big, expensive present once or twice a year, why not surprise them with subscription boxes for kids once a month? I have an 8-year-old and a 10-year-old, and they are thrilled when a package arrives in the mail that isn’t bills, replacement chargers from Amazon, or Garnet Hill catalogs.
Subscription boxes for kids can be useful educational supplements for homeschool or remote learning. Most are consumable, so your kid can have a treat that won't be left to molder in a corner of a playroom until they're 25. They're also handy to have around the house if you can’t send your sniffly kid to school or a big indoor birthday party. As a bonus, they’re usually affordable. I tested some of the subscriptions on this list, like the Lovevery Reading Skill Set 3-box set ($160), and I bought others for my kids and their friends. These are our favorites. Be sure to check out our other buying guides for kids, including the Best Strollers, the Best Kids Bikes, and the Best STEM Toys.
Updated November 2025: We refreshed information on all the crates, added new pictures, and added the Lovevery reading skill set box, CrunchLabs Creative Kits, Bookroo, and Enlightened Generation. We also updated links and prices.
- Best Box for All Ages KiwiCo Kiwi Crate We subscribed to Kiwi Crate's monthly subscription for so long that the company sent us a cautious email asking whether it was OK that we were getting repeat boxes. I now check in every year to discover that yes, the company's boxes are still amazing. Each box comes with a single, delightful, themed activity that's appropriate for a kid aged anywhere from a few months old to 18 years. A recent Delivery Bot ($24) aimed for 9+ years entertained my 8-year-old son for an afternoon. I can't extoll the virtues of this crate enough. The instructions are clear enough for young kids to follow. The pieces are easy for little fingers to manipulate (he did need some adult help adjusting the wheels), and the final project is always delightful: a little remote-controlled delivery bot that you can put things in and drive your sister and mother (literally) crazy! Kiwi Crate offers various gift boxes for all ages, from toddlers under 2 to teenagers. You can also select one-off boxes for specific interests, such as music, mazes, holiday crafts, and robots, or different themes, like Atlas Crates for geography or Doodle Crates for drawing. Kiwi is noted for its careful curation—the projects are fun and age-appropriate, but it doesn't break my kids' hearts when they inevitably lose or destroy them. If you're looking for just one crate, get this one and no one in your house will be disappointed.
- Best Clothing Box Stitch Fix Kids Clothes Box As my kids have gotten older, shopping for their clothes has become more and more difficult. One child has sensory issues. He hates stiff or tight fabrics, clothes that are too fuzzy, certain colors, and all jackets. The other is a budding fashionista who is on a running team and dances and needs workout clothes, baggy jeans, or whatever else happens to not be in her closet at the moment. Whenever I find a sweatshirt they will wear, Target immediately discontinues it and my cycle of living hell continues. Stitch Fix will cure what ails you, and you can start or stop your subscription as needed. You enter your child's age and size; color preferences and patterns to avoid; themes that they like; features to avoid (no crop tops); activities they like; and most importantly, budgets for every category. Stitch Fix sends you a box and you and your child keep what you like and send back the rest. I recently re-tested the box with my now-10-year-old, and both of us liked the new picks. I was able to easily get an assortment of athletic clothing for her, as well as a cloud sweater she adores. This is an easy way to update wardrobes for kids who grow out of everything instantaneously and are really hard to shop for. ★ Alternative: I also tried a box from Kidpik (starts at $100) for my now-8-year-old. Kidpik's selection is so appealing and stylish that my husband asked if the clothes came in his size. The clothes are much sturdier than the Stitch Fix selections. However, the selection is much smaller, and my son rejected half the clothes that Kidpik sent. Stitch Fix's extensive style quiz ensures that there's at least a fighting chance that your child will like any given garment.
- Best Puzzles Highlights Puzzlemania Book Club Subscription My kids are 8 and 10, and they are obsessed with puzzles of all kinds. This is great because they are at the age when they need to practice reading, and there are only so many times you can force them to reenact The Lord of the Rings trilogy. The classic children's publisher Highlights also offers a few different reading and activity boxes, in addition to the iconic magazine. My kids and I tried the I Can Read book club ($14/month) and the Puzzlemania subscription ($4/month). Puzzlemania was delightful. Each puzzle book is 32 pages and has a wide variety of puzzles, including sticker puzzles, word searches, Mad Libs–style storytelling, and riddles. We spent several afternoons filling in sticker puzzle pieces and playing the Highlights version of Sudoku. They both loved this puzzle pack so much that I bought the Highlights Great Big Book of Really Hard Puzzles ($13), which I'm anticipating will keep them occupied for at least one weekend trip or two.
- Best Science Box CrunchLabs Hack Pack This is coming with a big disclaimer: CrunchLabs, the company founded by former NASA engineer and YouTuber Mark Rober, says that its Hack Pack is for people over 14 years old. However, my 8-year-old put it together with minimal help in an afternoon, although it did take him much longer than the 60-minute estimated time for a teenager. ("Why are you so worried, Mama?" he admonished me when I showed skepticism. "The drawings show you exactly what to do.") Each box has a robot to assemble that illustrates a STEM principle, complete with a battery and an Arduino microcontroller. You can also unlock a video, but the drawings in the included manual were clear and big enough that we could put it together without the help of the internet. Our box had the infrared turret to illustrate the principle of infrared communication. My 8-year-old was thrilled, hiding it and using the infrared remote to ambush his sister with a barrage of foam darts. You can also unlock a web-based coding console to hack the robot by locking out other users. It's expensive, but the price-per-payoff valuation is worth it—the STEM principle it illustrated was interesting, the build process was engaging without being frustrating, and the project itself was very fun. ★ Alternatives: I love Mark Rober, so this is obviously the best box, but there are a ton of different science boxes. Kiwi Crate has a dedicated science crate. For much younger kids, Little Passports has an Early Explorers box ($25/month) aimed at children as young as 3. Science Expeditions is aimed at children over the age of 8; the projects are a little bizarre, like extracting the DNA from a strawberry. Neither my child nor I knew what we were supposed to do with this. Finally, a lot of people like Steve Spangler's Science Club STEM kits ($35), which are huge and come with multiple projects. These are fairly simple, like a marshmallow masher that you could Google yourself and make with stuff you probably have at home. However, I thought it was worth it to have the lesson and objects bundled so I didn't have to drink and empty a plastic soda bottle myself.
- Best Craft Kit CrunchLabs Creative Kit CrunchLabs is great, but it is aimed at older kids—my son needed a bit of help. The newly launched Creative Kit is aimed at 6- to 10-year-olds, so it's for a slightly younger demographic. I'm shocked at how well-thought-out these kits are. CrunchLabs sent the Ice Cream Stand and the Architect's Treehouse. The morning after both of the crates were assembled, both begged to get more. Even after my 8-year-old son had put together the tiny ice cream stand, he continued to play with it all afternoon. It comes with delightful little accessories, like moldable ice cream in different “flavors” (colors), little toppings, and tiny cones and cups. (I was just offered a tiny scoop of “Super Strawberry Smash.”) Unlike most tie-dye or pinwheel kits, the Creative Kit encourages play long after the craft has been completed. My 10-year-old likes these better than the Kiwi Crates because “it's like building a tiny town!”
- Best Reading Support Box Lovevery Reading Skills Support Box Now, my third-grader is a voracious reader. But it took him a few years and some hurdles to get to this point. In that time, the Reading Skill Set ($155) by Lovevery was invaluable. These books and games are a complete homeschool reading curriculum aimed at kindergarten through the second grade, but we used them as supplementary materials. Each set comes with three separate components: lovely, sturdy games; a few books; and parent course materials to explain both. The set was particularly crucial for my son during the second grade years. I particularly liked that the skill set addressed common errors and advanced vowel rules. It is really hard to remember what the letter “e” does in a word! My son found the board game to be very fun, like Chutes & Ladders but for word play. It was almost a disappointment when we realized, at the end of the summer, that he could actually read perfectly.
- Best Book Club Literati Book Club If you and your family are struggling to find reading material for your required 20 minutes of reading per day for school (that's not Wings of Fire over and over again), I highly recommend a book subscription. We paid for a Literati subscription until its curation system worked against them. Literati offers book clubs that take newborn children up to their teens. Literati will send your child five books each month. Return any books you don't like and pay Amazon's list price for the rest. Every book was a hit, and each kid had to have every book in every box. For the sake of my wallet and our already-groaning bookshelves, I had to stop the subscription. You can gift a subscription or a one-time, age-appropriate theme box with a card, personalized stickers, and artwork. It's a great way to expose your children (and yourself!) to wonderful new works of art or literature without dragging them to a bookstore. ★ Alternatives: Having to send back books your kid loves is a trap. If you want to just get and keep a book subscription, Bookroo ($20) is what you want; my son's first box just arrived with The Map Trap, of Andrew “Frindle” Clements fame, and he loves it. Also, if you or your child is bilingual, you might want to consider Curio ($58/quarterly), which currently offers themed books and audio reading guides in different age ranges for Spanish, Chinese, and French.
- Best Snack Box Universal Yums Snack Box This is the best box. And kids need to snack every day anyway, so you might as well read and learn while you're at it. My kids tear into the Universal Yums snack box like a very small pack of very tiny wolves. My colleague Louryn Strampe recommends it in her Best Snack Boxes guide and Best Subscriptions guide. You can choose a small, medium, or large box, and it includes an informative booklet, games, and trivia. Food is a great way to learn about geography and different cultures. Every month, my kids and I open the box, look at a globe, and do a lot of Googling. We have liked several foreign candies enough to start ordering them separately on Amazon. Even when the snacks aren't a hit—I got the salted truffle French fries all to myself—my kids always try them and ask a lot of questions about why a country is called the Kingdom of Butterflies and when we can visit.
- Best Coding Box Lingo Subscription Box Lingo was founded by Aisha Bowe, a former NASA scientist, and is intended to bring STEM skills to children who may have been underexposed. That description does not precisely apply to my 7-year-old, but he nevertheless enjoyed this kit. We tried In the Driver's Seat ($75), which teaches you how to build a backup sensor for a car. Mileage will vary, and the kit is technically aged for sixth to 12th graders. However, my son and I found it easy to follow along once we figured out how to log in to the Lingo portal and access all the videos on his iPad. We followed the video instructions in the portal to learn how to build circuits on a breadboard using lights and resistors, and program to turn the lights on and off. I particularly like that it doesn't purport to teach children coding via puzzle pieces or blocks but uses an actual circuit board and a real programming environment. Lingo also offers teacher support if you get stuck. However, I should note that while the kit contains all the hardware components you need to build the sensor, you will need your own iPad or laptop to access the videos and instructions.
- Best for Preschoolers Lovevery Play Kit We first received a Lovevery kit when my son was 2 years old. Now he’s 8, and I still find the company’s sturdy, Montessori-inspired toys in use around our house. Lovevery (pronounced “love-every”) promotes what it calls stage-based learning. At each stage of development, babies need different (beautiful, colorful, durable) toys to help them develop different parts of their brain. It’s pretty cute to term every stage with a different focus, like The Inspector or The Explorer, although I have to admit that I’m not so sure my son enjoyed experimenting with gravity that much more at 10 months than at a year old (he still dropped things on the floor is what I’m saying). My much older daughter also enjoyed arranging giant, gorgeous felt flowers just as much as my son did. If you’re a special person in a little one’s life and want to send them attractive and sturdy toys to pass down to others, this is the best toy subscription to get. ★ Alternative: Is your toddler going through a specific (very annoying) phase, and you need some help? Lovevery also offers parent course packs (starting at $50) to address needs like potty training or getting a new sibling. The course pack offers access to the Lovevery app, video content, toys, and books.
- Best for Babies Lalo’s Play Boxes are made for the littlest people in our lives. There are 10 different boxes of toys that are designed for different months within the first two years of a kiddo’s life, starting at the zero-to-12-month infant stage. It’s available both as a subscription or a one-off purchase of a specific developmental window, such as three to four months or 16 to 18 months, and you can add it to a registry on Babylist. The toys are beautifully made with nontoxic materials. Most of the toys I tested with my son were made of wood, like the wooden blocks he likes to knock over from the 19 to 21 month box and the drum he plays from the 13 to 15 month set. Each box comes with a little Play Guide to describe how the toy is meant to be used and to stimulate their age group. I also liked when the booklet gave tips on how to use the toys when my son got older, too. I tried out two different Lalo Play Boxes and was happy to see that my son was usually interested in at least three of the items consistently, which is pretty great for a toddler! I’m honestly jealous of how pretty some of the toys are, and regularly resist the temptation to steal the cute Stacking Rocket for my bedside table. —Nena Farrell
- Best for Artists SketchBox Art supplies—drawing, painting, pastels—are the delight of my family's life. SketchBox is a monthly box, and each month has a theme that's put together by an artist. My daughter's charcoal box was assembled by mixed media artist Nikoli Shaver and included a graphite starter kit, a small pack of media-appropriate paper, an eraser, charcoal pencils, and more. This box has an amazing value—the Nitram starter kit alone costs $16, and my 10-year-old spent several days sketching, tapping, and blending. If you're unsure of where to start with watercolor or oil pastels and find wandering Blick's aisles to be intimidating, these boxes are a great place to start. You can get a basic box for $25 or a premium one for $35, which has a higher-quality selection plus a piece of art to inspire you. ★ Alternatives: Art subscriptions are a great way to buy an assortment of materials so that you don't find yourself with 400 extra pipe cleaners on your hands. The Kids Art Box ($38) is aimed at children 3 to 7 years old. It's expensive, but five activities are quite a lot, even though I did have to hunt through my house for supplementary materials like extra paintbrushes and jars. Finally, one of my favorite boxes is the Zollie (starting at $40) craft kits. These boxes are not subscription-based, but you can order up to five kits at once. Each kit has everything you need to complete several small fiber-art projects, like embroidering flowers or knitting washcloths. My 10-year-old spent several happy afternoons looking up the QR code, watching the videos, and teaching herself how to do slip stitches and French knots.
- Best Baking Kit Bake Eat Love Baking Kit Cooking and baking subscription boxes are some of the best subscription boxes I've tried. Feeding kids every day is a chore, and I welcome any way to get some variety. Bake Eat Love is the first kit I was just as excited to try as my kids. That said, the Bake Eat Love boxes are probably best suited for an older age group, with slightly more sophisticated palates. We tried the sampler box with tiramisu cupcakes. While I love the light, fluffy texture of tiramisu and the innovative recipe, my son was perturbed to find that a cupcake he assumed was chocolate tasted more like Mommy's coffee. The kit does include a few prepackaged ingredients, but as with most cooking and baking sets, you do have to have a basic set of cooking utensils and a few ingredients that might require an extra shopping trip, like mascarpone. ★ Alternatives: I have gifted several Raddish Kids cooking club subscriptions ($24) to several nieces and nephews. The recipes are extremely easy for little kids to follow (my children particularly loved making pretzels), and the included tiny utensils are adorable and perfect for tiny hands (and for moms who just like using tiny things). We also tried Eat2Explore ($30), which was founded by a graduate of the French Culinary Institute. Each box features fun tools, nonperishable seasonings, recipe cards, and educational booklets from different countries. The salmon teriyaki was not the right pick for a child who has described fish as smelling like “stinky garbage,” but he did love using the included chopsticks. This is a fun, relatively affordable way to try to expand a kid's picky palate.
- Best Sticker Club Stickii Club My kids' appetite for stickers is endless. I find them constantly, on the mirrors in our house, on their school planners and water bottles, and occasionally stuck to the back of my chair or in the car. Stickers are also an accessible way of supporting independent artists. Maybe you can't buy a painting or a T-shirt, but a sticker only costs a few dollars and you can display it everywhere. For $12 a month, Stickii Club offers three different sticker styles—Cute, Vintage, or Pop—along with a storage sleeve and three stationery items, like a notepad, card, or stamp. The club works with independent artists and illustrators (no AI-generated art yet) to produce sheets of original designs. We tried the Pop subscription. These stickers are marvelous. There's a huge variety in the sheets sent. Some are vinyl, some are transparent, but all are high quality and intricately detailed. The artist is also noted on each corner so we can look them up ourselves. My kids were delighted and traded them with each other like currency. I am now investing in Stickii folios (from $18) in the hopes that I can keep these just a little bit more organized (and sticking a few on my laptop while I'm at it). ★ Alternative: You can't pick the style of box with a Pipsticks Kids Club sticker pack ($20), but with such a big selection, there are bound to be stickers that your child or children will love. It includes 15 sheets of Pipstickers, collectible stickers, a postcard, an activity book, and more. I have two kids who love stickers, and even we found the classic pack to be a bit much; Pipsticks also has a petite pack option for $14.

Congratulations on making it to the end of the week. This is Jonathan Wosen, STAT’s West Coast Biotech & Life Sciences Reporter. We’ve got an eclectic lineup for you today, including a look at how declining vitamin K shots are impacting infants, why medical records often don’t tell the full story about women’s health, and results on health and science-related ballot measures across the country.
Oh, and a study that unearths evidence of cannabis use from a 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb (pun intended). Let’s dig in.
143%
That’s how much higher the risk of brain bleeding during the first six months of life was in infants who didn’t receive a vitamin K shot, compared to those who did. Babies are born with low levels of vitamin K, which plays an essential role in forming blood clots. That’s why the American Academy of Pediatrics has for more than 60 years recommended that newborns get the one-time shot shortly after birth. But medical mistrust has led a growing number of parents to turn down the injection; the share of newborns who weren’t given vitamin K rose from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025.
That trend has had grim consequences, according to a study published Thursday in the Journal of the American Medical Association. Researchers looked back on data from more than 5 million infants born between 2017 and 2025 and found that, compared to infants given vitamin K, those who weren’t given K had a 47% higher risk of bleeding during their first six months and a 169% higher risk of dying while bleeding shortly after birth.
What is Kratom?
In recent years, the Kratom plant and related synthetic products have become omnipresent across smoke shops and gas station shelves, buoyed by proponents who extol these products’ pain-relieving powers. But public health experts have raised serious concerns about the potential dangers of kratom — and the fact that these products are not closely regulated.
It’s a debate that is confusing to many; two-thirds of Americans have never even heard of kratom. STAT’s Theresa Gaffney has you covered with this timely explainer on the drug. The piece covers how a plant that has been chewed and brewed for centuries in Southeast Asia due to its stimulant-like effects has quickly risen in popularity in the U.S., where some users say kratom has eased chronic pain and helped them get off opioids.
Theresa also digs into 7-OH and MGPI, semi-synthetic related products that some experts worry are especially addictive. Clinicians who run addiction treatment centers say that they’ve seen a rise in patients seeking help to get off 7-OH in particular. But for now, data on overdoses and deaths are murky.
Medical records often don’t tell the full truth about a woman’s health
You might think that your medical records are an objective account of your health. But they’re not, write epidemiologist Annemarie Hirsch and sociologist Jennifer Silva. The pair recently published a study in which they paired electronic medical records and interviews with 87 women about pain, illness, and encounters with the health care system.
Many of the women described trust-breaking encounters with health care providers and misdiagnoses, but these moments were rarely documented. The authors point to the story of a woman who lived with debilitating pelvic pain for more than a decade as a poignant example. Doctors at first dismissed her pain as related to obesity, pivoting to mental health after she lost weight. Notably, the turning point only came after her husband joined her for an appointment, and she was ultimately diagnosed with endometriosis. Her medical records chronicle this diagnostic odyssey, but they don’t capture the frustration and disillusionment she experienced after years of having her pain downplayed. Hirsch and Silva write that such stories raise concerns about the use of AI to advance women’s health.
“These tools are only as good as the data in the medical record,” they write. “If a woman’s symptoms are filtered through assumptions about her weight or mental health, and the true story of her pain is omitted, AI may learn and reproduce how the woman is framed in the record.”
Ballot measures lay bare divisions on abortion and trans issues
Many Democrats are still celebrating the blue wave that handed their party control of both the House and Senate. But that momentum didn’t fully translate to health-related ballot initiatives across the country. As of late Thursday, voters in Arizona, Colorado, and Washington had approved or were on track to endorse measures that would prohibit transgender youth from participating on school sports teams aligned with their gender identity. Voters in four states with abortion-related ballot measures chose to preserve the status quo, with Missouri, Nevada, and Virginia choosing to maintain abortion rights while Idaho preserved the state’s existing ban.
Meanwhile, California voters appear on track to endorse Proposition 38, which would authorize $8.4 billion in bonds to fund immunology research. The measure has sparked controversy because its main backer is also the co-founder of an institute poised to receive half the funds. South Dakota voters rejected an amendment that would have conditioned a state Medicaid expansion on federal financial support holding steady. And Massachusetts voters can breathe easier (well, sort of) after a measure to repeal the state’s recreational marijuana law was defeated handily.
You can read more from me and Theresa Gaffney. But first, let’s stick with weed for a moment longer.
New evidence for ancient cannabis use
Early writing by the ancient Greek historian Herodotus — known for his foundational text on the Greco-Persian wars and banger quotes like, “of all possessions a friend is the most precious” — is a key source used by historians to support the idea that prehistoric communities were smoking weed. Archaeological evidence is hard to come by (plants are perishable!) and just as tricky to interpret. But a new paper, published yesterday in Science, offers compelling evidence of ritual cannabis use in a 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb.
The monumental burial mound included a log cabin-like structure, one coffin, and the remains of multiple individuals and horse sacrifices. There, archaeologists found hundreds of cannabis seeds, a handful of which were analyzed and dated to the first decade of the eighth century BCE. But there was an even rarer finding: two long braids of human hair containing significant amounts of the psychoactive compound cannabinol. “Although proving intent in a prehistoric context will remain impossible,” the authors wrote, “the evidence is strongly in favor of intentional consumption for the plant’s psychoactive properties.”
Admittedly, this is not our usual fare. But the study is a good reminder that drug use is not a modern issue, but rather a phenomenon that’s been with us for millenia. — Theresa Gaffney

The story so far: The Sample Registration System (SRS) Statistical Report of 2021, released by the Office of the Registrar General of India recently, showed that India has maintained its Total Fertility Rate (TFR) at 2.0 — the same as reported in 2020. While the national average for TFR has remained the same, there is a wide regional variation in TFR data for States and Union Territories (UTs) reported independently.
The highest TFR was recorded in Bihar at 3.0 and the lowest was reported for West Bengal and Delhi at 1.4. The data went on to reveal that in the decade between 2009-11 and 2019-21, TFR has been on an overall decline, in States, and nationally, albeit at different rates.

Demerit system for contractors ‘not ruled out’, Hong Kong development chief says
Government also considering new conditions for homeowners under subsidy scheme, including having a long-term maintenance plan and funds for it
The Hong Kong government has not ruled out the possibility of introducing a demerit system for contractors, according to the development chief, after an independent inquiry into last year’s deadly Tai Po fire identified unscrupulous consultants and building professionals as the main culprits of the tragedy.
Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho said in a television interview on Sunday that authorities were also considering introducing new conditions for homeowners who applied for the government’s building maintenance subsidy scheme, including a long-term plan and fund for property maintenance.
“I do not rule out the possibility of introducing a demerit points system in the next stage if we can formalise the mechanism further. However, we have not considered it at this stage,” Linn said.

Following a busy cold open that saw Texas Senator-elect James Talarico overshadow Donald Trump and a monologue crashed by his future movie co-star Emma Stone, “SNL” host Druski — who made history as the first digital content creator to preside over the show (who had yet to achieve crossover success, a la Issa Rae and Quinta Brunson) — got to finally flex his sketch-comedy chops in a parody of the Nathan Fielder/Elizabeth Holmes docu-phenomenon “You Can See Everything.”
Yes, prior to Fielder’s stay in Billy Evans (played by Ben Marshall) and Holmes’ (the talented Jane Wickline) home, they were visited by another comedian: Druski.
The trio re-enacted a number of scenes from the doc in a new trailer for “Druski Sees Everything,” including the moment where Evans snatched away the bowl as Holmes was beating eggs (because she wasn’t doing it hard enough to his liking) and that uncomfortable staredown.
“We’re so glad you’re here,” offered Wickline’s Holmes, replicating her deep voice. “I just want people to see me as an ordinary person. Can you do that, Druski?”
“Based on what I’ve seen so far, I’m going to go ahead and say, ‘No.’ Y’all got some of the weirdest, freakiest vibe I’ve done ever seen,” cracked Druski, before snatching away the bowl and beating the eggs himself.
Then came the stare-down sequence.
“You being real right now?” asked Druski.
“I’m always being real,” replied Holmes.
“Hold up — you trying to f*ck me?” Druski said.
Holmes nodded slightly. Cue Druski: “I ain’t mad at it. I just… I wanna try something,” closing each of her glaring eyes shut with his fingers.
Later on in the trailer, they did the stare-down scene once more — only this time, Druski was in whiteface as Holmes, facing off against Wickline’s Holmes. The digital creator has gone viral a number of times in the past for his whiteface sketches, from playing a rowdy redneck to Erika Kirk.
“I’m always being real,” said Druski’s Holmes.
“No, I’m always being real,” fired back Wickline’s Holmes.
“I could do this all day, b*tch,” exclaimed Druski’s Holmes.
The trailer also included a quote from your very own Variety: “Somehow, this makes Nathan Fielder seem like the reasonable choice.”

Bengaluru airport declares full emergency after security threat on Lucknow-bound IndiGo flight
A full emergency was declared at Bengaluru airport after a suspected hijack threat note was found in the washroom of a Lucknow-bound IndiGo flight.
A full emergency was declared at Kempegowda International Airport (Terminal 1) in Bengaluru on Saturday after a suspected hijack threat message was discovered inside the lavatory of an IndiGo flight scheduled for Lucknow.
IndiGo flight 6E-451 was en route from Bengaluru to Lucknow when crew members detected the threatening note inside the aircraft's washroom. Adhering to strict safety protocols, the pilots immediately turned the aircraft back to Bengaluru to initiate security procedures.
Upon landing, airport security personnel and aviation law enforcement authorities took control of the aircraft, isolating it to execute thorough anti-sabotage and safety sweeps.
An investigation is currently underway to identify the origin and author of the threat message found on board.
Addressing the security threat, an IndiGo spokesperson issued an official press statement.

US and China must join hands to measure rising AI tide
Before deciding how to respond to developments in artificial intelligence, Beijing and Washington need a better sense of just how quickly the tide is rising
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
The next US-China talk on artificial intelligence should begin with a simple question: do the two governments actually understand how rapidly AI’s capabilities are improving? Before deciding what to do about the technology, Washington and Beijing need a common way to measure its progress.
Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are expected to meet in Shenzhen soon, and AI is set to remain high on their agenda. Their continued exchanges on this transformative technology are a positive sign, but AI is advancing so fast that governments may have less time to prepare for its consequences than they assume.
AI is fundamentally reshaping work across very different fields, including some once thought difficult to disrupt. In China, over 90 per cent of new microdramas in the first eight months of the year were AI-generated – without cameras or live actors. A production that once required as many as 100 people can now rely on just two to five to complete the work in one week. AI has wiped out much of what was once lucrative work for actors.

Sewing is having a moment. Here’s why
Increased interest in sustainable fashion and analog hobbies are driving some Canadians to learn to sew
Depending on the corner of the internet you inhabit, you may have noticed that the feeds are full of sewing enthusiasts.
Look up "thrift flips" on Instagram or TikTok and you'll find creators remaking second-hand garments into new ones, or old quilts into hoodies and track suits.
On Pinterest, searches for "sewing ideas" are up 118 per cent year over year by its Canadian users, while those for "beginner sewing projects" rose 67 per cent, according to data provided to CBC News by the platform.
Sewing hobbyists and the people who teach them say a number of factors — including renewed interest in analog hobbies and growing concern about the impacts of fast fashion — are driving more Canadians to pick up a needle and thread.
"A generation raised on fast fashion is rediscovering the value of making and repairing their own clothes," said Sabine Weber, a professor of fashion at Seneca Polytechnic College in Toronto whose PhD research focused on sustainable fashion.
"And now they have discovered thrifting."
Referencing data from Trendex North America, a Canadian apparel market intelligence firm, Weber says the clothing resale market was forecast to grow from around $3.8 billion in 2022 to almost $6 billion in 2026.
Students from Seneca Polytechnic on a visit to the Textile Museum of Canada in Toronto. (Submitted by Sabine Weber)
That shift in shopping habits has prompted people to learn how to make small repairs to thrifted finds, and from there to try more ambitious upcycling projects, she says.
"And then you want to really … show your individuality and your self-expression by making your own clothes."
In Victoria, Erin Kerr says she began in earnest to develop her sewing skills a few years ago. "I had a scrunchie brand called Hair of the Dog that ended up doing pretty well … but I was just kind of sewing rectangles over and over," Kerr told The Current.
Once she expanded her repertoire, Kerr began to offer sewing lessons to get more out of her studio space and bring in a little extra cash.
"We immediately had an email list of hundreds of people that were interested in learning to sew from us," she said.
What started as a weekend project has since morphed into the Sewing Club, a specialty shop and school that offers patterns, fabric, tools and a range of sewing workshops.
"There's definitely a lot of people that want to take their time with sewing and are into the whole kind of slow fashion movement," said Kerr. Others want to learn to alter clothes that don't fit well off the rack, or start from scratch and make something new.
Embracing the analog
There's also the offline nature of the craft, says Weber.
"It's a very big contrast to all the typing we do and all the machines and phones and iPads and whatever."
Branislava Pavlovic started sewing in spring 2025 and one of her most prized projects is this jumpsuit made of vintage Toronto Blue Jays bedsheets, which she wears to games. (Submitted by Branislava Pavlovic)
As Branislava Pavlovic points out, "it's literally impossible to be on your phone and sew at the same time."
She took up sewing in the spring of 2025 with beginner classes at the Neon Needle in Toronto and now works there as studio manager and instructor.
"We find that there's a lot of people who are in tech jobs, engineers and administrators, that just want to come and just do nothing like what they do all day, but actually do something for themselves and be creative."
Candice Alvarez, who sews and designs patterns from her home studio in Burlington, Ont., says she thinks the increased interest coincides with a shift in people's understanding of the impacts of fast fashion. (Amanda Grant/CBC)
Ishmam Sarker says he was inspired by some of the sewing content he was seeing on Instagram and TikTok.
"I've always been into fashion … And then I guess the algorithm worked in my favour. It slowly started to push some sewing-specific content on it," Sarker said.
He followed a tutorial on how to make a tote bag and took on more ambitious projects from there.
"I started just getting patterns from Fabricland and a bunch of other places online as well," he told The Current at a fabric swap in Toronto.
YouTube, he said, "helps a lot."
Candice Alvarez says she thinks social media has pushed hobbies like this to the forefront.
"And I think that's incredible because honestly, I had no idea that people were sewing their own clothes before I started," she said.
Alvarez, who now sews and designs patterns from her home studio in Burlington, Ont., says she also thinks the increased interest coincides with a shift in the way people look at fashion.
"Like fast fashion — for a while, people loved it," she said. "You could buy a T-shirt for $10 and it was amazing."
Whereas "people now, their eyes are opened to the fashion industry and how damaging it can be to the environment, and the labour [conditions] and like all of it."
Getting started
Those who are thinking of taking up sewing can check out an endless supply of tutorials online.
But brick-and-mortar studios where people can take in-person classes seem to be increasing in number.
The Neon Needle in Toronto is a sewing studio that offers a range of sewing classes and workshops. (Submitted by The Neon Needle)
For example, in Toronto, the Neon Needle transitioned fully from tailor shop to sewing-lesson studio in February 2024. Downtown Sewing opened in April 2025 and SewBar, a combined sewing studio and coffee shop is set to open soon.
Hey Soft Spot opened in Vancouver in September, Calgary's Sew Happy in August and Winnipeg's Lilax Studio in April.
Back in Victoria, at the Sewing Club, Kerr recommends keeping expectations modest at the start.
"I would say don't get too emotionally attached to your first project because it's probably going to look bad," she said. "So don't focus too much on the outcome. It's more the process and building your skills."

What Ottawa's 'RRSP for life' plan means for Canadian seniors
Experts say the plan cuts complexity, but ignores bigger issues for many Canadian seniors
Canada's new federal budget proposes a tweak to Registered Retirement Savings Plans (RRSPs) aimed at simplifying financial planning for thousands of seniors every year.
Tax and personal finance experts say while the new "RRSP for life" measure would be more convenient, it does not address seniors who are struggling under rising living costs.
An RRSP is a Canadian savings account that lowers your tax exposure today, and lets your savings and investments grow without being taxed until you retire. They can hold a wide variety of financial assets, including cash, stocks, guaranteed investment certificates (GICs), and exchange-traded funds (ETFs).
For the 2026 tax year, individuals can contribute up to 18 per cent of their earned income in 2025, up to a maximum of $33,810. If you have a workplace pension, the value of those pension contributions is deducted from that 18 per cent limit.
What are the proposed changes?
Currently, RRSPs must be withdrawn or converted into a Registered Retirement Income Fund (RRIF) when the account holder turns 71. In the new federal budget, Ottawa proposes to allow Canadians to keep their RRSPs after they reach that age.
Currently, if someone dies after age 71 with a RRIF, the account can be transferred to a spouse without closing it or triggering tax paperwork. That's not the case today with RRSPs.
Ottawa's budget proposal would "allow a surviving spouse or partner to become a successor holder of an RRSP, and simplify tax-free transfers to qualified survivors after the death of the account holder."
A public consultation on the plan started on Thursday, and will run until Jan. 8, 2027.
- 7 takeaways from the Carney government's 2nd budget
- Carney's new budget aims to end homelessness in 10 years
Jamie Golombek, managing director, tax and estate planning at CIBC Private Wealth Management, says today most 71-year-olds choose to convert their RRSPs to RRIFs to avoid the tax applied if they choose to cash out.
"It's a complex administrative thing for hundreds of thousands at least every year," he told CBC News.
"What the government is saying is, 'Why not have an RRSP for life?' In other words, an RRSP that you basically have until the day you die."
Under the proposed change, the government would require RRSP holders to withdraw a minimum percentage of their savings each year, starting at age 72. These percentages are based on average life expectancy to ensure that retirement savings is paid out and taxed gradually for the rest of the owner's lifetime.
John Fragos, press secretary to Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, confirmed to CBC News that under the government's proposal, RRSP account holders cannot contribute after age 71.
Why do the changes matter?
Aaron Hector, senior wealth advisor at Calgary-based Tier Wealth says simplifying the financial landscape for seniors is a smart move by the government. He also praises the proposal to allow RRSPs to be easily transferred after death.
"Not needing someone to go through the paperwork process of converting an RRSP into a RRIF just makes a lot of common sense for me," he said. "Heaven forbid it slips through the cracks. It could create some issues for people."
Li Zhang, director of social impact at Chartered Professional Accountants of Canada, sees the government's "RRSP for life" proposal as "more of a nomenclature change," that ignores bigger issues for seniors.
Firstly, she estimates only 33 to 37 per cent of Canadians actually have access to a pension.
"You're not actually talking about a lot of people who have a lot of retirement savings assets," she said. "If you've walked by food banks, and you look at the line, it's the really young or the really old."
She says another problem for RRSP holders is that the mandatory withdrawals can make it difficult to balance their income. "That then triggers higher levels of taxation," she said.
While the consultation period for this plan runs until Jan. 8, Golombek expects it could take much longer to enact these changes if Ottawa elects to make them.
"I think it's going to be a few years before we see the ultimate merger of these, or at least the elimination of the RRIF."

Woman who lost 9 family members in Wayanad landslide begins new chapter, gets married
Shruthi lost her family of nine in the catastrophic 2024 Wayanad landslides, and later lost her fiancé in a road accident.
S Shruthi, who lost her family and her home in the catastrophic landslides in Keralam's Wayanad district in 2024, began a new chapter on Saturday as she got married at the Guruvayur Sree Krishna Temple.
Shruthi lost nine members of her family, including her parents and younger sister, in the landslides that struck Chooralmala and Mundakkai villages of Wayanad on July 30, 2024.
Her fiancé, Jenson, with whom she got engaged in June, later died in a road accident in September that year.
Shruthi tied the knot with Sandeep, a native of Mananthavady, on Saturday morning in the presence of her surviving relatives, friends and public representatives, reported news agency PTI.
CPI MLA and former minister K Rajan, who coordinated the rehabilitation efforts during the landslides, was also present on the occasion.
Also Read | 149 more Wayanad landslide-affected families allotted houses in township through draw of lots
Speaking to reporters, Shruthi said she was happy about the occasion. "He came forward to accept me after knowing everything about my life. I pray that we live a happy life together," she said, thanking everyone who supported her.
Rajan expressed happiness for Shruthi and highlighted the LDF government's support for her after the tragedy. "This is a happy moment for everyone. We stood by her during her difficult times. I am happy that I could be part of this crucial moment in her life," he said.
Shruthi's tragic life
The tragic story of Shruthi, 24, an accountant at a hospital in Kozhikode district, touched people across Keralam after she lost her family of nine two years ago. Shruthi lost around ₹4 lakh in cash and around 15 ‘sovereigns’ of gold, along with her newly built home that was destroyed in the Wayanad disaster.
Her only support during those times was Jenson, with whom she got engaged on June 2, 2024 after a 10-year-long courtship.
The couple had visited the Puthumala graveyard on August 29, where some of her family were buried, and had reaffirmed their commitment to each other. They were initially set to get married in December, but opted for a simple court-registered marriage in September.
However, before they could go ahead, Jenson got critically injured when his vehicle collided head-on with a bus on September 10 that year and later succumbed to his injuries.
Shruthi and some other family members of Jenson were also injured in the accident.
Considering her hardship, the state government appointed her as a clerk in the Revenue Department. Her husband Sandeep also works as a government employee at the Wayanad Collectorate.

Why a US-Russia showdown left Morocco celebrating
- Published
Morocco has welcomed the end of a decades-long UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara, after a diplomatic showdown between the US and Russia left the Security Council unable to agree on its future.
The council failed on Friday to renew the mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (Minurso) after Russia vetoed a US-backed proposal. A rival Russian draft to extend the mission also failed to secure enough votes.
The decision raises questions about the future of Africa's longest territorial dispute and the fragile ceasefire between Morocco, which claims Western Sahara, and the Polisario Front which has been fighting for the territory's independence for more than 50 years.
Here is what you need to know.
Why is Western Sahara disputed?
Western Sahara, on Africa's north-west coast, was a Spanish colony until 1975. It has significant phosphate reserves and valuable fishing grounds along its Atlantic coast.
As Spain prepared to withdraw, both Morocco and Mauritania claimed the territory.
The International Court of Justice found historical ties of allegiance but no territorial sovereignty that overrode the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination.
Morocco's then King Hassan II responded by organising the Green March. On 6 November 1975 about 350,000 Moroccan civilians entered the territory in a mass demonstration intended to put pressure on Spain.
Days later, Spain signed the Madrid Accords with Morocco and Mauritania, agreeing to transfer administrative control. Morocco took the northern two-thirds and Mauritania the southern third. The agreement did not settle the question of sovereignty.
The Polisario Front, an independence movement founded in 1973, opposed the deal. It saw it as replacing Spanish colonial rule with Moroccan and Mauritanian control.
Mauritania renounced its claim in 1979, but Morocco continued fighting Polisario.
Algeria became Polisario's main regional ally, providing military support and hosting its leadership and thousands of Sahrawi refugees in camps near the city of Tindouf.
The North African country says its position is based on the right to self-determination, while Morocco sees Western Sahara as an integral part of its territory.
Morocco and Algeria fought a brief border war in 1963 over disagreements about territory inherited from French colonial rule. Their relationship has remained tense, with Western Sahara at the centre of their dispute.
What was the UN's mission role?
After 16 years of fighting, Morocco and Polisario agreed to a UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991, with the territory divided by a sand wall, or berm, to keep the rival forces apart.
The UN established Minurso to monitor the ceasefire and organise a referendum on the territory's future. Sahrawis were meant to choose between independence and integration with Morocco.
The vote was scheduled for 1992 but never took place. The two sides could not agree on who would be eligible to participate, with disputes over voter identification becoming a major obstacle.
In 2007, Morocco put forward a proposal for autonomy, which would see Sahrawis managing their internal affairs, while Rabat retained control over defence and foreign relations.
The Polisario Front and Algeria rejected the plan, insisting on a referendum that included independence as an option.
Years of UN-sponsored negotiations failed to produce a breakthrough.
The ceasefire broke down in November 2020, when Polisario said it was resuming armed struggle.
But following a long diplomatic campaign by Morocco, the UN Security Council voted in 2025 in favour of a resolution backing the autonomy plan as the "most feasible" solution for the disputed territory.
While most Sahrawis live in the part of Western Sahara controlled by Morocco, tens of thousands are estimated to be in refugee camps in Algeria.
What happened at the UN?
The US proposed extending Minurso's mandate for another year, but its draft went beyond the usual renewal.
It would have removed the word "referendum" from the mission's name and made Morocco's autonomy proposal the sole basis for further negotiations.
The draft received the support of 11 of the Security Council's 15 members, including France and the UK but Russia vetoed it, arguing that it was too favourable to Morocco.
Russia then proposed extending Minurso's mandate without changing its terms. That draft also failed, receiving only two votes in favour.
Minurso's mandate expired at the end of Saturday, 31 October. The UN said the following day that the mission had entered a liquidation period, with a reduced team overseeing the transfer of military equipment and other assets.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres said the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination must be respected and warned of the risk of renewed hostilities.
The Polisario Front condemned the US proposal. Its representative, Sidi Omar, thanked Russia for vetoing it, saying it would "torpedo the foundations of the UN peace process" and threaten regional and international peace.
Morocco, meanwhile, said the mission's personnel and equipment should leave the territory in the coming days, arguing that Western Sahara issue should no longer be considered by the Security Council.
Minurso had 155 military personnel and was expected to cost $62m (£46m) in the financial year beginning in June, according to a UN report.
Why is Morocco celebrating the end of the UN mission?
Morocco's royal palace welcomed the failure to renew Minurso's mandate.
In Laayoune, the territory's largest city, footage showed people celebrating, waving Moroccan flags and displaying portraits of King Mohammed VI.
"The decision is an opportunity for Rabat to challenge what it sees as an international mechanism that has failed to resolve the dispute," Issam Laaroussi, a Moroccan expert in international relations, tells the BBC.
He said Morocco would now have more room to push its autonomy proposal and shift negotiations away from a referendum on independence towards autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty.
The decision does not, however, change Western Sahara's legal status or amount to international recognition of Moroccan sovereignty.
Western Sahara remains on the UN list of non-self-governing territories, while the African Union officially recognises its independence, as the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (SADR).
But the decision comes after several countries backed the position of Morocco, which in recent years has made securing international support for its claim a central part of its foreign policy.
In 2020, the US recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara as part of an agreement to establish diplomatic relations between Morocco and Israel.
France also backed Morocco's autonomy plan as the basis for resolving the dispute in 2024.
Morocco rejoined the African Union in 2017, more than three decades after leaving its predecessor, the Organisation of African Unity, in protest at the SADR's admission.
Since returning, Rabat has sought to build support for its position from within the organisation. At least 10 African countries have opened diplomatic missions in the territory in support of Rabat.
"Morocco is not necessarily seeking to abandon the UN process, but to change the framework for negotiations and draw greater support from regional organisations," says Laaroussi.
Addressing a special joint session of parliament on Monday, House of Representatives Speaker Ahmed Touizi hailed the end of Minurso as a victory for the country's diplomacy.
He said the country should now move from "managing the dispute to implementing its autonomy plan under Moroccan sovereignty, while pressing ahead with development projects in the territory."
Could this lead to a renewed war?
The fear is that Minurso's departure could lead to renewed fighting.
The mission has monitored military developments and helped reduce the risk of escalation.
Aid organisation Oxfam warned that losing its monitoring and de-escalation role could undermine stability, with serious consequences for civilians.
Laaroussi admits that the mission's departure could create security gaps.
"Minurso's departure does not create the original conflict, because the conflict is already there, but it could aggravate an already fragile security environment," he says.
The UN decision has also fuelled nationalist rhetoric online.
Several Moroccan users have shared AI-generated images of themselves in military uniform, declaring their readiness to fight for Morocco's sovereignty over Western Sahara.
In Morocco, Western Sahara is widely regarded as a national cause. Political parties that are often divided on other issues are united in supporting the country's claim to sovereignty over the territory.
Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita has said the end of the mission does not mean the end of the ceasefire, and that Rabat remains committed to it "within respect of its security and sovereignty."
Polisario has not said what it will do next.
Any resumption of fighting could well draw in Algeria, as tensions with Morocco remain high.
According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), both countries significantly increased military spending last year, with SIPRI citing their dispute over Western Sahara as a key driver.
Algeria spent an estimated $25.4bn, more than four time Morocco's $6.3bn.

Paraguay's former president faces prosecutors after his removal over bank collapse
Paraguay's former President Santiago Peña has been taken to the attorney general’s office for questioning
Paraguay’s former president was taken to the attorney general’s office for questioning Saturday, just hours after being ousted by Congress over the collapse of a major bank. The Central Bank said it was working to compensate hundreds of thousands of people who were locked out of their accounts this week.
Drone footage taken by Paraguay’s Telefuturo showed ousted President Santiago Peña arriving at the attorney general’s compound in a black SUV, escorted by police officers. He wore navy blue pants and a white shirt and was not handcuffed.
Paraguayan prosecutors on Friday ordered the arrest of Peña and former Central Bank chief Carlos Carvallo as part of a criminal investigation into alleged breach of trust and other offenses tied to the collapse of Ueno Bank. Peña was transferred to a military base late Friday as hundreds of protesters gathered outside his home.
The arrest order was issued soon after the Senate removed Peña from office in a unanimous vote. The verdict came just three days after regulators seized Ueno Bank, freezing nearly 3 million customers’ access to their savings and triggering a political crisis.
Peña was replaced by Vice President Pedro Alliana, who began naming a new Cabinet Saturday. The Central Bank said Saturday that 1.2 million Ueno customers had received partial or full reimbursement of their insured deposits under Paraguayan law.
Lawmakers accused Peña of using his political influence to steer hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds into Ueno while regulators overlooked risky insider lending. Peña has denied wrongdoing.
The removal of U.S. President Donald Trump's ally marks the biggest political crisis in Paraguay in over a decade. The landlocked country of 6 million people returned to democratic rule in 1989. Since then, it has mostly been governed by the conservative Colorado Party.
Peña submitted his resignation Thursday, but Congress did not accept it and pressed ahead with an impeachment trial. Opposition lawmakers insisted on his removal to prevent him from leaving office with immunity.
“He must go, but not home. He must go to a maximum-security prison,” opposition Sen. Yolanda Paredes told reporters. “The public is fed up with impunity.”
In a farewell message released shortly before he was ousted Friday, Peña expressed hope his departure would spare Paraguay further harm.
“I do not want my presence to be a cause of greater division or instability,” he wrote. “My responsibility is to put the country above my personal fate.”
Public outrage has intensified by the day. Thousands of protesters demanding access to their frozen savings and accountability for Ueno’s failure have clashed with police firing rubber bullets and pepper spray this week. Paraguay’s largest teachers’ union, which has more than 40,000 members, plans to begin an indefinite national strike Monday to press for protection of public pension funds.

If you've been coveting one of Rocco’s smart designer minifridges, you might be interested to know the brand's biggest sale of 2026 starts today, featuring the brand-new Rocco Essential for under $1,000 and the OG Classic in this year’s new Beige colorway, as well as white and two rare blue colors, for $1,495—as low as the Classic ever gets.
Today also marks the rerelease of the Classic's Icy Blue and Royal Blue, two rarely seen colors that Rocco says are not coming back after this year.
The Essential
The Essential was just released in August and just began shipping in September; I'm currently testing it now. It's only been about a week and a half, but early impressions are positive. It has the same smart sight system as the Classic, but the biggest difference is obviously the look. Vintage-inspired fluted glass and rounded edges are out; sleek minimalism is in. The tinted dark glass door takes up the entire front, with a color-matched metal handle you can swap out for midcentury-inspired oak for an extra $95.
It's only got one temperature zone as opposed to the Classic's two, but my favorite part so far has been the interior—instead of the Classic's old-fashioned wire racks, the Essential sports smooth-glide drawers lined with a rubbery material and grip strips. This makes it much more accommodating to oddly shaped drinks, and prevents cans (it can hold up to 77) from rolling around every time you open your Rocco. It also gets colder than the Classic model—down to 34 degrees Fahrenheit instead of 37. My main frustration so far is that the sight system has been a little spotty and slow to recognize when drinks have been removed, but I'm having that problem with the Classic as well, so it's not specific to this model. All colors (Cream, Sage, Graphite) of the Essential are currently discounted.
The Classic
The handsome, vintage-inspired model is the one that started it all. Its thick steel body comes in a range of fun colors, the fluted glass refracts potentially drink-damaging light, and it comes with a color-matched metal tray so it can double as a bar cart. It's got two isolated temperature zones for red and white wine (or extra-crispy Cokes), plus five full-sized racks and one half-rack—enough for 88 cans or 27 bottles of wine. The wire racks don't pull out as smoothly as the Essential's rubber-lined drawers, but this is otherwise a top-of-the-line beverage cooler with an impressive 10-year warranty.
You can also control the interior lights from your phone. The sight system, however, is buggy—my Classic is currently displaying a rack of Dr. Pepper and Stella Artois bottles I had left over from a party in July (they were consumed not long after that), so I would not recommend buying one of these for the sight system alone. (Note this sale is on the Beige, White, Royal Blue, and Icy Blue Classic only.)
Back in Blue
I’m partial to the Classic’s forest green, but even I've got to admit the blue hues look pretty good. They sold out almost immediately around this time last year, so if you've been wanting one and you see this, I wouldn't wait to add it to your cart.

Before Attempting SD Card Recovery
Before performing a recovery of your SD card, here are a few methods that you can follow to improve the chances of recovering your lost files on your SD card:
First, don’t copy new photos or record new videos on this SD card. This prevents new data from being written to the memory card. Also, don’t transfer new files to the affected card. If needed, use a different SD card, especially if you are in the middle of recording or need to transfer your files quickly.
Next, do not format or initialize the memory card, even if the device you connected to asks you to. This also includes repair solutions commonly offered by devices such as PCs to recover your memory card; we strongly recommend avoiding them, as they can change the stored data.
Finally, before attempting recovery, make sure your missing files aren’t already saved somewhere else. Check your camera memory cards, your computer import folders, and any external hard drives or backups to confirm. If you find copies, open the files to confirm they work as expected so you don’t have to recover them again.
Finally, check the condition of your SD card. In general, recovery software works best when the computer detects the SD card and the connection stays stable throughout the recovery process. You can also recover files even if they won’t open.
If your memory card is physically damaged, overheats, fails, your device doesn’t detect it, or you see many warning signs, we recommend stopping immediately and seeking professional data recovery services.

Step 3: Scan Your SD Card
Once everything is selected, tap on “Start Scan,” and Recoverit shows the files in the sidebar. You can browse each file by capture time and original folder from the sidebar.
You can also preview and select files during scanning and watch for any errors, slow scanning, partition problems, and video fragmentation problems in real time. If any problems occur, follow the software’s guidance.
Step 4: Preview and Recover Your Files
You can now preview and recover your files. Browse the scan results by photo, video, and capture time, and view photos and videos separately; filter by various options, including capture time.

Select the files you need to recover, then click the “Recover” option. Next, choose a separate storage location. If some of your recovered videos won’t play, there are many possible reasons. The most common reason is that interrupted video recordings can become corrupted, since video recovery is more complicated than recovering deleted photos.

Final Thoughts

Yes, as long as your card is still recognized, you may be able to recover deleted files, but you need to ensure the memory card is readable and the data hasn’t been overwritten.
