The Delhi High Court has given the National Medical Commission (NMC) and the Delhi government’s Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) two weeks to submit a joint inquiry report on the medical qualifications of two doctors accused of mishandling a child during treatment.
Justice Neena Bansal Krishna passed the order on October 30 while hearing a contempt petition filed by the child’s mother, Sapna Jain, on behalf of her minor son.
According to the petition, the child suffered severe brain damage “after being mishandled by two unqualified doctors (misrepresenting as super-specialists) in the Neonatal ICU of Fortis Hospital, Shalimar Bagh”.
The petition claims that the child is now in a permanent vegetative state and suffers from West Syndrome, epilepsy and cerebral palsy. It also states that he continues to experience severe pain and suffering.
In March 2025, the High Court had called for affidavits clarifying whether the qualifications claimed by the two doctors “are qualifications entitling these Respondents (doctors) to undertake specialisation practice in this country.”
In May 2026, the court further directed the NMC Secretary and the DGHS to conduct a joint inquiry into the doctors’ qualifications and submit a report within eight weeks.
However, the fresh contempt petition alleged that the deadline of July 24, 2026, passed without the authorities submitting the report or seeking an extension from the court.
“The matter concerns the qualifications of doctors treating critically ill newborns. The NMC, being the statutory regulator, is duty-bound to ensure transparency and accountability, and its continued failure to place a clear and conclusive report before this Court raises serious questions regarding its fairness and credibility and that of its officers. The DGHS has likewise failed to discharge the joint duty cast upon it by this Court,” the plea said.
The court has posted the case for hearing on December 16.

You’ve probably been hearing a lot about data centers this week.
This election’s biggest AI story isn’t about data centers
Democrats are putting AI executives on notice. Here’s an early look at their plans.
Candidates in several races made regulating data centers a key part of their campaigns. Now, 40 ballot measures to slow or stop data centers have passed. And in an exit poll, when respondents were asked how important AI and data centers were in their vote for Congress, 56 percent answered that it was a “crucial or a major factor.”
Data centers are the physical infrastructure that powers AI, and they’ve become deeply unpopular not just because of their noisiness, ugliness, or electricity demand, but because of what they symbolize: the acceleration of a technology that many Americans fear and that they feel Silicon Valley is foisting upon them.
Key takeaways
- Key figures to watch include Abdul El-Sayed, Jon Ossoff, and Scott Wiener. And Sen. Maria Cantwell has already put out a framework that could have bipartisan appeal.
- Data centers have grabbed the headlines, but the bigger story is the sweeping success of candidates who prioritize AI safety.
- These leaders will be poised to rein in the tech itself through hearings and lawmaking.
If you’re one of the Americans worried about AI — or just prefer a more serious regulatory approach over the hands-off, Trump White House approach — there’s a problem with confining your attention to data centers. Even a successful push against them won’t address the bigger issues around the technology. And picking off data center projects one by one will slow, but not stop, the buildout. AI companies will still find jurisdictions that are willing to let them build — it’ll just cost them more.
The election outcome that matters far more, though it was far less trumpeted, is that voters just elected a new crop of leaders promising to actually push to regulate the tech itself. These are people who are concerned not just about AI’s physical infrastructure, but about AI regulation and safety. And they’ve signaled that they’ll push for laws that address the full spectrum of risks from AI — from cyber hacks and job losses all the way to bioweapons, power concentration, and even the possibility of human extinction.
In fact, for AI watchers, one of the most striking things about this election cycle is how safety-pilled many candidates have become since the major AI hacks this summer.
“If you go back before the summer, most conversations from policymakers around AI were at a very, very high level of abstraction. Few of them were focused on how these AI models may be highly capable and may pose rather unique risks,” Mackenzie Arnold, an analyst at the Institute for Law & AI, told me. “But there’s been a big shift.”
The midterm results — and the Democrats’ stunning takeover of Congress — improve the odds of reining in AI. But now, the big question is: Can the new victors use the momentum they built up around data centers — the kitchen-table issue that initially brought many voters into the tent — and broaden out beyond that to mobilize for greater AI safety? They may have a lot of ideas, but are they any good?
The new (and newly emboldened) crop of AI safety advocates
Among the newly elected Democrats, a striking number are very vocal about AI risks. And a few have clearly taken the time to educate themselves on the finer points. So before considering what concrete changes they can actually implement, it’s worth getting to know what they’ve proposed.
Abdul El-Sayed, who won the Michigan Senate race, said that we need a “full-on pause” on frontier AI research. He’s also advocated for global coordination on a slowdown, including a treaty with China aimed at avoiding an arms race dynamic. He supports a ban on recursive self-improvement, where AI models build the next, even smarter AI models. He also wants a new federal safety agency that would inspect companies and block releases if necessary.
Even if not all his ideas resonate with experts (like the simplistic idea of a “kill switch” for dangerous models), having him in the Senate means that AI safety advocates will have an easier time arguing for a pause on frontier research.
Another winner to watch is Jon Ossoff, who prevailed in his Georgia Senate race. In his victory speech, he lambasted AI developers, saying, “The titans of Silicon Valley dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction.”
Back in September, he impressed safety advocates by explicitly mentioning “catastrophic risks” like AI-engineered bioweapons. Conveying his priorities, he said, “A capable president would move swiftly to secure and reassure the American people, rush inspectors into frontier labs, fortify the nation against bioterrorism, demand legislation from Congress, and lead the world toward an AI treaty. But President Trump is compromised.”
Two other Democrats with strong AI safety bona fides and specific policy ideas have emerged victorious this week. Scott Wiener — the longtime California state senator who was behind two important pieces of legislation, SB 1047 (which was ultimately vetoed) and SB 53 (which was signed into law) — won Nancy Pelosi’s seat this week. He’s said he’ll work to institute strict federal safety standards and “guard against catastrophic risk from AI.”
And Manny Rutinel — who cosponsored a 2024 law that sought to regulate AI use — won his race in Colorado. Rutinel has ties to effective altruism, a movement long preoccupied with AI safety, and you can hear it in the way he talks: “This technology has a 10 percent risk of wiping out human civilization,” he recently told The New York Times. “I don’t want human civilization to come to an end.”
Sam Forstag, who just became Montana’s first Democratic member of Congress in decades, also stated that AI poses an “existential risk to all of humanity.” Troy Jackson, the Democrat who won his Senate race in Maine, has vowed that he’s “not going to let the billionaires write the rules,” adding, “We are not that far from ‘Terminator,’ and I don’t want to be ‘hasta la vista, baby.’”
You can expect these new victors to be reliable votes supporting the cause of AI regulation come early 2027. But what, exactly, might that look like?
What Democrats plan to do now on AI
As Democrats are poised to take power in Congress, they will have two big levers to pull on AI safety: hearings and lawmaking.
Now that the election is over, expect a whole lot of hearings. Sen. Ed Markey, who won reelection in Massachusetts, signaled that he’s coming for Big Tech executives. “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” he posted on X.
What will it look like if these executives are called to testify under oath? “Some of the hearings are going to be focused on safety practices — and evidence that the company’s practices are not up to snuff,” Arnold told me. “Asking for answers to questions of: ‘Why didn’t you find that earlier? Why didn’t you tell us?’ And while that doesn’t get you all the way [to safety], this public pressure is why so many companies have adopted voluntary practices, why they’ve improved their internal monitoring, their incident reporting, their response time to various incidents.”
As for lawmaking, experts I spoke with are now bullish that we’ll see much stronger AI legislation in 2027 than we’ve seen to date. Sen. Maria Cantwell, who’s slated to chair the Senate Commerce Committee, is a key player to watch. She’s already put out a framework for governing AI that could have bipartisan appeal, which she’s called a precursor to legislation. It requires mandatory safety standards for cutting-edge AI models, independent testing and audits that models would have to pass before release, and prompt reporting of safety incidents.
“Cantwell is going to push that, and she’s in a place to basically be the voice of the caucus on that,” Brad Carson, an advocate for stricter AI policies who leads Americans for Responsible AI and a former congressman, told me. “Every single Democrat supports it, and all they need is five or six Republicans to beat the filibuster, and I bet you they can find that.”
Carson is hopeful that Democrats can get Republican votes “especially as the gravitational pull of the White House eases,” he said. “Trump has led them down the primrose path of defeat. A lot of smart politicians are going to be distancing themselves.”
Yes, President Donald Trump ultimately holds veto power. And he’s allowed American tech companies to race ahead on the technology with very few guardrails. But as AI companies make more and more concessions to safety in light of security incidents, the president may be more willing to sign on to some safety regulations.
“He’s mercurial enough that I can see him signing something like this,” Carson told me, “especially if some of these Republicans say, ‘Look, we’re getting battered on data centers and AI. This is a terrible thing. Let’s do this.’”
Of course, the most surefire way to gain control of AI lawmaking, unobstructed by a veto, would be to lay the groundwork for a Democratic White House in 2028. And the midterms showed that a focus on reining in AI can help propel Democrats to victory. “The road to 2028 starts today,” wrote Alex Bores, the New York Assembly member who has made AI his main focus. “In order to maintain voters’ trust and avoid catastrophic risk, we need a unified baseline around AI safety in the Democratic Party.”
Although many voters focused on data centers this election cycle, it’s reasonable to predict — as cyber breaches and other security incidents proliferate — that they will move from symbol to substance, focusing more on safety in the run-up to 2028.
“We shouldn’t view voter sentiment towards data centers and AI as stagnant or static,” Arnold told me. “I think it will continue to update to events in the world, and I think it will increasingly focus on AI itself as we see events in the world that make that very obvious to people.”
Or as Greg Casar, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus that sets policy and legislative strategy, put it, “The revolt against data centers was one of the top issues of the 2026 election, and in a few years we will look back on it as just the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics.”
The savviest politicians are already preparing with that earthquake in mind.

Indian wrestler Taniya made history at the 2026 Youth Olympics, becoming the first Indian to win a medal in beach wrestling.
Competing in the women’s 75 kg category, Taniya beat Matilda Ann Hruby from the United States to enter the gold medal match, and secured silver after losing 1-2 to China’s Min Zhao.
Taniya had brought in valuable international experience into the competition, having won bronze in the women’s freestyle 69kg category at the U-17 World Wrestling Championships 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan, and silver at the U-17 Asian Championships, earlier this year.
She started her campaign in the women’s 75kg category with a 3-1 victory over Germany’s Mia Bauer, and got the better of Greece’s Vasiliki Karavanou and Estonia’s Merily Vaester in her next two group-stage clashes to book a spot in the semifinals of the event.
It was the seventh medal for India at the Youth Games in Dakar, which includes three silver and four bronze medals.

It was a big night for doctors to win seats in Congress, riding the blue wave
The U.S. Senate will soon have a practicing physician who's a Democrat for the first time since 1938, with the election of Dr. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in South Carolina.
Her win — among many other physician candidates Tuesday night — marks a dramatic shift when it comes to doctors with political power across the country. Historically, doctors have been elected to Congress more often as Republicans, not Democrats. But that changed this cycle.
Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news out of Washington, D.C.
In the recent past, the Republican party attracted doctor-candidates who were essentially small business people who had concerns about high taxes and government overreach. The new crop of candidates from health professions often work for large hospital systems and are interested in issues that align with Democratic priorities like public health, equity and affordability.
Andrews told NPR before she won that she was motivated to enter politics after watching parents worry about the cost of things like inhalers for asthma patients and insulin for kids with diabetes.
"I watch as worried parents leave the hospital in the evening so that they can go work their third shift job just so they can make ends meet," she said. "And then, like the majority of pediatricians in America, I've cared for kids who've been shot." Guns are the leading cause of death for children in the U.S.
"It really clicked to me that the path to catalyzing this change that I want to see in America for the children in America is through politics," she explained.
Blue wins, red losses
In the current Senate, all four of the physicians are Republicans. Two of them, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R.-La., and Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan, lost their reelection bids this year. With the election of South Carolina's Andrews and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist, in Michigan, there will now be an equal number of Republican and Democratic physicians in the upper chamber. (El-Sayed trained as a physician but did not do a residency or practice medicine, instead pursuing public health.)
In the House, the six members of the Democratic doctor's caucus will be joined by at least two more: New Jersey's Dr. Adam Hamawy, a former U.S. Army surgeon, and pediatrician Dr. Richard Pan in California. In the GOP doctor's caucus, neurosurgeon Dr. John Cowan was elected in Georgia, but at least two incumbents lost their seats, with a few races still too close to call.
A big recruiting effort
Many of these new Democratic physician-lawmakers were recruited and backed by 314 Action, a name that refers to the mathematical constant pi. The organization supports progressive candidates with science backgrounds to run for office, and it invested more than $30 million in dozens of Democratic candidates competing in state and federal races, including 48 physicians.
The group's president, Shaughnessy Naughton, says that the organization does leadership development and recruits scientists to run across the country, then helps candidates in a variety of ways.
"We work to help them put together their campaign strategy, communication strategy, media training, we help to get them local and national media exposure, work with them on their fundraising, and fundraise for them," she explains.
Those candidates won big time on Tuesday. In addition to big national names like Senators-elect Andrews and El-Sayed, and Governor-elect Dr. Amy Acton of Ohio, many of the downballot candidates 314 Action supported won as well. Among them are several incoming state legislators who will be the only elected physicians in their chambers: Dr. Nikhil Wagle in Iowa, Dr. Amelia Gallitano-Mendel in Arizona, and Dr. Jarod Fox in Florida.
Naughton attributes that success to health care and affordability being front of mind. Also, polls show the public trusts doctors, and the candidates effectively countered messaging from Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime anti-vaccine activist who has downplayed ongoing measles outbreaks.
"People were sick of it," Naughton says. "We should not have American children dying — or anyone dying — of measles in 2026. And yet, not only did we have that happening, we had a health secretary that only made the situation worse."
A key vote, a damaging investigation
Outgoing chair of the powerful Health, Education, Labor and Pensions committee, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R.-La., spoke often from the dais about how his experience as a physician shaped his perspective as a lawmaker and committee chair.
During Kennedy's confirmation hearing in Jan. 2025, Cassidy memorably spoke about the root of his passion for vaccination. "In the early 2000's, I was loading a patient onto an air ambulance, an 18-year-old young woman, to go to get a liver transplant from acute liver failure due to hepatitis B," he said, noting the expensive surgery and ongoing hospital bills she would face, if she lived. "It was the worst day of my medical career, because I thought: $50 of vaccines could have prevented this all."
Still, Cassidy ultimately cast a key vote to confirm Kennedy into the job, despite Kennedy's long history of anti-vaccine activism. Kennedy flaunted vaccine-related promises Cassidy said he made to earn that vote, and even supported the Republican primary challenger who managed to unseat Cassidy earlier this year.
In a surprise Tuesday night, Dr. Roger Marshall, R.-Kan., also lost his reelection bid — another senior member of the HELP committee. Marshall is an OBGYN and staunch supporter of Kennedy. In September, the New York Times reported that Marshall had sued more than 700 patients for unpaid medical bills. One of the patients filed a class action lawsuit against him last week. Marshall described his actions as a way to "keep the lights on" in a last-minute social media video. He lost to challenger Adam Hamilton, a Methodist minister, by four points.
All the way back to 1776
Dr. Chadd Kraus has studied physicians in Congress. Kraus is now an emergency room doctor and the vice chair for research for the Department of Emergency and Hospital Medicine at Jefferson Health Lehigh Valley in Pennsylvania. Two decades ago, after studying political science as an undergrad and pursuing a masters in public health, he worked on an analysis of the physicians in Congress.
"In 1776, 10.7% of the signers of the Declaration of Independence were physicians," the paper notes. Kraus explains that was an era where practicing medicine involved leeches; germs hadn't been discovered and antibiotics hadn't been invented. Kraus suggests those physicians happened to be "part of a class that owned land that was educated."
In the next two hundred years, medicine transformed, and for a time, very few physicians served as federal lawmakers. "In the period of time that we studied [from 1960-2004], there were 25 physicians total who had served in the U.S. Congress, whether the House or the Senate," he explains. "In the current Congress, there are as many physicians — nearly — as there were in that whole period of time that we studied, which was several decades."
The new count
To be specific, there are 20 physicians in the current Congress, and Republicans outnumber Democrats two to one. There are six Democrats and 10 Republicans who serve in the House. All four doctors in the Senate are Republicans.
In the new Congress, there will be at least 18 physicians in Congress, 10 of them Democrats. Depending on the outcome of several House races, Democratic physician-lawmakers may outnumber Republican physician-lawmakers. Another notable win was in Ohio, where oncology nurse practitioner Kristina Knickerbocker flipped a Republican House seat. Nurse Lauren Underwood, a Democrat, held onto her House seat in Illinois.
In addition to Republicans Cassidy and Marshall losing their Senate seats, in the house, Rep. Neal Dunn of Florida, a urologist, retired, and Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, an ophthalmologist in Iowa, and Jen Kiggans, a nurse in Virginia lost their seats.
Kraus says, when it comes to making laws, "physicians have a valuable perspective, not a monopoly on good policy," he says. "And the need for physician voices in government has grown, I think, over the course of time, as healthcare has become more complex and politically consequential."
He says the emergency department, especially, is a place where you can see the effect of health policy in real time. He recalls at the beginning of the opioid crisis, how emergency physicians were among the first to sound the alarm to policymakers. When the uninsured rates increase, they see patients coming in sicker than they would otherwise be, he says. "We see the challenges of health policy and the consequences of it," he says
A health policy shake up?
Many of the new members of Congress campaigned on health policy issues, like the cost of health insurance and prescription drugs. There's widespread dissatisfaction with the cost of health care across the political spectrum. Democratic leaders have said that reversing Republican cuts to premium subsidies for health insurance and work requirements for Medicaid will be at the top of their agenda.
Beyond those immediate issues, more than 15 years after the passage of the Affordable Care Act, there may be political appetite and public demand for major new health legislation in the coming years. Some candidates ran on Medicare-for-all, a national health insurance plan, which has become increasingly popular in public opinion surveys.
"I think we all certainly agree, no matter one's political views or perspective, that there is the potential for a better system," Kraus says. "I do think that having physicians and other health care professionals meaningfully incorporated into the policymaking process is really critical to finding what those innovations might be."
Naughton of 314 Action says the health-professional candidates her group supported care about and have ideas about how to change the health care system, but that hasn't been their only pitch to voters.
"I do think that they really lead with what they essentially are, which is problem solvers," she says. "We can fix this problem — we can make health care accessible and affordable — and not make it a choice between life or debt."
Lexie Schapitl contributed reporting to this story.

Perspective: Simon Winchester was here to tell a story
I met Simon Winchester decades ago, covering a big story in a small town. The Menominee Warrior Society had seized an abandoned Catholic monastery in Gresham, Wisconsin, and other indigenous rights activists - including the actor Marlon Brando - came to join them.
I was a young reporter who had traveled up from Chicago. Simon Winchester was there for The Guardian newspaper, wearing a Sherlock Holmes-style hat and a tweed cape. We wound up in the same local rooming house, and I would creep onto the stairs at midnight to hear Simon, on a payphone, read his elegant copy to an editor in London between quaffs of brandy.
"Analysis is just so much gabble," I remember him remonstrating to an editor one night. "I'm here to tell a story."
Simon Winchester, who died this week at the age of 82, told so many stories. He covered Bloody Sunday in Derry, Northern Ireland; the Watergate scandal in Washington DC; and the Falklands war - during which Argentine authorities accused him of spying for the British government and threw him in jail for three months.
"Who on earth would make me a spy?," he used to ask in re-telling the story. "As if I could keep a secret!"
Simon Winchester went on to author dozens of bestsellers that ranged around the world, and humanity. He wrote about earthquakes and cities, explorers on open seas, mountains, and in laboratories, the English language, and the human mind and soul.
"It was a brave man," Simon wrote in his book about the Atlantic Ocean, "who ate the first oyster."
This week, as exit polls show so much human anxiety over Artificial Intelligence, I wondered if Simon Winchester might want people to hear some of the final, surprisingly buoyant thoughts from his 2024 book, Knowing What We Know.
"An existential intellectual crisis looms," he wrote. "If machines will acquire all our knowledge for us and do our thinking for us, then what, pray, is the need for us to be?...
"But what if the opposite is true?" asked Simon Winchester. "What if mental leisure gives us the time and space to suppose, ponder, ruminate, consider, assess, wonder, contemplate, imagine, dream?...
"And by doing so perhaps come to know not simply what we do know, but what we should know, in order to be fully human."

'I cannot teach you integrity': How employee theft is hurting small businesses in Africa
- Published
When popular Kenyan food creator That Girl Boina took a two-week holiday to Europe, she expected to relax. A week into the trip, an Instagram direct message exposed a problem that would ultimately lead to the closure of her business.
"I was at your studio, I liked everything. The only problem was that I was asked to send money to a different number. It wasn't the number on the wall," a customer wrote to her.
Boina had opened Waxaholic Studio, a waxing and hydrafacial parlour in Nairobi's central business district, on 1 September 2024. A year later, she had hired a receptionist and two specialists and felt confident enough to take a two-week holiday, her first international trip of the year.
"I trusted them. It's two rooms and a reception - how do you mess that up?" she recalls thinking.
"It never occurred to me that maybe I was getting clients and someone else was stealing from me," she tells the BBC.
The discovery prompted Boina to examine the business more closely. Although the business had made a profit in the first few months, revenue began to fall in early 2025. She initially dismissed the decline as a seasonal slump but then realised there was a problem.
"Everyone around was making money apart from me," she says in hindsight.
She had already considered closing because it was not making a profit, but her initial investment, three employees depending on the business and her vision for it kept her going. The customer's message became the turning-point.
"If I am not making money and I am willing to wait and see where this goes and you guys are not giving me the same energy, then why are we still open?"
Rather than confront the employees, Boina decided to close the studio. That weekend, she put it up for sale but found no buyer. She sold some of the equipment and took others, including decorations, home. Waxaholic Studio closed in October 2025.
"I remember my friend taking me to a restaurant, and I started crying. We were both silent."
"What else would we do?"
Boina describes the experience as the worst feeling she has ever felt. The closure was not just a financial setback, but the loss of something she had built to secure her future.
In September, nearly a year after the business closed, Boina shared a video on TikTok recounting the experience, explaining that she had needed time to heal before speaking publicly about what happened.
The video went viral after being reposted on X, formerly Twitter, garnering close to one million views. It drew responses from many Kenyan business owners who described how theft, ranging from payment diversion to stock theft and the sale of expensive equipment, had pushed their businesses to the brink, forcing them to fire staff, sell their businesses or shut down.
"Although I have recovered emotionally, I am yet to recoup the money I invested in setting up and running the studio," says Boina.
The reaction to her story showed that employee theft is a huge problem for many small businesses owners in Africa, where a handful of employees may control payments, stock and supplier transactions, often with limited oversight.
A 2022 survey by PwC, one of the world's biggest consultancy firms, found that 63% of respondents in East Africa said their organisations had experienced economic crime, compared to a global figure of 46%.
The risks are not confined to small businesses. Some of East Africa's biggest supermarkets have also reported significant losses linked to employee fraud and stock theft. Tuskys and Nakumatt have both collapsed this decade amid wider financial and operational problems partly attributed to employee theft.
At its peak, Tuskys had more than 6,000 employees and over 60 branches across Kenya and Uganda. In 2015, the retailer hired loss-prevention firm Hipora Business Solutions East Africa to help tackle fraud. An audit found that Tuskys was losing more than 100m Kenya shillings (£581,000; $770,000) a month to employee theft, Business Daily reported. The alleged schemes included cashiers pocketing money, manipulating till transactions, and colluding with suppliers over goods received.
Nakumatt also suffered significant stock losses attributed to employee theft before going under, with a Kenyan policy firm reporting that more than $100m (£75m) worth of stock was unaccounted for.
Hipora, which works with businesses across East and Southern Africa, says employee theft is a huge problem, estimating that it accounts for more than 60% of losses recorded by small businesses.
Employee theft has evolved over the years, Hipora boss John Wanjohi tells the BBC. "Employees are like a cartel that colludes with clients and suppliers to perpetuate theft."
Employee theft does not always involve money being diverted to an employee's phone. It can sometimes take subtle forms, making it harder for business owners to detect.
For Cris Njoki, founder of IKOJN, a Kenyan ready-to-wear clothes brand, the problem lay further up the supply chain.
"I found out that one of my staff was asking our suppliers to quote higher for some of the raw materials we were getting from them," she says.
The employee allegedly colluded with a supplier to inflate prices, with the two sharing the excess money after the company paid the invoices. Njoki investigated the scheme and confronted the employee with the evidence. The employee subsequently left the company.
Since then, Njoki has tightened her firm's procurement controls.
"We have now centralised the procurement process and created a paper trail. Finance speaks to the supplier and then makes payment," she tells the BBC.
Across the continent in Accra, Ghana, employee theft came close to bringing Muftawu Nabila's business to an end.
The Joy News sports journalist says he was robbed by two different employees in the four years he has run his electronics shop. But theft by a third employee, he says, nearly forced him to close it altogether.
His first employee was let off with a warning. The second tripled monthly sales but left when her university semester resumed.
Before traveling to the United States to cover the Fifa World Cup in June 2026, Nabila hired a third attendant, leaving the business with little supervision.
"She almost collapsed my shop," he says.
While other employees had taken smaller amounts, sometimes as little as 50 cedis ($4; £3) at a time, the third attendant was operating on a larger scale, he says.
"Assuming we are making a sale of $200 (£150) a day, she could take up to $30," he says.
The theft continued for two months. When Nabila tried to restock the shop, he realised the money coming in was not enough to replenish his shelves. He began counting his stock every morning.
When he confronted the employee, she denied the allegations. But a stock count she conducted herself revealed a significant gap between inventory and sales receipts.
"I just told her: 'If you go home today, don't come back,'" he says.
His salary from his journalism job allowed him to rebuild the business.
For him, the shop is a way of creating jobs, making the theft particularly frustrating.
"We have to generate the money from the shop for me to pay you. So if I pay you, pay electricity bills, shop rent and you steal some, where am I expected to generate money?"
Theft happens in businesses around the world, but its consequences can be particularly severe for small businesses in Africa.
Many operate on tight margins, with limited access to finance, high borrowing costs and unpredictable tax environments.
Purchasing power is also lower in many African markets, limiting how much businesses can recover through sales or pass on to customers.
This is especially significant in a continent where the informal economy accounts for a large share of employment and economic activity.
For businesses without much of a financial cushion, the loss of cash, stock or equipment can threaten their ability to pay staff, restock or keep operating.
What might be a manageable loss for a larger company can push a small business to the wall.
Wanjohi says many small businesses lack proper safeguards to prevent theft.
At one struggling pharmacy branch, his team tightened controls over cash handling, stock movements, and cashier operations. Wanjohi says daily sales subsequently increased from 80,000 Kenya shillings to 200,000 after the changes.
Wanjohi says many businesses seek help from loss-control specialists only after the problem has become serious.
Detecting suspected theft, however, is only part of the challenge. Employers must also follow the law when investigating allegations and deciding whether to dismiss an employee.
Judith Guserwa, an advocate, says employers must investigate suspected theft, gather evidence and allow employees to respond before taking disciplinary action.
If employees admit to theft and choose to repay, let it be in writing: "If they don't, you terminate with a valid reason and press charges," she says.
The experience has changed how Boina approaches hiring.
She says she will now be slow to hire and quick to fire.
"I cannot teach you integrity," she concludes.

Three-time Formula One world champion Ayrton Senna is beloved in motorsport, and this year’s Sao Paulo Grand Prix marks 35 years since his first home win. Tributes to Senna regularly take place around the anniversary of his death or during the São Paulo Grand Prix. This year’s most notable ones include newly crowned World Champion Kimi Antonelli’s special helmet, as well as his visit to the grave and a meeting with the family.
Despite thirty-two years having passed since his death, Senna continues to receive more tributes than any other driver and has sold more merchandise than any inactive driver. Part of the reason is that both the sport and the company keep finding new ways to keep the memory alive.
Senna won 41 Grands Prix in a career spanning 10 years, with 80 podiums from 161 starts. His 65 poles were the highest number any driver had until Michael Schumacher broke the record in 2006. His proper self-introduction to the F1 world came at Monaco in 1984, in his rookie year, where he showcased his wet-weather skills to finish second in a generally uncompetitive Toleman-Hart. Just a month before the masterclass in Monaco, Senna had won the 1984 Nürburgring Race of Champions in equal machinery against nine Formula One world champions, as well as his future rival Alain Prost, once again in light rain. The Senna-Prost rivalry is one of the classic rivalries in motorsport history, and it turned into a friendship after Prost’s retirement in 1993, along with plans to start a racing team together, before Senna’s untimely death in 1994.
The 1994 San Marino Grand Prix was one of the darkest weekends in F1 history. Rubens Barrichello survived a 95G crash in practice, Roland Ratzenberger fatally crashed on Saturday at the Villeneuve curve, and Senna lost his life in a fatal crash on lap 7 of the race at the Tamburello curve, which had no shock-absorbing installations. Senna’s death remains Formula One’s last death on a race weekend, and it prompted major reforms in driver safety.
Senna’s funeral took place back in Sao Paulo, with the largest funeral procession in the country’s history and three days of national mourning. Senna was a national hero to Brazil because he was openly patriotic and proud, waving the Brazilian flag almost ritualistically during his victory laps at a time when Brazil was dealing with a turbulent economy and its self-esteem was at an all-time low. Senna was also a philanthropist, secretly donating millions of US dollars to poor children, and he had created the core framework for a charity aimed at Brazilian children, which became the Instituto Ayrton Senna after his death.
Senna’s name is managed by two bodies, both run by his family: Senna Brands, which handles licensing, and the Instituto Ayrton Senna, an education charity founded by his sister Viviane in November 1994. According to Máquina do Esporte, a Brazilian sports-business outlet, licensed Senna merchandise has sold more than USD 2 billion at retail over the past thirty years, and the royalties and image rights paid to the Instituto add up to more than USD 500 million. In 2024 alone, the Instituto reported USD 4.8 million in royalty income, of which USD 1.5 million came from Senna’s image (the rest came from the Instituto’s own logo). Senna Brands, meanwhile, says its revenue has grown eightfold since 2020, and it now has more than 65 partners in over 70 countries. Even Netflix’s Senna series, made with the family’s cooperation on a reported budget of USD 170 million, drew a record number of brand tie-ins for Netflix Brazil.
This posthumous income is fundamentally different from that of others like Michael Jackson or Elvis Presley, because the person under discussion did not leave behind a music catalogue or acting credits that would promise a steady income in the form of residual cheques. For this comparison, I do not count income from investments that may have been made by each estate, only the money earned posthumously solely from the person’s name, image, likeness and associated marks (number, helmet, signature, branded products, et cetera). I also used Forbes’ annual list of highest-paid deceased celebrities since 2001, adjusted to 2025 dollars. And this comparison list is surprisingly small.
The only comparable option is the American pro golfer Arnold Palmer, whose estate has earned between $235 million and $250 million since his death in 2016 from licensing his iced-tea-and-lemonade drink to AriZona. Kobe Bryant, on the other hand, has posthumously earned $35-80 million from his Nike line and licensing deals. Marilyn Monroe’s brand management company has earned $268-368 million since 2001, and the combined income of Monroe, Palmer and, surprisingly, Albert Einstein comes close to Senna’s posthumous income. I estimate Senna’s figure to be higher, because it has never been publicly audited and if we factor in the years when Senninha (“Little Senna”) toy and comic sales were at their peak.
Having grown up in India idolising cricketers and film stars, I expected to find an Indian equivalent of Senna’s legacy, but surprisingly the list comes up short among both Indian and international athletes and stars. Pelé’s brand was held by Sport 10, a US company; after his family failed to buy it back, it was sold to NR Sports, the company of Neymar’s father, for an unconfirmed $18M in 2025. Maradona’s death in 2020 led to six people claiming exclusive rights to his name, and unlicensed products never approved by his family showed up everywhere, including wine and cigars.
In India, within a year of actor Sushant Singh Rajput’s death, films based on his death had been announced. When his father approached the Delhi High Court to stop such films, the court refused, saying that a posthumous right to privacy is not permissible. Sidhu Moose Wala’s parents, on the other hand, have released about a dozen songs since he died in 2022, and very recently a hologram world tour opened in Toronto. Puneeth Rajkumar’s posthumous film James crossed 150 crore rupees at the box office. None of these come close to the figures Senna is earning, especially given the culture of tribute and the merchandise that follows.
Senna earns more than everyone else because his legacy has stayed with his family from the start, unlike Pelé’s or Maradona’s, and its foundations were laid before his death. The Senna “S” logo has existed since the early 1990s as part of his personal branding, and the Senninha comics, launched in January 1994, drew in children throughout the nineties and have since expanded into more than 370 licensed products, video games and a cartoon series. Later generations of adults were drawn in by documentaries and, more recently, by Netflix’s Drive to Survive and the Senna series, which introduced him to fans born long after his death, myself included. Special editions such as the McLaren Senna hypercar keep his name in places where a racing driver’s name rarely appears. The sport itself keeps him alive through tributes every year at Interlagos and, until this year, at Imola.
The money does have a purpose, as royalties from Senna and Senninha fund an education charity that claims it has reached more than 36 million Brazilian children. Senna Brands became a separate company in 2020, and its CEO, Senna’s niece Bianca, admitted that chasing revenue and running education programmes under one roof had started to clash, indicating that maybe a lot of these tributes are revenue generators. None of the posthumous F1 champions’ estates is run like businesses, except those of Senna and James Hunt. Michael Schumacher is the only one among Senna’s contemporaries with an organised programme, the Keep Fighting Foundation, and it is charity-led, while other contemporaries mostly sell signed memorabilia.
Senna stands unique in this regard: he is the only non-active driver to have a marketing portfolio that outdoes those of most current drivers. Interpolating from Forbes estimates and adjusting for inflation, it is also reasonable to assume that Senna earns more posthumously from his image and likeness alone than he did from his actual racing career. This does raise an ethical concern for me. Heartfelt tributes are one thing; every fan does them, every driver does them. But is a tribute that has become a whole industry built on a death watched live, pulling in at least half a billion dollars so far, really a tribute? The answer, in my opinion, sits in a very morally grey area. The main message, amid the hero worship and the tributes leading up to the Brazilian Grand Prix, is from Senna himself: “I have no idols. I admire work, dedication and competence.”
[Mithun Meenakshi Subramanian is a PhD student in computer science and an avid fan of motorsports]

Blue Origin packed a lot of news into one afternoon Thursday with the reveal of a new kick stage for the New Glenn rocket, a new rocket engine design, and the minor and widely expected delay for New Glenn’s return-to-flight mission from December until January. SpaceX vets work on water-fed propulsion. Three brothers who worked at SpaceX in the Falcon 9 era are now building satellites that run on water, a potentially harvestable resource on the Moon and found all over the Solar System, Ars reports. In late 2022, the three Carlisle brothers founded Argo Space to build infrastructure in space. Their vision was not just in-space transportation but also removing the need to use propellants from Earth to move around the heavens. Argo Space’s satellites will use water not only as a propellant, but also as a coolant and radiation shield.
How does this work? … Argo Space flew its first mission in July, but the spacecraft failed after one of its solar arrays didn’t deploy, and there wasn’t enough time to test the propulsion system. Two more missions are on Argo Space’s schedule for 2027 to demonstrate the company’s water-based thrusters. The propulsion system is basically a small rocket that uses hydrogen and oxygen as propellants. However, instead of launching with separate tanks of liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen, the satellite carries a reservoir of liquid water. In space, the vehicle uses solar power to split water into hydrogen and oxygen gases and burns them to generate thrust.
JAXA backs small satellite launcher. Japanese launcher startup Interstellar Technologies has secured the backing of the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) for its Zero rocket program, Aviation Week & Space Technology reports. The company said JAXA selected it for its Acceleration of Commercial Rocket Launch Demonstration program under the Space Strategic Fund. The government-funded program supports development and flight demonstrations of private launch companies with grants of up to $76 million per company, with the goal of fostering a growing commercial launch industry in Japan. Interstellar previously raised more than $250 million, with roughly equivalent funds from government and private capital.
Zeroing in … Interstellar is using the money to complete development of its Zero rocket, a two-stage launcher designed to carry up to 1 metric ton (2,200 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. “We have achieved critical technical milestones, including Japan’s first successful firing test of an orbital-class methane engine,” said Satoshi Nakayama, director of the board and president of Interstellar. “We have now reached the stage where we must swiftly turn these proven development results into operational commercial services.” The most recent update from Interstellar indicated a first launch of Zero in 2027.

Launch demand outpacing supply. A new report from analytics firm Quilty Space confirms that, outside of China, the world faces a significant shortage of rockets over the next five years, Ars reports. The firm estimates that between now and 2030, there will be a shortfall of about 150 launches compared to demand from satellite operators and civil space agencies. If demand from the US military is added in—and SpaceX does not extend the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy program to accommodate increased national security needs—the shortage could be doubled.
Worse than we thought … “What we wanted to get at is to understand how severe this launch crisis is and when will it be resolved,” said Caleb Henry, director of research at Quilty Space. “What we learned is that the launch crisis is more severe than we thought and that it will not go away this decade for sure, and it might not abate until sometime late in the 2030s.” Why is this happening? Quilty puts the blame on several factors: the war in Ukraine taking Russian rockets off the Western market; Amazon Leo demand; developmental delays in a new generation of rockets, from New Glenn and Vulcan to Neutron, Terran R, and Nova; and more recently, the retirement of the Falcon 9 as a rocket for commercial service.
China continues launching mega-constellation. Another 18 satellites for China’s SpaceSail Internet network launched Tuesday (Monday, US time) from a spaceport in the country’s northwestern desert. The mission marked the second launch—and first operational flight—of the Kinetica 2 rocket developed by a Chinese startup known as CAS Space. The SpaceSail constellation, also known as Qianfan, now consists of some 275 flat-panel satellites from a series of launches that began in August 2024. The network’s first phase will number 1,296 satellites.
A mini-Falcon Heavy … The Kinetica 2 is an interesting launch vehicle, with three side-by-side boosters arranged in a manner similar to SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy. But the Kinetica 2 is a much smaller rocket, with three kerosene-fueled engines on each booster instead of nine. Its lift performance to low-Earth orbit is about 12 metric tons (26,000 pounds). CAS Space plans to eventually recover and reuse the Kinetica 2 boosters.
India launches strategic navigation satellite. A Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) rocket launched on October 30 with a satellite to restore India’s regional navigation system, NDTV reports. The NVS-03 satellite is the third spacecraft in India’s second-generation navigation network. Some of the fleet’s older satellites suffered from atomic clock failures, rendering them partially or totally unusable. NVS-03 carries multiple clocks of different designs in an attempt to overcome the system’s reliability problems.
A “naughty boy” … India’s medium-lift GSLV has now launched 20 times since debuting in 2001. The rocket doesn’t fly as often as India’s smaller launcher, the PSLV, and hasn’t always performed well when it has. Six of the 20 flights ended in total or partial failures, but most of the mishaps occurred early in the rocket’s history. GSLV’s track record earned it the title “naughty boy” from Indian space officials. The most recent launch was a different story. The head of India’s space agency, V. Narayanan, declared that the GSLV’s recent flight was the “most precise launch of any rocket in the world.” We’re not sure what metric Narayanan used to make that claim, but the launch was, indeed, a success.
China reveals roadmap to lunar landing. Chinese space officials confirmed that the Asian nation plans to land its astronauts on the Moon within three years, Ars reports. At the Seventh Manned Spaceflight Conference in Beijing, officials, including Wang Xiang, chief designer for the lunar exploration program, laid out the country’s most publicly detailed plans yet for a series of missions leading up to a crewed lunar landing “before 2030.” China’s lunar landings will involve a lunar-orbit rendezvous similar to what NASA did in the 1960s and early 1970s with the Apollo program. However, lacking a rocket as powerful as the Saturn V vehicle, the crew and lunar lander will launch separately to the Moon.
These are the rockets … China’s Long March 10 rocket family will be the workhorse for the country’s initial crew missions to the Moon. The next big test will be the demonstration flight of a Long March 10A rocket, which flies with a single core booster, and China’s new Mengzhou Moon ship to low-Earth orbit in early 2027. The larger Long March 10, with three boosters connected together, will launch China’s Lanyue lunar lander on an uncrewed test flight to the Moon in 2028. The next year, a follow-up mission will involve the concurrent launch of two Long March 10s, one with an uncrewed Mengzhou spacecraft and the other with a Lanyue lander that will dock together in lunar orbit. Then, before 2030, another dual launch of Long March 10s will occur, this time with crew on the Mengzhou spacecraft, leading to the crewed landing mission.
Blue Origin’s big reveals. Blue Origin announced two significant upgrades to its New Glenn rocket on Thursday, reducing the cost of manufacturing the vehicle and expanding its capacity for payload delivery to geostationary orbit and the Moon, Ars reports. With these upgrades, the company aims to eventually position New Glenn to launch more than 1,000 times a year. One of the announcements involved a new engine, called Northstar, that will eventually replace the BE-4 engine that powers the first stage of New Glenn. The other piece of news was that Blue Origin is developing a hydrogen-oxygen third stage for the rocket to give it an extra kick for high-energy missions.
Blue’s Northstar … The Northstar engine is a simplified but more powerful version of the BE-4 engine. It has half the number of parts and 30 percent less mass, and about 65 percent can be 3D-printed, all while providing a thrust increase over the BE-4. Blue Origin believes it can manufacture the engine at 25 percent the cost of a BE-4 engine. The kick stage is somewhat of an engineering marvel in itself. The stage will use a lightweight composite fuel tank, but officials were not sure the structure could contain leak-prone hydrogen at high pressure. The company recently had a breakthrough at Launch Site One in Texas, when it completed its first composite liquid hydrogen tanking test, giving engineers confidence to move forward with the design.
New Glenn won’t return to flight this year. Blue Origin now plans to resume launches of its New Glenn rocket in January, delaying the much-anticipated flight of the vehicle after a destructive launch pad explosion in May, Bloomberg reports. The Jeff Bezos-backed company had been driving to launch New Glenn again before the end of the year in its quest to challenge SpaceX. But Blue Origin Chief Executive Officer Dave Limp told employees on Wednesday that they are now targeting a flight early in 2027.
What’s a month? … The slight delay is unsurprising, and a January launch would still put Blue Origin well head of initial fears of how long it would take to rebuild its launch pad in Florida. New Glenn has a busy launch manifest after the return-to-flight mission, including a crucial launch in the spring of Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 1 lander, an uncrewed precursor to the company’s future human-rated lander for NASA’s Artemis missions.
Artemis II tore through the atmosphere. The launch of NASA’s Artemis II mission in April caused significant disturbances in Earth’s ionosphere that could have triggered temporary, localized errors in GPS positioning, a new study has found, Space.com reports. The study by a team of researchers from National Cheng Kung University in Taiwan analyzed data from high-precision networks of fixed, ground-based GPS receivers. The researchers used the GPS measurements to reconstruct how the passage of the Artemis II mission’s Space Launch System rocket changed the concentrations of free electrons in the upper atmosphere.
Disturbing the peace … The measurements found that the ionospheric disturbances resulting from the Artemis II launch were more significant than any caused by other rocket launches to date. Curiously, they were up to 10 times more intense than those observed following the test launches of SpaceX’s Starship, which is twice as powerful as the SLS based on liftoff thrust.

The Congress party's receipts from donations above ₹20,000 plunged nearly 75% to ₹130.69 crore in 2025-26, the steepest annual fall in such contributions in a decade, an analysis of the party's filings with the Election Commission shows.
The party had received ₹517.39 crore in such contributions in 2024-25, according to its 2024-25 contribution report submitted to the commission.
A comparison with the preceding 12 financial years shows that the last steeper fall was in 2015-16, when Congress' disclosed donations dropped roughly 86% from ₹141.46 crore the previous year.
The latest decline follows two years of higher collections. Congress received ₹281.48 crore in disclosed donations in 2023-24, rising to ₹517.39 crore in 2024-25, the year Lok Sabha elections were held.
BJP received ₹6,074.02 crore in donations exceeding ₹20,000 in 2024-25, nearly 12 times Congress's collection. BJP's corresponding figure for 2025-26 is not available as the party's contribution report has not been made public by the ECI yet.
The BJP collected more than the Congress in each of the 12 financial years examined.
Funding through Prudent Electoral Trust accounted for a substantial part of Congress' latest decline. The trust's contribution fell from ₹216.34 crore in 2024-25 to ₹25 crore in 2025-26, a drop of about 88%.
Prudent was the only electoral trust listed in the party's latest contribution report.
Also Read | The murky world of political party finance
Among other large contributors were Star Cement, which gave ₹5 crore, Sajjan Bhajanka, who contributed ₹4 crore, and Prem Kumar Bhajanka, who donated ₹2 crore.
The Congress' 2025-26 fund collection, though sharply lower than the previous year, was not its lowest over the period examined.
Its disclosed donations were lower in several earlier years, including ₹74.52 crore in 2020-21, ₹95.46 crore in 2021-22 and ₹79.92 crore in 2022-23.
These figures exclude electoral bonds, which were reported separately when the scheme operated. Including bond receipts in the earlier years, the Congress' latest collection in 2025-26 was its lowest since 2020-21.
The contribution report does not show the party's total income, which also includes smaller donations, membership fees, coupon collections and interest.
The Congress' audited account for 2025-26, which has not been uploaded yet, is needed to establish its overall financial position. In 2024-25, coupon collections alone brought the party ₹350.12 crore.

Macau jails pro-democracy campaigner in city's first national security case
- Published
Macau has sentenced an ex-lawmaker and pro-democracy campaigner to 12 years and six months' jail in the city's first national security case.
Following a closed-door trial, Au Kam San, 69, was convicted on Friday of "subversion against the political power of the state", among other offences.
His wife Virginia Cheang condemned the ruling, calling the case a "groundless persecution designed to humiliate Au".
Macau was handed back to China in 1999, ending over 400 years of Portuguese administration. Its national security law came into effect in 2009, criminalising acts of treason, secession, and subversion against the Chinese Communist Party.
The law was revised in 2023, broadening its scope to include non-violent acts of secession, and again this year, to allow for trials to be held behind closed doors.
Prosecutors had accused Au of assisting and collaborating with "external hostile organisations" by collecting, preparing and disseminating information that was "manifestly filled with political claims of a subversive nature against the state".
These took place "over a long period of time", the prosecutors claim.
Au was arrested in July 2025 and later charged with three counts of subverting the state's power, three counts of endangering national security by establishing contact with foreign organisations, and one count of breach of confidentiality.
He was found guilty of four of the seven charges following a three-day trial which ended in September. A judge had ordered that the trial be held behind closed doors "to ensure that no prejudice is caused to the interests of national security".
Macau's authorities never publicly disclosed the details of the case. Au's family had earlier told the media Au was not allowed to seek his own legal representation and had instead been assigned a lawyer by the court.
Au's wife Cheang said she hoped authorities would grant her and her family permission to regularly write to and visit Au in prison.
"I dare not hope for more as I believe that will only lead to greater disappointment," she said in an open letter on Friday.
Au, who was formerly a primary school teacher, was elected to the Legislative Assembly in September 2001. For 20 years, he served as one of only a handful of pro-democracy lawmakers in the legislature, largely made up of pro-Beijing loyalists.
Au had co-organised annual vigils in Macau to commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing.
These vigils were previously tolerated in places like Macau and Hong Kong, but have effectively been banned in both cities since China imposed a sweeping national security law on Hong Kong in 2020.
Au's jailing comes a day after Hong Kong sentenced Joshua Wong, the face of its now-quashed democracy movement, to 10 years in jail. Wong, 30, whose activism started when he was just a teen, has been in custody for the last six years.

A 22-second-long clip shared by X user Vijay Thottathil (@vijaythottathil) showing a massive crowd in a large open area went viral on November 1.
Thottathil posted the video with the caption, “Early in the morning itself Ramlila Maidan is packed #ChaloDilli,” thus claiming that the crowd had gathered for the INDIA’s bloc’s rally on November 1 to protest against electoral irregularities and demand the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Early morning itself Ramlila Maidan is packed ✊🏼 🔥
#ChaloDilli https://t.co/oM5kSpCNoH
— Vijay Thottathil (@vijaythottathil) November 1, 2026
The post by Thottathil, who was till recently a social media manager of Kerala Congress, amassed over 243,000 views and was reshared over 1,400 times. (Archive)
Congress leader Harish Rawat, too, shared the video on Instagram, claiming that the visuals were from the November 1 protest rally.
View this post on Instagram
Various other X handles posted the same 22-second clip, claiming that they are visuals from the ‘Chalo Dilli’ rally held on November 1. A few of them are shown in the gallery below:
Fact Check
In the comments of the video posted by Vijay, X users were quick to point out that the video was not from the November 1 ‘Chalo Dilli’ protest, and instead was from another rally held at an earlier date.
To determine the veracity of these claims, we ran a reverse image search on a few of the keyframes, which led us to a video uploaded by Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on December 14, 2025.
This video, captioned “‘वोट चोरी’ के खिलाफ जनसैलाब 🔥🔥” (A public outpouring against “vote theft”), was uploaded during the “Vote Choro, Gaddi Chhodo” protests of December 2025.
View this post on Instagram
The comparison of certain keyframes of both videos reveals stark similarities, including the backdrop, the size of the crowd, a flag being waved in the front, and even a blue tent visible in the clip. See below:
A deeper dive revealed that Congress leader Harish Rawat had himself shared the video during the “Vote Choro, Gaddi Chhodo” protests on December 14, 2025. He has now shared the same clip again as scenes from the INDIA bloc rally of November 1, 2026.
To sum up, the viral clip with the massive crowds gathered at Ramlila Maidan shared by Thottathil is an old clip from the “Vote Choro, Gaddi Chhoro” protests that was organised by Congress in December last year. Several users have falsely presented it as visuals from the recent ‘Chalo Dilli’ march on November 1.
