In March this year, on the sidelines of Razorpay’s annual flagship event FTX, CEO Harshil Mathur told Inc42 that what mattered most to him was how Razorpay stands in the public markets, and not the fact that it went public. Eight months on, that test now has a rough date as the company sets off on the last leg of its IPO journey. Razorpay has received SEBI’s approval for its proposed IPO. The fintech major is looking to raise ₹5,000-6,000 Cr through a mix of fresh issue and offer for sale at a valuation of around $5 Bn, with a listing likely between January and March 2027. Axis Capital, Kotak Mahindra Capital, JP Morgan and Citi are the reported bankers. The headline number when it comes to Razorpay’s listing, or for that matter any listing within fintech circles, has been that of valuation.Sources suggest that Razorpay may be looking to list at a $5 Bn valuation, a markdown from the $7.5 Bn valuation that the company commanded in December 2021. But back in 2021, fintech valuations were sky high amidst a pandemic led funding boom that witnessed sharp corrections years down the line. Another fintech major, PhonePe, paused its mega listing in March 2026, with reports suggesting that volatile geopolitical tensions and valuation concerns led the payments company to put its IPO plans on hold. It has since revived them on the back of MDR. Sources told Inc42 in September that PhonePe is targeting a listing between February and March 2027 at a valuation of about $10 Bn. But Razorpay has a different story to tell the public investors as it seeks ₹5,000-6,000 Cr from them. The first part of that story is profit. “When you take out that one-time cost of the reverse flip, Razorpay was profitable — that profitability streak is maintained throughout. We hope the financials will continue to improve from here as a company that’s continuously growing,” Mathur had told Inc42 earlier. In FY25, Razorpay slipped into the red, weighed down by ₹1,209 Cr in ESOP expenses and one-time restructuring and tax costs from moving its domicile to India. It did not disclose the size of the loss. The reverse flip tax bill has been reported at about ₹1,245 Cr, or about $150 Mn. A year earlier, in FY24, its payments business had reported a ₹34 Cr profit against a total revenue of ₹2,068 Cr or a net margin of 1.6%. The company claims to lead India’s digital payments processing market in terms of total payments volume and is expanding across Southeast Asia and other geographies, but monetising this scale has always been a problem when it comes to payments companies. The 0.4% merchant discount rate (MDR) on large UPI payments, due after Diwali, would be the first fee on a bulk of these payments, and it would arrive just ahead of the listing window. How much reaches Razorpay’s bottom line depends on two things: how it negotiates with the banks that receive the fee and the large merchants that pay the MDR. Sources we spoke to suggest that much of the revenue bump that companies like Razorpay will get out of MDR would not boost their topline significantly, but could feed profits strongly because it is a fee on rails that companies have already built. For Razorpay, it’s a boost to its search for the right valuation just in time. MDR on UPI would likely narrow the gap between the company’s sought valuation and its bottomline. It also gives Razorpay a growth story to take to public investors as it heads into the IPO. A Profitable Core Unlike many of its contemporaries eyeing a listing at the scale of Razorpay, the fintech has no major debt overhang and nearly half of the IPO proceeds are expected to be allocated for OFS. Company sources told us that the core online payments business is EBITDA profitable and generating strong cash flows, which is why the company is making bold investments in allied businesses and AI. Sources pointed towards capital allocations “between mature, cash-generating units and high-potential growth bets”, with AI-first products, financial infrastructure and new verticals taking the investment. The company has also given a timeline on profitability. “By the end of FY26, our India business should be solidly profitable. At the consolidated level, we’ll reach profitability about two to three quarters after that,” the company’s CFO, Arpit Chug, told Inc42 in October 2025. But FY26 has since closed, and Razorpay is yet to make those numbers public. The biggest factor in Razorpay’s IPO will be the profitability and the margins earned by its core business. In lieu of actual profit figures, Razorpay’s pitch to public investors rests on scale. It described itself in 2024 as India’s market leader in digital payments processing, with a majority share, and said in 2025 that it served 105 of India’s 119 unicorns. It claims to be processing a total payments volume (TPV) of over $180 Bn (as of 2024 end). When compared against its primary competitors Cashfree and PayU, Razorpay stands out for its scale and its focus on small and medium businesses. Razorpay claims to lead on overall volumes, enterprise accounts drive the bulk of volumes at Cashfree, Inc42 reported earlier. Razorpay, on the other hand, claims that 80% of its client base comprises SMBs and startups. Among the three, PayU India leads in terms of the topline. Its payments business alone earned $523 Mn (about ₹4,420 Cr) in FY25. It pulled ahead of Razorpay which reported ₹3,783 Cr in FY25, while Cashfree stood at ₹640.1 Cr. PayU owner Prosus claims the company has a 25% share of the Indian online payments, while processing $90 Bn in TPV in FY26. In a bid to race past the competition, Razorpay has been eyeing overseas markets by strategic tie-ups and acquisitions. Mathur earlier said that international was its fastest-growing business, with payments growing about 40% and newer segments at 70-90%. Outside India, Razorpay currently operates in Malaysia and Singapore and is eyeing expansion into the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam as its next Southeast Asian targets. The company, according to sources, is expanding majorly within Southeast Asia and expects the revenue from these countries to contribute 15% of its overall topline by 2030. Razorpay entered Malaysia by buying a majority stake in Curlec in 2022, launched its gateway there in 2023 and entered Singapore in March 2025. Closer to home, the biggest expected lever is UPI and the introduction of MDR soon after the festive season. About half of the payments flowing through Razorpay are on UPI, and that rail is about to start earning the fee that can feed the company’s bottomline. The Two Negotiations Behind Razorpay’s MDR Upside The first critical negotiation for Razorpay will be with banks. Payment aggregators such as Razorpay get no fixed share under NPCI’s stated framework, because they are not direct members of the UPI network and are part of it only through sponsor banks. So the aggregator’s cut has to come out of the acquirer bank’s share in the MDR, under a private contract between the two. Reports suggest that the talks have centred on aggregators keeping 50-80% of the acquiring bank’s MDR share. But there is also a flip side to it. Payment aggregators and gateways already earn technology, checkout and reconciliation fees from merchants, and with MDR coming into effect, the merchants can move to the aggregators and gateways that offer more reasonable take rates. Pine Labs CEO Amrish Rau has already flagged that talks with merchants have yielded this view among the primary customer base for payments aggregators. “From a commercial standpoint, I absolutely do believe when it comes to the largest of large merchants that we have with us, there will be a commercial conversation to be had, for sure,” Rau said in October 2026 after the Q2 results. Notwithstanding the restructured commercial agreements that the payment aggregators and gateways will sign with banks and merchants for the MDR regime, sources say that the fee could support higher valuations for IPO-bound companies such as Razorpay and PhonePe. “The headline MDR pool is not the same as revenue accruing to an individual participant. It depends on eligible transaction volumes, merchant mix and the prescribed distribution across the ecosystem,” PhiCommerce CEO Rajesh Londhe told Inc42. Listed peer Paytm has already put a number on what MDR will bring to the table. With its Q2 results, Paytm said it expects an uplift of about 2.5 bps in its overall payments processing margin, and that the actual outcome may stabilise in 2-3 quarters after implementation. As per sources, MDR could bring Razorpay ₹192-461 Cr of revenue a year once implemented, which would be about 5-12% of its FY25 revenue and 15-36% of its FY25 gross profit. As a result, analysts believe that Razorpay could see a valuation bump of $300 Mn-$1 Bn from the existing ask. That’s what the MDR effect can actually unlock, though much would also depend on the commercial agreements with banks and merchant talks. Razorpay’s technology prowess and merchant scale could be a huge lever in any talks with banks and merchants. However, what matters more than the scale will be the value of transactions and the scale of the clients themselves, which would directly boost revenue and improve margins. Nearly 80% of Razorpay’s customers are small businesses, digital-first brands and startups, and it has not disclosed how many of their tickets cross the ₹2,000 threshold required for the MDR boost. There is also no certainty as yet on the timeline by which fintech companies can expect the MDR outcome to start showing up on their P&L. Analysts tracking the industry, however, say that the companies would need a few quarters of data to give investors a credible outlook. For Paytm, that could be 2-3 quarters, and with Razorpay coming to the IPO table, investors would want to hear a number for the company. Will a listing between January and March of 2027 be enough to give investors a clear answer? The AI Story Needs Numbers Then there’s the AI story, which we had written about extensively earlier this year. According to Mathur, Razorpay is building a long-term business bet on AI and this is not related to the IPO and its outcome. The fintech sector has been one of the earliest adopters and partners of frontier AI models such as ChatGPT and Claude, experimenting with AI use cases for the millions of merchants on its platform. Razorpay’s Agent Studio, built on Anthropic’s Claude, offers small businesses task-specific agents for abandoned carts, disputes, subscription recovery and cash flow forecasting. Mathur wants Razorpay to be known as “an operating system for businesses” which is run on AI. That story gives investors a reason to look past the thin margins in the payments business, but the AI theme is not strong enough in the case of Razorpay yet. It has to make a bigger splash in terms of the outcomes it is seeing. . Rivals Cashfree, PayU and Pine Labs are also accelerating their AI led partnerships to offer new products to their existing merchant base. All these AI offerings have been particularly concentrated towards agentic workflows and ecommerce enablement. However, there is still little public evidence of what these agents earn. Mathur earlier told us that it will take a few years to assess the real term monetisation value that these AI capabilities can unlock for any fintech. Hence for an IPO-bound Razorpay, its core payments business is the only true and measurable metric for the public investors. The future bets may fructify but for now, they are unlikely to be a factor for investors. Even at a reported $5 Bn valuation, Razorpay goes to market with some real strengths such as 65% YoY revenue growth in FY25, about $180 Bn in annualised TPV, and a profitable core. While it is banking on the MDR regime to solve a lot of headaches, investors will want to see a lot more to justify the valuation ask. Whether the price holds depends on disclosures still to come, including its FY26 and subsequent financial performance and the results of its MDR negotiations with banks. And only then will Razorpay find out how much of its story the public market is willing to pay for.

I live in the Hamptons year-round, and my children are growing up in a place often associated with wealth, status, and luxury. They see beautiful homes, boats in the harbor, expensive cars, and designer shops lining the streets.
My children have many luxuries surrounding them, but our family is not rich.
As a parent, I'm very conscious of teaching them that happiness does not come from expensive things, exclusive places, or what other families may have. I want them to know how to live with comparison without feeling ashamed of what they do not have or entitled to have.
Everything is expensive
Every day prices can make that lesson difficult. At Candy Kitchen in Bridgehampton, two eggs currently cost $10.95, and pancakes are $12.95. Elsewhere, a smoothie can cost more than $30 (including my favorite spot for that Mint Chip Smoothie in Sag Harbor). Even taking two children for ice cream adds up quickly once everyone chooses a cone and toppings (on average, it costs $28 for two frozen yogurt sundaes).
I don't want my children to think these prices are standard, or that every trip outside the house should include an ice cream or a visit to the card shop. I will tell them in advance, "If you want candy or cards today, bring money from your piggy bank." This gives them a choice while helping them understand that money is finite.
At the same time, I don't believe that raising grounded children means never going out or enjoying what is around us. Alongside the designer stores are nostalgic places such as Kites of the Harbor and The Wharf Shop, where casually browsing the toy collection, sterling silver jewelry, and handmade home decor can feel like a part of childhood. It is important to experience these places and find a balance.
We talk openly about finances
We openly discuss savings and finances to a degree they can understand. I don't burden them with adult worries, but I don't pretend that everything is affordable. When they spend their own money, they look at prices differently. They weigh how much they want something and whether it is worth giving up something else later.
I try to show them that some of the best experiences here cost nothing. The library offers an abundance of free in-person and online classes, activities, tutoring resources, reading programs, children's fairs, and museum passes. Their camp has family fun days, and their school holds heritage fairs. We go to the beach, spend time in nature, and watch the sailboats in the harbor, identifying the different types. I take them paddleboarding and crabbing, and bring them back to my roots growing up in North Haven.
These activities help them see the Hamptons as a community and a home, not a backdrop for luxury. Interestingly, the area has a tremendous range of wealth. People from many different demographics live and work here, and my children's friends come from families with varied financial circumstances. The wealthiest residents do not always flash designer brands. In those moments, we are reminded that possessions do not necessarily tell you who a person is.
I'm teaching them skills
Resourcefulness is one of the most important things I can teach my children. We make homemade scrubs and find projects to do with what we already have. They learn practical skills: styling hair, sewing, building things, cooking, and fixing simple household problems. I have friends who are private chefs, and cooking with them shows my children that making something well is both creative and useful.
I also teach them to be organized and self-reliant at home, to know where their belongings are and take care of them, because things can pile up quickly.
I encourage my children to think about buying things that can generate income instead of things that will remain idle. I want them to ask: Can I make something with this? Can I use it to learn a skill? Could this help me earn money one day?
Both of my children ice-skate and play tennis. I explain that those are not just hobbies. Skills can eventually become work. Someone who understands tennis may learn to string racquets or work at a tennis shop. A strong skater may become an instructor or an ice-skating attendant. They do not need to choose a career at this young age. However, I do want them to recognize that ability, reliability, and hard work do create options.
Most of all, I want my children to leave home believing they can take care of themselves. I want them to be practical, to work hard, and to have a skill set that sets them apart. I want them to appreciate what they receive without expecting anything.
The Hamptons will always give them opportunities to compare. My job as a parent is to give them something stronger to measure their lives by: what they can make, what they can contribute, how they treat people, and how much joy they can find in what is already around them.

Meghan's father Thomas Markle under house arrest after child sex abuse material charge
- Published
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida after being charged over possession of child sex abuse material.
Markle, 82, was arrested in Florida on a federal complaint alleging he held images that show child sex abuse, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) said.
He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, the DoJ said. Markle has previously denied allegations of possessing images of child sex abuse, calling them "sick lies".
In a 30-minute court hearing on Friday he was also ordered to submit to electronic monitoring, but no plea was taken.
At the court hearing, the charges were laid out against him by federal prosecutor Courtenay Derry, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
He was brought into court in a wheelchair, escorted by two US Marshals. Markle was wearing black trousers and a black t-shirt.
No plea was taken during the hearing, and an arraignment date in California will be determined in due course, a joint statement from the DoJ and the US Attorney's Office Central California said.
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have not commented on Markle's arrest.
Markle was arrested after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in LA registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year, the DoJ said.
Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.
FBI director Kash Patel said authorities "moved quickly" when arresting Markle.
"Mr Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions," Patel said.
He added that the FBI would "use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide".
Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.
In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.
Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.
Markle Sr moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was then reportedly living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having his leg amputated.
In October, London's Metropolitan Police confirmed that it had received a letter in 2019 making a "number of claims" relating to Markle Sr.
The Met said information contained in the letter, which related to allegations against Meghan's father outside the UK, was passed on to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, but it did not share it with other law enforcement agencies.
The force has since voluntarily referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IPOC) over its handling of the letter.
In a statement released in October after the allegations against Markle Sr emerged, the Duchess of Sussex said: "I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year.

As the air quality of the national capital deteriorated to the 'very poor' category for the first time this winter season, the Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and adjoining areas (CAQM) on Monday (November 2, 2026) announced Stage 2 of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP).
The air quality is likely to be in the 'very poor' category for the next three days, as per the Central government’s Air Quality Early Warning System for Delhi. The last time Delhi’s air quality was in the 'very poor' category was on February 11 this year.
Stage 2 of the GRAP mandates NCR State governments to enhance vehicle parking fees to discourage use of private vehicles. The GNCTD (Delhi government) and NCR State governments also have to “stagger timings for public offices and municipal bodies in the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the districts of Gurugram, Faridabad, Ghaziabad and Gautam Buddha Nagar”.
Considering the restrictions on vehicles, the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) has decided to run additional trips on weekdays. While the DMRC was running 20 trips since October 28, when the GRAP-1 was enforced, 20 more trips will be run now. “This is to encourage people to use public transport rather than their private vehicles and help mitigate pollution,” said a senior Metro official.
Other directions to State governments include implementing existing measures to control air pollution, such as mechanical sweeping of roads or sprinkling water on roads, among others
The GRAP is a set of short-term emergency measures to reduce air pollution and is divided into four stages. The CAQM announces the different stages depending on the level of pollution recorded or forecast for the near future.
The 24-hour average Air Quality Index (AQI) of Delhi stood at 324 (very poor) at 4 p.m. on November 2, 2026, up from 261 (poor) a day earlier, as per the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)’s daily bulletin, which is treated as the day’s AQI. A higher AQI indicates worsening air quality.
‘Very poor' levels of air pollution could lead to “respiratory illness on prolonged exposure”, as per the CPCB. On February 11, 2026, the AQI was 305 (very poor).
Every winter, air pollution spikes in the Delhi-NCR and many parts of the larger Indo-Gangetic Plains, mainly due to meteorological factors such as lower wind speeds and a drop in temperature. Pollution from stubble burning during October and November and bursting of firecrackers during the festive season also add to existing pollution from vehicles and dust, worsening the air quality.

How do spam callers get your number in the first place?
Spam calls getting you down? Here's how robocallers got your number in the first place.
Whether it's spam calls or text messages, the modern world is dominated by flooded inboxes and phone scams. If you find yourself inundated with notifications about packages you didn't order or services you've never used, you might wonder how all these ads and cons made their way to you. Luckily, you can stem the flow of slop.
There are many ways to stop spam calls on Android, iPhone and other devices, but an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. If you want to get ahead of spammers, you need to know how you're getting spammed in the first place.
Unfortunately, many of these causes are out of your hands, such as random robocaller dials and data breaches. On the bright side, there are some steps you can take to keep your number from spreading further.
How spam callers get your number
A good portion of spam calls and texts come from sheer bad luck. Sometimes you need to use your number for an important account, only for that site or service to be hit by a data breach. Either that, or an illegal robocaller has randomly dialed your number or stolen it from a public record, like a court directory, property deeds or corporate filings.
Even if you're registered with the FTC's Do Not Call Registry, which restricts most telemarketing calls, you can still be spammed by charities, political parties, debt collectors, telephone surveyors and other exempt callers.
The bulk of numbers available to spammers and scammers, however, have been bought from data brokers. In many cases, this data is legally resold to third parties after you sign up for accounts, loyalty programs, contests, sweepstakes and more. You probably agreed to these sales, either as a mandatory condition of using a service or while rushing through web pages with deliberately confusing checkboxes.
You may also have fallen victim to a phishing scam, handing over your information by filling out a fake login page, making an account on a sketchy website, applying to a fake job listing or signing up for a bogus app or service. If you've signed up for anything with your phone number, there's a strong likelihood your information has been sold.
How to keep your phone number safe
Your devices do have a level of protection against phishing, from browser warnings about risk sites to Android's enhanced protection against bank scams. But there are also ways to take precautions with your number.
Always keep an eye on the sites you use and avoid ones that are stuffed with ads or that you don't recognize. You can be extra safe by searching for reviews and scam reports about a site before you sign up. In general, though, hide your number on any public profiles and be mindful of how many accounts you create and which boxes you check.
If you're under attack from robocallers who just won't stop, signing up for the FTC's registry is one way to limit your risk. If you want to find out how your number may have gotten out, check whether an associated account was part of a data breach by searching your email address on a site like Have I Been Pwned. You can also google your own phone number in quotes to see if it pops up anywhere.

New Delhi: The government is considering amending a 1953 law governing its coir industry, aiming to update rules for a sector that employs more than 750,000 people and exported a record ₹6,614 crore of products last fiscal year, according to two people aware of the matter. The Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSME) ministry wants to broaden the Act’s definitions to cover a wider range of products and reduce the delays and paperwork firms face, the people said. Shipments rose 52% to ₹6,614 crore in FY26 from ₹4,343 crore in FY25. “The work on some amendments to the Coir Industry Act has begun. Some discussions have happened on this, and the broad direction for this exercise is to modernise and rationalise,” said one of the people, a government official who requested anonymity. The industry is concentrated in southern India, and about 80% of workers in fibre extraction and spinning are women. The amendment exercise would also re-examine the existing definitions under the Act, with the aim of making these terms fulfil modern requirements, the first person said. Queries emailed to the MSME ministry and the Coir Board on 5 November remained unanswered. Indian coir products such as mats, pots, coir fibre, and handicrafts have found key export markets such as the US, China, the Netherlands, and Spain, among others, according to the MSME ministry’s FY26 annual report, as these products are commonly biodegradable. Experts say that coir, a natural fibre, can be an alternative to synthetic fibres. “It has the potential to fetch a high premium in the replacement of products using synthetic fibres, such as mattresses, for instance. Similarly, coir ropes have an edge over synthetic ropes, as they hold their knots more reliably than plastic knots, which easily come loose,” said Gurudas Nulkar, professor and director of the Centre for Sustainable Development at the Gokhale Institute of Politics and Economics. Nulkar said that besides coir, coconut shells also make good industrial substitutes. “Coconut shells are used to activate carbon, a crucial part of household water filtration systems. Another upcoming use of this is that it can be converted to biochar, which is eligible for carbon credits,” he said. While exports are rising, it is important to understand that profits from exports mostly benefit traders, but putting more money in the hands of coir farmers and workers is essential to building a local market for coir products, Nulkar added. Lobby groups say the sector would gain from covering newer coir products and easing compliance. Vinod Kumar, president of the India SME Forum, which represents nearly 100,000 MSMEs, said the law should “explicitly recognise the full range of commercially relevant coconut husk products, including coir pith, cocopeat, husk chips, growing media, geo-textiles and composites”. Reform must go beyond adding names, he said, by “removing ambiguity around newer materials and applications and ensuring that eligible enterprises can access development support”. “Compliance should become simpler through a single digital interface, and fewer repetitive submission,” he said. Modernisation also needs shared facilities for processing, drying, grading, testing and water treatment, plus husk storage, affordable working capital and stronger buyer links, he added. Export disruptions hurt artisans too, Kumar said, citing a March 2026 pile-up of export-ready products worth ₹200 crore. “Even an artisan who never exports directly can be affected when an overseas buyer postpones an order,” he said. After 28 years, the gamer’s game is getting a big remake.
A fully redone version of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time arrives Thursday exclusively on the Switch 2. Nintendo has been releasing trailers and screenshots in the run-up to the launch, and the imagery, while whetting appetites, has also left fans with an overwhelming question: Why does Link look like that?
Specifically, child Link. Ocarina of Time allows players to time-hop and explore levels as child and adult versions of the game’s main protagonist. Gameplay starts as child Link in the Kokiri Forest, which looks more lush and verdant than ever in the remake. But aesthetic upgrades have also been applied to child Link, resulting in a curled-eyelash, laminated-eyebrow, douyin-lipstick yassified elf boy.
Fans have been quick to compare the design to the human-vampire hybrid Renesmee from Twilight and the Gerber Baby. “He looks so microwaveable,” one Reddit user wrote.
The changes feel all the more stark when juxtaposed with the remake’s background nonplayer characters, who remain noticeably simpler and more reminiscent of the original game’s character designs.
The original Ocarina was limited to minimal polygonal shapes and textures because of the small storage capacity in N64 cartridges, and these technical limitations produced what became a recognizable and beloved visual style. Thanks to the Switch 2’s larger storage capacity and higher memory bus speed, designers have been able to add details to Link and the other main characters that wouldn’t have been possible in the original.
Beyond better technology, though, people have different expectations of video games from major publishers. Interconnecting level designs, intricate storylines, and highly realistic environment and character model details are table stakes for contemporary AAA games. Video games are also more mainstream, and once-regional media like anime and manga have become global phenomena over the past three decades, influencing taste in the larger culture.
Clayton Lundgren, a former quality assurance tester for the game developer Naughty Dog who currently streams Ocarina of Time along with other games on Twitch, sees nothing accidental about Link’s new look. “For a decision as important as the key art for the main character, this is the kind of thing that is gonna go past a lot of quality inspection higher up than the person that drew it,” he says. “This is 20-plus years of merchandising that you’re committing to.”
Links to the Past
Since The Legend of Zelda launched the franchise in 1986, Link has existed in many forms. Though his long hat, pointy ears, blond hair, green tunic, and Master Sword are staples of his design, none of these characteristics have been stable across his 40 years. He’s had pink hair, his tunic has been blue and red. He’s even been a tree.
The remake takes the evolution a step further, though. Lundgren, who has at least 1,000 hours in Ocarina across speed runs, challenge runs, and community competitions, immediately realized that this week’s release is a ground-up remake when he watched the game’s new trailer. For many fans, the rich detail of the underbrush and sunbeams in Kokiri Forest visible in the teaser video were proof this isn’t the same Ocarina. But Lundgren saw something else: The undulation in the ground was different.
Unlike the 2011 Zelda remake for the 3DS, which uses the same underlying geometries as the original, the 2026 remake is a complete overhaul, from the superficial textures to the bones underneath. And if everything is different, how is this the same Link we’ve played and loved before?
Luke Cuddy, a philosophy professor at Southwestern College who has edited books about The Legend of Zelda, offers the “Ship of Theseus” thought experiment as a way to think through the conundrum. The famous philosophical riddle asks whether the true ship is the one Theseus is currently sailing or the original constituent parts that have been replaced over time. If one thinks the true ship is the one Theseus is currently sailing, they believe there is something beyond the physical body that makes something what it is.
“There are only a few minimal features that are continuous over time with Link,” says Cuddy. Aside from a few visual and narrative touchstones—and the occasional “Hyah!” or “Hyup!” voice line—there isn’t much else that Link is. “For me, that allows for a lot of malleability.”
That malleability is cushioned by other forms of continuity. Beyond aesthetic similarities and a shared title across Zelda games, contemporary games that were influenced by the original Ocarina are now shaping the remake in turn, and norms of play set by speedrunners and challenge runners of the original continue to shape engagement across gaming communities.
But another force is fueling the current scrutiny and anxiety over the remake, one that haunts every contemporary artistic endeavor: Was generative AI involved?
Artificial intelligence has long been part of video games designed to respond in real time to players’ actions. But these days, when the topic of AI use in video games comes up, it’s usually in reference to AI tools being used to make the visual parts of a game, the storyboards, the written scripts, or the spoken dialog.
The backlash to these tools is growing, rooted in concerns about the environment, artists’ intellectual property, and aesthetic taste. Players are increasingly worried that they’re engaging with media that betrays their values, and for a game like Ocarina, the possible juxtaposition of the original’s groundbreaking design with derivative and cannibalistic tools feels like a long way to fall.
Cuddy compares the “super-enhanced version of Link” in the remake to the output of an AI filter, and other fans are questioning why the designs look like they were run through DLSS 5, an animation upscaling tool that uses generative AI. Nintendo has confirmed its use of AMD FSR, a competing upscaling tool, though when WIRED asked if generative AI tools were also used in the character design process for the new game, the company declined to comment.
When one of the most beloved entries in a beloved game franchise gets a new coat of paint, fans of the game are of course going to scrutinize every aspect of the remake’s design. But Lundgren predicts that, based on Zelda fans’ history of embracing Link’s many incarnations in the past, “in two years we’ll think it looks great.”

The 2026 West Bengal elections were legally invalid, according to former Chief Election Commissioner SY Quraishi. At the same time, he said some parts of the election might have been valid. Quraishi called for checks where Muslim voters could have been removed in large numbers. He said fresh polling should take place where necessary. “Was the Bengal election legally valid or not? I believe it wasn’t,” Quraishi said. “Maybe the whole election isn’t ruined, but at least (the Supreme Court should) point out where there is suspicion,” he added. Quraishi raised concerns about the elections in Kolkata on November 5. He delivered the keynote address at the Hashim Abdul Halim Memorial Lecture. He questioned how officials had revised the voter lists before the elections. He said the matter was before the Supreme Court and hoped for the right decision. Quraishi criticised the special intensive revision (SIR) of the voter lists. He alleged that officials had used it to indirectly check citizenship. According to him, the process lacked transparency and had raised several questions. He expected the court's judgment to clarify what officials did right and what went wrong. He said voters should be able to exercise their rights without having to plead. He recalled that voter cards were earlier delivered to people's homes. He said voters did not have to negotiate to get their names on the lists. “Many people asked me: is the SIR NRC through the back door? My answer is that SIR is NRC through the front door. In fact, it is the father of NRC,” The Wire quoted him as saying. “There, they followed legal procedures for years to reach a conclusion. Here, in one stroke, within 15 days, across Bengal, I read that in 49 constituencies, 70-80% of Muslims were cut, calling them all Bangladeshis,” he added. Quraishi also spoke about how the Election Commission of India should take decisions. He said the rules would first call for all three commissioners to agree. If they cannot agree, the majority should decide. He said the Chief Election Commissioner alone cannot have the final say. “If the CEC is left alone, he is not the Election Commission. Teens worldwide aren't getting enough exercise — especially girls
The World Health Organization recommends adolescents spend at least one hour a day exercising enough to basically break a sweat — a brisk walk or a more intense pick-up soccer game. Lot's of research suggests this level of activity is crucial for supporting growing bodies and minds.
But new global data suggests only a small minority of kids and teens get that much. In fact, one in four report not hitting 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous exercise any day of the week, according to a new study in The Lancet Global Health. Girls, as well as adolescents from middle- and lower-income countries reported even lower levels of exercise.
"The findings are disappointing, because one of the major results is that the trend over the last 15 years is flat," says Fiona Bull, head of the physical activity unit at the World Health Organization, who co-authored the study. "These data are a call for us to relook at what we're doing. Business as usual will not change these trends."
Changing habits in those teen years could have a lifelong impact, says Solveig Cunningham, a global health researcher at Emory University. "As an adolescent, if your baseline is zero days of physical activity, that's going to be your baseline as you go into adulthood."
What 3 million teens revealed
So how do researchers know whether adolescents are — or aren't — working up a sweat? It's tricky. Researchers would love to be able to strap smartwatches to kids to get detailed data, but that would be costly. The next best strategy is to ask a basic question — how many days during the past week were you active for at least 60 minutes?
The report draws on data from surveys posting some version of this question to over 3 million adolescents from 140 countries over the past 15 years. Only about 14% of kids worldwide reported getting an hour a day of exercise. Globally, the average adolescent reported less than 3 such days a week, the study found.
Kids from low- and middle-income countries tended to be less active than their counterparts from wealthier Western countries, the study found. There's no one explanation for this pattern, but a few likely causes stand out.
"Physical activity is an issue of opportunity," says Andrea Ramirez Varela, an epidemiologist at the University of Texas Health Science Center in Houston. In many lower income countries, she says that the environment — where they live, go to school and play — often restricts opportunities to be active. The study didn't break down the urban and rural divide, but some research suggests rural adolescents in lower-income countries move more, she says, often out of necessity. In increasingly populated urban areas, activity is lower.
Many cities aren't designed to be walkable, says Varela. In Latin America, where she does most of her research, "many parents think it's unsafe to just let your kids walk alone to and from places," she says — much less go out and play independently. In some urban centers, air pollution can make being active outdoors unhealthy too.
Screens may play a role as well. After school, "kids and adolescents, when they arrive home, they start watching TV, they are in front of a screen," says Valrela. "Because this digital world is so attractive, they are going to be sedentary the rest of the day."
Cultural barriers
The report also revealed a stubborn gender gap.
Girls were less active than boys in virtually all countries. Nearly 30% don't exercise at all during the week compared to 22% of boys. Only 11% of girls were active daily compared to 17% of boys. And girls' weekly average of active days was lower (2.4 vs 3).
"It's very worrying to see this gender difference so early," says Bull, noting that the difference often persists into adulthood.
Different norms around what's appropriate for girls often drive that divergence.
"In many places, when girls reach puberty, there are taboos to engaging in physical activity," says Cunningham. Take India, for example, where Cunningham has focused much of her research. "Mothers or grandmothers will say, 'Well, you know, we don't want girls spending a lot of time outside. Their skin might get darker. That might have negative implications for whether they can get married."
Cunningham notes that girls are active in other, often less intense ways. "In South Asia, as well the United States, a substantial proportion of girls' active time is doing chores," she says "If the guys are outside playing and the girls are inside sweeping, they're both active, but it's kind of not the same thing."
What would get them moving?
Improving these trends won't be easy, experts told NPR. Redesigning cities to be more walkable, for instance, takes many years and substantial investment. Many experts point to schools as a practical place to start. "To move the needle, we need to focus on the settings where kids and adolescents spend most of their time," says Varela.
In fact, data suggests that countries with higher levels of adolescent exercise tend to have more structured time for sport during or after the school day. Building up such programs in other countries might help close the gap, says Varela, especially if done in ways that make sport accessible and affordable.
Such efforts will require sustained attention from policymakers, Varela says, who face pressures from all sorts of competing interests. But she says it's worth it.
"Not solving the problem in this stage of life will perpetuate the problem in adulthood," she says, where the costs to society, in terms of poor physical and mental health, only become greater.

The Union Health Ministry has proposed expanding the network of authorised entry points for the import of drugs, medical devices and cosmetics into India, adding 10 inland container depots (ICDs), a Special Economic Zone (SEZ) and an international airport to the existing list of notified locations.
The proposed amendment to Rule 43A of the Drugs Rules, 1945, is aimed at easing import operations, reducing inland transportation distances and improving the movement of healthcare products across the country.
The additional locations proposed include ICD Sonipat, Piyala and Harsaru in Haryana; ICD Dadri in Uttar Pradesh; ICD Gandhidham/Mundra in Gujarat; ICD Sanath Nagar and Thimmapur in Hyderabad, Telangana; and ICD Whitefield in Bengaluru, Karnataka. The Ministry has also proposed including SEZ Bommasandra in Karnataka and Noida International Airport in Uttar Pradesh for the import of drugs by air.
The proposed additions will supplement the existing network of authorised import gateways, which includes ICDs at Dhannad and Tihi in Indore, Madhya Pradesh, besides airports already notified for drug imports.
Rule 43A specifies the ports, airports, railway stations, road crossings and other entry points through which drugs can be imported into India.
According to the Ministry, expanding the network is expected to allow importers to clear consignments closer to their manufacturing facilities, warehouses and distribution centres. This could reduce inland transportation requirements, optimise logistics costs and minimise delays in the movement of imported consignments.
The move is also intended to improve operational convenience for importers and strengthen the supporting infrastructure for the supply of medicines, medical devices and cosmetics.
The Ministry has invited objections and suggestions from stakeholders on the draft amendment. Responses can be submitted to the Under Secretary (Drugs Regulation), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, or emailed to drugsdiv-mohfw@gov.in.
The amendment will be taken forward after consideration of the objections and suggestions received, noted a release issued by the Ministry.

Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader
- Published
Joseph Kabila was a commander in the rebel alliance that brought his father to power in the Democratic Republic of Congo in 1997, went on to succeed him as president and now, at the age of 55, he is a rebel leader once again.
In an even stranger twist, the man he has sworn to topple is the very man he handed power to after 18 years at the helm, and with whom he had formed a coalition government after stepping down. While one of the rebel groups he had fought against as president is part of his new alliance.
His career reflects the ever-shifting nature of politics in DR Congo, where alliances are ephemeral, with the use of force a constant threat.
When Kabila was named leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), earlier this month, it confirmed what many Congolese had long believed – that the former president was working with the M23 rebels, who last year seized much of eastern DR Congo, including the region's main cities of Goma and Bukavu.
Nevertheless, the confirmation sent shockwaves through DR Congo – a vast country two-thirds the size of western Europe, with huge deposits of gold, diamonds and even more importantly minerals used to make everything from the mobile phones to batteries for electric vehicles.
For Kabila, the alliance offers a possible route back to the power he had lost.
For the M23 rebels, his involvement brings the experience and networks of a former head of state to a movement whose military advances have yet to translate into broad national legitimacy.
But it is far from certain that they can achieve their stated goal of ousting President Félix Tshisekedi.
Policy analyst Henry-Pacifique Mayala told the BBC that Kabila had been left with few options for regaining political influence.
"He actually was left with no other choice," he said.
Facing a death sentence after being convicted in absentia of treason, as well as US sanctions over his alleged support for the M23, Kabila may have sought assurances that the partnership could serve his interests, Mayala suggested.
"I'm not sure that he is making this huge leap in the dark without having received considerable assurance," Mayala said, adding that the M23's military strength could give Kabila greater leverage in any future negotiations with the Congolese government.
Kabila's involvement also raises questions about whether the conflict could spread beyond the east.
The M23's territorial gains have been concentrated in the country's eastern provinces, some 1,500km (1,000 miles) from the capital, Kinshasa.
Kabila's political networks could give the rebellion a broader reach, but that does not necessarily mean it has the capacity to extend its military campaign across the country.
And it is not clear how far Kabila's national reach extends.
While he was in power, after being named following the mysterious assassination of his father Laurent in 2001, he was often seen as something of an outsider in Kinshasa. He was far more at home speaking Swahili, the lingua franca of eastern DR Congo, as well as east Africa, rather than the Lingala spoken in Kinshasa.
His father's rebel group actually walked across the country to Kinshasa, also starting in the east, over a period of seven months, before eventually seizing power in May 1996 and ousting long-time ruler Mobutu Sese Seko, who had governed the country as his own personal property for more than 30 years.
There is little suggestion that Joseph Kabila's FRN would try to repeat that feat but earlier this week, he likened Tshisekedi to Mobutu.
"You have a tyrant who wants to impose and dictate what he thinks is right and not necessarily follow the constitution, which is the supreme law of the land," he told Conspiracy Trackers Great Lakes (CTGL), a pro-M23 research group.
Kabila accused the government of using the death penalty, ending the moratorium introduced during his own presidency, to intimidate civilians, politicians and members of the military, as well as himself.
"This is personal," he said.
He framed his confrontation with Tshisekedi as a fight against authoritarianism, invoking Section 64 of the constitution, which calls on citizens to resist anyone who seizes power or exercises it in violation of constitutional provisions.
Tshisekedi is rumoured to be planning to change the constitution to allow him to seek a third term in office, with the C64 coalition of opposition parties named after that same section of the constitution, campaigning against such a move.
But in a sign that he may not get everything his own way, the C64 coalition this week refused to back Kabila's rebellion, saying that Congo's multiple security crises cannot be resolved by military means alone. Instead, it announced plans to seek direct talks with both Tshisekedi and Kabila in pursuit of what it called a "genuine and inclusive national dialogue".
Richard Moncrieff, a Great Lakes analyst with the International Crisis Group think-tank, said President Tshisekedi retained substantial advantages.
"Tshisekedi has strong American backing. He has a lot of money. And he generally controls the political system and, as far as we can see, the military system," Moncrieff said.
In his first public reaction to Kabila being named FRN leader, Tshisekedi was damning: "In my view, it's simply proof that he has never loved this country, and even less its inhabitants," he said last week.
And yet Kabila is widely believed to have helped ensure that Tshisekedi succeeded him, rather than Martin Fayulu, who was the true winner of the 2018 elections, according to leaked results provided by the Catholic Church, which had observers around the country.
Indeed, the former head of the electoral commission who announced Tshisekedi as the winner, Corneille Nangaa, has said as much.
Now one of Kabila's deputies in the FRN, he claimed that Kabila and Tshisekedi had reached a political agreement before the final election results were announced.
"I can confirm that I helped draft the deal," Nangaa told France 24 in September 2023. "Tshisekedi is a liar. He knows there was an agreement and he knows what was contained in the deal."
Tshisekedi has maintained that he won the election legitimately.

After the disputed election, Kabila and Tshisekedi entered a power-sharing arrangement that allowed Kabila's coalition to retain control of parliament even after Tshisekedi took office in January 2019.
The arrangement unravelled in December 2020, when Tshisekedi moved to break Kabila's parliamentary dominance and build his own majority. The former allies became rivals, and Kabila went into self-imposed exile in South Africa.
From exile, Kabila's criticism of Tshisekedi grew louder.
He returned to DR Congo in 2025 and appeared in rebel-held Goma. In September that year, a military court sentenced him to death in absentia on charges including treason and financing violence in eastern Congo.
At the time, he rejected the accusations.
Yet another intriguing sub-plot to the announcement is Kabila's relationship with Rwanda's President Paul Kagame.
In the early years of his presidency, ties were strained between DR Congo and Rwanda, which accused its giant neighbour of not doing enough to remove ethnic Hutu militias involved in the 1994 Rwandan genocide from its territory. Their presence in what is now DR Congo has been used to justify Rwanda's repeated military involvement in its giant neighbour, going back to its backing of Laurent Kabila's rebellion.
The M23 was formed in 2012, vowing to stand up for the rights of ethnic Tutsis and to protect them against these militias, but also battling the Congolese army, under the control of Joseph Kabila.
From the start Rwanda was accused of backing them. It has always denied these allegations, as it still does despite overwhelming evidence.
However, relations later improved and Kabila's government worked with Rwanda against the Hutu militias.
Alex Adams, Africa programme director at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said Kabila's appointment as rebel leader could bring his interests into alignment with those of Rwanda's president, even though their objectives differ.
"Kabila wants to recover political influence nationally, while Kagame is primarily concerned with Rwanda's security and strategic position in eastern Congo. This is an alignment of convenience rather than a partnership built on deep trust," he said.
Policy analyst Mayala said Kabila's involvement could help Rwanda counter accusations that it was interfering in Congo's internal affairs.
"This is a former president. It's finally a Congolese rebellion," he said.
Even before the announcement of Kabila as the rebellion's leader, fighting was continuing despite a peace accord overseen by Donald Trump last year.
Part of that deal saw the US sign an agreement to extract DR Congo's mineral wealth and the US has since seemed to side with Tshisekedi by imposing sanctions on various Rwandan officials and bodies, accusing them of prolonging the violence.
Elections are scheduled for 2028, but Tshisekedi has warned that fighting in the east could delay voting.
Against this backdrop, Kabila has questioned whether elections alone can resolve the country's political crisis.
"Does Congo need elections or a revolution?" he asked, arguing that lasting peace required a fundamental overhaul of the country's executive and legislature.
International security analyst Ovigwe Eguegu argues that Kabila is banking on military force to regain political influence, while Tshisekedi seems to be trying to extend his time in office beyond what the constitution allows.
"It looks like the Congolese people are going to lose either way, because neither of these two sides present a credible economic transformation plan for both the eastern Congo and the entirety of the country," Eguegu said.

Sao Paulo GP: Can Max Verstappen, Lewis Hamilton come from the back again as Lando Norris hopes for rain to fight Kimi Antonelli
Lando Norris starts on pole in Brazil from Kimi Antonelli but there will be plenty of attention further down the field with Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton starting at the back; watch Sunday's Sao Paulo Grand Prix live at 5pm on Sky Sports F1, build-up from 3.30pm
Saturday 7 November 2026 23:26, UK
A mixed up grid and rain on the forecast has set up the prospect of a thrilling Sao Paulo Grand Prix on Sunday.
For the third year in a row, Lando Norris will start on pole position in Brazil with new F1 world champion Kimi Antonelli alongside him on the front row.
Unusually though, there will be plenty of attention further down the field as power unit changes for Red Bull's Max Verstappen and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton mean they start at the back, while Ferrari's Charles Leclerc starts 14th for a 10-grid place penalty.

And Mercedes' George Russell, who was left frustrated to not qualify first after a strategic error from the team, starts seventh following a five-place grid penalty for a new internal combustion engine, so several of F1's biggest names will begin the Sao Paulo Grand Prix - lights out at 5pm on Sunday with build-up from 3.30pm, live on Sky Sports F1 - out of position.
"It's almost a reverse grid race, no?" Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff told Sky Sports F1.
"Yeah, exciting. I think we want to lock in the points for the Constructors' Championship. But it's all floodgates open, the better. Let's race."
How far can Verstappen and Hamilton climb up the field?
Verstappen is no stranger to making his way through the pack at Interlagos after his remarkable victory from 17th in 2024 in the rain.
The Red Bull driver, who has won three times in Brazil, gained 11 places in the opening 11 laps before making the right strategy call to take a crucial victory.
Last year, Verstappen started from the pit lane and impressively charged his way to the podium in dry conditions, but he thinks it will be more difficult to get towards the front this time around.
"It's going to be a bit harder to overtake. The Overtake Mode doesn't really do a lot around here. Everyone is draining their battery from the last corner to Turn 1. Everyone has their wings open, so the effect is less than normal," he told Sky Sports F1.
"That will make it a bit harder to overtake once you get to the cars that are similar on lap times. The first few cars are not a problem. The others will be a little harder."
Hamilton memorably went from 20th to fifth in the 2021 Sprint in Brazil, after he was disqualified from Qualifying, then won the Grand Prix after starting 10th.
However, Hamilton will not have the same car advantage from five years ago with Ferrari struggling this weekend compared to their recent form.
But, the high chance of rain means Hamilton, and Verstappen, will have the chance to showcase their extraordinary skill and could still find themselves towards the pointy end of the field with a special performance.
"It will be tricky conditions but I love racing in the rain," said Hamilton.
"I was basically using the qualifying as a test to make sure the engine is working, and making sure the car felt good. I feel good for tomorrow."
Leclerc has less cars to overtake from 14th and feels he learned a lot from the wet qualifying by experimenting with set-up tweaks which will benefit him in the race.
"It's going to be very tricky. My biggest strength in the junior categories has been wet driving. Since my nine years with Ferrari, we have never found a way around it," he told Sky Sports F1.
"I still believe if we manage to find the right window of this car, we can fight for much better than top six."
Norris hoping for 'dark, gloomy day' to fight Antonelli
Perhaps quite fittingly, last year's F1 world champion Norris will start on pole from the new world champion Antonelli in the first race since the latter secured this year's title a week ago in Mexico.
McLaren have brought a new front wing, rear wing, beam wing and floor elements to their car this weekend and it appears to have made an immediate performance impact.
Norris and Antonelli traded lap times throughout Friday's practice sessions in the dry but the McLaren driver feels he needs rain to beat Antonelli on Sunday.
"I expect a battle no matter what. If it's dry, I probably expect a bigger battle because I don't think we quite have the speed compared to them," he told Sky Sports F1.
"That's why I feel like we had a very good day today. We made the most of conditions where it's not so much about who has the best car, it's more who can push things to the limit and make the most of that opportunity.
"I'm hoping when I wake up it's a dark, gloomy day because we will have a better chance then."
Norris pointed to Antonelli's impressive long run pace in the dry on Friday as the reason he's hoping for rain, whereas the Mercedes driver says he's open to any conditions.
"Hopefully, we can get off the line well, and let's see if it's going to be wet or dry," said Antonelli.
"In the dry, I felt very good over a single lap and on the long run, especially in FP2. So let's see. I'm looking forward to it.
Mercedes have a big opportunity to win the Constructors' Championship with Antonelli starting in second and Russell in seventh, while the two Ferraris are outside of the top 13.
If Mercedes outscore Ferrari by three points, or more, they will seal their ninth title since 2014 but the result of the race itself appears to be more important to the drivers, and Russell is hoping for more rain following his impressive qualifying.
"I felt really confident in the rain. I think my pace, along with Lando's, was by far the best out there," he said
"In the rain here, it's always a challenge. I hope it is wet. I feel I've got a greater chance if it's wet."

PM Modi extends Diwali wishes, to celebrate festival with jawans today
PM Modi extended Diwali greetings to people across the country on Sunday. He will be celebrating the festival with the jawans.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday extended Diwali greetings to the people across the country, wishing everyone on the occasion of the festival of lights.
On Saturday, the Prime Minister had conveyed his festive greetings, wishing the people happiness, peace and prosperity. He reiterated his tradition of celebrating Diwali with jawans, continuing his annual gesture of spending the festival with armed forces personnel.
“Diwali wishes to everyone! Heartfelt Diwali wishes to my family members across the country,” PM Modi said in his latest post on X.
‘Festival of light reflects our resolve against darkness’
On Saturday, PM Modi had extended Diwali greetings to the nation through a video message, highlighting the festival as a symbol of light’s triumph over darkness and expressing hope for happiness, peace and prosperity for all citizens.
In a 50-second video message shared on social media platforms including X, Modi appeared in traditional attire with a tilak and addressed people directly, extending his greetings on the festival.

He said the country was glowing with lights on the occasion of Deepavali. “This festival of light is a reflection of our resolve against darkness,” he remarked. Offering “very best wishes” to everyone, he prayed that the festival and the “days ahead remain filled with happiness, peace and prosperity.”
The Prime Minister also spoke about his personal practice of celebrating Diwali with great enthusiasm. He said that spending the festival “among the country’s jawans” has become his “regular routine every year” which “will continue this year as well.” He concluded the message by once again conveying heartfelt Diwali greetings.
PM Modi’s annual Diwali celebrations with jawans since 2014
PM Modi’s annual visits to military locations on Diwali have become a consistent feature of his tenure since 2014. He began the practice at the Siachen Base Camp, the world’s highest battlefield.
In subsequent years, he marked the festival with troops in the Punjab sector near Amritsar in 2015, Sumdoh near the China border in Himachal Pradesh in 2016, the Gurez sector in Jammu and Kashmir in 2017, and Harsil in Uttarakhand in 2018. He was in Rajouri along the Line of Control in 2019, Longewala in Rajasthan’s Jaisalmer in 2020, Nowshera in Jammu and Kashmir in 2021, Kargil in 2022, Lepcha in Himachal Pradesh in 2023, Sir Creek in Gujarat’s Kutch in 2024, and aboard the indigenous aircraft carrier INS Vikrant off the Goa-Karwar coast in 2025.

Protests across Nova Scotia oppose AI data centres
EverWind Fuels plans to build the first phase of a Cape Breton data centre next year
Rainy weather did not deter people from turning out across Nova Scotia on Saturday to oppose the construction of AI data centres in the province.
The protests follow EverWind Fuels' plan to build the first phase of a data centre in Point Tupper by next year to support American AI giant Anthropic's chatbot, Claude.
The largest protest was in Halifax, where hundreds turned out in front of Province House, many bearing placards. About 200 people gathered in Kentville, roughly 150 in Port Hawkesbury and dozens assembled at Centre Square in Truro.
Speaking at the Halifax protest, Rowan Swain of the Ecology Action Centre said he is concerned that the province is being promised a future where corporate profits are prioritized.
"Nova Scotians deserve better than this," Swain said. "There are options for this province that can grow our economy without sacrificing the health of our communities and our environment and our fresh water."
Rain didn't stop data centre protesters from turning out in Truro on Saturday. (Luke Ettinger/CBC)
Many of the placards highlighted concerns about the water and electricity needed to run data centres.
EverWind has said it intends to draw electricity from the provincial energy grid until onshore turbines are built. It holds approvals for the wind farms but has not yet started construction.
Sadie Beaton in Kentville is concerned that Mi'kmaw consent has not been given.
Beaton protested to ensure the responsibilities of the Peace and Friendship Treaties are upheld.
Benjamin Lauzon, one of the organizers of the Port Hawkesbury protest, said it is important to speak out when people see something wrong happening.
He wants Premier Tim Houston to convene an emergency session of the legislature to allow an open debate on the Point Tupper data centre.
"The MLAs have a duty to bring the public's concerns to the legislative assembly," Lauzon said. "Right now, it's not a decision for him alone to make."
EverWind, province respond
Earlier this week, EverWind held a public meeting in D'Escousse, a small coastal community in Cape Breton's Richmond County, on the matter.
"There are concerns with projects such as this and what's really important from our perspective is that there's measures in place to ensure that we're developing these projects responsibly and we're developing them in line with the federal guidelines and we're developing them in line with the provincial expectations," said Mark Stewart, the company's director of engagement.
There was also a public meeting held this week in Lower River Inhabitants.
In a statement, the province said that it accepts and expects that Nova Scotians have questions and concerns about the data centre. It also said the potential for a $10-billion investment is something to be open minded about.
"Our government has been clear that a data centre can only proceed if they can meet and exceed provincial and federal guidelines, which include protecting water, the environment, and power rates and capacity," it said.

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows a real incident of a girl being kidnapped while walking along a road in Bihar. In the video, a group of men travelling in a Bolero vehicle with a covered number plate is seen abducting the girl. She attempts to break free from their clutches, while a passing motorcyclist who records the incident can be seen trying to stop the kidnappers. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
