Fact: The video is scripted and does not show an actual kidnapping in Bihar. Muklesur Ali, who creates videos with Isa Stunt, confirmed to NewsChecker that the incident was scripted and that all the people seen in the video were members of his team. The Instagram and YouTube accounts associated with them also feature similar staged videos created for entertainment purposes. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to an Instagram post uploaded by an account named ‘Isa Stunt’ on 11 October 2026, featuring the same video (archived). However, unlike the viral clip, this version had no audio and instead featured background music. Further, the accompanying caption provided no specific information about the incident.
Upon reviewing the Instagram account, we found several other videos similar to the viral clip. Many of these videos (here, here, and here) featured the same Bolero vehicle, motorcycle, and man seen in the video of the alleged kidnapping and scuffle. This suggests that the videos may be staged and do not depict actual incidents.
We also found a YouTube channel linked in the bio of the Instagram account ‘Isa Stunt’, which featured several videos similar to the viral clip, depicting incidents such as a girl’s kidnapping, a street assault, and a road accident. However, the video descriptions and the channel’s bio stated that the content was created for entertainment purposes.
We also noticed an Instagram account named ‘Muklesur Ali’, which was tagged in several videos (here, here, and here) posted on the ‘Isa Stunt’ account. Upon reviewing Muklesur Ali’s account, we found several videos similar to the viral clip, including a video depicting a similar staged kidnapping. We have previously debunked (here, here, and here) several videos created by Muklesur Ali that went viral on social media and were shared as depicting real incidents. This further suggests that the viral video is staged and was created for entertainment purposes rather than documenting an actual kidnapping.
NewsChecker reached out to Muklesur Ali, who told them that he and Isa create scripted videos as a team. He confirmed that the viral video depicting the girl’s kidnapping was also scripted and that all the people seen in it were members of his team.
To sum up, this viral video of a girl being kidnapped on a road in Bihar is scripted and does not show a real incident.

Concerns have been raised over the sudden rise in number of Turkish nationals facing removal from the UK as a result of mistakes, prompting accusations that the Home Office has failed to learn the lessons of the Windrush scandal.
Since the start of the year, there has been a sharp rise in the number of rejected applications for indefinite leave to remain for those on European Community Association Agreement (ECAA) visas, a longstanding route to residency for Turkish nationals seeking to set up a business in the UK.
The rise in refusals appears to apply to applications lodged since September 2025, shortly before Shabana Mahmood announced controversial proposals at the Labour conference for tougher conditions on those applying for leave to remain.
The home secretary said at the time: “In solving this crisis, you may not always like what I do. We will have to question some of the assumptions and legal constraints that have lasted for a generation and more.”
The Home Office maintains that there has been no change to the rules but doubts about this have been raised, including by the former foreign secretary David Lammy, who said there “seems to be a sudden change” in the government’s policy, which had “devastated” the lives of those affected and evoked memories of the Windrush scandal.
Hundreds of ECAA holders have been refused permanent residency since the start of the year, a big uptick compared with previous years, while the number of successful applications has plummeted from the usual several thousand to just a few hundred since January.
Refusal letters have been riddled with basic errors, made-up requirements and a disregard of human tragedies, which were previously treated with discretion.
Many of those being denied arrived in the UK within the past seven years and have set up successful businesses. Among them is a woman who started treatment for cancer in Turkey after being diagnosed on a trip during the Covid-19 pandemic, when the NHS restricted such care. Her application was denied because she “chose” to begin treatment in Turkey, even though her medical team advised that transferring clinical care treatment “carried significant clinical risk”.
Despite a review, the Home Office stood firm and informed the woman in October that she and her three young children “should now leave the United Kingdom”.
Another refused applicant was told his window-cleaning business was not legitimate because he did not have a social media presence, a requirement that does not exist. One woman whose father in Turkey lives with terminal Alzheimer’s was denied indefinite leave to remain because the Home Office said his condition had been “known for several years”, meaning her absences from the UK did not stem from an “urgent unforeseen situation”.
Lammy, the MP for Tottenham, a constituency with a large Turkish-speaking population, said: “I have been contacted by constituents whose lives have been devastated by what seems to be a sudden change in Home Office policy – people who have built their lives and families here and played by the rules.
“I can’t help remembering the Windrush scandal when I hear these terrible stories. The Home Office needs to urgently revisit and consider the Lessons Learned review. This is entirely unacceptable. I would like to see justice for Britain’s Turkish-origin community.”
The number of ECAA applications under administrative review, a process where the Home Office re-examines a refusal, has soared since the start of the year, according to a freedom of information request, jumping from 145 in 2025 to 395 from January to mid-August 2026. Lawyers dealing with ECAA cases have told the Guardian there have been long delays for applications lodged from September 2025, beyond the usual six-month wait time.
Data from the department shows a stark fall in the number of Turkish nationals applying through this route being granted indefinite leave to remain. From January to June 2025, there were 3,378 grants of settlement in the UK for ECAA applicants. For the same period in 2026, this plummeted to 745, a 78% drop.
Lawyers have said these types of cases were previously routinely approved because of guidance on compassionate circumstances but that a harsher shift occurred for applications lodged from last September.
Home Office caseworkers also appear to be making significant errors or applying requirements that do not exist. In one refusal, which was eventually overturned, the department said it had been “unable to locate a website for your business” or any “evidence of any online presence, for example social media presence” and falsely claimed the applicant did not provide a complete set of bank statements. In another, the Home Office wrongly calculated the number of days the applicant was out of the country, incorrectly claiming they were out of the country for more than 180 days within a 12-month period.
The Home Office’s approach to ECAA holders appears to contradict certain recommendations made in the independent review into the Windrush scandal, which Priti Patel, the home secretary at the time, accepted and promised to act on. These included establishing clearer guidance on the burden and standard of proof, increasing direct contact with applicants, and revising the criteria and process for assessing cases involving vulnerable applicants.
A Home Office spokesperson said: “There has been no change to how ECAA settlement applications are considered. Every application continues to be considered on its individual circumstances, in line with the published rules and guidance.”

Indian investors who held Apple, Amazon, Tesla, and NVIDIA, shares allege they logged into their Stockal accounts to find those investments replaced with shares of a thinly traded Chinese microcap. Nearly 30 investors say their portfolios were altered without consent on October 15. Their established US stock holdings were allegedly liquidated and the proceeds used to buy Nasdaq-listed Zhibao Technology shares. One investor told Moneycontrol that securities worth $3.1 Mn, or around ₹29 Cr, were sold within two minutes, followed by purchases of 30.5 Lakh Zhibao shares within 15 minutes. Another reported that holdings worth $335,768 were sold and 3 Lakh Zhibao shares purchased. Media reports put investor-reported losses above ₹100 Cr. Inc42 has not independently verified this aggregate or authenticated the investors’ account details and alleged transactions. An FIR has reportedly been registered in Bengaluru. The dispute now centres on how the accounts were accessed, whether safeguards failed, and who bears responsibility across Stockal, its parent Borderless Investing, and US brokerage partner DriveWealth. How The Trades Unfolded Founded in 2016 by Sitashwa Srivastava and Vinay Bharathwaj, Stockal enables Indians to invest overseas through US stocks, exchange-traded funds, and curated portfolios. It has raised over $15 Mn from investors like ScaleX Partners, Arc Ventures, July Ventures, HDFC Securities, and Cadenza Ventures. The startup partners with DriveWealth to facilitate US stock investments. Bharathwaj left Borderless in 2022 and is currently the founder and CEO of “AI-first money intelligence and advisory platform” Cruise Money, as per his LinkedIn profile. Investors allege the October 15 transactions replaced holdings in companies including Alphabet and AMD with Zhibao shares, leaving them exposed to a thinly traded microcap. Borderless said DriveWealth notified it on October 16, India time, of suspicious trading across 13 accounts. Its assessment indicated an unauthorised third party had accessed 26 accounts using valid login credentials. In 13 accounts, large-cap US equities were liquidated to acquire thinly traded microcap securities. Borderless said it restricted access shortly after receiving the notification. An investor told Moneycontrol that Borderless contacted him on October 18, acknowledged suspicious activity, and said DriveWealth had restricted transactions in his account. Zhibao’s subsequent decline deepened investors’ reported losses. Against an average purchase price of around $1.05 cited in investor accounts, the shares closed at $0.42 on October 23 — a fall of approximately 60%. Differing Accounts Of Access In an October 30 letter to an investor, DriveWealth reportedly said the unauthorised access occurred through the Stockal interface and attributed responsibility for associated security lapses to Stockal. It reportedly said it froze the account on Stockal’s instructions. Responding to Inc42’s questions, DriveWealth said, “The Stockal incident is unrelated to DriveWealth’s systems. It occurred on Stockal’s app, not our platform. DriveWealth does not have a customer-facing app through which trades are placed, and our systems and client data were not affected by this incident.” Borderless’s public statement offered a possible explanation – social engineering involving information exposed in another company’s data breach several weeks earlier. It stressed that this connection remained unverified and under investigation. Borderless said its investigation found no evidence of a breach or compromise of its platform, interface, infrastructure, or internal systems. It also said no funds were withdrawn from affected accounts, based on findings available so far. This distinction leaves the disputed trades themselves central to investors’ concerns – their allegation concerns changes to their holdings without consent, irrespective of whether money left the accounts. Safeguards Under The Spotlight The precise access method remains under investigation. However, the incident raises questions about whether possession of valid credentials could have been sufficient to execute the disputed trades. Yash Kadakia, founder and CTO of cybersecurity firm Security Brigade, told Inc42 that stolen credentials are a common entry point, but platforms cannot shift responsibility entirely to customers when compromised passwords enable financial transactions. He said layered safeguards should include two-factor authentication, SIM binding, device and geographical checks, and separate transaction-level authentication. Behavioural monitoring is also critical. Multiple accounts accessed from one IP address, or similar trading patterns across accounts within a short period, should trigger scrutiny, he said. Such monitoring could explain DriveWealth’s detection of suspicious activity, Kadakia suggested, although the actual detection mechanism remains unclear. He added that implementation and enforcement remain challenges despite stronger SEBI cybersecurity requirements for regulated entities. Borderless Sets Out Its Position Borderless said it had engaged independent cybersecurity specialists, introduced additional authentication and account-protection measures, and found no evidence of a wider threat to its platform, products, or other customer accounts. It maintained that unauthorised trading identified so far was restricted to 13 accounts. The company said it had been engaging affected customers and working with DriveWealth to reconstruct events, examine disputed transactions, and explore avenues for a fair resolution. However, it said assistance should not be construed as an admission of liability, negligence, wrongdoing, or responsibility. It said it was cooperating with authorities and regulators. Borderless also maintained it had provided substantive responses to media enquiries before publication and cautioned that its public account could change as the investigation progressed. Inc42 has separately sought answers on the transactions, investigation, and investor concerns. The story will be updated upon receiving a response. Who Bears The Responsibility? The controversy has also drawn attention to Stockal’s former partnership with HDFC Securities. Launched in 2019 through globalinvesting.in, their operational association ended in July 2024. HDFC Securities has clarified that it is not named among the accused in the FIR and said it would cooperate with regulators and law enforcement authorities. While HDFC Securities has clarified its position, questions about the disputed trades remain unresolved. How were the accounts accessed, why were the transactions not intercepted, and what recourse do affected investors have to restore their holdings or recover losses? Cross-border investing divides responsibilities across the customer interface, trade execution, and custody of securities. Establishing each intermediary’s obligations and the safeguards applied will be central to determining accountability. For affected investors, the immediate issue remains whether the investigation will explain the disputed trades and deliver a resolution. For now, neither the source of the alleged compromise nor responsibility for the claimed losses has been conclusively established. Edited by Vinaykumar Rai

This is an updated version of an article first published in August 2026
Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
And now Kimi, who turned 20 only in August, has dominated F1 in only his second season, and become the youngest world champion in the sport's history.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he entered, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments, including pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He took the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli took six poles and six wins in the first 11 races, establishing a 50-point lead in the championship.
Mercedes lost their dominant form in the second half of the season in the face of challenges from first McLaren and then Red Bull.
But Antonelli remained a consistent threat at the front, and he killed off his Monza ghosts in the Italian Grand Prix with a stunning victory after an engine penalty led to him starting 19th on the grid.
He put in a drive of clinical excellence and, with help from a safety car, chased down and caught Russell in the final laps to take a win that will go down in folklore.
The extent of his turnaround in form has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not [fitting the stereotype of] a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says.
"We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said 'Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1'," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

If the vote to impeach Hegseth passes in the House, the Senate must then vote to either acquit or convict Hegseth on the articles of impeachment. Under the Constitution, convicting and removing a public official from office requires a two-thirds majority in the Senate.
Shortly after Election Day, a rumor spread that U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., planned to force a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in response to the Democrats' outsize victories in the 2026 midterms — which were widely seen as a rebuke of President Donald Trump's policies, particularly his war in Iran.
The rumor circulated on X and Facebook. Snopes readers searched the website for information on a possible Hegseth impeachment trial.
In short, the claim is true. It originated with a CNN article titled "Republicans quickly turn against Pete Hegseth after midterms rout." Here's what the story said about Massie (emphasis ours): 
House Republicans are expected to vote to directly repudiate the defense secretary in a matter of days. Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, the famously anti-Trump GOP lawmaker, told CNN he plans to trigger a vote to impeach Hegseth when Congress returns next week — and multiple GOP sources said they expect it to pass.
Massie then referenced CNN's reporting in a Nov. 4 X post (archived) that confirmed he planned to reintroduce articles of impeachment against Hegseth. (Massie previously forced a vote on impeaching Hegseth in September, which failed.)
"There is one contingency in which I won't reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns," Massie said on his official X account, which has a gray checkmark badge verifying that it authentically represents a government official.
Snopes has not independently verified CNN's report that at least some Republicans believe Massie's impeachment articles against Hegseth will pass.
The House passes impeachment articles through a simple majority. The Senate must then vote on whether to convict Hegseth on those articles of impeachment before he would be removed from office — and the Constitution requires a two-thirds majority vote in the Senate to convict.
Congress has never successfully removed a Cabinet member from office under the impeachment process.
After several news outlets reported that Hegseth did not intend to step down and that Trump was showing support for him — at least publicly — Massie said in a Nov. 5 X post that his impeachment resolution was a "much gentler version of what's coming when Dem's control Congress."
(While Democrats won majorities in both congressional chambers, they won't actually take control of the Senate and House of Representatives until the new members are sworn in in January.)
Following Massie's Nov. 5 post, Hegseth shared a video that same day calling Massie a "disgruntled, defeated congressman" who, alongside Democratic allies, "dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly" (at 4:12).
In the video, Hegseth compared the impeachment efforts against him to lawmakers' previous attempts to impeach Trump.
"It's all about the politics of personal destruction," he said. "Didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me."

It might be too early to start talking about an on-field crisis at Manchester City, even though it fell to a third straight Premier League defeat.
City coach Enzo Maresca was certainly not panicking.
After opening the campaign with seven wins in a row, City lost at struggler Nottingham Forest 3-1 to fall six points behind league leader Arsenal after the defending champion beat Hull 1-0.
“We are conceding too many goals unfortunately and we need to improve that," Maresca told the BBC.
"Use the international break to understand why and try to avoid in the future. Always concerned but we need balance — seven wins in a row then three (defeats) in a row. Need the balance. No panic. We need to understand but no panic.”
Liam Delap, a City academy graduate, netted two goals for Forest — which had yet to score at home this season coming into the match.
It was only a second win of the season for Forest, which moved two points out of the relegation zone — with Manchester United taking its place in the bottom three ahead of Sunday's (November 8) match against Aston Villa.
Forest got off to a dream start.
Jair Cunha caught City defender Josko Gvardiol in possession and he surged forward, finding a gap to slide the ball into the bottom left corner and give his team the lead in the sixth minute.
More defensive mishaps from City, which again lost the ball, allowed Delap to sprint from inside his own half and between two defenders before firing into the back of the net to double Forest's advantage in the 18th.
City managed to get one back early in the second half. Jeremy Doku latched onto a long ball over the top on the left flank and his cross was deflected into the path of Rayan Cherki, who drove it into the top left corner.
City was pushing hard for the equalizer but Forest restored its two-goal advantage in the 74th, with Delap finishing off a rapid counterattack with a fine shot that went in off the inside of the far post.
Forest coach Oliver Glasner sprinted half the length of the field to celebrate with his players.
“One of my best running stats, I guess," Glasner told the BBC. "I will be fatigued tomorrow but I can be because it's the international break so I can have a rest!”
Defending champ grinds out narrow win
Earlier, it seemed as if Arsenal was in for a frustrating day, with things not clicking against a well-organized Hull, before Martin Ødegaard found a way through in the 72nd minute.
Noni Madueke cut in from the right wing and Konstantinos Tzolakis managed to parry his effort but not nearly far enough and the captain was there to slam home the loose ball.
Controversy at Leeds
Substitute Noah Okafor had been on the field for only 97 seconds when he scored to send Leeds to a 1-0 victory over Tottenham in a match marked by controversy.
A throw-in was headed on by Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Harry Wilson pushed the ball into Okafor's path to drive home in the 79th.
It was Leeds' first victory in almost two months and lifted the team into eighth, two points above Spurs — who were looking for their fourth straight win after none from their first six matches.
Tottenham will feel Leeds should have played the second half with 10 men after a nasty challenge by Jayden Bogle on Mathys Tel in the 34th. It wasn't malicious but the late tackle saw Bogle's studs land on the trailing ankle of Tel, leaving the Tottenham forward writhing in agony.
A long VAR check for a possible red card for Bogle ended with no action deemed necessary. Tel tried to continue but came off a few minutes later.
Newcastle drew at Fulham 1-1.
No FA Cup fairytale again for Macclesfield
There will be no repeat of Macclesfield's heroics in the FA Cup this season as the team lost at Mansfield 3-0 in the first round.
Non-league Macclesfield pulled off the biggest upset in the history of the competition last campaign when knocking out holder Crystal Palace.

JD Vance’s bad week gets worse
Is the GOP presidential nomination wide open?
Hi readers, happy Friday! What a week, right?
My colleague Caitlin Dewey has spent the last two days unpacking some of the midterm results and their implications for you, and there will be lots more of that to come. But before we head into the weekend, I’m going to take a quick second to look ahead — to 2028.
Specifically, to the future of the Republican Party, which just found itself on the wrong end of what may be the biggest electoral landslide since 1976. It’s a comprehensive, crushing repudiation — and one that has already cast the future of MAGA’s heir apparent, Vice President JD Vance, into doubt.
Vance has long looked like the presumptive Republican presidential nominee in 2028, with the clearest claim to President Donald Trump’s legacy. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, also considered a potential 2028 candidate, has previously said he would defer to Vance were Vance to run.
But that may be changing. The downside to being so closely linked to the president, after all, is that it’s hard to run very far when the president gets hit with Electoral Ragnarok. Vance didn’t help his case on Wednesday, with a strange and lengthy post on the social media site X blaming the Iran war for his party’s electoral woes.
Also implicated in questions about Vance and the 2028 primary is a bigger question about the future of the MAGA movement. Specifically: Is MAGA dead?
No more MAGA? No, more MAGA!
If you ask conservative writer and Vance ally Rod Dreher — and we did! — the answer is easy: Yes, after a historic electoral thrashing, MAGA as a political movement is dead. And it is possible that, as a vote-getting enterprise, MAGA is at the end of the road. But the Trump White House has no plans to let up on the MAGA agenda.
We got our clearest post-midterms sign of that fact on Friday afternoon, in the form of one Stephen Miller. Trump, in a post to Truth Social, announced that Miller would take over as White House chief of staff starting Monday, replacing current chief of staff Susie Wiles.
Miller’s ascension is a foreboding sign: Through one and a half Trump terms, he’s been the driving force behind many of Trump’s cruelest and least popular policies — some of the same policies, particularly around immigration, that helped Republicans lose the midterms in a blowout.
Trump’s decision to promote Miller, with just a little over two years left in the White House, means that we can expect the administration to double down on those same policies, with predictably unpopular results.
That all spells more bad news for Vance, already limping out of the midterms after tying himself tightly to failed Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who was behind one of the ugliest attack ads in recent political memory.
And it may embolden other potential contenders, like Rubio (who is reportedly eyeing an exit from the administration in an attempt to save face) and even outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who Dreher described to Vox as “the only national Republican politician not tainted by Trumpism.” (Mostly because he got flattened by Trump in the 2024 Republican presidential primary, but never mind that now.)

The Indian government has moved to reduce the price of cancer drugs after a retired bank clerk took her case to the supreme court.
From next month, 137 cancer drugs in India will be cheaper as the government tries to tackle the tragedy of poorer patients either forgoing treatment, selling land or falling into debt to meet the high cost of some medicines, which are making large profits for hospitals and pharmacists.
Sarojam Radhakrishnan, a former bank employee in Kerala, was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2021. Doctors prescribed life-saving targeted treatments but the monthly cost, of more than 63,000 rupees (£500), was far beyond her family’s means.
Realising that thousands of families were being ruined by the cost of such drugs, Radhakrishnan filed a petition to the Kerala high court in 2022 demanding government intervention to lower the costs.
When the case reached the supreme court, the judges looked at hospitals’ and retailers’ mark-ups on cancer drugs and called the situation “carnage” and “extortion”.
During a hearing on 29 September, justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta noted how a life-saving cancer drug supplied to hospitals at 2,700 rupees carried a vastly marked-up price of 27,000 rupees.
The judges found that hospitals, distributors and chemists enjoyed large margins on medicines. Analysis by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority revealed a trade mark-up on some cancer drugs averaging 170%, with some extreme examples stretching to more than 700%.
A 30% trade margin cap on the price of 42 drugs has been in place for some years but many others remained off this list. Now, prodded by the supreme court’s findings, the government has imposed the cap on 137 other drugs.
“The measure is expected to reduce medicine prices by up to 70% and help cancer patients save 2,500 crore rupees [£199m] annually, significantly reducing the amount they pay from their own pockets,” a statement from the Department of Pharmaceuticals said.
People on low incomes in India dread illness, as the cost of treatment can mean financial ruin, particularly for cancer patients.
Whenever the Indian Cancer Society holds a free diagnosis camp in Gurgaon where he lives, Krishan Kalra urges local drivers, maids, cooks and tailors to turn up because tests they cannot afford are offered free.
As a former member of the council of the Rajiv Gandhi Cancer Institute and Research Centre, Kalra knows the importance of early diagnosis, but he said very few people attended. “When I ask why, they say they’re too scared – if something serious like cancer is detected, they haven’t got the money to pay for the treatment so they prefer to remain in the dark,” he said.
With the cost of cancer drugs ranging in price from 38,000 to 380,000 rupees, many families quietly walk out of the doctor’s consulting room upon hearing the estimated cost of treatment.
Studies by the Public Health Foundation of India show that spending on healthcare pushes about 55 million Indians a year below the poverty line.
Few Indians can afford the premiums for comprehensive health insurance. The government’s nationwide insurance scheme, Ayushman Bharat, covers treatment for some cancers but it provides only 500,000 rupees’ worth of annual cover for a family – the cost of just one dose of Kadcyla (ado-trastuzumab emtansine), a drug used to treat breast cancer. Patients may need up to 14 doses.
Dr Ravi Kannan is a surgical oncologist and director of Cachar cancer hospital and research centre in Silchar, Assam. He has worked in hospitals elsewhere in India and is familiar with doctors’ trauma of seeing patients walk out to go home and die.
“Some families start the treatment, hoping against hope to manage the cost. They start but they don’t come back for chemotherapy or radiation. They can’t sustain the cost,” he said. “The decision is a welcome step if the outcome is that more patients can access the drugs they need.”
India records about 1.56m new cancer cases annually – up from 1.39m cases in 2020 – making it a significant public health challenge.
As the supreme court delves deeper into the subject, what was clear, said Jyotsna Singh, co-convener of the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments, a civil society network, was that a “total overhaul” of the healthcare system was needed.
“Right from the cost of manufacturing a drug to the point of sale, we need to make the system transparent and regulate the entire supply chain. Only then will these drugs become available to those who need them,” she said.
Singh said companies and hospitals were likely to try to find legal loopholes to wriggle out of the 30% cap, suggesting that hospitals may offset the lower price charged for a drug by raising charges on other items.
The supreme court judges have also asked the government’s lawyers why the cap should apply only to cancer drugs and not the entire range of non-patented drugs. The court has given the government until 27 October to respond.
Unfortunately, the court’s ruling came too late for Radhakrishnan, who died in September 2022 while her case was still pending in Kerala.

WTA Finals in Indian Wells: Who's winning the end-of-year extravaganza? Aryna Sabalenka and Coco Gauff are in the frame
The season-ending championship heads to Indian Wells for the first time, with Aryna Sabalenka and Coco Gauff among the stars competing; You can watch the WTA Finals live on Sky Sports from 8-15 November
Sunday 8 November 2026 07:57, UK
Marion Bartoli, Madison Keys and Laura Robson give their predictions ahead of the season-ending WTA Finals in Indian Wells.
Four players are returning to the year-end event, with three set to make their debut in the absence of world No 1 and reigning champion Elena Rybakina, who pulled out on Saturday night due to her body "not being physically ready to compete".
Who will win the tournament in the California desert and who will be the dark horse? We've asked our panel of experts for their predictions.

Marion Bartoli's winner is...
I'm picking Aryna Sabalenka.
Sabalenka has won 85 per cent of her hard-court matches this year, 34 wins from 40, which is the best percentage of the eight qualifiers. The strongest argument for me is what she did in March. She won 12 matches in a row to complete the 'Sunshine Double', beating Rybakina in the Indian Wells final and again, in straight sets, in the Miami semi-final before beating Coco Gauff for the title. Add the Brisbane title and finals at both hard-court Grand Slams, and you can see how consistently she's put herself in a position to win on this surface.
November in Indian Wells is a different test. The cooler desert evenings could change how the ball comes through the court.
She's played only three matches since the US Open final - so three and a half weeks between her last match and the start of the Finals. I'd expect her to have fresh legs, which matters if she goes deep into the week. The question is how quickly she finds her competitive rhythm. As a coach, I'll be watching how deep she returns and how balanced she is when she goes after that first groundstroke. In a round robin, you can recover from an early loss, but your first opponent is already one of the best players in the world.
Laura Robson's winner is...
Aryna Sabalenka.
Marion Bartoli's dark horse is...
My dark horse is Mirra Andreeva. She's already world No 3 and a Grand Slam champion, so nobody in that locker room is overlooking her.
Look at who she beat to win Indian Wells last year. She beat Rybakina, Svitolina, Swiatek and then Sabalenka, coming back from a set down in the final. That run tells you a lot about her. She dealt with Rybakina's ability to take time away, with Svitolina making her earn every point, and with the weight of shot that Swiatek and Sabalenka can put on you. Those are very different problems to solve in the same week, especially when you're 17.
This year she's won Adelaide outdoors on hard, Linz indoors on hard and her first Grand Slam at Roland-Garros. She also reached the final in Beijing, so we've seen her play well on hard courts deep into the season. What tips it for me is the quality of the players she's already beaten here and how well her game matches up against the two favourites.
What I love about her game is that she can absorb a very hard ball and change direction before her opponent has recovered. Against Sabalenka, watch for the backhand down the line after she's taken a heavy ball crosscourt. Suddenly Sabalenka has to hit on the move.
If Andreeva can take away the easy angle on that first groundstroke, she has a much better chance of getting into the rally. And when she's stretched, she can change the height of the ball to give herself time to recover. If the cooler evening conditions give her a fraction more time to defend, that helps, provided she gets enough depth on the next ball.
The test in her first WTA Finals is whether she can protect her own second serve and be brave enough to attack theirs.
Her movement and backhand will keep her in points. To beat the best players in this field, she'll also need to step forward when she earns the short ball. She's already shown she can do that against both favourites at Indian Wells. That's why I can see her winning the whole thing.
Martina Navratilova's dark horse is...
Jessica Pegula hasn't won a Grand Slam this year, so maybe this is the big one for her this year.
Madison Keys' dark horse is...
Mirra Andreeva. She's a great player, and the conditions in the desert really complement her strengths. I think that's a big reason why she's enjoyed so much success there and has been able to produce some of her best tennis, including her title-winning run in 2025.
Laura Robson's dark horse is...
Elina Svitolina.

Hajra Begum rolls a potato in her hands, checking its skin for cuts, soft spots and signs of rot. After a day harvesting in her family’s field in Chorwan, a remote mountain village in Gurez, Indian-administered Kashmir, she is sorting the crop for winter storage. Some of the potatoes will feed her family through the cold months; others will be saved for planting in spring.
“It should be perfect for planting,” she says. “If you keep a bad potato, you will waste the whole next year.”
Begum, 40, is preparing to lower the potatoes into a khraw, a traditional underground storage pit lined with straw and sealed against the cold. For generations, khraws have kept potatoes, turnips and cabbages through Himalayan winters, when heavy snowfall cuts villages off from the Kashmir valley and temperatures fall below -20C (-4F) – cold enough to crack pipes and freeze diesel.
But the practice is slowly dying out. As roads have improved and young people have left for work and education, fewer families maintain the pits. Their decline threatens not only a traditional way of storing food but also the local potato varieties themselves and the knowledge of which ones store well, resist rot and produce reliable harvests.
“When I was young, almost every family had three or four pits,” Begum says. “Now, down in the main valley, they have abandoned the practice altogether. Only a handful of families still use them. The rest buy from the market or subsidised ones from the government.”
Begum learned from her mother how to tell potatoes that store well from those that rot or sprout too quickly. She is passing this on to her daughter, but is unsure whether the skill will survive into another generation.
Gurez is a high-altitude Himalayan valley perched near the Line of Control, the heavily militarised boundary separating Indian- and Pakistani-administered Kashmir. About 80 miles (125km) from Srinagar, the valley remains cut off each winter when snow closes Razdan pass, its main road link, which sits at roughly 3,600 metres.
It is home to the Dard-Shin people, an Indigenous community who speak Shina and have a culture that is distinct from Kashmiri, with community links across the border in Gilgit-Baltistan, administered by Pakistan.
Potatoes account for about 45% of Gurez’s cultivated area, according to a 2019 study by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research’s National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources (ICAR-NBPGR), a government body that studies and conserves India’s crop diversity. Yet the genetic diversity of the valley’s potatoes has not been systematically documented.
Dr Sheikh M Sultan, a senior scientist based at ICAR-NBPGR’s Srinagar station, surveyed the valley and later struggled to find some of the varieties he had once encountered. “When I first visited, I saw many varieties,” he says. “Later, I could hardly locate even one sample of some. The loss of genetic diversity is tremendous.”
Sultan says migration, improved roads and changing lifestyles have contributed to the decline. As traditional farming disappears, so does knowledge about selecting, cultivating and preserving local varieties.
“When people stop producing their own seeds and start relying entirely on commercial varieties, the loss can be irreparable,” he says.
He warns that research institutions often prioritise introduced varieties over indigenous crops whose characteristics remain poorly understood. “Our indigenous varieties may possess valuable characteristics, including tolerance to cold and resistance to certain pests and diseases,” he says.
“These are resources we should be studying and improving, rather than neglecting.”
Climate breakdown is adding to the pressures on farmers across the Himalayas. People in Gurez report drier springs, reduced snowfall and water shortages, which they say have affected potato production.
Abdul Jabbar Mapnoo, 70, a farmer in Chorwan, remembers winters when deep snow covered the valley. “Every house used to have two or three khraw, each holding about five quintals – 500kg – of potatoes,” he says. “The springs are drying up, and there is less snow in winter. Potato production has fallen. I remember winters when six feet of snow would cover the valley in January or February.”
As farming becomes more difficult and markets easier to access, households have less incentive to grow their own potatoes. Varieties adapted to local conditions over generations could disappear from cultivation before researchers establish what makes them distinctive.
Dr Parveen Kumar, a scientist at the Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology of Kashmir, says locally adapted varieties should not be overlooked. “Climate change is a reality, and farmers need to be aware of adaptation strategies,” he says.
Pressure on farmland poses another risk. In Gurez, where cultivable land is scarce, the Kishanganga hydroelectric project has affected land in the valley through acquisition and submergence. Among the areas affected is Badwan, a village known for its potatoes.
One potential route for preserving the varieties could be through using geographical indications – a designation granted by the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization, and is similar to the French appellation d’origine contrôlée. It can be used on goods that have a specific origin and possess qualities or a reputation linked to this – which can help increase the market value and give them greater recognition. This, and the globally important agricultural heritage systems programme have helped areas such as the saffron-growing landscape of Pampore in Kashmir.
However, recognition alone will not preserve the varieties. They must be identified and documented before they disappear from cultivation, along with farmers’ knowledge of how to select, store and replant them.
In Chorwan, Begum unloads the last sack of potatoes into the pit and covers it, ready for another winter. Some will feed her family; the rest will be replanted in spring. Knowing which potatoes to eat and which to save as seed relies on knowledge passed down through generations.
If these varieties are not documented while they are still being cultivated, Kashmir may lose a living agricultural treasure trove before scientists can fully understand what it contains.

Former Australia head coach Darren Lehmann has denied the claims of Usman Khawaja that the entire team was aware of the infamous Sandpapergate scandal during the 2018 Test series against South Africa, saying he was unaware of the discussions and that responsibility may have varied from player to player.
“No, no,” Lehmann told ABC when asked whether he knew about the conversations surrounding the incident.
“Again, there’s conversations going on everywhere about lots of things in the game of cricket. That would be one for Smith and Khawaja to discuss. But for me, when you’re in conversation about the game of cricket itself, you know reverse swing is happening. So it certainly was talked about how we’re going to combat reverse swing. Because they were doing it very well, South Africa, and making the ball swing.”
Lehmann’s comments came after Khawaja questioned the long-standing account of the scandal, which saw Steven Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft identified as the main people responsible.
Speaking to Nine, Khawaja said the entire Australian team had been involved in the episode.
“It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us. In an ideal world, I don’t want to do this. I don’t want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now,” Khawaja said.
Lehmann, who was Australia’s head coach during the 2018 tour, said he could not speak for the other players and suggested that knowledge of the ball-tampering may not have been universal.
“I don’t think everyone would have known,” Lehmann told ABC. “But you do know ball-tampering is going on because it’s been happening for 150 years. So it’s just how it’s being done and how you would know to that extent, I suppose, and how the bowlers would know, how other players would know.
“So that’s an individual case-by-case… on the players, and I suppose they’ll respond with their thoughts and what they know. I can’t speak for them at all. I can only know what I know, and I know that ball-tampering was a big part of the game of cricket. Now it’s obsolete. But that doesn’t make it right either, but that’s the case, and we paid a heavy price for that.”
Former Australia fast bowler Jason Gillespie also reacted to the claims, calling Khawaja’s account ‘fascinating’.
“Usman claims that he went and addressed the whole team and said, ‘We need to take collective responsibility for this.’ He said everyone was in that room. So, I found that really fascinating,” Gillespie said in a video posted by ABC Sports on X.
Lehmann, meanwhile, also questioned the timing of Khawaja’s revelations, suggesting that the publication of the latter’s account could be linked to his book.
“That’s part and parcel of selling books, I suppose. I don’t know what he’s getting paid. He’s probably getting paid a lot of money to do it. Is it worth it? I don’t know. Maybe I’ll write a book. Things are left unsaid sometimes for the good of the game and the good of the people. But it is what it is. You’ve just got to deal with it, don’t you? Each time it comes up. It’ll happen somewhere else, I’m sure.”
Lehmann said he had not spoken to Khawaja about the claims, adding that the Sandpapergate episode does bring back difficult memories.
“It’s not easy to talk about even now, and then you go back there, and I don’t know any way else to say this, but it puts you back in a bad place. So hopefully I can just get through this, and we move forward again,” he said.
Smith and Warner were handed 12-month suspensions from international and domestic cricket after the scandal, while Bancroft was sanctioned for nine months. Lehmann, despite being cleared of his involvement in the scandal, resigned as head coach after the tour and also apologised for Australia’s actions.
