The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) seized drugs and cosmetics worth ₹34.51 lakh, cancelled 122 licences and suspended 422 others following enforcement action across the State in October 2026, according to a press note issued by the department on Thursday (November 5, 2026).
The FDA conducted 1,986 inspections of drug manufacturing, sales and other regulated establishments during the month and issued 674 notices. Of these, 1,694 inspections were conducted at drug sales establishments and 292 at manufacturing and other regulated establishments. The department cancelled 105 licences and suspended 367 licences of sales establishments, while 17 licences were cancelled and 55 suspended in the manufacturing and other categories.
The department also carried out 11 search and seizure operations involving alleged violations related to the manufacture, storage and sale of drugs and cosmetics. Two FIRs were registered, and four persons were arrested under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act in connection with the illegal sale of narcotic drugs.
Among the major seizures, FDA officials recovered allopathic drugs worth ₹22.03 lakh from the premises of Phoenix Medicorp in Nagpur on October 7. According to the department, the establishment had stored drugs at unlicensed premises despite surrendering its licences.
In Mumbai, FDA officials seized spurious drugs identified as Empirime tablets and Cardiurex 2 ml, worth ₹1.01 lakh, from INHS Asvini in Colaba on October 29, according to the department.
In separate operations in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar on October 14 and 25, officials seized 199 Nitrosun 10 tablets containing Nitrazepam. Four persons were arrested in connection with their alleged illegal sale.
The FDA also seized cosmetic soaps worth ₹4.05 lakh from Vedas Herbals Mahila Gruh Udyog in Baramati, Pune district, on October 14, for alleged manufacturing without a licence. In Vasai East, officials seized raw materials, packaging materials and machinery worth ₹1.83 lakh from G.B. Cosmetics on October 10 in connection with alleged unlicensed manufacture and sale of nail polish.
The Konkan division recorded the highest number of inspections in October at 556, followed by Pune with 375 and Greater Mumbai with 322. Konkan also accounted for the highest number of regulatory actions at 156, followed by Greater Mumbai with 105 and Pune with 77.
Between April 1 and October 31, the FDA conducted 7,950 inspections across Maharashtra, issued 2,888 notices, cancelled 555 licences and suspended 2,074 licences. The department recorded 2,629 regulatory actions, comprising licence cancellations and suspensions, during the seven-month period.
The FDA urged citizens to report instances of illegal drug manufacturing or sales, as well as suspected substandard drugs, medical devices and cosmetics, to its commissioner’s office or the nearest district office.

"The race is too hard for women. They are simply not tough enough to do it."
Those are the words of Lazarus Lake, race director of the Barkley Marathons - one of the world's hardest ultramarathons which to date, of the approximate 1,000 people who have started, only 20 have ever completed.
Speaking in 2015 and daring for someone to prove him wrong, it took nine years until a British ultra-runner did just that.
Completing the extreme 100-mile course with just one minute 39 seconds to spare of the 60-hour cut-off, Jasmin Paris from Midlothian made history and cemented her name in the ultra-running history books.
But now, increasingly, she is not alone.
Last summer, there was a female one-two for the first time in the gruelling Montane Summer Spine Race from Derbyshire to Scotland. Rachel Entrekin set a new course record and became the first woman to win the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May, while last month Sophie Woods smashed the overall record by six days to complete the Via Alpina.
It appears female runners are no longer just taking part in ultra-endurance events, they are competing with their male counterparts, breaking records and in some cases, winning races outright.
All of this has prompted suggestions that they are perhaps better suited to these kinds of challenges.
But is there any scientific proof? Do women really have any physiological or psychological advantages in endurance exercise (anything that takes more than six hours)? And if so, could we see more of these records fall in the future?
In running distances up to the marathon, there is on average a 10-12% performance gap between males and females.
Men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine.
But as the distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow.
The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study of more than 20 years of amateur ultra-race data conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners,
Anything further than 195 miles and women have the potential to be faster.
So why might this be the case?
For Professor Andy Jones, an expert in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, there are three potential physiological explanations why women could perform better over longer distances or durations.
Fat metabolism – women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer.
Muscles – women have more oxygen-efficient muscle fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities.
Fatigue resistance – women retain more strength over hours of endurance exercise.
However, Jones, who played a key role in Eliud Kipchoge's sub two-hour marathon challenge in 2019, is keen to point out that the science in this area is "behind".
"There isn't as much hard evidence as there would be for shorter distances, which have been studied for a long time in quite some detail," he adds.
That is a view shared by Dr Richard Burden, co-lead of female athlete health and performance at the UK Sports Institute, who feels a lot more information needs to be gathered before conclusions can be made.
"At the moment we are speculating … there are definitely some physiological adaptations that you see more in women than men that are favourable for ultra-type events. But those need to be better established and more studies would need to be done."
Physiology, however, only gets you so far. The realities of ultra-endurance exercise - multi-day events, sleep deprivation, extreme terrain and conditions, to name but a few – mean the journey to the finish line is as much mental as it is physical.
And for Sophie Woods, this is where women have the edge.
"It's not necessarily about being the fastest person at the start," she says. "It is about preparation, it is about mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong."
During the New Zealand runner's record-breaking run of the Via Alpina, she was forced to expect the unexpected – from disruption caused by wildfires that made her route longer and more dangerous to swarms of horseflies.
"I was so tired and there were so many of them and I wanted to have a complete meltdown and just cry, but I couldn't because if I stopped moving, they started biting me," she says.
"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing and just knowing that once we start something, you've just got to keep moving until you get to the finish."
That view is echoed by Yngvild Kaspersen, who last month became the first woman to win the prestigious Ultra-Trail Mont Blanc CCC race in the Alps twice. She credits her victory to the "mental game" she puts herself through in training.
The Norwegian, who balances life as a professional runner with her job as a GP, also believes female ultra-runners are so strong because camaraderie in the community is unrivalled.
"We're competitors but we're also motivating each other, inspiring each other, pushing each other to do better in the races," she says. "If you see the podiums for the women this year [at UTMB], how close we are and how we're running together out there - that's very special and I'm very proud to be a part of that community and that group of women."
So can we explain why women might be more resilient?
Sports dietitian Renee McGregor, who specialises in athlete nutrition and hormonal health, believes the answer comes from the female body itself.
"The moment women step into puberty, we are dealing with a fluctuating hormonal system," she says. "We never ever give ourselves credit for that, it's just an accepted part of being female. But actually, it is an endurance in itself and I think that's probably where a big part of our resilience comes from."
McGregor, an ultra-runner herself, points to research that suggests female runners display more disciplined and even pacing strategies than men in distance races, maximising on what she terms the female "brain bank".
"I don't think women go into these races without a lot of thought and contingency planning," McGregor adds.
"For example, if you've been through a pregnancy and you've dealt with nausea, if you've had a baby and dealt with the lack of sleep or if you've gone through fertility treatment, you have to go through so much discomfort, but you know you can get through it. And I think it's that knowledge of 'I can get through this, I can find a solution'."
One of the biggest reasons why we cannot talk with any certainty about the potential physiological and psychological advantages that women may have in this field is because participation numbers are low, with women making up roughly only 20% of those on ultramarathon start lines.
Research by SheRACES, a network set up by British ultra-runner Sophie Power to correct gender disparities in running, suggests the reasons for this range from societal perceptions around women's abilities, to concerns around the time needed for training, or access to the right support at the events themselves.
Slowly but surely, however, things are starting to change.
Earlier this year, a trail race in New Zealand became the first UTMB World Series event to achieve a 50:50 gender split, while a leading UK race provider has launched a new initiative to target gender parity at its events.
And now, according to Dr Burden, society is talking about the limits of human performance in a different way too.
"Historically, the majority of the time it [the limits of the human] will be established from male models or male sports," he says. "Now we're starting to break it up into the limits of male performance and the limits of female performance and that's a distinction that needs to be made … but to make better comparisons, we would need more women taking part in ultra events."

When it comes to participation, visibility is key.
Kaspersen describes Rachel Entrekin's historic victory at Cocodona 250, one of the most demanding ultramarathons in the world, as an "inspiration" among the elites to "dare to try".
And at the amateur level, there are those like Emily Fairs, a 22-year-old ultra-runner who documents the realities of her training and races on social media as part of her mission to get more women of all ages on start lines.
"When it comes to endurance training, there are so many components that come into it and that we are fearful of but by seeing another woman do it you think 'right, if she can do it, if she has the tools, she has the knowledge, she has the ability to do all these crazy difficult challenges, then so do I. I'm no different to her. She's no different to me'," says Fairs.
Fairs says she has received thousands of messages from women about how her content has encouraged them to lace up their trainers, and believes recent trends of female success in ultra-running are just the start.
"When the proportion is so low, we have no clue what women are capable of. We're starting to see more women get faster and enter the sport and push themselves and break records. So, who knows where we'll be 10-15 years later down the line?"

Gurdial Singh Bhangu, the former coach of the Indian women’s hockey team that won the 2002 Commonwealth Games, has passed away aged 86.
“His contribution to Indian hockey will always be remembered. Our heartfelt condolences to his family and loved ones,” Hockey India said in a statement on Saturday.
Bhangu was born in 1941 in Lyallpur — now known as Faisalabad in Pakistan — in pre-independent India. He grew up in Ambala and played university-level hockey before joining the National Institute of Sports (NIS), Patiala, where he was an understudy of hockey legend Dhyan Chand as well as 1956 Olympics gold medallist Balkishan Singh.
Bhangu was also head coach of the Nigerian women’s team from 1972 to 1976, helping it qualify for its first World Cup in 1976.
He took charge as India’s women’s head coach in 1998 after the team finished 12th in the World Cup. He inspired the team to an Asian Games silver medal a few months later, only to take the team to larger heights a few years later.
At the Commonwealth Games 2002 final, India beat England 3-2 in Manchester, with Mamta Kharab scoring a golden goal in extra time.
Bhangu was honoured with the Dronacharya Award in 2000, becoming the first hockey coach to receive it. He later moved to Surrey, Canada, and passed away there on Friday.

Indian security personnel carrying batons and shields and accompanied by riot control vehicles surrounded the site of a planned opposition protest in Delhi on Sunday that is set to demand the resignation of the country’s election chief over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Authorities warned of traffic diversions ahead of the protest march and rally that will be led by Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi. The opposition says it expects hundreds of thousands of people to participate in what it says will be a major challenge to the prime minister, Narendra Modi, and his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
Opposition parties, student organisations and the youth-led Cockroach Janta party have held near-daily demonstrations since last month demanding that the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, step down over the voter list revision that critics say favours the BJP.
The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol, while the BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Analysts say the youth protests, and growing support for the opposition, form the worst crisis for Modi since he came to power in 2014. But his government remains stable and the next general election is not due until 2029.
The opposition parties have announced they will hold a nearly 1.5km march on Sunday from central Delhi to the Ramlila Maidan, a ground that is the designated site for their protest rally.
Visuals from news agency ANI showed riot control vehicles and dozens of security personnel armed with batons and shields outside the rally venue, where announcements were being made urging people to ensure smooth traffic movement and cooperate with police officials.
Delhi traffic police said a “large gathering” was expected at the venue, and traffic regulations and diversions would be implemented “as required”.
“People have started coming to participate in this rally ... we have ensured proper arrangements at the venue, and arrangements are also planned on the route of the march that will happen in a few hours from now,” senior police officer Rohit Rajbir told ANI.
The protests demanding Kumar’s resignation erupted after the Indian Express newspaper reported in September that his two deputies had raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.
The change, which began last year, removed over 130 million names from voter lists, including 28 million who died, 63 million who relocated and 30 million who could not be traced.
Opposition parties allege the deletions disproportionately affect Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party – allegations the poll panel and BJP reject.

He was briefed at the Sukna-headquartered 33 Corps, near Siliguri.
“Sukna and its surrounding region is a critical hub for the movement of supplies, weaponry, food, medical provisions and personnel to forward locations. Its geographical sensitivity necessitates round-the-clock operational readiness,” Singh said.
Deep Dive
Army chief General Dhiraj Seth, Eastern Army commander Lieutenant General VMB Krishnan, and corps commander Lieutenant General Man Raj Singh Mann were present.
The defence minister is scheduled to visit the Sherathang war memorial in Sikkim on Diwali to pay tribute to Indian soldiers killed in the 1967 Nathu La and Cho La clashes with China. The battles ended in a decisive Indian victory, with one account putting Indian casualties at 88, against 340 on the Chinese side.
In Bagdogra, also near Siliguri, Singh asked the armed forces to strengthen cyber resilience, information integrity and domain awareness to boost combat readiness and tackle emerging threats. Security landscape has become more complex, with warfare stretching beyond conventional engagements along the borders to include “asymmetric warfare, proxy wars, cyber-attacks, drone swarms, information operations and narrative management,” he said while interacting with air warriors at Air Force Station, Bagdogra.
“Often, the adversary avoids direct confrontation and instead seeks to exploit our vulnerabilities. Through social media, the adversary may attempt to sow doubt in the minds of the local population and our soldiers by spreading misleading information. In such a scenario, your role extends beyond that of an ordinary soldier,” Singh said.
IAF chief Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit was also present.
Singh described Bagdogra as a strategically important region and a crucial link in India’s security framework, particularly for the North-east.
A December 2025 report of the parliamentary committee on external affairs contained pointed mentions about Chinese activities in areas surrounding the so-called “chicken’s neck,” or the Siliguri Corridor—the territory linking India’s strategic northeastern states to the rest of the country.
The report on “Future of India-Bangladesh relationship” said China’s increasing footprint in Bangladesh, especially through infrastructure and port development and military cooperation, is a concern though the government is taking all measures to safeguard India’s national interests.
Singh said that the air warriors deployed in the region serve as a robust shield for the security of the eastern sector, and their preparedness is fundamental to maintaining stability in the region. “The more you engage with the local community, the weaker the adversary’s conspiracies will become.”
He described the revamped Agnipath scheme as a Diwali gift for Agniveers, while reiterating the government’s commitment to the welfare of military personnel and their families. The new Agnipath framework will apply only to existing Agniveers who miss out on retention, giving them two more years in uniform and another shot at becoming permanent soldiers, as first reported by Hindustan Times. Essentially, all current Agniveers will become permanent after this two year extended service, subject to meeting specific eligibility criteria and individual consent

Cheavon Clarke hands Chris Billam-Smith first stoppage loss in stunning upset win over former world champion
Cheavon Clarke beat former world champion Chris Billam-Smith at the Copper Box Arena in London; Billam-Smith had never been dropped before but Clarke put him over twice before the referee halted the Bournemouth star
Sunday 8 November 2026 01:51, UK
Cheavon Clarke scored a stunning stoppage win over Chris Billam-Smith at the Copper Box Arena in London.
He not only knocked the former world champion down for the first time in Billam-Smith's career, he put him over twice and handed the Bournemouth star a first stoppage defeat.
Halted on the ropes, as Clarke's right hooks streaked in, Billam-Smith at once shook his head to protest as the referee waved it off.
Clarke, after a thrilling win over Jack Massey last time out, was looking for a big-name scalp that would launch him into the top class of the division. He got it.
Billam-Smith had been seeking to exact some personal vengeance too. Clarke had beaten him in a pivotal national amateur championship final 10 years ago. The Bournemouth man had subsequently converted himself from amateur nearly man to elite professional champion. But, a decade on, Clarke once again handed him a bitterly painful defeat.
They began the first round busily with frenetic work. Clarke, full of energy, winged shots over. His head swung in too wildly, but it was a right hand over the top that gave Billam-Smith pause for thought.
Clarke popped Billam-Smith with a left hook as the former champion charged after him. Rolling under a left hook, Clarke moved off. He snuck his right round Billam-Smith's guard. Billam-Smith swallowed another right but dug in an uppercut with his backhand.
A right flew in and Clarke grabbed him in a clinch. He then answered with a cracking right to the jaw himself. But Billam-Smith, renowned for his toughness, took it stolidly.
In the third round Clarke blasted an excellent right uppercut between Billam-Smith's elbows. He touched his chin with the left hook and reached Billam-Smith with a long cross.
Manoeuvring for position in a clinch, Clarke whipped his left hook over. Billam-Smith bulled into him in a physical, frenetic fight, finishing the fourth round swinging hooks.
Early in the fifth round Clarke went for Billam-Smith. They traded hard hits.
The clinching, a frequent feature of the fight, appeared to leave them both frustrated. Clarke popped in a clean jab, but Billam-Smith ground forward onto the front foot.
Billam-Smith hit out with thudding power in the sixth round. Clarke sighed out a breath and stepped back, briefly losing the shape of his boxing.
But in the seventh round it was stunning to see Clarke bomb Billam-Smith over with a right. The Bournemouth man struggled back to his feet and Clarke swarmed forward. As Billam-Smith tried to escape from the ropes, Clarke knocked him down again.
He attacked Billam-Smith once more on the ropes. Billam-Smith's leg stuttered, but he had his feet under him when referee Lee Every moved in to end it.
'I'd love to run it back'
"I'm fine. It was a good shot. He buzzed me, obviously," Billam-Smith said afterwards. "It was a great shot. I made a mistake, but I felt like I was winning the fight.
"Fair play to Chev. We've had three fights now and he's got them all. I'd love to run it back and get him eventually."
Clarke beamed: "Underdog to who? Not us!
"I don't care about a label. I'm Chev Clarke and that's all that matters."

The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.
The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.
Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.
His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.
Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.
In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.
Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.
The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.
It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.
In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated to the Shakahola forest, police said.
The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.
Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.
Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.
The plight of his followers began to emerge in March 2023, when a man told police his brother and wife had starved their children to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.
Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date on which he told his followers the world would end. Police rearrested him and started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.
Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.
Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.
Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.
Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

The 5pm performance at the Hong Kong Cultural Centre involved nearly 600 musicians and singers from six choirs: the Hong Kong Philharmonic Chorus; the Learners Chorus; the London Philharmonic Choir; St Paul’s Co-educational College Senior Mixed-Voice Choir; Ying Wa College Choir; and the Hong Kong Children’s Choir.

The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?
- Published
Republicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that powered Donald Trump to three straight presidential nominations imploded in spectacular fashion in the 2026 midterms.
The stunning election defeat immediately raised questions about the party's future post-Trump.
But there are no easy answers as Republicans face the choice of doubling down on Trumpism or trying to chart a new path forward in his final years in office.
The depth of the problem was captured by outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans".
Others struck a more optimistic tone. Vice-President JD Vance, who blamed the midterm results on public anger over the war with Iran, argued the party could turn things around. Nevertheless Vance acknowledged the fallout will be messy.
"There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why," Vance said.
The wide range of reactions on the right highlights deep fault lines in the party that formed around Trump's improbable rise to the presidency in 2016 and never really went away.
It's too early to tell which faction will win out. But while Republicans are still licking their wounds, the intraparty battle Vance predicted is already under way.
The party must decide whether it will be "centred on one figure, one guy, or on a wider set of ideas like conservatism that can win outside the deepest red places," Rina Shah, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.
Critics on the right - the "Never Trumpers" who opposed his first White House campaign - are pushing for a return to the Republican Party's pre-Trump roots, citing the historic losses around the country on election night.
But simply turning back the clock on Trump will be extremely difficult if not impossible to do.
The party has been wholly transformed during Trump's decade-long reign. Most Republicans have shifted to the right on domestic issues like immigration, and rejected the interventionist foreign policy of the George W Bush era that led to the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.
In Congress, the more moderate establishment wing of the party that disliked Trump from the start has almost entirely disappeared, replaced by conservative Trump backers who echo his nativism and populist rhetoric.
That trend continued this year, as old-guard Republicans like John Cornyn in Texas and Maine's Susan Collins, both of whom clashed with Trump over the years, were voted out of office.
Three days after the election Trump appointed Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.
The move signalled Trump has no plans to moderate his policies or message in his remaining years in office. Miller, who had been serving as the president's chief domestic policy adviser, is a longtime Trump aide known for his hardline immigration policies.

One of the architects of the Make America Great Again (Maga) movement, Steve Bannon, predicted a "civil war" in the party after the midterms.
Afterwards, he blamed the Republicans' defeat on the economy and "foreign wars". "I don't think we implemented the Maga programme," he said, calling on Trump to double down on mass deportations.
But other Republican strategists said the midterms were a wake up call for Make America Great Again (Maga) loyalists who want Trump's political movement to outlast his presidency.
"There's still plenty of Maga voters out there who have supported Donald Trump through thick and thin," said Whit Ayres, a Republican strategist.
"But there is also a significant portion of the Republican Party that's non-Maga, and that's a majority now."
Should Republican hopefuls distance themselves from Trump?
The party lost control of the House and Senate, as well as governorships and state legislatures in red states like Texas and Kansas where Democrats had been shut out of power for decades - and where Trump won by double digits when he was on the ballot.
The stunning upsets underscored the fickle nature of political coalitions.
Trump expanded the Republican base in 2024, increasing support with Latinos and younger voters among other key groups. Republicans hailed the gains as a sign of future strength for the party.
Just two years later, the party lost ground with nearly every critical voting bloc. According to a New York Times analysis of voter data, Latino support for Democratic candidates increased by 29 percentage points from 2024-26. Support from young voters 18-29 years old increased by 33 points.
The swings reflected polling ahead of the midterms that found widespread disapproval with Trump's handling of the economy, immigration and the war with Iran.
Democrats also capitalised on a public perception that the Trump family and administration is rife with self-dealing and corruption. The president's focus on the White House ballroom and other Washington construction projects also contributed to a sense among voters that he was more focused on his legacy than addressing affordability issues.
It's a sentiment shared by Benjamin Shrader, the leader of the Young Republicans in Austin, who was still shell-shocked when he spoke to the BBC in Texas the morning after his party was almost wiped out in the state by a Democratic "blue tsunami".
Shrader said Trump was still a "force of nature" when asked to reflect on how the president had used his first public appearance after the results to show off the White House ballroom project.
He hesitated before adding: "I would focus on issues that are not ballrooms, that are not renaming things. I would focus on what matters."
The evidence in the immediate aftermath of the midterms suggests that Republicans could benefit by distancing themselves from Trump ahead of 2028.
'Vance was the favourite - now the race is wide open'
Vance tried to thread the needle with his midterm assessment blaming the Iran war and calling for a return to "America First." It was a nuanced critique that broke with Trump on an unpopular war, but embraced a broader political brand that remains popular with the Maga base.
Trump's next moves on Iran will be watched closely by the party for their 2028 implications. An escalation would risk fuelling the concerns voiced by Vance and other "America First" proponents.
In his postmortem statement on X, Vance also echoed the growing calls on the right to reexamine US support for Israel. But he also signalled an openness to making some immigration enforcement changes. That clashes with Miller, a Vance ally who has speared the administration's second-term immigration agenda.
Party strategists said the midterm drubbing complicated Vance's path to the nomination.
"Before this midterm, JD Vance was the odds-on favourite to win the Republican nomination in 2028. After this midterm, the nomination battle is completely wide open," Ayres said.
Potential Trump successors have some time to consider their options, but they'll have to make up their minds relatively soon. Any 2028 presidential hopefuls will face pressure to announce White House bids in the next few months. Some could launch campaigns before the end of the year.
Vance's election analysis was widely interpreted as an unofficial signal of his plans to run. It will likely be a crowded primary field.
Other rumoured White House contenders include Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Florida Governor DeSantis, former US ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, to name a few.
In the next election cycle, Republican presidential and congressional candidates alike will have tough decisions to make on key issues of the day, from US support for Israel to tariffs to the AI boom.
Trump's power may be diminished as he enters the final two years of his second term, but he'll still have the loudest voice in the party over the next two years. It's unclear whether he will get deeply involved in the process or take a hands-off approach.
Trump has praised Vance and Rubio at different times, but typically deflects questions about who he'd like to see succeed him.
His endorsement will loom as the biggest wildcard in the 2028 Republican primary race.
"It remains to be seen who will jump into that race," Ayres said.
"But I think it's going to be a lot larger and more diverse than we anticipated before the midterm election."

Vietnam withdrew on Monday a proposal allowing children aged 15 to 17 to donate their organs after death following public criticism in a country where deceased donor transplants remain limited.
The Southeast Asian country began kidney transplants in 1992 and performs the most annual transplants in the region, according to state media.
However, the vast majority of transplants in Vietnam rely on living donors. Transplants in many other nations mostly use organs from deceased donors, expanding their donor pool.
Officials in Vietnam say they are seeking to update a 2006 law on organ and tissue donation, aiming to increase life-saving transplants while safeguarding donors.
A draft submitted to the National Assembly last month proposed allowing 15- to 17-year-olds to donate their tissues, organs or bodies after death, provided the child's parent or legal representative consented.
But, after online backlash, officials removed the under-18 donor provision from a revised draft dated Sunday, with the government saying it had accepted recommendations from lawmakers that only legal adults should be permitted to donate their organs.
Dissent is heavily restricted in communist Vietnam, but opposition centred on whether parental consent could adequately protect child donors from pressure or exploitation.
Criticism also focused on a survey of schoolchildren as young as seven conducted in October to gather feedback on the draft law.
The poll prompted questions about whether minors could understand complex medical, legal and ethical issues, state outlet Tuoi Tre News said.
It said "the provision allowing minors to register as posthumous organ donors prompted considerable controversy and differing opinions among the public".
"Taking these concerns into account, the government has revised the draft," stipulating that only people aged 18 or older may donate their organs, Tuoi Tre said.
National Assembly deputy Pham Khanh Phong Lan urged lawmakers last month to oppose allowing child organ donors, saying: "You cannot sacrifice one child to save another."
One Threads user posted on Monday: "The power of public scrutiny has paid off. It is a relief to see this draft proposal rejected."
The newly revised draft still allows living minors to donate regenerative tissue, for bone marrow or stem cell transplants, to family members when no suitable adult donor is available.
The procedure would require health assessments, counselling and consent from both the child and their legal representative.
A draft law is expected to be approved this month.

Israel's Arab-led parties in spotlight after inconclusive election
KUFR QASI, Israel — In recent years many Palestinian citizens of Israel shunned elections, believing there was little to gain from participating in the politics of a state which, they say, regularly marginalizes their communities and oppresses their fellow Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.
But last month, Palestinian Arabs in Israel came to the ballot boxes in record numbers, helping strip Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's most far-right government in Israel's history of its majority, and giving Arab-led parties the votes they needed to become a powerful force in Israeli politics.
"We blocked the government of Netanyahu from continuing," said Jamal Zahalka, chairman of the High Follow-Up Committee, the main umbrella body representing Palestinian citizens of Israel. "It's a historical achievement. I think our community found its strength."
Neither Netanyahu's coalition, nor his main challenger Gadi Eisenkot's center-right opposition, reached the threshold of 61 seats needed to form a government. Arab-led parties won 19 out of 120 seats – enough to give them a critical role in the negotiations that will now determine who governs Israel at this turbulent moment in the country's history.
The election results strike at the heart of the decades-long questions about how Israel defines itself and the role of Palestinian Arabs in its society.
'The Story Still Isn't Over'
At a park in the Palestinian-majority town of Kufr Qasim two days after the election, hundreds of people gathered for the annual commemoration of residents gunned down in 1956 by Israeli border police on the opening day of the Suez Crisis in the violent early years of the state, when Israel, Britain and France attacked Egypt after it nationalized the Suez Canal.
"And today we stand here, 70 years later," the speaker told the large crowd from a podium: "And the story still isn't over."
The crowd at this event, mostly dressed in black — some wearing the keffiyeh, the black and white stitched scarf symbolizing Palestinian resistance — mourned not only their lost relatives all those years ago, but also the suffering of Palestinians now: the sharp rise in discrimination against their communities in Israel since the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023; Israel's war against Hamas in Gaza that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and left a population to survive amid the ruins of the enclave. And the actions of Netanyahu's extreme right-wing government in the occupied West Bank, where rights groups and the U.N. say it has armed and supported settlers as they force Palestinians from their homes and agricultural lands with unprecedented violence.
Worsening rights inside Israel was one reason, residents of Kufr Qasm told NPR, why so many Palestinian citizens in Israel went to the ballot boxes. "There is no freedom anymore," said Intisar Sarsur, 65, sitting with relatives beside an olive tree in the park in Kufr Qasim. " We are seeking for our basic rights as human beings."
"Everybody that I know participated in the elections. Not one person stayed home," Sarsur said. She and her family were sharing platters of mutabbaq, a sweet Palestinian layered pastry, and freshly pressed olive oil from this year's olive harvest – usually a joyous moment in the Palestinian calendar, that she said now felt bittersweet. This year the olive harvest for Palestinians in the occupied West Bank was marred by frequent attacks by Israeli settlers trying to disrupt this economically and culturally significant time of year.
Palestinian citizens of Israel, descendants of those who remained as the state of Israel was established in 1948 (when a majority of the prewar population was forcibly expelled or fled during the war) now make up about 20 per cent of the population.
This election, Arab-led parties received a 64 percent increase in votes compared to the last elections, according to the Central Elections Committee. The gains they made have stirred anger, and even fear, among many on Israel's political right, who see them as a threat to the country's Jewish character.
Fear Factor
Netanyahu and his allies made the large Arab turnout a rallying cry. On election day, Netanyahu posted a video calling it an "emergency". Itamar Ben Gvir, the far-right national security minister, filmed his own appeal at the entrance to Kufr Qasim: "If you want this country to remain Jewish and Zionist … then get out and vote!"
As results came in, Netanyahu's Likud party went further. It claimed Arab parties had "stolen" the election through bribery, threats and forgery, and later warned of a foreign takeover of the Knesset and the "Islamization of Israel." The party has made no evidence public. Police say they found no basis for the claims, and election officials say there was no widespread fraud. The head of the elections committee separately asked the Shin Bet security service to investigate suspected foreign funding of efforts to boost Arab turnout. But he and the attorney general say the vote was conducted properly and the results were not compromised.
The messaging by Netanyahu's bloc is widely seen as an attempt to prevent Eisenkot's center-right grouping from partnering with Arab parties — a reality that would give Eisenkot the majority he needs to form a government. But the sharp rise in anti-Arab sentiment since the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks, in which some 1,200 people were killed, has made an alliance with any Arab party potentially politically treacherous and could cause other Jewish right wing members of his bloc to split off in fury.
Eisenkot is not a natural ally for Arab parties either. A former military chief of staff whose son was killed fighting in Gaza, he served as an observer in Netanyahu's war cabinet early in the war. And he still cuts a hawkish figure. As a general, he is credited with formulating the "Dahiyeh doctrine," which he laid out in 2008: using "disproportionate force" against villages from which militants fire on Israel, which he called "not civilian villages" but "military bases." It is named after Beirut's southern suburbs, a Hezbollah stronghold that Israel largely decimated in heavy bombardment in 2006.
So Arab parties are divided on how to use the power they gained in this election. Ra'am, a socially conservative Islamist party, campaigned on joining a governing coalition and put a Jewish former police official second on its list. But for now the Joint List alliance that won 11 of the 19 Arab-led party seats in this election won't formally partner with Eisenkot. Its leaders have said they could back his government from the outside, but won't join it, citing Israel's ongoing war in Gaza and its occupation of the West Bank.
President Isaac Herzog has been consulting with parties over who they would support to try to form a coalition. He is expected to announce which candidate he'll give a mandate to next week, to try to form a coalition. That candidate will have 28 days and can ask for a further two-week extension. If he fails, another candidate is given only 28 days (without extension) to try to form a government. And if no one manages to form a coalition, there will be repeat elections next year.
In Kufr Qasim, as the readings and re-enactments of the 1956 killings unfurled on stage, Mansour Shaaban said he would vote again in an instant. Aged 33, this was the first election he had voted in. But now he said it's necessary to try to stop what he called the racism and oppression of Palestinians by Israel's extreme right. "There are Israelis we eat with and live alongside," Shaaban said. But Netanyahu and Ben-Gvir and other leaders in these last years he said "are making it impossible to co-exist," he said.
"Even if we don't succeed to create change this time," he said, now right-wing Israeli politicians know that Palestinian citizens of the country have found their voice.
Nuha Musleh contributed to this report

The TDP and its allies, the JSP and the BJP, continued their stellar performance in the elections to the Zilla and Mandal Parishad Territorial Constituencies (ZPTCs and MPTCs) after crushing the YSRCP in the Urban Local Body (ULB) polls. Japan announces emergency cybersecurity package following a wave of attacks
Japan has announced an emergency cybersecurity package that includes AI and cyber rescue teams
TOKYO -- Japan on Friday announced an emergency cybersecurity package that includes the use of artificial intelligence and cyber rescue teams after a wave of massive data breaches hit major companies and government agencies.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told a ministerial meeting Friday that a rapid response to potential attacks is essential in the era of AI-generated attacks. She urged both government agencies and companies to step up their preparedness.
The emergency package comes after dozens of companies and government agencies were hit by unauthorized access to their systems and leaks of client data, prompting uneasiness across Japan.
"At this very moment, cases of unauthorized access and data breaches are occurring, causing a major impact on daily lives of the people and corporate activities,” Takaichi said. “Let us increase the response capability across Japan by devoting all government resources.”
Measures in the 10 billion yen ($63 million) package are designed to build a resilient society in which the public and private sectors share information, provide swift assistance to the affected and recover from damage.
It aims to acquire one of the world’s highest levels of cybersecurity.
The government will enhance its capability to access servers used by hackers as a preemptive measure known as “active cyber defense,” which was legalized in October.
In case of a possible challenge to Japan’s national security, the government will deploy a support team of officials from the Defense Ministry, the National Police Agency and the National Cybersecurity Office.
Under the measures in the package, a “top gun" team of cybersecurity experts will be set up by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry by the end of November. Team members will use AI to counter hackers and detect weaknesses in network systems. They are to cooperate with technology companies and advanced AI developers of friendly nations to keep Japan's security expertise up to date.
There will also be a “cyber rescue team” of experts from the public and private sectors to provide initial responses to companies affected by cyberattacks. A separate team will help vulnerable companies to strengthen their defenses.

OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI have all asked creator Matt Husk to collaborate following the viral success of his videos trolling AI models.
During the WIRED World Fair on Wednesday, Husk told the crowd “all the big AI companies” have inquired about working with him, including Elon Musk’s xAI, which Husk claimed offered a Tesla for a week if he made videos exclusively for the firm.
The comedian has gained some 2 million followers combined across Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube, as well as a deal with the talent agency Unicorn, through videoing himself making deadpan requests to ChatGPT’s voice model—asking it to count to 100, or to beatbox, for example. His viral videos have exposed the weaknesses of OpenAI’s LLM, which comically botches the tasks and swings between sycophancy and gaslighting Husk, and earned him the title of “Sam Altman’s worst nightmare.”
In April, Altman, nodding and smiling, admitted on tech podcast Mostly Human that the model’s inability to set an accurate timer was a “known issue” and would be for another year, after being shown a Husk video in which he asked ChatGPT to time him running a mile and found that it measured a span of a few seconds as lasting “around 10 minutes.” When Husk says “I swear I was faster than that,” it replies with a sympathetic tone: “It can feel faster in the moment.”
During his interview at WIRED World Fair with Shell Game podcast host Evan Ratliff, Husk said OpenAI offered him early access to a patch for the timer issue if he shared his account. He declined. The company had previously emailed Husk asking to collaborate on a video. “They offered me the smallest amount,” he said. “I was just like, ‘No.’” The firm then offered to send him gifts and asked for his home address; Again, Husk declined.
OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI (which was recently rolled into SpaceX to create SpaceXAI and then SpaceXSI after President Trump renamed artificial intelligence “super intelligence”) did not respond to requests for comment.
AI labs are increasingly pitching their products as capable of handling everyday chores. On Tuesday, OpenAI announced its model had scored “very highly” on a benchmark built to model its ability to help people in their personal lives, such as meal prep and enrolling a child in kindergarten. “The way they promote it is like ‘It can do anything,’” Husk said, “so I’ll put it to the test—see if it can order bread for me.” In one of his videos, Husk asks AI to help him negotiate some bread on Craigslist down from a starting price of $10,000 to $5. The model accepts a price of $400.
Husk began publicly trolling chatbots about a year ago. He told Ratliff, a WIRED contributor, at the time he liked to make TikToks asking people questions, but there weren’t many around while he was working his landscaping job, and he ran out of ideas. So he recorded himself telling ChatGPT a nuclear bomb had gone off. The model’s response, “I’m rooting for you,” and advice to take shelter “was not helpful at all,” he said. “I thought it was a pretty bad video,” he told Ratliff, “and the next morning I had 100,00 views, and I was like, ‘Let’s tell it I got hit by a train.’”
Since then, Husk has secured brand partnerships with CeraVe and Ninja. He also has an upcoming original series with The Onion, where he learns complicated skills, like being a mime, over Zoom. “I'm spending too much time talking to AI,” Husk explained, “so I'm going to branch out and learn stuff from humans.”
While Husk finds himself talking to AI a lot to scope out ideas for videos, “I don't really use it in that creative sense,” such as to generate ideas, he said, because they would all be “too similar.” “I'd rather just have my worst idea at least be my idea rather than AI's idea for a video,” he said.

Ramayana – Part I, starring Ranbir Kapoor and Yash, has begun its fourth day on a strong note at the Indian box office. The much-awaited mythological epic has collected Rs. 25.29 crores nett across all languages as of 12 noon on Sunday, November 8, registering substantial growth over the corresponding collections on its previous three days. However, with Sunday coinciding with Diwali and Lakshmi Puja, the film faces an unusual challenge, as evening festivities could impact theatrical footfalls.
To put things into perspective, Ramayana had collected Rs. 20.37 crores nett by 12 noon on its opening day, Thursday, November 5. The corresponding figure dropped to approximately Rs. 10 crores on Friday before improving to Rs. 17.84 crores on Saturday. Sunday's Rs. 25.29 crore collection represents growth of 41.76% over Saturday and 24.15% over Thursday at the same reporting time. Compared with Friday, collections have more than doubled.
The improvement is particularly noteworthy considering that the film collected Rs. 67.80 crores nett on Saturday, its highest single-day business so far. With Sunday starting ahead of Saturday at the corresponding reporting point, the film has demonstrated strong early-day demand.
On Day 4, Ramayana registered morning occupancy of 35.9%, which improved to 39% for afternoon shows. Evening occupancy has been reported at 46.7%, although the figure remains provisional and could change as more show data becomes available.
Sunday, November 8, coincides with Diwali, one of the most important festivals in India. Traditionally, theatrical business can face challenges on Lakshmi Puja day, particularly during the evening. A large section of the audience is occupied with religious ceremonies at home and in offices, while many families spend the evening visiting relatives and friends. Consequently, even films enjoying strong audience interest may witness a slowdown during certain evening hours on Diwali. The potential impact of Lakshmi Puja on evening footfalls will therefore be a crucial factor in determining Sunday's eventual box office total.
Karnataka and Maharashtra lead; Bengaluru and Mumbai emerge as strongest cities.
In terms of geographical performance, Karnataka and Maharashtra have emerged as the two biggest contributors to Ramayana's Sunday nett collections so far.
At the city level, Bengaluru occupies the top position, followed by Mumbai.
