Italian chef fired after refusing to put pineapple on pizza
- Published
An Italian chef sacked from a Brisbane restaurant had refused to put pineapple on a pizza because it was an "insult to his culture".
Davide Tamburella was fired from the now-closed La Costa restaurant in May, a fortnight after a meeting with management who had a string of complaints about the chef's behaviour.
Among them were Tamburella's refusal to provide ham and pineapple pizza for guests at a function. At the time, the chef had stated that any direction from management "need not be followed when it is offensive to his culture".
The details came to light after the chef went to Australia's Fair Work Commission claiming he had been unfairly dismissed.
In its ruling released on Tuesday, the commission noted that Tamburella's refusal to put pineapple on the pizzas was because "he considers, as an Italian, that putting pineapple on a pizza is an insult to his culture".
It also noted that it was the third time Tamburella had refused to use the fruit on pizzas in the past four years.
He had previously requested his boss to "check how important it is for Italians not to put pineapple on a pizza".
The state of Queensland, where the restaurant is located, is considered Australia's pineapple heartland and produces all of the country's commercially-grown pineapples.
On the Sunshine Coast, visitors regularly stop to take photos next to The Big Pineapple, a heritage-listed 16m-tall fibreglass model of the fruit, which has become a local landmark.
Other concerns were raised about Tamburella using foul language, his communication style and "escalation of frustration in the workplace".
The ruling also detailed an incident at work in April this year where Tamburella fractured bones in his right hand when he struck a metal hand rail.
Tamburella had been hoping the restaurant would sponsor a visa for him that allows skilled workers to be permanent residents.
However after his sacking, the restaurant ended that process, the tribunal heard.
He lost his unfair dismissal claim on the grounds that the application had been filed too late, according to the ruling.
The restaurant's managing director, Elliot Ingram, told the Daily Mail there was "more to this story than a pizza topping".
The BBC has approached Tamburella for comment.
On the chef's LinkedIn profile, he describes himself as someone who, throughout his career, has focused on "delivering exceptional food" and "improving business performance".
Three months ago he posted a "letter for chefs" with the theme "respecting the ingredients".
The LinkedIn profile states he now works at another Brisbane restaurant. A BBC check has found that pineapple is not on that restaurant's menu.

Pope Leo begins a 12-day, 3-country South America tour after his cancer surgery
MONTEVIDEO, Uruguay — Pope Leo XIV has arrived in South America for a 12-day, three-country journey that will be his longest and most far-reaching trip yet, and his first major overseas visit since undergoing lung cancer surgery.
Along the way Leo will take 12 flights, including two helicopter rides, give 36 speeches and visit 10 cities including Cusco, Peru, which sits more than 11,000 feet above sea level. Even the heartiest of travelers can experience altitude sickness there and may require supplemental oxygen.
Last month, Leo underwent surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung. Vatican officials say he has completed his two-week recovery period and requires no further treatment.
The Vatican's new communications chief Maria Montserrat Alvarado said the pontiff was eager to begin his journey. "His doctors are very confident and he'll have plenty of medical care on board should something happen," she said.
First stop Uruguay
It's a puzzling choice for the first leg of the pope's anticipated return to South America, where he spent two decades in Peru, first as a missionary then as Bishop of the coastal city of Chiclayo. Uruguay, a small nation of around 3.5 million people, where adoring crowds will be small, is famously Latin America's most secular nation.
When asked why go to Uruguay at all, given the high rate of atheists and strict separation of church and state, communications chief Alvarado answered simply, "Why Not?" Adding, "the Gospel is meant to go everywhere."
Few welcome banners are seen throughout the capital Montevideo, except for large posters of a waving Pope Leo adorning city churches. A huge banner drapes down the facade of the Blessed Sacrament Church, in Montevideo's upscale Pocitos neighborhood, where 70-year old retiree Ana Maria Saprissa was heading for quiet prayer.
We are thankful, agradecida, she says that the pontiff is coming to visit. "His visit gives us such joy because … he remembered us all here in this tiny country that has so many needs," she says.
Uruguay's tradition of separating religion from government and public life dates back more than a century. Christmas has long been officially referred to as Family Day, while Easter week is given the vacation-friendly name Tourism Week.
Only about a third of Uruguayans identify as Catholics and even less say they practice the religion, according to political analyst Mariana Pomiés , director of the public polling firm CIFRA.
But as a practicing Catholic, Pomiés says sometimes Uruguayan and especially officials misinterpret what secularism is. "Secularism is not anti-religion, it's the neutrality of the state in religious matters. But here the neutrality se convirtió en un absoluto … it became an absolute."
Pope celebrates "positive secularism"
Dozens of volunteers cleaned streets, mowed lawns and erected a simple stage outside the tiny brick Our Lady of Guadalupe Church. It's the focal spot for many in the Casavalle neighborhood, a working-class city about a half hour north of Montevideo, where the pope is scheduled to visit on Saturday.
"I am very happy, very glad, very grateful … that eyes have been set here," where many are forgotten and stigmatized, said Father Pablo Coimbra who's served as the community's pastoral leader for the past six years
"For the first time many people who live their lives always on the margins, on the margins of opportunities, of possibilities, of the future, on the margins of a loving gaze ... well, today they are in the heart, in the center," he said.
A proposed papal address to the parliament triggered a swift rebuke from the public and politicos alike and was quickly scrapped. However, Uruguay's left-wing President Yamandú Orsi is overseeing a welcome ceremony outside Montevideo's main cathedral, where Leo is celebrating evening prayers, vespers with church leaders and laypeople.
Sunday mass will take place in Florida, about an hour outside the capital, a town replete with Catholic and national pride. Every Nov. 8, church goers commemorate the Virgin of the Thirty-five, a symbol of Uruguay's independence movement from the Brazilian empire in 1825.
A long awaited Papal return to Argentina
By Sunday, Pope Leo will be in neighboring Argentina, fulfilling a wish of his predecessor, Pope Francis, who had hoped to return to his homeland but never made the trip.
Before his death, Francis had said he didn't want a papal visit to become entangled in Argentina's intensely polarized politics.
Pope Leo's visit to Argentina offers an early test of how he will address the Catholic Church's differences with right-wing populist leaders gaining ground across Latin America. Those tensions have also surfaced in the U.S., where Leo has clashed with President Trump over immigration and the treatment of migrants.
Far-right President Javier Milei's sweeping austerity measures, which have pushed millions of Argentines into poverty, could put him at odds with Leo, who has long championed the poor.
Milei has also embraced data centers and a largely unfettered approach to artificial intelligence regulation, while Pope Leo's inaugural encyclical called for ethical caution and safeguards to protect human dignity in the age of AI.
Saving the best for last?
The final leg of the trip will take Leo back to Peru in what has been billed as a homecoming.
As a missionary priest and later appointed Bishop of the coastal city of Chiclayo, Pope Leo spent two decades in the country. He became a naturalized Peruvian in 2015, and has said the country shaped his life more than anything else.
He will visit several cities and towns where he lived and will meet with President Keiko Fujimori, the daughter of former Peruvian dictator Alberto Fujimori.
As a priest during the Fujimori dictatorship, Leo was openly critical of military violence and human rights abuses and supported efforts leading to Peru's Truth and Reconciliation Commission following the return to democracy.
But for many Uruguayans Pope Leo is not very well known. Walking past the huge stage set up for Leo's welcoming ceremony, Juan Martin Guerreiro said he wasn't sure he would attend the pope's speeches.
"He doesn't feel as influential to me … as Pope Francis," said Guerreiro. But he said he's willing to give the new pope a chance because he is South American.
When reminded that Pope Leo was born in Chicago, Guerreiro said he wouldn't hold that against him.

As a single mom, I always loved the idea of living with friends later in life. I pictured something like "The Golden Girls" — gray hair, grown children, and long days laughing with my closest companions.
I never expected that lifestyle to happen at 41, while I was still raising my kids on my own and figuring out what came next. But that all changed this past summer, when I texted my friend Jennifer and asked if she'd consider moving in with us.
Jennifer and I weren't very close before this. Sure, we checked in on each other from time to time, and would go to dinner or a movie together every few months, but that was it.
Even though we weren't best friends, I still thought she and I would be ideal roommates because we're both clean, organized, and responsible.
Plus, we were both looking for a financial reset. I'd been planning a move to Paris and had put my side hustles on the back burner, but when the move fell through, I was stretched thin as a single mom covering a mortgage alone.
Similarly, at 49, Jennifer was burned out from leading a media network and a mental-health nonprofit. She was also single, living alone in an apartment — since her kids are all grown — and shouldering all her expenses.
We realized that sharing a home could help us both save some money while we figured out our next steps. Because we weren't super close friends to begin with, we didn't have to worry about the arrangement infringing upon our relationship.
And as long as my two teenage kids were fine with it, I felt good about the decision. So, after two weeks of discussion, Jennifer moved in.
Sharing expenses made room for small joys again
The first weekend we lived together, I was surprised there wasn't any awkwardness. She fit right in, asking about our shower schedules, what time we woke up and went to bed, and the WiFi password.
Thankfully, our two-story home gave everyone enough privacy, with my room on the first floor and Jennifer's and my kids' rooms on the second, so we never felt like we were stepping on each other's toes.
Before long, we experienced the biggest payoff: financial relief. Within just a few months of living together, I was finally able to save money again.
It's often said that living alone is a flex, but living with my friend has given me financial breathing room I wouldn't have had otherwise.
My mortgage is around $2,000 a month, and Jennifer pays me $500 for rent. When my children and I are gone for long stretches, she offers to pay a portion of the electricity and water bills. Groceries are our own responsibility, but we share the cost for household items like paper towels and laundry detergent.
Now that I have a roommate who is contributing to the expenses, I can have dinner with girlfriends once a month or buy a book from the bookstore without feeling guilty.
I also can take my kids to lunch at a café or treat them to dinner without feeling panicked.
Plus, Jennifer is less stressed about finances now and can be more selective about the entrepreneurial projects she takes on.
Jennifer became more than a roommate to my kids and me
Beyond the financial benefits, welcoming Jennifer into our home has brought us closer together and made us feel like one large family.
She takes a vested interest in my kids' well-being — offers rides to and from school if they need them, shares her snacks with them, and talks to them about their creative dreams, goals, and projects they're working on.
Even in the simple moments of drinking our morning coffees together, we talk about everything from disappointing encounters with men to our hormones as we get older.
It's not unusual for our Sunday dinners to spill into the late evening with wine, pasta, and long, candlelit conversations around the dinner table.
We all love playing games, or simply sitting at the kitchen island while I read the newspaper, and Jennifer quotes a film nobody else has seen.
Although the arrangement has been beautiful, we've both had to give up some freedom. For example, we have a mutual rule that we don't bring men we're dating back to the house, out of our respect for each other and for my kids' safety.
We've learned to be more conscious of everyday habits, from remembering whose laundry is in the washer to keeping the noise down late at night.
I've also learned to be more intentional about keeping the common areas clean, since the space is no longer just for my kids and me.
Jennifer and I have been living together for six months, and even though I'm not moving abroad anytime soon, I am still very much in transition. I am picking up the pieces of a future I thought I'd have, re-imagining it, and changing direction. It's a relief to do that with someone helping me out.
At this time, we don't know how long we'll live together. Eventually, I would love to move to New York City to be closer to family, which means my time with Jennifer as my roommate would come to an end.
Regardless, both of us have said we'd do it again, and we'd choose this over moving in romantically with a man.

A promising new medicine against heart disease fails unexpectedly
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
An experimental drug doctors hoped would be the next big advance in preventing heart attacks and strokes failed a crucial test, researchers reported Saturday.
The medicine, which reduces levels of a particle in the blood associated with heart attacks and strokes, didn't protect volunteers in a closely watched study.
"I was shocked. I had high hopes for success," says Steven Nissen, a cardiologist at the Cleveland Clinic who led the study. "Cardiovascular disease is still the leading cause of death in developed countries. And so we really were hoping to find additional therapies that would reduce risk."
The research aimed to help people who seem to do everything right. They keep their cholesterol and blood pressure low, eat well, maintain a healthy weight, and exercise regularly. But many still suffer heart attacks and strokes.
"That sort of patient we see very frequently, and we were really doing our best to try to find a way to help those patients," Nissen says.
Many of these patients have elevated blood levels of a cholesterol-carrying protein called lipoprotein(a) or Lp(a), which has long been thought to increase the risk for heart disease.
"About 20% of the global population have elevated levels. And that's about a billion people. So it's a common disorder," Nissen says.
Researchers have been searching for a drug to lower Lp(a)
Until recently, doctors didn't have any drugs that could lower Lp(a) levels. But several drug companies have developed experimental new medications in recent years that can slash elevated Lp(a).
So Nissen and his colleagues gave 8,350 adults who already had heart disease either a placebo or a drug called pelacarsen, which cuts Lp(a).
The drug did suppress Lp(a) levels by about 78%, the researchers showed. But after five years, that drop didn't translate into saving people from suffering cardiovascular complications.
"Very disappointing, terribly disappointing," says Nissen, who presented the first details about the study at an American Heart Association meeting in Chicago Saturday and published more specifics in the New England Journal of Medicine and the NEJM Evidence.
Drugmaker Novartis, which sponsored the study, announced last month that the study results hadn't met its goals but without releasing specifics.
In a statement, Novartis said the study "provides meaningful evidence" about the relationship between Lp(a) and heart disease and may "help inform future approaches to cardiovascular management." "Progress in science depends on pursuing challenging questions and studies [like the pelacarsen study] play a crucial role in moving the field forward, even if the results are not what we had hoped for," the company said.
What went wrong?
The failure of the drug to help patients is stunning because so many scientists, doctors and drug companies hoped Lp(a)-lowering drugs would provide the next major weapon in the fight against cardiovascular disease, which kills more than 900,000 Americans each year.
"I think it's a big deal because the expectation was so high that this would end up being positive," says Harlan Krumholz, a Yale University cardiologist. "And so it was really jarring to see this."
Researchers are scratching their heads about what went wrong.
It could turn out that high Lp(a) doesn't actually cause heart attacks and strokes, but instead is a marker for something else that increases the risk.
There could be other reasons for why the study failed.
"Maybe you need to treat longer. You may need to treat earlier, before people have advanced hardening of the arteries," says Roger Blumenthal, a cardiologist at Johns Hopkins University.
Another possibility is that Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only help people with higher Lp(a) levels.
"Maybe a higher Lp(a) should have been required for entry into the trial," says David Maron, a Stanford University cardiologist who serves as the president of the American Society for Preventive Cardiology.
The pelacarsen study could also have failed because Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only benefit people whose blood pressure and bad cholesterol weren't as well controlled, several experts said.
Another explanation could be that there's something about pelacarsen, the experimental drug, that doesn't produce a benefit.
It's possible other Lp(a)-lowering drugs might.
Several other drugmakers, including Amgen and Eli Lilly, are testing other experimental Lp(a)-lowering drugs. The results of those trials are expected to become available over the next few years.
"The take-home message is the story's not over," says Karol Watson, a cardiologist at the University of California, Los Angeles. "It's kind of just starting."

Book Box: Diwali and the books we give each other
A reflection on parent-child bonds, nostalgic reading, and recommended books for the festive season.
Dear Reader,
It is Diwali morning in Mumbai. Four days ago we left the new home we are still making. The carpenters caught a bus home to Mandi, the masons to Bajaura, the polisher to Bilaspur. The Other Reader and I drove down to the plains, to Chandigarh, and flew to Mumbai to spend Diwali with my parents and my siblings.
In Mumbai, my mother needs containers for her kitchen. Little jars for cardamom, cinnamon, cumin. We go together to the neighbourhood market. The shop down the road is crammed with containers of every kind. My mother finds what she wants. Flushed with the hunter-gatherer thrill of a successful expedition, we go for cold coffee at Poetry and Cheesecake. We share a frappe and talk about how to parent adult children.
The waitress, a friendly young woman in her twenties, brings us the bill inside an anthology of poetry.
My mother pays. Then she opens the book. “’There was a ship,” quoth he,” she begins, and we are both gone. Back to a bungalow in Jamshedpur. Back to the evenings when she read to us, sometimes The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, sometimes The Highwayman.
“It’s been so long,” she says, “since I read aloud.”
She asks if she can buy the book. The waitress smiles and says no. They don’t sell these. It is the only copy, kept for bringing bills to customers. Then she looks at our faces and says, “You can borrow it.”
I want to tell her how much this means to me. My mother has been a little sad and overwhelmed of late, and these poems are just what she needs. I want her to know that this small gesture has made my mother very happy.
Instead, I say, “Thank you, thank you. I live just down the road. I’ll leave my number.”
“That’s okay,” she says. “Just drop it back.”
In the car my mother worries. “I hope she doesn’t get into trouble.” But she is already turning pages, finding her favourites one by one. “Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?” she reads.
“These are the poems I really love. And this print is large enough for my eyes,” she says.
Tonight, after the diyas, we will read them aloud. Tomorrow morning I will take the book back. I hope the young woman is there. I want to tell her what it meant to my mother.
Yesterday the book club met, and it was different. We came dressed in saris. We swapped books, which seemed apt for Diwali. We laughed and joked and squabbled a little. Everyone wanted Leftovers:A History of Food Waste and Preservation by Dr. Eleanor Barnett. Everyone wanted Prayers for Rain, a murder mystery by Dennis Lehane. Nobody wanted Swallowing the Sun by Lakshmi Murdeshwar Puri, a striking hardback with a beautiful cover and a slow-moving story inside.
If you are still looking for books to give this Diwali, here are a few possibilities.
· The one everyone’s talking about: Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke, a satirical suspense novel about a tradwife influencer.
· Feel-good novels about human relationships : Whistler by Ann Patchett or The Correspondent by Virginia Evans.
· Poetry for the shelf: Glass, Irony and God by this year’s Nobel laureate Anne Carson, which includes the extraordinary The Glass Essay. And perhaps an anthology of the fifty greatest poets : something to dip into, and something to read aloud.
· Non-fiction: London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe, a true story about a London teenager’s death set against an extraordinary landscape of crime in the city. Or Marginlands by Arati Kumar-Rao, a book that explores India’s vulnerable landscapes and the people who live in them.
Our borrowed poetry anthology is on the table by the door, to be read aloud and then given back.
Happy Diwali and happy reading. I’d love to know: is there a poem someone read to you as a child that you still remember?
Sonya Dutta Choudhury is a Mumbai-based journalist, Founder of Sonya’s Book Box, and a teacher of Storytelling in Business. Got a knot in your life, a dilemma at work, or a reading slump you can’t shake? Send your questions and book requests to sonyasbookbox@gmail.com, and she promises to give each one her most earnest consideration.

Nearly every state in the US experienced a bump in household income last year, yet it's still not enough to afford the typical home.
States like Rhode Island and Virginia saw fairly large increases in income from 2024 to 2025 — 9.02% and 7.85%, respectively — but an additional five figures is needed to afford a median-priced home in each state, according to data from the US Census and Realtor.com.
Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones said that even though households are bringing in more money, an increase in mortgage rates since last year isn't helping.
"Mortgage rates are more than one percentage point higher than a year ago, which cuts into buyer budgets and offsets the affordability gains from softening home prices and rising incomes," Jones said. "Nationally, the median household income is not enough to afford the median-priced home in any state."
The national median household income was $84,780 in 2025 — a roughly 3.8% increase from the previous year. However, with the national median listing price at $419,250 in September 2026, that's $31,136 short of the recommended income to buy, assuming a mortgage rate of 7.32% and a 10% down payment, according to Realtor.
Realtor calculated the additional amount needed above the median income to afford the typical home in each state, and found that some require a couple thousand dollars, while others require nearly six figures.

A British national is among six people dead in a shooting in Krakow, police have said.
The person, who has not been identified, is one of four women and two men who were killed in the drive-by shooting in the city’s main market square at around 3pm.
The gunman drove into the tourist spot and began firing shots, local police said, adding that the suspect was shot and arrested.
Two police officers were also injured, including one who is in a critical condition after suffering three gunshots.
On Saturday evening, Poland’s police commander-in-chief, Marek Boron, said a British national was among the dead. Three of the other victims were Polish, he added. The identity of the remaining two dead is still unknown.
Earlier, Poland’s interior minister Marcin Kierwinski said the 25-year-old suspect, who is in hospital in a serious condition, was influenced by far-right ideology. He said: “Police officers are on-site, as are agents from the Internal Security Agency, both here at the scene and at the individual's family home."
The country’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, called the shooting an “act of terror”.

While you might be pondering whether to replace a smartphone with one that has a slightly better camera or a second screen, the Federal Aviation Administration is planning a much bigger leap in technology for the country’s air traffic control system.
The FAA said yesterday that it will stop using floppy disks as part of a long-awaited upgrade that will give air traffic controllers faster access to data needed for crucial safety alerts. The new Enterprise Information Display System (E-IDS) will be installed in 435 facilities, replacing several information display systems dating to the 1980s.
The FAA “is continuing its historic modernization of America’s air traffic control system by replacing outdated floppy disks that contain vital weather and other critical information with a streamlined, 21st-century system,” the agency said. E-IDS will be “deployed to operational control positions at more than 400 facilities across all air traffic control domains,” and “provide operationally essential information for controlling aircraft,” the FAA said.
The change has been in the works for over six years. “No more floppy disks or paper strips,” then-Acting FAA Administrator Chris Rocheleau told the House Appropriations Committee last year.
The FAA said E-IDS will replace older tools that have “technical end-of-life issues” and address two of the aviation agency’s top safety concerns: distribution of weather alerts to pilots (known as PIREP for Pilot Report); and timely distribution of Notices to Airmen (NOTAM), which include information on abnormal statuses and hazards.
“E-IDS gives air traffic controllers the information they need to make timely decisions and keep the flying public safe,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said. “We’re moving away from outdated, manual processes and replacing technology that once relied on floppy disks with a modern system that allows controllers to instantly share critical flight alerts, restricted airspace schedules and pilot reports across the National Airspace System.”
Upgrades will take a year
It’ll take a year or so to make the upgrades at every facility. The first sites to get E-IDS will be Atlantic City International Airport, Nashville International Airport, Greater Rochester International Airport, and data processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City. The FAA said it plans to complete the upgrade at 435 sites by the end of 2028.

A man in his 20s showed up to a UK hospital with the hilt of a knife sticking out of his face. The 15 mm-wide blade hidden within went completely through his right eye and through his brain, with the tip of the blade hitting the top of his skull.
Despite the ghastly injury, the man was alive and conscious when he arrived. He could still talk and move all four limbs. His doctors described him as being in a state of agitation. On the Glasgow Coma Scale, he scored a 12 (E3 V4 M5), indicating a “moderate” brain injury, just one point above “mild.” He could open his left eye when told, but otherwise kept it closed (E3 score); he could talk and answer questions, but was confused (V4); and he intentionally moved away when pressure was applied to his body (M5).
In a report published Friday in BMJ Case Report, his doctors said they were concerned that in his confused, agitated state he may try to pull the knife out on his own. So, they swiftly sedated and intubated him. They put him on prophylactic treatments for bacterial infections, including tetanus. Then they used images to see what was going on in his head.
“Pull-and-see”
The blade was entirely through the right eye socket and eyeball. It traversed the left frontal and temporal lobes of his brain, passing through in front of—and without apparently injuring—the corpus callosum, which connects the two sides of the brain and is full of nerve fibers. The blade also missed the left internal capsule, which holds another bundle of nerve fibers.
In terms of damage to major blood vessels, doctors found that the blade was close to the left internal carotid artery, a major blood vessel, but didn’t seem to have damaged it. Doctors did find, however, that a branch of the middle cerebral artery looked to be indented by the knife.
After consulting with various medical specialties, the man’s doctors moved to emergency neurosurgery. They opted to remove part of his skull to directly see into the brain, but used a conservative “pull-and-see” method to slide the blade out rather than invasively excavate it. After it was out, the doctors saw no signs of significant hemorrhaging. The brain wound was cleaned and drained before surgeons patched up his skull. His right eye, however, couldn’t be saved. Given its extensive damage, it was removed.

Iran executed three men on Sunday (November 8, 2026) after they were convicted of carrying out operations for Israel and the U.S. and taking part in armed unrest during anti-government protests in January, state media reported.

The executions are the latest in a series Iran has carried out in recent months over the January protests, including of people accused of links to Israel and the U.S.
Hassan Dioband, Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh were accused of using firearms, grenades and Molotov cocktails, setting fire to public facilities and damaging an electricity substation in the city of Karaj, causing power outages in some areas, according to the judiciary.
The judiciary said Mr. Dioband was arrested on January 11 after investigations identified him as a suspect in attacks on public property and incitement to violence.
Ten others accused of participating in the unrest under his supervision were subsequently arrested.
The three were sentenced to death and ordered to have their assets confiscated. Their executions were carried out after the Supreme Court upheld their sentences, while the other defendants received prison terms of 5 to 10 years.

Tesla will end production of the Cybertruck at its Texas Gigafactory next year.
It’s a uniquely toxic electric vehicle, between its divisive design and Elon Musk’s embrace of you name it. That toxicity certainly contributed to subpar sales, along with a number of recalls.
But the end of the Cybertruck is also another sign that the era of big EVs—particularly big trucks—is waning. That’s great news for pedestrian and biker safety, but also for the battery supply chain at a time when more people need to get behind the electric wheel.
The Cybertruck uses a massive 123 kilowatt-hour battery that clocks in at around 1,600 pounds, or around a quarter of its weight. That’s on par with the battery that powered Ford’s F-150 Lightning, another electric truck that was canceled late last year. (The company also killed a three-row EV in 2024.) Ford’s behemoth batteries ranged from 98 kilowatt-hours up to 131 kilowatt-hours.
Seeing both trucks canceled within a year of each other, while automakers have announced a bevy of smaller EVs and gas-powered autos with electric motors that can extend range, indicates there may be a shift afoot. Ford is planning to launch the Fathom next year. The sub-$30,000 electric pickup is expected to be about the size of the automaker’s compact gas-powered Maverick pickup. Though Ford hasn’t announced the battery sizes available in various trims, it’s a safe bet they won’t be anywhere near the size of the F-150 Lightning or Cybertruck. The company is also planning to relaunch the Lightning as an extended-range model.
Startup Slate is also launching a tiny electric pickup that can be converted to an SUV, with a bare-bones base model starting below $25,000. It also features a svelte battery and has seen a massive surge in preorders—though, to be fair, so did the Cybertruck, and we saw that turned out.
Then there’s the Rivian R2, which launched this year. While the SUV isn’t as tiny or cheap as Ford and Slate’s vehicles—its battery has 88 kilowatt-hours of capacity and weighs in at around 1,200 pounds—it’s still smaller than the company’s flagship R1S. Rivian has also teased the R3, an even more-slimmed down SUV, in the coming years.
That’s not to say big EVs are dead. The Kia EV9, for example, is among the top 10 EVs by sales in the US, as is the R1S. There’s also a torrid resale market for the F-150 Lightning. But the rest of the top 10 new EV sales are all crossovers, sedans, or mid-sized SUVs with moderately sized batteries, and a number of newly announced EVs are trending on the smaller side or function as extended range vehicles.
Building smaller vehicles is, of course, one way to make EVs cheaper. With less weight to propel, you can rely on a smaller battery. And given that the battery pack is the most costly component of an EV, that can in turn help automakers offer more affordable vehicles at a time when the price of so many other consumer goods is skyrocketing. That includes the current crop of EVs: The average transaction price for a new model is now $55,800, according to Cox Automotive.
Going small—or smaller, anyway—also means making the most of a limited battery supply chain. The vast majority of Cybertruck drivers are doing the same thing with their vehicles as Hyundai Ioniq 5 drivers: getting groceries, commuting, and driving kids to soccer games. But a standard range Ioniq 5 driver is doing it with a battery about half the size.
After President Donald Trump’s administration killed EV incentives last year, sales plummeted. The Iran War and rising gas prices have led to an uptick in interest, though sales still lag behind the global average. (Used hybrid sales have also picked up, reflecting the pain people have been feeling at the pump.) Even with a Democratic-controlled Congress, EV incentives coming back under Trump are about as likely as defense secretary Pete Hegseth putting pronouns in his email signature. But should Democrats take the White House in 2028, marking the culmination of Woke 2.0, support for would-be EV buyers becomes much more likely.
Automakers pivoting to smaller cars could be much better-positioned to meet pent-up demand if that happens, while also lowering the risks of delivery delays.
Even Elon’s announcement killing the Cybertruck points to where the market is heading: He claims Tesla is ending production to make room for cranking out more Cybercabs. The battery size in those vehicles? Just 48 kilowatt-hours.

It was a curious way of conducting negotiations. Ahead of the 2025 climate summit, in the Amazonian port of Belém last year, the Brazilian hosts had taken off the table the issue that most had assumed would be at its heart: concrete plans from each country laying out exactly what they would be doing to cut their greenhouse gas emissions.
Brazil was insisting, instead, that these plans – the bedrock of the Paris agreement – were the business of national governments and not up for negotiation. “In that case, it will be a very short Cop,” one seasoned global south negotiator told the Guardian shortly before, reflecting a widespread unease. “There is nothing to negotiate.”
“They have decided that there is no appetite for negotiation, with the US out of Paris,” said another developing country diplomat. “Countries won’t engage.”
The summit ended with a deal, although few loved it. But, as the faultlines from the Brazilian decision deepen going into this year’s summit, it is clear that the Paris agreement, and climate action around the world, has reached an impasse.
And it is not just Cop insiders who are worried. For many outside the vast white air-conditioned conference halls, the question, as this year’s summit begins, will be: what is the point?
Those same governments have pledged year after year since the Paris agreement was signed in 2015 – and entered into force a year later – to limit global heating to 1.5C above preindustrial levels. Yet temperatures for two years have exceeded that threshold, and the UN revealed a few weeks ago that its most optimistic estimate was now for about 1.7 to 1.8C of heating.
There could be no clearer evidence that the Paris agreement, on the face of it, has failed. It is impossible not to wonder whether the Cop process itself is just not fit for purpose.
The charge sheet against Paris is long, with the central issue being the failure to achieve its goal. Beyond that immediate failure, the negotiation processes are endlessly convoluted and cause their own problems. It took more than five years just to negotiate the Paris “rulebook” under which the treaty is interpreted and put into effect.
The convention that all resolutions must pass by consensus has given bad actors free rein. Donald Trump’s allies – in Saudi Arabia, Russia, Venezuela and some other petrostates – frequently veto measures and obstruct progress.
It took more than 30 years of negotiation since the UN framework convention on climate change was signed in 1992 for fossil fuels even to be addressed directly. This was at Cop28 in Dubai in 2023, where countries agreed for the first time to “transition away from fossil fuels” but failed to set a timeframe or any policies to back up the resolution.
The US, the world’s biggest economy and responsible for about one in every eight tonnes of carbon dioxide emitted today, has withdrawn from Paris under President Trump.
Even parts of the developed world which support the process have mostly failed to come up with convincing plans: Australia, co-host of Cop31, has set no end to fossil fuel exports; its fellow co-host Turkey plans to increase its carbon output. The UK is opening a gasfield and mulling a new oilfield, Germany has dropped its electric vehicle sales targets and scrapped a renewable heating law. Meanwhile, most rich countries are reducing their contributions to climate finance for the poor.
Most of all, the slow pace of the Paris timetable might have seemed fine in 2015, when temperatures were rising at 0.2C a decade. Today, the rate of rise is 0.4C a decade and still accelerating.
“The structures of Cops and Paris are labyrinthine, bureaucratic, and ultimately dispiriting,” said Paul Bledsoe, a former Clinton White House climate adviser, now with the American University. “It may be time to streamline them to focus more deliberately on national emissions reduction goals.”
As ordinary people watch these failures outside and inside the process, some are losing faith. The Paris agreement was a sensation, celebrated around the world. In the years since, the aura of Cop has faded, as meetings seem to disintegrate into arguments over wording and compromise.
“A lot of the commitments, the promises that were made, just turned out to be a bunch of hot air,” said Juan Carlos Monterrey, former climate envoy for Panama, now chief executive of the Vanglabs consultancy. “Under that measure, we have failed.”
Johan Rockström, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said: “The fact that global warming is accelerating, that we inevitably will be breaching the 1.5C limit within three to five years, that tipping points are coming closer fast, that Earth’s resilience is showing worrying signs of decline, and that we still allow ourselves to follow a global path that will take us to a catastrophic 2.6C-3C, and that this is allowed to happen within the framework of the Paris agreement, cannot be considered as anything but a global failure.”
But, like most involved in international climate efforts, both refuse to concede that Paris is done for. “On the other hand,” said Rockström, “Paris is all we have. And we know that the global climate crisis can only, in the end, be solved if all countries in the world simultaneously move away from planet-damaging heat injection.”
Monterrey agrees. The most important fact about the Paris agreement, and the Cop process, he says, is that they exist. “Paris is our moral compass. It has told us where we should go. The speed of travel is not what it needs to be, but Paris has set the direction.”
A messy compromise
This year’s Cop is the first to have a split presidency and host. Being held in Turkey but presided over by Australia, Cop31 is a messy compromise between two countries whose other chief point of commonality is an admiration for coal.
Unexpectedly, however, the skies are a little brighter over this year’s meeting than anyone might have expected. Brazil has decisively re-elected Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva who has already overseen the biggest reductions in deforestation for decades.
The US midterms delivered a drubbing for the right, while in Serbia and Hungary this year democracy has won out over authoritarianism. Though the far right is still on the march across much of Europe, and autocrats still rule in most of the countries with the biggest fossil fuel industries and highest emissions, the replacement or weakening of anti-climate authoritarians by pro-climate parties is a positive sign. Globally, a large majority of people support climate action.
Action beyond the framework of Cop is marching on. After the failure of last year’s Cop30 in Brazil to provide a strong statement on phasing out fossil fuels, a group of nearly 60 countries held an alternative meeting in Colombia in April and agreed to draw up their own national roadmaps for the “transition away from fossil fuels”.
Three major countries have so far done so: France, Germany and the Netherlands. Bledsoe wants to use this model for more side agreements on the “super pollutants” such as methane, refrigerant chemicals called HFCs, ground-level ozone, nitrous oxide and black carbon, or soot.
Cutting methane by 40% could alone hold down temperatures by about 0.3C in the next decade, and deeper cuts beyond that could yield a 0.5C decrease by 2100.
“Paris was never intended to do all the hard work itself,” Bledsoe said. “We need to use the G7, the G20 and other forums too, and we need to elevate the climate to the level of national security concern, and see it as an economic threat.”
While the failures of Paris might seem obvious, its “moral compass” has also translated into greater success in the real world than many people realise.
“The solar panels on my roof and the BYD Dolphin [electric car] my neighbour drives are exhibit one and exhibit two of Paris’s success,” said Claudio Angelo, of the Observatório do Clima thinktank. “Will Paris prevent overshoot of 1.5C? No way. Will it prevent 2C of warming? Unlikely. But the transformation it has triggered can’t be exaggerated.”
Perhaps the clinching argument lies in China, the world’s biggest emitter of greenhouse gases and second-largest economy.
“China is taking multilateral climate efforts more seriously than many other countries, and certainly more seriously than it did a few years ago,” said Li Shuo, director of the China climate hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute. “The reason is simple: its economic stakes have grown enormously. If the world abandons decarbonisation, where will China sell its solar panels and electric vehicles?”
And, stung by high fossil fuel prices, many developing-country consumers are grasping clean technology without waiting for assistance. In Pakistan, plagued by blackouts and grid supply issues, rooftop solar panels have taken off, now making up about a quarter of electricity use in the country. Similarly, drivers in Vietnam are increasingly opting for cheap electric vehicles from China, which now make up more than 40% of its car sales.
Meanwhile, the conference hosts themselves, from unpromising beginnings, have brought forward one of the biggest new ideas in the last decade for putting the world on track to lower emissions – changing fuel sources for cars and heating to electricity. The electricity should be from clean sources where possible – but its efficiency means that even if the energy source is fossil-based, it still uses less power.
Jan Rosenow, professor of energy and climate policy at Oxford University, estimates that the superior efficiency of electricity over fossil fuels will mean that the world’s total final energy use can be halved by switching to electric for everything – meaning we need to generate a lot less, too.
If countries can agree a target at Cop31 of deriving 35% of final energy use from electricity by 2035, up from 23% today, that would be a major boost to decarbonisation efforts. Adair Turner, former chair of the UK’s climate change committee and now co-chair of the Energy Transitions Commission thinktank, said: “Electrification is the single most important thing you have to do [to reach net zero emissions].”
Cops provide a place where countries can come together to share experiences, to seek advice, to find support and fellowship. “That’s very valuable,” said Ilana Seid, ambassador of Palau and chair of the Pacific Small Island Developing States. And in a world in which the bulk of current and future emissions, and fossil fuel production, comes from non-democracies or authoritarian states, Cops also provides one of the few forums where they can be held to account.
That “societal pressure” is crucial, said Seid. “We small islands and vulnerable nations are on the frontline. For us, this is existential. We are all very committed to Paris.”
After all, despite all the doubts, the power of a decision at Cop should not be underestimated. While “coalitions of the willing” are a “good thing” according to Nick Stern, the economist, the universality of the Paris agreement and Cops give them a unique authority.
Sue Biniaz, a former US climate negotiator, said: “Any time you have a consensus decision, it sends a signal to investors, to people who finance things, and to countries. I think that’s true these days with the geopolitics of the world – if something can be agreed by the whole world, it’s impactful.”
Cop31 may bring progress on electrification, on climate finance and on the transition that countries, rich and poor, need to make to a low-carbon world. But we already know that whatever the summit produces, it will not be enough.
However flawed yet substantive they are, Cops last only a fortnight, while efforts to tackle the climate crisis will require such wholesale transformation of our economies and societies that they should top governments’ agendas all year.
“Imagine you have lost your loved one without having their bodies to bring back home. Lost livelihood where you spent your whole life to accumulate those assets. We faced a horrific situation,” said Sujeeta Mathema, executive director of ActionAid Nepal, who was quickly on the scene to help people after the catastrophic glacier collapse there.
“It feels like living with grief, fear and uncertainty about the future. The devastation is not just physical; it is deeply emotional and psychological.”
People are traumatised, she says, and deeply feel the injustice of how the climate crisis is created by the rich while hurting the most vulnerable. But Cop can still be a place of hope, Mathema adds.
“Cop is an important space for us to raise our voice, clearly putting our agenda. Cop can help prevent such disasters if the commitments come off paper and are put into action.”

The 57th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu explores how researchers are using advanced imaging and reconstruction techniques to create detailed, three-dimensional maps of the human brain.
Zubeda Hamid, senior assistant editor, The Hindu, speaks to Mohanasankar Sivaprakasam, Head of the Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre at IIT Madras, about the technology, how the maps are created and what they could reveal about the human brain.
The episode looks at C-STROKE, a recently released three-dimensional atlas of a stroke-affected brain. Unlike conventional MRI scans, which provide images of the brain at a particular resolution, the new approach allows researchers to examine brain structures in greater detail and build comprehensive 3D maps.
The discussion explains how researchers prepare brain tissue, use imaging techniques and reconstruct the data to create these maps. It also looks at the different scientific and technological disciplines involved in the process and how detailed mapping could help researchers study the brain’s structure and changes associated with neurological conditions.
Another focus is the Centre’s plan to map more than 100 human brains across different stages of life. The project aims to build a larger collection of brain maps that could help researchers understand variations in brain structure, study neurological conditions and expand the available resources for brain research.
The episode also examines the potential applications of these atlases in clinical research and healthcare, including how they could contribute to a better understanding of stroke and other brain conditions. It discusses the possibilities as well as the work needed before such maps can be translated into clinical applications.

Amid a sweep of Democratic victories in Tuesday’s midterms, some online commentators jokingly declared “Woke is back.”
There was little congressional pushback over the past two years as the Trump administration terminated hundreds of grants meant to chronicle and remedy medical inequities, shuttered programs intended to diversify the science workforce, and opened investigations into universities and medical schools it accused of discriminating against white and Asian applicants. Will that change now that the Democratic Party has won control of the 120th Congress?
Two newly elected candidates with science credentials told STAT they hope to change that: Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and former health disparities researcher, and incoming Rep. Jasmine Clark of Georgia, a microbiologist who will be the first Black woman with a STEM Ph.D. in Congress.
Democrats have a long list of priorities, and with President Trump still wielding his veto power, passing bills related to health equity will still be an uphill battle. The White House posted on X Thursday, “FYI: DEI is still dead.” But, the introduction of at least two lawmakers with personal connections to health equity work could offer a counterweight to such policies for the rest of the second Trump administration.
“I know firsthand what DEI initiatives can do for students who are trying to find their way, and they don’t actually quite know all of the options that are available to them,” Clark told STAT in an interview Wednesday. A former professor, she said such programs have opened up opportunities for her students in the sciences.
El-Sayed, interviewed a few days before the election, said, “The war on diversity, equity, and inclusion is about a vision of an America that doesn’t include certain kinds of people. I will always stand for an America where everybody is included and empowered, and I think that’s critical for us as we move to the future.” During his time in academia, he did research on disparities in maternal health and within the Arab American community. He added, “we need to be able to document the ways in which our systems are allowing for and, in some respects, creating the differences in the ability for people to live long, healthy lives. It’s important work, and it should help guide where public policy gaps are and where we need to fill them.”
The second Trump administration has seen unprecedented changes to the scientific ecosystem. Some of the most major have drawn forceful responses from Congress. Proposals to cut the National Institutes of Health’s budget, cap funding for overhead costs at universities, and exert more political control over federal funding have all been rebuked by Congress. With the Democrats taking control of both chambers, further pushback may be coming.
The NIH did not respond to a request for comment.
A number of physicians and scientists who won their races have noted that accountability for health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is high on their list of priorities. Part of that accountability should be understanding which communities and researchers were affected by policies like grant terminations over the past two years, said Jennifer Jones, who directs the Center for Science and Democracy at the Union of Concerned Scientists. “I want to know who was most harmed by this because there’s absolutely a justice and equity issue at play when you clearly attack issues of diversity, equity, and inclusion,” she said.
While equity work is sometimes portrayed as controversial, Philip Alberti, the founding director of the Association of American Medical Colleges Center for Health Justice, said polling he has done has shown broad support for health equity initiatives across ideological groups. “Three-quarters of U.S. adults support the goal of ‘all communities having a fair and just opportunity to be healthy,’ and 65% of adults who have ever heard the term ‘health equity’ support it, too,” he said. “This was true across all subgroups, including across groups defined by self-identified ideology. This is not controversial.”
Clark trained as a microbiologist before taking to politics during the first Trump administration. She said she would seek an assignment on the House oversight committee and has a number of questions she’d like to pose to appointees like Kennedy. For one, she would like to understand why the administration has repeatedly pushed for a controversial hepatitis B vaccine study in Guinea-Bissau. Clark likened that trial to the Tuskegee syphilis experiment, an unethical study conducted by the U.S. Public Health Service and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention that withheld treatment for syphilis from nearly 400 African American men from 1932 to 1972.
Another way she has seen the fallout of the administration is that her former lab, which studies HIV transmission, had to pause some of its longitudinal studies in Africa because of restrictions on international collaborations. Even if the lab is able to find more funding, “you basically have to start from scratch, or you just have a big hole in your data. That’s not what we need to be doing if we want to actually do things like end the HIV epidemic,” she said.
She also lamented the process of grants for federal funding being screened for certain terms and phrases to determine if they are related to “DEI.” This process has particularly affected researchers studying health disparities, and has made it difficult for some to apply for new funding. In September, a handful of researchers sued the agency, arguing this process infringed on their first amendment rights.
“Having the ability to write in your research grant that you’re looking at the disproportionate impact without having to dance around those words because any grant that has the word ‘disproportionate,’ or ‘woman,’ or ‘Black,’ or ‘gender,’ or anything like that all of a sudden gets flagged,” she said. “That’s not the environment we should be operating under if we actually want to answer real-life questions. So I look forward to being a part of a Congress that will prioritize moving toward and not immediately dismissing research because they are trying to answer questions about why one group is impacted more than another.”

This man refused life-saving treatment because of his religion - days later the rules changed
- Published
In August this year, 26-year-old Isaac Valdez had an epileptic seizure while browsing in his local library, causing him to convulse and strike his head against the ground.
He lost consciousness. Later, in hospital, it transpired Isaac had hit his head with such force it had led to a brain haemorrhage.
Treatment was seriously complicated by the fact that, as a Jehovah's Witness, Isaac carried a "No Blood" card, an indication that he would not accept treatment involving any form of blood transfusion because of his religious beliefs.
As a result, a procedure to drain fluid from Isaac's brain did not take place.
But his family, from Waxahachie, Texas, were encouraged by the fact that he regained consciousness and even started to talk again. He was able to confirm that he stood by his "no blood" beliefs.
The family's relief at his apparent improvement was short-lived. Isaac slipped into a coma and his condition worsened rapidly.
A neurosurgeon told Isaac's family the only way to save his life was an emergency operation, but that it was one that required blood transfusion.
His family took the decision to abide by Issac's wishes as a lifelong Witness not to accept such a procedure.
Isaac - who his twin brother Jacob Valdez describes as an intelligent man who loved volunteering and helping the elderly - died on 26 August 2026 when doctors turned off his life support.
Just 23 days later, the Jehovah's Witnesses' Governing Body announced a seismic change in teaching that would, in effect, have given Isaac the religious green light to have the life-saving treatment he had refused.
The change suddenly means the vast majority of medical procedures using donated blood are no longer prohibited to followers. Now, decisions on whether to accept such treatments are to be left to individuals.
Jacob, already dealing with the death of his twin, was angered at the Jehovah's Witnesses' leadership for not coming to their conclusion sooner. He told BBC News he believes Isaac could well still be alive if they had.
The original rule on blood transfusions dates back to 1945, towards the very end of a war during which the use of blood transfusions had been increasingly widespread. The leaders of Jehovah's Witnesses announced that their believers were not permitted to accept transfusions.
This was based on their interpretation of Bible verses from both the Old and New Testaments prohibiting the consumption of blood, including one from the Book of Acts that instructs believers to abstain from blood, from food offered to idols, and from things that had been strangled.
So, why has the Jehovah's Witnesses' Governing Body, based in New York state, now decided to change the rules, 81 years after introducing them?
It comes after years of pressure from both within and outside the faith, but that is not how leaders of the faith describe the decision.
"The change is basically the application of Bible principles to modern medicine and its methods," says the Jehovah's Witnesses international spokesperson, Paul Gillies, who described it as both a fresh look at scripture and at medical advances.
We meet Gillies at the Jehovah's Witnesses UK headquarters set in 85 acres of Essex countryside. It is a vast modern complex where hundreds of volunteer followers of the faith live and work without pay.
He insists the basic teaching has not changed and that the transfusion of whole blood is still prohibited. However, for decades, most transfusions have not used whole blood, instead using the specific components of blood that are needed by the patient.
The change is being justified by permitting the use of blood components, like plasma and red blood cells and platelets, in the huge numbers of medical procedures that were previously banned.
Gillies says the Bible references "abstaining from blood" but not "various components that could be extracted from blood".
He says the Governing Body felt it their duty to avoid scriptural "overreach" and only apply what was specifically described in the Bible.
But that explanation has stunned many and led them to ask if it was not a huge overreach 81 years ago to ban blood transfusions in the first place, when transfusions are not specifically mentioned in the bible.
Others are then also asking why it has taken so long to come to this landmark decision, given that transfusions that do not use whole blood have been the norm for decades.
These are questions Jacob asked as soon as the ban was lifted, just days after a memorial service for Isaac.
Jacob, who had already left the Jehovah's Witness faith he was brought up in, texted prominent figures from Isaac's congregation in Texas after Isaac's death. The messages are full of angst, and painful to read.
He asked them to consider "the part you played in encouraging so many people to sacrifice their life for something that was never God's will".
Most did not reply, but one "elder" responded saying he could not understand why Jacob was so angry and fixated on the policy shift.
This all further infuriated Jacob, who particularly wants the faith's decision-makers to be accountable for all the lives lost.
"I want to ask them if they could apologise directly, I would like not to have a deflected answer, just straightforward apology," he says.
It is extremely difficult to say how many Jehovah's Witnesses, among the estimated nine million followers of the faith worldwide, died each year having refused treatment involving blood transfusions. But research in one medical journal in 2016, The Obstetrical & Gynecological Survey, put the figure at around 1,100.
"We're sympathetic to their feelings, and if individuals have lost family members and are concerned about some of these questions, they deserve to be heard compassionately," says Gillies.
But there was little clarity about why the change did not come earlier.
"Why has it taken this time? Well, I guess because it takes time, it doesn't necessarily mean that there is some magic change that's taken place," says Gillies.
And when asked, Gillies deflects calls for the leadership to apologise, saying that many lives had, in fact, been saved because faithful Jehovah's Witnesses had not been exposed to blood contamination scandals.
He also insists that even after the new edict, some Jehovah's Witnesses could still decide they did not want to accept a transfusion, and that may have been the case even if the edict had come years ago.
Indeed, the BBC spoke with Alex Ball, 58, a Jehovah's Witness from West Sussex, who says in 2012 a doctor told him he would not survive the chemotherapy he needed to treat his blood cancer unless he also had a transfusion.
"I wanted to adhere as closely to the scriptures as possible when I was sick, and I think I did that well."
With help from what is called "a Jehovah's Witness Hospital Liaison Committee", Alex found an American consultant who could perform a treatment to boost Alex's blood cells without the need for any products from someone else. His UK consultant agreed to treat him using the new method and it worked.
More than a decade later, Alex says he would make the same decision again, despite the change in blood policy that would have permitted the transfusions he had been told he needed.
It is not just receiving blood which has been an issue.
Elisha Cummings, 50, a Jehovah's Witness from Trinidad and Tobago, was unable to donate blood to her aunt, who died, because of the rules.
They also cost her her marriage too, with her husband of 10 years leaving the faith and divorcing her after it came to light that he had had a blood transfusion as a child, something that was looked down upon in her Witness community.
"Since the blood policy change, I have not been myself," she says. "It left me in a sort of depressed mode."
"How many houses did I go to trying to convince people about the blood doctrine? And you're coming now and it's something totally different," Elisha says.
Elisha says her beliefs as a whole have been shaken, yet she feels reluctant to leave the faith, partly because it is what provides her with her community and she fears isolation.
In the past, those who disagreed with "blood doctrine" were ostracised or felt like they needed to leave the faith. Will they now be able to come back?
"Any individual that wants to come back to the faith is warmly welcomed," says Gillies, speaking of those who had left the faith because they had accepted a transfusion for themselves or a relative.
"If they would like to become one of Jehovah's Witnesses again and would like to speak to the elders, then they're very welcome to do so."

The lobbying group for the U.S. pharmaceutical industry spent an estimated $59 million on search advertising over a recent seven-year period to influence how Americans view the highly charged issue of prescription drug costs, according to a new analysis that used data to model the spending.
Of that, the Pharmaceutical Research & Manufacturers of America spent roughly $32 million on ads linked to insurance and health plan searches, while $28 million was spent directing people to its web pages and domains criticizing pharmacy benefit managers, which drugmakers argue are the true culprits behind the rising prices for many medicines.
Spending also surged around well-publicized legislative and regulatory actions, such as when Medicare began drug price negotiations in 2023. In all, PhRMA used more than 283,500 distinct keywords to generate 17.1 million paid visits from 2019 through 2025, according to an analysis published in Clinical Pharmacology & Therapeutics.

The Union Health Ministry has proposed amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945, to immediately suspend the manufacturing licences of drugs declared Not of Standard Quality (NSQ) on specified critical quality parameters.
The government said on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) that the proposed amendments seek to enable prompt regulatory intervention upon detection of substandard medicines, prevent their continued manufacture and distribution, and strengthen the mechanism for ensuring compliance with prescribed quality standards, in the interest of patient safety and public health.
Under the existing provisions of the Drugs Rules, 1945, suspension or cancellation of a manufacturing licence is preceded by the prescribed regulatory procedure, including issuance of a show-cause notice. This may result in a time gap between the declaration of a drug as NSQ and the initiation of regulatory action. During this period, the drug may remain in circulation, posing potential risks to public health and making effective recall more challenging.
To address this regulatory concern, the Ministry has proposed a provision for immediate suspension of the manufacturing licence of the drug by the Central Licensing Approving Authority or the State Licensing Authority upon receipt of a government analyst’s report declaring the drug as NSQ with respect to assay, dissolution, related substances, impurities or sterility.
“These parameters are critical to determining the quality of medicines. The proposed provision aims to ensure that instances of non-compliance involving these specified parameters are met with prompt regulatory action, thereby minimising potential risks to patients,’’ the Ministry said.
The proposed amendment provides for mandatory corrective measures before revocation of the suspension. The suspension shall continue until the manufacturer undertakes an effective root cause analysis to identify the reasons for the quality failure and implements appropriate Corrective and Preventive Action (CAPA) to the satisfaction of the licensing authority.
Suspension can be revoked after the requisite corrective and preventive measures are implemented and then verified by the licensing authority. This mechanism will ensure that identified quality deficiencies are adequately addressed and necessary safeguards are put in place to prevent their recurrence.
“To further strengthen regulatory coordination and facilitate timely action, consequential amendments have also been proposed to Form 13, relating to the test report of the Government Analyst. Under the proposed mechanism, the Government Analyst’s report would be endorsed to the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI), the concerned State/UT Licensing Authority under whose jurisdiction the manufacturing site is located, as well as the manufacturer and marketer of the concerned drug,’’ the government said.
It added that the proposed arrangement is aimed at ensuring timely communication of NSQ findings to the relevant authorities and stakeholders, thereby facilitating coordinated regulatory action and strengthening accountability across the drug manufacturing and marketing chain.
The proposed amendments follow deliberations at the 65th meeting of the Drugs Consultative Committee, held on December 20, 2024, and recommendations of the 92nd meeting of the Drugs Technical Advisory Board, held on April 24, 2025.
The amendments are expected to strengthen post-marketing regulatory surveillance, facilitate timely action against substandard medicines, promote greater accountability among manufacturers and marketers, and reinforce public confidence in the quality of medicines available in the country.
The draft amendments have been notified for public consultation, inviting objections and suggestions from stakeholders and members of the public within 30 days from the date on which copies of the Gazette of India containing the draft rules are made available to the public.

Anthropic is holding firm on the pledge made in its Super Bowl commercial this year to keep Claude ad-free. The company’s recent IPO filing didn’t even mention the possibility of selling ads to make money from the AI chatbot. It’s easy to maintain the high ground with about $112 billion in investor cash.
The chatbot industry, though, may find selling ads necessary to defray the high costs of generating AI responses. OpenAI is all in, with over 100,000 customers advertising in ChatGPT since ads debuted there in February. Last week, Google expanded ads in its search chatbot AI Mode to 10 more countries beyond the US and declared that users “find them highly relevant.” Advertisers are far from satisfied with the experience, but they expect it to improve.
Ads stand to be particularly vital for the long-term viability of niche chatbot platforms, which can’t rely on the same degree of venture capital largesse as the top AI labs or the massive revenues of tech giants. I recently spoke with Koah Labs, one of a number of new ad technology companies focused on AI experiences. The San Francisco startup markets itself as bringing ads to over 200 apps, such as DeepAI, which offers tools for creative queries, and Liner, which focuses on providing citations in AI answers. It works with brands like telehealth giant Hims and flower delivery service UrbanStems.
Koah has attracted just a tenth of the advertisers OpenAI has, but CEO Nic Baird still believes he’s getting a good sense of what’s working and what’s fuzzy as chatbots take over from traditional search engines—and what their rise will mean for your AI experiences.
Machine-Crafted
Ads composed partly by AI rather than fully by a human generate double the clicks, Baird says. It’s difficult to assess exactly why, but AI-generated marketing copy likely feels more natural next to the output of an AI model.
Because ads shown by Koah are grounded in product details and imagery supplied by the advertiser, users don’t seem to be encountering AI-hallucinated, erroneous information. But some advertisers, such as drugmakers, face government requirements on what they must—or cannot—say in ads, Baird says. These companies default to more human control over their ads, generating weaker results, according to Baird.
Since ads with dull messages or that feel like clutter could drive users away, the onus is on ad tech companies to find a middle ground that’s engaging to users without triggering risk-averse brands. That balance might be harder to strike when a human is out of the loop.
Creative Targeting
Google searches for “help with stress” are likely to bring up ads for therapists. Chatbots can get more creative, in Baird’s view. For instance, ads for spas have performed well within Koah’s network when shown after users’ prompts related to “stress,” he says.
The key difference, according to Baird, is that Koah can select and customize the ad based on “not only the prompt, or the Google search, but also the response from the AI platform, which brings context from the rest of the conversation thus far.” In addition, chatbot prompts tend to be at least double the length of Google queries, giving Koah more information to determine a relevant ad.
Baird claims users are accustomed to navigating through multiple topics within a chatbot conversation, which could make them more receptive to adjacent marketing than they are in traditional search. Koah says users are clicking on about 3 percent of ads, about on par with the performance of the more mature Google ads system.
All the Context
When called on to show an ad, Koah generally receives a user’s entire conversation up to that point to help inform what it displays. While traditional search queries generally look for specific information, people often use chatbots as not just conversation partners but confidants. It’s unclear whether users will accept the privacy trade-offs that come with personalized chatbot ads as they begin to proliferate.
Baird says Koah anonymizes the queries it receives and stores them in a de-identified way, but he declined to comment any further on the data collection and storage. While acknowledging that personalization can become intrusive, he argues that there are benefits for users and advertisers alike as the tech matures. Nonsensitive information about chatbot discussions, for instance, could inform personalized content on the page that loads after an ad click. Perhaps someone expressed interest in a specific feature, or the AI model didn’t highlight a particular downside of a competing product. The advertiser could fill in the gap.
Koah doesn’t have data on whether people actually want these customized pages, but the tech industry has long argued that people prefer when ad experiences feel relevant. Having the conversation history also could benefit advertisers when Koah enables retargeting, or repeating, an ad to the same user.
Negative Triggers
By Koah’s estimate, one out of every four chatbot queries about a retailer or brand concerns a return, exchange, or other support issue. Baird believes chatbots provide an opportunity not replicated easily elsewhere for advertisers to address what they might politely call a “customer success” matter.
He expects manufacturers and retailers will eventually target disappointed customers to remind them about warranties, engage them in an AI-intermediated support, and potentially steer them away from a more costly customer service interaction. It’s possible that the AI chatbot’s response may provide users with similar help, but buying an ad guarantees companies get their message across.
The ideal outcome is users reaching resolution they can live with more swiftly than through other means. In the worst case, it's a wasted ad buy and a more irate consumer.
Great Unknown
None of the apps Koah currently serves ads in offer users AI agents that can shop on their own. However, apps like Instinct and Meta’s Muse are starting to take over shopping chores for some users. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently said Muse could become the company’s biggest source of revenue but suggested it would come from transaction fees rather than ads.
That doesn’t mean advertising will be entirely cut out from bot-dominated ecommerce, with initial studies suggesting that ads could influence AI agents.
Baird expects an opportunity to give “the user's agent the best possible recommendation, and that’s going to be a combination of a great discount, a really relevant product,” and an easy digital path to make the purchase. The chatbot must make “abundantly clear” to the agent what content is sponsored or else risk losing user trust, Baird says.
It’s also possible the chatbot ad market fizzles out before agents take hold if more AI developers adopt Anthropic’s stance. Kevin Baragona, CEO of DeepAI, says while ad revenue has been meaningful, he’s not committed to it because the experience just doesn’t feel right yet in terms of privacy, design, and more.
“I don’t think the ads are working terribly well for anyone,” he says.
