An Indian Air Force (IAF) IL-76MD heavy-lift transport aircraft has landed at the Nyoma airbase in eastern Ladakh at an altitude of 13,629 feet, setting a world record for the highest-altitude landing by an aircraft of its class. The achievement marks a significant milestone in India's strategic airlift capabilities, demonstrating the IAF's ability to operate heavy military transport aircraft in some of the world's most challenging high-altitude terrain. It also strengthens India's logistical reach close to the Line of Actual Control (LAC) with China. The Russian-origin four-engine aircraft, known as the 'Gajraj', landed at the airbase on Friday. Located approximately 25 km from the LAC, Nyoma is emerging as a key military infrastructure asset for India's forward deployment and logistical operations in eastern Ladakh. The development comes amid continued military sensitivities along the India-China border. Although the two countries have completed disengagement at several friction points and resumed patrolling arrangements since October 2024, a complete de-escalation of troops in eastern Ladakh remains a broader strategic concern. The successful landing demonstrates the IAF's ability to operate a heavy strategic transport aircraft at an altitude where thin air, reduced engine performance and difficult terrain pose considerable operational challenges. The IL-76MD can transport approximately 40–45 tonnes of cargo, depending on its configuration and operating conditions. This includes heavy military equipment and platforms such as infantry combat vehicles and other armoured assets. Its ability to land at Nyoma could significantly improve the movement of troops, equipment and supplies to forward areas, reducing dependence on airfields located farther from the China border, including Leh and Thoise. The aircraft also played an important role during the 2020 India-China military standoff in eastern Ladakh, when the IAF used its heavy-lift capabilities to transport military equipment and other essential assets to the region, according to an Indian Express report. The IAF announced the latest achievement in a post on X, describing it as a "remarkable demonstration of the aircraft's enduring capability", backed by the skill, precision and professionalism of its crew. It added that the landing was a milestone reinforcing India's strategic capabilities. The landing also highlights the growing operational importance of the Nyoma airbase, which has been developed as a strategic military facility close to the LAC. The airfield, located in the Nyoma subdivision of Leh district, was originally constructed in 1962 as a mud-paved landing ground but remained largely inactive for several decades. It was reactivated in 2009 after an AN-32 aircraft successfully landed there, demonstrating its potential for military operations. Following the 2020 border standoff with China, the airstrip supported the operations of several IAF aircraft, including the C-130J and AN-32 transport aircraft, as well as Apache attack helicopters and Chinook heavy-lift helicopters. The airbase was subsequently upgraded under a Border Roads Organisation (BRO) project estimated at around ₹214–218 crore, as per Indian Express. Its approximately 2.7–3-km runway, built with a rigid pavement surface, is designed to support the operations of military transport aircraft and fighter jets. Nyoma's proximity to the LAC makes it particularly important for rapid mobilisation. The ability to move heavy equipment and personnel directly to a forward airbase could reduce logistical turnaround times and strengthen India's capacity to sustain troops deployed in eastern Ladakh. The facility is especially valuable given the region's difficult geography and extreme weather conditions. Situated in the cold-desert terrain of the Changthang plateau, Nyoma experiences temperatures that can fall to around –30°C. Its high altitude and rugged mountainous surroundings also make infrastructure construction and aircraft operations challenging, with the construction window limited to a few months each year. The IAF has demonstrated its ability to operate military transport aircraft at extreme altitudes in eastern Ladakh before. In 2013, an IAF C-130J Super Hercules successfully landed at the Daulat Beg Oldie (DBO) airstrip, situated at an altitude of approximately 16,614 feet. That landing demonstrated the IAF's ability to operate transport aircraft at even higher elevations. However, the latest Nyoma landing is significant because of the aircraft involved. Unlike the C-130J, the IL-76MD is a much heavier strategic transport aircraft, with a substantially larger payload capacity. Operating an aircraft of this size at high altitude presents additional challenges because thinner air reduces lift and engine performance, requiring careful calculations of payload, runway requirements and operating conditions. The successful landing therefore demonstrates a different dimension of India's strategic airlift capability, particularly its ability to transport heavier military equipment closer to forward deployment areas. Despite the achievement, the landing also draws attention to the challenges facing India's ageing strategic transport fleet. India acquired 17 IL-76 aircraft between 1985 and 1989, making the Gajraj fleet one of the IAF's oldest heavy-lift assets. The aircraft have faced serviceability challenges over the years, particularly because of difficulties in sourcing spare parts following the collapse of the Soviet Union. These challenges have been further complicated by the Russia-Ukraine war. There have been discussions about extending the technical service life of around a dozen IL-76 aircraft. At the same time, the IAF is pursuing its Medium Transport Aircraft (MTA) programme, which is intended to replace both the IL-76 and AN-32 fleets. The latest landing at Nyoma is significant not only as an aviation milestone but also as a demonstration of the capabilities India continues to rely on to maintain military readiness along its disputed border with China. Often derided as a “B-class” cuisine, Japanese curry was adapted from the British navy in the late 19th century but has grown to be its own paradigm.
Mildly spiced, usually store-bought bases are bulked up with meat and vegetables before being infused at home with ingredients akin to family secrets: apple, honey, soy sauce and miso are all common kakushi aji (literally, “hidden flavors”) — components that may not register overtly but elevate a dish overall.
Making curry roux cubes, complete with your own kakushi aji, is surprisingly simple. When mixed with water, each cube from this recipe will make approximately 550 milliliters of curry, a generous portion for four adults when combined with other fillings. There is no chile whatsoever in the base recipe, but there is room for adaptation. Feel free to incorporate as much or little heat as you like, adding or subtracting other spices or kakushi aji as you like.
Makes 6 125-gram cubes
Cook time: 45 minutes
Ingredients:
Whole spices for toasting
- 7 1/2 grams cumin seeds
- 7 1/2 grams coriander seeds
- 7 1/2 grams fennel seeds
- 7 1/2 grams cinnamon stick
- 7 1/2 grams black peppercorns
- 5 grams cardamom pods
- 5 grams fenugreek seeds
- 2 1/2 grams cloves
- 2 1/2 grams allspice
- 2 bay leaves
Powders and kakushi aji:
- 10 grams dried kombu (I used shaved tororo kombu)
- 5 grams dried shiitake
- 5 grams dried mandarin peel
- 10 grams salt
- 10 grams cocoa powder
- 5 grams ground turmeric
- 5 grams powdered ginger
Roux:
- 350 grams butter
- 275 grams all-purpose flour
- 50 grams honey
Directions:
- In a small pan, add all of your whole spices and toast over medium heat for about one to two minutes or until fragrant. If you use powdered spices, skip the toasting.
- Place everything in a spice grinder or mortar and pestle in batches with the kombu, shiitake and mandarin peel. Pulse to grind until it reaches the consistency of a powder. Once done, mix in your salt, turmeric, ginger and cocoa to form a curry powder.
- In a medium pot, melt your butter over medium heat. When the butter begins to lightly brown, add the flour and stir constantly until the roux turns dark brown. This could take up to 10 minutes. A richer color equals more flavor, but do not allow it to burn or stick to the pan. Remove from heat and add the curry powder. Stir until completely combined, then add in the honey.
- Carefully pour out the hot mixture into six silicone muffin molds or freezer containers. You can also leave the mixture to set as a single piece, then carefully divide it later. Place it in the refrigerator to harden.
- Once completely solid, remove the roux pieces from the mold or container and place them in an airtight container. They will last a month or more refrigerated or six months in the freezer.

Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan's RSF fighters, BBC investigation finds
- Published
A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.
UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings "deeply disturbing", saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes.
The RSF has rejected the BBC's findings.
The paramilitary group's health minister described the allegations as propaganda and a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF's reputation.
Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 - some hit multiple times.
Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict.
The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC's data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly "disappeared" or abducted.
"The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state," says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC.
"The RSF started hitting these areas so citizens have no longer any way to stay there. It was intense. It was deliberate. It was planned."
The investigation comes a year after the fall of el-Fasher, one of the most brutal chapters of the civil war which erupted in April 2023 between the RSF and Sudan's military.
Both sides have been accused of attacks on health facilities.
In March 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the bombing of al-Daein hospital in RSF-held eastern Darfur, which killed dozens and forced the site to close. Sudan's military is believed to have carried out the drone strikes, although it has denied responsibility.
But events in el-Fasher represent "one of the clearest and most severe examples of the wider impact of the conflict on health care in Sudan," the WHO said in response to a BBC query.
UN investigators have reported that the fighting in el-Fasher bore the "hallmarks of genocide", where historical ethnic animosities have seen Arab militias - now the backbone of RSF forces - target non-Arab groups such as those that populate the city.
The BBC's investigation reveals for the first time a detailed chronology of attacks on healthcare during the long siege of the city.
- A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan 
  - Published13 November 2025
- Reports of mass killings in Sudan have echoes of its dark past 
  - Published31 October 2025
Some medical facilities in el-Fasher closed down within weeks of the country's civil war starting in April 2023.
Crucially this included one of the main hospitals - the Teaching Hospital - located in a conflict zone in the middle of the city.
Its operations were moved to el-Fasher's South Hospital. There medical services continued, although increasingly hindered by power cuts and dwindling supplies.
The situation changed dramatically a year later, when the RSF mounted its siege of el-Fasher.
In late May and early June of 2024, the South Hospital was shelled several times as paramilitary fighters pushed forward from their positions in the east of the city.
The first bombing came as a shock, says Dr Suliman.
The area around the hospital that was hit was "very crowded because it was the only working hospital in the city providing surgical services", he says.
On that day medical staff operated on 16 injured patients, he added.
The attacks culminated in an RSF raid on 8 June. Hospital staff were taken by surprise - many of them escaped over the back wall as the RSF fighters entered the building, says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, a pharmaceutical specialist.
But the director general of the hospital, surgeon Izzeldin Ahmed Dawaud Asow, encountered a group of the paramilitaries outside his office.
They did not know he was a doctor, he said, but denounced him with ethnic slurs.
"There are no citizens here. You are Falangi," they said, using a derogatory term implying that non-Arab Sudanese are foreigners.
Dr Asow says he was beaten with rifle butts and lost consciousness at one point. Ultimately, he saved himself by pretending to be dead.
"They put their hand on my chest, and I stopped breathing. And they said: 'Leave him, leave him. The rubbish has died. Leave him.' They left me."
That same day the RSF was driven out by the Sudanese military and its allies and Dr Asow returned to find the bodies of several patients and the surgical equipment in his operating room thoroughly destroyed, he said.
The hospital closed and later fell into RSF hands when the army retreated.
Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud, a prominent Sudanese surgeon who has joined the RSF-backed civilian government as health minister, insisted the South Hospital was being used as a military base.
According to international law, hospitals can lose their protection if they are used by a party to the conflict to commit an "act harmful to the enemy".
In an interview with the BBC, Dr Nugud declared that missile launchers were set up on the grounds and shared a video showing remains of weapons filmed more than a year after the hospital closed, which he said supported his claim.
He also showed us what he called maps of landmines planted around the Teaching Hospital, which is located next to Sudanese military headquarters.
Doctors told us the hospital was not incorporated into the base and said they visited it to pick up medical equipment during the war.
The BBC has found no independent evidence of Dr Nugud's allegations. And the government of the Darfur region categorically rejected the charges.
After the South Hospital shut, its staff and remaining equipment were moved to the Saudi Maternity Hospital in the west of the city, where the army had its main bases.
Within days the pace of attacks on the facility picked up. At this stage the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) sounded the alarm.
"We do not know if hospitals are being intentionally targeted, but… the belligerents are not taking any precautions to spare them," it said in a statement.
However, in the course of our investigation we spoke to six doctors who described a pattern of systematic targeting.
They told us how Saudi Hospital was repeatedly struck - on some days up to 25 times, with a mix of shelling and drones, the latter "intelligent rockets" with precision-guided attacks.
Smaller medical facilities also came under fire. The BBC's timeline records the steady closure of private hospitals and neighbourhood clinics.
Furthermore, when some of these healthcare buildings shifted locations, the alternate venues were also attacked.
The Specialised Children's Hospital, which shut down at the beginning of the war along with the Teaching Hospital, moved to two other locations, both of which were then shelled and forced to close.
Similarly, the main dialysis centre was struck and then attacked again after it relocated.
By the time the RSF seized the city in October 2025, the Saudi Hospital was the only functioning health facility left.
The medical staff there had rallied to try to keep working as conditions worsened.
Doctors described how sandbags were set up to protect the building.
They built underground bunkers out of steel containers and established a number of alternative sites to house and receive patients and conduct surgery as the threat of attacks and the damage to the main structure steadily increased.
Dr Asow said this makeshift surgery was attacked five times in 2025.
In one case, he says, he was operating on a patient's neck when the building was shaken by an explosion - the medical staff ran out in fear, but he stayed.
In another case, health workers had prepared the theatre for an operation, but he told them to move the patient elsewhere because it needed a deep clean given the relentless case load. Shortly afterward the room was destroyed by shells - and the patient survived.
"From that day, some of my staff called me 'Mr Deep Cleaning' because they think that the issue of deep cleaning saved that patient," he said.
Dr Asow also describes how drones tracked the movement of patients.
On 15 March 2025, people carrying the injured from the site of an attack to one of the temporary wards were followed by a hunting drone, he says.
It struck as they reached the gate of the building, killing nine people.
On 17 August of the same year a donkey cart was transferring patients to the alternative operating theatre because all the ambulances had been destroyed, Dr Asow told the BBC.
It was hit by a drone, killing two patients, the driver and the donkey, he says.
The RSF health minister dismissed these accounts as "a continuation of lies" by the military (SAF) and their local allies, known as the Joint Forces.
"Even the medics, and many of the people who were there, because of this conflict, these tribal issues, these racial issues, they are allied with the Joint Forces and with the SAF. That's why you don't depend on that narrative," he said.
Doctors told the BBC they believed RSF fighters deliberately targeted medical facilities because army or allied fighters were among their patients.
The onslaught of shelling and bombing culminated on 25 October 2025 with the RSF storming the hospital amid allegations of a massacre that killed more than 460 patients and their companions.
The RSF has denied a massacre occurred, although the WHO condemned the reported killings and satellite imagery appeared to show clusters of bodies on the blood-soaked grounds of the hospital.
The BBC shared details of its investigation with the UN human rights chief, who said our findings were "deeply disturbing", and consistent with the analysis of his office.
"Our monitoring and documentation shows the RSF repeatedly struck el-Fasher's main hospitals and makeshift health facilities, destroying or seriously damaging them and severely impacting access to health services for thousands of civilians trapped in the city," Türk said.
Healthcare in el-Fasher is now being run by the RSF-backed government. It has released several videos showing the Saudi Hospital and the Teaching Hospital re-opened, cleaned up and seeing some patients.
Dr Nugud says South Hospital is also set to reopen. He denied that doctors were forcibly abducted, telling the BBC that instead they had chosen to stay on to work.
"I have a video in front of the children's hospital when we freed a consultant, a doctor and six of the medical staff who were working with the SAF, and then when el-Fasher got liberated, there was a forgiveness for all of them.
"We liberated them," he said.
The BBC spoke to one of the doctors in the video, Dr Al-Haj Mohamed Ahmed. He told us he had no choice: "I was forced to be there.
"If I spoke out of line, they'd put a bullet through my head."
He was among several medical workers captured while trying to escape the city and sent back, along with Dr Mustafa Ahmed.
They distinguished themselves by bringing a cholera epidemic in a temporary prison at the paediatric hospital under control and were subsequently taken to Saudi Hospital.
"They started to say that you are the people of the city, and we take the city, so we need to work together for the sake of the city," says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, who describes waking up several mornings in a row at the prison to find 50 inmates dead of cholera.
A year on from the fall of el-Fasher, the trauma of this dark period in Sudan's civil war is still painfully sharp.
The front lines have shifted elsewhere with no signs of a resolution to the conflict. And attacks on healthcare continue as part of a wider and devastating humanitarian crisis.

The disadvantages of owning smart refrigerators
Before paying extra for a smart fridge, it helps to know what it could mean for your budget, your privacy, and software support over the years.
If you haven't shopped for appliances in a while, you may be surprised by how common smart models have become. To be clear, "dumb" ones do remain on sale. But even cheaper products frequently offer some smart home functionality, and the high-end models can include features like cameras and custom touchscreen controls. There are actually ovens with cameras despite what you'd assume from the heat involved.
The king of smart appliances, though, is the fridge. Once connected to Wi-Fi, many fridges will let you do things like check and adjust their temperature zones, or get alerts when maintenance is needed or the door is left open. The most advanced models — like Samsung's Bespoke Fridge with AI — can turn your fridge into a digital bulletin board, and even keep track of its contents.
In a sense, it's about time that appliances started feeling as advanced as the rest of our devices. But there are several potential drawbacks, among them data collection and obsolescence. You're probably better off with a smart display like an Echo Show if you want a family hub.
The literal and figurative costs of smart refrigerators
For most buyers, the overriding concern is cost. Shop around, and you'll likely find that the difference between a dumb fridge and one with bare-bones smart features (temperature status, door alerts, and the like) tends to be minor. As things become more advanced, however, the premiums can become exorbitant. In September 2026, Samsung was selling two versions of a four-door Bespoke fridge sized at 29 cubic feet: a $5,000 AI model with a display, and a $3,600 variant with some smart features that swaps the screen for a beverage center. Given that you could buy a complete second appliance with those savings, you should probably double-check your priorities.
Smart fridges also raise privacy and security issues. While your home is unlikely to be a target, commercial freezers in Europe were recently sabotaged by hackers, and with a smart refrigerator, you're adding another potential entry point into your network. Also, manufacturers are constantly collecting data from smart appliances. In some circumstances, this is for practical purposes, but it's also used for marketing. Samsung's touchscreen fridges display ads unless you disable them.
In the long term, your bigger concerns may be repair and obsolescence. While smart tech can help with diagnosis, you're also increasing the number of things that can break, and the potential service costs. On the obsolescence front, think about how rapidly other device makers cut off software support for older products. This is evident in how you can't even install watchOS 27 on the 2022 Apple Watch Ultra. Home appliances last eight to 19 years on average, so you're taking a huge gamble that a manufacturer won't cut off your apps and services the moment supporting old hardware looks bad on its bottom line.
Can it still be worth buying a smart refrigerator?
Ultimately, this is subjective, but if you're cost-conscious, you're probably better off focusing on the features that count most with any fridge: space, power efficiency, and balanced cooling. A touchscreen hardly matters if you can't fit a gallon of juice or if your leftovers are frozen when they're not supposed to be. Besides, generations of people have lived without needing an app to remind them about the door or whether they need more milk.
As we suggested up top, if you want the sort of communal hub promised by touchscreen fridges, it's far more cost-effective to buy a smart display. Amazon's Echo Show 16 is $500, doubles as a TV, and can easily be replaced on a whim. Apple fans now have the option of the $300 HomeView. Heck, you can use an iPad or any Android tablet if you like, though those aren't optimized for family sharing.
Because of discounts or other perks, a smart fridge can be tempting whether or not you were planning on getting one. Remember, though — you don't have to activate those smart features. You can stay disconnected and remove every concern except that initial sticker shock.

The blue wave that handed Democrats power in both the House and Senate did not filter neatly through ballot measures across the country.
Measures on abortion, marijuana, science funding, and Medicaid largely reflected a more liberal national sentiment. But multiple states voted to implement or enhance restrictions on transgender youth.
In Arizona, Colorado, and Washington, voters approved or were poised to approve measures to enact or expand prohibitions on transgender youth participation on school athletics teams aligned with their gender identity. Colorado also was on track to approve a new ban on gender-affirming surgery for minors.
While critics called the measures on transgender rights “ballot candy” for Republicans, there was no correlation between the measures and winning candidates’ affiliations. Colorado Democrats, for example, won the Senate, most House seats, and both the governor and attorney general offices.
The results indicate that many voters are concerned about gender, sports, and fairness in particular, but those worries may be outsized compared to the number of young transgender people these laws will apply to. Existing data suggest around 300,000 youth ages 13 to 17 nationally identify as transgender, and some 40% may participate in sports. In late 2024, the NCAA said that there were fewer than 10 transgender athletes among more than 500,000 total. And in response to a recent poll, an NCAA representative confirmed that zero transgender athletes currently compete in women’s leagues.
Data is limited and murky on the physical advantage that people worry transgender women may have in various competitions, but research so far does not suggest any inherent edge. When it comes to medical care, data show that top surgery is rare among minors, while bottom surgery on a minor’s genitals is already virtually nonexistent.
The Trump administration has relentlessly targeted youth gender-affirming care in the last two years, leading many hospitals to stop providing care like puberty blockers and hormones, even in states where the care is still legal. It’s unclear what that fight will look like now, as candidates like Abdul El-Sayed and James Talarico, who have expressed support for transgender youth, won across the country. Locally, six transgender candidates won seats in state legislatures that have never previously elected transgender representatives.
“The voters rejected the anti-trans rhetoric used against candidates while still stripping away our rights at the ballot,” Chase Strangio, who leads the ACLU’s LGBT & HIV Project, said on Instagram. Strangio argued that ballot measures are “a function of funding more than anything” and should not be used as justification for more restrictive legislation.
The blue wave could have trickle-down effects on Colorado’s ballot measures. Both proposals are statutory changes, which means that even once they officially pass, the state legislature can make amendments before enacting them. On Wednesday, the state’s governor-elect said the restrictions would need “a long, hard look,” before implementation, The Denver Post reported.
Abortion votes stick to the status quo
Four states voted on ballot measures related to abortion, and all preserved the existing legal status.
The most contentious vote was in Missouri, where just two years ago voters narrowly approved a measure to enshrine the right to reproductive freedom in the constitution. The state legislature asked voters to reverse that decision, tying a potential abortion ban to a more popular proposal to constitutionally ban gender-affirming care for minors. (That care is already illegal in the state, but not constitutionally prohibited.) Voters unequivocally rejected the bid, with nearly 56% of the vote against it.
In Nevada and Virginia, where abortion is already legal, strong majorities voted to enshrine that right in the state constitutions. Four years after the Supreme Court overruled Roe v. Wade, 26 states have some type of legal protections on abortion.
But stalwart red Idaho denied the right to abortion, preserving the state’s existing ban.
Weed smokers are safe in Mass.
A measure to repeal Massachusetts’ recreational marijuana law was defeated handily, with nearly 76% of voters choosing to keep the grass growing. Polling showed the measure had little chance of passing, yet out of the state’s nine ballot questions, it became the most expensive. The measure was almost entirely funded by Smart Approaches to Marijuana, a national nonprofit that advocates against legalization that put $3.7 million into the campaign. Opponents paid $2.8 million.
While no other states considered measures to legalize drugs like marijuana or psychedelics, Idaho voters preserved their right to do so in the future. More than 66% rejected a proposal that would have given all power to legalize psychoactive drugs to the legislature.
But results on other drug policy measures seem to complicate the narrative of a big blue wave. Voters in two states approved measures that appear to endorse the Trump administration’s punitive approach to drug policy from his executive order naming fentanyl as a weapon of mass destruction. Arizona approved a measure naming drug cartels terrorist organizations and directing the state’s Department of Homeland Security to address the threat, while Colorado voted to increase criminal penalties for the possession, manufacture, and sale of fentanyl. (Colorado’s governor-elect said this, too, may need to be reconsidered.)
Californians friendly to $8.4 billion research fund
Golden State voters appeared on track to pass California’s Proposition 38, which authorizes $8.4 billion in bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research. The result suggests that the state’s voters were eager to defend research funding after the Trump administration’s slew of grant terminations, delays, and disruptions. But the measure has generated controversy because of where that funding will likely go.
Prop 38 will direct half the funds, $4.2 billion, to a single institute that isn’t named explicitly but which must meet a long list of criteria that experts in California politics call “oddly specific.” Only one institute appears to meet those criteria: the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy. This institute, also known as CIII, was cofounded by Gary Michelson, a billionaire philanthropist, retired surgeon, and Prop 38’s leading backer. Michelson poured more than $40 million of his own money into the Yes on 38 campaign; fellow CIII cofounder and treasure Meyer Luskin contributed $5 million in support of the measure. As of mid-October, the No on 38 campaign had raised less than $9,000.
CIII is still under construction and went from having zero employees during the 2024 calendar year to three last month, according to documents filed with the Internal Revenue Service and reporting by CalMatters. STAT’s own reporting revealed that the American Association of Immunologists, the field’s leading scientific society, seriously considered pulling its endorsement of Prop 38 once it became clear half the funds would likely go to Michelson’s institute. The organization decided to maintain support after its governing body met with Michelson in August.
The measure also drew support from more than 70 organizations, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and the state’s Democratic and Republican parties.
Proponents argued that this investment would help researchers working to cure or treat new treatments for Alzheimer’s, heart disease, and cancer. They also framed Prop 38 as a way for voters to protect California from abrupt turns in federal science funding.
A Medicaid win, a school meals loss
Other health-related ballot initiatives saw mixed results, reflecting voters’ overarching concern with affordability and funding.
As national Medicaid cuts loom, South Dakota voters rejected an amendment that would have conditioned the state’s expansion program — already approved by voters — on the federal share of funding remaining at 90%. Proponents of the measure argued that decreases in federal funding would make it too expensive for the state. But it also would have meant a sudden loss of coverage for the tens of thousands of residents who are enrolled through the expansion program.
Arizona voters approved a measure to require voter approval for any local taxes on groceries, and to cap any such tax at 2%. (There’s no statewide sales tax on groceries, but local jurisdictions can enact them.)
North Dakota voters narrowly rejected a proposed constitutional amendment to require public schools to offer all students free breakfast and lunch. The program would have cost $124.3 million to $134.3 million every two years, per the North Dakota Monitor.

Ex-NYPD cop arrested for fatal slashing of Brooklyn jogger
Katie Suarez, 28, was discovered fatally injured on running path by her father

An ex-New York City police officer who was kicked off the force after being deemed psychologically unfit has been arrested in the fatal stabbing of a Brooklyn jogger.
Sayed Mohassib, 27, was charged with second-degree murder, tampering with physical evidence and criminal possession of a weapon Saturday in the October 30 killing of Katie Suarez. The 28-year-old was fatally stabbed in the neck while running along the Shore Parkway Greenway near her home.
Mohassib, who was working as an elementary school aide at the time of his arrest, allegedly told investigators he had no memory of the attack but woke up covered in blood and holding a knife, according to police sources cited by the New York Post.
Investigators tracked Mohassib to his Bensonhurst home after surveillance footage allegedly showed him leaving the park around the time Suarez was attacked. Police believe he disposed of the weapon in the garbage, which was taken to a Staten Island landfill before eventually ending up at a New Jersey dump, the outlet reports.
Suarez, a TD Bank teller training for an upcoming race, was following her usual waterfront running route after work on October 30. She planned to meet her parents afterward.
She spoke to her dad on the phone around 7:56 p.m., telling him she was about half a mile away and would meet him shortly, according to NYPD Chief of Detectives Joseph Kenny. When she never arrived, her dad went looking for her and found her unconscious beneath a tree along the waterfront path around 8:16 p.m.
Suarez was taken to the hospital with serious neck injuries. She was later declared brain dead but remained on life support so her organs could be donated. She died three days after the attack.
The circumstances surrounding Mohassib's arrest prompted interest in his previous time in law enforcement and the military.
Mohassib initially worked as a paraprofessional for the NYC Department of Education before joining the NYPD in 2022. However, he spent only about six weeks on the force before leaving to enlist in the Marines, according to the Post.
The military later discharged him after determining he was psychologically unfit for service, police sources told the outlet. Mohassib subsequently attempted to rejoin the NYPD but was denied and returned to working for the city's education department.
He was employed as a paraprofessional at PS 200 in Bensonhurst, just blocks from the waterfront area where Suarez was attacked.
Mohassib returned to the elementary school in the days after the stabbing, but colleagues reportedly became concerned by his erratic behavior and incoherent speech. They alerted police, although those reports were not what ultimately led investigators to him, according to the Post.
Resurfaced photographs of Mohassib also show him wearing an NYPD dress uniform and posing in a Brooklyn College basketball uniform. He attended Brooklyn College during the same period as Suarez, although investigators have not established whether the two knew each other, according to the outlet.
Police believe the attack was random, according to ABC7. The investigation remains ongoing.

Iran says it has lifted its self-imposed limit on missile ranges, and other Mideast news
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard has lifted its self-imposed limit on the range of its ballistic missiles, hinting at potential developments for longer-range capabilities
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard says it has lifted a self-imposed limit of 2,000 kilometers (1,200 miles) on the range of its ballistic missiles, suggesting the country may seek to develop missiles capable of reaching more distant targets as fears of renewed all-out war rise.
Meanwhile, airstrikes near Yemen’s capital killed 25 people, according to a spokesman for Yemen’s Houthi-run Health Ministry. Heavy rains lashed the Gaza Strip, flooding tents and intensifying the misery of hundreds of thousands of Palestinians.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Saturday. Read our full coverage here.
The comments by the spokesman of Iran’s paramilitary Revolutionary Guard came days after the country’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khomeini, warned that “any kind and level of threat” from the U.S. or Israel would face a response without geographic limits.
Asked at a Tehran news conference about the limit on missile ranges, Gen. Hossein Mohebbi said, “That restriction has been lifted for us.”
He did not say whether Iran had missiles capable of exceeding the limit, saying only Iran would “demonstrate these capabilities in practice” rather than make statements.
Iran is not known to have missiles that can go beyond the 2,000-kilometer (1,200-mile) limit — a range that puts parts of Greece and the Balkans, the entire Arabian Peninsula, the Levant and most of Egypt within reach. However, U.S. officials have said technology from Iran’s space program can be repurposed to build intercontinental ballistic missiles.
The Iranian military, meanwhile, said a tanker east of the Strait of Hormuz had hit a mine and caught fire. It did not identify the tanker's flag or destination. It said the vessel had turned off its navigational beacon and was sailing in a “prohibited area.”
Airstrikes in a village near Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, killed 25 people and wounded 30 others, mostly women and children, Anees Alasbahi, a spokesman for Yemen’s Houthi-run Health Ministry, said.
The Associated Press could not independently verify the claims. The Houthi spokesman accused Saudi Arabia, whose Information Ministry did not immediately reply to an AP request for comment.
Since the summer, fighting has escalated between the Iranian-backed Houthis — who control Sanaa, the north and the west of the country — and their Saudi-backed opponents based in the south and east.
In the Gaza Strip, displaced families spent a sleepless night as heavy rain flooded their fragile tents, soaking mattresses and belongings, and turning camp pathways into pools of muddy water.
The rain marks the start of another difficult winter for the more than 1.6 million Palestinians living in tents or other makeshift shelters in the territory, where nearly the entire population has lost its homes during Israel’s campaign triggered by the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks.

Majed Al-Omari, who lost a limb during the war, struggled to make his way between tents on crutches after the rains tore down the wooden frame and plastic sheeting of his shelter.
“We will have to sleep in the street tonight, or find somewhere else to stay,” he said.
The U.N. humanitarian office has said 294,250 families need shelter assistance for the rainy season, but available supplies are enough to provide only partial assistance to 18% of those in need. It said a lack of funds, slow procurement procedures and delayed approvals by the Israeli authorities mean additional supplies may not reach Palestinians until more than halfway through winter.
The results of the U.S. midterm elections suggest that long-standing U.S. support for Israel is on rocky grounds on both sides of the aisle. Democrats, who gained control of Congress, are fiercely divided, and many Republicans are increasingly critical of Israel’s government, particularly its wartime conduct in Gaza.
On Tuesday, as Americans went to the polls, President Donald Trump suggested cutting off aid to Israel. Then, a staunch critic of Israel, Abdul El-Sayed, became the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate.
The Democratic senator-elect from Michigan addressed U.S. Vice President JD Vance as “JD, habibi” — a common Arabic term of affection — in his victory speech. And Vance partly blamed the Republicans’ massive electoral losses across the country on U.S.-Israel relations, including the war in Iran the two countries launched jointly on Feb. 28.
“Something fundamental has shifted,” said Michael Oren, a historian and former Israeli ambassador to the U.S.
U.S. Central Command said Saturday that “strict enforcement” of the U.S. blockade on Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz continues.
It also announced a new task force focusing on hampering Iran’s options to transport what it called “advanced weapons and other materials” through its land borders and the Caspian Sea.
Iran established a chokehold on the strait, a vital strategic waterway in global trade, at the beginning of the war, and has claimed attacks on tankers. The U.S. says its blockade had redirected 144 commercial vessels through the end of October.

Hong Kong must show real remorse for the Tai Po fire tragedy
A bow and a resignation are not enough. The government must deliver long-overdue reforms, support survivors and take genuine responsibility
3-MIN READ3-MIN
Christine Loh is chief development strategist at the Institute for the Environment, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. 
When Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu and seven principal officials bowed deeply before the cameras on October 29, Hong Kong witnessed something rare: a collective government apology.
It came 11 months after the Wang Fuk Court fire claimed 168 lives and uprooted 1,984 households. A minister has resigned. Many reforms have been promised. Yet public reaction remains divided. That division reveals what people expect an apology to achieve, and how differently they understand political responsibility.
A political apology should acknowledge failure, accept responsibility and express remorse. It should also commit the government to preventing a recurrence. The purpose of a political apology is to bring closure. While the chief executive would like closure, he cannot yet declare that it has been achieved.

Dozens of global health and environmental organisations called on the World Health Organization on Tuesday to revise decades-old standards for nitrate levels in drinking water, arguing they do not reflect recent scientific evidence about potential health risks.
In an open letter, 85 organisations, including Greenpeace International and the World Organization of Family Doctors (WONCA), called on the United Nations health agency to include nitrate in an upcoming review of its drinking water guidelines.
The toxic effects of nitrates -- a residue left behind by intensive farming -- are widely recognised as particularly dangerous for children and pregnant women.
But the current WHO guidelines -- which set the maximum acceptable nitrate level in drinking water at 50 milligrammes per litre as nitrate or 11.3 milligrammes per litre as nitrate-nitrogen -- date back to 1958 and are "outdated", the organisations warned.
That level was set specifically to prevent so-called "blue-baby syndrome" -- a deadly blood disorder in which the blood's capacity for carrying oxygen is reduced.
But the limit "has not been updated in response to robust epidemiological evidence linking chronic, low-level nitrate exposure to long-term human health risks", Tuesday's letter said, pointing in particular to "colorectal cancer and adverse birth outcomes".
"Studies now link nitrate in drinking water, at levels well below the current WHO limit, to bowel cancer and premature birth," WONCA chair Pratyush Kumar said in a joint statement.
Decisive action
The letter was sent to coincide with WHO's annual One Health Day, which aims to raise awareness about the interconnected health of humans, animals, plants and shared ecosystems.
Surface water models indicate that hundreds of millions of people globally are exposed to elevated nitrate levels, the letter warned.
"Water should be life-giving, not life-threatening," Amanda Larsson, the global project lead for agriculture at Greenpeace, said in the statement.
"We cannot protect human health without protecting the groundwater and rivers that sustain us," she insisted.
"Governments must take decisive action to curb the growth of intensive livestock farming and actively support producers in transitioning to ecological farming practices -- ensuring that clean, safe drinking water isn't a luxury but a guarantee."
The organisations pointed to findings published last year by an expert panel commissioned by the Danish government indicating that the current international standard was insufficient to protect public health.
That expert panel recommended reducing the nitrate limit to 6.0 mg/L -- nearly 10 times below the current WHO benchmark -- something Denmark committed to earlier this year.
But most national governments base their drinking water standards on WHO guidelines, the organisations said, stressing that updating those guidelines was "vital for global policy reform".

CJP’s Abhijeet Dipke predicts ‘Modi govt’s defeat in 2029’ at anti-SIR rally in Kochi: ‘He will definitely go’
Dipke alleged that the government was waging a war against the country's youth to protect Gyanesh Kumar and questioned why he was so important to the PM.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke on Saturday predicted that the Modi government would be voted out of power in the 2029 Lok Sabha elections and urged people to prepare for a change of government at the Centre.
Addressing a protest meeting organised as part of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)'s 'Jantar Mantar at Kochi' campaign against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, Dipke said a change of government would come only through elections and reiterated his demand for an independent and impartial electoral system. Track live updates on anti-SIR stir in Kochi
Referring to the BJP's assertion that Modi would remain in power, Dipke said, "Be prepared for 2029. He will definitely go."
He repeatedly asked the gathering whether Modi would lose power in 2029, drawing cheers from the protesters.
"The change in the government will only happen through elections," he said, adding that the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar was necessary to ensure a fair electoral process.
"Gyanesh Kumar has to go. If he goes, Narendra Modi will also go," he said.
Dipke alleged that the government was waging a war against the country's youth to protect the Chief Election Commissioner and questioned why Kumar was so important to the prime minister.
Referring to his arrest in Delhi along with CJP leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka for entering Jantar Mantar with the national flag, he said he would continue carrying the Tricolour wherever he went.
"I was sent behind bars for raising this Tricolour. Saurav and Ashu, my two brothers, were also sent behind bars for raising it. The last time this happened in India was when we were ruled by the British," he said.
Comparing the Modi government with British rule, Dipke alleged that the present dispensation was attempting to restrict people's freedom.
"I want to tell Narendra Modi that I will carry this Tricolour everywhere, in every part of this country. If you want to arrest me, you can arrest me in Delhi, Maharashtra, Keralam or Tamil Nadu. Arrest me from every part of the country, but I will come back again and raise this Tricolour," he said.
He alleged that the government was gradually attempting to control what people eat, whom they marry and whom they vote for, and claimed that the SIR exercise was being used to influence electoral outcomes.
"They first wanted to control what you eat, then whom you can marry and love, and now they have come to a point where they want to control whom you vote for," he said.
Dipke said the country was founded on the ideals of three leaders -- B R Ambedkar, Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru. Describing Gandhi as the soul of India, Ambedkar as its backbone and Nehru as its mind, he said Prime Minister Narendra Modi did not have the stature to become greater than the three leaders.
"Even if you remain in power for 120 years, you will never become bigger than Ambedkar, Gandhi and Nehru," he said.
Rejecting allegations that the CJP was receiving foreign funds or working to destabilise India, Dipke accused Modi of acting at the behest of foreign powers, particularly US President Donald Trump.
He alleged that Modi had compromised India's interests to protect his image and avoid being humiliated by Trump on the global stage.
"Who is selling the interests of this nation? It is you, not the CJP and not the cockroaches," he said.
Dipke said the country had remained largely silent for the past 10 to 12 years, but the Jantar Mantar protest had helped people regain their voice and courage.
"For the last 10-12 years, somewhere this country had lost its voice. But what happened at Jantar Mantar, because of that, the country has found its voice again," he said.
He alleged that the government was cracking down on young protesters because they had begun questioning those in power.
Dipke also accused the BJP of dividing people on religious lines and alleged that riots were being caused for political interests.
"This is the youth of this country whom you are calling anarchists. No, sir, we are not anarchists. We are Ambedkarites, we are Gandhians. Don't you dare call us anarchists," he said.
He claimed that India was more democratic during the tenure of former Prime Minister Manmohan Singh, when people were allowed to openly criticise the prime minister.
"First UAPA will be slapped on Modi if he pulls out those speeches that he spoke against Manmohan Singh. But that was India; that was more democratic," he said.
"I am not saying that government was perfect. But that India was more democratic, where you were allowed to criticise the prime minister. And that is how democracy should be," he added.
The protest meeting at Rajendra Maidan was attended by a large number of people from different age groups. Leaders of various youth and socio-cultural organisations also took part in the event, where cultural programmes were organised.
Earlier, a protest march from Marine Drive to Rajendra Maidan was led by actor Prakash Raj.

A video circulating on X, bearing the logo of M World, purports to show Russian foreign minister Sergey Viktorovich Lavrov saying that India is merely an oil-trading partner to Russia and that the two countries share only a commercial relationship. In the video, Lavrov is also heard claiming that India has no right to interfere in Russia’s foreign policy or advise Moscow on matters concerning Russia, Ukraine, the United States or any other country.
Supreme Court advocate and activist Prashant Bhushan shared the video on his X account (@pbhushan1), which he later deleted. In his post, he criticized the Indian government and questioned what kind of advice external affairs minister S Jaishankar gave to Russia.
Another X account, Diya Kapoor, also shared the video with the similar claim of Sergey Lavrov drawing clear boundaries about the relationship with India.
🚨🇷🇺🇮🇳 RUSSIA DRAWS A CLEAR LINE!
“India is a trading partner, nothing more. We supply oil, and India pays for it. This commercial relationship does not give New Delhi the right to dictate or interfere in Russia’s foreign policy.”
Sergey Viktorovich ⚠️🌍 https://t.co/uX1x0adl0G
— Diya kapoor (@DiyaKapoor113) November 2, 2026
Some X accounts also shared this video with the claim of Sergey Lavrov dismissing India.
Fact Check
After a closer examination of the video, the movements of Sergey Lavrov while speaking appear unnatural and seem out of sync with the audio. This suggests that the clip may have been edited or manipulated. Using this as a lead, we performed a Google reverse image search on several keyframes from the video and found a video with the same background and clothing uploaded by M WORLD on October 31.
A comparison of the two videos shows that Sergey Lavrov’s clothing, background, head movements, and hand gestures are the same, with only the audio being different. Even the ‘M World’ YouTube channel logo appeared in both videos, confirming that the original video had been digitally manipulated. Both videos also feature the exact same glitch at the same moment.
In the original video, Sergey Lavrov is seen refusing the reports from Ukrainian officials claiming that Russian President Vladimir Putin refused to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and stating if Zelenskyy wants a direct meeting, he must travel to Moscow, where Russia will guarantee his safety and security.
Media outlet DW News posted the original video on October 31 showing the conversation about President Putin and Ukrainian President Zelenskyy meeting.
Furthermore, the official X account of the Russian Embassy in India, Russia in India (@RusEmbIndia) has also debunked the video. “Please stop copying silly AI fakes,” it said in a comment to the X post by Diya Kapoor.
@DiyaKapoor113 Please stop copying silly AI fakes
— Russia in India 🇷🇺 (@RusEmbIndia) November 3, 2026
Union government’s official MEA fact check account, too, flagged the post as fake.
Fake Alert!!! 🚨🚨🚨
The video of the Russian Foreign Minister being used in this post is fake! https://t.co/jpEX6qu19p
— MEA FactCheck (@MEAFactCheck) November 3, 2026
To sum up, the viral video claiming that Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov publicly dismissed India’s diplomatic standing is completely false and an AI-generated deepfake. The original footage contains a briefing regarding Russia-Ukraine relations, and there is no mention of India.

There's AI agent drama in startup land, and it poses a big legal question.
It started with an accusation from Josh Manders, founder of the cloud hosting platform Primcloud. Manders asked why Jake Runzer, an employee of Railway, a competing cloud provider, was "trying to breach" Primcloud's infrastructure.
Hey @Railway, is there a reason employee's of yours are trying to breach my infrastructure?
Your employee Jake Runzer, just attempted to tonight.
— Josh (@joshmanders) November 3, 2026
Railway CEO Jake Cooper responded and tagged Runzer.
"That was indeed me," Runzer wrote, saying that no malice was intended. "I've been running some agents to do signups + agentic testing on similar platforms. Just halted the harness I was designing around this as it was definitely going off the rails and reaching too far."
Ah yup. That was indeed me. No mallace intended. I've been running some agents to do signups + agentic testing on similar platforms. Just halted the harness I was designing around this as it was definitely going off the rails and reaching too far
— Jake (@jakerunzer) November 3, 2026
Runzer's post quickly circulated across the web as X users questioned the legality of AI agents attempting to breach a company's infrastructure. Cooper apologized and said that Railway would ban any testing of the models on external organizations that wasn't performed manually.
The legal threat of the AI era
Runzer said that his agent went "off the rails." The drama drives at a key question of the AI age: If an agent gets in trouble, who could be held legally responsible?
It's a question that has challenged lawyers, especially after the OpenAI-Hugging Face hack. Since AI agents can operate autonomously, proving liability can be complicated.
Mark Rasch, the general counsel of threat advisory firm Unit 221B, said that prosecutors would have to prove two things: that the AI agent actually attempted to illegally access another computer, and that the user intended for it to do so.
That second part — proving the user's intent to illegally breach a system — is thorny. In the case of a bug bounty, or a deal offered from a company to security researchers who can find flaws in its system, users look for security vulnerabilities but have no intent to break the law. "The problem is that the AI agent, once they find a way to break in, might say: 'Huh, this might work, let me try it,'" Rasch said.
Then there's the question of negligence. Elimu Kajunju, a cybersecurity lawyer at Rimon Law, said defendants could try to shift blame onto the AI companies that built the agents.
Kajunju thought these cases were becoming harder to defend, because it's difficult to claim surprise. "This has happened multiple times now," he said, speaking generally. "We really can't say that anymore."
Both Rasch and Kajunju said that the legal precedent was still forming, making it a pressing question for lawyers and AI users alike.
Where the spat stands
Railway's CEO later posted a longer explanation of the incident.
Cooper said that an employee, on his own time, had created a tool for "proactive identification + reporting of bug bounties within the broader community," using an externally hosted service running on DeepSeek. The employee's tool was used only once, the CEO said, and the employee "halted it proactively within 15 minutes of starting."
"Railway does not condone these actions," Cooper wrote. "We create an environment where internal red teaming has strict guidelines, and when bug bounty disclosures must occur, we follow every letter of responsible disclosure. We have addressed this incident with the employee directly and have taken appropriate action. We are also reinforcing our expectations for employee conduct to help prevent similar situations."
Manders countered that he doesn't have a bug bounty program. Primcloud considers any attempt to "probe, scan or test" its vulnerabilities as a security violation in its acceptable use policy.
To further complicate Railway's week, the company sustained multi-day outages starting Wednesday. By Friday, it said that some customers' service had been restored.
It's not clear whether Manders will sue. Manders, Runzer, and Cooper did not respond to requests for comment from Business Insider.
Cooper had some thoughts on who was to blame.
"You operate the machinery, you are responsible for that what that machinery does," he wrote.

Teenagers are reportedly turning to a prescription cancer drug in the hope of gaining a few extra inches, as a social media trend called 'heightmaxxing' fuels anxiety around physical appearance and height. The trend is part of the wider 'maxxing' culture, in which young people share methods they believe can help them achieve an ideal version of themselves. One prominent offshoot is 'looksmaxxing', where young men exchange tips on improving their facial features, physique and overall appearance. According to a report by Rolling Stone, some teenagers have started taking erdafitinib, a drug used to treat certain cancers, believing it could help them grow taller. Online, they refer to the medicine as 'erda' and share updates about their height, duration of use and reported side effects. Interest in the drug appears to have been fuelled by medical reports of unexpected growth in children who received erdafitinib during cancer treatment. However, it has not been approved or established as a height-enhancement treatment. One teenager featured in the report is Zak, a 17-year-old TikTok user from New York, who said he had been taking erdafitinib intermittently since he was 15. He reportedly purchased the medicine from overseas online sellers, initially paying $300 (approximately ₹28,206) for a month's supply. Aware of the risks of taking a cancer drug without medical supervision, Zak said he had started setting aside money for potential hospital bills. He attributed his height-related insecurities partly to social media videos discussing how tall men should be to find partners, as well as being teased at school for being shorter than girls in his class. Zak reported side effects including nosebleeds, extremely dry skin and severe joint pain. Although he has since stopped taking the medicine, he said he was satisfied with the growth he believed he had experienced and was considering taking it again. According to his own measurements, he grew several inches between 15 and 17. Erdafitinib, sold under the brand name Balversa, blocks proteins known as fibroblast growth factor receptors (FGFRs), which play a role in regulating cell growth. Initially approved in the US in 2019, the prescription drug is used to treat certain adults with locally advanced or metastatic urothelial cancer, a type of cancer that commonly affects the bladder, when their tumours have specific genetic alterations. A study titled Accelerated Linear Growth during Erdafitinib Treatment: An FGFR-Related, but Growth Factor and Sex Steroid-Independent Mechanism?, published online on July 31, 2024, examined two children treated at the Medical University of Vienna. The researchers reported accelerated linear growth and changes in the children's growth plates, including widening and increased mineralisation. Both children had received the drug through a compassionate-use programme after standard treatment options and clinical trial possibilities had been exhausted. However, the findings do not establish that erdafitinib is safe or effective for healthy teenagers seeking to increase their height. Adalbert Raimann, a paediatric endocrinologist at the Medical University of Vienna, explained that the medicine blocks proteins involved in regulating bone growth. He warned that the long-term consequences of interfering with these processes in otherwise healthy children remain unknown. Andrew Dauber, a paediatric endocrinologist at Children's National Hospital, also said he would not prescribe erdafitinib to help children grow taller, describing the practice as too dangerous. The parents of a 13-year-old girl have sued Google claiming she planned a potential suicide and funeral using its AI technology on a school-issued computer.
Filed Monday in a California court, the complaint is the first known case accusing Google of negligence related to AI integrations on Chromebooks, the tech giant's low-cost laptops used by millions of students in the United States and around the world.
The teenager was not able to access Google's Gemini app, nor OpenAI's ChatGPT, because they were blocked by her school. She was nonetheless still able to use Google's search engine, which contains AI-powered tools.
Those features were notably not among the tools that Google announced this week will be disabled by default for students.
"Schools should turn search off and keep it off until Google removes AI mode from search or ensures that every single student is always safe when they're interacting with AI," Andrew Liddell, one of the family's attorneys, told AFP on Thursday.
The complaint alleges that the child had been a "happy 13-year-old girl" in North Carolina who received great grades, played music and participated in Girl Scouts.
Despite "no history" of mental illness, within months of using Google's AI-powered search on her school laptop, she began a "quiet spiral into a severe psychological crisis" according to the complaint.
On March 17, the school's monitoring software flagged a document titled "Funeral," and the school notified her parents.
Her mother then saw the child writing a farewell letter in real-time after logging into her daughter's account, and her father intervened.
"We are reviewing the claims in the lawsuit and we take this very seriously," Google spokesperson Jose Castaneda told AFP.
Google argues that AI mode includes safeguards against self-harm and attempts to bypass them.
But the child "was able to keep going back over and over and over again," Liddle said. "Whatever safeguards they think they put in place were obviously insufficient."
Developers of fast-evolving AI technology are facing a litany of similar lawsuits in the US.
OpenAI faces several wrongful death suits, including from the parents of 16-year-old Adam Raine, a teenager who committed suicide allegedly using methods advised by ChatGPT.
Google and the startup Character.AI agreed in January to settle several lawsuits filed by families of teenagers out of court.
On Wednesday, Google, TikTok and Meta each separately sued California to block a law that prohibits social media companies from providing addictive features to users under 16.
Governor Gavin Newsom signed the law in September, and it goes into effect on January 1, 2027.

Hawaii has the highest proportion of Asian American eligible voters among all US states, with the community accounting for 37% of its electorate, according to a new analysis by the Pew Research Center. The finding highlights the growing significance of Asian Americans in the country's electoral landscape, particularly in states where they represent a substantial share of the voting population. Based on an analysis of the 2024 American Community Survey, Pew found that California ranked second, with Asian Americans making up 15% of its eligible voters. Nevada followed at 9%, while New Jersey and Washington each recorded an 8% share. The figures offer a snapshot of the demographic composition of the US electorate as political parties assess the results of the November 3, 2026, midterm elections. Pew's figures refer to eligible voters, defined as US citizens aged 18 and above, rather than the overall population. The Asian American category includes people who identify as Asian alone and are not Hispanic. Hawaii's 37% share places it considerably ahead of other states, with the proportion more than twice that of California, the second-ranked state. The state's demographic composition is distinct from much of mainland America. Asian Americans have a long-established presence in Hawaii, with generations of families tracing their roots to migration from countries such as Japan, China and the Philippines. Much of this migration was linked to plantation labour and the development of the islands' economy. Over time, these communities established deep-rooted family networks and successive generations of US citizens, contributing to the relatively high proportion of Asian Americans eligible to vote. Hawaii's position also reflects the state's broader demographic profile, where Asian Americans constitute a particularly significant part of the population and electorate. California, despite having one of the largest Asian American populations in the country, has a substantially lower proportion of Asian eligible voters at 15%. Nevada, at 9%, completes the top three, followed by New Jersey and Washington at 8% each. The growing electoral significance of Asian Americans comes against the backdrop of a broader expansion of the community's voting strength across the United States. Pew's analysis shows that Asian Americans accounted for 13.65 million eligible voters in 2026, an increase of approximately 2.25 million, or 20%, since 2022. This makes them one of the fastest-growing racial groups in the US electorate. However, population growth does not automatically translate into voting power. Citizenship and age are two important factors determining how much of a community can participate in elections. According to Pew, approximately 60% of the Asian American population in the US was eligible to vote in 2024. This compares with 81% of White Americans, 74% of Black Americans and 52% of Hispanic Americans. The relatively lower eligibility rate among Asian Americans is partly explained by the community's immigrant population. Around 25% of Asian Americans were non-citizens in 2024, compared with 21% of Hispanic Americans. The composition of the Asian American electorate is also distinctive. Pew found that 65% of Asian eligible voters were naturalised citizens, while 35% were born in the US. These differences help explain why states with large Asian American populations do not necessarily have equally large shares of Asian eligible voters. The Pew analysis also highlights significant geographical differences in the distribution of other racial and ethnic groups across the US electorate. Maine has the largest proportion of White eligible voters, with the group accounting for 92% of its electorate. Vermont and West Virginia follow at 91% each, while New Hampshire stands at 89% and Iowa at 87%. Among Hispanic eligible voters, New Mexico has the largest share at 43%. California ranks second at 33%, followed by Texas at 32%, Arizona at 25% and Florida at 23%. The figures underline the significant electoral presence of Hispanic communities in several states, particularly in the southwestern US. Meanwhile, the District of Columbia has the largest proportion of Black eligible voters, at 41%. Mississippi follows at 36%, while Georgia and Louisiana each have 31%. Maryland rounds out the top five at 30%. Unlike Hawaii's Asian electorate, however, Black eligible voters do not constitute the largest racial or ethnic group in any state's electorate, according to the analysis. The demographic findings come at a time when Asian American and Pacific Islander (AAPI) voters are attracting greater attention from political parties and election strategists. A survey conducted for the 2026 Midterm Election Voter Poll by BSP Research and the African American Research Collaborative, in partnership with several national organisations, points to a shift in voting preferences among Asian American voters. According to the survey, 64% of AAPI voters supported Democratic candidates in US House races, compared with 33% who backed Republicans. This represented a nine-percentage-point swing towards Democrats compared with the partisan balance recorded in the 2024 presidential election. The survey also highlighted the importance of younger voters in the community. One in eight AAPI voters said they had cast their first ballot in the 2026 elections. More than half of AAPI voters under the age of 40 reported having first voted in 2022 or later. The findings suggest that Asian American voters are becoming an increasingly important electorate, particularly in competitive congressional districts where relatively small shifts in voter preferences can influence election outcomes. The political environment has also been shaped by concerns over anti-Asian hostility and immigration policies. A September 2026 report by Stop AAPI Hate found that 48% of South Asian adults surveyed had experienced a hate-related incident because of their race, ethnicity or nationality in 2025. The organisation also documented a significant rise in anti-South Asian slurs online between 2023 and 2025. Death toll from air strikes near Yemeni capital rises to 33, Houthis say
The death toll from Saturday's air strikes on a village near Yemen's capital, Sanaa, has risen to at least 33, with 39 wounded, Houthis said, in one of the deadliest reported attacks since fighting between Saudi Arabia and the group resumed in July.
The Houthis' Saba news agency said the strikes were carried out by Saudi Arabia. Riyadh has not claimed the attack.
The Houthi-run health ministry said the strikes hit homes in the Bani Hushaysh area, a Houthi stronghold east of Sanaa, and that most of those killed were women and children.
Abdul-Aziz al-Dailami, director of Sehatuna Hospital in Sanaa, said many victims remained trapped under the rubble, including first responders.
"The strikes keep coming. Just as rescuers arrive, another strike hits. We have even lost some of our own medical responders, who have been martyred," he told Reuters.
"We received a number of wounded individuals in very critical condition, with injuries to the head, chest and legs, as well as fractures," al-Dailami added.

Several tanker ships linked to Iran have been loitering over subsea Internet cables in the Gulf of Oman near the Strait of Hormuz—a possible indication that the Iranian government is preparing to attack such undersea infrastructure in response to any renewed US and Israeli strikes.
The movements of three sanctioned tankers and an Iranian fishing boat have been tracked near major undersea cables by the maritime intelligence firm Windward in October, according to the Financial Times. Six active cables currently cross through the contested Strait of Hormuz, linking the Middle East to Europe, Africa and Asia, with two more cables having segments under construction in the region.
Four countries, including Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar, depend entirely upon such subsea telecommunications connections running through the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint to link with the outside world. But other countries also depend heavily on the region’s undersea cable network—one third of India’s westbound Internet traffic goes through the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz.
One cable under construction, the 2Africa cable, is owned by a tech consortium that includes the US company Meta. That was one of the major cable corridors visited by the drifting Iran-linked ships.
Windward used both ship-tracking data and satellite images to track the vessels as they slowed down and looped around near multiple cables, with some ships then “going dark” by switching off their automatic identification system (AIS) transponders that normally broadcast their location and other information.
Such movement and behavioral patterns suggest the Iran-linked ships may be “mapping the cable routes, or placing charges or mines on them while dark,” Windward told the Financial Times.
Windward highlighted the examples of two sanctioned tankers linked to Iran that spent days drifting “directly over regional cable corridors… both with no commercial reason to stop” in a blog post on October 26. Both ships carried no commercial cargo.
