Claim: Video of Muslim MPs performing Namaz together inside the Israeli parliament.
Fact: The video shows Jordanian MPs performing the Dhuhr (noon) prayer inside the Jordanian parliament in Amman on 03 November 2026. There are no reports of Muslim MPs performing namaz in the Israeli parliament. Hence, the claim made in the post is False.
First, we searched for reports of any such act happening in the Israeli Knesset recently but couldn’t find any credible reports to support it. Moreover, the parliament announced that Israel’s newly elected Knesset will hold its inaugural session on 10 November 2026, during which lawmakers will be sworn in, and the speaker will be elected.
Next, a reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to the same visuals published by BBC News Arabic and Jordanian media outlets (here, here & here). These reports state that the footage shows members of parliament performing the Dhuhr (noon) prayer inside the House of Representatives of Jordan (the Jordanian Parliament) in Amman on 03 November 2026.
The prayer was reportedly led by MP Dr. Ahmad Al-Raqab right before a scheduled legislative session to elect members of the parliament’s permanent bureau. He can be seen leading the prayer in the extended video published by some media outlets.
Furthermore, the presence of Jordan’s national emblem in the viral video, along with matching interior visuals, conclusively proves that the footage is from the Jordanian parliament and not the Israeli parliament.
To sum it up, the video from Jordan’s parliament is being falsely shared with the claim that it shows Muslim MPs performing Namaz in the Israeli parliament.

Victorian premier vows to make 'whatever changes' after delivery driver fatal stabbing
In short:
Victorian Premier Ben Carroll says community safety is his top priority, after a deadly attack involving two delivery riders in Melbourne's CBD.
Jianming Feng, 47, was fatally stabbed on Friday night while making a delivery for Hungry Panda.
A 51-year-old man has been arrested over the incident.
Victorian Premier Ben Carroll has vowed to make "whatever changes are necessary" following the fatal stabbing attack of a delivery driver in Melbourne's CBD.
Chinese national and father of two, Jianming Feng, was fatally stabbed on Friday night while making a delivery run for Hungry Panda near the Queen Victoria Market.
Another food deliver rider, aged 34, was injured in the alleged altercation.
On Sunday, Mr Carroll said he would continue to work with the Transport Workers Union and other representatives to ensure the safety of gig economy workers.
"As premier I will ensure I do everything I can with the Chief Commissioner of Victoria Police that, no matter where you work, no matter where you shop, no matter where you live, that you are safe," he said.
"We do know that often people in the gig economy, people who are doing transit deliveries, are some of the most vulnerable Victorians and they do need proper protections in place and workplace safety."
Homicide Squad detectives have arrested a 51-year-old Footscray man over the incident.
Safety concerns on the rise
Last night hundreds of people attended a vigil for Mr Feng, with many raising concerns about safety in the city.
"This is not how we're picturing Melbourne would be like," international student Xi Ip said, who was among those at the vigil.
"We were expecting a safer community. We don't want anything like this to ever happen again. That's a 47-year-old man who has a family to support.
"This is a pure tragedy … We want police to protect not just citizens but all of the community in the city."
Another student Xenith Yen said she was considering moving back home to Shanghai.
"I feel so unsafe in this city and I am paying a very high rate of tax but I don't get anything back from this city. I want to go back home."
Student Casper Ge called on the state's leaders to do more.
"It's everyone's right to have a safe city when they're doing their job. I feel very bad for this poor man."
Ria Li, who lives next to the scene, said she had lived in Melbourne for two years and was concerned about her safety because of drug use in the CBD.
She said she wanted to see steps taken by the government and Hungry Panda, which she said was a well-used delivery service among the Chinese student community, to improve driver safety.
"In Melbourne's CBD, international students are not a small group," she said.
"It's very depressing, it's very unfair that … someone's husband, someone's son and someone's dad got killed. It's really depressing as a Chinese to see such tragedy happen right next to my apartment."
Hungry Panda and the Chinese consulate in Melbourne have been contacted for comment.

The Republicans' defeat in the U.S. midterm elections was watched closely in Russia, where some observers are predicting it could herald more support for Ukraine when the Democrats take over Congress in January.
But if the Kremlin is hearing the ticking of a clock on its nearly 5-year-old full-scale invasion of its neighbour, it seemingly remains unperturbed.
Asked if the election's outcome could stymie U.S. attempts to help negotiate a settlement between Moscow and Kyiv, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov voiced hope that U.S. President Donald Trump will continue to pursue his peace efforts.
“There is groundwork already in place, and another round of trilateral negotiations is set to take place very soon,” Mr. Peskov said of talks planned for Tuesday (November 10, 2026) and Wednesday (November 11) involving Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. representatives in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates.
He also praised the “successful humanitarian peace-building efforts” by first lady Melania Trump, adding that “we hope that all of this will continue.”
Last week's limited ceasefire around the Russia-occupied city of Oleshky, brokered with her help, allowed for the delivery of humanitarian aid and the evacuation of some residents.
Mr. Peskov shrugged off a question from reporters on whether the new Congress would challenge Mr. Trump's stance on Russia and Ukraine. He called it an “internal matter” for the U.S.
Trump's recent moves have appeared to favour Moscow
Trump’s recent moves appear to favour Moscow
In recent months, Mr. Trump's actions appeared to favour Moscow
Last month, he struck a diesel fuel import deal with Russia in a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on the Kremlin, to the dismay of Ukraine and its European allies. He also claimed that Kyiv's attacks on Russian oil refineries caused a spike in diesel prices in the U.S. He urged Kyiv to halt the strikes, even though rising global energy prices were largely driven by the Iran war.
Mr. Trump also issued an executive order to put on hold sweeping new sanctions that clamped down on the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause was in the national interest. Lawmakers from both parties blasted Mr. Trump's move as benefiting Russian President Vladimir Putin.
At the same time, Ukraine reported a throttling of Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX. Mr. Trump denied being behind the brief slowing of Starshield, but the move to limit the system that serves as the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and battlefield communications was widely seen as part of Washington's efforts to pressure Kyiv.
The diesel deal appeared to falter this week after U.S. federal and state officials warned that handling any shipments could bring legal consequences, and two U.S.-bound tankers changed course. The Kremlin sought to play down the development, saying deliveries will continue.
Kyiv desperately needs to replenish its supplies of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors to fend off Russia's ballistic missile attacks. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has made repeated requests for Washington to speed up delivery of the defensive systems, but U.S. stockpiles have been exhausted by the Iran war, and the U.S. has prioritised replenishing its own arsenals.
On October 30, the Trump administration said it has approved a proposed $2.1 billion sale of Patriot interceptors for Ukraine after Kyiv had accused the Pentagon of delaying delivery.
Mr. Trump also appeared to echo the Kremlin's view that Mr. Zelenskyy was an obstacle to peace while saying Mr. Putin was more open to a deal.
Mr. Trump on Thursday (November 5) conferred with Mr. Putin's envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who attended a White House ceremony with the first lady recognising last week's humanitarian truce. The President didn't meet any of the Ukrainian officials also at the event but hinted that some kind of grand deal about European security was in the works.
Many in Russia argue that the Democrats' victory could put congressional pressure on Mr. Trump to tread more carefully and toughen his stand on Russia.
Dmitry Medvedev, who served as Russian President in 2008-12, predicted that Mr. Trump would be less inclined to press Ukraine when a new Congress is seated.
"He doesn't need an extra confrontation with Democrats,” said Mr. Medvedev, who now serves as deputy head of Russia's Security Council.
New House and Senate could boost aid to Ukraine
There has been strong bipartisan support for Ukraine, raising the prospect of veto-proof passage of more aid to Kyiv or tough new sanctions on Moscow.
On Wednesday (November 4), Mr. Zelenskyy told German broadcaster ZDF that while there has been backing for Kyiv from both parties, the Democrats “speak very clearly about supporting Ukraine."
In other remarks on Thursday (November 5), the Ukrainian leader also noted the midterm elections could have a positive effect on U.S. assistance, including speedier delivery of the Patriot interceptors. “I believe our chances of getting additional assistance from the United States may now grow,” he said.
Abbas Gallyamov, a former Putin speechwriter-turned-political analyst who lives abroad, argued that his old boss had missed a chance of striking a deal on Ukraine before the Democrats won and now could face a less cooperative Washington.
“Putin's prospects have significantly worsened,” Mr. Gallyamov wrote in a commentary. “He thought that the time was on his side and wasn't in a hurry to use the window of opportunity that had opened after Trump's victory, and now this window is starting to close.”
Some policy experts, however, cautioned against expectations of a dramatic shift.
The Democrats could put more funding for Ukraine on the agenda and increase pressure on Mr. Trump over the diesel deal or Russia sanctions waivers, but hard limits on the President's power are unlikely, said Jorn Fleck, senior director of the Atlantic Council's Europe Center.
“Even with a strong majority in both chambers of Congress, Democrats will struggle to impose meaningful limits on Trump's conduct of foreign policy, given his constitutional powers and willingness to push the envelope,” Mr. Fleck said in a commentary.
“Unshackled from having to face voters at the ballot box again, Trump may shift into deal-making overdrive to cement his legacy.”
Some expect a more hard-lined Trump
Konstantin Kosachev, a Deputy Speaker of the upper house of the Russian parliament, argued that Mr. Trump's executive powers in the foreign policy sphere would allow him to pursue his course regardless of congressional opposition.
He said if authorities in Kyiv believed that the Republicans' defeat would make the Trump administration more receptive to Ukraine's requests, they could be mistaken.
“They will not find a more pliable or constrained Trump," Mr. Kosachev said. “Rather, they will face a more resolute one, who is no longer looking over his shoulder at upcoming elections.”
For all the importance of Congress, "the U.S. President's role in foreign policy remains paramount — a fact Trump understands better than anyone else,” he said.
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna struck a similar tone in an interview on Thursday (November 5) with The Associated Press, saying "the President is President Trump,” and he has the ability to dictate foreign and security policy. “Unpredictability” should be expected, he added.
Mr. Kosachev said that by pinning their hopes on a victory by the Democrats, Kyiv and its allies in London, Brussels and other capitals in Europe have sided with Mr. Trump's domestic political adversaries.
"Consequently, they are all but guaranteed two years of a hard-line Trump,” he said.

Democrats plan to widen their probes of fatal ICE shootings
The morning after Tuesday's midterms was gloomy and rainy in Minneapolis, but people still gathered at the place where Border Patrol agents shot and killed Alex Pretti, a VA nurse and U.S. citizen, last January. All week, community members have come here to place their "I Voted" stickers at the memorial.
Nicki Adams, who dated Pretti and was his close friend for nearly 17 years, watched quietly as a woman added her sticker to a street lamp completely covered in the red decals.
"I wanted to see all the stickers. I just wanted to be here," she says. "It just means a lot to me. I think it would mean a lot to Alex, too."
A few blocks away, people left their stickers where an ICE officer killed Renee Good, a mom of three and a U.S. citizen, just a few weeks before Pretti's death. In Houston, they left them where an ICE officer killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a father of three and a Mexican immigrant, in July.
Adams says these stickers, and the election results this week, send a clear message to Congress: "You work for us, and please carry on these values that we care about … We want to be seen and heard and taken care of and have our neighbors taken care of."
The deaths of Pretti and Good during the ICE surge in Minneapolis marked a pivotal moment for the country, sparking intense public backlash to President Trump's aggressive deportation efforts. But federal law enforcement officials have given little indication they're progressing in investigating their deaths, or the deaths of at least seven other people killed by federal immigration agents since Trump took office again last year. DHS did not respond to an NPR request for the status of those investigations.
Now, after Democrats' sweeping wins this week, their deaths at the hands of immigration agents will likely be the targets of renewed investigations. With a majority in Congress, Democrats can issue subpoenas to the major players in Trump's mass deportation plan, compelling them to testify under oath before the legislature.
That could include White House Border Czar Tom Homan, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, former Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino, and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, among others.
Congress can also demand internal documents like use-of-force reports.
"They can dissect these individual shootings, and really unravel the story of what happened," says Naureen Shah, who leads the ACLU's immigration policy work.
Democrats have already held shadow hearings on the ICE shootings, during which they've called in family members and witnesses to testify.
But Shah says now Congress can ask key questions of top decision makers: What orders were given to immigration officers in the field? What was training like for these officers?
Who made the decision to paint Good and Pretti as threats, including calling Pretti a "would-be assassin" and a domestic terrorist, when video showed otherwise?
"It's like we can turn the faucet on and actually find out so much more," Shah says. "There's an aspect of this that is really about a kind of reckoning with how it's possible that things that seemed unthinkable could happen on American streets. How do you have that reckoning if you don't actually have the ability to force people to explain themselves?"
Democratic leaders have already said that's the plan.
Maryland Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, who is expected to lead the House Judiciary Committee, told NPR in a statement that Congress will use "every tool" at its disposal to investigate ICE and that it is time for the agency to "start answering to the American people."
California Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia, expected to lead the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, vowed to take on DHS and ICE abuses in a two-word statement: "Lawyer Up."
Mississippi Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson, expected to lead the House Committee on Homeland Security, sent a letter on Wednesday to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, demanding the agency "comply with all document preservation requirements."
Illinois Democratic Rep. Delia Ramirez wrote on social media that Noem, Miller, Homan, Bovino and Mullin should "clear" their schedules.
In response to that, DHS general counsel James Percival said Democrats are "more interested in political shenanigans than in governing" but said the agency is prepared to "deal with this nonsense."
There are key limitations to what Democrats in Congress can do with their majority when it comes to ICE accountability, says Rachel Moran, a professor at the University of St. Thomas School of Law.
Major changes, like clawing back funding for the agency, would require a veto-proof majority, something the Democrats don't have.
"You still have a president who has shown a complete lack of interest in accountability for federal agents and in fact, a great deal of knee jerk defensiveness about their conduct," Moran says.
In a statement, a White House spokesperson told NPR "if Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."
Democrats, the statement added, "should be reminded that we still control the federal government and all of its powers."
But that's not true. Congress has its own powers, one of them being the ability to compel testimony. Moran says a deeper probe into the shootings could still serve important purposes, like making evidence available for states to use in their own criminal investigations.
Minnesota officials, for instance, have been fighting with the federal government to get evidence related to the Pretti and Good killings.
Brent Ganger, Renee Good's brother, says learning more information about his sister's death will be hard to hear, "but I think it's also super important for us to understand what happened that day. I don't want history to keep repeating itself."
It was painful, he says, to watch immigration agents kill more people after his sister. He thought her death would be a turning point. In a way, it might have been the start of one. After the surge in Minneapolis, most Americans said ICE had gone too far.
Ganger, who considers himself a moderate, was happy to see the Blue Wave this week. On election night, he was scrolling Instagram when he saw a photo of his sister's memorial site, with all the "I Voted" stickers.
"I was very grateful to see the repudiation of this administration from the country. It felt very supportive of my entire family," he says.
The next morning, in his home in Colorado, he got up and made biscuits and gravy, his sister's favorite breakfast.

Refugee athlete to make history for second time at Youth Olympics
- Published
When he started running, Yiech Pur Biel had to compete barefoot. Far from home in a new country, it was the first step towards rebuilding his life as a refugee.
"That's when I decided now it is time to depend on myself and also to start a new life with determination," he tells BBC Newsbeat.
In 2016, Biel made history competing in the 800m event as part of the first Olympic refugee team at the Rio summer Olympics in Brazil.
Ten years on, he's making history again leading the first refugee team for the Youth Olympics as their Chef de Mission.
Joining almost 3,000 athletes, the small team of six will be wanting to make sure their debut counts - but Biel says they're also hoping to send a message that "refugees still need our help".
Hosted in Senegal, Saturday's opening ceremony will launch the first ever Olympic sporting event on African soil.
Africa is home to nearly 45 million displaced people, out of almost 120 million globally, representing the world's biggest displacement crisis.
Biel says for the refugee team, the Youth Olympics is "a chance for them to tell the world and also to represent the population, especially the refugee population, in Africa".
"It's about representing the hope of young people who are living in a refugee camp, who have lost their motivation or their talent."
Biel was a child when he was forced to flee his home in South Sudan after his village was attacked.
He ended up in Kenya, telling BBC Newsbeat: "It traumatised me, starting a new life, being alone in Kakuma," referring to the major refugee settlement close to the border between Kenya and South Sudan.
"But I started a new life, I believe that school helped me a lot. It helped me to interact with young people who faced the same challenges."
The rest of his childhood was spent on the refugee camp where he took an interest in football.
After realising it wasn't the sport for him, he gave running a go during trials set up by the International Olympic Committee - where he raced without shoes.
It made him "believe that if I can work harder by myself, I can achieve", he says.
One of the athletes on the refugee team, Arno Yafunga Botay, also lived at Kakuma after fleeing his home in the Democratic Republic of Congo in 2017, when he was six.
Now 15, he will be competing in judo and told BBC Sport Africa he's promised to bring back a gold medal which he'd like to take to the refugee camp.
"I think if I achieve [a] gold medal, I can go there and teach them the value of judo," he said.
As for Biel, he says it's an honour to be chosen as the team's Chef de Mission.
"This is so important for them, to learn from my experience as an athlete and also as a refugee who is coming from a refugee camp," he says.
"So this role means a lot to me and also means a lot to those young athletes who are going to compete."
Competition at Dakar 2026 begins later, with the opening ceremony on Saturday.

Diwali is more than a festival of lights. For generations, it has also been an occasion for Indian businesses, traders and households to review their finances, begin new accounts, buy gold and make investments.
While these customs have retained their significance, the way people observe them has evolved. Physical account books have given way to digital ledgers, gold purchases now include investment-oriented products, and younger investors are exploring financial markets.
Here is how five Diwali traditions connect culture, commerce and India's economy.
An occasion for wealth creation
Diwali has traditionally been associated with prosperity and the worship of Goddess Lakshmi, the deity of wealth. For households, it is an occasion to buy valuables, purchase gold, set aside savings and plan finances for the year ahead.
Wealth creation is no longer limited to physical assets. Alongside gold and traditional savings instruments, households are exploring mutual funds, shares and other financial products. Diwali or Dhanteras can also serve as a starting point for investing.
Dr Shunil Tripathi, an NCFE trainer empanelled with the RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and PFRDA, said festivals can provide a cultural and emotional motivation to move from saving to investing. 
The challenge is to turn an occasional decision into a regular habit through financial awareness and long-term planning.
“The basic philosophy, however, remains similar: save today to secure tomorrow,” he said.
Inculcating regular investment habits
Younger investors may mark the occasion by starting a mutual fund systematic investment plan (SIP), buying Gold ETFs or opening a Demat account. These serve different purposes: a SIP enables regular investment, while a Demat account holds securities. The larger shift is towards using the festival to think about long-term financial goals.
GenZ's new traditions
Red account books to digital ledgers
For many Indian trading communities, particularly in Gujarat, Diwali marks the beginning of a new business year. One prominent tradition is Chopda Pujan, the ritual of worshipping account books before beginning a fresh set of financial records.
Traditionally, business families closed old accounts and worshipped new 
bahi-khatas
 during Lakshmi Puja. The books were marked with auspicious words such as 
Shubh
 and 
Labh
, symbolising prosperity and a fresh beginning.
Diwali traditions linked to finances
The practice continues in some families, even as formal accounting has shifted to digital systems. GST has added to businesses' formal record-keeping and compliance obligations, including maintaining transaction records, issuing tax invoices and filing periodic returns. Accounting software and digital ledgers are now part of routine operations.
There is also an important distinction between customary Diwali-to-Diwali reviews and statutory accounting. Financial reporting, income-tax filings and GST compliance follow the April-to-March financial year. Some traditional businesses nevertheless maintain 
bahi-khatas
 alongside formal records and compare their net worth from one Diwali to the next. Net worth is calculated by subtracting liabilities from assets.
Chartered accountant Balvinder Singh Oberoi said festive-period sales were another important measure. “One financial metric they do track religiously is festive period sales,” he said, referring to businesses comparing sales during the Diwali period with the corresponding period a year earlier.
Dhanteras and the gold rush: Buying precious metals
Buying gold on Dhanteras is among India's most enduring festive traditions. Associated with prosperity, security and wealth preservation, the occasion is particularly important for jewellery retailers, bullion dealers and precious-metal businesses.
Buying patterns are evolving. Consumers are showing interest in lightweight designs, smaller denominations of gold coins and bars, and exchanges of old gold for new jewellery. High prices have encouraged some buyers to adapt the size and design of their purchases rather than abandon the tradition.
This year's Dhanteras, observed on November 6, brought fresh momentum for jewellers as gold prices eased from record levels. Reuters reported local gold prices at around Rs 1,41,800 per 10 grams on Friday, after falling to Rs 1,37,863 earlier in the week, their lowest level since March 24. The correction brought some buyers who had been waiting for more favourable rates back to jewellery stores ina addition to those who waited for the cultural significance.
The gold rush in festive season
The All India Gem & Jewellery Domestic Council (GJC), in a preliminary assessment after Dhanteras, estimated gold sales at around Rs 60,000 crore, up 15-20% in value terms from the previous year. Volumes were expected to remain broadly unchanged, suggesting that higher prices accounted for much of the increase in sales value.
Demand also extended to diamond jewellery, with wedding shoppers and families contributing to purchases. Senco Gold MD and CEO Suvankar Sen told TOI that demand for diamond jewellery had grown 25-30% during the festive period.
The Diwali economy: Where does India's festive money go?
The festive season is a crucial consumption period for several industries. Alongside FMCG, automobiles, consumer durables, jewellery and apparel, spending also benefits travel, hospitality and premium gifting. Ecommerce has also been a key contributor in this aspect, allowing quick deliveries, festival sales and wide variety.
Ravi Kapoor, partner and leader for the retail and consumer sector at PwC India, included travel and premium gifting among the categories that gain from festive demand. He pointed to the long holiday period as a reason more families are open to travelling. “A lot of families actually now are quite open for travel,” he said.
Kapoor estimated that “in automobiles roughly a quarter to 30% of volumes happen in this period”. He added: “Same is the number for durables. 30 to 40% durables get sold right.”
The demand story is also spreading beyond metropolitan households. Kapoor said e-commerce, digital payments and better physical infrastructure had widened access to consumers in smaller cities and towns. “The access has become much, much better, much easier,” he said, pointing to the growing contribution of Tier-II and Tier-III markets to new online customers.
However, higher festive sales do not automatically mean that households have become more financially comfortable. The source of the spending matters: purchases supported by improved incomes and savings may point to stronger consumption, while those financed by stretching household budgets may be harder to sustain.
Economist Dr Rohit Kumar Singh said this distinction was central to assessing demand. “Are households spending more because their incomes and savings have improved, or are they stretching their budgets to make room for festive purchases?” he asked.
Anand Ramanathan, partner and consumer industry leader at Deloitte South Asia, also highlighted the gap between financial confidence and spending capacity. Deloitte's March 2026 ConsumerSignals survey found that 79% of Indian consumers were confident about meeting upcoming payments and 60% were comfortable with their savings. However, only 65% were willing to make large purchases, down five percentage points from the previous month. Just 43% said they could afford to spend on things that brought them joy.
Festive shopping: Online vs offline
The findings suggest that financial confidence does not always translate into a willingness to make discretionary purchases. Whether consumers continue spending after the festive season will be a better test of how durable the demand is.
Muhurat trading: When Diwali meets the stock market
Diwali's association with wealth and prosperity also extends to India's stock markets. Every year, the BSE and NSE hold a special trading session on Diwali, known as Muhurat trading, marking the beginning of the new Samvat year.
Many investors consider the session auspicious and use it to make a symbolic investment or begin a longer-term investment plan. The tradition dates back to the BSE's introduction of the session in 1957; the NSE began holding it in 1992.
How have markets performed?
Both the Sensex and Nifty closed higher in eight of the last 10 Muhurat trading sessions from 2016 to 2025. The two exceptions were 2016 and 2017. The indices then recorded eight consecutive positive sessions from 2018 through 2025. In the 2025 session, the Sensex gained 63 points, while the Nifty rose 25 points.
These gains, however, reflect movement during a single special session, not returns over the full Samvat year. An auspicious start does not guarantee market gains. Investors still need to assess companies, understand their risk appetite and maintain a diversified portfolio.
Muhurat trading brings together faith and finance, giving the stock market a cultural connection beyond its regular trading calendar. The more meaningful step is to carry the discipline of that beginning into the rest of the year.
Experts decode: What the festive season tells us about India's economy
Diwali sales offer a snapshot of India's consumption economy, but the festive rush also raises larger questions. Is spending broad-based or concentrated among affluent households? Are consumers buying more, or simply paying higher prices? And does the demand generated during the festive season translate into sustained growth for businesses?
A more selective household wallet
Anand Ramanathan, partner and consumer industry leader at Deloitte South Asia, said India's festive consumption story reflected a larger market but more selective spending. Consumers are reallocating budgets towards purchases they consider worthwhile.
“The story is increasingly one of a larger consumption economy combined with a more selective household wallet,” he said.
Smaller discretionary purchases are increasingly spread throughout the year, while big-ticket items such as appliances and electronics remain linked to festive discounts and financing. Food, sweets and entertaining, meanwhile, generate occasion-led demand. Ramanathan described Diwali as “a blend of accelerated demand and occasion-created consumption”.
The wider economic impact
Economist Dr Rohit Kumar Singh said festive demand supports more than retailers. Manufacturers, transporters, warehouses, packaging companies and MSMEs also benefit, while seasonal hiring creates temporary employment. “The festive season also supports a much wider network of businesses. Manufacturers, transporters, warehouses, packaging companies and MSMEs all benefit from the increase in activity,” he said. However, smaller businesses can face unsold inventory, delayed payments and working-capital pressure. Higher input costs, including crude oil, can further squeeze margins.
How festive season supports businesses
Dr Shunil Tripathi, the NCFE trainer empanelled with RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and PFRDA, said Diwali could be an opportunity to review income, expenditure, savings, investments and financial goals. Traditional practices of setting aside money, grains or gold reflected the idea of preparing for the future. “The basic philosophy, however, remains similar: save today to secure tomorrow,” he said. But social pressure and the desire to keep up with others can also lead to unnecessary purchases and borrowing.
From auspicious trades to long-term investing
Chartered accountant Balvinder Singh Oberoi said the symbolic investment made during Muhurat trading could be a starting point for greater financial awareness. “Muhurat trading provides that crucial first step to getting started,” he said. The real value lies in using the occasion to understand markets and build a consistent, long-term investment habit rather than treating a token purchase as wealth creation.
Festive trends versus lasting shifts
Ravi Kapoor, partner and leader for the retail and consumer sector at PwC India, cautioned against treating every festive-season trend as a permanent change in consumption. One structural shift, he said, was the movement from unbranded to branded products, including in categories such as sarees, jewellery and food.
“The long term consumption story is very clearly the growth of formal consumption, the growth of formal economy in the country,” he said.
Kapoor also described India as an “E-shaped economy”, with affluent households relatively insulated from economic changes, middle-income consumers spending cautiously and lower-income groups facing tighter constraints. Whether festive demand continues after Diwali, and whether the shift towards organised brands persists, will offer a better indication of the economy's underlying consumption trends.
K-shaped economy
Ultimately, Diwali's economic significance goes beyond a surge in shopping or a promising start to the business year. It brings together consumption, investment and traditional practices, while offering a window into changing household priorities. Whether this festive momentum translates into sustained demand and long-term financial discipline will become clearer in the months ahead.

On 02 November 2026, Union Home Minister Amit Shah participated in the BJP’s ‘Loktantra Bachao, Arajakata Hatao’ Maha Padayatra in Hyderabad. Organised by the Telangana unit of the BJP, the march began near the Dr Babu Jagjivan Ram statue in Basheerbagh and concluded at Moazzam Jahi Market. Shah was accompanied by Union Ministers G Kishan Reddy and Bandi Sanjay Kumar, Telangana BJP president N Ramchander Rao, and other party leaders and workers. The march was organised as part of the BJP’s campaign against the INDIA bloc’s allegations concerning the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls (here, here, and here).
Amid this incident, a video is circulating on social media (here, here, and here), claiming it shows people protesting against Union Home Minister Amit Shah and chasing him away during the BJP’s Loktantra Bachao, Arajakata Hatao’ Maha padayatra in Telangana on 02 November 2026. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows people chasing Union Home Minister Amit Shah away during his Telangana padayatra on 02 November 2026.
Fact: The video dates back to July 2023 and shows Rahul Gandhi travelling in a car amid a crowd waving Congress flags in Khammam, Telangana. Rahul Gandhi attended the ‘Telangana Jana Garjana Sabha’ in Khammam on 02 July 2023. On the same day, Amit Shah attended a programme in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, after virtually inaugurating the Akshar River Cruise in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. We found no reports of him visiting Hyderabad that day. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to an X post (archived) dated 4 July 2023, featuring a clearer version of the same video. Rahul Gandhi is clearly visible inside the VIP car, with people waving Congress flags. The post’s caption identifies the location as Khammam district in Telangana and states that Rahul Gandhi was returning after delivering a speech. This suggests that the video is from a Congress event held in Telangana.
On 02 July 2023, Rahul Gandhi attended the ‘Telangana Jana Garjana Sabha‘ in Khammam, Telangana, as part of the Congress party’s campaign ahead of the Telangana Assembly elections. Rahul Gandhi also shared videos from the event on his official YouTube channel, while the Congress party issued a press release about the programme.
To verify whether Amit Shah was in Hyderabad on 2 July 2023, we conducted a Google search and found that he was scheduled to attend the ‘Jan-Swabhiman Divas‘ programme at the Indira Gandhi Pratishthan in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, organised to mark the 74th birth anniversary of Dr Sonelal Patel. He attended the event as the chief guest and addressed the gathering between 2:30 pm and 4:30 pm. Earlier that day, he had virtually inaugurated the Akshar River Cruise at the Sabarmati Riverfront in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, through video conferencing. These reports indicate that Amit Shah was engaged in public programmes in Ahmedabad and Lucknow on 2 July 2023; However, we found no reports indicating that he visited Hyderabad that day.
To sum up, this viral video does not show Union Home Minister Amit Shah being chased away during the Hyderabad padayatra on 02 November 2026.

Dolly Parton always loved whipping up feasts of Southern comfort food for her loved ones, including her goddaughter, Miley Cyrus.
The late country icon loved it so much that she even wrote a cookbook with her sister, Rachel Parton George, which came out in 2024.
My favorite section of "Good Lookin' Cookin': A Year of Meals" is dedicated entirely to Thanksgiving dishes. And the best recipe of the bunch is Parton's sweet potato casserole.
Here's how to make it.
Dolly Parton's sweet potato casserole has a nutty twist.
To make the sweet potato casserole at home, you'll need:
- 5 large sweet potatoes, peeled and quartered
- 2 cups of miniature marshmallows
- ½ cup of chopped raw pecans
- ½ cup of light brown sugar, packed
- ½ cup (1 stick) of butter at room temperature, plus more for greasing
- 1 teaspoon of vanilla extract
- 1 teaspoon of salt
- 1 teaspoon of ground cinnamon
First, I preheated the oven and prepped my potatoes and baking pan.
I set the oven to 350 degrees Fahrenheit and buttered a 9-inch-by-13-inch pan.
I also washed, peeled, and quartered my sweet potatoes.
I placed my sweet potatoes in a large pot and covered them with cold water.
I brought the pot to a boil over high heat, then lowered the heat to maintain a low boil for 20 minutes while the potatoes cooked.
You'll know they're ready when the potatoes are fork-tender.
I drained the potatoes, placed them in a large bowl, and added the butter and seasonings.
I threw in the brown sugar, vanilla, salt, cinnamon, and butter, adding the latter in knobs so it'd be easy to mix.
Then it was time to mash.
The recipe recommends using a potato masher to mix the ingredients until they're "well combined." I don't own one, so I simply used a big wooden serving fork — it worked like a charm!
I transferred my mashed sweet potatoes to the baking pan, smoothing the top.
I sprinkled the pecans on top, then evenly covered the casserole with my miniature marshmallows.
I covered my pan with aluminum foil and threw it in the oven.
The recipe says you should bake your sweet potato casserole for 20 minutes.
Once the 20 minutes were up, I baked the casserole uncovered for five additional minutes.
The marshmallows should turn golden brown, but mine were still white as snow after five minutes passed. So I turned on the broiler and baked the casserole for two additional minutes to give them some color.
I let my sweet potato casserole cool for 15 minutes before serving.
I was slightly disappointed when the sweet potato casserole came out of the oven. The marshmallows got a little overcooked by the broiler and now only covered half of the casserole. Next time, I think I'll just let the marshmallows cook uncovered the entire time.
Unphotogenic marshmallows aside, this sweet potato casserole was delicious. The crunchy pecans added a delightful twist, and the combination of brown sugar, vanilla, and cinnamon was well balanced. The texture was satisfyingly creamy, and the dish made my kitchen smell delicious.
I brought this to a Friendsgiving, and the pan was empty within minutes — despite having a lot of competition!
I'll definitely be missing Dolly during this holiday season. Serving up a casserole that's warm and sweet seems like a fitting tribute.

Delivery of various services in government hospitals and health centres across Keralam are likely to get affected in the coming days as the job contracts of 1,495 temporary staff working under the National Health Mission (NHM) have been terminated from October 31.
According to sources, those who lost their jobs include doctors, nurses, pharmacists, accountants, physiotherapists, lab technicians, and the staff who coordinate the activities of Accredited Social Health Activists. The services of special newborn units in district hospitals and activities of ‘Ashadhara’ project, the digital and decentralised healthcare initiative launched by the government through the NHM to manage haemophilia and other rare genetic bleeding and coagulation disorders, may be hit. Functioning of urban health centres and labs and pharmacies in many hospitals and other healthcare institutions too may get affected.
Leaders of the Centre of Indian Trade Unions-affiliated NHM Employees Federation say that the highest number of the affected staff are in Ernakulam and Thrissur districts, 183 and 180, respectively. Ninety-nine people have lost their jobs in Kozhikode district alone.
Assembly elections
Meera Nimeesh, State general secretary of the federation, says that the contract staff are appointed for a one-year period from April to March. However, this year, the contract was extended till May, because of the model code of conduct for the Assembly elections. After the new government assumed office, their tenure was extended twice, till October 31. Ms. Nimeesh adds that though the staff had earlier undergone one round of performance appraisal in May, they were asked to do it again in October. Following this, their services were terminated.
Ms. Nimeesh claims that even those with close to 20 years of experience, who have consistently recorded good performance, found themselves jobless one fine morning. She alleges that the government’s action is politically motivated as those who don’t align themselves with the United Democratic Front government have been singled out and terminated.
In a statement, the federation says that the services provided by NHM staff—spanning areas such as immunisation, maternal and child care, communicable disease control, management of lifestyle diseases, palliative care, laboratory services, day-to-day operations of hospitals, and field-level health activities—constitute an integral part of the healthcare system. Meanwhile, it is learnt that the Health department has issued a notification for the appointment of new staff.

White-tailed eagles reintroduced into England and Wales imperil endangered seabird populations and risk wiping out some colonies, ecologists and conservationists are warning.
Puffins, guillemots, razorbills, fulmars and kittiwakes are among the birds for which breeding populations could collapse if large numbers of white-tailed eagles are released, according to some academics and conservationists.
“Amidst all the excitement and enthusiasm for reintroducing white-tailed eagles, the fact that these birds will probably destroy our seabird colonies seems to have been completely overlooked,” said Tim Birkhead, an emeritus professor of ecology and evolution at the University of Sheffield.
The return of white-tailed eagles to Britain after they were driven to extinction in 1918 has been a great conservation success story in recent decades. But proposals to release up to 60 eagles in Gwent, south Wales, on top of 20 young birds already being released over the next three years on Exmoor, is dividing nature lovers.
The Gwent Wildlife Trust is supporting the proposed Gwent reintroduction while the Wildlife Trust of South & West Wales (WTSWW) is opposed.
Last month an eagle from the Exmoor release was sighted over the south Wales island of Skomer, a renowned seabird sanctuary where David Attenborough was filmed encountering puffins and shearwaters for his Wild Isles series. British seabirds have suffered the worst declines of any group of birds over the last five years, with populations falling by a fifth, but the seabird populations in south Wales are relatively healthy.
Sarah Kessell, the chief executive of WTSWW, said: “We’re increasingly alarmed about the reintroduction of white-tailed eagles across the UK as more evidence comes to light of their impact on cliff-nesting seabirds.
“The islands of Skomer and Skokholm are a sanctuary for globally important seabird populations, which are already under threat. The extra pressure of disturbance and displacement from white-tailed eagles could have a significant impact on breeding seabirds. We have an overwhelming obligation to protect the seabirds on the islands that we manage.”
White-tailed eagle chicks brought over from Norway to reintroduce them into Scotland in 1975 has led to a wild population now of 200 breeding pairs, with 45 birds successfully reintroduced to the Isle of Wight since 2019. Although there has been repeated illegal killing of the huge avian predator, the first English-born wild bird fledged from a nest in East Sussex in 2023. Wales has not yet restored the species to its skies.
Prof Geoff Hilton, the head of wetland evidence at the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT), which is leading the Gwent reintroduction, said: “Conservation action has and always will carry an element of risk. But what’s essential is that we carefully evaluate those risks early, use robust evidence to investigate the scale of those risks, and balance them against potential opportunities.”
Hilton emphasised that white-tailed eagles were generalist feeders with a varied diet including carrion, fish and small mammals. Research published in 2020 of eagles east of the Baltic Sea found that birds of particular conservation concern in the EU accounted for approximately 1% of identified prey in a long-term study of eagle diets.
He said: “With careful phasing, we aim to establish seven to nine breeding pairs of white-tailed eagles over the next 10 years. Therefore, we don’t expect this reintroduction to significantly reduce or impact any single species population. We do, however, expect to see healthier, more balanced ecosystems and landscapes, as apex predators like these eagles start to thrive once again.”
In evidence submitted by WTSWW against the Gwent proposals, Stephen Votier, a professor of seabird conservation and ecology at Heriot-Watt University, said: “It is clear that white-tailed eagles can have severe impacts on seabird populations – they seem especially vulnerable because the eagle can indirectly affect social aspects of breeding.”
As well as directly predating seabirds and their young, indirect effects are likely to be much greater, say some researchers, because the fear induced by white-tailed eagles causes adult seabirds to temporarily desert their breeding sites, exposing chicks to predation by other birds including gulls and corvids.
Birkhead, who has studied the guillemot population on Skomer since 1972, said he would “love to see white-tailed eagles” but said scientific evidence of the predators hastening the extinction of seabird colonies in Scandinavia must be properly considered.
In 2023, a scientific paper found that in northern Norway an increasing abundance of white-tailed eagles accelerated the loss of a kittiwake colony in Røst in 2020 by “many years”. The colony was already in decline but the eagles’ impacts were greater because fewer fish for the kittiwakes compelled the birds to spend more time foraging and less time defending their young from predators.
Annette Fayet and Tycho Anker-Nilssen, co-authors of the study, said that although Røst only had two to three breeding pairs of eagles, large numbers of immature eagles gathered there and disturbed the nesting seabirds.
Asked about the applicability of their findings to Wales, they said: “We cannot assume that the situation in Norway will be reproduced in south Wales but find it impossible to rule out that something similar could happen there too, in time.”
Roger Morgan-Grenville, the author of a book about white-tailed eagles that will be published next spring, said there was a consistent association between the rising number of white-tailed eagles on the Baltic coast and the reduced breeding success of the cormorant, and similar negative impacts on northern gannets and kittiwakes in western Norway. He said: “I’m absolutely in favour of these magnificent birds covering our skies again but we need to listen to all voices, and not just the loud ones, and we need to accept that the landscape that the white-tailed has come back into is a far more depleted one than it left in 1918.”
Natural Resources Wales is assessing the application for the release of white-tailed eagles in Gwent, with a verdict expected by the end of this year. A spokesperson said: “If we are minded to grant a licence, there will be a public consultation process from late 2026 into early 2027 before any final decision is made.”

The best laptop display ever made, bar none. The notch is gone! Having a touchscreen is occasionally useful. Much lighter to carry. Somehow, even better speakers. Glowing Apple logo returns.
TIRED
Touchscreen implementation feels half-baked. High price for the same performance as last year’s model.
Apple doesn’t change its mind very often. Its history is one of sticking to its guns, even when pressed on certain design or technology decisions. And yet, I’ve been working on a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen for the past few days—a device I never thought would come into being.
Ignoring the (very reasonable) arguments about the poor ergonomics of touchscreen laptops made in the past, Apple has brought such a display to the MacBook Pro in the most un-Apple way I could have imagined. I’m not sure why it’s here, but it is.
I do know, though, that I love the new “PROLED XDR” screen. Combine that with a hole-punch cutout for the webcam and the return of the light-up Apple logo on the lid—and it's enough improvements to call this a big upgrade over the rest of the MacBook lineup. But compared to a similarly specced MacBook Pro from a year ago, the OLED model costs almost $1,000 more by comparison.
Small Touches Add Up
Photograph: Luke Larsen
With the arrival of the OLED MacBook Pro, Apple now offers two flavors of its flagship premium laptop. The standard Mini-LED option now comes with the M6 processor with improved graphics and battery life, but otherwise looks largely the same as before.
The OLED MacBook Pro, however, is the biggest change since 2021. You won’t notice it immediately on the outside. Color options are still just Silver and Space Black. You still have a choice between 14- and 16-inch. Ports are the same. Open it up, and you’ll see the familiar keyboard and trackpad. It’s all there as you’d expect.
The only visual indication that you’re using something different is the glowing Apple logo on the lid. As a feature only available in the very expensive OLED MacBook Pro, it’s a pure, unabashed status symbol. And I love it. It even matches the display’s brightness, so it doesn’t distract in a dark room.
Another discernible difference in the OLED MacBook Pro is something you’ll notice with your hands rather than your eyes. The 16-inch model I tested now weighs just 4 pounds, well over half a pound lighter than the non-OLED equivalent. Most of the weight savings come from OLED, which uses much thinner, lighter layers (more on OLED later). This is a very large laptop, but the weight reduction makes it much easier to carry around in a bag.
Photograph: Luke Larsen
And the notch is gone! No Apple design feature has bothered me more than this large cutout at the top of the screen, which houses the webcam and sensors (it remains in the non-OLED model). The punch-hole camera is a huge improvement. As someone who found the notch a complete eyesore since it was introduced, this might be the change I’ve been most excited about. Like on newer iPhones, the MacBook Pro is also getting Dynamic Island, which makes the punch-hole camera more useful. It can show interactive Live Activities, such as timers or currently-playing music. I imagine it won’t be used too often, though it does its job by hiding the punch-hole and showing off those narrow bezels.
There are some subtler tweaks. The rubber feet on the bottom have softer, rounded edges. The bezels around the screen are slightly smaller.
Even Brighter OLED
It’s been over two years since Apple first brought its tandem OLED displays to the iPad Pro. In that time, MacBook Pro users have been patiently using the same Mini-LED display. Nevertheless, the OLED MacBook Pro has finally arrived, and Apple has pushed the tandem OLED panel further than ever before. This is the brightest laptop display I’ve ever tested, capable of reaching up to 1,000 nits in SDR. That’s on everyday content throughout the operating system and across all apps. The screen can, however, crank out 2,000 nits of brightness—but only in specific circumstances.
Photograph: Luke Larsen
For example, under very bright light or outdoors, the ambient light sensor built into the webcam module will detect those conditions and tune the display beyond the 1,000-nit upper limit. Combine that with the optional nano-texture screen, and you have what is undoubtedly the best laptop for working outside. That’s especially impressive considering glare is a big problem with typical OLED laptop screens. (You’ll need to turn on the “Automatically adjust brightness” setting, which I typically don’t.) Apple sent me the OLED with standard glass for testing, which comes with an antireflective coating that the company calls “groundbreaking." Next to the non-OLED M6 MacBook Pro, it looks about as reflective. If you really want to use this thing outside, the nano-texture upgrade is well worth it.
HDR content is the second situation in which the screen can be cranked up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness. Here, the idea isn’t to blast your eyes with brightness; it’s about details. In HDR-rendered photos, videos, movies, and games, 2,000 nits would be bright enough to deliver incredible depth of detail and color. I’ve never seen HDR like this on a laptop, and you really have to experience it to truly get it. In my HDR testing, my OLED MacBook Pro never quite reached 2,000 nits, maxing out at 1,849 nits. But amazingly, it can even produce this in a 25 percent window, and 1,025 nits with every pixel lit up. The only place you’ll find brighter OLED is in the very latest OLED TVs.
Now, this is actually only 12 percent brighter than the Mini-LED MacBook Pro, which I retested to make this comparison. But when you pair a brighter OLED screen with the deep blacks it can produce, you have absolutely stellar HDR, giving the content a range of depth never before seen on a laptop.
I watched a number of professional HDR footage, side-by-side with the Mini-LED MacBook Pro. That difference is very noticeable. Is it something only TV nerds and videographers will care about? Maybe. The Mini-LED MacBook Pro is already a great laptop for watching movies on. All I can say is the OLED model is noticeably better. And for those who work professionally with HDR footage, this should open up new possibilities. My hope is that, as these HDR-capable devices proliferate, we’ll see more HDR video produced—even just for the web.
The speakers also make the OLED MacBook Pro an ever better movie-watching device. Apple says the six-speaker sound system has “50 percent deeper bass.” That’s hard to measure, but like the screen, you notice a difference when you compare it side-by-side with the previous-gen model. The bass really does stand out more, giving you a fuller sound both for music-listening and movie-watching. And just to be clear: Apple already had the best speakers in the game.
Like an iPad
Photograph: Luke Larsen
In the time I’ve had with the touchscreen MacBook Pro so far, I tried to remind myself of its new powers. But when I’m deep in work, I completely forget the touchscreen. It just has no place in my workflows. That doesn’t mean it’s not ever useful, though. Sometimes, swiping away a notification with a finger feels intuitive. Or if you’re lounging on the couch and use your thumb to scroll through your Instagram feed as you would on an iPad, it works. But those times are few and far between. I’m certainly not going to be poking three fingers up at the screen to swipe between Spaces when I could do that on a trackpad without even lifting my hand.
I’ve noticed the same tendency when I use an iPad Air or iPad Pro connected to the Magic Keyboard. It’s just easier and faster to keep your hands where they are. The difference here on the MacBook Pro is the software. The interface doesn’t exactly draw you in to touch it. Everything that could click you can now touch, but tapping tiny icons and controls with your finger feels clumsy, as it always has. It’s the same problem in Windows 11. To be fair, Apple has put in more effort than Microsoft ever has, tweaking macOS to optimize for touch—not unlike iPadOS.
One of my favorite optimizations happens when you tap on the window controls (the three buttons to close, minimize, or fullscreen). After you tap, it pops out and lets you select one of the three more precisely. The drop-downs in the menu bar are also more spaced out, and you can tap and drag your finger to select options more easily. These visual touches are handy, and some of Apple’s apps have found ways to make certain tasks touch-based.
Photograph: Luke Larsen
I admit I don’t benefit much from a touchscreen laptop, but Apple also hasn’t made any hardware changes to make touching the screen feel more natural. Would Apple ever put a 180- or 360-degree hinge on a MacBook? I would have thought no—then again, I never thought a MacBook would have a touchscreen in the first place. Not even the Apple Pencil is supported here (not that it would ever be comfortable to use at an angle).
The bigger problem is that third-party apps have to optimize for touch. Even though click-to-touch will work in all apps right out of the box, not all developers will put in the effort. Also, I’ve noticed some apps translated through Rosetta (which lets Intel-based software run on Apple silicon, such as Steam) don’t support some features, like the zoom-in window controls. I can’t see myself adjusting my behavior when you can’t reliably expect consistency across these apps.
Apple has been selling the OLED MacBook Pro’s touch capabilities to creative pros—the kind of user who would use this laptop. The ideas are mildly interesting, whether it’s drawing directly on the screen with Pixelmator Pro or applying brush textures onto 3D models in ZBrush. I’m not an artist, but I use Logic Pro. You can now touch the screen to play drums right on the screen or draw automations into Remix FX. But that’s where I started to think these are more gimmicks than real features creatives will actually benefit from. Even amateur musicians will always have a physical MIDI keyboard, and playing musical instruments on the laptop keyboard (a Logic feature that’s been around forever) feels more natural than tapping the screen. I’ll wait for Adobe to prove me wrong.
Here’s the thing: In all my discussions with Apple about the touchscreen, I never got the impression that touch was supposed to replace the keyboard and trackpad as the primary input method. That’s a safe, smart play if the goal is to not rock the boat too much. For so many years, Apple sat back and watched Microsoft fumble its own touch implementation through the disaster that was Windows 8. It’s certainly true that in today’s world, it feels strange that you can’t control a MacBook screen with your fingers. As someone with kids, my MacBook is safe from their fingerprints. This feels more like a “catch-up” feature we’ve long been without, but I hope Apple commits more to touch and engineers a more unique way to integrate it.
The Same M5 Max
The 2026 OLED MacBook Pro uses the same chips as the previous generation: the M5 Pro and M5 Max. This is the first time Apple has done this since introducing Apple Silicon in 2020. Each new version of any Mac has always come with an updated chip. Either Apple’s pace is slowing down, or the company thinks the OLED touchscreen will be a strong enough draw to convince buyers to refresh.
To be fair, the M5 Max and M5 Pro were already at the top of their game. Even compared to new Nvidia RTX Spark laptops like the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra, the M5 Max dominates in overall power. Time to rest on their laurels, I suppose. Rumor has it that Apple will skip the M6 Pro and M6 Max altogether, saving those more powerful configurations for the M7 generation. Again, that would be a first for Apple Silicon since its introduction.
On the other hand, Apple claims the OLED MacBook Pro internals have been completely redesigned to support the PROLED XDR display. The goal is performance parity with the non-OLED M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro—nothing more. And in my testing, that’s precisely what I saw. Scores were very similar to the previous-gen MacBook Pro in Cinebench 2026, as well as in the games I tested. I won’t go too in-depth here—check out my review of the previous M5 Max MacBook Pro if you want more performance analysis.
Photograph: Luke Larsen
If you already own an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro, it’s very difficult to justify upgrading to the OLED version, even if you’re able to sell it for a decent price. Unless you have a specific use case for the OLED display, I can see many people wanting to wait until next year for the performance upgrade. On the flip side, if you want to upgrade from an M1 Max or M2 Max, you face a tricky decision between the OLED and non-OLED MacBook Pro. For now, Apple is still selling both models in its lineup.
The OLED model costs $400 more, which is steep for a display upgrade. This is on top of the price increase from earlier this year, which already added an extra $500 to the M5 Max MacBook Pro. The 14-inch OLED MacBook Pro starts at $2,899, while its 16-inch sibling starts at $3,399—startling pricing to be sure.
For my review, Apple sent me a souped-up 16-inch model with the M5 Max with an 18-core CPU and 32-core GPU, a standard glass OLED (nano-texture is an optional $150), 128 GB of unified memory, and 2 TB of storage. This configuration costs $7,399, and it’s not even the most expensive!
There’s little hope prices will come down anytime soon, as the memory shortage continues to tighten. If the OLED touchscreen is what draws you to these devices, the 14-inch M5 Pro is the way to go. Just know that you’re leaving a decent amount of performance on the table by not choosing the M5 Max.
Luke Larsen is a product writer and reviewer at WIRED, covering laptops, PCs, Macs, monitors, and the wider PC peripheral ecosystem. Strait of Hormuz could reopen under Qatari plan to end US war with Iran
Iranian media reports fresh strikes on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz with diplomacy on ice

Qatar has floated a new plan to restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and end the conflict between the United States and Iran, despite reports of renewed US strikes on a key Iranian island.
Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, the emir of mediating Qatar, spoke with US president Donald Trump about their vision for a deal to end the eight-month war, Qatari media reported on Friday.
Al-Thani said on Saturday that the Trump administration was willing to find a solution after the midterm elections, which produced a damning verdict of the conflict and its impact on fuel prices last week.
Under Qatar’s proposal, the US would lift its blockade on Iranian ports and release some of its £6bn worth of frozen Iranian assets, according to the Guardian.
Iran would also agree to visits by IAEA nuclear watchdog inspectors to its main facilities, before reopening the Strait of Hormuz to commercial traffic on the second day, the newspaper said.
Under the Qatari deal, and crucially for Trump, who casus belli was that Iran should never be able to acquire nuclear weapons, the regime would apparently not have to give up its nuclear stockpiles.
The Islamic Republic has made overtures to controlling the vital Strait, through which around a fifth of global oil normally passes, with Oman after the war and could begin charging fees for safe passage.
Under the Qatari deal, Tehran would reopen the route already agreed with Muscat, to be jointly lodged with the International Maritime Organisation (IMO).
Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, has separately spoken with Iran about the future administration of the Strait, including the need to register the proposal with the IMO.
Muscat has its own long-term proposal for the running of the channel, which would only see shipping companies charged for services, not tolls per se.
Iran has also sought to resolve a number of secondary issues thrown by the conflict, which began with US-Israeli strikes on February 28.
Ending the parallel clashes in Lebanon, pulling US forces back from the region and paying war reparations are all new obstacles that will require mediation.
Tehran has been proposing its own seven-day plan to end the war since September, but that has so far been rejected by Trump.
It calls for Washington to lift its blockade, unfreeze assets and approve an Iranian-backed route through the Strait of Hormuz, after which the contested waterway would be reopened.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Thursday that Tehran has also submitted a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar.
They said the US was reviewing its but that future discussions would still depend on Washington first meeting Tehran’s seven stated demands.
Ali Bagheri Kani, the deputy head of Iran's top security body, told Iranian state television on Friday that they were still not satisfied with “paper commitments” and must see practical steps from the US.
With diplomatic efforts still on ice, Iranian media on Saturday said it appeared two missiles had struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran has repeatedly said it would respond to new attacks by striking at US and Israeli targets in neighboring countries.
The United States has not yet announced any attack on targets inside Iran.
