The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.
Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party.
The former liberation movement is projected to lose its status as the biggest party in the two most populous provinces, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, as parties began coalition negotiations behind closed doors. The final results are expected to be announced on Sunday.
The ANC was on 31.8% of the vote nationally, almost 14 percentage points below its 2021 local election result. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance (DA) had 24.1% of the vote, while the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma was on 9.3%.
Turnout also rose in Wednesday’s poll. The election commission estimated that 54.5% of registered voters cast their ballot, up from 46% five years ago.
The final shape of coalitions in some of the country’s biggest cities remained unclear with the final votes still being counted. Senior figures in key parties said they would talk with almost anyone, while keeping negotiating strategies under wraps.
In Johannesburg, South Africa’s commercial capital and biggest city, with 4.8 million people, voters have had to contend with regular water and power cuts, uncollected rubbish and potholes. The municipality, which has seen 10 changes of mayor in the last decade amid unstable coalitions, has admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog.
With just over half of votes counted in Johannesburg, the DA was leading with 40%, having run an energetic campaign under Helen Zille, a 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor. The ANC, which leads the current coalition, was in second place on 17.5%. ActionSA, a rightwing party led by Herman Mashaba, was on 15.5%. Mashaba has pledged never to work with Zille, whom he calls “racist”, something she vehemently denies.
Many of the ANC’s township strongholds have yet to report full results. The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a respected thinktank, has projected the DA will finish with 34%, the ANC 20% and ActionSA 16.8%.
Coalitions in Gauteng’s three city municipalities are often negotiated together. The DA is leading in all three.
The MK party, led by 84-year-old Zuma as he continues to weather and deny numerous corruption allegations, is expected to displace the ANC as the largest party in KwaZulu-Natal. Founded in 2023, it mixes socially conservative Zulu nationalism with pledges to redistribute land and wealth from white to black South Africans.
With half of votes counted in eThekwini municipality, which contains Durban, the MK had 41%, meaning other parties could form a coalition to keep it out of power. Meanwhile, the DA is projected to maintain its majority in Cape Town, despite growing middle-class anger over rising housing costs.
Voters choose a local councillor and a party, with seats allocated via proportional representation. Councillors will then have two weeks to elect mayors and form municipal governments.

Joshua Wong, face of Hong Kong's pro-democracy protests, jailed for 10 years
- Published
Joshua Wong, once the face of Hong Kong's democracy movement, has been sentenced to 10 years in jail for colluding with foreign forces under the city's sweeping national security law.
Wong, 30, is among hundreds of campaigners and ordinary Hongkongers arrested under the law, which was imposed in 2020 following explosive pro-democracy protests against Beijing's growing control.
Critics say the far-reaching law has silenced dissent, but authorities argue that it is needed to maintain stability and deny it has weakened the city's cherished autonomy.
Wong, who has been in custody for the last six years, has already been imprisoned multiple times for his activism which started when he was a teen.
- Silenced and erased, Hong Kong's decade of protest is now a defiant memory 
  - Published30 November 2024
- What a defiant mogul's trial says about Hong Kong 
  - Published18 December 2023
On Thursday, Wong arrived in court wearing a dark blue long-sleeved shirt, khaki trousers and black-rimmed glasses. He looked slimmer compared to his previous public appearances.
He nodded in greeting towards members of the packed public gallery, and took notes intermittently as the judge read out the reasons for his sentencing.
A crowd had gathered outside the court, with dozens of Hongkongers having queued for hours hoping to get a seat in the public gallery. There was also a heavy police presence.
Wong is already serving time for subversion and was due to be freed early next year when he was handed the latest charges, which he has pleaded guilty to earlier in September.
Two months and two days of the 10-year term will be served concurrently with his ongoing sentence, the judge said on Thursday.
Prosecutors said that Wong had conspired with other campaigners, including self-exiled activist Nathan Law, to lobby for foreign sanctions and blockades against Beijing.
These activities took place between July and late November 2020, the court heard.
Wong and Law had been co-founders of Demosisto, a now defunct pro-democracy political party.
The charges against Wong "underscores the authorities' fear of prominent dissidents and shows the lengths they will go to keep them behind bars for as long as possible", rights group Amnesty International had earlier said.
Who is Joshua Wong?
Born to IT professional Roger and homemaker Grace in October 1996, Wong was diagnosed with dyslexia as a child, which made him struggle with school.
However, he was quick to challenge established rules and norms when they didn't make sense. In secondary school, he rallied with his classmates to protest against the high prices of canteen lunches on Facebook.
In 2011, Wong, then 14, co-founded the pro-democracy student activist group Scholarism, which quickly grew in size and influence.
The following year, the group rallied more than 100,000 people to protest against Hong Kong's plans to implement mandatory "patriotic education" in schools, forcing the authorities to back down.
Wong, who was just eight months old when Hong Kong was returned from British to Chinese control, has devoted much of his life thus far towards addressing the strictures Beijing has imposed on his home city.
By 2014, Wong, who was then at the forefront of a civil disobedience movement known as the "Umbrella Movement", had already become one of the most recognisable faces of Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement.
In 2016, he co-founded Demosisto with Law and Agnes Chow, an activist who is now also in exile.
But he often expressed discomfort at being labelled a "protest leader".
"We have a lot of facilitators in this movement and I'm one of them... Instead of having a top-down command, we now have a bottom-up command hub," Wong told The Financial Times in November 2019.
Demosisto disbanded in 2020, the year Beijing introduced the controversial National Security Law (NSL) in Hong Kong.
Law left for the UK and continued his advocacy abroad, while Wong stayed on in Hong Kong and tried to run for a seat in its legislature – but was barred, with authorities citing his opposition to the NSL as one of the reasons.
Meanwhile, the court cases against Wong were stacking up.
On 23 November 2020, he pleaded guilty to several charges related to his involvement in protests outside the Hong Kong police headquarters in 2019.
Then came the NSL charges. While still in prison in February 2021, Wong was among 47 people charged with "conspiracy to commit subversion". The group became known as the Hong Kong 47 and remains the largest prosecution so far under the NSL.
Wong was still serving his 56-month sentence for the subversion conviction when he was charged with collusion under the NSL last year.
On 22 November 2020, the day before he pleaded guilty to the protest charges, Wong wrote in a post on Instagram addressed to "the people of Hong Kong": "To be honest, I have never had much faith in Hong Kong's politics, but I have every confidence in the people of Hong Kong.
"Even as political power now poses a comprehensive challenge to the resilience of our civil society, I believe the people of Hong Kong will, as always, find a way to see things through."
The harshest NSL sentence thus far had been handed to former media tycoon Jimmy Lai, who was jailed for 20 years, also for colluding with foreign forces.

Usman Khawaja insisted on Sunday he did not “throw anyone under the bus” by claiming the entire Australian team was in on the 2018 “Sandpapergate” plot and defended taking eight years to go public.
The retired batter re-ignited the infamous ball-tampering scandal in Cape Town on Saturday ahead of the release of his autobiography this week, where a chapter is dedicated to the issue.
He alleged that it was not just Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft -- who were all subsequently banned -- who were responsible.
“It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us,” he said.
Khawaja claimed Australia also employed the tactic during the previous Test at Port Elizabeth.

In response Darren Lehmann, who was head coach at the time, denied there was widespread knowledge of the plot while Cricket Australia said it was “comfortable” with the findings of its original investigation.
That probe found only Smith, Warner and Bancroft were in the know.
“When I mentioned it was all of us, that’s implying that whether we like it or not, we’re all responsible for what happened together as a team,” Khawaja said in a lengthy Instagram post on Sunday.
“We need to take that collectively. That is all.”
He added: “I haven’t thrown anyone under the bus.
“The guys that are currently in the team right now and the other people that were there on the South African tour, including me, we’re not the victims.
“These three guys (Smith, Warner and Bancroft) took the blame for all of us.

Khawaja, who retired this year after 88 Tests, defended waiting so long to make the claims, denying it was a marketing ploy to sell his book.
He said he wanted to go public in 2018 once Smith, Warner and Bancroft were suspended.
“But Smudge (Smith) being the man and leader he was, he talked me out of it.
“He wanted to take the blame. I argued with him, but he was having none of it. That’s the first time I tried to come out.”
Khawaja said he again almost spoke up in 2021 when bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon all denied publicly that they knew about the ball-tampering.
But after extensive talks with then-coach Justin Langer he decided not to.
The 39-year-old said he never felt comfortable talking after that while back in the Australian team from 2022.
“Call me a chicken or whatever you want. I didn’t know how to do it because I was still in the team,” Khawaja said. “I was always conscious of putting my team first, but I’m not in that team anymore.”

The National Basketball Association (NBA) says it removed Rwanda's army team from its African league because of US sanctions imposed on the country in March.
The NBA had previously said the Rwandan army-funded Armée Patriotique Rwandaise (APR) club would not participate in the 2026 Basketball Africa League (BAL).
However this is the first time the NBA has revealed the reasons behind the APR's removal.
The association was responding to complaints by two US senators, who sent a letter asking them to reconsider their partnership with the Rwandan team. The US placed sanctions on the Rwandan army, accusing it of fuelling the conflict in the Democratic Republic of Congo in March.
The senators said the NBA risked "becoming complicit in sportswashing by accepting money from a Rwandan government that systematically abuses human rights".
Last week, the US also imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry over its support for the M23 rebel group which has seized control of large parts of eastern DR Congo. Rwanda denies backing the rebels despite overwhelming evidence.
Rwanda is an official BAL partner and pays the league to host its finals at the 10,000-seat BK Arena in the capital, Kigali.
The BBC has asked Rwanda for comment.

In the letter to the NBA dated 23 October, Democratic Senator Jeffrey Merkley and Republican counterpart Marsha Blackburn gave the association until 2 November to give a written response regarding its continued partnership with Rwanda.
"What is the NBA red line for accepting money from foreign governments that commit human rights abuses?" the senators asked.
Among other queries, they also questioned how the association could "reconcile its continued partnership with Rwanda with its purported commitment to justice".
In its response, NBA deputy commissioner Mark Tatum said the Rwandan team "had been withdrawn" from the BAL following the sanctions imposed earlier in the year, American sports website ESPN reports.
The NBA said the APR basketball club would remain barred while the US sanctions are in place.
The APR is one of Rwanda's top basketball teams and represented the country in the BAL in 2024 and 2025, when it came third. It was replaced by the RSSB Tigers this year.
The BAL is a pan-African basketball league established and co-organised by the NBA and the basketball's world governing body Fiba.
It is a professional league featuring 12 club teams from across the continent.
Rwanda has hosted all but one of the league's final and playoff matches since the inaugural match in 2021.
The NBA reportedly receives millions of dollars annually from the country for the marketing and partnership rights.
DR Congo has repeatedly condemned Rwanda's high-profile international sports deals, including with the NBA, European football clubs and Formula 1, asking them to end their campaigns.
It argues that these help Rwanda clean up its global image, while the conflict continues in eastern DR Congo.

Health intel-sharing group warns industry in wake of cyberattack on French blood bank
In a new security bulletin, the information sharing and analysis center devoted to the healthcare industry, Health ISAC, alerted members to a recent wave of cyberattacks targeting refrigeration controllers — including one incident that affected a major French blood bank.
"This alert is issued for situational awareness, highlighting how recent operational technology (OT) attacks against specific refrigeration brands directly intersect with emerging threats to the health sector," reads the bulletin seen by NPR. Operational technology refers to the machines that control physical processes in the real world, from cooling systems to water pumps.
Cyberattacks on grocery stores and food processing plants everywhere from Europe and Israel to U.S. military bases have drawn headlines in recent months, particularly as attacks have resulted in spoiled food, fires, broken machinery, and major business disruptions. Attackers are clearly aware of the vulnerability of these systems and are taking advantage.
However, until news broke that the French blood bank, known as the French Blood Establishment, had also been targeted, there was less public attention focused on the potential consequences of refrigeration controllers failing in other industries, particularly healthcare, where lifesaving implements like blood and vaccines often require finely tuned temperature-controlled environments to remain viable.
"This incident underscores a stark operational reality: cybersecurity in healthcare is fundamentally about patient safety," wrote Errol Weiss, the chief security officer at Health ISAC in an email to NPR. "When threat actors manipulate operational technology like cold-chain storage and refrigeration units holding donor blood, plasma, or critical therapies, they aren't merely stealing data or locking down administrative files, they are directly endangering the physical resources required to sustain human life."
On Thursday, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the FBI, the Department of Health and Human Services, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture published their own fact sheet about threats to industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems, tools they identify as critical to multiple industries from healthcare to chemical production, food and agriculture, and transportation.
The FBI Cyber Branch Operations director, Brett Leatherman, said the bureau is tracking bad actors targeting these systems "across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk."
"Industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems protect food, medicine, and other temperature-sensitive products, making them attractive targets for malicious cyber actors," Leatherman said.
Iran, Russia and the search for the culprits
The French blood bank confirmed in a press release Tuesday that one of its vendors used in cold storage rooms was targeted by malicious cyber activity, resulting in the defrost and temperature thresholds being raised dangerously high. The French Blood Establishment ultimately managed to detect the suspicious activity in time to rescue blood samples.
It remains unclear who is responsible for the global attacks on refrigeration controllers, and whether it's multiple actors or groups.
Iran has been linked to at least one incident in Israel earlier in the spring, though that breach involved a lot more sophistication and malicious activity. Investigators probing the disruptions at U.S. military bases are also considering Iran as the potential culprit.
Meanwhile, two pro-Russian hacking groups, NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance, belatedly released videos and posted on Telegram claiming responsibility for the attacks across Europe, publishing a sample of alleged hacked credentials that would've allowed them to access equipment including machines made by the Danish company Danfoss and the American company Copeland. Those machines can monitor and control temperature and other functions. The hacking groups have some history of targeting refrigeration controllers and other operational technology. However, it's unclear if the recent wave of attacks on refrigerators and freezers across Europe even required stolen credentials to execute, a factor that has led some cybersecurity experts to be skeptical of their claims.
Even so, it will require more evidence like access logs, configuration changes, and connections between maintenance accounts on the controllers to make any clear assessments, explained Tom Hegel, who leads threat intelligence research at cybersecurity firm SentinelOne.
"Russian-aligned actors are a credible hypothesis because there is a credible precedent, including the refrigeration-related attack DOJ attributed to CyberArmyofRussia_Reborn and NoName's history of politically motivated disruption. But that is only the context, not the missing evidentiary link to these European incidents," Hegel told NPR.
"It's important to note that such Russian threat actors often seek attention and claim to cause incidents even when false," he continued.
Regardless of who's responsible, the incident highlights how these nearly ubiquitous tools used to remotely manage critical systems are vulnerable to attack in several different ways.
For one, thousands of the refrigeration controllers in France alone were exposed to the open internet with almost no protection put in place before unidentified hackers went after them in October. Afterward, experts were still tracking hundreds of devices left unprotected. That's just a fraction of the tens of thousands of exposed operational devices online, many of them embedded in critical infrastructure.
Additionally, many of the major remote management systems used in refrigerators and freezers have security vulnerabilities. After alerting the companies to the problems, cybersecurity firm Claroty published research on vulnerabilities in multiple major refrigeration controllers, including those made by both the American manufacturer Copeland and by Danfoss.
While some of those vulnerabilities have been discovered and the vendors have designed patches to seal the hole, the problems don't stop there.
Experts warn it's difficult to patch operational technology because doing so often requires shutting systems down. In industries like healthcare, even minutes of downtime create extreme risk for patient safety. And for some aging models, it's impossible to patch, because the vendor is no longer offering updates — and companies can't afford to spring for a new model.
Sometimes, executives don't even know what machines are on their networks.
Additionally, for many companies, vendors that work with them demand remote access to systems like refrigeration controllers to regularly service them. It's often a requirement in the contract companies sign.
"Industrial chillers operate under vendor contracts that mandate persistent remote access," explained Nic Adams, CEO of 0rcus, a U.S. offensive security firm. "These commercial agreements leave national food and medical supplies defenseless against basic credential abuse."
Finally, hackers are now using AI to find these vulnerabilities faster than ever, and AI is also helping them to better understand the complex machines and the processes they control. Bad actors a world away no longer need to understand individual languages or industries, or even the physics involved to disrupt operations. In recent weeks, cyber incident responders tell NPR they're seeing a massive spike in attacks that are at least in part carried out by AI agents.
The good news is that a lot of these attacks, even if they incorporate AI, are not particularly sophisticated, novel, or stealthy.
Weiss of Health ISAC tells NPR there are basic steps the healthcare industry can take to prevent being a victim of these opportunistic attacks.
That process "begins" by "eliminating public internet exposure," wrote Weiss, then "enforcing strict network segmentation" in order to isolate refrigeration systems "from standard enterprise and guest networks" and finally adding on safeguards "that software overrides cannot bypass" like "hard-wired mechanical cutoffs" and "independent thermal alarms."
In the Health ISAC alert, the industry is urged to separate not just refrigeration controllers from hospital IT systems, but also medical gas monitors, for one, and train staff onsite on how to take physical manual control of machines in an emergency.
Finally, the alert urges hospitals to have offline backups of their systems.
Store managers on the frontlines
Sharing intelligence about these kinds of cyberattacks can help other potential victims avoid disaster.
While Estonian grocery stores were targeted in the most recent wave of attacks, many of those store managers were on high alert thanks to warnings issued by Estonia's Information Systems Authority, RIA. "When one Selver store was attacked on 2 November, the attackers managed to change the refrigeration system's temperature setting to +50°C. However, the service provider reacted quickly and prevented significant damage," said Annika Müür, a spokesperson for RIA. "So while we can't say that Estonia managed to prevent the attacks entirely, I think this case is a good example of the importance of monitoring threats internationally, acting on early warnings and working closely with businesses to minimise the impact."
Weiss of Health ISAC also urged companies across sectors that are being targeted by this recent wave of attacks to share information to help others defend themselves.
"The attack highlights why timely, trusted information sharing across borders and sectors is our strongest collective defense," he wrote.
"Rapid intelligence sharing allows hospitals and health facilities globally to recognize emerging attack patterns, verify vendor exposure, and harden critical infrastructure before threat actors can cause physical harm."

Formula One will continue to race at Sao Paulo’s Interlagos circuit through to 2035 after announcing a five-year contract extension on Saturday.
The existing contract, under an extension agreed in 2023, was due to run until 2030.
Interlagos, officially named the Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace after Brazil’s 1975 race winner, first hosted a world championship grand prix in 1973. It is currently the only South American round of the championship.
The atmospheric circuit has witnessed some major milestones in the sport’s history, including the late triple champion Ayrton Senna’s emotional home win in 1991, Kimi Raikkonen winning the 2007 title for Ferrari and Lewis Hamilton’s first with McLaren in 2008.

Given the opportunity, I'd happily travel everywhere by train. Luckily, I live in Southern California, where I can easily explore neighborhoods up and down the coast via the Amtrak Pacific Surfliner.
This beautiful coastal train runs all the way from San Diego to San Luis Obispo, and I've discovered tons of cool towns and cities simply by exploring the stops along the route. One of my favorites is the city of Ventura: It's an easy, $22 day trip from my nearest train station in Los Angeles.
Ventura is a historic beach town north of LA with a wealth of attractions, from relaxing, surfer-laden beaches to eclectic shopping and delicious food.
The train ride to Ventura is short and affordable
A one-way ticket from the Hollywood Burbank Airport station costs just $22 and gets me to Ventura within an hour and a half.
One of the perks of traveling by Amtrak, instead of by car or bus, is the café car experience. If I don't have time for Starbucks in the morning, I'll grab a coffee and a vegetarian breakfast burrito with cheese, eggs, and potatoes (and then douse it in hot sauce or ketchup).
I also love that Ventura's beach is just a block from the train station. This means I don't have to pay for parking or fight for a good beachside spot.
The beach is typically the first place I go upon arriving. I walk south toward the pier, down the paved promenade that runs along Surfers Point.
Sometimes, I'll roam the pier and get a fish taco or elote from Beach House Tacos. But usually, I just sit in the sand with a good book and lounge for an hour or so, relaxing in the sun.
Before I leave the beach, I like to indulge my inner child and use the swing at the small playground right on the sand. Swinging toward the ocean always makes me feel like I could soar right over the waves.
Downtown Ventura is full of thrift shops and quirky small businesses
One of my favorite reasons to take a day trip to Ventura at all (besides the beach) is to go thrifting. The downtown area, especially Main Street, has a plethora of vintage and thrift shops.
Coalition Thrift Store is always at the top of my list. It has an incredible, reasonably priced selection of both modern and vintage pieces. I run a vintage shop on Etsy and source some of my finds from there.
I'm also a huge bookworm, so the used bookstore, The Calico Cat Bookshop, and romance novel store Smitten are usually next on my list.
From award-winning fish tacos to tiki drinks, Ventura has a great food and drink scene
When hunger strikes, I'll usually grab some pub grub at one of the gastropubs in the area, like Finney's Crafthouse. I'm also a fan of Spencer Makenzie's, which has a fish taco that locals voted best in Ventura. Eating seafood when I'm next to the ocean is a must.
Depending on my mood later in the day, I'll either grab a fun drink at VenTiki Lounge to chill out or a vanilla chai from Palermo Coffee & Gifts as a pick-me-up.
My last stop of the day, however, is always Tony's Pizzaria, just a block from the train station. I'll grab a slice of cheese pizza for my trip home.
My favorite part is spending a day without driving
Ventura is such a great day trip because, unlike most of LA, it's easy to explore on foot. I can get my steps in, then relax with my feet up on the train ride home.
If I'm taking the train after 8 p.m., I might even treat myself to a cocktail during Amtrak's after-hours happy hour, something that's impossible to do while driving.
By the time I get back to LA, I've squeezed a beach day, some shopping, and plenty of good seafood into a 12-hour day trip — all without ever having to set foot in a car.

Women recruited from economically weaker sections were being offered ₹20,000 to ₹30,000 for an egg donation cycle, while those operating the alleged racket made an average of about ₹3 lakh from each cycle.
Malkajgiri police widened their investigation into the exploitation of women, falsification of records and the role of IVF and fertility establishments.
The 43 women rescued during simultaneous raids in Hyderabad have undergone medical examinations, including blood-group and fitness tests. Police are now verifying their medical histories with IVF centres to establish their treatment records.
The investigation has raised concerns over how the women were recruited and whether they gave informed consent for the procedures. Police said women from economically weaker sections were targeted and that, in some cases, intermediaries allegedly even completed their signatures on documents. Investigators are examining possible falsification of records and whether the women fully understood the procedures they were being recruited for.
Police are tracing the payments and commissions involving organisers, recruiters and intermediaries who connected the women with fertility-related establishments.
The investigation is now expanding to medical establishments. Police are preparing to serve notices to the District Medical and Health Officer (DMHO) and conduct searches at ART and fertility centres. Some hospitals have also approached police and informed them that employees found to have been involved had been removed.
Investigators are examining how women from West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and other states were recruited, transported and accommodated in Hyderabad before being referred for egg retrieval procedures. Their medical records, consent documents and the procedures they underwent are also being scrutinised.
All eight accused arrested in connection with the Hyderabad cases have been remanded to judicial custody. Further investigation is underway.

రోడ్డుపై నడుచుకుంటూ వెళ్తున్న ఓ బాలికను కొందరు వ్యక్తులు కిడ్నాప్ చేసిన ఒక వీడియోను బీహార్లో జరిగిన సంఘటన అంటూ సోషల్ మీడియాలో షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ). ఈ వీడియోలో నంబర్ ప్లేట్ను కప్పి ఉంచిన బొలెరో వాహనంలో వచ్చిన కొందరు వ్యక్తులు బాలికను బలవంతంగా ఎత్తుకెళ్లడం కనిపిస్తుంది. వారి నుంచి తప్పించుకోవడానికి బాలిక ప్రయత్నిస్తుండగా, అటుగా వెళ్తున్న ఓ బైకర్ ఈ ఘటనను వీడియో తీస్తూ, కిడ్నాపర్లను అడ్డుకునేందుకు ప్రయత్నిస్తాడు. దీని వెనుక ఎంత నిజముందో ఈ కథనం ద్వారా తెలుసుకుందాం.
క్లెయిమ్: బీహార్లో రోడ్డుపై నడుచుకుంటూ వెళ్తున్న ఓ బాలికను కారులో వచ్చిన కొందరు వ్యక్తులు కిడ్నాప్ చేసిన నిజమైన ఘటనను ఈ వీడియో చూపిస్తోంది.
ఫ్యాక్ట్: ఇది ఒక స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియో. ఇది బీహార్లో నిజంగా జరిగిన కిడ్నాప్ ఘటన కాదు. Isa Stuntతో కలిసి వీడియోలు చేసే ముక్లేసుర్ అలీ (Muklesur Ali) ఈ ఘటన ముందుగా ప్లాన్ చేసి చిత్రీకరించిందని, వీడియోలో కనిపించిన వారందరూ తన టీమ్ సభ్యులేనని తెలిపారు. అంతేకాకుండా, వారితో సంబంధం ఉన్న ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్, యూట్యూబ్ ఖాతాల్లో కూడా వినోదం కోసం ఇలాంటి అనేక స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియోలు ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేసిన వాదన తప్పు.
వైరల్ వీడియోలోని కీ ఫ్రేమ్లను ఉపయోగించి రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, 2026 అక్టోబర్ 11న ‘Isa Stunt’ అనే ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ ఖాతాలో ఇదే వీడియోను (ఇక్కడ) పోస్ట్ చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం (ఆర్కైవ్). అయితే, వైరల్ వీడియోలో ఉన్నట్లుగా ఈ వీడియోలో ఆడియో లేదు. దానికి బదులుగా బ్యాక్గ్రౌండ్ మ్యూజిక్ ఉంది. అంతేకాకుండా, ఈ పోస్టుకు జత చేసిన క్యాప్షన్లో కూడా ఘటనకు సంబంధించి ఎలాంటి వివరాలు లేవు.
ఆ ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ పేజీని పరిశీలించగా, వైరల్ వీడియోను పోలి ఉన్న మరికొన్ని వీడియోలు కనిపించాయి. ఈ వీడియోల్లో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) వైరల్ వీడియోలో కనిపించిన అదే బొలెరో వాహనం, మోటార్ సైకిల్, వ్యక్తి ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. దీన్ని బట్టి, ఈ వీడియోలు నిజమైన ఘటనలకు సంబంధించినవి కాకుండా ముందుగా ప్లాన్ చేసి చిత్రీకరించినవై ఉండవచ్చని తెలుస్తోంది.
తదుపరి, ‘Isa Stunt’ అనే ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ ఖాతా బయోలో ఇచ్చిన యూట్యూబ్ ఛానెల్ను కూడా గుర్తించాం. ఈ ఛానెల్లో వైరల్ వీడియోను పోలి ఉన్న మరికొన్ని వీడియోలు ఉన్నాయి. వాటిలో బాలిక కిడ్నాప్, రోడ్డుపై దాడి, రోడ్డు ప్రమాదం వంటి ఘటనలను చిత్రీకరించారు. అయితే, ఈ వీడియోల వివరణలు ఇంకా ఛానెల్ బయోలో ఈ కంటెంట్ను కేవలం వినోదం కోసం రూపొందించినట్లు పేర్కొన్నారు.
అయితే, ‘Isa Stunt’ ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ ఖాతాలో పోస్ట్ చేసిన పలు వీడియోల్లో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) ‘Muklesur Ali’ అనే ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ ఖాతాను (ఇక్కడ) ట్యాగ్ చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. ముక్లేసుర్ అలీ ఖాతాను పరిశీలించగా, వైరల్ వీడియోను పోలి ఉన్న మరికొన్ని వీడియోలు కనిపించాయి. వీటిలో ఇదే తరహాలో కిడ్నాప్ చేసినట్లు చిత్రీకరించిన ఒక వీడియో కూడా ఉంది. గతంలో కూడా ముక్లేసుర్ అలీ రూపొందించిన పలు వీడియోలు సోషల్ మీడియాలో వైరల్ కాగా, వాటిని నిజమైన ఘటనలుగా తప్పుగా ప్రచారం చేయడాన్ని మేము (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) ఫ్యాక్ట్-చెక్ చేశాం. ఈ వివరాలన్నీ పరిశీలిస్తే, వైరల్ వీడియో నిజమైన కిడ్నాప్ ఘటనను చూపించేది కాదని, వినోదం కోసం ముందుగా స్క్రిప్ట్ ప్రకారం చిత్రీకరించిన వీడియో అని తెలుస్తోంది.
NewsChecker ముక్లేసుర్ అలీని సంప్రదించగా, తాను, Isa కలిసి ఒక టీమ్గా స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియోలు రూపొందిస్తామని తెలిపారు. వైరల్ అవుతున్న బాలిక కిడ్నాప్ వీడియో కూడా ముందుగా స్క్రిప్ట్ ప్రకారం చిత్రీకరించిందేనని, అందులో కనిపించిన వారందరూ తన టీమ్ సభ్యులేనని ఆయన స్పష్టం చేశారు.
చివరిగా, బీహార్లో రోడ్డుపై ఓ బాలికను కిడ్నాప్ చేస్తున్నట్లు వైరల్ అవుతున్న ఈ వీడియో స్క్రిప్టెడ్, నిజమైన సంఘటన కాదు.

In China’s fierce race for success, mental health struggles are starting earlier
While competition once centred on getting into college, teenagers are increasingly under pressure to get a higher secondary place
6-MIN READ6-MIN

Caroline Linin Beijing
Moon Chen stared down at her textbook, struggling to make sense of the words on the page.
The 15-year-old felt a suffocating weight press into her chest, while her heart fluttered erratically.
Chen’s mother rushed her to a cardiologist – only to be told that she should see a psychiatrist instead.

Four content funds, jointly established by Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA) and local companies, presented the projects they’ve been investing in over the past year in a TCCF showcase today.
The line-up from the four funds – Chunghwa Digital Cultural and Creative Fund, Momomini Kids Content Fund, Joint Journey Creative and Enjoy Entertainment – include a wide range of films, series, live performances and immersive exhibitions.
Opening the presentation, TAICCA chair Sue Wang said: “These ventures are managed by professional fund managers, based on rigorous risk assessment and management. We want to ensure professional governance in planning the portfolios of these funds.”
Enjoy Entertainment – established by TAICCA, Far EasTone Telecommunications (FET) and Far Reach Entertainment – focuses on premium content and international co-productions.
Watch on Deadline
The fund has so far made 15 investments since launch one year ago, including into Our Blues, a Taiwanese remake of CJ ENM’s Korean series, which will premiere on Netflix on December 3; and two recent hit films: Taiwanese horror film The Rope Curse 4: Kuntilanak and action film 96 Minutes.
Gary Tsai, FET’s COO of Entertainment Service and GM of Far Reach Entertainment, said Rope Curse 4 had recently grossed $2.5M (NTD80M) in Taiwan theatres and has also been released in Malaysia, Indonesia, and soon Cambodia. “The film has Taiwanese taste and flavor but is still resonating with audiences across Asia,” Tsai said.
Enjoy Entertainment has also invested in the ID Music Festival in Huashan cultural park, live musicals Her Voice and Don’t Cry Dancing Girls and an immersive exhibition created by illustrator Jimmy Liao.
TAICCA is also partnered with Momomini, a Taiwanese media brand and YouTube content channel, in the Momomini Kids Content Fund, which specializes in kids content and has made six investments over the past year. In addition to TAICCA support, the fund is backed by the Fubon Cultural & Educational Foundation and DaWin Creative.
Phoebe TSAI, COO of Momomini Kids Content Fund, introduced the slate which includes animations such as comedy adventure Who’s Our Sub Today, and Feifei, based on stories by Taiwanese artist and author Bei Lynn; as well as live-action shows such as Mogu & Perol, a collaboration with France’s Zephyr, and reality series Having Fun In The Mountains.
The Momomini fund has also backed drama series Hello Mr President, about a kid who travels to Taipei to meet Taiwan’s president. “Very few production houses in Taiwan make drama for kids and teenagers – it’s been many years since any kids drama appeared on TV. So we’re very honored to have the opportunity with the support of TAICCA to invest in this drama,” said Tsai, adding that the show has finished shooting and will be on air from January next year.
Founded in 2025, Joint Journey Creative (JJC) is a joint venture fund between SET Group, TAICCA, Chunghwa Telecom and Japan’s The Far Eastern TV Entertainment.
Focused on investements in the transmedia and IP development space, the fund aims to connect Taiwanese creators with Asian and global markets. As one of its shareholders is Japanese, the fund has been building bridges between the content industries in Taiwan and Japan. Its investments include joining the production committee for multiple seasons of Japanese drama Midnight Diner, including season six.
“We’re able to create relationships and trust between Taiwan and Japan to pave the way for more collaboration with Japanese parties,” said JJC President Joanne Tsai.
JJC has also been running talent incubator programs including a romance drama series workshop that introduces Taiwanese talent to drama producers from Korea and Japan. “We’ve identified several quality scripts and here in TCCF we’re talking to our collaborators in Japan and Korea to see how we can bring them to screen,” said Tsai, adding that the fund is also working with partners in the rest of Asia, Europe and the U.S.
The fourth fund, Chunghwa Digital Cultural and Creative Fund, was jointly established by TAICCA, Chunghwa Telecom, and E.Sun Bank, again with a mission to help Taiwanese cultural content reach global audiences, with capital of around $30M (NTD1BN).
General Manager Lin Kun-feng explained that the fund is making equity investments into Taiwanese production company Damou Entertainment (The World Between Us) and IP development and publishing company Horiza Creations.
Chunghwa is also investing in a wide range of film and TV projects, including C’est La Vie, produced by and starring Esther Liu, Call Of Lobster, starring Chang Chen and Choi Siwon, and indie band Shallow Levee’s tour Speak in Silence.
While Chunghwa is the biggest shareholder in the fund with a 64% share, TAICCA holds 30%, E-Sun has 5% and CDCC Capital Management has a 1% share.

Agnipath scheme threatened national security, was introduced in haste: Congress’s Rohit Chaudhary
Congress demanded the scrapping of the Agnipath scheme, alleging that it weakens national security and disrupts military training and cadre management.
Congress on Friday demanded the scrapping of the Agnipath recruitment scheme, alleging that it weakens national security, disrupts military training and leaves young recruits without the job security and benefits available to regular soldiers.
“This was a major scheme that threatened to weaken our national security. The Modi government introduced it in haste, without adequate consideration,” Congress leader Colonel (Retd.) Rohit Chaudhary said.
Introduced in June 2022, the Agnipath scheme recruits personnel below officer rank for four years, with 25% of each batch eligible for retention in regular service. On November 4, the Union Cabinet approved an additional two-year engagement period for the remaining 75% of the recruited pool, after which they can be considered for regular enrolment subject to their willingness and meeting selection criteria. The move came weeks before more than 18,300 Agniveers from the first batch were due to complete their four-year tenure by December 31.
Deep Dive
Chaudhary questioned why the government was extending the service period instead of regularising all Agniveers. Referring to the Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani’s assessment that recruits had performed well, he asked, “If all of them performed so well, why are only 25% being made regular soldiers today? Why should the remaining 75 % have to wait?”
Arguing that the scheme could undermine operational preparedness, Chaudhary said, “We do not need a contractual army to guard these borders. We need a regular army.” He alleged that the short tenure had disrupted cadre management and limited opportunities for further training, especially for technical roles in the armed forces. “Over four years, we are unable to provide these recruits with the proper training required under the army’s established system,” he said.
“When you do not even know whether a person will remain in service after four years, the entire training system is disrupted,” said Colonel Sudhir from the Congress’s ex-servicemen department.
Lieutenant Colonel Navjot Singh Thind, who heads the party’s ex-servicemen department in Chandigarh, said there had been no need to alter the army’s recruitment system. “As a soldier, I certainly know that there was absolutely no need to tamper with the army in this manner. And if there was a need to do so, why have they now changed the scheme?” he asked.
Chaudhary also alleged that Agniveers faced unequal treatment compared with regular soldiers in terms of pay, leave, career progression and compensation for those killed in service. “Agniveers are given only 30 days of leave, whereas regular soldiers are entitled to 90 days…Living and working in such a stressful environment became extremely difficult for them,” he added.
He further called for families of Agniveers killed in the line of duty to receive lifelong pensions and benefits equivalent to those provided to families of regular soldiers.
The Congress leader said the revised service tenure for Agniveers was an acknowledgement by the BJP-led government of the scheme’s failure. “It [BJP] has effectively admitted that the Agnipath scheme was an unlawful, ill-conceived, unwarranted, anti-national, anti-military and anti-youth decision that needed to be rejected,” he said.
Chaudhary further announced the launch of “Jai Jawan Part Two”, renewing the Congress’s campaign against the Agnipath scheme. Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi launched the “Jai Jawan” campaign in 2024, demanding the scrapping of the Agnipath scheme and the restoration of regular army recruitment.

The Telangana government has expanded cancer treatment services to all 33 districts in the State, with day-care cancer centres providing chemotherapy locally to reduce the need for patients to travel to Hyderabad, Minister for Health C. Damodar Raja Narasimha said on Tuesday, November 3. The government has also initiated steps to establish Regional Cancer Centres to further strengthen cancer care infrastructure, he added.
The Minister made these remarks during a review meeting on medical services being provided to cancer patients in government hospitals.
Oncologist Dr. Nori Dattatreyudu, who also serves as the advisor to the Telangana government on preventive, curative and affordable cancer care, said 35,000 cancer cases have been registered on the dedicated cancer portal. “Declaring cancer a notifiable disease and effective use of cancer registry will help strengthen the State’s efforts in monitoring and controlling the disease,” he added.
Citing the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination programme as an example, Dr. Nori also appreciated the State’s efforts in prevention, screening and early detection of cancer. Of the 3.4 lakh eligible girls in Telangana, 2.3 lakh of them have been vaccinated against the HPV, achieving a coverage of 67%, he said.
During the meeting, officials briefed the Minister on cancer treatment facilities available at the MNJ Cancer Hospital and the Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS), besides the functioning of day-care chemotherapy centres established across the State. They explained that while patients initially receive treatment at MNJ or NIMS, chemotherapy services are subsequently provided at district-level centres. Patients are also being mapped district-wise to facilitate treatment and follow-up.
The Minister directed officials to improve facilities for patients receiving chemotherapy at district centres and ensure that the services were readily available at the district headquarters. “Patients should not have to travel to Hyderabad for chemotherapy when treatment could be provided closer to their homes,” he added.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Leela Rea, 37, who built a greenhouse in her California backyard. She now rents it out for small events and photo shoots, earning an average of $24,000 a month. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
Our family would always drive by this beautiful house in Vista. It had 100-foot trees, eucalyptus, smilax growing down the hills, and hydrangeas. It didn't feel like it belonged in Southern California, but more like the middle of the European countryside.
My oldest daughter would always say, "Mommy, that's the princess house," or, "It's the Christmas house." It just had so much character.
In 2024, we saw that the home was up for sale. Even though we were a week away from a European vacation, I told my husband, "We're absolutely buying this house."
We closed escrow while we were in Switzerland and bought the house for about $1 million. Its interest rate is nearly 8%, and our monthly mortgage payment is about $7,000.
A couple of years earlier, my husband and I had sold our wedding-venue business. Living in Southern California is expensive, and we owned multiple properties, including a home in Carlsbad, which was our primary home at the time.
We wanted a way to increase our income without having to return to work full time. For a while, we rented out our Vista home, along with the lawn and backyard, on Airbnb. We also considered building an accessory dwelling unit on the property to rent out.
We consulted a contractor, who gave us a quote for a three-bedroom, two-bath accessory dwelling unit (ADU). All in — with permits and construction — he told us to budget between $500,000 and $600,000, with room for error.
I was like, "There's no way this thing is going to cost me $600,000 to build, and I'd be earning like $3,500 a month." I have three young children, too. Would I even be able to trust them to run around with a stranger living on our property?
My background in the wedding industry gave me an idea
Instead of an ADU or tiny home, my husband and I decided to build a greenhouse in the backyard.
I'm not going to pretend that I just landed on this idea. I knew what I was doing. I previously worked in the wedding industry and have a pretty good idea of what people are looking for.
In Southern California, there are many beautiful venues, but not a lot that are small and intimate. For example, there's a beautiful wedding venue about 15 minutes down the street, and it's an insane property. But they do four or five weddings a day there, and their food-and-beverage minimum is probably around $50,000 to $100,000.
If you're having a rehearsal dinner or a baby shower, you're not going to want to spend $50,000. That's where we come in. We're like, "We'll meet you right here."
I've had greenhouses on my Pinterest board for 10 years. We almost went with a company from England to build ours, but the quote was way over our budget. So I sketched out my own idea, and I reached out to a friend who's a welder.
I have applied for a patent for my greenhouse design. It cost us almost $200,000 to build, including electrical work, flooring, and a fireplace. To help finance construction, we sold a couple of our real-estate properties, though not our Carlsbad home. All in, it took about 10 months to build.
We live in such a social-media, content-creation world. You give something a bomb aesthetic, people are going to come, and they're going to pay — especially with the rise of AI, people are craving something real that stands out.
Our house is on a hill, and the greenhouse is down below. There are two seasonal creeks on each side of the greenhouse. When it rains, they get really full. There are massive trees everywhere. On one path, we have a lavender field with about 150 French lavender plants, and you just kind of walk into the greenhouse. It's so sweet.
The business has taken off
We've done a lot of proposals, and photoshoots are our bread and butter. But our highest revenue events are the intimate ones, like rehearsal dinners, bridal showers, and baby showers.
A lot of the time, guests get married at the courthouse and then have a stunning little 20-person reception in the greenhouse.
I think, in this post-COVID world, people are more attracted to intimate events with their nearest and dearest. Nobody really wants a Taylor Swift wedding. You can't splurge when you have that many people.
With smaller events, you have money for the flowers, candles, live musicians, and food. You can really stretch your budget.
At first, I was posting everywhere to promote the greenhouse. There are different platforms that charge insane commission fees, which worked for some time. But now we get enough inquiries through social media that it just doesn't make sense.
We don't do a lot of events each year — maybe 10 to 15 intimate events. But we do a lot of photoshoots and content-creation shoots. They make good money, and you don't have to do anything for them.
When we first started, we charged $3,000 for a day rental, whether it was a baby shower or an intimate event. Now, our minimum for any event is $7,500.
For photoshoots, the minimum is $375 per hour for photoshoots. We also offer a full buyout of the house — which we now live in full time — but only when we're traveling. It's not like, "Hey, I want to rent your whole house today." Never. We have to plan for it. And unless we're bringing in at least $30,000 for the weekend, I'm not packing up.
On average, we earn about $24,000 renting out the greenhouse. Some of that money goes back into maintaining the space.
For events, I always provide refreshments, paper towels, and trash bags, which cost between $200 and $350 a month. We also hire a cleaning company that charges between $350 and $500. I used to do a lot of the cleaning myself, but I've paid my dues.
We're building more greenhouses based on my design
We've had a lot of manufacturers reach out and say, "Let us build a greenhouse, and we'll split the profits." But I reached out to the friend who built ours, and I was like, "Let's engineer this properly and figure it out together."
We are manufacturing here in Southern California, and there will be three sizes. I'm going to put the smallest one in our old house in Carlsbad. We already have a couple of preorders, so I'm really excited to start seeing them pop up.
This project is going to change our whole family's life.
In the beginning, even my family was like, "Who would pay to rent out your house and little greenhouse?" And I was like, "Oh my gosh, let me show you."
Through renting out our greenhouse, my husband and I are grateful not to have to work full time. Some months, we're earning as much as some people make in a year. We're also able to spend more time together as a family.
Our parents' generation was always told that getting an education or working a job for 20 to 30 years was the best way to build wealth. But I don't think our generation thinks like that.
It's such a fun, interesting time to be alive. We have all these tools to market and sell our ideas in ways previous generations never dreamed of.
I feel like people need to think differently to start living differently. And I hope more moms know that they can bet on themselves. Why not?

Kerala-born Nithya Raman has won the Los Angeles mayoral race, becoming the first Indian-American elected to lead the city. Incumbent Karen Bass conceded defeat and pledged a smooth transition, paving the way for Raman, an urban planner and city council member, to lead America's second-largest metropolis. Raman's victory makes her the city's first South Asian mayor. She began her political journey with her election to the Los Angeles City Council in 2020, becoming the first Asian-American woman and the first South Asian elected to the council. She secured another mandate in 2024. “Los Angeles, I am deeply honoured to be your next mayor,” Raman wrote on X on November 5. Bass said she had called Raman to congratulate her. “While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken,” Bass said. “I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition. Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us.” Bass becomes the first Los Angeles mayor in two decades to lose a re-election bid. Her first term was overshadowed by the deadly Palisades Fire, which broke out while she was out of the country and caught the fire department unprepared. Raman's campaign focused on housing accessibility, homelessness management and improving municipal services. According to LAist, her pledges included better maintenance of street lights and potholes, alongside structural policing reforms. She entered the mayoral race at the last minute, despite initially backing Bass's re-election bid. Her decision to file in the final hours before the deadline angered sections of the city's Democratic establishment, which had rallied behind Bass. People are “dissatisfied” with the “broken status quo” of Los Angeles, Raman told AFP ahead of the November 3 midterm vote. “This city's government has made solving problems look impossible for so long,” said the Ivy League-educated urban planner. "Hopelessness can be fatal for a city, but this campaign refused to accept that.” Born in Thrissur, Keralam, to a Tamil Brahmin family that moved to the United States when she was about six, Raman's political outlook was shaped partly by her work in Chennai. After graduating from Harvard and completing a master's in city planning from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, she returned to India in 2010. Between 2010 and 2013, she headed Transparent Chennai, a project under the Centre for Development Finance. Raman and her team mapped public toilets in slum resettlement colonies, documented informal waste pickers and recyclers, and pushed for their inclusion in municipal planning. She also co-authored research opposing the forced relocation of families from Chennai's waterways, including the Cooum River, to distant resettlement colonies. Her work involved collaboration with citizen groups such as Exnora and the Thillai Ganga Nagar Residents' Welfare Association. “The collaboration involved organising community forums, mapping local traffic issues, and collecting data on public transport, pedestrian safety, and civic infrastructure gaps to present actionable data to the Chennai Traffic Police and municipal corporations,” said V. Rama Rao, a civic activist. A former civic volunteer recalled: “She taught us that data could be weaponised.” Raman has credited this approach to community activism with shaping her political philosophy, which focuses on using data-driven urban planning to address housing affordability and homelessness. Raman's victory comes amid wider gains for Indian-Americans in US politics. Indian American Impact said her election reflected the growing political influence of South Asian Americans, particularly in California. The 5.5 million-strong Indian-American community also saw several candidates win elections across the country. Pia Dandiya of Florida and Dr Amish Shah of Arizona will join Representatives Ami Bera, Pramila Jayapal, Ro Khanna and Suhas Subramanyam in the US Congress. Other winners included Ranjeev Puri in Michigan, Aruna Miller in Maryland, Nabeela Syed in Illinois and Pooja Sethi in Texas. Jyot Singh won a seat in the Georgia State House, becoming the first Indian American and first Sikh American elected to the Georgia State Legislature. Nothing illustrates more poignantly the exalted status once enjoyed by temple elephants, and their subsequent fall, than the story of Kesavan — the elephant of the Adi Kesava Perumal Temple at Kanniyakumari’s Thiruvattar — who is the protagonist of writer Jeyamohan’s Mathagam.
A favourite of the King, even when he was a prince, Kesavan developed a sense of his own exceptional status. Even his chief mahout was afraid to command him. The mahout’s emaciated leg, a result of Kesavan’s fury, bears testimony to what the elephant was capable of. But the day the King died, Kesavan was reduced to the status of just another animal, a slave to humans. The elephant, which once commanded fear and deference, would now meekly extend its leg to help the mahout climb on to its back.

Measles strategy works – Now it must expand to more countries
Cape Town Measles Declaration pledges to cut measles deaths by half
At a landmark World Health Organization (WHO)/United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) meeting in Cape Town, leading players in the fight against measles spelled out what it will take to stop 2000 children dying every day from this preventable disease. Together with UNICEF special ambassador Angelique Kidjo, they issued a call for intensified efforts and the resources necessary to ensure all children are protected against measles.
“We can do it – we’ve done it before – in Afghanistan, Angola, in countries devastated by conflict and drought and every other form of disaster,” said Carol Bellamy, Executive Director, UNICEF. “In just three years, and against great odds, we’ve cut the number of children dying from measles by almost 25%. It’s one of the most dramatic declines in disease mortality in history. But the next 25% will be harder. With the political and financial support of donors and governments around the world, we can together save many more lives.”
The “Cape Town Measles Declaration” calls on governments to take strong action against one of the world’s most vicious and prolific vaccine-preventable childhood killers – a disease which kills 745,000 children every year. We must control this disease to meet the Millennium Development targets of a 67% reduction in under-five mortality by 2015. The world leaders are well aware of the urgency. Last year, the UN General Assembly Special Session on Children set a 2005 target date to reduce measles deaths from 1999 levels by 50%. This year, the World Health Assembly, which includes 192 member states, endorsed the WHO and UNICEF measles strategy to combat the disease.
“When 30 million children are affected and 745,000 children die every year, you have to think big,” said Dr. LEE Jong-wook, Director-General of WHO. “Since the launch of the WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths in 2000, we have delivered measles vaccine to more than 200 million children globally. We know the strategy works. An additional half a million children are alive today because of all the partners’ efforts. But if we’re to prevent more deaths, we must do more. And we’ll need help from governments and from the international community.”
The campaign against measles has been dramatic – hundreds of thousands of children saved, the virus almost banished from the Americas and transmission cut drastically in many African countries, where the Measles Initiative Partnership has been the driving force behind the campaign. WHO and UNICEF have identified 45 countries as the highest priority for mortality-reduction strategies, accounting for 95% of global deaths from measles.
“It has been astonishing to see the results of the immunization programme in Africa,“ said Dr Mark Grabowsky, Senior Technical Officer, American Red Cross. “Now we have proof that we can reduce measles mortality even in countries torn apart by conflict, if governments are committed, communities are engaged and we have the support of donors, NGOs and volunteers. What we have accomplished so far through the Measles Initiative Partnership gives great hope for the future, and the many thousands of children we can still save.” The foundation of the measles mortality-reduction strategy is the re-invigoration of national immunization systems. At the Cape Town meeting, delegates discussed strategies with governments and policy makers for strengthening routine immunization services and making the life-saving measles vaccine available to all children as a matter of course.
”It’s not just about reducing childhood deaths today. We need to be in this for the long haul and this means a sustainable reduction in childhood deaths, which only a strong national health system can guarantee,” said Dr Stephen L. Cochi, Deputy Director, National Immunization Program, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). ”This kind of international focus and commitment gives us the opportunity to build that strength – boosting safe routine immunization services, establishing international laboratory networks and increasing surveillance to detect and respond to outbreaks.”
“Today the call to action is clear,” said Mr Nick Farrell, Senior Programme Officer, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. “ We have to ensure every child receives a second opportunity for measles immunization in these 45 countries, no matter how remote or marginalized, regardless of barriers of conflict, culture and poverty.
“To date we have seen tens of thousands of health workers and volunteers trek across mountains and deserts in all kinds of conditions to find these children to ensure they receive the life-saving vaccine,” said Timothy E. Wirth, President of the United Nations Foundation. “We are witnessing incredible commitment from ordinary people. They need – they deserve to be backed up by the world’s political will and financial support.”
Ms Angelique Kidjo, Special UNICEF ambassador, believes that the Cape Town Measles Declaration indicates a clear path towards a giant achievement in children’s health.
”The world has committed, to drastically reducing the devastating, pointless waste of young life,” she said. “If we reach our targets for measles, we will have taken a huge step towards keeping that promise. I believe we can get there – but only if we make it a priority to turn this declaration into action. This goal deserves all we can give. We must do whatever is necessary.”
Further information:
- Of all the vaccine-preventable diseases, measles remains the leading childhood killer. Measles is an important cause of overall under 5 childhood mortality.
- Measles affects over 30 million children. More than 745,000 die each year from measles – more than half of them in Africa.
- A safe, effective and inexpensive measles vaccine has been available for over 40 years.
- Measles accounts for an estimated 50% of vaccine-preventable deaths among children.
- One million measles deaths are already being prevented each year with existing immunization efforts. With the successful implementation of the WHO-UNICEF measles strategy (including routine immunization and periodic supplementary immunization activities), an additional 500,000 measles deaths can be prevented each year.
- Measles is a highly contagious vaccine-preventable disease caused by the measles virus. It is one of the most readily transmitted communicable diseases and probably the best known and most deadly of all childhood illnesses. Measles causes a high fever, rash, cough and can kill. It affects mostly children, but also young adults. Children usually do not die directly of measles, but from its complications such as pneumonia and diarrhea which attack their weakened immune systems.
- It costs less than a dollar to immunize a child against measles.
- A critical goal is to reduce measles mortality by 50% by 2005 (compared to 875,000 deaths in 1999).
- The WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths includes: achieving and maintaining high routine measles immunization coverage – ‘the first opportunity’ to infants; Providing a ‘second opportunity’ for measles immunization for all children through periodic supplementary immunization campaigns; Ensuring high quality measles surveillance is in place to detect and respond to outbreaks; and improving management of complicated cases.
- Collaborating partners include: WHO, UNICEF, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the United Nations Foundation, humanitarian and non-governmental organizations, including the American Red Cross and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, governments of countries affected by measles, development banks, donor governments (e.g. Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America).
- The importance of developing long term immunization planning cannot be underestimated. This includes ensuring measles activities are fully integrated with other national health goals, establishing high quality surveillance, mobilizing necessary human and financial resources and planning for financial sustainability of measles mortality reduction activities.

Why a US-funded vaccine trial on babies was cancelled in Guinea-Bissau
- Published
A proposed trial of a hepatitis B vaccine on newborn babies in Guinea-Bissau has been cancelled following accusations that the trial was "unethical" and "neocolonial".
The trial was funded by the US, under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has a long record of expressing scepticism about vaccines.
Police have seized a batch of vaccines from the research centre at the heart of the controversy.
The proposed trial drew international criticism because it planned to withhold a vaccine recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) from half of the participating newborns.
Some public health experts argued that the proposed trial raised broader questions about whether vulnerable populations in African countries were being asked to take risks that researchers would not accept in wealthier countries.
The BBC has asked the US department of health and human services for comment.
Here is what you need to know.
What was the trial?
The study was planned at the Bandim Health Project, a research centre that has operated in Guinea-Bissau since 1978.
It was designed to involve 14,000 newborns, with half receiving a hepatitis B vaccine shortly after birth and the other half not being given the shot.
Bandim said the trial aimed to investigate whether the hepatitis B vaccine given at birth has broader health effects beyond preventing infection.
Previous studies in The Gambia and Guinea-Bissau have raised questions about a possible link to increased mortality.
Researchers argued that because Guinea-Bissau does not currently offer routine hepatitis B vaccinations at birth, despite WHO recommendations, they have a unique opportunity to study its effects before such vaccines are introduced in 2028.
But critics questioned the ethics of withholding the vaccine from some babies, particularly in one of the world's poorest countries, where the infection is widespread.
The Trump administration funded the proposed study, with the CDC awarding the University of Southern Denmark (SDU) $1.6m (£1.2m) in December 2025.
What did the WHO say?
Walter Kazadi Mulombo, the WHO representative in Guinea-Bissau, told the BBC they became concerned after receiving questions about the study and finding no publicly available protocol.
He said the main ethical concern was that the trial would withhold an intervention already proven to protect newborns against hepatitis B.
"The vaccine has been used for more than 30 years in more than 115 countries," he said. "A study that will withhold that intervention from other newborns is unethical."
He warned that babies could be exposed to the virus during childbirth if their mothers were infected, as well as later in life.
Nearly a fifth of the population of Guinea-Bissau are infected with hepatitis B, a viral infection that affects the liver.
Those infected during infancy are particularly likely to develop chronic infections, which kill up to 25% of people, mostly through liver failure or liver cancer, according to data published in 2020.
The WHO is working with the government to bring forward the birth-dose vaccine.
"The country had been expected to add it to its routine immunisation schedule in 2028, but officials are considering introducing it in the first quarter of next year," Mulombo said.
Guinea-Bissau currently vaccinates children against hepatitis B at six weeks, which means it is less effective.
Why did Guinea-Bissau reject the trial?
Guinea-Bissau's government prohibited hepatitis B vaccine trials involving children in January. At the time, it requested a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study.
Health Minister Quinhin Nantote said in October that the suspension remained in force and had not been overturned by the Council of Ministers after reports emerged claiming that the trial would be taking place after all.
"We were surprised to learn from media reports that the study might proceed," Nantote said. "We are outraged because even I, as the minister responsible for this sector, was not informed."
The dispute intensified after the SDU said a revised study protocol had received ethical approval "from the relevant authorities in Guinea-Bissau", which Nantote denied.
Dr Gavin Yamey, a professor of global health and public policy at Duke University in the US, criticised the proposal.
"The proposed trial reeks of neocolonialism," he told the BBC, questioning why the research was not being conducted in Denmark.
His criticism centred on the decision to withhold a recommended vaccine from some newborns in a country where hepatitis B is widespread.
SDU dean Jakob Grauslund said the trial had never started, no babies had been enrolled and no vaccinations administered as part of the research.
Was the trial approved by anyone?
The SDU said it had received a separate, positive assessment from the university's own research ethics committee.
Grauslund said the university had sought an additional independent assessment, although Danish law did not require one.
He added that the relevant Danish statutory research ethics bodies were unable to undertake the review.
Following the approval from the SDU's ethics committee, Grauslund decided that the project could proceed.
He, however, stressed that this did not replace the separate authorisation required from Guinea-Bissau's authorities.
What has happened to the vaccines?
On 19 October, Guinea-Bissau's Judicial Police searched the Bandim Health Project's facilities in the capital, Bissau, and seized a batch of hepatitis B vaccines.
Police said the batch was intended for vaccinating children but did not disclose how many doses had been seized or the specific grounds for the investigation.
They stressed that the seizure did not, in itself, mean the vaccines were defective or unsafe.
The police have not explicitly said whether their investigation relates to the proposed trial, the importation of the vaccines or other circumstances surrounding the batch.
Grauslund said he could not comment on the seizure of the vaccines.
Who is funding the research?
The proposed trial was funded by the US government at a time of significant changes to vaccine policy under President Donald Trump and Health Secretary Kennedy.
Under Kennedy's leadership, a US vaccine panel attempted to end a longstanding recommendation that all newborns receive a hepatitis B vaccine at birth, but a federal judge later blocked this, along with other changes to vaccine policy made by the Trump administration.
Critics have questioned whether the research could help support that policy shift, although the study's stated aim was to investigate potential effects of the vaccine beyond preventing infection.
Kennedy has praised the Danish researchers as "the deities of vaccine research", and cited earlier findings from their work in support of concerns about vaccine safety. A subsequent study by some of the same researchers, however, found no evidence of the previously reported effect.
There is no evidence that the proposed trial was designed to justify a change in US policy.
