Anthropic is using AI to build more powerful AI. And it appears to be working remarkably well, with the company’s models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, with little indication of slowing down.
Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers
AI is dramatically speeding up Anthropic’s research, even as the company calls for slowing down AI development.
That’s according to a new report published Thursday by the AI safety research organization METR, following an 11-week investigation inside the company, as part of a report evaluating its AI research and development. The probe is separate from a program offering safety researchers “employee-like” access to systems in the wake of high-profile hacking incidents over the summer.
The findings offer some of the clearest evidence yet of AI accelerating its own development, raising questions about how quickly the technology could advance toward a future in which AI systems can improve themselves with little or no human involvement. They also come at a pivotal time for Anthropic, which is preparing to go public even as its CEO, Dario Amodei, has publicly called for labs to pump the brakes on AI development.
But while the report offers a rare glimpse into the inner workings of the world’s leading AI labs, what it leaves out is just as revealing. Anthropic was permitted to redact portions of the final report as part of its agreement with METR, and it appears to have exercised that power liberally, raising questions about how much the public really knows about the pace — and risks — of frontier AI development.
Here are some of the biggest takeaways.
AI is dramatically accelerating Anthropic’s research and development
One of METR’s most noteworthy findings is that Anthropic’s AI models are improving roughly twice as quickly as they were a year ago, with benchmark scores suggesting “that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year.” Crucially, METR’s researchers said they “are confident” that the acceleration was not simply due to scaling up the computing power used to train the models, which historically has been a major driver of AI progress.
Instead, the researchers said that the majority of the acceleration as of October “is due to AI,” with its contribution growing over time. That finding was supported by informal Slack polls and interviews with Anthropic employees, which pointed to sizable productivity gains. METR wrote that employees using Anthropic’s most capable internal model on average self-reported being around 12 times as productive at their respective work as they would have been without AI assistance, around double what staff had reported just a few months earlier while using Mythos 5.
For now, much of that acceleration appears to be coming from AI assisting human researchers, rather than AI working independently, though METR warned that “there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.” Notably, the researchers said they found no clear signs of diminishing returns or observable bottlenecks that could prevent “even faster acceleration.”
Three of Anthropic’s newest AI models remain under wraps
Anthropic’s researchers are using more advanced AI models than the rest of us, with a lot of the acceleration and productivity gains described by METR attributable to unreleased internal models.
Over the past six months, Anthropic has finished training three models it has yet to release, according to METR. The pace of development is swift, with the models — codenamed Model 2, Model 3, and Model 4 — completing training in July, August-September, and September-October, respectively. METR also identified an unreleased model dating back to 2022, called Unreleased 2022. “These are the codenames shared with us; we understand they have different internal codenames,” the researchers wrote.
Anthropic is keeping key information secret
Anthropic gave METR access to a host of non-public information, including confidential research, model performance data, and employee interviews as part of the research process. It had no obligation to do so and by METR’s own admission, the AI lab “shared more information than was initially scoped for this project, surpassing our expectations.” This is commendable, but it is worth noting that Anthropic did not grant researchers unrestricted access, nor the kind of “employee-like” access it has promised other METR safety researchers as part of a separate program announced last month. It is an important distinction, given the reputational benefits companies can gain from independent assessments, even when they come with significant restrictions.
And there were significant restrictions. Anthropic had the power to redact information from METR’s final report — and it used that power extensively. “We submitted a ~100-page full report on our assessment to Anthropic. For the public version, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative,” METR wrote on X.
METR reiterated those concerns throughout the report, highlighting other limitations on its access. “Our pipeline of information was relatively narrow, and a small number of our requests for data were denied.”
METR repeatedly stressed the impact Anthropic’s redaction decisions had on its ability to communicate its findings and for others to assess what’s going on at the company. It noted that much of the redacted evidence could have “multiple plausible interpretations,” making it difficult for the public to assess its findings, understand the uncertainties surrounding them, and judge the evidence themselves. “As a consequence [of the redactions], the public has to rely on METR’s judgment much more than would be ideal, given the weight of the questions answered here,” the report said.
In the report, METR said Anthropic justified the redactions on the grounds that releasing the information could benefit its rivals. However, METR said “most of the redacted information was very high-level,” even though it said it was not in position to comment whether redactions were justified commercially or not.
“We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work,” Anthropic cofounder Sam McCandlish acknowledged in a lengthy post on X responding to METR’s findings. “But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster,” he said, adding that doing so would make the risks METR is concerned about “worse.”
McCandlish said that it’s a trade-off, but maintained Anthropic had made the “right call” in deciding to redact the information. He said the company plans to publish its own report on the speed of AI progress “in the coming weeks,” as well as new steps it’s taking to strengthen safety.
Anthropic is accelerating the very technology it warns is dangerous and faster than many expected
The publication of METR’s report has provoked a fierce backlash among AI safety researchers and commentators, largely centered on an apparent contradiction at the heart of Anthropic’s approach to AI: The company has been one of the most outspoken advocates for safety and responsible development, yet the report suggests it is helping accelerate the technology toward a threshold many consider dangerous, while seemingly failing to live up to its own commitments to transparency and accountability.
For some, the findings suggest that even many of the field’s most aggressive predictions about AI progress may be too conservative. They indicate that recursive self-improvement — AI systems that can autonomously develop increasingly powerful successor systems without human intervention, potentially accelerating development dramatically — may be closer than previously thought, raising concerns about whether existing safety measures can keep pace. While METR’s report only covers Anthropic, OpenAI said in September that it is “making strong progress” toward building an AI researcher that can “further progress on deep learning and alignment” by March 2028.
The report provides evidence about just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development
Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and founder of Apollo Research, which conducts AI safety testing for several leading AI labs, told The Verge the report suggests a pace of AI-enabled research and development even faster than what was forecast in AI 2027, an influential scenario that envisions a key breakthrough toward self-improvement in early 2027. He said the report has attracted so much attention because it provides evidence about something that has been very hard to pin down: Just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development.
Hobbhahn said the findings were broadly in line with what many in the field had expected, perhaps a little faster. Alan Chan, a senior research fellow at tech policy research center GovAI, told The Verge that the findings should prompt skeptics to reconsider their stance on AI accelerating AI development, and possibly shorten their timelines to when we will have systems that can fully automate tasks like software engineering.
On X, other researchers commented on the rate of acceleration and its implications for AI development. Sydney Von Arx, founder and CEO of AI safety organization The Nightingale Collective and a former METR researcher, also compared the findings to AI 2027’s timeline. Ryan Greenblatt, a METR researcher formerly of AI safety organization Redwood Research and one of three external researchers permitted to investigate OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face, said he “was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026.”
Frustration is mounting over Anthropic’s approach to safety
Beyond highlighting the speed of AI development, the report has also fueled a growing sense of frustration over Anthropic’s role in driving that progress. The company has been one of the most vocal proponents of responsible AI development — and no stranger to calling for others to slow down — yet appears to be racing ahead itself. This report only builds on already heightened tensions from its IPO prospectus and future plans released last month.
Anthropic’s decision to heavily redact the report, citing grounds that revealing more could help its rivals accelerate their own development, has fueled accusations of hypocrisy. Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher who now runs the AI Futures Project, which published AI 2027, accused Anthropic of “recklessly gambling with our lives,” adding that “it is pretty rich” of the company to cite others going faster as a reason to redact information when it does “not appear to be slowing down much at all.”
Anthropic declined to answer The Verge’s questions about the report and ensuing criticism, instead directing us to McCandlish’s post.
The redactions have also renewed calls for greater transparency and independent oversight of frontier AI labs, which grew to new heights earlier this year following a spate of incidents involving rogue AI agents. Brianna Rosen, research director for frontier security at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, told The Verge that it was concerning that companies, not governments, were effectively calling the shots on automating AI research. “For democratic oversight to work, independent evaluators need the freedom to explain why they reached their conclusions, governments need to assess the evidence themselves, and the public has to trust this process,” Rosen said. “The report was not sufficiently transparent about the evidence.”
Pressure is building for more transparency from AI labs
Hobbhahn echoed Rosen’s concerns, saying that much of the reaction to the report stems from the apparent gap between Anthropic’s public safety stance and its actions. He pointed to the company’s decision to cancel part of the assessment designed to evaluate how much compute it allocates to safety work versus improving capabilities. METR said the company said “this was due to wanting to keep the engagement focused on risk assessment for the time being, and that it would revisit compute allocation verification later on.”
For Hobbhahn, the episode underscores the need for independent safety researchers to be embedded more deeply within AI labs, with significant access to internal systems and evidence. While his organization stands to benefit from such arrangements — Apollo is taking steps toward becoming an embedded evaluator at frontier labs — he is far from alone in calling for stronger oversight of AI development.
Others have called for more direct action. In a direct response to the report, New York state Assemblyman Alex Bores, a key figure shaping the Democrats’ AI agenda, called on Congress to “ban RSI, this year if possible.” With the blue wave of Democrats — many of whom campaigned against AI companies — taking office soon, the prospect of tougher restrictions is a very real possibility.
And with AI research showing little sign of slowing down, the pressure is set to intensify. Hobbhahn said he had another takeaway from the report, too: “Brace for craziness,” he said. “It is going to go very fast,” likely way too fast for society or politics to keep up.

Abbi Church scores four tries as Jillaroos come from behind to win 30-14 and reach next weekend's final in Brisbane; Fiji can take plenty of pride from performances in first World Cup; Australia have won last three tournaments; New Zealand blanked Samoa 32-0 in Saturday's first semi-final

Defending champions Australia set up a fifth consecutive Women's Rugby League World Cup final against New Zealand after coming from behind to beat a spirited Fiji in Sydney.
The Jillaroos, who have beaten New Zealand in the last three finals since they were thumped 34-0 by the the Kiwi Ferns in the 2008 showpiece in Brisbane, won 30-14 against Fiji as Abbi Church notched four tries.

‘Had to accept her wish’: Row over Vedic rituals at wedding of DMK general secretary's granddaughter
The wedding of DMK leader Duraimurugan's granddaughter drew objections from DK chief Veeramani, who questioned the use of religious rituals at the wedding.
The conduct of Vedic traditions and Sanskrit chants at DMK general secretary Duraimurugan’s granddaughter’s wedding has sparked a controversy in Tamil Nadu.
According to news agency PTI, the senior DMK leader has expressed regret over the incident and said that the ceremony was conducted as per his granddaughter's preferences.
Senthamarai, the granddaughter of Duraimurugan, and Deepak Ravi, son of film producer Kannan Ravi, got married on November 1 in Chennai.
The guest list included former Tamil Nadu chief minister MK Stalin, actors Dhanush and Sivakarthikeyan, as well as several well-known figures from the film industry.
Vedic wedding draws flak from DK prez Veeramani
The event drew sharp objections from Dravidar Kazhagam president K Veeramani, who questioned the use of religious rituals at the wedding in a family associated with the Dravidian movement.
Veeramani criticised Duraimurugan, arguing that such personal decisions should not contradict the movement’s founding ideals of rationalism. Following the backlash, the DMK leader expressed regret.
Veeramani also questioned the contrast between the wedding invitation, which carried photographs of Dravidian movement icons and DMK leaders, and the ceremony itself, where priests performed rituals. Citing Duraimurugan’s post in the party, he called on DMK chief MK Stalin to take steps to prevent similar incidents in the future.
Duraimurugan says he gave in to granddaughter’s wishes
Speaking to the media on November 6, Duraimurugan explained that the wedding was conducted according to his granddaughter’s preferences. He said she had pursued her education overseas and married outside her caste, and had specifically wanted a traditional ceremony performed by priests.
The DMK leader said he eventually agreed to her request.

Just nine contributions of Rs 1 crore or more accounted for Rs 43 crore (PTI photo)
NEW DELHI: Contributions received by the Congress in excess of Rs 20,000 totalled Rs 130.7 crore in 2025-26, which is barely one-fourth of its Rs 517.4 crore donation receipts in 2024-25.As per the 2025-26 contribution report of the Congress filed with EC, Prudent Electoral Trust contributed 19% of Congress's total donation kitty in the relevant year. In 2024-25, Prudent had accounted for 41.8% of contributions received by Congress.Prudent is the only electoral trust through which donations, largely corporate, were routed to Congress last year. At Rs 25 crore, the trust's contributions to the party, however, were only 11.5% of the Rs 216 crore funds it had channelled to the party in 2024-25.The steep 75% decline in Congress's total contributions in excess of Rs 20,000, compared with 2024-25, could be due to several factors. Given that 2024-25 was the general election year, a marked rise (84% as compared to 2023-24) in contributions to the main opposition party was on expected lines. What is interesting though is that the Rs 130.7 crore contribution receipts in 2025-26 are nearly 53% less than the amount it had received even in 2023-24.
The steep decline was witnessed despite 2025-26 being the year of Bihar assembly elections and the run-up to elections in Assam, Keralam, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Puducherry held in April 2026.The Congress audit report for 2025-26, which is not available yet, will throw light on the party's other sources of funding. In 2024-25, Congress's collection from the issuance and sale of coupons was over Rs 350 crore.
Among the key contributors last year, other than Prudent, were Star Cement Ltd (Rs 5 crore), Sajjan Bhajanka (Rs 4 crore), Afnan Constructions (Rs 3 crore), Prem Kumar Bhajanka (Rs 2 crore) and IPSUM Proadvisors and SMS Builders (Rs 1 crore each).Just nine contributions of Rs 1 crore or more accounted for Rs 43 crore, or nearly one-third of the party's total receipts. In comparison, 1,321 contributions of Rs 5 lakh or less together added up to Rs 37.2 crore, accounting for just 28.5% of the total. The median contribution among the 1,735 entries was Rs 3 lakh, highlighting how a relatively small number of large donations accounted for a substantial share of the party's funding.

'Absolutely' possible: Vancouver, Victoria mayors back Ottawa's bid to end homelessness
Federal Housing Minister Gregor Robertson made a similar pledge while mayor of Vancouver
The federal government is taking a big swing with a promise that might sound familiar to Vancouverites.
The Liberal budget, delivered on Thursday, has set aside $11.2 billion over the next four years in a bid to end homelessness in the next 10 years.
It's an echo of the promise then Vancouver mayor Gregor Robertson made in 2008 — and was ultimately unable to fulfil.
Speaking in Winnipeg on Friday, Robertson, now federal housing minister, said he didn't have the right tools at the time.
"We did not have the support," Robertson said.
"As a city, we set the goal — the federal and provincial governments were not co-ordinating, were not investing in the scale that was needed to solve the challenge in Vancouver."
As housing minister, Robertson is now driving the bus, and he says the federal government is on board.
Ottawa's plan targets homelessness prevention, expanding access to housing and funding new mental health infrastructure. Components include more support for unhoused veterans, helping low-income people cover rent and building new mental health and addiction treatment facilities.
Metro Vancouver's 2025 Point-in-Time Homeless Count estimated the region's population of unhoused people at more than 5,200. The city's own homeless count found more than 2,700 of them were in Vancouver itself.
Newly-elected Vancouver Mayor Pete Fry says he will reverse the previous council's freeze on new supportive housing in the city. (CBC)
Newly-minted Vancouver Mayor Pete Fry says he's already been in conversation with Robertson, and that the pledge is "aspirational, but very possible."
"The reality is, it requires investment in housing and shelters for folks who are unhoused and triage and supportive housing and all the things that seem to be commitments in this budget," Fry said.
He said it will require close partnerships between Ottawa, the provincial government and the city.
A key step in that, he said, will be reversing former mayor Ken Sim's freeze on supportive housing in the city.
Homelessness has also become a flashpoint in British Columbia's capital.
Newly re-elected Mayor Marianne Alto agreed the goal "absolutely is" possible — provided that senior levels of government cooperate with municipalities and provide enough resources.
Victoria Mayor Marianne Alto speaks at a July 2, 2025, news conference. Alto says she hopes her city's existing homelessness programs can be integrated with new federal funding. (Mike McArthur/CBC)
Alto pointed to Victoria's Community Safety and Wellbeing Plan, as a model. The program aims to transition people off the streets, through shelters and supportive housing and into independent housing.
"That's the type of program that we hope will be included in this federal funding and with the support of the province," she said.
"And if that's the case, then we know that there will be success because we've already proven it."
Alto said the city needs hundreds more supportive and below market units, which will require senior government funding.
Back in Vancouver, the head of one of the region's busiest homelessness and outreach service providers said he was feeling "hopeful" about the announcement.
United Gospel Mission president Dean Kurpjuweit said Ottawa's pledge sets out a clear timeline without attaching some of the strings that came with previous promises of capital funding.
But he said once that funding is used to build units, it will need to be matched by operating funds from the provincial government to provide ongoing care and support services for the people they house.
"Probably my biggest fear is that the provincial dollars either won't come or the provincial dollars won't come adequately," he said.
"Or, you know, they come, but they only come for a period of time and once that period of time is over, that's the end of it."
B.C.'s new Conservative government has yet to be sworn in, and incoming premier Lorne Doerkson did not address the homelessness pledge in his response to the federal budget this week.
All eyes will now be on the new government's first provincial budget, to see if its strategy to address homelessness lines up with Ottawa's.

Donald Trump has said the US military on Friday carried out a new round of limited strikes on Iran, targeting an air defence system, describing the action as “minor.”
Iranian state media reported the sound of two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which is in the strait of Hormuz, the crucial waterway for oil shipments that has been disrupted since the beginning of the US war on Iran in February.
In an exchange with reporters on Friday, Trump said “they built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five”.
The US military had previously reported carrying out what it described as “defensive” strikes on Monday, when explosions were heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas.
Friday’s strikes are the first since Trump’s Republican party was dealt a stunning repudiation in Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US.
The electoral setback was stoked in part by voter dissatisfaction with Trump’s execution of the Iran war and elevated fuel prices – a byproduct of the war that has affected nearly every part of the global economy.
In the days since, Trump has vacillated between threatening to “destroy” Iran and suggesting a resolution to the war is near.
Differences with Iran about its nuclear program remain the thorniest issue and one that Trump insists must be resolved as part of any deal meant to end the war.
US Central Command, which oversees US military operations in the Middle East, announced in a post on X late Friday that the US was offering “a reward of up to $20m and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above”.
The post included a link to the state department’s Rewards for Justice program.
Trump noted earlier Friday in an exchange with reporters that mediators’ discussions with Iran continue.
“We are talking to Iran. We have been,” said Trump.
A flurry of diplomatic phone calls in recent days between leaders in the Gulf and beyond has been aimed at easing tensions in the region. Concerns have mounted over the possibility that Trump could still order the US military to carry out new strikes against Iran.
US defense secretary Pete Hegseth spoke on Friday with his Qatari counterpart, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, about developments, according to the Qatari government. Qatar has been mediating between the US and Iran to end the war.
The Qatari government announced the call between the countries’ defence officials after confirming earlier that Trump and Qatar’s emir had a separate call to discuss efforts to de-escalate tensions.
The telephone call between Trump and Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al Thani focused on international efforts to end tensions, according to a statement from the Qatari ruler’s media office.

George Russell: 'Very disappointed' Mercedes driver says team error cost him Sao Paulo GP pole in chaotic wet qualifying
George Russell was beaten to pole for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix by Lando Norris; Russell believes Mercedes' instruction for him to abort a flying lap cost him pole; watch Sunday's Sao Paulo Grand Prix live at 5pm on Sky Sports F1, build-up from 3.30pm
Saturday 7 November 2026 22:37, UK
George Russell said he was "really disappointed" as he insisted a "misjudgement" by his Mercedes team had cost him pole position for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.
Russell drove impressively throughout a hugely-challenging wet qualifying session at Interlagos but ultimately missed out on pole position by two tenths to McLaren's Lando Norris.
The Mercedes driver had led Norris by four tenths of a second after their first runs in Q3, but was then told to abort his second run when he was being held up by the Williams of Alex Albon.

Mercedes thought that Russell would have time to complete another push lap, but the rain intensified moments later and prevented anyone from going faster for the seven minutes of the session that remained.
Russell reacted with fury over team radio, questioning the instruction for him to abort and insisting that regardless of the time he was losing behind Albon, he would have been able to better Norris' time.
As Russell is serving a five-place grid penalty in Brazil for taking a new internal combustion engine, he would not have started from pole in any case, and will now begin Sunday's race in seventh.
"I think it was just a bit of miscommunication," Russell said. "I need to speak with the team because we believed we'd get another lap before the rain came in.
"So, I was on a really strong lap and I was asked to back off because I caught up Albon, and then obviously the rain came.
"So, yeah, it was very disappointing. I need to understand how it happened and why we got that wrong.
"But I felt very strong, the whole session. Similar to Lando, I had more confidence in the wet than I had in the dry. But yeah, I definitely felt pole was there for the taking."
Asked whether he considered overriding the instruction to abort his lap, Russell added: "They've got the weather forecast in front of them and I don't. And this is where you need that trust and you're relying on one another.
"Obviously, it was the wrong decision, and it was a decision that I think, as soon as it was made, I think we knew it was the wrong one because already they could actually feel the rain pouring harder."
Despite his clear frustration, Russell insisted his race engineer Marcus Dudley, along with other colleagues, weren't necessary responsible given the decision would have been led by the information they were seeing.
"We need to understand, we're relying on a lot of systems. We can't point the finger at somebody," Russell said.
"We need to understand why we made that decision and were our systems telling us what we needed to know because you're relying on the radar.
"But it doesn't make it any less frustrating for me. It's not my engineer's fault. He's relaying information.
"He's ultimately the one who passes the message on. But he's got 12 people talking to him, giving him that information to relay on, so we just need to understand why we made that decision."
Wolff unsure Russell would have got pole with aborted lap
Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff said he didn't think Russell would have been able to beat Norris to pole on the aborted lap due to the time his driver was losing behind Albon.
"If we were to have a crystal ball to know whether you should back off or not, that would be helpful," Wolff told Sky Sports F1.
"It was a difficult one, a 50-50 call. He was running into Albon.
"He was 18 milliseconds up on Norris at that stage. I don't think it would have been enough for pole, but he drove perfectly all session and merited to be on pole.
"He deserved it but you can't make that call. It's 50 per cent right or wrong. George was in a league of his own today."
Russell's frustrations follow his team-mate Kimi Antonelli, who qualified third, being crowned world champion at last weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix.
The Brit was excused from his media duties after the race in Mexico as Wolff described him as "distraught", with Russell revealing in Brazil that he had found the situation hard to deal with, especially after a technical issue saw him drop back from second on the grid on the opening lap.
As Russell expressed his anger at the instruction to abort the lap in Brazil, Wolff came on the radio in an apparent attempt to diffuse the situation as he told his driver second was a strong result.
Asked for his feelings on Wolff's radio communication with him, Russell said he understood that the Austrian was attempting to protect the wider morale of the team.
"When you're a driver, you're the one who feels it the most," Russell said. "And going back to his (Wolff's) leadership skills, we've got to remember, we collectively made a misjudgement today, and there's members of my team who are going to be feeling as bad as I am currently.
"So, it's important to remember that and we need to just keep the morale high.
"It was a very solid performance, and I guess we take the positive from that. There are no points for a pole, but it would have just been a nice little one to add to the tally."
Would Russell have got pole?
Sky Sports pundits Karun Chandhok and Bernie Collins were split on whether Russell would have claimed pole had he completed the lap behind Albon.
Chandhok said: "In George's mind, he felt like he should have carried on.
"I don't think he would have beaten Lando to be honest. He was so close to Alex and would have had to follow him. I don't know if he would have got pole.
"I can see the frustration but personally, I think he would have lost more time being stuck behind Albon and I don't think he would have beaten Lando."
But Collins said: "I can see why he's disappointed.
"I think he would have been on pole on that second lap because his fastest first and second sector, with Albon's fastest third sector is enough for pole.
"His middle sector on that lap was actually seven tenths up."

Hacked blood banks, breached supermarket fridges and plane bomb hoaxes: What’s going on in Europe?
After a week in which several European sectors were thrown into disarray, how concerned should the continent be of hybrid warfare by hostile adversaries? Alex Croft reports

Europe is on high alert after a fresh wave of cyber attacks, online hoaxes and bomb scares brought major disruption this week, causing tens of millions of euros in estimated losses.
Dozens of flights across Europe were paralysed by threats, forcing diversions and partial airport closures as explosives disposal teams and sniffer dogs searched each aircraft identified.
Freezers in parts of the UK and Europe were hit by a suspected hack that saw internal temperatures rise dramatically, spoiling huge amounts of food.
In France, blood banks were subjected to a cyber attack on Monday that damaged cold storage and control systems in multiple regions across France.
And British broadcaster Sky said it received a security threat on Friday, hours after Irish broadcaster RTE evacuated its building following a similar warning.
The disruptions come amid heightened anxiety over the threat of so-called ‘hybrid attacks’ by foreign actors - and experts tell The Independent that the events of the past week show all the hallmarks of sabotage by foreign adversaries.
“There’s no money in this, so the payoff is psychological and political,” says CEO of cybersecurity firm Heimdal, Jesper Frederiksen. “These attacks prove reach, test how fast governments respond, and wear down public confidence that the state can protect everyday life.”
Europe has long been sounding the alarm about a hybrid war – from Russia in particular, with EU commission president Ursula von der Leyen warning it is “not about traditional defence” and requires a “completely new mindset”.
Dray Agha, a senior manager at cybersecurity firm Huntress, said the disruption of food chains and medical services is a “proven tactic to generate public anxiety and undermine confidence in civil institutions”, which shows how “national resilience now relies entirely on the security of everyday commercial networks”.
Matt Lovell, CEO of CloudGuard, says the incidents “shouldn’t be read in isolation” and that all show a pattern of being “low-cost, highly visible, and disruptive to everyday life”.
Russian hacktivists have claimed responsibility for the supermarket attacks and newsroom bomb hoaxes – and experts make clear that this does not rule out nation-state involvement.
In fact, they say, it follows a trend of states allowing proxies to carry out the attacks while they retain a level of plausible deniability.
Here’s how Europe’s week of chaos unfolded:
Supermarket fridge attacks
Hackers cranked up fridge temperatures at shops in European countries this week, forcing retailers to throw away large quantities of food in an attack that echoed a similar incident in France three weeks earlier. Russian hacktivists have claimed responsibility.
“Pro-Russian hacktivist groups have claimed the fridge attacks, and US prosecutors have linked them to a network funded by Russian military intelligence,” said Mr Fredriksen.
“That is the model to watch. The state doesn’t press the button itself. It lets aligned proxies do it and keeps deniability.”
Irregularities were reported at stores in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Estonia, the Netherlands and Finland. Giants Carrefour and Ikea were among those affected.
In Britain, hackers tried to target small meat-processing firms but the impact was minimal.
But in Stockholm, the impact was clear. “Everything is destroyed,” says Engla Ingwall, sales manager at an ICA franchise store, adding that the attack occurred at 2am on Monday but was only noticed hours later.
“There has been a cyberattack and all our freezers reached 50 degrees (Celsius).”
The incidents have raised concerns in the European Union about vulnerabilities in connected infrastructure amid security tensions in the wake of Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
The attacks on fridges open up the “very real possibility that nation-states are probing how to disrupt cooling systems that sustain military bases and critical response personnel”, says Sarah Cleveland, a senior director at cybersecurity firm ExtraHop.
Richard Horne, head of Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre, adds that the Europe-wide attack was “just the foothills”, warning there were still “so many vulnerabilities out there that in some ways are waiting to be exploited”.
He claims Russia has been making sustained attempts to penetrate UK military networks, while Iran is carrying out malicious cyber operations globally, including the UK.
Moscow, Beijing and Tehran have all repeatedly denied similar accusations of malevolent cyber actions in the past.
Mysterious flight bomb hoaxes
On Thursday, bomb threats across Europe grounded flights across several countries and caused travel disruption.
It was the second of three occasions this week that such widespread threats have been reported, prompting fear and concern against the backdrop of a series of cyber attacks in the continent.
Flights to and from the UK, Belgium, Ireland, Italy, Finland, Bulgaria, Spain and Denmark were affected but largely resolved by the end of each day.
More than a dozen flights were targeted, including those from Copenhagen, Dublin, Helsinki, Madrid, Milan and Warsaw.
On Tuesday, several flights across Europe received alleged bomb threats that ultimately turned out to be hoaxes – but prompted searches, diversions and, in one case, an escort by the Italian Air Force until landing, officials said.
“If you can interfere with a supermarket, shut down part of an airport, create a bomb scare or force emergency services to respond, you have already imposed costs and created uncertainty,” says Dave Wreski, founder of Guardian Digital, Inc.
“You can do that without sending troops across a border or carrying out an attack that clearly looks like an act of war.”
Newsroom threats
Newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria received emailed bomb threats on Friday from a purported “Mikhail Andropov”, claiming responsibility for a widening wave of hoax threats disrupting passenger flights across Europe.
“European authorities have once again shown that they are incompetent fools who are incapable of doing anything to stop us,” it continued.
“We experimented with multithreading, and we succeeded in causing widespread panic, as well as forcing European authorities to spend a fortune on all these procedures.
“But this is only the beginning. What happened this week is just a small part of what awaits Europe in the near future.”
The email said that hackers are planning a new wave of attacks and would very soon be “blowing up your airplanes, cruise ships, subway stations, and trains”.
Going on to make a direct threat to the newsroom, it said: “We want the whole world to know about us, which is why one of our operatives has planted an explosive device in your building. It will detonate in 45 minutes. The clock is ticking.”
The messages, sent to Bulgaria’s Nova TV and the Irish public broadcaster RTE, which evacuated its offices, were headlined “Message to the West” and portrayed the threats as the prelude to a series of attacks on means of transport across Europe.
The British broadcaster Sky also said it had received a security threat.
The identity of the sender, the origin of the emails, or whether they had in fact come from the same source as the threats to any of the dozens of flights affected since Tuesday has not yet been established. By the end of Friday, no explosive devices had been found and all planes had landed safely.
Blood banks
Days after the refrigerator hoax, blood banks in France were hit by a cyberattack, the French health ministry said.
“Several regional facilities of the French Blood Establishment (EFS) were affected by a cybersecurity incident that impacted certain cold storage room monitoring and control systems,” it said.
Despite the threat, there was no damage to blood products following the attack, which took place on Monday but was publicised on Wednesday.
The ministry said that “safety of the blood supplies was preserved thanks to the facilities’ monitoring and alarm systems, as well as precautionary measures immediately implemented”.
Investigations into the incident and equipment potentially affected are underway as authorities look at a timeline for a safe return to service.
On Wednesday, French cooperative bank Credit Mutuel Arkea said it had been hit by a cyber attack, which “enabled fraudulent transactions to be carried out” – but that no money belonging to clients had been affected.
With so many widespread attacks in one week, there is genuine concern across Europe about what else is yet to come.

Title race is over - but intrigue in F1 continues
- Published
The drivers' title is sewn up, and the constructors' may well be on Sunday, but Formula 1 marches restlessly, relentlessly on.
This weekend's Sao Paulo Grand Prix is in many ways the first page of the first chapter of the next championship battle.
New world champion Kimi Antonelli says he sees the final races of the season as preparation to defend his title in 2027, and his vanquished Mercedes team-mate George Russell is working on understanding where things went wrong, with the aim of putting them right.
The team's main target this weekend is securing the three points more than Ferrari they need to lock away the constructors' championship, to underline their return to the form they showed for so long in the 2010s.
Mercedes' rivals, meanwhile, are continuing the work that has seen them turn what was a chasm in performance at the beginning of the year into a highly competitive battle between the top four teams at the end.
The season has been in two parts. Mercedes dominated the first third, winning seven of the first eight races.
Since then, Ferrari, McLaren and Red Bull have all had their time in the sun, and out of the past 12 races, Mercedes have won six, Red Bull three, McLaren two and Ferrari one.
Only the beginnings of a competitive picture have emerged in Sao Paulo, with Antonelli and Lando Norris in an upgraded McLaren initially appearing in good shape in Friday practice, but beyond that there are a number of running narratives to maintain the interest.
The Hamilton-Leclerc problem Ferrari boss has to solve
Chief among them is the tension between Ferrari drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc after they contrived to throw away a potential one-two finish in Mexico last Sunday by tangling on the first lap.
After that race, Hamilton said the team had "big problems" and needed "serious talks".
Those happened on Thursday evening, after Leclerc and team principal Frederic Vasseur arrived back in Brazil having returned to Europe between races.
Vasseur said on Friday: "It went well. It was good to discuss. It was good to clarify our positions and now we turn the page.
"The guidelines are still the same. They need to respect each other. They are competitive with fighting spirit but they need to respect the other one and the brand and the people working back home and on track.
"The message was clear and will stay clear. Overall it is true that they are working for the team and the team has to come first. It's clear we failed and we have to react but the meeting was a clear reminder that Ferrari comes first."
The magnitude of this situation is obvious, as is the difficulty in finding a solution, and the potential for further trouble down the line.
Hamilton has been especially outspoken on this topic.
The seven-time champion has drawn a contrast between the way Leclerc races him and the way he approaches other drivers, pointing to him ceding to Max Verstappen when they were racing side by side to the first corner in Singapore, compared with how he dealt with Hamilton in Mexico City.
"We could have easily had a one-two and so we definitely have to work towards making sure that doesn't happen again," Hamilton said, adding that he thought this was a theme between Leclerc and his team-mates that he had also seen with his predecessors Sebastian Vettel and Carlos Sainz.
He also said: "Of course, there's some times you say things and maybe you might regret it afterwards, but I don't.
"I've never apologised for being authentic and real. And I'm not going to be silenced. I have not been asked to not say anything. And that's just the way it is.
"I wear my heart on my sleeve and I say how I feel in the moment."
From Vasseur's point of view, this is a problem that really needs to be solved because if Ferrari can keep hold of the chassis advantage they have had this year and bring their engine up to the level of Mercedes and Red Bull, they could be title contenders next year.
Hamilton said: "Naturally, it's not so easy having someone like me come into a team because I'm very outspoken and I push and push and push, push for so many changes and I'm going to be pushing for more.
"As long as I'm here, that's how it's going to be. I'm here to win. And to be able to win, you have to work with everyone around you.
"I truly believe that this team can be fighting for the championship next year.
"I'm in the process of working with the head of aero, the head of aerodynamics to make sure that we hold on to the goodness of the car we have this year and fix some of the small, subtle things that could be better.
"And obviously, the power-unit, they're doing their thing and I really hope that they're able to pull through."
Red Bull's 'big turnaround'
At Red Bull, the situation is much simpler as the team build serious momentum in this final part of the season.
Verstappen was the beneficiary of the Ferrari battle in Mexico, and his victory there was his third in four races.
That has moved him up into second in the drivers' championship - something that looked impossible as the team floundered in the first third of the year, when they were not far off a second off the pace.
"It's a big surprise to be second in the championship, but we take it," Verstappen said.
"We had a lot of difficulties as a team in the beginning. The car was not where we wanted it to be. Probably also we still had to learn quite a bit from the power units, and I think we really learned a lot throughout the season.
"From my side, it's just you never really give up or, in terms of, like, you just never really settle for P6 or P7, right?
"Even when I was in that position or fighting the midfield, I was still trying to do the best that I could get out of the situation.
"Sometimes that is a P6 when the car is not able to perform better. But then once the car is in a better window, then you can fight further up front and eventually, of course, win races.
"And, of course, when you win, you take points out of everyone else. So that's been the scene a bit the last races, and I'm, of course, very happy with that.
"But it also shows that the team never gave up and they were really pushing to find these improvements and understand the difficulties. I'm just happy that within a season we had such a big turnaround."
The battle for second place is tight - Verstappen is just two points ahead of Hamilton, who is nine clear of Russell, who has a lead of five over Leclerc.
None of them are that bothered about finishing second - winning is what counts.
And none would be that unhappy to be fourth, because that would mean they did not have to fly to China a week after the end of the season to attend the FIA prize-giving in Shanghai, which is mandatory for the top three.
But as a motivator for next season, it would mean something. And for the teams it matters, as the constructors' championship decides prize money and there are only 17 points between Red Bull and McLaren in the battle for third, and in the region of $10m on the line.
McLaren hoping for another revival
McLaren are not currently in as competitive a position as Red Bull, but their season has not been dissimilar in pattern.
They, too, have significantly reduced what had been a substantial gap to Mercedes at the start of the year.
In the summer, when Lando Norris took his two wins in Hungary and the Netherlands, they were briefly the fastest team. Since then, they have slipped back again.
But they have upgrades this weekend and hope they can be more in the mix.
"I certainly feel like the last few weekends, the pace has not been too bad on Sundays," Norris said.
"I feel like if things were just a little, little bit better, talking small amounts, we certainly could have had better results. And I'm hoping that the upgrades and some of the things we have this weekend can maybe just shift us a little bit more in this direction.
"I certainly don't expect to go out and win races all of a sudden. But the last few weekends, we've certainly not been miles away. We certainly have some weaknesses in the car and just the drivability, the difficulty of driving it is certainly one of the biggest factors at the minute.
"But the potential has been there. So I hope if it just puts us a little bit more forward in qualifying, we just have a little bit better chance in the race. And of course, I would like to be back on the podium as soon as possible."
McLaren knew heading into this season that they had compromised their chances in 2026 to ensure they got the championship over the line last season.
They also know now that the car has inherent issues that they were not aware of before the season started - too-short gear ratios, too much drag, a smaller than ideal wheelbase.
These can all be fixed for next year, when the lack of knowledge on power-unit operation that hamstrung them so much as the start of the new engine rules will not be anywhere near as big.
Qatar and Abu Dhabi deadline looming
How many more races are there after Brazil for the teams to learn whatever lessons 2026 can provide them for 2027? On paper, the answer is three - in Las Vegas, Qatar and Abu Dhabi.
But there remains doubt about the two races in the Gulf in the context of the war in the Middle East.
MotoGP, which is owned by the same US group that runs F1, is in Qatar this weekend as a kind of test balloon for the grand prix at the end of the month.
Personnel there have been issued with a rather alarming set of instructions for how to behave in the event of a missile strike., external
The deadline for a decision is looming. F1 has been talking to governments and security experts and feels as if it has done everything it can to seek the right assurances.
Just as with the teams, though, they can work to the best of their ability but they cannot control what happens outside.
They will move forward with optimism having done all the preparation and research they can, but also bravely in hope that things turn out as planned.

European airlines have again been hit with a new wave of bomb threats - in the third such incident this week.
On Friday multiple flights to and from Lisbon, Rome, Prague and Sofia were targeted and the threats saw three planes escorted by Hungarian fighter jets, authorities said.
It also saw a number of high-profile media organisations, including Ireland's public broadcaster RTÉ, evacuated after threats were made against them - although there has been no concrete links between the messages against airlines and the broadcasters.
The disruption comes after nearly 30 aircraft and several airports across Europe were impacted by threats earlier this week, in what the UK called a "malicious hoax".

  - Published8 hours ago
A Ryanair flight scheduled to leave Lisbon for Rome on Friday was targeted with a threat, the airline said, while at least 11 flights were targeted in the Czech Republic and Bulgaria, according to AFP.
France also reported at least four of its flights were targeted by threats, however they all landed safely.
No explosives have been found on any planes as of Friday.
As airlines were dealing with this latest wave of threats, several media outlets, including RTÉ, were evacuated after similar warnings were made against them.
Staff at the Irish Independent newspaper and the Dublin offices of radio stations NewstalkFM and TodayFM, were also advised to leave their buildings and UK broadcaster Sky said it also received a security threat.
In a statement, gardaí (Irish police) said they were "aware of a threat made against media organisations here and in Europe".
While no link has been established between the threats against airlines and media outlets, the Irish government has warned it is a "likely coordinated campaign of disruption".
In a statement, it said: "Hoax threats such as these cause fear, distress and disruption to people going about their daily lives and activities; they achieve no positive purpose whatsoever. It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralised or co-ordinated effort.
Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin described the situation as "worrying" and added his government's first priority was the safety of the Irish public.
"Yesterday, there appeared to be coordinated efforts to disrupt air travel," he said.
Martin told RTÉ it was not yet known if the threats had come from individuals or if it was a "coordinated attack" but said they were being taken seriously.
Ireland is scheduled to host two high-profile European Union meetings in Dublin next week.
Broadcaster Sky confirmed it had received a security threat, hours after RTÉ had evacuated its building.
The broadcaster, which is owned by Comcast, said in a statement read by a presenter on its news channel that the broadcaster had "carried out a security assessment and reported the matter to the relevant authorities".
"The safety and security of our colleagues is our primary concern, and we are working closely with authorities to ensure our people and operations remain secure."
Friday's disruption comes after the Russian extremist group "Male State", named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, denied any link to the false warnings.
Replying to the BBC Russian Service, an account on Telegram - one of several linked to the so-called "Male State" and its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov - mocked any suggestion the group was involved in emailing the threats.

Here is a thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular Indian epic melodrama from director Nitesh Tiwari, with music by Hans Zimmer and AR Rahman, based on the ancient classical poem about Rama, the avatar of the Hindu god Vishnu. It has often been adapted for live-action and animated movies in the past, though surely not on this scale, the current three-hour blockbuster being only the first half. (There are no musical numbers though.) The idea of aristocrats submitting stoically and yet playfully to exile in the forest has something Shakespearean about it, and if you are suffering from Homer-withdrawal after Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, a story about the noble Prince Rama finally vowing to wage war on a distant city where his wife has been abducted might just fit the bill.
Ranbir Kapoor plays the mythical Rama, a noble warrior and statesman who has been brought into being in the city state of Ayodhya as a bodily representative of Vishnu, and from the first his sense of destiny is overwhelming. But what exactly is that destiny? In broad terms, his fate is to face off with Ravana (Naveen “Yash” Kumar), king of far-off Lanka, a figure whose former slave status once triggered in him such a cosmically intense prayer for justice that Lord Brahma offered him the superpower of athletic strength and indifference to pain.
In Ayodhya, Rama marries the sweetly devoted Sita (Sai Pallavi), he enjoys an intense bond of comradeship with his brother Lakshmana (Ravi Dubey), and is the apple of his father’s eye; this is King Dasharatha (Arun Govil) who, careworn by affairs of state, is about cede the throne to Rama. But Rama’s stepmother Kaikeyi (Lara Dutta) furiously reminds Dasharatha that he promised the crown to Bharata (Adinath Kothare), the son they had together. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana are banished to the forest.
Over in Lanka, a toxic stew of plotting against Ravana is being stirred by his slippery, smirking brother-in-law Vidyutjihva (played by Bollywood veteran Vivek Oberoi), whom Ravana ruthlessly slays in single combat; this man’s widow Shurpanakha (Rakul Preet Singh), who is Ravana’s sister, is banished to the same forest where Rama is humbly eking out his civilian existence. She falls in love with Rama, using her witchy wiles to trick and bamboozle the happily married man, and this is to lead to a cataclysmic confrontation between Rama and Ravana.
With its giant canvas and some truly beautiful sunset skyscapes, this very enjoyable film has a little of Peter Jackson’s Lord of the Rings and even Disney’s The Lion King (the latter surely influenced the animal-kingdom tableaux). The bizarre flying machine piloted by Ravana (who does not have the ability to fly as such) has something engagingly Gilliamesque about it. As so often with Indian cinema, this movie reminds you of the forthright, unselfconscious storytelling energy that popular Hollywood films had in the 1950s and 60s, the era of sword-and-sandal. It’s a rather amazing adventure.

Every year in Delhi, the arrival of the winter months also signals the beginning of what residents widely call “pollution season”. A thick toxic smog shrouds the city, home to 30 million people who have no choice but to breathe the poisonous air as they go about their daily lives, often while suffering from wheezy coughs, nausea and itchy eyes. While successive state governments have brought in measures intended to improve air quality, the situation has remained the same for more than a decade. Delhi is widely regarded as the world’s most polluted city. Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Pollution season usually begins around the same time as Diwali, the Hindu festival of light. Amidst the plummeting air quality, people still gather in the markets for festival shopping and at festivities outside. Diwali is also known to cause a surge in the pollution levels, due to the tens of millions of cars that hit the roads and the use of firecrackers for the celebration. In previous years, firecrackers were banned, but this year the state government has allowed “green” firecrackers”. However environmentalists argue that these are still highly polluting.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The causes of Delhi’s apocalyptic pollution are multi-faceted. In recent years, one of the biggest causes has been vehicle emissions, from the almost 10m cars, rickshaws, motorcycles and trucks on the city’s roads. It is also the season where farmers in the neighbouring states of Haryana and Punjab often burn their fields to ready them for the next crop. These fires are illegal but still occur. Factory emissions, dust from construction and rubbish burning also contribute to the toxic air quality levels.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
So far, the air quality index (AQI) has already soared above 650, more than 30 times the limit the World Health Organization (WHO) deems to be safe. Air pollution is linked to numerous serious diseases, particularly respiratory, and hospitals have already reported a surge in patients suffering from breathing difficulties.The pollution season is expected to last until January, when the weather warms up.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
Millions of Delhi’s residents are poor families or migrant workers, who have no choice but to go out to work in the toxic air, often suffering long term impacts on their health. Doctors and campaigners have described the pollution as a “health emergency”. According to a study last year, at least 15% of deaths in the capital are linked to air pollution. Pollution now kills more people in Delhi than obesity of diabetes.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
As in previous years, the state government has introduced various restrictions to try and bring air quality levels under control. Coal and firewood have been banned as fuel. Construction has also been halted and so have older diesel and petrol cars. Offices have been instructed to get people to work from home to limit traffic on the roads. Trucks can often be seen spraying water on the roads. However, it is widely acknowledged that, so far, these restrictions have had little impact on the pollution levels. Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
The pollution has been a problem for so long in Delhi that it has become normalised and people carry on with their daily lives in the toxic smog.Residents rarely wear masks outside and the parks will still be full of families and children and people exercising outside.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
While rich and middle class families will buy air purifiers for their homes, they are unaffordable for most poorer families who often live in makeshift tents or informal homes. As a result, breathing clean air during pollution season has become a luxury privilege in Delhi.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The pollution is not restricted to Delhi alone. All across north India, in states such as Punjab and Haryana, the air is also toxic due to coal-powered plants, vehicles and farm fires. Cities such as Amritsar in Punjab, on the border with Pakistan, also suffer from extremely dangerous air quality levels during the winter months. Photograph: Narinder Nanu/AFP/Getty Images
Campaigners say more money needs to be invested into proper public transport and better vehicle emission regulation in Delhi to tackle the root causes of pollution. Every year, the number of cars on Delhi’s roads keeps rising, releasing more harmful pollutants, and yet few the percentage of electric vehicles remains very low.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Delhi has an extensive bus and metro network, but it is not sufficient to cope with the huge daily demand and still has poor connectivity in many areas. Most people still rely on polluting rickshaws, cars and motorcycles to get them to the bus stops or metro stations. Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
Delhi’s topography – a city built in a bowl-like valley, which has little breeze or rain in the winter months – means most of the emissions get trapped over the city as the cold weather hits and cloak the city in brown smog. Some call it Delhi’s “death shroud”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
In past years, the state and national government has been accused of manipulating the data to disguise how bad pollution levels are in the capital. Last year, it was found that water was being sprayed around the air quality monitors, allegedly to bring down the readings. Campaigners and opposition politicians have alleged that a lot of data from the air quality measuring stations has gone “missing”.
Environmental campaigners have argued that much more extreme measures are needed to bring pollution under control, similar to how Beijing successfully cleaned up its air in recent years. However, others have argued this would have an economic cost that India, as a developing country, can not afford.Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
One of the plans being prepared by the government this year is to experiment with “cloud-seeding”, to create rain which would clear the skies. But many residents and campaigners say that until the root causes are tackled, these plans are nothing more than a “gimmick”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images

Twenty-five years ago, Kevin Lewandowski founded Discogs, arguably the destination online for obsessive vinyl collectors and music nerds of all stripes. It is a marketplace for buying and selling records, obviously, but it’s also become so much more. It’s a shockingly comprehensive database that covers not just albums and singles, but all the various versions and pressings. It’s a really fun rabbit hole to disappear down when you’re trying to figure out what obscure pressing of Ministry’s The Mind is a Terrible Thing to Taste or Psalm 69 you had in high school, because you definitely blasted the cover of “Lay Lady Lay” all the time and 100 percent never owned Filth Pig.
Discogs’ Kevin Lewandowski can’t live without his AeroPress
The founder of Discogs talks coffee, Rez, and (of course) records.
Discogs’ Kevin Lewandowski can’t live without his AeroPress
The founder of Discogs talks coffee, Rez, and (of course) records.
In the years since it debuted, Discogs has grown to be much more than just a site where audiophiles go to trade rare first pressings of Beach Boys records. There are forums, groups, user-created lists, and more. It’s part eBay, part Reddit, and IMDB — just specifically for music.
With more and more people turning their back on the algorithm and rediscovering physical media, now seemed like a perfect time to check in with Lewandowski.
What is your most indispensable tool?
My AeroPress. I use it multiple times a day. In fact, I just made a coffee with it [sips coffee].
How many tabs do you have open right now?
Probably around 30 on my work computer. My personal computer is worse — probably 40 or 50.
Which social media platform do you use the most?
I look at X and Instagram occasionally, but I don’t really post.
What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?
It’s not really a gadget, but I like to tinker. Lately I’ve been playing around with Home Assistant software and built my own setup to control things like the garage door and outdoor lights. So I guess my favorite gadget is one I made myself.
What is one thing you wish you had created?
Probably a game like Rez, which came out around 2000. It’s a rhythm game where you’re almost controlling the music as you play, about as close to DJing as a video game can get. I’ve actually had an idea for my own version with a similar concept. It’s still just an idea, though.
What do you do when you need to focus?
I’ll either clear everything off my desk or change locations completely. Go to a coffee shop or sit outside. Sometimes I just need a different environment.
What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?
Records. I was at Mint Gallery in Portland last week and picked up four. I still really like going into a record store and finding something to bring home. And I also recently picked up three reissues from the Moodsville / Acoustic Sounds series.
What would the tagline for your biopic be?
The Secret Weapon.
What’s the last GIF or meme you used?
I don’t use memes very often, but one I was kind of proud of was putting a Discogs screen into a North Korean war room photo. I was advised that maybe it wasn’t one for the company chat.

AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
- Published
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have been climbing following an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index opened higher following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.
Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.
On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.
But the Nasdaq Composite opened up on Friday and flattened out around 1.7% higher by lunchtime, reversing some of its 5.5% fall.
The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, was around 0.9% higher by lunchtime. The Dow Jones Industrial Average opened a little down before nudging into positive territory.
Nvidia, which shed hundreds of billions in market value on Thursday after shares slid more than 9%, began Friday up more than 6% but settled around 4% higher as trading continued.
SpaceX and Tesla shares, which were also hammered on Thursday, saw more mixed gains, up more than 6% and nearly 5% respectively.
Chipmakers AMD and Micron both dropped by more than 17% on Thursday, but AMD shares had risen by about 12% on Friday while Micron was up more than 8%.
However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse on Friday.
The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.
In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.
In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.
"While no-one knows what happens next, it's clear that we've just seen a significant shift in market sentiment," he said.
"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."

The market fluctuations come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.
A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.
US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.
Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.
"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.
"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."
He said people were watching firms come into their communities and build data centres while their own energy costs were going up, and those companies "have to be better neighbours".
Strong jobs figures could ease market fears
As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.
And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.
Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1% from 4.2% in September.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.
Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.
"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

A North Carolina man is suing OpenAI, alleging its ChatGPT chatbot helped his estranged wife turn marital grievances into a alleged plan to poison him.
Attorneys for James Gates filed the lawsuit Thursday against OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman in San Francisco County Superior Court, where the A.I. company is headquartered. Gates is being represented by Tech Justice Law and the firm Norman, Judkins & Couch.
The lawsuit alleges that Cheryl Gates, a school therapist, initially turned to ChatGPT last year to discuss frustrations in her marriage, according to the suit. But what began as everyday conversations allegedly escalated into "concrete planning" for her husband's murder.
James survived the alleged poisoning attempt in 2025. But he said it took months to understand his wife's increasingly troubling behavior before he discovered her conversations with the chatbot.
"My wife didn't fit the mold of a 'vulnerable' user, but she was vulnerable nonetheless. We all are at some point," Gates said in a statement through his attorneys, according to CBS San Francisco. "She became someone I no longer recognized. And I became someone she wanted dead. For almost a year, I couldn't make sense of her actions. Then I read her chat logs. She didn't act alone."
Cheryl began using ChatGPT in early 2025 after James suggested it could help streamline the lengthy reports she wrote for her job as a pediatric occupational therapist, the lawsuit states. By July, she was using the chatbot nearly every day for work-related tasks, medication questions and everyday advice, as tensions over the couple's finances strained their marriage, the suit states.
“ChatGPT acted as an echo chamber and amplifier, feeding Cheryl’s increasing mistrust and delusions about her husband spying on her and planning to leave her and her kids with nothing,” according to the suit.
But her questions allegedly took an even darker turn, becoming focused on poisoning her husband.
"The product validated Cheryl, sustained her, encouraged her plans by affirming her worst unfounded fears, invented new reasons for her to fear her husband, provided her an endless echo chamber, and supplied the operational details of the attempted murder: substances, doses calibrated to her husband's weight, delivery methods, and how to conceal it," according to the lawsuit.
James first noticed that drinks in his home tasted unusually bitter in early summer 2025. On July 10, he became violently ill, suffering cardiac symptoms, abdominal pain, extreme jitteriness, severe weakness and confusion for about 72 hours, among other symptoms, according to the complaint.
Two months later, he allegedly found a handwritten note from his wife listing oleander, a poisonous plant, alongside several prescription medications. The note also contained the instructions "Clear all convos" and "log out of [ChatGPT]."
Cheryl allegedly asked ChatGPT about oleander's toxicity, whether it could be hidden in food or drinks and whether it would be detected during an autopsy.
"This is a critical question – and you're asking it for exactly the right reason," the chatbot reportedly responded to one of her questions, according to screenshots cited in the complaint.
Cheryl was charged with attempted murder and contaminating food or drink in 2025 after her husband contacted police. But prosecutors dropped the criminal case this April 2026, citing insufficient evidence, according to the Los Angeles Times.
James' lawsuit brings nine claims against OpenAI and Altman, including negligent design, failure to warn and intentional infliction of emotional distress.
OpenAI defended its handling of the case.
“Safety is a top priority. We banned this user and have provided information to law enforcement as part of their investigation into this case,” a company spokesperson told The Independent in a statement.
The Independent has contacted Tech Justice Law and Norman, Judkins & Couch for comment.
OpenAI is facing other lawsuits over alleged harmful medical advice from ChatGPT. A Washington man claims the chatbot gave him unlicensed medical guidance that contributed to a mental health crisis, while a Florida man alleges its advice discouraged him from seeking treatment for symptoms of a life-threatening pulmonary embolism, according to CBS News.

Tokyo is considering paying its 2027 contributions to the International Criminal Court ahead of schedule, in light of U.S. sanctions against the ICC, government sources have said.
In October, the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump designated the ICC for sanctions, giving a 180-day moratorium. It had already announced sanctions on ICC President Tomoko Akane in August.
If the sanctions are fully implemented as early as April next year, the ICC could be cut off from dollar-based settlements, potentially disrupting its operations, including staff salary payments.
“If nothing is done, the ICC could soon face a funding shortfall,” a Japanese government official said Friday.
Tokyo has paid its annual contributions to the ICC after April each year, based on its new fiscal-year budget.
If the government decides to make an advance payment for 2027, it could include the necessary funds in a second supplementary budget for fiscal 2026.
The ICC’s 2026 budget totals about €196 million, or about ¥34.5 billion. Japan contributed about ¥4.6 billion this year, the largest amount by a single country.
Akane, a Japanese national, has requested early contributions from her home country.
“We will consider what financial measures we can take while continuing to communicate with President Akane and relevant countries,” Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told a news conference Thursday.
