You’re going to hate shopping in an AI economy
Why AI agents will make the “rage economy” worse.
If you’re like most Americans, the answer is “probably not very well.” And that may be understating it: As of 2025, according to the “National Customer Rage Survey” — yes, it’s a real thing — nearly 80 percent of Americans ran into a “product or service problem” in the past year, and nearly two-thirds experienced “rage” in attempting to resolve it.
We have, in short, entered into a rage economy, where high prices and inflation have made everyday products unaffordable at the same time as our experiences buying those products have filled us with fury.
The landscape isn’t really improving, either: As a consumer, you’re faced with terrible customer service, unhelpful chatbots, and products that are worse than they used to be.
If you listen to the big AI companies, however, there’s a light on the horizon: AI agents, which can step in and do the things you don’t want to (like waiting on hold or dueling it out with aforementioned unhelpful chatbots). But are AI agents really the key to fixing our rage economy? Or will they just be what brings it deeper into chaos?
Charlie Warzel, a staff writer at The Atlantic, recently went deep on what happens when we bring AI agents into our already contentious consumer experience (along with his colleague Matteo Wong).
Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with Warzel about how AI agents are being used for the grating parts of our lives, what happens when companies use their own AI agents to deal with consumers, and where this all might leave us.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
Charlie, we spoke about how the economy and how customer service works is making everyone rage out. Are AI agents going to make it better or worse?
In the early time, it’s probably going to make it a lot worse. What we are essentially seeing right now is that these agents are inundating the internet with persistence.
These are relentless things that are tasked to do the onerous activities that we don’t want to do. And they’re already flooding call centers. They’re flooding restaurant reservations. They’re flooding plumbers and people who run small businesses with requests and queries. And they’re not people.
It’s going to make a lot of people feel, honestly, pretty awful. The world has all of a sudden become very inhuman or there are these inhuman burdens being put on the humans who don’t have agents yet to work on their behalf. And that imbalance is going to make a lot of people pretty mad.
You wrote for The Atlantic that we are not ready for our coming AI agent future. How are we not ready for this?
If it reaches a critical mass, the argument is that we aren’t ready for it because the economy is built off of, and in a lot of ways thrives off of, inefficiency — off of the fact that people aren’t paying perfect attention to everything.
People aren’t moving their money from savings account to savings account every day because they’re getting the margins on a slightly better interest rate or something like that. This entire subscription economy is based off of inefficiency. You don’t cancel the thing that you don’t use for a long period of time or it lays dormant for a while.
But what these AI agents offer in their most idealized fashion is that they pay perfect attention to everything, all the time. They are hypervigilant and able to act on your behalf in inhuman ways. And if a large portion of the population is using these to do their banking, to do their e-commerce, and at the same time you have these large organizations like banks, healthcare companies, platforms like Amazon and Walmart, you’re going to see just incredible amounts of chaos.
The economy would, in that way, start to behave more like the stock market, where prices fluctuate on the order of milliseconds. And from watching the stock market over decades, I don’t know if we want diapers to behave like securities.
One of the more speculative but also illustrative ideas here is what people refer to as an agentic bank run. This is the idea that, say, 5 million people are using the same agent to do all of their banking and they all identify at the same time that there is a high-yield savings account that everyone should be in. So they move money en masse: millions of agents pulling money out of one account to the next, and then those banks are struggling because they’ve just lost all of these deposits at once. It’s theoretically possible that something like that could happen all of the time.
Is this a two-way street? Are the companies also adopting agents into every part of their processes and consumer relations?
Yes. It’s slower on that end, but I like to think of this as an arms race.
A lot of retailers, especially Amazon, have blocked a number of these agents from accessing their platform. Because even though Amazon can make good money off of these sales, they don’t yet want these companies to have access to their backend infrastructure.
There are a lot of corporate secrets like inventory and who’s buying what and who’s selling what. These agents can act as really good intelligence gatherers if they’re granted access to these platforms.
What you’ll see eventually is that the retailers are going to have demands: “You guys can let the agents on the platform, but you can’t undercut our prices in this way.” It will just be something that you have to trust that your AI agent company is making a deal in your best interest.
I think that that’s really interesting because you could end up having this future where everything feels really good as a consumer because it’s frictionless: “My agent’s going to do all this stuff for me while I sleep or while I’m hanging out with my family or whatnot.” And in reality, what’s going to happen is you’re just having someone do something for you, but nothing else has really changed. You’re not getting a better deal. It’s not that much more helpful to you because these companies have taken care of themselves first.
But that is the promise. That is what Sam Altman and Mark Zuckerberg are trying to sell us.
Do you think it’s a pipe dream or do you think there is some reality, one day, when we as a society will say, “This consumer-facing AI agent world of ours is better than the one we had a hundred years ago”?
Something that I think is really funny is Meta, with Muse, has really dominated the conversation about these AI assistants. And this is the company that wanted to connect the world, that says that us being together is this universal good, it is strengthening the bonds of humanity.
This is a tool that is fundamentally antisocial. You don’t have to interact with those people if you don’t want to. I’m not trying to romanticize running really annoying errands when you’re busy and your kids are sick and you’ve got work deadlines and things, but there’s also the experience of interacting with people on a day-to-day basis that is foundational to our humanity and these things basically want to automate that away.
That’s a real thing that we need to think about and grapple with. And the other part of this is, what are we freeing this time up for?
I’m always wondering that myself, because that’s what they keep promising. You’re going to have so much time…to do what? To then just spend more time scrolling your platforms?
To spend more time scrolling your platforms, spend more time working. There is a lack of thought about what a human is for if we fully embrace automation in all these different ways, right? It’s one thing to say, “I wish it was easier to buy paper towels on Amazon.” It’s another to say—
It’s pretty easy, though. I don’t do it that often, but I’m pretty sure it’s really easy.
It is. I think it’s good to have those interactions and it’s okay to sand down some of them, but this future suggests, what if you never had to do anything you didn’t want to do? And I don’t know if they’ve thought that through.

Trillions of bacteria living in the human gut may play a role in Parkinson’s disease, a brain disorder that causes tremors, stiffness, and slowed movement, according to a new study involving patients from Keralam.
Researchers from the Cochin University of Science and Technology (CUSAT) and the Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences and Technology (SCTIMST), Thiruvananthapuram, found significant differences between the gut bacteria of Parkinson’s patients and those of healthy individuals. The findings were published online in npj Parkinson’s Disease, an international scientific journal.
Parkinson’s disease occurs when nerve cells in the brain that produce dopamine, a chemical that helps control movement, gradually die. Scientists have long suspected that the gut and brain communicate continuously, and that an imbalance in gut bacteria could contribute to inflammation affecting the brain. Studies have shown that non-motor symptoms, including constipation and other gastrointestinal problems, can appear years before the tremors begin in Parkinson’s patients.
The study involved 65 Parkinson’s patients attending SCTIMST’s Comprehensive Care Centre for Movement Disorders and 65 healthy individuals, most of whom were the patients’ spouses. Spouses were included as healthy individuals for comparison, as they were more likely to share similar diets and living conditions.
Metagenomic sequencing
Researchers analysed stool samples using metagenomic sequencing (16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing), a technique that identifies the bacteria present and helps assess their potential functions in the gut. They found higher levels of bacteria potentially associated with inflammation and lower levels of beneficial bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids, which help maintain the gut lining healthy and regulate the immune system, in Parkinson’s patients.
The researchers suggest that the shift in bacterial communities could weaken the gut barrier and allow inflammation to spread.
“The study found that differences in the abundances of these bacteria were strongly associated with disease severity and other clinical features of Parkinson’s disease,” said Baby Chakrapani P. S., director of the Centre for Neuroscience and assistant professor in the Department of Biotechnology at CUSAT. “The findings also suggest that gut bacteria may be linked to disease progression through their influence on processes involving dopamine, glutamate, and GABA, chemicals that play important roles in brain function.”
Funded by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), the study was conducted by Aneesa P. A., a research associate at CUSAT, under the supervision of Mr. Chakrapani and Dr. Syam Krishnan of SCTIMST.
Gut bacterial composition is influenced by factors such as diet, age, sex, and lifestyle. Differences in these factors, as well as genetics, could explain why studies in different populations have reported inconsistent associations between particular bacteria and Parkinson’s disease.
According to the researchers, this is the first study in an Indian population to integrate gut microbiome composition with its functional role in Parkinson’s disease. The findings could help future research into simple tests for early diagnosis of the disease and treatments aimed at restoring gut health.

Russell Brand's convictions renew spotlight on media — and a culture — that may have looked away
Russell Brand's convictions this week for rape and sexual assault have renewed scrutiny on the BBC and other media employers that may have looked the other way
LONDON -- For three straight years while he worked at BBC radio stations, Russell Brand was awarded a notable distinction by The Sun, Britain’s largest tabloid: “Shagger of the Year.”
It was, of course, in perfect alignment with the bad-lad image Brand cultivated that rode a thin line between outrageous and offensive, as he became one of Britain’s most famous comedians.
Brand’s convictions Thursday for rape and sexual assault have turned a spotlight back on the BBC and other media employers, renewing questions about whether bosses enabled his behavior or chose to look away. They also highlighted the ways in which his excesses were overlooked by the culture at large.
“When Brand was at his most famous, his wrongdoings were indulged or ignored by his employers and, to be fair, the public too,” Ann Olivarius, an attorney specializing in sexual misconduct, said in an email message.
The BBC apologized last year for a culture of silence that, it said, prevented staff from complaining about Brand’s behavior at its radio stations between 2006 and 2008 because they felt he was too powerful.
It reiterated that apology after his conviction.
“It was of great concern to us that some people felt unable to raise concerns about Brand’s behavior,” the BBC said Thursday in a statement. “We apologized to those impacted, for both the culture and failings at the time.”
Britain’s public broadcaster had launched the internal probe after The Times and Channel 4, in a joint investigation, aired accusations in 2023 from women who said they had been sexually abused and degraded by Brand.
The resulting articles and documentary brought women forward who provided the evidence that led to his conviction. But it was no secret Brand had misbehaved during his time as a shock jock at the BBC or TV host at Channel 4. He wrote in a memoir, for example, about how he had sex in radio-station handicapped bathrooms with contestant winners from the BBC station 6 Music.
“Nobody ever mistook Russell Brand for a Boy Scout,” said Allen Adamson, co-founder of marketing consultancy Metaforce. “His brand was R-rated from Day One."
The 51-year-old was convicted Thursday of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault involving multiple women. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault. He faces sentencing Monday.
Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy of London’s Metropolitan Police called the conviction “a testament to the extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them.”
“Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women,” Furphy said. “As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement.”
Of the eight complaints the BBC investigated, only one — that Brand had urinated in a cup in front of staff — had been made formally during his time at the stations. The review found it was “not dealt with effectively.”
In his second memoir, “My Booky Wook 2,” Brand spoke of how “incredibly tolerant” Lesley Douglas, the Radio 2 controller at the time, was about his behavior and that he took advantage of the “lots of room” she gave him.
He acknowledged going “too far,” though, when he claimed, on air, that he would be under the desk performing an intimate act with a female newsreader while she was reading the headlines.
The newsreader “was a bit upset,” he said.
Liz Kershaw, a longtime BBC radio DJ, wrote in The Telegraph on Thursday that she had complained since 2006 to BBC management about how Brand’s behavior was tolerated.
“Brand was a creation of some of the most powerful players in the media,” Kershaw wrote. “They were in his thrall. And he was egged on. He was their performing monkey. He made ‘great telly.’ His colleagues were collateral damage.”
In 2008, Brand finally went too far during an on-air prank and had to resign. Brand phoned actor Andrew Sachs, best known for the 1970s program, “Fawlty Towers,” and left a message claiming to have had sex (he used an expletive) with his granddaughter.
Brand resigned from Radio 2 and Britain’s broadcast regulator hit the BBC with a record fine of 150,000 pounds, the equivalent of $219,000 at the time.
While a Channel 4 documentary helped bring down Brand, the broadcaster was also connected to one of the criminal charges at trial from his days as a TV host there. Channel 4 apologized in 2024 to a former employee after an internal review found it had not investigated a serious complaint a staffer made against him in 2009.
Brand was convicted Thursday of sexually assaulting a former employee while working on a project for the channel in 2009. The staffer testified that two members of Brand’s entourage had asked her to give Brand a massage and then watched and laughed as the comic put his head into her crotch.
One of Brand’s associates, Jack Bayles, did not testify but said in a statement that he did not recall the incident but was sorry for missing something at the time or failing to recognize the distress it caused.
“I was in the early stages of my career, and it was a frantic, pressured and toxic working environment,” Bayles said. “Brand was chaotic, dismissive and manipulated the people around him.”
He said he stopped working with Brand in 2010 and had not been in touch with him since.
Some analysts noted that it was precisely Brand’s outrageous image that may have protected him from suspicion of criminal activity.
Adamson, the marketing consultant, noted “the sex, the drugs, the open shirt, the leer" that defined Brand. “That is exactly why the behavior never registered as a warning sign; it was him marketing his brand,” he said.
Blame goes also to the media at the time, Adamson noted. “The media did not just cover the persona — they co-authored it. When a national newspaper hands you a trophy three years running for sleeping around, you are not hiding anything. You’re building your brand."
Attorney and anti-misogyny activist Cheyenne Hunt noted that Brand’s raunchy behavior almost served as a pre-emptive defense.
Someone like Brand "is trying to create a persona such that if someone comes forward, there is this ... defense available to them, that is, ‘Well, what did you THINK was going to happen?’" Hunt said.
The role that comedy played was also key, said Hunt, who leads the group Reckoning Action, which she founded after her role in exposing sexual misconduct allegations against U.S. politicians Eric Swalwell and Graham Platner.
“I tell people to beware of the clown and beware of the jester,” Hunt said. “Because it makes their behavior appear as though they’re joking or like it’s some kind of absurdist comedy, and folks don’t take them literally. But what they’re doing is building a permission structure to do exactly what they’re telling you they’re going to do.”
"And that is very much Russell Brand’s MO, and I think he learned from many other folks who have the same playbook.”

European air traffic is targeted by new threats after a week of hoaxes
BERLIN — Officials across Europe reported a fresh slew of bomb threats against multiple flights on Friday, following a string of hoaxes that have caused flight diversions this week. Two broadcasters also received security threats.
No suspicious items were found and no one was injured, but the threats have raised concern because they came as Europe digests other recent disruptions — including attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems and drone incursions.
Overall, the threats have caused minimal disruption to aviation across the continent, according to the European air traffic authority. Eurocontrol said it was aware of bomb threats against 14 flights on Thursday — only 0.05% of all of the nearly 26,300 flights across the European network that day — and seven on Tuesday.
In Hungary, the defense minister said military fighter jets escorted three separate passenger planes Friday across the country's airspace within an hour after each received bomb threats. Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said they were flights from Brussels to Sofia and from Prague to Cyprus and Romania.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu's office said Friday that "four new bomb threats were made today against aircraft flying over French territory." The planes landed safely at Paris' Orly Airport and bomb disposal experts were conducting inspections. The office didn't give details of the flights affected.
Other incidents included threats against a Prague to Bucharest flight operated by Romanian carrier Tarom, and a Ryanair flight traveling from Lisbon to Rome. A WizzAir flight from Prague to Rome was diverted to Venice after a bomb alert, and passengers were evacuated after the aircraft landed.
Security inspections were carried out and no explosives were found.
Eurocontrol said Friday it was monitoring the situation and working closely with airlines, airports, navigation service providers and other groups across Europe "to mitigate any disruption to air traffic flows."
At Prague's Vaclav Havel Airport, spokesperson Denisa Hejtmánková said a total of nine flights were threatened, including arriving flights from Denmark, Spain and Britain, and departing flights to the Netherlands, Cyprus, Romania, Italy and Britain. Czech police said security measures were taken that had "a minimal impact on the normal operations at the airport."
In the Danish capital Copenhagen, police said Friday they went to the airport for a second consecutive day "in connection with threats directed at air traffic" as a precautionary measure. They said they assessed that there had been no danger to passengers or to others at the airport.
No clear evidence on who is behind the threats
More than two dozen flights were affected by threats earlier in the week, with some diverted as authorities scrambled to rule out any danger.
Fake bomb threats are relatively common but it is unusual to see so many in such a short period.
It remains unclear who is behind the wave of airline hoaxes, which come at a time of increased geopolitical tensions and warnings from authorities that Russia may be ramping up so-called hybrid threats in Europe.
Authorities have not attributed the threats to any group or state actor, and no evidence has emerged linking the hoaxes to a government. An email containing the threat sent Thursday to airport authorities in Rome and reviewed by The Associated Press purported to come from a group describing itself as anti-feminist and claiming it was targeting a "feminist regime." Another European airport received a threat with similar wording, but it was unclear if it came from the same sender.
Bomb threats are on pilots' minds and create unnecessary tension, but crews are prepared to respond professionally, said Paul Reuter, vice president of the European Cockpit Association. Pilots review procedures with cabin crews, identify airports where they could divert and may carry extra fuel, he said.
Reuter called the use of civil aviation for geopolitical disruption or hoaxes "totally unacceptable."
Broadcasters also received threats
In Ireland, the Dublin headquarters of national broadcaster RTE was evacuated Friday after a bomb threat, and live broadcasts were replaced with pre-recorded programs. Staff returned to the building after a few hours, once police and sniffer dogs had searched the area and declared it safe.
Ireland's police force, An Garda Síochána, said it has been liaising with Irish media organizations and the threat will be investigated.
Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin said the threats to RTE and others "just illustrates how relatively simple it can be to cause disruption and to undermine the normal operation of society through unconventional activities of this kind, which are designed to cause fear and anxiety."
He said there would be a "very significant security operation" in place next week when Dublin hosts meetings of the European Political Community and European Union leaders.
Separately, U.K.-based broadcaster Sky said it had also received a "security threat." In a statement reported by Sky News channel, it said that "we are working closely with authorities to ensure our people and operations remain secure." Sky News remained on air.
It's not clear if the incidents were linked.

Kenyan pharmacists warn against viral craze of using allergy drug for vaginal tightening
- Published
Kenyan pharmacists have warned women against inserting allergy tablets into their vaginas in an attempt to make them tighter, following the spread of potentially dangerous medical advice on social media.
The warning follows a wave of social media posts promoting cetirizine - a widely available oral antihistamine used to treat allergies - as a way of tightening the vagina, supposedly to enhance sexual pleasure.
Although antihistamines can sometimes cause dryness as a side effect, experts say this does not strengthen vaginal muscles.
"Dryness is not tightness... instead, it may increase friction, discomfort, and the risk of tissue injury," the Pharmaceutical Society of Kenya (PSK) said.
"Inserting oral tablets is unsafe. Cetirizine tablets are made to be swallowed. Their ingredients have not been tested on delicate vaginal tissue," it added.
Cetirizine is commonly used to relieve symptoms such as sneezing, a runny nose, itchy eyes and skin reactions, including hives.
The controversy began earlier this week when posts circulated on TikTok claiming that cetirizine could reduce vaginal moisture and create a sensation of tightness during sex.
This sparked widespread debate, with some users promoting the practice while others questioned its safety.
There have also been local media reports of the price of the drug rising and increased demand in some pharmacies, especially in the capital, Nairobi.
"Cetirizine is an allergy medicine, taken by mouth. It is not approved or tested for any other purpose, and definitely not for vaginal use," the PSK, a professional body representing pharmacists in Kenya, said in a statement issued on Thursday.
"If you have already tried it. Stop. See a doctor if you have pain, bleeding, burning, itching, unusual discharge, or fever," it advised.
The society also urged social media influencers and content creators to take care when sharing health information, saying that unverified claims could put people's health at risk.
The warning comes a day after Kenya's health ministry expressed concern about the trend.
Ouma Oluga, a senior health official, said some social media users appeared to be treating the medical advice from experts as a joke, without considering the possible consequences.
He suggested that the authorities could introduce a system to track the distribution and purchase of medicines to help identify possible misuse.
However, no formal decision has been announced on such a initiative.
The PSK said it was aware of reports of increased demand for cetirizine, rising prices and shortages at some pharmacies.
It urged retailers not to exploit the trend, warning that people who genuinely needed the medicine for allergies could struggle to obtain it.
It went on to encourage its members not to knowingly dispense medicines that would be misused - and report any side affects to the health authorities of those that had been.
The PSK ended its statement by saying that unverified online trends should never trump what the experts say: "Check with a pharmacist before using any medicine for a purpose it was not made for.
"Do not rely on social media for medical advice."

Homes and temples glow across India as Diwali celebrations begin
- Published
Millions across India are set to celebrate Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, illuminating homes, temples, offices and streets with oil lamps and colourful lights to symbolise the triumph of light over darkness.
The festival falls on the darkest night of the Hindu lunar month of Kartik, when the moon is not visible in the sky.
Although Diwali traditions vary across India's regions and communities, the festival is widely marked by prayers, family gatherings, the exchange of sweets and the lighting of firecrackers.
But the celebrations come amid growing concerns over air pollution, particularly in northern India.
Seasonal weather conditions and the burning of crop residue contribute to deteriorating air quality, while firecrackers set off during Diwali can make the situation worse.
In the capital, Delhi, the air quality index (AQI) reached 391 on Friday morning, placing it in the "very poor" category ahead of the festival. There are fears that pollution levels could rise further after the celebrations.
India's financial capital, Mumbai, has also experienced high pollution levels in recent weeks, with its AQI reaching 322 on 24 October. Although air quality has improved in recent days to reach "moderate" levels of 104 on Friday, there are concerns that Diwali fireworks could trigger another spike.
In an effort to limit pollution, India's Supreme Court on Monday permitted the manufacture, sale and use of certified "green" firecrackers in Delhi and surrounding areas for a limited period.
These firecrackers are designed to produce 20-30% less emissions than conventional fireworks. But critics have questioned how effective they are in reducing pollution and raised concerns that conventional firecrackers could still make their way into the capital from neighbouring states.
Despite the debate over fireworks, Diwali is about much more than firecrackers.
The festival celebrates the return of Lord Ram to Ayodhya after his victory over over Ravan, the main antagonist in the Hindu epic Ramayana, and symbolises the triumph of good over evil.
In the days leading up to the festival, families clean and decorate their homes with flowers, colourful lights and traditional oil lamps known as diyas.
The celebrations also bring families and friends together for prayers, elaborate feasts and the exchange of gifts, and lots of traditional Indian sweets.
Colourful patterns known as rangoli are created at entrances to homes, while markets bustle with shoppers buying festive essentials beneath brightly lit decorations.
The celebrations began on 6 November with Dhanteras, when buying gold, silver or new utensils is considered auspicious and believed to bring good fortune.
The second day, known as Chhoti Diwali, or small Diwali, is marked by the lighting of oil lamps and, in some households, setting off firecrackers.
The third day is the main celebration, when families offer evening prayers to Lakshmi, the Hindu goddess of wealth and prosperity, before gathering for festive meals and fireworks.
The fourth day is celebrated differently across India, with family gatherings and New Year festivities in some communities. The fifth and final day, known as Bhai Dooj, celebrates the bond between brothers and sisters.
The festival is also celebrated by Sikhs and Jains along with other important religious observances.
Sikhs mark Bandi Chhor Divas, or Prisoner Release Day, commemorating the release of their sixth guru, Guru Hargobind, from imprisonment at Gwalior Fort in the early 17th Century.
For Jains, Diwali marks the attainment of moksha, or liberation from the cycle of rebirth, by Lord Mahavira, the 24th and last Tirthankara, or spiritual teacher, of the current era.
With Indian communities spread across the world, Diwali is also celebrated internationally, with families and friends coming together for festive gatherings and exchanging gifts.
The festival is considered an auspicious time to make new purchases, which many believe bring prosperity and good fortune. India's stock exchanges even hold a special one-hour trading session for investors who consider buying and selling shares on Diwali auspicious. Known as known as Muhurat trading, it will take place on 8 November this year.
Although rooted in Hindu traditions, Diwali is celebrated by people across different faiths and communities.

A New Game Plan
Regional gaps in safe sport rules remain a 'major' concern for Canada's sport integrity agency
Report identified 'major inconsistencies' in policies across levels of sport and jurisdictions
More than six months on from a report that rang alarm bells about the prevalence of abuse and maltreatment in sport, the head of Canada’s sport integrity agency continues to have “major” concerns about regional gaps in safe sport rules.
Sport Integrity Canada maintains Canada’s Safe Sport Program public registry, which includes the names of more than 80 people who’ve been sanctioned across more than two dozen different sporting bodies.
The registry captures violations of the Universal Code of Conduct to Prevent and Address Maltreatment in Sport, a set of rules governing behaviour around sport that all national sport organizations in Canada had to adopt as a condition of federal funding. It applies to coaches, volunteers, athletes and other leaders across sport.
A New Game Plan Series
The behaviours captured in the registry range from physical, psychological and sexual maltreatment to neglect and retaliation, among others. Some of the people on the list have been convicted of crimes. Some have been banned from sport permanently. Others faced sanctions such as suspensions or additional education.
It’s a snapshot of abuse and maltreatment in sport in Canada, but far from a fulsome picture.
That’s because most provincial and local sporting organizations aren’t required to adopt the Universal Code of Conduct. Details of maltreatment at those levels may not appear on Sport Integrity Canada’s registry.
“We know that individuals who cause harm in this way can move from one sport to another sport at one level to another level, where their names aren’t being appropriately placed on a registry so people know about it,” Sport Integrity Canada president and CEO Jeremy Luke said.
“It's a major concern for us. It was a very clear recommendation coming out of the Future of Sport in Canada Commission report and it needs to be put in place in Canada to protect participants who are participating in these sports.”
It’s also not a new concern. Reporting from CBC’s Shattered Trust project chronicled the problems with implementing safe sport rules at the grassroots level, and the consequences of the gaps that exist there, over the last few years.
The evidence shows that despite growing awareness and policy efforts, maltreatment remains deeply rooted in Canadian sport.Future of Sport in Canada Commission report
The Future of Sport in Canada Commission’s final report, released in March, described a system with a longstanding “culture of silence,” and one where racism and discrimination are major issues.
The commission’s work began after a number of athletes spoke publicly and testified in front of Parliament about the harm they experienced during their sporting careers.
“The evidence shows that despite growing awareness and policy efforts, maltreatment remains deeply rooted in Canadian sport,” the commission, led by former Ontario Chief Justice Lise Maisonneuve, wrote. “It affects individuals at all levels, including at the grassroots. These systemic problems require immediate and sustained government action. Although it is not possible to eliminate maltreatment entirely, governments and sport organizations must work together to strengthen and align prevention and response measures so that all participants can safely experience sport’s benefits.”
There are plenty of rules at the national level, where Sport Canada has the power to withhold federal funding to national sport organizations that don’t follow safe sport rules.
It’s below the national level that a hodge podge of safe sport policies persist, from the education every athlete and coach receives, to something as simple and important as background checks, the commission found.
“Participants noted major inconsistencies in safe sport policies across levels of sport and jurisdictions, emphasizing the need for a shared understanding of maltreatment and consistent standards ‘from coast to coast to coast,’” the commission wrote, describing interviews with more than 1,000 participants in the Canadian sport system. “They supported the development of clear and harmonized expectations and remedies for all participants, regardless of sport or level.”
‘Urgent’ need for harmonization
The Future of Sport in Canada Commission said there’s an “urgent” need for more uniformity when it comes to how maltreatment is handled across the country.
More than seven years ago, sports ministers from provinces and territories across the country signed the Red Deer Declaration, agreeing that sport should be a safe place free from maltreatment and abuse. They agreed to work together on issues like monitoring and education.
The declaration led to the Universal Code of Conduct at the national level, but implementation at the provincial and territorial level has been “uneven,” the commission found. Quebec has its own safe sport legislation, for example, while British Columbia created a non-profit called Sport Safeguarding BC to oversee complaints in that province.
Some jurisdictions still don’t have a centralized place for people to file complaints. Many rely on third parties to handle those complaints, a set-up that the commission described as “costly, inconsistent, and affected by perceived or real conflicts of interest.”
The commission called for a pan-Canadian safe sport program that would harmonize rules, education, and the handling of complaints. But that will “take time and political commitment to build,” the commission said.
Luke envisions a system where Sport Integrity Canada can take a leadership role and provide guidance on sharing information and making sure there are consistent rules.
That includes closing the gaps on the registry.
“I think it's a priority, but I also think we need to get to a place where a priority becomes action and that we can put in place the necessary systems to make it occur,” Luke said.
“There are some challenges around putting in place registries, but what's most important is that we protect people who participate in sport, particularly vulnerable people, and that we agree as a country that we want to have a registry so that we can properly protect participants in sport from the grassroots level all the way through to the national level.”
Funding for safe sport
In the last year, the federal government has earmarked more than $1 billion, spread over several years, to a sport system in transition.
Sport Canada has put $17.3 million into Sport Integrity Canada in 2026-27, up from $12.6 million in the previous fiscal year. The Sport Dispute Resolution Centre of Canada also saw a boost, from $1.94 million, up from $1.5 million.
Adam van Koeverden, Canada’s secretary of state for sport, gather sport leaders from across the country for a national summit in Ottawa next Monday and Tuesday, and safe sport will likely be on the agenda.
“Sport Integrity Canada has been among the strongest organizations in terms of their ability to apply for additional funding and demonstrate very, very clearly where the gaps lie and what they need in order to achieve stronger and safer sport systems,” van Koeverden said in a recent interview with CBC Sports. “They're one of our most important partners and certainly a regulated, mandated organization within the Canadian sport system.”
But the real heavy lifting to close the gap will require a pan-Canadian solution, something the federal government alluded to in an October press release announcing sport funding.
It will take all provinces and territories on the same page with the same vision, and it’s not clear how long something like that might take.
“Addressing maltreatment is a shared responsibility that requires commitment and collaboration from all levels of government across Canada,” the press release from Sport Canada says. “The federal government continues to work closely with provincial and territorial partners to advance safe sport priorities, including independent complaint mechanisms, awareness and education initiatives, and the exploration of a national safe sport registry. Together, these efforts look to build a more coordinated, consistent and effective approach to safe sport from coast to coast to coast.”
Looking abroad
Sport Integrity Canada works with other sport integrity organizations across the world through the International Integrity Group. Canada will serve on the organization’s executive through 2028.
The group includes Sport Integrity Australia, the similarly named organization that has wrestled with many of the same issues as Canada has faced.
More than five years into its existence, Sport Integrity Australia is trying to tackle the fragmentation between levels of government by adding national integrity managers at the state level to help integrate safe sport policies. Australia is also a federation, with powers divided between the federal level and provincial/state bodies.
“It gives us that formal connection from the national to the state level,” Sport Integrity Australia CEO Dr. Sarah Benson told CBC Sports. “By having those integrity managers in place, they'll also be a connection through to the community level.”
Dr. Sarah Benson, CEO of Sport Integrity Australia, is spearheading a review on the effectiveness of national integrity framework that guides that country's safe sport. (Karissa Donkin/CBC)
Australia doesn’t have all the answers. Still a young agency, Benson is spearheading a review on the effectiveness of the national integrity framework that guides safe sport in Australia.
She’s also hoping to use a home Olympic and Paralympic Games in Brisbane in 2032 as a vehicle for culture change in Australian sport.
“How can we do things differently that would actually benefit and put the athlete at the centre of what we're doing?” Benson said. “How can we use sport to actually try and make a difference in those areas that we've really been challenged to really shift the dial on in the past?”
But Australia’s sport integrity framework is rooted in legislation that makes it easier to cooperate with law enforcement agencies that are investigating the same issue as the sport integrity body.
It’s something Luke said Canada is missing. Sport Integrity Canada regulates abuse and maltreatment, as well as doping and competition manipulation.
“They [Sport Integrity Australia] have a lot of authority being a government agency that enables them to be able to cooperate with law enforcement and cooperate with other governmental bodies and be able to investigate matters perhaps in ways that we can't in Canada, given we're not a government agency and we're not founded in legislation in the same sort of way,” Luke said.
“I think that's a model we want to continue to consider the pros and cons of as we look to implement some of these recommendations in Canada and whether that’s a place that we should be evolving to.”

A shipment of Nvidia hardware valued at $11.4 million vanished in transport between Oakland and Texas over the summer, and more than two months later, police have announced no arrests or recovery of the cargo.
As reported by The Mercury News, six pallets of unknown Nvidia equipment left Oakland on August 29 on a truck bound for Fort Worth, Texas. The hardware was reportedly picked up as scheduled by a truck bearing the logo of a food transportation company before vanishing off the grid. The theft wasn’t noticed until early September, when the buyers realized that the shipment had never been received. Police attempting to trace the truck’s route found it had made several multi-hour stops after picking up the hardware before losing the truck somewhere in San Bernardino County, California.
Oakland police confirmed that there was a grand theft report filed on September 13 and that the investigation remains ongoing. Authorities have not said what Nvidia hardware was stolen or exactly how the theft was carried out.
The theft in Oakland is the latest in a wave of increasingly bold hardware heists. As Ars’ Ashley Belanger reported recently, thieves have made off with more than $100 million in similar shipments since June. According to investigators cited by NBC News, the criminals have shown planning and sophistication by employing techniques like GPS location spoofing and even arranging collisions with police escort vehicles. Stolen components can be stripped down and sold in gray-market transactions or shipped overseas where access to US tech hardware may be restricted.

A new UK law banning porn featuring choking and “fauxcest,” or simulated incest, may have unintended consequences for content creators and smut fans all over the world, some experts warn.
As of November 6, amendments to the Crime and Policing Act will outlaw the “possession or publication of pornographic images of strangulation or suffocation”—a law intended to curb violence against women and girls. Yet some experts warn that the legislation is written broadly enough that it could potentially criminalize far more innocuous content, including “breast smothering,” “jeans facesitting,” and even potentially oral sex, ostensibly because people could have their airways impeded during these activities.
“I would encourage both content creators and consumers to underscore the risks of this law,” says Myles Jackman, an obscenity lawyer in the UK. “Because to me, it genuinely seems like one of the greatest acts of suppression of free speech in global history.”
The new amendments were inspired by a lengthy pornography review authored by Baroness Gabby Bertin, a Conservative member of the UK House of Lords. The legislation bans various depictions of sex acts, including “pornographic images of strangulation or suffocation,” as well as content showing performers role-playing as minors under the age of 16.
It also takes aim at “fauxcest,” an extremely popular porn niche that depicts simulated sexual relations between family members who are not related by blood, such as stepsiblings or stepparents. In Bertin’s review recommending the ban on such content, she cites “anecdotal evidence” suggesting that fauxcest “can be used between an abuser and child to permit interfamily child sex abuse,” describing it as a “fig-leaf” of sorts for actual sexual abuse.
Under the new law, those caught distributing or in possession of such content face up to five years in prison and a fine.
The impending UK legislation has prompted panic among some adult creators, many of whom are currently combing through their content libraries and removing clips that could get swept up in the ban.
“The problem is always how broad [the legislation] is,” says Alexandra Snow, an adult content creator and educator. “And we won't know how they're going to interpret it until they start making people's lives hell.”
Snow says she is particularly concerned about how the aspect of the legislation pertaining to “suffocation or strangulation” will affect kink creators, who may make content related to collaring or leather fetishes. She’s also worried about AI image-recognition software, which is already in widespread use among the platforms, potentially flagging content that isn’t violative at all. “They use a very broad, heavy-handed approach,” she says.
Cami Strella, an OnlyFans creator in the US who estimates that 60 to 70 percent of her content depicts some form of role-play, including step-“fauxcest,” is also concerned about the legislation. She says that the content she makes is “just playing a fantasy,” and that more sex education and literacy is required to teach people about the risks of various behaviors.
“I don’t think banning it is going to do anything,” she says. “If anything, it’ll just push even worse content that is actually illegal or immoral underground, so you’ll have to access it away from these platforms. This is just a slippery slope we’re getting into.”
The new UK law is seemingly targeted at the trend of choking in porn, which has been linked to real-life instances of fatal choking during sex. Though the practice is highly risky, potentially leading to brain damage or death, it’s increasingly common among young adults, largely due to the prevalence of eroticized choking depictions in the media and in porn. The death of a 16-year-old Australian girl in August, who authorities say lost consciousness after she was choked consensually during sex, has led to renewed calls for legislation banning depictions of the practice in online porn, which has “absolutely sort of normalized this kind of sexual violence,” Bertin recently told the BBC.
The UK has a history of imposing stringent restrictions on internet pornography, particularly compared to the United States, where statutes like Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act of 1996 largely exempt platforms from liability for hosting objectionable content. Long before many US states started requiring users to verify their ages before visiting porn sites, for instance, the UK communications regulation agency Ofcom has been slapping websites with fines of up to 10 percent of their worldwide revenue for failing to comply with age-verification requirements.
“The UK is really pushing for limits on free speech,” says Michael Fattorosi, an adult industry attorney based in Italy. “This is just something they're throwing on top of the heap of restrictions.”
In a statement to WIRED, Clara Coleman, a spokesperson for the UK’s Ministry of Justice, denied that the legislation was intended to curb sexual expression. “We’re committed to halving violence against women and girls in a decade, and that includes preventing harm before it starts,” Coleman says. “[These] laws aren’t about policing people’s sexual freedom, they’re about cracking down on content that normalizes violence against women, encourages unlawful behavior, and can cause real-world harm.”
Jackman, the lawyer, says that he has no issue with the provision banning strangulation, as its risks are proven and there are existing laws banning strangulation in the UK. He cautions, however, that the law is written broadly enough that relatively innocuous content could also potentially be penalized.
“It would be up to a court to decide this on a case-by-case basis, but given that it would appear that face-sitting by a vagina owner is now arguably suffocation, the insertion of a penis could equally be considered suffocation because it blocks the airways,” he says. In other words, “the UK could have just banned blow jobs” in online pornography.
Though the law currently applies only to consumers and creators in the United Kingdom, the stiff penalties for “possession” of such images—which the law defines as an image being stored on a phone, a hard drive, or in cloud storage—is of particular concern to Fattorosi.
“As far as creators are concerned, if you visit the UK, if you’re going there on holiday, if you’re going there for a conference, you should probably be careful about what you keep on your phone,” he says.
The subscription-based platform OnlyFans is particularly vulnerable, he adds. Though most American porn companies don’t have a substantial presence in the UK, making it difficult for Ofcom to go after them, that doesn’t apply to OnlyFans. The subscription-based platform’s parent company, Fenix International Limited, is based in the United Kingdom and has already faced steep fines from the agency for failure to adhere to age-disclosure requirements.
“If I were OnlyFans,” Fattorosi says, “I’d be very worried about this.” (In a statement, OnlyFans tells WIRED the platform “complies with applicable laws and regulations in all jurisdictions in which it operates and has longstanding, proactive safety measures in place that meet UK legal requirements.”)
In advance of the new legislation taking effect, adult content platforms have issued updated guidelines for creators. The platform IWantClips has already started complying, publishing a new set of guidelines for creators and fans based in the UK and removing clips that could potentially be swept up in the legislation. The laundry list of sexual niches and categories banned now includes “breast smothering,” “ass smothering,” “jeans facesitting,” “BBW facesitting,” “plastic fetish,” “scissorhold,” and “butt drops.”
Trans Princess Jezebel, a dominatrix and adult content creator in the UK, says she has already started going through her content library on IWantClips and OnlyFans, removing videos that may be seen as violative. She’s heavily reliant on clips to advertise her services as a dominatrix, and she’s concerned that once the law takes effect on November 6, she’ll take a huge financial hit.
“When the state starts regulating which types of pornography people are allowed to watch, a dangerous precedent is set,” she tells WIRED in an email. “Where will it end?”
But even though the UK is, for the time being, an outlier, Jackman warns it may not be for long. He says he has heard of lawmakers in Italy, the Netherlands, and Spain discussing similar legislation, as well as members of the evangelical lobby in the United States.
“In terms of free speech,” he says, “the lights are going out across the globe.”

Judoka determined to prove refugees belong at Dakar 2026
- Published
Arno Yafunga Botay was six when his family fled the Democratic Republic of Congo after threats to his father's life culminated in an attack on their home which claimed the life of his seven-month-old sibling.
Following a spell living in the Kakuma refugee camp in north-west Kenya, the family settled in Nairobi. There, Arno used to watch his father Arnold practising judo and eventually asked him to teach him the sport.
Now, having coming through trials in East Africa, he will compete for the Refugee Olympic Team in the under-55kg category at the Dakar 2026 Youth Games.
"I didn't expect to be selected," the 15-year-old told BBC Sport Africa.
"I was so excited. I was crying tears of joy."
This is the first time that a team of refugees will appear at a Youth Games.
"It [means] a lot to me to represent other refugees, represent my community," Yafunga Botay added.
The family have been in Kenya since they were forced to leave DR Congo in 2017.
"There were people who wanted to kill me," Arnold said.
"At the time, I was detained somewhere when people came to our house and attacked my family. The situation led to the death of my child."
- All you need to know about the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics 
  - Published5 days ago
- Africa prepares for historic Olympic moment at Dakar 2026 
  - Published23 July
After finding safety, Yafunga Botay and his elder brother Christian would watch their father training before he headed out to work as a labourer.
Yafunga Botay began receiving instructions in judo rules and techniques at the age of seven.
However, life in their adopted East African nation provided its own challenges.
"I [did] not have the judogi clothes or transport fees for local competitions," he explained.
"It's been difficult going to school. There's no money for school fees.
"My father has no work. He needs to go to work and give us money to go and pay the school fees.
"And here we don't have support. As a refugee, to stay in Kenya, you need to have documents.
"[Thankfully] the IOC (International Olympic Committee) came with this programme of helping refugees achieve their dreams."
An Olympic first for refugees
The Refugee Olympic Team was first introduced at the Rio 2016 Olympics and Cameroon-born boxer Cindy Ngamba won the team's first ever medal at Paris 2024 when she claimed bronze in the women's 75kg category.
In a double first, the team will now make its Youth Olympics debut at Dakar 2026, which is the first Olympic event hosted on African soil.
"As a refugee, we have a right to compete," Yafunga Botay said.
"A refugee is a human being like other people."
Father Arnold says the team serves as a message of hope to people around the world who have been displaced.
"Being a refugee does not mean your life is over," he said.
"Refugees can also do things that surprise people.
"My message to fellow refugees is don't give up. Keep pushing until the end."
The six-strong team competing in Senegal is being mentored by two-time Olympic marathon champion Eliud Kipchoge.
"He teaches us [to] respect the coach, focus on what you are doing," Yafunga Botay said.
"I promised him I'll bring the gold medal [back] so he can see [what] I achieved."
Discipline and respect
Judo has become a central part of life for the family.
Arnold still coaches Yafunga Botay and Christian, now 17, occasionally serves as his younger brother's sparring partner.
The teenager describes his father as "strict" even at home, with a firm focus on the importance of discipline.
"Maintaining his weight is not easy. He [Arno] has to keep training consistently," Arnold said.
"Judo teaches him respect and helps him interact with others, whether at school or at home.
"Those lessons follow him everywhere. In judo, every time you fall you gain the strength to keep going."
The owner of the dojo in the Kenyan capital where Yafunga Botay has trained since 2020 says his selection for Dakar 2026 has "changed perceptions" of judo in the community.
"It is helping parents understand that judo is not just a fighting sport - it has real value," Lawrence Karisa Nyundo told the BBC.
"I have received calls from parents who want to enrol their children.
"It is a big achievement for this club that one of our athletes is going to compete at the Olympics. We are praying that he performs well."
After Dakar, Yafunga Botay hopes other refugees can benefit from his experience in the future.
"In Kakuma, there are good judokas.
"I think if I achieve [a] gold medal, I can go there and teach them the value of judo."
Competition at Dakar 2026 begins on Friday, with the opening ceremony a day later and judo events running from 1-3 November.

Bangladesh’s Towhid Hridoy converted his maiden century into a double century to lift his team into a dominant position in the second Test against West Indies on Saturday. Hridoy was unbeaten on 242 off 359, smashing 22 fours and 11 sixes.
His double ton helped Bangladesh reach 386, taking a 30-run lead in the first innings after a poor start. West Indies ended the day’s play at 7 for no loss when bad light forced stumps.
Hridoy became the fourth Bangladeshi batter to hit a double century after Mushfiqur Rahim, Shakib Al Hasan and Tamim Iqbal and also passed Mushfiqur’s 219 to become the highest individual scorer for the country.
“It’s unbelievable how he was still able to find boundaries and hit sixes even when he started getting tired,” Bangladesh coach Phil Simmons said of Hridoy. “He showed outstanding game awareness, knowing which shots to play and when to give the last three batsmen the strike. Everything he did in this innings was exceptional.”
ALSO READ:BAN vs WI: Amir Jangoo’s unbeaten 111 leads West Indies revival from 27-3 vs Bangladesh
Resuming at 88-3 on Day 3, Hridoy and Mushfiqur negotiated the West Indies bowlers well before Jomel Warrican dismissed Mushfiqur, ending their 73-run partnership.
Warrican and skipper Roston Chase then sparked a collapse as Bangladesh lost three wickets in quick succession to be left at 184-7. Hridoy then helped the side stage a comeback by adding 117 runs with Taijul Islam in the eighth wicket. He raised his maiden century off 171 balls, which also took the side past 300.
After the century, Hridoy became more adventurous, unleashing a spectacular attack on West Indies bowlers. Ten of his 11 sixes, the highest by any Bangladeshi batter and also the second-highest in cricket history, came during this period.
Warrican, who took 4-104, finally broke through with the wicket of Taijul for 22. But Hridoy was unstoppable, as he shared an 85-run partnership with Taskin Ahmed in the ninth wicket to edge Bangladesh ahead. He raised his double century in 304 balls.
“We were thinking about what lead we could have got or how big the lead could have been, but the way Hridoy batted was special,” Warrican said. “We have to reflect on things that we could have done better. As a unit, we still have to keep our heads up because there’s a job to be done. We have to come back well tomorrow.”
Bangladesh bowlers lost two reviews in the first over before West Indies openers Joshua da Silva and Brandon King kept the side unscathed by safely negotiating four overs.

After Macklemore called out some of the venues that would not host his Free Palestine Tour, Madison Square Garden has responded.
In a recent statement, an MSG spokesperson claimed the decision to reject the tour was due to “extremely limited availability” and the fact that he’s “not an arena level act,” despite quickly selling out the tour’s arena shows in Dublin, Paris and London last month.
“We have some of the busiest venues in the world with extremely limited availability and he’s not an arena level act,” the MSG rep said in a statement.
The statement came after Macklemore called out some of the venues that “have turned us down” including MSG, Prudential Center, Barclays Center, UBS Arena, Intuit Dome, Kia Forum, Crypto.com Arena, Chase Center, and Climate Pledge Arena.
Watch on Deadline
“By mid-September, we received available dates at these arenas through the end of the year. But once they found out these were my benefit shows for Palestine, those dates were suddenly off the table,” he said. “The doors were closed. The conversations were all different, but the result was the same. The shows were not going to be allowed to happen in these venues.”
Macklemore added in part, “I’d rather lose every opportunity in this industry than spend another day protecting people who value their business relationships with Israel more than they value Palestinian human life. We live in a country that prides itself on freedom of speech. Yet we’ve reached a point where a handful of billionaires can decide which causes are acceptable, which voices are welcome and which human lives are worth defending. Today it’s Palestine. What will it be tomorrow?”
	In September, Macklemore announced the Free Palestine Tour, which is “supporting the Palestinian people and movement,” after Ed Sheeran dropped Macklemore from his tour amid an outcry around the opener’s “Free Palestine” onstage remarks. Opting to remain publicly neutral on the issue, Sheeran subsequently released a statement saying it was the “promoter’s decision” after Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft assembled several of the tour venues to give him an ultimatum.

Houthis say at least 25 killed in Saudi air strike
- Published
Media linked to the Houthi movement in Yemen say that at least 25 people, including women and children, have been killed in airstrikes by Saudi Arabia.
There has been no comment from the Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognised government in Yemen.
Live video footage on Al Masirah - a television station run by the Houthis - has shown rescuers pulling bodies out of the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.
The bodies of young children can be seen among those dug out from the ruins.
The television station has also shown a number of injured people being carried on stretchers to hospital.
Saba news agency, which is also run by the Houthis, said the attack was carried out by Saudi Arabia.
The Saudis have led a coalition that has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government.
The war in Yemen had been dormant for several years but reignited as a result of the Iran war.
A truce began to fall apart when Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Sanaa - which is controlled by the Houthis - to prevent an Iranian plan landing there.
The Tehran-backed Houthis subsequently targeted Abha airport in Saudi Arabia, then began hitting Saudi ships that have been using the Red Sea off the coast of Yemen as an alternative oil export route to the Strait of Hormuz.
Major fighting has since resumed in Yemen between the Houthis and forces fighting for the Saudi-backed government of Yemen.
On Friday, an attack on a market in Taiz province, which has been the focus of much of the recent fighting, is reported to have killed 30 people.
The Houthis accused the Saudis of carrying out the strike, while government forces accused the Houthis of having fired a missile at the site.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.
The Saudis have regularly bombed Houthi positions, while the group has fired multiple missiles at targets inside Saudi Arabia, including airports and oil facilities.
Hours before the strike that hit al-Shariyah, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a missile heading towards Riyadh.
A Houthi leader, Mahdi al-Mashat, has vowed that the group will take revenge for the latest attacks in Yemen.

New Zealand poised for weeks of political wrangling after knife-edge poll
AUCKLAND: New Zealand faced the prospect on Sunday (Nov 8) of weeks or even months of political wrangling after a knife-edge election that produced no clear winner.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon declared his right-wing coalition has a mandate to form the country's next government - while conceding results remained too close to call definitively.
Preliminary results have his National party winning the most seats, giving them a very slim majority of just two if combined with their coalition partners, the populist NZ First and the libertarian ACT.
"New Zealanders have given us the biggest seats in parliament, forty-two seats as it stands today, and a pathway to form a government," Luxon told journalists on Sunday.
"There's no doubt about it. We've got a mandate."
He said his National party had done well given the war in the Middle East and subsequent global fuel shock that has been widely blamed for New Zealand's economic difficulties.
"What we achieved, I think, was pretty good last night."
Opposition Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins has joked that while the country had spoken, "it may take us a little bit longer to figure out exactly what it is that you've said".
But the results show he has only a very narrow path to power for his left-wing grouping, which also includes the Green Party and the Maori party.
"EVERYONE'S OVER POLITICS"
Luxon will run a caretaker government until the final votes are announced on Nov 27.
"I think everyone's over politics, so let's all just have a bit of a break for the next three weeks," he said.
That final tally will include nearly 400,000 so-called "special votes" - among them around 100,000 votes cast overseas and by people within New Zealand but outside the local electorate in which they live.
Historically, special votes leaned left, potentially giving the Labour or Green parties an additional one or two seats at the expense of the right-bloc.
This week's knife-edge poll drew intense attention to the country's minor parties, in particular the upstart centrist Opportunity Party.
Under the country's mixed-member proportional representation system, voters must tick two options - a general party list as well as an individual member to represent their electorate.
Results put Opportunity winning seven seats, potentially giving the party a kingmaker role in the next government.
With 100 per cent of the preliminary count done, Luxon's National are on 42 projected seats and Labour on 36, according to the electoral commission.
The Green Party is in third place with 16 seats, while ACT are on 13 and NZ First have 12. Te Pati Maori have five.
Luxon said Sunday that while it was "unlikely" he would need the Opportunity Party to form a government, he was willing to work with leader Qiulae Wong on issues on which they agree.
"We can work with our current coalition partners to form the government," he said.
"What I've also said, though, is that there is a need for us to go forward in cross-party collaboration in a lot deeper way."
Many Kiwis are struggling to make ends meet - the price of basic goods remains stubbornly elevated, and unemployment at its highest in more than a decade.

The Kerala Water Authority (KWA) has kicked off a major drive to rid the Pipeline Road on the Peroorkada-Aruvikkara stretch of encroachments and unauthorised constructions. The water utility said on Saturday that it has intensified action against encroachers.
As part of the drive, illegal structures were removed at the Vazhayila junction on Friday. The effort will continue in the weeks ahead, the KWA said on Saturday. “These measures are being taken to protect the Pipeline Road and the allied KWA assets and to ensure access for carrying out repairs and maintenance works,” the KWA said.
The Pipeline Road is important for the KWA as the transmission main carrying water from Aruvikkara to the capital city passes through it.
The water utility has requested encroachers to vacate the premises voluntarily, so as to avoid action. KWA officials are also serving notices to encroachers under provisions of the KWA (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupation and Removal of Unauthorised Constructions) Regulations, 2014.
If the encroachers fail to vacate the premises within the timeframe stipulated in the notice, the Executive Engineer concerned will issue the final speaking order. Failure to vacate within the 30-day deadline prescribed in that order will attract eviction measures with the assistance of the police, according to KWA.
In August this year, the KWA had ordered that all permanent, semi-permanent and other encroachments be removed from the Pipeline Road in Kochi. The drive in Kochi was held as part of the preliminary measures for the laying of pipelines to the city from a proposed 190-mld water treatment plant.

The deportation of two more Uyghurs to China from Thailand would put their lives in grave danger, activists have said, with one of the men saying he would be “like a slave” if he was sent back.
Last year, Thai authorities forcibly deported 40 Uyghur men to China despite pleas from the men themselves and the UN.
 
The US and Canada had reportedly offered to resettle them, but Bangkok appeared to want to avoid upsetting Beijing. The UN has said the returnees’ whereabouts remain unknown.
Now, two more men fear becoming the latest victims of Beijing’s repressive crackdown against the largely Muslim ethnic group, condemned by the UN as a potential crime against humanity.
The girlfriend of one of the men said her boyfriend, whose name is being withheld for security reasons, told the Guardian he wanted to go “anywhere else but China”.
Human rights groups said two Uyghur men were at risk of deportation after recently being transferred to an immigration detention centre and they feared Thai authorities may once again give in to pressure from Beijing.
Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, called for the men to be allowed to travel to a safe third country. “Previous Thai governments have kept Uyghurs in inhumane detention for years and then complied with Beijing’s demands to send them to China, where they were forcibly disappeared,” she said.
The men had been serving a seven-year prison sentence for offences related to an attempted escape from immigration detention in January 2020. They were part of a group of more than 200 Uyghur men, women and children who were apprehended by Thai police in 2014 near the border with Malaysia after they fled from China.
Since 2014, women and children in the group have been released to Turkey, while the men have been deported to China, in separate batches, attracting criticism from the United Nations and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio.
Uyghurs, a Turkic minority mainly from the Xinjiang region in China, have been subjected to decades of oppressive and discriminatory treatment from the Chinese authorities. This has included the incarceration of hundreds of thousands of people in detention camps aimed at stamping out their cultural identity.
Beijing has defended its policies in Xinjiang as being aimed at poverty alleviation and counter-terrorism.
In July, Marzeyya Kasem’s (who asked to be referred to by her Islamic alias) boyfriend wrote to her in a letter that he would be “like a slave” if he was sent back to China. “Sometimes I thought why I’m a human being. What I do wrong against China … no want to go back to China,” he wrote. She shared the letter with a Thai rights group.
The two men facing imminent deportation reportedly pleaded their case to Thailand’s office of the National Human Rights Commission on Wednesday.
Relatives of Uyghurs have said the Chinese government was “paranoid about Uyghurs going to a safe country in large numbers and living together”, and preferred to have them deported.
It is not clear whether China has issued a formal extradition request for the two men. But Chaipruak Doungprapat, Thailand’s national security council chief, told reporters that the men, along with three other Uyghurs who are still in prison, had arrest warrants outstanding in China.
Some have questioned whether criminal warrants could be credible considering that at least one of them, Kasem’s boyfriend, was a minor when he left China. “If they are really wanted for a crime in China, why didn’t China immediately issue a [Interpol] red notice [when they were detained in 2014]?” asked Kasem.
Kasem believes that because Thailand was criticised for last year’s mass deportation, this time the authorities were trying to establish a more credible legal basis for the move.
A spokesperson for China’s foreign affairs ministry said: “The cooperation between China and Thailand in combating cross-border illegal and criminal activities such as smuggling is consistent with the laws of the two countries, international law and international practice.”
A spokesperson for Thailand’s foreign affairs ministry declined to comment.
