Gadi Eisenkot, the main rival to Benjamin Netanyahu, secured endorsements on Thursday from a majority of lawmakers to try to form a government but Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, said it was still unclear who could break the deadlock and that he would decide on Sunday which of the two men should try first.
Of the Knesset’s 120 elected lawmakers, 67 had endorsed Eisenkot through several days of talks with Herzog, while 46 endorsed Netanyahu. Herzog said on Thursday that while the “results of the consultations may appear clear”, there were “mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves” that make it difficult to say who has the best shot to form a government.
He said he would make a pick on Sunday, and that he would hold “personal talks with some of the party leaders” over the Israeli weekend, which runs Friday-Saturday.
A bitterly contested election last month, seen by many observers as one of the most consequential for Israel in many decades, ended with neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot, a former military general and chief of staff, securing a clear pathway to power.
Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority, dropping from 68 to 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. The Change bloc of Zionist parties led by Eisenkot has 48 seats, leaving parties representing Israeli Palestinians as potential kingmakers with a record 19 seats. The Joint List has 11, while the more conservative, Islamist Ra’am has eight.
In Israel’s political system, the otherwise largely ceremonial president decides which candidate has the best initial chance of building a stable coalition to rule.
Both Arab-majority parties reported backing Eisenkot, according to Haaretz. United Torah Judaism, though often aligned with Netanyahu, did not endorse either man.
Turnout among Arab Israelis – Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, who constitute 20% of the population – more than doubled to about 80%, transforming the political landscape. Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza had no vote.
The leader of Israel’s main Palestinian coalition has admitted to “disagreements with Eisenkot on many issues” but said on Thursday that Palestinian voters wanted change after facing intensified racism, discrimination, crime and exclusion under the current coalition.
“We are not choosing between good and better but between what we see as bad and even worse,” Yousef Jabareen said, according to Israeli media.
Last month, Jabareen told the Guardian that the first demand of Arab Israeli voters was to get rid of the Netanyahu government, and in particular its most extreme members, Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister, and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister.
Eisenkot has also put conditions on any potential coalition with Arab parties: they have to recognise that Israel is a Jewish state, accept compulsory national service – either civil or military – and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.
Jabareen and the Joint List have suggested they would support an opposition from the outside with tactical voting in the Knesset. Ra’am has said it would join a new government led by Eisenkot.
Herzog, who met delegations from the Palestinian Israeli parties and other small parties, has called on all to help avert another round of elections.
“Any reasonable person need only look at the security and diplomatic challenges before us, at the changing region around us, and remember the issues tearing us apart from within, to understand that an immense responsibility rests upon us,” Herzog said.
Netanyahu remains prime minister in a caretaker government until a new coalition is formed or there is another election, which must be held if no candidate succeeds.
Though the 77-year-old political veteran did better than expected in the vote and his Likud party won the most seats, his nationalist-religious coalition, the most rightwing government in Israel’s history, lost its governing majority.
Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, has seized on an investigation by election officials into possible vote tampering to cast doubt on the results, accusing Israeli Palestinian-led parties of stealing the vote. Critics accuse Netanyahu and his partners of trying to undermine the results, which he denies.
Israel’s Central Election Committee said on Wednesday that the election’s integrity had not been compromised. The head of the committee, the supreme court justice Noam Sohlberg, has called on the country’s elected officials to protect public trust.
“This is a real danger. One of the foundations of democracy is the peaceful transfer of power,” Sohlberg told Herzog at his residence on Wednesday. He said high voter turnout, including among the Arab minority, was a blessing.
Netanyahu’s allies on the far right, including Ben-Gvir, have called for the immediate arrest and interrogation of Arab party leaders.

Addressing social media debates over the scientific validity of Temple's eponymous brain-monitoring wearable, founder Deepinder Goyal issued a statement directed at “Concerned Indian Doctors”, asserting confidence in the R&D behind the wearables. Goyal pointed out that Temple had already spent $30 Mn on its development, including $20 Mn of his personal money. He also noted that the company is raising funding from its employees and customers. “Selling a few thousand devices recovers a small fraction of this investment. A scam that pays nothing is not a scam anyone would run,” the CEO wrote in his post. Goyal further said the product’s 14-day no-questions-asked return policy would validate its product in the market. On questions over Temple’s credibility and scientific validation, he argued that many wearable makers initially relied on internal studies before publishing external validation. He said the company would release pre-prints before peer-reviewed publications and it expects independent studies to emerge once the device becomes available more widely. In a follow-up post, Goyal also said, “Temple is a fitness tracker, and wellness device. We are not a medical device,” adding that the device hasn’t been clinically validated. Important to highlight that pre-orders for the wearable officially opened on November 1, with a hefty listing price of ₹85,000. Units are hand-made to order and expected to begin shipping roughly three months after purchase, starting in early 2027. What Doctors Say About Temple? For context, several medical experts had criticised Temple over its claim that a wearable sensor placed near the temple can reliably measure cerebral blood flow. Hepatologist Dr Cyriac Abby Philips, popularly known as The Liver Doc, published an Instagram carousel calling the product “the biggest health scam and wellness fraud in India,” saying the device can only detect when blood rushes to one’s face. Gurugram-based gastroenterologist Dr Zubin Sharma also noted that blood flows to the brain via arteries in the neck and back of head, not the temple. Additionally, many on social media pointed out that studies published on Temple’s website were not peer-reviewed, and were funded and conducted by the company itself. They also raised questions about the validity of Goyal’s Gravity Ageing Hypothesis, which links the long-term effects of gravity on blood circulation to ageing. In fact, Dr Philips doubled down on the criticism of Temple in a reply to Goyal's latest post, calling out Temple's claims of reading blood flow to the brain and the company's explanation of its proprietary 'Entropy' score. The Temple Journey So Far Goyal’s move into brain-monitoring wearables has been taking shape through a series of bets on longevity research. This began with his personal research initiative Continue Research, which he referred to as his personal health and wellness venture back in 2024. The initiative remained largely under wraps for over a year before unveiling its first hypothesis, Gravity Ageing, in November 2025. The hypothesis proposed that gravity's effect on cerebral blood flow (CBF) could be an overlooked contributor to human ageing. Temple emerged around the same time as a commercial extension of this research. Inc42 first reported in November 2025 that Goyal was exploring a wearable device company focused on health monitoring. The device, which he had been seen wearing near his temple, was being used experimentally to measure blood flow to the brain in real time. “I left the Eternal CEO role to chase purpose with Temple. This is not about money. I have enough of it to last for generations. My incentives are fully aligned with getting the science right. I am not staking a reputation earned over 20 years on making a quick buck,” Goyal said. On the product front, Temple has been developing a wearable that sits on the forehead near the temple and tracks signals associated with cerebral blood flow. Goyal revealed a smaller version of the device in August, claiming it was less than half the size of its earlier iteration. It has worked with contract manufacturers Zetwerk and Ethereal Machines to scale production, while retaining some manufacturing capabilities in-house. The startup began taking shape as a standalone venture earlier this year. In February, Temple raised $54 Mn (around ₹493 Cr) in a seed funding round at a post-money valuation of approximately $190 Mn. The round was led by Goyal, who invested a little over ₹100 Cr, with participation from Steadview Capital, Peak XV Partners, Vy Capital, Info Edge Ventures, among others. More than 30 employees also participated in the round. Temple subsequently expanded its ambitions beyond hardware. In July 2026, it acquired London-based longevity medicine practice Longevous for an undisclosed amount, bringing clinical and scientific expertise into the business.

4 of family, including 2 children, killed in Odisha fire; short circuit suspected: Cops
The cause of the fire is yet to be ascertained, though a short circuit is suspected, the police said.
Four members of a family, including two children aged 11 years and eight months, were burnt alive in a fire that broke out in their house in Odisha’s Jajpur district, police said on Sunday.
The incident occurred around 8pm on Saturday, at Sk Nizam Uddin’s residence in Nalipur village under Badachana block of Jajpur district. The cause of the fire is yet to be ascertained, though a short circuit is suspected, the police said.
According to local resident Ajay Kumar Samal, Nizamuddin arrived from Gopalpur on Saturday with his daughter and grandchildren. "The fire broke out when his elder daughter-in-law was cooking. His daughter, daughter-in-law and the two children died in the incident," Samal said.
On being informed, fire services personnel from Chandikhol and Balichandrapur police rushed to the spot and launched firefighting and rescue operations.
The deceased were identified as Nizamuddin's daughter Gul Afsa Parveen (26), daughter-in-law Tabassum Parveen (40), granddaughter Roshni Parveen (11) and an eight-month-old grandson, Jajpur Superintendent of Police (SP) Yashpratap Shrimal said.
A youth sustained serious burn injuries in the incident. He was initially admitted to the Badachana Community Health Centre but later shifted to Cuttack after his condition deteriorated.

Paraguay judge orders detention of impeached ex-president amid corruption investigation
Santiago Peña charged with breach of trust, administration for personal gain
A Paraguayan judge on Saturday ordered former President Santiago Peña held in pretrial detention at a military facility while prosecutors investigate his ties to digital lender Ueno, whose collapse has left millions of customers struggling to access their accounts.
Judge Humberto Otazú ordered Peña, who has been charged with breach of trust and administration for personal gain, held at the facility, saying detention was necessary to ensure he remained in the country while the case proceeded.
The detention, a day after Peña's removal from office, deepens a political and financial crisis that has prompted protests in Asunción, swept up senior officials and led regulators to try to contain risks to the wider financial system.
Peña's attorney, Ricardo Preda, told journalists that Peña was pleading not guilty to the charges.
"We will submit to the investigation and I am sure that when this investigation is over the result will be the dismissal," Preda said.
Protesters gather outside Peña's residence in Asunción on Friday. (Cesar Olmedo/Reuters)
Otazú also ordered former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo to pretrial detention in a holding center after prosecutors charged him with breach of trust, producing false public documents and administration for personal gain.
Carvallo did not respond to a request for comment.
Prosecutors allege that Peña used his position as president to influence decisions by government agencies and state-owned entities to keep large amounts of public money deposited at Ueno, despite maintaining financial ties to the lender.
They say that relationship created a conflict of interest as Peña encouraged, facilitated or influenced decisions benefiting the bank.
Customers trying to access their funds are seen outside a closed Ueno branch in Asuncion on Thursday. (Cesar Olmedo/Reuters)
Peña, who was a shareholder in Ueno’s holding company until March 2025, has denied wrongdoing and said the bank's problems were a regulatory matter.
Peña had arrived at the Attorney General’s Office earlier on Saturday to appear before prosecutors following his dramatic removal from power on Friday.
Vice-president takes power
His ouster brought Vice-President Pedro Alliana to power, with the longtime ruling Colorado Party politician sworn in on Friday to complete Peña’s term through August 2028.
The two charges against Peña could carry a sentence of up to 10 years in prison each, the prosecutor said.
Carvallo resigned as central bank chief earlier this week as the crisis surrounding Ueno escalated. He had previously headed the digital lender until 2023.
Ueno Bank executives arrive in custody at the anti-corruption prosecutor's office in Asunción on Wednesday. (Jorge Saenz/The Associated Press)
The collapse has left millions of customers struggling to access their accounts and prompted protests in Asunción.
The scandal has also swept up senior officials and former Ueno executives, while regulators have sought to reassure markets and contain risks to the wider financial system.
The central bank on Saturday said the equivalent of $160 million US had been paid out to nearly 1.2 million savers, under the state deposit guarantee scheme.

Let’s get that out there right away, because for a lot of people, it will be the only thing that matters. As with so many things in life, though, you get what you pay for. There’s no questioning the quality of the laptop’s display or most of its other hardware components.
But should you buy it? Well, that’s a complicated question in 2026.
We’re in a time of great uncertainty when it comes to buying a computer. Prices are at levels we’ve not seen in recent history, and they may well keep climbing. Meanwhile, users paying close attention to the early developments in both local and agentic artificial intelligence are asking an important question: “What will computing even look like in a few years, and what does that mean for the computer I should buy today?”
Apple’s new MacBook Pro sits at the intersection of all of this uncertainty. In multiple ways, it’s also straddling different worlds.
It arrives amid a changing of the guard in Apple’s leadership, potentially raising questions about the future direction of Apple’s ecosystem. It’s a mass-market consumer product, but configuring it with enough RAM and storage to make it feel future-proof pushes its price into territory mostly only well-funded businesses can afford. It’s firmly rooted in the computing paradigms of the past 20 years, but it shows early signs of flirtation with new AI workflows. It’s a conventional Apple laptop in most ways, but it also has a touchscreen—something that would never have happened in a prior Apple era.
It’s an outstanding, high-quality product, but whether it’s something you should buy depends on you—what you’re doing right now, what you’ll be doing in the future, and what you value.
Specifications and performance
For most of the specs we look at, Apple isn’t claiming any difference here. The new MacBook Pro promises 24 hours of battery life (though you’d have to use it in a conservative way to achieve that), it has the same ports (three Thunderbolt, one HDMI, one SDXC, and MagSafe), and it has the N1 chip for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 connectivity.
And like its immediate predecessor, it offers the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as options. Running synthetic benchmarks, we found no meaningful difference at all compared to when we ran the same tests on the previous model, so we won’t spend time discussing their performance today. We’ve covered both thoroughly in prior reviews, and you can read up there if you’d like.
The chips are more than fast enough for normal workflows for the foreseeable future, including most 3D work. AI inference is the main area where they may be less future-proof. To be clear, they’re strong enough for now, but the field is evolving rapidly, and there’s reason to expect significant improvements in future chips on this front.
According to Bloomberg, Apple is skipping Pro and Max versions of the M6 chip that was introduced earlier this year to focus its attention on a significant rework for the M7 due in 2027. “The M7 line is designed primarily around major advancements to on-device AI processing,” Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman wrote. The line would emphasize memory bandwidth, which matters for fast, efficient AI inference.
Even without Bloomberg’s report, I’d expect Apple to prioritize those areas in its next high-end chip refresh. That’s partly because there’s another tea leaf to read here: Apple made just such an update with the A20 Pro, which debuted in its latest iPhones several weeks ago. That update brought a substantially improved Neural Engine and a significant increase in memory bandwidth. We also found that the A20 Pro delivered improved 3D graphics performance in some cases.
Similar improvements could come to Macs, meaning it might be worth waiting another year if you’re focused on AI workflows or even 3D applications—especially given the high cost of these machines. That’s part of what makes this such an uncertain time to buy a laptop. We’re in a moment when these companies are revisiting the architecture of these chips because of these new workflows, and we don’t know what the end result is yet.
A monster of a display
Here’s one thing that’s not at all uncertain: The display on the MacBook Pro is the best I have ever used in a laptop. If the display is your primary concern, this is a big moment.
Apple calls it a “tandem OLED display,” meaning a panel with two emissive layers. This approach helps achieve a higher peak brightness, but perhaps more importantly, it can reduce the risk of burn-in. Most of the time, the display won’t need both layers running at full power. Instead, they can share the load and run at a reduced current, helping extend the panel’s lifespan.
The new display can achieve up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness on HDR highlights, but it’s rated for 1,000 nits of sustained brightness. In general, I like the way Apple handles HDR for this at the OS level, too.

The brightness matters for HDR content, sure, but what really makes OLED stand out is per-pixel illumination—meaning each pixel can turn on or off independently. That allows for absolute black levels and very strong contrast. The MiniLED display in the previous MacBook Pro offered good contrast for an LCD display, but OLED has a fundamental advantage here, and it shows.
As you’d expect, the screen offers native support for both P3 and Adobe RGB color gamuts. It also has a variable refresh rate from 10 to 120 Hz, just like many of Apple’s other products. As before, the MacBook Pro comes in roughly 14-inch (3,024×1,986 pixels) and 16-inch (3,472×2,226 pixels) variants. There’s also a nano-texture glass option to fight glare, though that will set you back another $150.
It’s one of the most impressive displays I’ve used in any device, and it’s certainly the best I’ve ever used on a laptop. The colors are vibrant, the contrast is outstanding, the blacks are inky, and it can get very bright when it needs to—not just with highlights but full-screen brightness as well. And on the whole, it’s extremely precise. Uniformity appears basically flawless. It’s what you’d expect from an ultra-high-end TV or reference monitor, not a laptop or computer screen, and it’s genuinely striking.
We’ll see about longevity, but OLED has come a long way in recent years, and my first impressions are that Apple has made all the right choices here.
I find myself trying to find something negative to say about the MacBook Pro’s screen to avoid sounding too effusive, but I can’t think of anything substantive. The best I can do is complain that Apple’s proprietary “PROLED XDR” label is silly and eye-roll-inducing.
Branding aside, the screen is the main reason to pay extra for this model.
Design
With its lid closed, the new MacBook Pro looks identical to its predecessor. The dimensions are largely the same. It’s slightly thinner, but you’d have to check the spec sheet or handle them side by side to notice.
Pick it up, though, and you’ll find that it’s noticeably lighter than the last model, by about half a pound. It’s not in a totally different weight class, but you can notice the change, and it’s a nice improvement. The reduction is partly due to the display technology switch; it’s easier to make a light OLED screen than a light MiniLED one.
Open the MacBook Pro and turn it on, and you’ll see one of a few other notable differences, depending on whether you’re behind or in front of it. From behind, you’ll see the Apple logo on the lid now lights up, as it did on MacBooks of yore. It’s arguably a little tacky, but it’s also neat and nostalgic. I don’t hate it.

From the front, you might notice that the already barely there bezels are even more barely there, though that’s subtle. More likely, you’ll see that the top-of-screen camera notch has been replaced by a cutout just like the Dynamic Island Apple introduced on the iPhone.
A comparatively sensible camera cutout
When I reviewed the first iPhone with a Dynamic Island, I was largely positive about it. No, it’s not ideal to have a cutout on the screen, but Apple has handled it as intelligently as possible, and I would even go so far as to say it has turned what should be an albatross into an attractive feature.
Thanks to the OLED display, it’s possible to make any of the pixels around the camera cutout just as black as it is. Apple has designed live activities, the volume bar, and more to appear as if they are expanding out of and around, and contracting back into, this little dot. It remains ingenious.
When the Dynamic Island first arrived on the iPhone, it helped unify several previously disparate approaches to displaying notifications in iOS, making it especially useful. This time, it doesn’t solve as many problems, but it’s an improvement over the dead weight of the notch. It also helps that the MacBook Pro’s much larger screen means the cutout takes up a small share of the screen’s real estate.

The Dynamic Island works the same with full-screen apps as the notch did. By default, the top of the viewport ends just below the Dynamic Island, so it just looks like there’s a taller top bezel, and it doesn’t cut into the application interface. The menu bar, clock, and other system elements still occupy the space above the application (set against a totally black background) when you move the cursor up there.
I tested a few fullscreen games with it, like World of Warcraft and Cyberpunk 2077. Some behaved by default like the default fullscreen app behavior I just described, but others tried to occupy the whole thing, making the cutout visible. Vitally, every video app I tried avoided the cutout in fullscreen.
This isn’t something to upgrade for, of course. But on the whole, I think it’s an improvement over what we had before.
The most touchable MacBook Pro ever
Apple has finally added a touchscreen to the MacBook Pro. I say “finally” because the possibility has floated around for about two decades. Steve Jobs was famously opposed to the idea; there’s even video of him explaining why he thought it would make for a poor user experience.
A couple of years ago, reliable reports emerged that Apple was moving forward with the idea regardless. When I first heard about it, I imagined what could be a really exciting implementation: a convertible laptop that would let you use it in a tablet-like mode, with Apple Pencil support for drawing and writing.
As a game developer, I imagined quickly sketching 2D game maps with an Apple Pencil, using a local AI model to convert them into 3D geometry, and then switching to a laptop configuration to start testing and coding. I also imagined using it like an iPad to more comfortably watch movies on a flight.
That’s not what we got, though. The laptop has the same form factor as the previous MacBook Pro model—no tablet mode or Pencil support. Instead, it just lets you reach up from the keyboard and trackpad to touch the screen. That feels like a missed opportunity.
Some creative apps have implemented touch features that might justify the touchscreen functionality if you use them a lot. For example, you can play the on-screen virtual piano keys on Logic Pro with multiple fingers, which could be nicer than clicking on them. I imagine many people already have workflows built around other approaches, though.
If you were specifically waiting for a touchscreen on your MacBook Pro, this seems like as good an implementation as you could hope for without turning the laptop into a convertible. Apple has put real care into it. For example, it has re-engineered the hinge so the screen is not particularly wobbly when you touch it. It’s fast, accurate, and responsive. It supports multi-touch gestures like pinch-to-zoom or swiping with three fingers to switch desktop spaces.
There’s one use case I find compelling as a developer. Testing iPhone and iPad apps in the Simulator has always been a minor hassle because of the difference in input methods. You either have to approximate only a subset of the interactions available to users with a trackpad and mouse or connect an iPhone or iPad to test them that way. A touchscreen could provide a more elegant way to test such apps in Xcode, Unity, or whatever else you might use.
Unfortunately, some of the UI elements in macOS are too small for my large fingers, so I have to tap very carefully. I also keep forgetting the touchscreen is even there for hours at a time and go back to my normal habits, partly because there’s nothing you can do at the OS level that you can’t do just as easily with trackpad gestures. And as Jobs predicted all those years ago, my arm got tired while I was using it.
For me, it feels faster, easier, more comfortable, and more natural to use the keyboard and trackpad 100 percent of the time, but I admittedly have decades of muscle memory and habits built around them. There’s apparently a generation coming up with the same kind of familiarity with touch interfaces, so this feature may appeal to them. Plus, touchscreen laptops have been a thing on Windows forever, and some people seem to want to buy them, though I never quite got why without an added tablet configuration.
It’s unlikely to account for a big portion of the device’s cost compared with the rest of the OLED panel, memory, storage, and so on. So, my own bafflement aside, I’m not unhappy it’s here. I imagine it will serve those who want it well enough.
The same excellent workstation—if you can afford it
As noted earlier, whether this laptop is worthy of a recommendation depends on you and how you use your machine. That’s always been the case, but it seems more so here.
If you’re a creative professional or a display enthusiast who wants the best laptop screen you’ve likely ever seen, you won’t be disappointed if you shell out for it. And hey, maybe you can show me your workflow and prove me wrong about the touchscreen!
If you’re just looking for a great laptop with strong performance for everyday use, consider the non-OLED, non-touchscreen model that’s still in Apple’s lineup—or even a MacBook Air, which compromises relatively little for most users. And there is, of course, the entire world of Windows and Linux laptops.
If you’re a developer—especially one working at the frontier of AI workflows—well, that’s where things get tricky. Will waiting be worthwhile? So much about how those workflows will evolve and what they’ll demand from your hardware is still so up in the air that I can’t make a confident recommendation. (For what it’s worth, I fit best in this category, and I’m still holding onto my M1 Max machine, though my resolve is wavering.)
All that said, in most ways, this is still the same MacBook Pro we’ve reviewed again and again for the past few years. Touch adds a feature aimed at a particular niche, or perhaps it’s there to roll out the welcome mat for a newer generation. The display is a more substantial update and makes a compelling case for upgrading, especially if you’re coming from an older, pre-MiniLED laptop.
But this is an expensive machine. The configuration I reviewed here (16-inch, M5 Max, 128 GB of RAM, 2 TB SSD) retails for a whopping $7,399, though you could at least shave $1,600 off that by going to a more typical-for-most-people 64 GB. (The cheapest configuration starts at $2,899.)
For the vast majority of buyers, the pre-OLED version that’s still in Apple’s lineup or another MacBook altogether will offer more bang for your buck. If you’re the kind of person who wants OLED or a touchscreen, though, you probably know that already. Based on my time with the new MacBook Pro, both features deliver on their promises, even if the latter isn’t as ambitious as some of us had hoped.
The good
Outstanding display that offers notably better and more accurate image quality while modestly reducing the weight of the device
The M5 Pro and M5 Max are still plenty fast for the majority of users
Strong build quality, solid port selection, and everything else we had positive to say about the last MacBook Pro, too
The bad
For certain workflows, the M5 Pro and M5 Max are already a few months old in an environment where things are moving very quickly
The RAM and SSD price crunch is real, and these prices are a formidable barrier for most people

Hollywood video engineer here. What's important for the displays we use is that they are reference displays; they meet the intended spec (normally within <1 CIE ΔE2000), and are calibrated to both make sure they do, and to know that they do.
You could say the same about music recording studios: Why bother working with massively expensive, "perfect" speakers in a pristine acoustic environment, where nobody will be listening to the music this way?
It comes down to, there is no "representative" mediocre consumer display that would be worth working on: What's out there in the world varies massively by the monitor's technology, age, price level, and viewing (or listening) environment.
A few mastering studios that could afford it, have put together rooms full of various consumer displays to do what you said: Look at the same content (in an identical environment!) to gauge what do contemporary TV's do to it. It's expensive (yes, even for Hollywood facilities), it's a moving target, and eventually it doesn't tell you a ton. There is a spec of what color on TV's should look like (ITU Rec.709, SMPTE ST 2084, etc.), and it's the TV companies' job to work off it.
And a colorist who's in a room with a director setting the look of a show, can't sit every day staring at 10 screens and playing guessing games. Similarly, audio monitor have a "flat" reference response curve that doesn't represent any common, bass-loving consumer headphones.
That said, the colorist or audio mixer's job includes understanding what consumer tech is like out there, and for example, they may absolutely consider that not everyone has an OLED TV when dialing in the dark shadows. And yes, colorists and producers watch the shows at home on their consumer TV, and they better be happy with the results!
FYI High-end consumer TV's can be very close to the pro monitors. For TV / streaming content, what's often in the room is a reference monitor (e.g. Sony BVM-HX310) and a consumer "client monitor", which may be an off-the-shelf consumer TV like an LG G5 (albeit professionally and carefully calibrated).

The countertop kitchen composter is a lovely thought. Instead of a smelly bucket of vegetable scraps and coffee grounds breeding fruit flies on your counter or attracting rats to your backyard, you could just put it all into a nifty electric gadget. Then, at some undetermined point in the future, you'll have a bountiful supply of nutrient-rich compost to use in your garden.
Unfortunately, none of the more popular electric kitchen composters do exactly this. Though some of these devices are marketed as “composters” and include instruction booklets and companion apps detailing the many ways to use compost, most will only grind up and dry your food scraps. You will greatly reduce your food waste output, and it will no longer smell, but if you’re hoping to put eggshells and banana peels into a machine and magically scoop out the kind of compost you’d buy at the garden center, that’s just not going to happen.
That said, you can mix small amounts of these grounds into potting soil in tiny ratios or use them as a feeder for a “real” compost pile. But again, most of these machines are meant for reducing the volume of household food waste. This is, itself, a legitimate goal, as cast-off food makes up an estimated 24 percent of municipal solid waste, resulting in the release of methane, a destructive greenhouse gas, as it breaks down in the landfill.
Or maybe you'd just like your food grounds to be odor-free and shelf-stable before adding them to your green waste bin for municipal composting or your backyard compost. In any case, despite critics’ cries of greenwashing and corporate astroturfing, there is indeed value to these devices. They make people more aware of their food waste. They don't use a huge amount of power (around 1 kilowatt-hour was typical in my testing). And my top pick, the Reencle Essential (8/10, WIRED Recommends), even produces something close to compost.

As I mentioned above, none of these machines makes truly ready-to-use, biologically stable, fully decomposed compost, but Reencle comes closest to creating what you'd scoop out of a traditional compost bin or pile. Popular in South Korea years before it appeared in the US, Reencle machines arrive with a starter bag of Reencle Compost Starter (which you can purchase separately for $52) containing activated carbon, wood pellets, glucose, and a trio of patented thermophilic microbes ready to chow down. There's also a prefilled charcoal filter that slots into the back.
The Essential is Reencle’s newest—and least expensive—model, with a refreshed, contemporary exterior; controls on the front instead of the top; and a lid that opens and closes manually. It's too large for a kitchen counter, but it conveniently operates much like a heated trash can. The lid opens via a manual button on the top of the unit, and in goes your organic matter. That's it. There are no cycles, tablets, or auxiliary buckets to worry about, and the cycle is barely louder than a refrigerator fan—about 28 decibels. Within hours to days, depending on the item, the scraps break down into a material resembling a cross between dirt and sawdust.
The smell isn't always pleasant, but you can usually mitigate this with the control panel's Dry and Purify buttons or by adding what, in composting lexicon, is called “browns”—dry, carbon-rich materials, like bread or shredded paper. The Reencle also tends not to stink when you feed it its preferred diet of 1.5 to 2.2 pounds of scraps per day. Unlike other machines, it can also accept meat and dairy.
When the volume reaches the fill line, it’s time to scoop out the grounds. At this point, you can mix the grounds with potting soil at a 1:4 ratio and leave it to cure for three weeks. (I used a large tub in my garage for this step.) Afterward, you can use it for both outdoor and indoor plants. I’ve used the resultant mix to positive effect both indoors and outdoors.

Most kitchen “composters" simply grind and dry your food scraps, but the Lomi 3 countertop composter does the best job of this of the bunch. All of these machines do a great job breaking down food scraps in some way or another, but none fully address what to do with them, absent a yard or compost pile. Adding them at a 1:10 (or even 1:15!) ratio to potting soil is kind of a pain, and many people don't have the space to store all this dirt. The Mill is the only device that solves this issue by allowing users to ship their grounds in a box via USPS to a farm in Washington state that repurposes the broken-down scraps for chicken feed (for an extra fee).
When I first tested the Mill in 2024 (6/10 WIRED Recommends), I didn't care for this idea, which seemed inefficient at best and canceled out the benefit of recycling the food waste at worst. I also didn't love the coarse texture of the grounds, having tried to use them in my garden and finding them too easily rehydrated. The price also seemed over the top for what's essentially an oversized Lomi. But if you're looking to reduce the amount of food waste leaving your house, the Mill has the best ease of use, requiring the least amount of work on a user's part.

There's an almost encyclopedic directory of what can and can't go in the machine, as well as a tracker that shows how many pounds of waste you've diverted over time. The Mill also has a massive capacity that only needs emptying about once a month—a claim I found to be accurate during my testing period. It's on the louder side at around 60 dB, so I highly recommend scheduling its processing cycle to run at night.

The Analog OG
In order to understand the intended purpose of electric composters, one first needs to know about the original indoor home composting method: the bokashi bin. Unlike traditional outdoor composting, which is straightforward anaerobic decomposition, the bokashi method, invented in Japan in the 1980s, is anaerobic fermentation. This method is a bit like quick-pickling your food waste to prep it for the decomposition process. The food scraps still need to decompose, but this gets it part of the way there with the least amount of hassle and time. In fact, some gardeners even prefer bokashi to compost, as the output retains nitrogen, a critical plant nutrient.
To start, put your food scraps in the included bucket, and once you have about a 1-inch layer of waste, add a sprinkling of microbe-infused bran (a 2-pound bag of bran with a little spouted measuring cup is included with the Bokashi Living kit). The instruction booklet for my Bokashi Bin also recommended putting a plate inside the bucket to push down the contents. Compost “tea,” or liquid byproduct of the fermentation process, can drain through a spigot on the bottom every couple of days and then be added to your outdoor plants. The smell is reminiscent of kombucha brewed in a hot dumpster with diapers and stale beer, so be sure to rinse out the cup each time.
Once your bin is full, let it sit for two weeks, and your food waste will have broken down enough to bury in your garden or add to your backyard compost. I admit I struggled with this part—after two weeks, my scraps looked much the same, only stinkier and slimier. Bokashi Living says on its website that this is normal: If it has a pickle-like smell and produces bokashi tea, it's a success.
I’ll admit it was refreshing at first to have a device that didn’t make noise, need maintenance, or use electricity, but a few weeks into testing the Bokashi Bin, I found myself sorely missing my Reencle. I didn’t keep a separate scrap bin on the countertop, so every time I needed to add refuse to the bucket, I had to peel the lid off with my dirty hands and remove the plate, which then made my hands even dirtier. The smell of fermenting food waste would then immediately—and as time went on, almost violently—permeate the kitchen and its vicinity. I certainly prefer any of the electric options listed above, but bokashi has its devoted adherents. If what I've detailed above doesn't sound bothersome to you, it may be worth a try.

Other Kitchen Composters I Tried
Clear Drop Organics Collector (OC) for $399: From the makers of the innovative Soft Plastic Compactor, this simple white box does not claim to grind, process, or compost your food scraps; it simply stores up to 3.5 gallons' worth of them in an enclosed container with a fan and carbon filter for odor control. For its part, the OC did this well. I also appreciated the included paper-bag liners, which made it easy to drop off the scraps at a nearby collection bin, as my town does not have municipal compost. I also loved the sensor-activated lid that slides back and forth. Clear Drop posits that municipal composting is the best option overall for reducing waste via compost, because the process can be standardized for quality and is easy for everyone to comply. I agree, but let's be real: You can get a carbon-filter compost canister for less than $30. If taking the compost out every couple of days instead of every seven days is a chore you're willing to pay $400 to avoid, then knock yourself out. But you should know that the OC makes a loud fan noise—40 decibels on my decibel meter—which annoyed everyone in my household so much that I didn't even make it through the full test period.
Vego Countertop Kitchen Composter for $360: This grind-and-dry processor is roughly the same size as the Lomi, with many of the same operational features, but it is significantly less expensive. However, there are definitely some inconveniences that come with the lower price point. For one, you need to add scraps into the bucket while it’s seated in the machine. You can remove the bucket, but unlike with the FoodCycler, there's no separate lid for the bucket, and the metal mechanism underneath is exposed. Further, the machine’s lid is a bona fide pain to get on and off, requiring precise alignment of notches and two hands to wrench it open or closed. Needless to say, this is no easy feat with fists full of scraps. Vego claims its Vego mode does create a biologically active soil amendment when processed with one of the included VegoTabs (packet of 30, $30 if purchased separately). In all modes, but Vego mode especially, the barrel turns every couple of minutes, emitting a loud whirring. Because the sound isn't constant, it's more noticeable. Even from 10 feet away, I found it obtrusive enough to want to turn up the TV volume.
GEME Terra II for $700: Billed as the first “AI-powered kitchen appliance that uses industrial-grade microbes to turn waste into living soil,” this machine was the largest and bulkiest one I've tested (12 inches long, 22 inches high) and operates much like the Reencle, with a heated, enclosed container and a bag of proprietary starter microbes. Instead of a replaceable carbon filter, it uses a metal-ion purification system. Also similar to the Reencle, the GEME does not make ready-to-use compost but, rather, pre-compost that can be mixed with dirt. The role AI plays in this process is unclear: I couldn’t find an explanation on the website, on the machine itself, or in the instruction booklet. (GEME says it is working on an improved description.) The Terra II's signature feature is that its industrial-grade microbes can withstand the supposed high heat of the breakdown process. However, when I put a temperature probe into the Terra II's pre-compost after I'd had it running for about a week, it was 97 degrees Fahrenheit—nowhere near hot enough to kill pathogens. Further, during my testing period, this machine emitted a constant fan noise, like a range hood on medium speed—46 decibels on my decibel meter, which was loud enough to be disruptive.
FoodCycler Eco 5 for $500: Like the Eco 3 above, this is a food recycler and doesn’t claim to create true compost. It’s a large, quiet machine; my 3-year-old likes to turn it on when I’m not looking, and I don’t notice until I see that the blue light is on. The result doesn’t look like compost, but it does get ground down to some bare-bones food bits after several extra cycles my son initiates with his sneaky button-pushing. Each cycle runs between four and nine hours. It hasn’t been stinky, and I’ve found it handy to have nearby in the kitchen for food waste. It is quite large, though—nearly as bulky as my robot vacuum station due to its 5-liter capacity. The cheaper Eco 3 is likely a more efficient use of space in the kitchen, unless you have a ton of food scraps on a regular basis and really need the larger-capacity bin. —Nena Farrell
How I Tested
I cook daily for my family of three, and I've been processing our kitchen scraps in these composters in my home kitchen since the summer of 2024. I tested each machine under typical household use for a minimum of four weeks each, and in several cases, six weeks or longer. I tested all cycles offered, with all manner of foods allowed, according to each manual. I even attempted to use the finished product in my yard and potted plants (to varying effect). I acquired the units either by purchasing them myself or receiving them as samples from companies (with no expectation of coverage). When I completed testing, I donated or returned some units and kept others in office storage.

Your iPhone Duo can do more than multitask! These 10 quirky apps turn the foldable into a retro computer, cassette player, Nintendo DS, accordion, instant camera, virtual fridge, and even a grilled cheese toaster. Some are free, others paid, but all make clever, fun use of its folding design.
The iPhone Duo is perhaps the most radically different iPhone since the original iPhone. While its arrival was rumored for over a year, Apple finally launched it this September. The phone can fold in half to become nearly passport-sized and can be unfolded to shape-shift into a bigger, tablet-ish smartphone. Ever since its launch, we have been constantly hearing about its multitasking prowess, its computer-like processing abilities, how well it handles productivity apps, yada yada yada…
But all this is pretty basic, something we expect with all new iPhones, or rather flagship smartphones at this point. With the kind of price and specs these high-end smartphones come with, it hardly is a surprise that they can handle power-hungry tasks with ease. The foldable form-factor and the added display real estate make it a different experience, surely. But surely there is way more to the device than the same old tasks and apps? So, we are on a mission to make your iPhone Duo fun, using all that processing and multitasking magic that it possesses.
The result is these ten apps.
They are not at all useful. But they make the Duo a-not-just-another-serious (read: boring) device out there. They add an element to it that we all so need to survive – they make it fun. Got an iPhone Duo? Download! (Note: relax, all of these are optimized for the iPhone Duo)

Tiny Computer (USD 3.99): Unfolding Retro computer feels
Imagine getting a vintage PC feel on something as new and pristine as the iPhone Duo? That is exactly what the app Tiny Computer can deliver. Using the half-fold setting of the iPhone Duo, the app turns your phone into a proper vintage computer. The upper half of the screen becomes the display while the lower half becomes the keyboard. You get to choose from ten different computers in total, including the Apple Macintosh, IBM PC, iMac G3, IBM ThinkPad, Windows XP, Amiga 500, and more.
It is not just all show; you can actually use some retro paint apps, run old command-line interfaces, play games like Solitaire, and even type on clicky keyboards. Each machine also hides secret commands and files paired with occasional crashes to make the whole experience even more believable.
Deck Man (USD 4.99): Go cassette crazy!
Another app that brings retro feels to the Duo is the Deck Man. It is one of the most visually appealing apps for the Duo because it essentially turns your iPhone Duo into a 1980s cassette Walkman player. The app uses the unfolded version of the phone as the collection of cassettes in your music library that you can browse. You then “insert” the cassette of your choice into the deck, and once you fold it, the secondary screen mimics the look of a cassette Walkman player.
The app has realistic mechanical clicks, background tape static, and if you fast-forward or rewind it too aggressively, the virtual tape inside can get all tangled and then would have to be untangled manually, just like a retro cassette player. “Tape” this one to your Duo!
MD Vinyl (Free): Spin those discs!
If cassettes are “too” modern for you, then you can go even further back in the music era with the iPhone Duo by installing MD Vinyl. This essentially turns the Duo into a virtual turntable with spinning records and album art. The record design determines the aesthetics of the app. The app allows you to pick and drop the needle to play or pause the tracks. It can pair with music apps like Apple Music and Spotify. It is not a new app and has existed for years, but it attains a whole new dimension on the Duo, adding a vintage touch to the modern audio experience.
Fold Accordion (USD 2.99): Fold and unfold to create music
If there is one app that makes the most use of the iPhone Duo’s form factor, it is the Fold Accordion. It literally turns the hinge of the iPhone Duo into working accordion bellows. When you launch the app, it places the keys on the display, which you can press with your right hand while opening and closing the Duo with the left hand to create music of your own. The app comes with a learning mode which highlights keys you have to press to create something pleasant, instead of getting straight to the chaos of keys. A great way to test that folding mechanism too.
Delta (Nintendo DS) (free): Double screen gaming magic, DS style!
Popular Retro Game emulator Delta has launched an updated version of its app, specifically for the iPhone Duo. The app brings specially designed skins for the iPhone Duo, and the most interesting one of the lot is the Nintendo DS portable gaming console, which interestingly was the world’s first mainstream foldable device. The app uses the inner display of the iPhone Duo to bring a DS-style layout and controls across the displays. The game even enters sleep state when the device is folded, similar to the Nintendo DS. Trust the Duo to bring back the magic of double-screen gaming.
Toastie (USD 2.99): Smartest thing since sliced bread!
Unleash the inner chef in you with the absolutely useless but equally fun app called Toastie. This app turns the iPhone Duo into a – wait for it – virtual grilled cheese toaster. You get 15 seconds to assemble your sandwich, and once you are done, you have to hit the ‘grill’ button and physically close the iPhone Duo shut. You then have to wait, listen to the sizzle, or get a slight peek to ensure your toastie is grilling well. If you open the phone too soon, the cheese won’t be melted; if you wait too long, it might end up getting burned. Once you are done with it, you serve it, and you get a star based on your accuracy, recipe, timing, and so on. Useful? Not. But definitely the smartest thing since sliced bread. Actually, the smartest thing done to sliced bread!
TypeDraw (USD 4.99): Paper-like Moleskine
The iPhone Duo looks like a handy pocket notebook or a passport, and TypeDraw literally converts it into a handy little Moleskine-like notebook. It even comes with a digital thread, just like you find on a notebook, which you have to move or swipe aside to open the notebook (or just open the Duo). You can write anywhere on a page using an Apple Pencil or your finger and can even fiddle and curl up paper corners, as well as choose fonts (you can convert your handwriting into one, if you wish), types of paper, and even plain, ruled, dotted, or grid patterns on paper. And the page turns on the internal display are absolutely paper-like. It is like carrying a real notebook.
Snapshots ($1.99): Unfold to Polaroid
Snapshots is an app that helps your Duo morph into an instant camera. It is one of the very first community-developed apps optimized specifically for the iPhone Duo. When bent in half (90 degrees), the top half of the primary display becomes the viewfinder while the bottom half holds the controls. Once you hit the shutter, the photo captured on the upper half of the viewfinder is virtually printed on the lower half with the same mechanical sound and effect as on an instant camera. Just like with a real instant camera, the photo does not appear right away but takes a few seconds to develop, giving us those Polaroid feels.
Phridge (free): Chill…literally!
This is perhaps the most quirky and our personal favorite app in the list. It turns the iPhone Duo into a – wait for it – refrigerator. When folded, you can decorate the ‘door’ of this fridge with magnets, to-do lists, photographs. And when you open it, you can see groceries and food and drink inside and arrange them. This is when the real fun happens, because you can topple something over, drop a fizzy drink, or break a glass jar or bottle. You can also place your hand in a slingshot to shoot stones at the shelves, or get a sword to slice things in half, if you feel like some chaos. You can only close the fridge when you fold the phone shut, making the hinge integral to its operation. How cool is that? Just chillin…
Chompduo (Free): Jaw-dropping (and closing) stuff!
We all need an app that adds six hungry monsters to your iPhone Duo. Well, we do, anyway. That is exactly what ChompDuo does. When installed, it unleashes six hungry monsters on your Duo that open their huge mouths when the device is unfolded, making the inner display a giant mouth. You can tap on the open mouth to make it bite or drag it to squeeze it shut. When you fold the phone, the jaws close shut with a chomp sound, and a pair of googly eyes appear on the outer display, which can jump when you tap on them. What more does one need on a foldable?

The Enforcement Directorate (ED) conducted searches at three premises linked to crypto exchanges CoinDCX and Delta Exchange India (DEI) over alleged unauthorised cross-border transactions involving crypto derivatives and tokenised foreign stocks. In a statement, the agency said the searches were conducted between November 4 and November 5 across Bengaluru. The crypto trading transactions in question run into thousands of crores of Rupees, as per ED. “ED Bengaluru has conducted search(es) at three premises linked to Neblio Technologies Pvt. Ltd. (CoinDCX parent) and Excelium Technologies Pvt. Ltd.(which operates Delta Exchange India) under FEMA 1999 in the case of large scale unauthorised cross-border financial transactions involving crypto token derivatives and real world asset tokens,” said ED in a statement. As per the directorate, ED began its probe into the matter after receiving information of alleged forex violations by CoinDCX and Delta Exchange India. The agency alleged that CoinDCX and Delta Exchange India facilitated spot trading, futures and options (F&O) trading and trading in tokenised shares of foreign companies – all through cryptocurrencies. ED also claimed CoinDCX advertised these products despite not being authorised to offer them. While CoinDCX is yet to issue a statement on the matter, Delta Exchange India said that it cooperated “fully” with the officials and furnished the information sought. In a post on X, the crypto exchange further claimed that it is not involved in “any cross-border transfer of VDAs (virtual digital assets) in any form or manner”. “We acknowledge the Enforcement Directorate’s statement regarding their visit to our premises on 4th & 5th November… We cooperated fully with the officials and provided the information that they sought. We remain committed to extending our support and cooperation as may be required…,” said Delta Exchange India. CoinDCX's Alleged Modus Operandi According to the ED, user funds (deposited in Rupees) were allegedly converted into stablecoins, primarily USDT, and then transferred to overseas crypto platforms including Binance, KuCoin, Gate.io and Bybit. The agency alleged that these transfers circumvented forex rules governing cross-border money transfers. For spot trades, the ED alleged that CoinDCX used an account, opened in the name of a Costa Rica-based entity, to send the USDT to foreign crypto platforms. Describing the Costa Rican company as a mere “paper entity”, the agency alleged that the transactions were allegedly actually executed directly through CoinDCX APIs. The directorate also made similar allegations for CoinDCX’s F&O product. ED said that the homegrown platform allegedly opened matching positions via APIs on foreign platforms after users placed orders, with settlements occurring overseas when positions were closed. The ED also claimed that tokenised-stock trading on CoinDCX was routed through Hyperliquid, an overseas decentralised crypto trading platform. It said that user funds were converted into USDT to open positions, with settlements completed on the overseas platform. The alleged volumes of spot, derivatives and tokenised-stock transactions were described as running into thousands of crores of rupees. The ED also alleged that CoinDCX paid hundreds of crores in transaction fees to foreign platforms in stablecoins. This, the agency said, contravened forex rules. Delta Exchange India Under ED Radar Just like CoinDCX, the Enforcement Directorate also alleged that Delta Exchange India offered spot trading, crypto derivatives and tokenised foreign stocks via cryptocurrencies. It alleged that a large volume of DEI’s derivatives and tokenised-stock transactions was routed through CoinDCX, which in turn executed them on foreign platforms. The agency alleged that Delta Exchange India also transferred hundreds of crores of Rupees to overseas associate entities. These transfers are under investigation, added the ED. In a statement, the ED said the fintech products offered by both crypto exchanges appear to have prima facie contravened norms under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956, the SEBI Act, 1992 and the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. The investigation remains ongoing. The searches are part of ED’s broader clampdown on forex violations involving crypto platforms. Just days ago, the directorate launched a probe into alleged FEMA violations involving crypto platforms Mudrex and Saber.money as well as decentralised finance (DeFi) protocol Instadapp and its associated platform, Fluid, over alleged unauthorised cross-border fund transfers worth more than ₹4,940 Cr. Prior to this in June this year, the ED had also searched six premises linked to five platforms, namely Transak, Carret, Xpat, Onramp.money and Onmeta, over alleged unauthorised cross-border crypto transfers.

Kemi Badenoch says Donald Trump 'deserved to be thrashed' in the US elections and has denounced his 'dirty' style of politics.
In a sweeping attack on the American President's record she criticised him over the Iran War, for threatening Canada and Greenland, imposing swingeing tariffs and “squabbling with allies” like the UK.
Trump's heavy defeat in the US mid term elections was “entirely self inflicted”, she told The Independent Editor-in-Chief Geordie Greig.
Controversially, Badenoch said she would have been content if Trump had never won a second term in the White House and his Democrat opponent, Left winger Kamala Harris had become President in 2024 instead.
WATCH IN FULL: Kemi Badenoch’s interview with The Independent
In the wide-ranging exclusive interview for The Talk Show, Badenoch also savaged Tory predecessors Boris Johnson and Liz Truss for their “mistakes” in government.
She said Andy Burnham was more “fun” than Keir Starmer, but behind the “charm” he was “dangerous.”
She called Nigel Farage's Reform Party “bonkers” and ruled out serving in a Conservative-Reform Coalition led by him.
But she conceded that before his dip in popularity, Farage had made an “emotional connection” with voters that the Tories had lost until she became leader.
Badenoch's outspoken condemnation of Trump's policies and personality may come as a surprise, especially to Tory supporters, some of whom urged her to copy him after he won power.
Asked if he deserved to be thrashed, she did not hesitate: “Yeah. He has not been acting in the way that I would consider conservative. Where is the push for free markets and better trade... rather than protectionism, America first, the squabbling with allies? That's not what conservatives do.
“Trump is very charming in person, but you see the way that he talks about journalists, about individuals. It doesn't meet the standards a statesman should meet - always wanting to get dirty in terms of insults and and so on.
“When he was rude about Keir Starmer... I didn't like that at all. What they did to President Zelensky in the White House was awful.”
Trump had won power “with an extraordinary coalition of Latinos, more Black voters than any other Republican” - and wasted it.
“What's the first thing he does? Tariffs, and then talking about Greenland and Canada. A lot of people were wondering, ‘what are you doing?’”
She understood Trump's initial decision to go to war with Iran - which she had backed.
“We don't want them getting nuclear weapons. But where's the plan?”

His defeat in the mid term elections was “entirely self-inflicted”, she said. “Voters want results.”
Ms Badenoch claimed she would have been happy if Trump had lost the last presidential election - and revealed a hitherto unknown admiration for fellow black female politician Kamala Harris.
“People ask me who did I prefer, Kamala Harris, Donald Trump? I would say I like them both equally. Make of that what you will.”
While refusing to 'name and blame' former Conservative PMs Johnson and Truss, she was fiercely critical of both their records in No 10. They were guilty of “gimmicks, mistakes and short termism. Everybody made mistakes. Obviously, the leaders were responsible for most of them. Immigration was too high.”
Did she mean Johnson and the so called 'Boris wave' of immigration?
“People know who the prime minister was then,” she said, removing all doubt.
Truss got equally short shrift. Badenoch savaged the disastrous budget that saw Truss kicked out of Downing Street after six weeks.
“You can't just announce £150 billion bailing out people's energy bills and £45 billion of tax cuts with no spending cuts at all,” she said disbelievingly.
“Those are the wrong way of doing things.”
READ MORE Kemi Badenoch: 'I watched a man being beaten to death in front of me'
Rather than call out Johnson and Truss personally, Badenoch, a Methodist, quoted St Augustine: “Hate the sin, love the sinner.”
She deflected the notion that Burnham's “charm” has revived Labour fortunes since awkward Starmer's demise.
Calling him a “foot in mouth” politician, she says: “He says things first and then thinks about it later.”
He is more genial. I'm not sure I would call it charm. He looks like he'd be more fun company at a party, (but) that makes him more dangerous because he wants to please everybody.”
With the latest polls indicating the Conservatives have narrowed the gap with Labour to two points, she insists she has his measure, boasting: “The more Andy Burnham sees of me, the less he wants to have an early election.”
She is equally confident about seeing off the challenge from Farage, whose ratings have fallen in the wake of a series of scandals to hit him and Reform. It has coincided with the Conservatives overtaking Reform in the political ratings war.
“At the moment, I am beating him, and I think he's very worried about that.”
She freely admitted Farage initially struck a chord with the public at a time the Tories were floundering.
“What worked for him was having an emotional connection and an authenticity which we as a party had lost, sounding very technocratic.”
That had all changed now she was Tory leader and the shine was coming off Farage.
“One of the things going wrong for him was that he pretended to be this everyman.
“A lot of his supporters... don't understand how he's getting £5 million and they're not able to pay their energy bills.”
It was up to a Commons inquiry to decide if Farage's £5 million donation from a crypto currency billionaire was “corrupt”, said Badenoch. But she has made up her mind.
“His story doesn't add up.”
She is just as adamant she would never serve under 'Prime Minister Farage.'
“No, because he would not be good for this country. I simply wouldn't.”
Some of Reform's ideas, such as a recent proposal to ‘nationalise Poundland' were plain “bonkers”.
She claimed Farage did her a favour with the acrimonious defection of defeated Tory leadership rival Robert Jenrick to Reform earlier this year.
Getting rid of Jenrick was like defusing an “unexploded bomb” - leaks from the Shadow Cabinet ceased overnight, she said.
Badenoch joked: “The only thing I haven't done is written a thank you card to Nigel Farage for taking these problems away. I'll write it in his Christmas card!”
She defended her aggressive style at the Commons despatch box.
“You have to be a fighter to survive. There are 400 Labour MPs screaming and shouting. I need to put some of those people in their place. It's a kill or be killed arena.”
Which explains why she refused to say sorry for calling ex Education Secretary Bridget Phillipson “spiteful” for the closure of private schools as a result of Labour's VAT on school fees.
“Spiteful. What's wrong with that?” she retorted.
“She hurt many, many children. They had to leave their schools, which closed down. It was class war. So yes, I will call it like it is.
“We've spent a lot of time dressing things up in fancy words where most of the public don't understand what we're talking about.”
After putting a difficult start as Conservative leader behind her, Ms Badenoch said Labour and Reform jibes do not get under her thick skin. Even if they did she would not show it.
She is proud of being a 'cool customer,' adding: “I'm a poker player. I have a very good poker face.
“I remember saying to some people I get better every day, and they mocked it. But it's true. I believe in continuous improvement.”

Large language models are already communicating with humans in dozens of languages everyday. Turns out it may not be a stretch to use them to talk with dolphins, too.
That’s the premise of research by Denise Herzing, the founder and director of the Wild Dolphin Project. Herzing first began thinking about how the marine mammals communicate while on a 1985 trip to the Bahamas to study Atlantic spotted dolphins after hearing their telltale clicks and whistles.
It’s been a 40-year wait, but AI is finally allowing Herzing to untangle what dolphins are saying, she told the audience at WIRED World Fair. Her research group has gathered countless hours of video and audio footage of dolphins, and it’s now working with scientists at Georgia Tech as well as Google DeepMind to give structure to dolphins’ language—if not fully translate it yet.
“With AI, we can find patterns,” she said, adding, “This is a powerful new tool. I’ve personally been waiting for it.”
The team has used some of that research to even attempt two-way communication by rigging up an underwater, wearable computer that can play dolphin sounds. That includes using sounds to indicate items like a scarf and habitat like sargassum—a seaweed. Two researchers would model behavior—one researcher would play the scarf sound, for instance, and then the other would play with it—and then see how the dolphins responded.
One of the challenges, though, is decoding communication from mimicry. “Even though we had these whistles and are labeling toys, there’s a big difference between mimicking and understanding the function,” Herzig said. “That’s hard to do in the wild.”
Working in a sanctuary or more controlled environment might help researchers suss out the difference, she said.
What dolphins are actually saying to each other remains a bit of a mystery. While Herzig’s team has done a job of finding patterns, a two-way conversation remains a ways off. That’s because while humans have made pretty decent headway in understanding dolphin social hierarchies and behavior, there’s more work needed to really enable a conversation.
“We might have the data and the structure, but what does it mean in dolphin culture?” she said. “That’s going to be an exploration on its own.”
Being able to talk with dolphins would, of course, be very cool. (Who hasn’t dreamed of talking with animals after all?) But ultimately our attempts to understand dolphins could help us understand more about ourselves and our relationship with the planet. Herzig said that when she asks people what they think dolphins would say to us, the most common response is along the lines of “the dolphins would say ‘Why are you messing up our ocean?’”
That answer, she said, “tells you how we are thinking about the world.”
