The measure, which may face legal challenges, requires girls who want to play in girls' sports to produce documentation from a healthcare provider who has verified "the student's biological sex" relying on the student's reproductive anatomy — in other words, a genital exam — genetic makeup or their natural testosterone levels. Due to how expensive genetic and testosterone testing can be, the genital exams are the most accessible option.
In the aftermath of Election Day, social media users circulated a rumor that Washington voters passed an anti-trans measure that would allegedly subject girls who want to play school sports in the state to genital inspections. 
The rumor spread on X, Threads and Bluesky. Some posts shared additional alleged context, claiming that the ballot measure would subject children who want to play in girls' sports to genital inspections. Others dismissed these claims as a "fantasy."
Washington voters did, in fact, pass a measure called Initiative 26-638 aimed at banning trans girls from playing in girls' sports. The act requires medical providers to "verify" a student's biological sex using reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup or naturally produced testosterone levels.
In theory, the law does not explicitly require genital exams for anyone because it provides three options for sex verification. In practice, due to how expensive genetic and testosterone testing can be, the genital exams are the most accessible option, according to child advocacy groups and medical providers who oppose the provision.
It is worth noting these tests cannot necessarily definitively determine a person's biological sex, which scientists say is a complex category.
The measure subjects every girl who wishes to play in girls' school sports to sex verification, but does not subject students who wish to participate in boys' sports to the same scrutiny. The Washington Interscholastic Activities Association reportedly said earlier this year that it was aware of 10 trans student athletes total in the state; it's unclear how many of these athletes are trans boys, as opposed to trans girls. 
While the Washington secretary of state website indicates that there are still ballots left to count, as of this writing, support for the measure has a 13-point lead over opposition. Furthermore, The Associated Press called the race, stating that the "Yes" vote won.
Snopes, like many credible media publications, relies on AP calls for elections. As such, we have rated this claim as true.
(Some posts stated that the measure was "winning" or had won before AP called the race; ultimately, those posts turned out to be true, even if they called the race early.)
It's worth noting that the act may face legal challenges.
"Many have said that I-638 is likely unconstitutional and we understand there are legal groups and organizations considering litigation," said No Hate in WA State, the main coalition opposing the measure. The American Civil Liberties Union-Washington said in its own statement that it was "exploring all potential next steps to uphold the rights of transgender girls and their access to school sports."
I-638's text, examined
The complete text for I-638 is available on the Washington secretary of state's website. Here's the relevant section (emphasis ours):
NEW SECTION. Sec. 3. A new section is added to chapter 28A.600 RCW to read as follows:
(1) Policies, procedures, rules, and other requirements adopted in accordance with RCW 28A.600.200 by a school district board of directors or a voluntary nonprofit entity must prohibit biologically male students from competing with and against female students in athletic activities with separate classifications for male and female students if the athletic activity is:
(a) Intended for female students only; and
(b) An individual or team competition activity.
(2) A student who elects to participate in individual or team competition activities intended for female students only governed under subsection (1) of this section shall provide, as part of the required routine sports physical examination, a health examination and consent form or other statement signed by the student's personal health care provider that verifies the student's biological sex, relying only on one or more of the following: The student's reproductive anatomy, genetic makeup, or normal endogenously produced testosterone levels.
As opponents to I-638 have noted, a birth certificate would not be an acceptable form of sex verification under I-638. About 28% of K-12 school-age girls in Washington do not have a personal doctor or nurse, meaning that it's likely many families would not be able to rely on an established medical history with a health care provider.
The nonpartisan Washington State Parent Teacher Association, the largest volunteer and child advocacy organization in the state, opposed I-638 on the grounds that it would likely require many girls to either undergo an intimate, embarrassing and medically unnecessary genital examination or forgo playing in girls' sports. Here's what the organization said (emphasis ours):
Two of the three permitted methods, genetic testing and testosterone measurement, are expensive and unlikely to be covered by insurance for this purpose, since neither is clinically indicated. That makes an examination of reproductive anatomy the most accessible pathway for most families.
The burden falls hardest on rural, uninsured, and lower-income families, and on families without an established relationship with a healthcare provider — who face the added problem that the measure never says what qualifies someone as a student's "personal health care provider."
Doctors and medical professionals opposing the initiative shared similar warnings and noted that major medical organizations advise against pelvic exams for adolescent girls, with some citing psychological harms and potential future avoidance of medical care. The Washington Academy of Family Physicians and the Washington State Nurses Association opposed the measure.
The Seattle Times reported that doctors may interpret the measure differently, given that it's vague and, in some views, "poorly written."

Toll in Old Delhi's Chawri Bazar building collapse rises to 3 as another body pulled out
The deceased was identified as Pankaj Sharma, a resident of Hanuman Nagar village in Bihar’s Khagaria district.
The body of a 40-year-old man was recovered from the debris of the collapsed building in Old Delhi’s Hauz Qazi in the early hours of Saturday, taking the death toll in the incident to three, police said.
The deceased was identified as Pankaj Sharma, a resident of Hanuman Nagar village in Bihar’s Khagaria district, deputy commissioner of police (central) Rohit Rajbir Singh said.
With the latest recovery, five people have now been pulled out of the debris, including three who died and two who sustained injuries. Both injured workers have received medical treatment and are stable, officials said. Rescue operations were continuing at the site at the time of filing this report.
The Hauz Qazi collapse
The recovery comes two days after a three-storey building under construction collapsed in the narrow lanes of Chawri Bazar on Thursday morning, trapping construction workers under the debris.
The building, located in Gali Sitara near Chawri Bazar Metro station, reportedly collapsed in two stages around 9.30am while construction work was underway.
The collapse has also raised questions about alleged negligence during construction, with the police arresting three contractors in the early hours of Friday. The contractors allegedly ignored repeated warnings from workers about the poor quality of the construction materials and the structure's inability to support another concrete slab, according to the first information report (FIR) registered in the case.
DCP Singh identified the accused as Siraj, Tajuddin and Furkan, all residents of the Ajmeri Gate area. They were arrested from Sirohi village in Faridabad's Dauj tehsil.
Workers raised concerns
In his complaint to the police, Firoz, a 37-year-old construction worker from Bihar who lives in Mandawali and survived the collapse, alleged that the contractors repeatedly disregarded workers' concerns about the building's structural stability.
According to his statement, he and other workers had been engaged by the contractors to carry out construction on a plot measuring around 70 square yards. Three concrete slabs, locally referred to as lanterns, had already been laid at the property.
The workers allegedly warned that the existing slab was not strong enough to support another slab and that it required additional cement and wooden support.
“We had informed the contractors that the lintel had not dried up and we cannot put another one... to support the lintel, more cement and wood is required... but they asked us to continue, saying that the cost would increase,” Firoz said in the FIR, a copy of which was accessed by HT.
Firoz also told the police that they had attempted to raise their concerns with the property owners. However, the owners allegedly told them that the contractors were handling the construction and that they should approach the contractors instead.
Around 9.30am on Thursday, Firoz and the other workers were carrying out construction when the building suddenly gave way. Two of his fellow workers were trapped under the debris, while he was working in the rear portion of the structure and managed to survive.
The FIR
The FIR names Tajuddin and Furkan as accused and invokes sections 105 (culpable homicide not amounting to murder), 290 (negligent conduct with respect to pulling down, repairing or constructing buildings), 125(a) (negligent act with respect to buildings) and 3(5) (common intention) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS).
The collapse has also brought renewed scrutiny on the civic authorities, particularly after it emerged that Delhi Police had alerted the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) about construction activity at the property nearly five months before the incident.
Police flagged construction
In a letter dated June 15, the station house officer of Hauz Qazi police station had alerted the deputy commissioner of MCD's City SP Zone about new residential construction spread over around 70 square yards at property number 4547-48 in Wali Sheesh Mahal, Ajmeri Gate, and sought action.
The MCD acknowledged receipt of the communication but said a subsequent inspection found that the owner was undertaking repair work that its maintenance department had advised in April.
However, an inquiry by the civic body alleged that the owner used the repair advisory as a cover to clandestinely undertake fresh construction on the second and third floors without the requisite permissions.
The MCD inquiry report also flagged discrepancies in the property's tax declarations, alleging that excess floor coverage had been declared to mislead authorities and to claim protection under laws applicable to older structures.
The building reportedly lacked a sanctioned building plan, raising questions about how construction was allowed to continue despite earlier police communication to the civic body.
Issues facing rescue
The rescue operation on Thursday was severely hampered by the extremely narrow lanes of the walled city, which prevented heavy machinery, including JCB excavators, from reaching the site of the collapse. Fire personnel and other rescue teams had to rely largely on manually removing debris to reach those trapped beneath.
Residents of neighbouring buildings were also evacuated after police warned that one of the adjoining structures was in a precarious condition.
Meanwhile, chief minister Rekha Gupta ordered the immediate suspension of the junior engineer and assistant engineer concerned, a detailed inquiry into the collapse and registration of an FIR against the contractor. She also directed officials to ensure the best possible medical treatment for the injured and provide ex gratia assistance to the families of the deceased.
Police are continuing their investigation into the circumstances leading to the collapse, including the alleged violations during construction and the role of the contractors and property owners.

First Diwali where Naxalism has been eliminated: PM celebrates with jawans in Bastar
Prime Minister Narendra Modi celebrated Diwali with security personnel in Bastar, Chhattisgarh, calling 2026 a historic year in India's fight against Naxalism. He credited soldiers and security forces for helping free every district from Maoist insurgency.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday credited his government's policies and the determination of security forces for the progress made in India's fight against Naxalism, saying that not a single CRPF personnel had lost his life while on duty in the past year.
Addressing security personnel during his Diwali visit to Bastar in Chhattisgarh, Modi said the country had witnessed a major change in its fight against Maoist insurgency since 2014.
He said the political will to confront internal security threats had strengthened after the BJP-led government came to power in 2014.
“To take the country forward, we must confront and defeat the enemies of the nation with strong determination and a well-planned strategy. The political will that was lacking in the country to do this was strengthened in 2014,” Modi said.
He added that the people had given him an opportunity to serve the country and that the situation had begun to change after he assumed office.
“For a long time, we had seen more of our soldiers being killed than Naxalites. However, for the first time in 47 years, something remarkable happened: not a single CRPF jawan lost his life while on duty during the past year,” he said.
The Prime Minister described this as a victory for the government's policies and the courage, restraint and determination of security personnel.
PM MODI COMPARES NAXALISM FIGURES BEFORE AND AFTER 2014
Modi cited figures from 2004 to 2013 to criticise previous governments' handling of Naxalism. He said the number of security personnel killed every year during that period was higher than the number of Naxalites killed.
“Unfortunately, the governments of that time treated Naxalism as an incurable disease and left it unaddressed,” he said.
The Prime Minister said the fight against Maoist insurgency had been difficult, with Naxalites attacking security personnel and civilians and disrupting democratic processes in affected areas.
He said Naxalites had even deprived people of their right to vote and that the country had witnessed as many as 2,000 Naxal attacks in a single year.
Recalling the violence in Chhattisgarh in 2010, Modi referred to the killing of 76 CRPF personnel in an encounter with Naxalites in Dantewada. He also cited another incident in the district that year in which 44 civilians were killed.
“This land was soaked in the blood of our brave soldiers. But not a single voice of anguish was heard from those influential leaders living in their palaces. Not a single tear was shed by them,” he said.
Modi said such attacks continued for decades and that more than 1,000 security personnel had been killed in Chhattisgarh alone during the period.
He again referred to the 2004-2013 figures, saying that security personnel were being killed in greater numbers than Naxalites during those years. He criticised the governments of that period for failing to address the insurgency.
“No country can function with an approach that simply accepts that things will continue this way in the face of its enemies,” he said.
PM CALLS 2026 DIWALI SPECIAL AFTER NAXALISM FIGHT
Earlier, Modi described Diwali 2026 as special, saying India had won its decades-long battle against Naxalism and Maoist terror.
“This is the first Diwali when the country has won its decades-long battle against Naxalism and Maoist terror. This is the first Diwali when every district of the country is free from Naxalism,” he said.
He added that crores of Indians could now celebrate the festival without the fear of Naxalism and credited security personnel for the achievement.
The Prime Minister said he had visited Bastar on behalf of 140 crore Indians to express gratitude for the sacrifices, dedication and service of security personnel.
He compared the role of forces guarding the country's borders with that of personnel protecting internal security, saying both were essential to safeguarding India's unity and integrity.
Modi also extended Diwali greetings to security personnel deployed across the country and said millions of Indians were proud of their service.

Elon’s Edsel is no more. Last night, Tesla CEO Elon Musk revealed on social media that his car company is ending its failed attempt to wrest control of the American pickup truck market. The Cybertruck will cease production in the middle of 2027, liberating that space in Tesla’s cavernous factory for other uses—more Cybercabs, most likely.
Musk first revealed the Cybertruck in late 2019, back when Tesla was still trading at a theoretically understandable price-to-earning ratio. The pickup’s unusual angular shape owed more to low-res video game models than any concessions to practicality. At the time, Musk made fanciful claims that the truck would use a stainless steel monocoque construction, telling his audience that “the body and bed don’t do anything useful” on a normal truck. While some race cars use carbon-fiber monocoques for strength and lightness, making a pickup truck with a stainless steel monocoque chassis would only make sense if someone had an awful lot of stainless steel lying around and needed something to do with it all.
The truck was supposed to go on sale for less than $40,000, and Tesla made its usual stratospheric sales predictions that (had they been accurate) the bare metal EVs would be as ubiquitous as the Model 3 and Y.

In late October and early November, a photo circulated on social media supposedly showing U.S. President Donald Trump, late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and singer Beyoncé aboard a private jet. The image shows Trump and Epstein sitting shirtless next to each other, with Beyoncé standing behind them.
"The Epstein files have leaked again !! As Jeffrey Epstein, Trump and Beyonce are all seen chilling on board," one X post (archived) captioned the image.
(X user @TomthunkitsMind)
The image spread primarily on X and Facebook.
In short, the photograph wasn't real. We didn't find it in any reputable news outlets and AI-detection tools indicated it was artificially generated. Google Gemini detected a watermark showing that the image was created or edited using Google AI. As such, we have rated the image fake.
How we know the image is fake
First, we didn't find the image in news outlets or any other credible sources — it spread solely on social media. If it were real, it would likely have been widely reported by news organizations. Another sign that the image was fake was Trump's physical appearance, as he looked much older than he did when Epstein was still alive.
Moreover, an analysis using Hive Moderation, an AI-detection tool, determined with 99.8% confidence that the image was "likely to be AI-generated."
(X user @TomthunkitsMind, Hive Moderation)
We also ran the image through Google Gemini's SynthID check, a tool that scans for watermarks embedded by artificial intelligence software. That scan detected a SynthID watermark and concluded, "this image contains a SynthID watermark, which indicates that it was generated or edited with Google AI."
(Google Gemini)
Readers who want to check whether an image contains a SynthID watermark can do so by uploading the photo to Google Gemini and asking, "Does this image have a SynthID watermark?" However, the absence of a SynthID watermark does't automatically mean an image is authentic, as it could have been created using other AI tools.
It's unclear who created the image, but it has circulated online at least since Oct. 26.
Some social media users sharing the image suggested Beyoncé was involved in Epstein's crimes. While the singer's name does appear in the Epstein Library, the references we found don't accuse her of any wrongdoing and, for example, concern such matters as tickets to her concerts:
(www.justice.gov/epstein)
(www.justice.gov)
All in all, while genuine photographs of Trump and Epstein together exist, the image above isn't real. It's one of many fabricated images of the two that have circulated on social media.

Fast, fearsome, and fragile were words often associated with former New Zealand fast bowler Shane Bond, whose promising cricket career was drastically curtailed by injury.
He debuted as a 26-year-old against Australia in Hobart in 2001, but it was in his next series, against Bangladesh, where he truly announced himself.
He took 11 wickets in two Tests at an average of 13, and it looked like the beginning of a long and lucrative career.
But Bond's back had other ideas. A stress fracture kept him out the game for almost two years from 2003.
A meeting with back surgeon Grahame Inglis offered him hope he could overcome his injury by undergoing a little-known surgery that is now commonplace in the fast bowling fraternity.
"If I can't fix this, then the career is potentially over," Bond said of his decision to undergo pars stabilisation surgery in 2004.
"He [Inglis] talked about a procedure that he had done, one on a New Zealand high jumper and one other athlete.
"He thought that the chances I came back and bowled fast were slim, but ... I was prepared to give it a go."
While other injuries limited Bond to just 14 more Tests before he retired in 2009, his back didn't trouble him again.
Last surgeon standing
Renowned New Zealand spinal surgeon Rowan Schouten was working with Dr Inglis at the time and said Bond was "patient zero in this whole story."
The success of that surgery laid the groundwork for a procedure that Schouten and his team have now performed on around 30 professional cricketers.
When surgeons in the UK stopped performing the procedure and Dr Inglis retired, Dr Schouten became the world's leading authority on repairing spinal stress fractures in fast bowlers.
"We were kind of left as the last man standing with experience on international fast bowlers and since then it's taken off essentially," he said.
"We're dealing with calls and connections from all around the world, from the UK, India, South Africa, Europe, Bangladesh, everywhere."
Bond still helps fast bowlers who have struggled with back issues and is often approached for advice.
He's coached Jofra Archer, Jason Behrendorff and James Pattinson, who all had the surgery and returned to play at the top level.
What is pars stabilisation surgery?
When a fast bowler is considering spinal surgery, like Australia's Lance 'Wild Thing' Morris did in 2025, it sounds like a drastic step.
Loading Instagram content
But Dr Schouten said the surgery was straightforward and "not that extreme".
It involves grafting the spine to stimulate repair, before putting screws and wires around the injured portion to provide stability.
"We've got a few little added components to it that we believe are important ... but it's a pretty standard technique," he said.
The injury, often referred to as a stress fracture, is common across sport and very prevalent in cricket.
Dr Schouten stressed the surgery is not a fusion, and most stress fractures do not need it.
"You need to preserve all that spinal motion that these guys need to be able to bowl full pace," he said.
If a player did opt to go under the knife, the recovery involves a six-to-nine month rehab program.
"Some stress fractures in some players become a recurring theme," Dr Schouten said.
"And then if you do that, if you have that two or three times in a row over multiple seasons, it can really disrupt a career."

Snow has fallen across parts of NSW, Victoria and Tasmania as an unseasonal cold blast whips through Australia’s south-east.
Thredbo, Perisher and Mount Hotham all recorded falls, while snow also fell on Kunanyi/Mount Wellington in Hobart.
The snow had been forecast by the Bureau of Meteorology (BoM), and though uncommon, it is not entirely unusual – many of the places hit by snow in the past 24 hours also recorded a fall in November 2022.
The falls brought a rush of posts on social media from those puzzled by the unseasonal spring weather.
“You will not believe this, it’s springtime in Australia, in November, and it’s snowing,” Madeleine McVie, a retail manager at Thredbo, posted on Instagram on Saturday afternoon.
“Like, not just a little bit. It’s fully snowing.”
McVie posted another clip on Sunday morning of her riding empty chairlifts through the park as the snow continued to fall.
Kingston Crows cricket club in Tasmania posted an image of the Kingston Beach Oval on Saturday that showed it coated in hailstones.
The BoM said a weather system, filled with cold air moving north from towards Antarctica, had caused the wintery chill with apparent temperatures much cooler than forecast maximums. South-westerly winds were also causing the apparent or “feels like” temperature to be lower.
At midday, Adelaide, Melbourne, Hobart, Canberra and Sydney all had temperatures that felt cooler than 13C.
The highest temperature at that time was in Adelaide, with a top of 17.5C that felt like 12.3C, with Canberra the lowest (a maximum of 12.9C that felt like 5.3C).
Brisbane, Perth and Darwin, meanwhile, were all enjoying temperatures in the 20s or 30s.
Warmer temperatures are forecast for Monday, and all capital cities are expected to reach at least 20C by Tuesday.
It may be one of the last cold snaps of the year – the BoM, as well as the UN and other bodies, have warned of the likely effects of a “jaw dropping” supercharged El Niño.
The climate crisis, caused by pollution from fossil fuels, is already supercharging extreme weather and killing people. The El Niño is expected to ratchet up the effects even further, and has already begun to affect regions across the planet as weather patterns are altered.
The southern hemisphere summer is predicted to be hotter and drier as a result of the huge El Niño, meaning greater wildfire risk and droughts in Australia and southern Africa.

Protesters break into Microsoft data center in Amsterdam as Europe backlash spreads
Protesters have broken into a Microsoft data center construction site in Amsterdam
THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- Protesters broke into a construction site for a new Microsoft data center in Amsterdam on Friday, with some climbing a crane and setting off flares while others clashed with police.
Nathan Timmer of the protest group Geef Tegengas, a phrase that translates as Push Back, told local broadcaster AT5 that protesters were occupying the site in an effort to stop construction.
Campaigners against data centers in Europe are expected to stage protests and other actions in several countries on Friday and Saturday, demanding a moratorium on large-scale developments to address social and environmental concerns around the energy-hungry behemoths.
“We don’t want it to be built. Nobody needs it,” Timmer said. “The only thing this will be used for is AI slop. AI warfare, data surveillance, and committing genocides. We don’t want that,” he added, vowing to continue protesting until construction is halted.
Pro-Palestinian activists also joined the demonstrations in the Dutch capital. By late afternoon police were escorting activists off the construction site, though some still remained, local media reported.
Microsoft said it was aware of the Amsterdam demonstration. “We understand that people feel strongly about the project, and we respect their right to express those views peacefully," a spokesperson said. “However, we do not condone any actions that are unlawful or that put people’s safety at risk.”
The demonstrations come days after the U.S. midterm elections ushered in a wave of Democrats promising to clamp down on data centers, which face resistance around the world due to the massive amounts of computing power and water they use.
Dozens of civil society and grassroots groups have said they will join the “Stop Dirty Data Centres” events on Friday and Saturday in 15 European countries, including Ireland, Poland, Denmark, Finland, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, France and the U.K., organizers said.
“There’s a gulf between where elected leaders are at in terms of buying into the hype about AI and where people are at,” said Owen Espley, coordinator of StopDirtyDataCentres.eu.
In Germany, a dozen protesters gathered in front of a data center on the outskirts of Berlin on Friday.
“We want to put a stop to this blind construction of data centers around Germany, regardless of any environmental concerns,” said the protest spokeswoman Caro Weber. “This is really, really dangerous for our future.”
Around 100 people also protested against data centers in front of the Polish parliament on Friday, representing communities around Warsaw where new centers are planned.
In Italy, the fast-growing data center industry faces an equally rapid rise in grassroots opposition, particularly in the northern Lombardy region, the country’s main hub for digital infrastructure.
Activists argue that the boom in facilities serving cloud computing and artificial intelligence is moving faster than public consultation and environmental oversight.
The movement reached a milestone on Oct. 10, when more than 1,000 people and representatives of around 40 local committees gathered in Milan’s Piazza della Scala for what organizers described as Italy’s first national demonstration against data centers.
Protesters called for a moratorium on new projects and demanded a national strategy governing the industry’s growth. The demonstration followed a series of increasingly large mobilizations in towns around Milan.
Europe is projected to attract $5.6 trillion in cumulative data center capital expenditure from 2026 through 2050, accounting for around 18% of global investment, according to PwC’s Global Data Centre Outlook 2026–50.
The U.S. is forecast to attract $15.1 trillion in capital spending on data centers during that period, the report said.

Naishadham reported from Madrid. Associated Press journalists Giada Zampano in Rome, Pietro De Cristofaro in Berlin and Claudia Ciobanu in Warsaw contributed to this report.

India’s anaemia burden is not in doubt. The fifth National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5) found that more than half of women and about two-thirds of young children are anaemic. In this context, double-fortified salt (DFS) — fortified with iodine and iron — is often proposed as a potentially transformative solution. However, the case for DFS rests on convenience: everyone consumes salt, so why not add iron to it? But convenience is not efficacy, and a policy that asks the country to continue consuming salt to deliver iron deserves closer scrutiny.
Iron fortification of salt is a vehicle that cuts against public health. Indians consume, by most estimates, roughly twice the five grams of salt a day recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). About one in three adults has hypertension, and India’s own non-communicable disease (NCD) action plan commits to a 30% relative reduction in salt intake.

Insurtech Go Digit reported a 31.1% year-on-year (YoY) decline in its net profit for the September quarter (Q2 FY27) to ₹142.4 Cr from ₹206.8 Cr in the corresponding quarter last year. The insurtech major's profit also declined 62.4% sequentially from ₹378.61 Cr in the June quarter. The decline in profitability came despite a marginal increase in insurance revenue, which rose 1.7% to ₹2,720.5 Cr during the quarter from ₹2,674.9 Cr in Q2 FY26. Sequentially, insurance revenue increased 2.1% from ₹2,665.6 Cr. Segment-wise, Motor Third Party (TP) insurance remained Go Digit's largest business, contributing ₹1,066.1 Cr to insurance revenue in Q2 FY27, up 8.3% YoY. Motor Own Damage (OD) insurance revenue grew at a faster pace of 11.4% YoY to ₹640.64 Cr. The company's gross written premium for the quarter dipped by 3.6% YoY to ₹2,571 Cr while gross direct premium, dipped 1.2% to ₹2,351 Cr. However, the company's insurance service result, which reflects the profitability of its insurance operations before investment and other financial income, sunk 73.4% YoY to ₹43 Cr from ₹161.98 Cr in the year-ago quarter. The figure also fell 62.3% sequentially from ₹114 Cr. The deterioration in the insurance service result came as insurance service expenses increased 22.4% YoY to ₹2,607.73 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹2,130.85 Cr in the corresponding quarter last year. Incurred claims rose 9.2% to ₹1,968.03 Cr from ₹1,802.96 Cr, while employee benefit expenses increased 4.3% to ₹95.48 Cr. Commission expenses, on the other hand, declined 2.6% YoY to ₹781.88 Cr from ₹803.10 Cr. Other insurance service expenses increased 1.7% to ₹94.52 Cr. On the investment front, Go Digit reported a 20.6% YoY increase in investment income to ₹368.4 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹305.5 Cr in the year-ago period. However, investment income declined 39.2% sequentially from ₹606.47 Cr. The company's net finance result, which includes investment income and insurance finance income or expenses, increased 28.6% YoY to ₹196.94 Cr. Consequently, Go Digit's profit before tax (PBT) declined 31.2% YoY to ₹190.18 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹276.30 Cr in Q2 FY26. The figure was also down 62.4% sequentially from ₹505.96 Cr in Q1 FY27. Total tax expense stood at ₹47.79 Cr during the quarter, comprising current tax of ₹3.93 Cr and deferred tax of ₹43.86 Cr. This compared with a total tax expense of ₹69.51 Cr in Q2 FY26. For the first half of FY27 (H1 FY27), Go Digit reported a 3.2% YoY decline in net profit to ₹521 Cr from ₹538.23 Cr in H1 FY26. Insurance revenue increased 4.5% YoY to ₹5,386.09 Cr during the six-month period. Shares of Go Digit ended today’s trading session 1.05% higher at ₹260.30.

The Supreme Court has refused to lift the ban on the preparation, sale and storage of non-vegetarian food near Gujarat's Somnath Temple. The court said a balance needed to be maintained and declined to interfere with an interim order of the Gujarat High Court that keeps the restrictions in place. A bench of Justices MM Sundresh and PB Varale heard a petition filed by restaurant owners challenging the restrictions imposed by the Gir Somnath district administration. During the November 6 hearing, the owners argued that the ban was affecting their businesses and livelihoods. The Supreme Court, however, refused to grant immediate relief and asked the Gujarat High Court to decide the pending appeals preferably within two months. "We need to maintain a balance. We don't say anything," the bench observed. The dispute began with a notification issued by the Gir Somnath District Magistrate on 10 August, 2026. It prohibits the preparation, sale and storage of non-vegetarian food, including meat, fish and eggs, at restaurants, hotels, shops and roadside stalls in specified areas around the Somnath Temple. The restrictions cover designated routes in Prabhas Patan and areas within 500 metres of the temple. Six restaurant owners challenged the notification in the Gujarat High Court. They argued that it affected their right to carry on a lawful business and threatened the livelihoods of people working at their establishments. Some of the restaurants had reportedly been operating in the area for 35 to 40 years. On October 30, a single-judge bench of the Gujarat High Court set aside the notification, holding that the restrictions went beyond the powers available under the Gujarat Police Act, 1951, and affected the owners' fundamental right to carry on a trade under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. However, the Gujarat government challenged the decision, following which a division bench stayed the single judge's order. This brought the restrictions back into force. During the hearing, senior advocate Huzefa Ahmadi, representing the restaurant owners, argued that the restrictions would affect businesses, particularly during the festive season. He also questioned the need to regulate people's food choices. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Gujarat government, defended the restrictions by referring to the religious significance of the Somnath Temple. He argued that restaurants could continue selling non-vegetarian food outside the restricted areas. The Supreme Court chose not to interfere with the High Court's interim arrangement. It did not deliver a final ruling on whether the ban was legally valid. The Supreme Court has asked the Gujarat High Court to decide the pending appeals preferably within two months. The matter is scheduled to come up before the High Court on 25 November, 2026. Until then, the restrictions will remain in force. Restaurant owners will have to wait for the High Court's decision before they can resume preparing and selling non-vegetarian food in the notified areas. The Supreme Court's refusal to lift the ban does not mean it has finally upheld the restrictions. Their legality is still being examined by the Gujarat High Court. ‘Apologise to Ram Bhakts first’: Yogi Adityanath ahead of Akhilesh Yadav's visit to Ayodhya
UP chief minister Yogi Adityanath said the same forces that had opposed the Ram temple movement were now trying to take political mileage from it.
Ahead of Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav's proposed visit to Ram temple in Ayodhya, chief minister Yogi Adityanath on Saturday sought an apology from those who opened fire at karsevaks in 1990. Without addressing Yadav directly, Adityanath demanded that an apology be tendered to 'Ram Bhakts' before visiting Ayodhya.
The chief minister was referring to the firing that took place on October 30 and November 2 in 1990, during the government of Samajwadi Party patriarch Mulayam Singh Yadav. The SP has maintained that the then government had to act to maintain law and order.
ALSO READ: Akhilesh Yadav to visit Ayodhya Ram Temple with family for first time since consecration
Akhilesh Yadav is set to visit the Ram Temple in Ayodhya with his family on December 12. This will be his first visit to the temple since its consecration in January 2024.
Taking aim at Yadav, Adityanath said, "Tender an apology to Ram Bhakts first for firing on karsevaks before coming to Ayodhya." The chief minister was addressing seers at Ram Katha Park in Ayodhya at the 10th edition of Deepotsav.
"Those who got bullets fired on karsevaks, who shed the blood of Ram Bhakts on the streets of Ayodhya, are coming here to seek blessings. First, they should apologise to the karsevaks, to the seers, and to the people of Ayodhya," the chief minister said.
Adityanath also said Ayodhya does not belong to any one party or family. "Ayodhya is the land of Maryada Purushottam Shri Ram. Those who insulted the sentiments of crores of Ram Bhakts cannot wash away their sins merely by visiting the temple," he said.
The chief minister said the same forces that had opposed the Ram temple movement were now trying to take political mileage from the Ram temple. “Earlier, they used to say Ram did not exist. Today they are coming to Ayodhya. This is the victory of the faith of the people," he said.
The chief minister further claimed that Ayodhya has transformed from a neglected town into a global spiritual destination under the double-engine government. Adityanath credited 10 years of Deepotsav, the construction of the Ram temple and infrastructure development for restoring Ayodhya's ancient glory.
"For decades, Ayodhya was kept in darkness. Today, 30 lakh diyas (earthen lamps) are being lit here. This is not just Deepotsav, this is the celebration of the return of Ram Rajya," he said.
He also warned that those who play with the sentiments of Sanatan Dharma will not be forgiven by the people. "The people of Uttar Pradesh have seen who stood with Ram and who stood against Ram," he added.
The seers present on the occasion welcomed the chief minister's remarks with chants of 'Jai Shri Ram'.
Vice-President CP Radhakrishnan was the chief guest at the Deepotsav where governor Anandiben Patel was also present
Earlier in the day, Samajwadi Party leader Tej Narayan Pandey alias Pawan Pandey had said SP national president, along with his family, would visit the Hanuman Garhi temple and Ram temple in Ayodhya on December 12.
“Akhilesh ji is coming with his family for darshan of Hanuman ji and Ram Lalla. This is a matter of faith. The BJP should not do politics on faith," said Pandey, former SP MLA from Ayodhya Sadar assembly seat.

On 4 November 2026, the results of the 2026 US midterm elections were announced, with the Democratic Party winning a majority in the House of Representatives & the Senate. Against this background, a video is being widely shared on social media (here, here, here) with the claim that it shows US President Donald Trump destroying his office following the Republican Party’s defeat in the 2026 US midterm elections. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals showing US President Trump vandalizing his office after the Republican Party’s defeat in the midterm elections of 2026.
Fact: We found no credible reports confirming such an incident. This is an AI-generated video by a creator named Iman Rus. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
We found no credible reports confirming such an incident. A reverse image search using keyframes led us to the original video, which was uploaded on 4 November 2026 by the Iranian Embassy in Lebanon on X. The video clearly carries the label “AI Generated” in the upper-right corner. It also credits the creator, Iman Rus, at the end.
A keyword search based on the information gathered above led us to the same video uploaded on the YouTube channel ‘Iman Rus’ on 4 November 2026. The video title clearly identifies it as AI-generated. Additionally, YouTube’s AI disclosure in the video also confirms that the content was created using AI.
We also analysed the viral video using AI detection tools, Hive AI and SynthID, both of which indicated the video was AI-generated.
To sum up, the viral video claiming that Trump vandalised his office following the Republican Party’s defeat is AI-generated.

10 useful iPad apps that could make your daily life easier
Put your iPad to good use with apps for journaling, discovering art and much more.
Your iPad should make every day easier. Whether you want to build new habits or improve your routines, we've rounded up apps that put the best iPads to work in your daily life.
We found these by digging a bit deeper. These aren't first-party Apple apps or subscription-only Adobe staples. It's free to get started with each, though most charge for extra features, which we've noted where applicable.
Our favorite apps are elegant and well-designed, taking advantage of the entire iPad display. They also keep AI to a bare minimum. There may be machine learning to help with search and transcriptions, but you won't find fake images or bogus text generators here.
1. Sofa: downtime organizer
If you're a voracious consumer of media, you need Sofa to help keep track of it all. Start with books, TV shows and movies, then add whatever other categories you'd like. Sofa has a clean interface that grabs title images and info to give you an overview of everything you watch (or read).
Sofa's tracking feature is especially useful for remembering which episodes you've seen. Mark them off as you watch them and add notes if you like, or rely on the included summaries. Sofa tracks two different series at once for free, while paid subscribers can track unlimited titles.
Sofa's free tier offers all its best features without advertisements or pop-ups begging for more. If you want to fine-tune your media tracking with custom ratings that you create and smart lists that populate based on your filters, Sofa offers a subscription for $5.99 per month, $49.99 per year or $249.99 for a lifetime membership. Unless you're a professional TV critic, you'll likely be fine with the free features.
2. Bear: Markdown notes
Instead of Apple Notes or Google Keep, try Bear, an app for capturing thoughts. Bear has become a productivity favorite by keeping its interface deceptively simple; it's a large notepad app without a glut of buttons and menus. While it's powerful, you don't have to use advanced features you don't need.
Bear is built around smooth Markdown styling and supports tags to organize your thoughts. For example, if you find yourself often complaining about your job, tag that post with #job. You can add links, tags or even to-do tasks that are easily searchable. If that sounds complicated, ignore what you don't need and you're left with an elegant, attractive note-taking and journaling app.
Bear has a reasonably-priced subscription tier ($3/month or $30/year) that offers a few extra features if you're hardcore about your notes. With it, you can sync your Bear notes between devices, as well as publish your notes using HTML or ePub to use the app as a blogging tool.
3. Flipboard: the social magazine
After a few minutes with Flipboard, you'll wonder why it isn't preloaded on every iPad. This decentralized social experience transforms the touchscreen into a magazine with a clean layout and large images. If you read a lot of news, Flipboard is the best way to stay current.
The app starts by having you select from an endless list of topics to find stories. These can start as general as sports, music or science. Or by dialing down, you might find "UEFA Champions League," "blues music" or "sustainable design."
If any sources arise that you don't want to see, block them. In general, the selection is great; you can follow individual authors and sites the same way you follow topics.
The best part about Flipboard is that it's totally free: it doesn't make you cough up a fee for the best content, and you can sometimes find stories that are normally trapped behind a paywall.
4. Happy Spoon: easy meal planning
HappySpoon is an (artificially) intelligent meal planner that helps you create a menu for the week ahead following whatever ideas or guidelines you set. The app uses AI to understand plain-language requests that you make, like "I need to use up all my chicken breast, so make a bunch of different chicken recipes." Once you've created your menu, it even generates a handy shopping list sorted by grocery store aisle.
I asked the app to generate "breakfasts that are simple and on-repeat, like a big batch of muffins or oatmeal to eat every day" and it did exactly that. It also understood the rule "no lunches" and left that spot blank on my weekly menu.
HappySpoon automatically resizes your portions and recipes to match your eaters. You can specify adult-sized or kid-sized appetites, and it will conform: the grocery list populates with the right amounts.
You don't need to use HappySpoon's AI features; in fact, they're only free for two weeks. That's enough time to get started and use the AI for help generating a variety of menus. There are plenty of other AI tools that can create recipes, but if you want to stick with HappySpoon, the fee is $5.99 per month or $49.99 per year. I found the AI tools useful at first, but after a couple of weeks, the extra AI benefits didn't seem necessary.
5. MindNode: mind mapping
Whatever you need to organize, MindNode is a perfect starting point. Whether it's a meeting agenda, a workout plan or your life's goals, MindNode offers a simple canvas to connect and organize thoughts. You'll find features to enhance, stylize and reorganize your finished maps.
Start with the big idea in the center and then branch out. A map can grow large the more you dig in, but MindNode makes it easy to keep your idea maps looking neat. You also have the option to view your maps as a text outline instead.
If this sort of mental organization appeals to you, the premium subscription may offer enough bonus features to make it worth the asking $2.99 per month or $24.99 per year. With the subscription, you get more editing tools, the ability to add photos and emoji to your nodes and some professional-strength features for teams working together.
It also unlocks real-time collaboration with others so you see edits and additions as they happen. You can set each node as a task with a reminder and checklist. And Apple Intelligence will enhance the experience by offering new ideas, summarizing what it sees and similar. The AI extras aren't necessary, but are available with the premium plan.
6. Journey: a diary of your life
Journey is a place to store your memories, including journal entries, calendar appointments , major dates, photos, multimedia and maps of the places you've been. The more you use Journey, the more it rewards your dedication, with features that track your habits later on.
The available templates are Journey's secret weapon. If you're planning a trip, for example, the travel planner template includes fields for details like your hotel address, flight information, car rental details and even a budget planner that tracks your anticipated versus actual spending.
Templates include tons of other categories, from personal goal trackers to a 30-60-90 day plan for starting a new career. Once you've built a journaling habit, you're able to track your progress through Journey's graphs and statistics. If you tag each journal entry with a mood, you'll see how your feelings ebbed and flowed throughout your journaling experience.
By paying $6.99 per month or $49.99 per year (or $199 for the app's lifetime), you get premium features that could be helpful if you share a journal with someone else. There's also a premium AI feature included, though thankfully it doesn't offer to write journal entries for you. Instead, you can ask "how many entries did I write last month?" or tell it to "summarize my summer vacation from 2026."
7. Libby: the library app
Libby is your local library in app form, which should be enough to earn an immediate download. Did you know you can borrow ebooks from your library? Just register your library card with Libby — go get one if you don't have one! — and you're ready to download the glut of digital content you might not have even known your library offered.
Libby handles the borrowing and serves you the book in its own ereader interface, or you can put titles on your Kindle. Libraries have limited copies even for ebook titles, and Libby lets you join a waiting list for the latest best-seller if you can't grab it right away.
There are audiobooks available as well, in addition to other common library finds like periodicals, graphic novels and comic books. If you can't find the title you want, Libby has an option to send requests so your local library secures a copy. And because it's a library, there's no premium offering; just borrow books and enjoy them.
8. Day One: starter journal
If journaling seems like a chore, Day One does the grunt work for you. Every time you start an entry, it records the time and date, your location, the weather and even the phase of the moon. The app isn't shy about prompting you with topics to get your journal started. If you've wanted to start a journal but don't know where to begin, Day One is ready for you.
There are several categories of prompts, including Reflection, Fitness and The Year Ahead. Under Mindfulness, you might find simple prompts like "How am I feeling right now?" or introspective questions like "How often do I observe my thoughts without judgment?"
If you don't want to begin with a prompt, Day One is able to access your photos, maps and calendar to pull together a summary of your day. You can add a calendar event, the map of where you went and the photos you took there. Day One puts an emphasis on privacy, with an app-specific passcode to protect your journals. There's a setting to turn off all AI-based features if you prefer.
Day One will record an unlimited number of journal entries without paying a dime, but if you want to add unlimited photos and videos, or audio recordings, you'll need to pay a subscription fee. For $49.99/year you get all that, plus interesting integration with IFTTT (If This Then That) and other markup tools.
9. Habitify: habit tracker
Habitify can help you build habits without being intrusive or making you do so much work that the app becomes its own "habit" to maintain. You design a habit or goal, then Habitify monitors your progress in the background as much as it can. It's the rare app that you barely need to use to get value from.
You tell Habitify what you want to do and on which days you'll repeat the habit, then give it a specific goal. Habitify integrates neatly with Siri, so you often won't need to open the app to log your habit since Siri will. Siri can even update you on your progress — just ask how you're doing with your goals and Habitify will feed Siri the answer.
There is a paid option for $49.99 per year, which is useful if fitness is your goal since Apple Health and Google Health integrations sit behind that paywall. You can connect Habitify to your Apple Watch or Fitbit so it knows you kept up your routine. It works with Apple Health and Google Health to gather data, with your permission. The paid option can also monitor your screen time if limits are part of your habit goals.
10. DailyArt: history and culture
DailyArt is for art world enthusiasts who want to go beyond the most prolific canvases and dive deeper into the lives of the artists who created them. One recent offering was a gorgeous Autumn Landscape created in 1899 by the pseudonymous Hishida Shunsō. In addition to the image, the app offers a brief history of the work and artist, with an explanation of the style it exemplifies. You can select the artist name or other links to see more artwork, or wait until tomorrow to see what DailyArt serves up next.
The feature are robust, so if you have a burgeoning curiosity in the art world, this is a great way to start. It offers collections grouped by artist, artistic movement or other qualities. You'll find a collection of paintings that all depict people working with their hands or a collection of cats in art, for example. There are also quizzes and games if you want to have a bit of fun.
DailyArt has an unobtrusive ad bar near the bottom of the screen, plus a premium option for $4.99 per month or $29.99 per year. Along with removing ads, this also gives you unlimited searches in a vast library of high-quality artwork, with accompanying information to build your art knowledge.

Who is the Opportunity Party, this year’s potential kingmaker?

Who is the Opportunity Party, this year’s potential kingmaker?

The centrist minor party, whose policies include a land tax and a $370 a week universal basic income, says it is looking to “market-driven solutions” while being committed to a low-emission future and evidence-based policy.
Opportunity will negotiate first with the party that secures the highest number of votes.

For anyone tuning in who needs a refresher on the MMP electoral system, here goes:
MMP means voters are asked to vote twice – once for their preferred party and the second time for an electorate MP.
There is a single chamber of parliament which generally has 120 MPs. This is the overhang issue which I think we’re going to be talking about tonight as results come in.
Under MMP it is very uncommon for a single party to form a government.
If there is no majority winner, the major parties will start negotiations after the election and can either form a coalition or confidence-and-supply agreements with minor parties. The party with the largest number of votes does not necessarily win, and negotiations can take days or weeks.
Some senior National heavy hitters will, remarkably, be out of a job if National’s party vote goes badly tonight.
Those most at risk include:
Nicola Willis (finance minister), Chris Bishop (like Willis, is tipped as a potential future leader of the party), Paul Goldsmith (justice minister) and Gerry Brownlee (speaker of the house).
Some background: All the pre-election polls looked bad for any National MP who was relying on the list vote to return them to parliament; such as Willis and Brownlee, who are list-only candidates. Goldsmith (Epsom) and Bishop (Hutt South) are both engaged in tense, marginal electorate battles. If either loses, they are then reliant on winning via the list. We’ll be watching all this closely.
Some of the Labour party candidates are locked in neck and neck races, with tensions high for those at the Labour party event watching the candidates in Hutt South. With more than 20% of the vote counted, Labour’s Ginny Anderson has edged just ahead of the incumbent, National MP Chris Bishop, by just a handful of ballots.
Green MP Julie-Anne Genter is just holding off Labour challenger Craig Renney in Wellington North, while Labour’s Kieran McAnulty is winning against National’s Mike Butterick in Wairarapa.
Elsewhere in Wellington, Labour party MP Ayesha Verrall was hoping to win Wellington North off the incumbent Green MP Tamatha Paul, but early votes suggest this won’t be the case. Paul is leading comfortably, at almost twice Verrall’s count in an electorate where Green is also leading the party vote.
Another key feature of this election has been the possibility of an overhang - where a party wins more electorates than its share of the party vote.
If that occurs, more seats will be added to parliament to make up the difference and could dictate which coalition can form a government.
Te Pāti Māori (the Māori party) has been calling on supporters to engineer an overhang for its party - by voting for its candidates in the Māori seats, and not giving them a party vote. This could benefit the left bloc.
Meanwhile, if National holds on to a good portion of its seats but its party vote falls short, that will give the party an edge to form a government but could see some of its most prominent MPs out of parliament.
Elsewhere in the Upper Hutt Cosmopolitan Club, punters were ordering crate bottles of local beer Tui and listening to a band kick up a rendition of Tennessee Whiskey.
For Hutt locals, the Cossie Club is a social hub; karaoke on Thursdays, Bingo on Sundays, and a jug of lager for $14 during happy hour.
While everyone spoken to by The Guardian voted for Hipkins in the Remutaka electorate – “he’s a local boy,” – party votes were otherwise split between Labour, the Opportunity party, and NZ First.
“I’ve always voted Labour, Chris knows that,” said Gladys Cooney, 96. “I haven’t heard anything from them this election, I don’t think anyone has gone deep enough.” The cost of living was appalling, she said. “Everything you touch has gone up.”
Fellow local Paul O’Riley also voted for Hipkins, but party voted NZ First. “I worked for 50 years in this country as a truck driver, Winston [Peters] does the most for us.”
Seven of the seats in New Zealand’s 120-seat parliamentare Māori electorates. Voters of Māori descent can choose to vote on the Māori roll – allowing them to vote for these seats – or the general roll. More than half of Māori voters are on the Māori roll.
They still get two votes; one for the electorate, and one for their preferred political party.
Last election, Te Pāti Māori won six of the seven seats. But internal turmoil has plagued the party since. Tonight, eyes will be on Te Tai Tokerau – covering the geographical area from New Zealand’s most northern point in Cape Reinga to West Auckland – where the Green’s candidate Hūhana Lyndon could help the party nab their first Māori seat.
Latest polls put her leading the race, followed by Labour’s Willow-Jean Prime and Te Pāti Māori candidate Aperahama Edwards.
Te Pāti Māori remain ahead in most other electorates, aside from Ikaroa-Rāwhiti and Te Tai Tonga (the biggest electorate, covering the entirety of the South Island and Stewart Island) where Labour candidates lead polling.
In an election night that has come down to Chris vs Chris, it’s important to know the difference.
Christopher Luxon, 56, the incumbent, leader of the National party and PM since 2023, is the former chief executive of the country’s national airline, Air New Zealand, and previously worked a slew of corporate jobs worldwide. He entered parliament in 2020, winning the Auckland electorate of Botany. A father-of-two, he is Christian but doesn’t discuss his faith, and has emphasised his business credentials — in 2023, his party was elected on its economic pledges.
Chris Hipkins, 48, the career politician who leads the center-left Labour party, is having a second crack at being PM tonight. Following the resignation of Jacinda Ardern in January 2023, Hipkins, also a father of two, took the reins for nine months ahead of that election, which his party lost. He’s held the Remutaka electorate in parliament since 2008. Some voters still associate him with Covid-19 and strict lockdown measures, while others connect with his pledges for better healthcare and improved cost of living.
National party faithful are starting to trickle into its event at the cavernous Viaduct Event Centre on Auckland’s waterfront. The room is awash in blue light.
People are grabbing drinks and milling around. The reaction is flicking between nervousness and excitement as the first numbers show the race is - as predicted - neck and neck.
As the first results of the night flashed up onto the big screen, Labour party volunteer Jasmine, 22, who works in the public service and didn’t want to use her last name, stopped talking mid-sentence.
A hush fell over the room as the first poll results show the main parties neck and neck . “That’s close,” she said, exhaling. “It’s great that Opportunity is over 5%, I’m happy about that. It’s just overwhelming; this is years of work, and that’s real numbers.” She’s been working for the party since she was 16.
Cheers are going up in the room as electorate results begin to come in. About 200 party supporters are expected here tonight.

Pope Leo urges faithful in Uruguay to build bridges of fraternity and faith
Pope Leo XIV has urged an estimated 40,000 people in Uruguay to build bridges of fraternity and faith
MONTEVIDEO, Uruguay (AP) — Pope Leo XIV urged Uruguayans on Saturday to build bridges of fraternity and faith, as he delivered an ode to the region's beloved mate tea and raised the profile of the Catholic Church in Latin America's most secular country.
Leo spent his first full day in Uruguay pointing to the church’s historic roots in the country and the work it’s doing today. He drew an estimated 100,000 people at a prayer vigil and visited a violence-ravaged neighborhood of Montevideo where church groups have built homes, provided job opportunities and run drug rehabilitation programs.
The aim, on the first stop of his three-nation South American tour, is to propose the Catholic faith as a response to today's challenges and the church a willing helper in a country where even Catholic holidays have secular names and God cannot be mentioned in oaths of office.
Leo traveled first to Paysandú, in western Uruguay on the border with Argentina, for his first Mass in South America. The Vatican said 40,000 people -- many from Uruguay but also from neighboring Argentina and Brazil – came out, despite the morning rain and blustery gray skies.
The crowd erupted in the stadium chant of “Olé, olé, olé, olé, pope, pope!” when Leo’s plane landed in Paysandú, around 375 kilometers (230 miles) from the capital, Montevideo. They cheered again, blew horns and waved yellow handkerchiefs when he arrived in his open-sided popemobile at the Mass site in a park.
Speaking to the crowd in Spanish, Leo reminded them that the Catholic faith had been “part of the life of the Uruguayan people since their earliest days, and it must be passed on to future generations with creative courage!”
Because of its accessible location on the Uruguay River, the city was chosen to host Leo’s first Mass at the start of his 12-day South American tour that was in doubt after he underwent lung cancer surgery on Oct. 13.
“He’s the representative of Christ but he’s human. And we weren’t sure if he could make it, but he pushed through for us,” said Soledad Sánchez, 73, who had driven to Paysandú from northern Uruguay, her eyes filling with tears. “He made it here to give us a message of peace because he knows our world needs it right now.”
Leo asked the faithful to build bridges of fraternity, recalling the nearby bridge over the Uruguay River that connects Uruguay and Argentina and over which many pilgrims crossed to attend the Mass.
He also pointed to the ritual of drinking mate, the bitter herbal tea that Uruguayans and their neighbors carry everywhere, as a poignant symbol of unity and encounter that he suggested should be applied to spreading the faith.
“It teaches us to share and to be together, strengthening the bonds that unite us as brothers and sisters,” he said. “It is a sign of welcome, integration and shared values.”
Mate, a cherished national symbol in Paraguay, Argentina and Uruguay, is above all a sharing ritual. The leaves are steeped in a hollowed gourd and the drink is sipped through a metal straw called a bombilla, and the gourd passes from hand to hand among friends, family and sometimes strangers, refilled for hours.
Everyone drinks from the same straw, and Uruguayans drink more mate per person than people anywhere else, roughly 9 kilograms (about 20 pounds) of the dried leaf a year, according to industry estimates.
“We must reflect on these symbols that we share, which give us identity and a sense of belonging, which speak to us of our origins and point us toward the future,” Leo said.
The message landed.
“I’m not religious. I’d never go to Mass if it weren’t the pope, but he surprised me. He made it appealing, the way he talked about things we all have in common, like mate,” said Jorge Monzón, 64, from Paysandú. “I personally felt a sense of communion.”
Leo pressed the message of the church's commitment to helping Uruguayans later Saturday by visiting Casavalle, a Montevideo area of small neighborhood s beset by drug trafficking and gang violence. In Borro, the Our Lady of Guadalupe Parish builds homes and supports addicts in their recovery, with donations including from The Papal Foundation, the U.S.-based group of wealthy Catholics who fund special papal projects.
Leo toured some of the new homes and praised the work church groups were doing, all while the crowd chanted “León, amigo, el barrio está contigo!" (Leon, my friend, the neighborhood is with you!")
He said Christians must commit themselves to the charity and closeness shown by the biblical figure of the good Samaritan, “who did not remain indifferent upon seeing misfortune, but took responsibility for his brother’s life.”
“We cannot turn a blind eye to the fact that there are children in Uruguay who do not go to school for fear of never returning home,” he said.
Uruguay has universal access to primary school and enrolls nearly all its children, but only about half of Uruguayans finish high school, one of the lowest rates in Latin America, according to the National Institute for Educational Evaluation. The graduation rate is even worse for children from the poorest households, where only one in four graduate compared to nearly nine out of 10 from the wealthiest families.
Jonathan Tropiano, 28, is one of the many in the area whose lives were transformed by the church.
He dreamed of becoming a rapper but was arrested after falling into crime and violence. Once out of prison, at the age of 20, Tropiano became closer and closer to the local church.
“My life was horrible, with so much suffering. But then I found God and that was when I started to be a better person,” he said.
Late Saturday Leo presided over an evening prayer vigil at Montevideo’s Centenario Stadium, which hosted Pope John Paul II during the last papal visit to Uruguay in 1988. The Vatican said some 70,000 people were inside and another 30,000 outside watching on TV screens.
Leo told them that the relatively small number of Catholics in Uruguay wasn't a calculus the church considers important, recalling that Jesus was born in a small stable in Bethlehem.
“God chose Bethlehem, and that choice alone is enough to prevent us from equating smallness with insignificance,” Leo said.
Saturday was Leo's only full day in Uruguay before heading Sunday afternoon to Argentina for the second leg of his trip, which was to end next week in his second homeland of Peru.
Many Argentines, though, took advantage of the Paysandú Mass to see him since it was located just across a bridge from the eastern Argentine city of Colón and was closer than any of his Argentine stops in Buenos Aires, Luján and Córdoba.
“Argentina is a much more religious country than Uruguay, and there’s this desire to be here to witness something historic,” said Luciana Lobato, 20, an Argentine tour agent who organized buses for 180 pilgrims from across the border.

Janice Tjen continued her winning streak while Magda Linette pulled off yet another comeback to set up an interesting singles final at the WTA 250 Chennai Open on Saturday.
World No. 75 Tjen, who clinched her maiden Tour-level title here last year, was largely untroubled during her 6-3, 6-4 victory over USA’s Robin Montgomery as the top-seeded Indonesian notched up her ninth straight win at the SDAT Stadium in Nungambakkam.
Later, Linette, who finished as runner-up in the inaugural edition in 2022 but did not play here last season, had to dig deep for a 2-6, 6-2, 6-3 win over big-hitting Russian Anastasia Zakharova in the 34-year-old Pole’s third three-setter this week.
Amidst the cacophony of firecrackers bursting the bubble of silence usually created around a tennis fixture, Tjen blitzed to a 5-1 lead in the opener against left-handed Montgomery.
World No. 151 Montgomery stopped the bleeding as she converted her fifth chance to finally break Tjen’s serve, but the 24-year-old Indonesian eventually bagged the set.
Montgomery, 22, was much more patient with her play in the second essay as she looked to open up the court before going for the winning shot. It earned her a break point at 40-30 in the fifth game but Tjen saved it with a superb forehand lob. Former World No. 95 Montgomery had one more chance but her forehand only found the net in response to a 136km/h second serve from Tjen.
Tjen escaped and immediately got the decisive break in the next game.
Serving for the match, Tjen showed yet another example of her court craft as she won a 13-shot rally on match point with a forehand down the line.
“This is the first time that I’ve played in this kind of outside environment. It’s definitely not easy for me and I’m pretty sure it’s also not easy for anybody else as well because we’re so used to playing in a quiet environment. So,I was just trying to be focussed there,” said Tjen when asked about playing with firecrackers bursting in the background.
“We were told by the supervisor that there will be fireworks going on during the match and knowing that in advance definitely helped. I was trying to just tune it out as much as possible. It’s definitely not easy because you don’t know when it’s going to happen. It is constantly happening but it’s at random times.”
Linette, who came to Chennai with seven first-round exits since her semifinal finish at the WTA 250 event in ‘s-Hertogenbosch, Netherlands, was on the backfoot as the 24-year-old Zakharova’s aggressive style of play completely broke her forehand in the first set.
But the third-seeded Pole, former World No. 19 and 2023 Australian Open semifinalist, showed her experience as from the second set, she focussed more on using the pace of Zakharova’s shots and redirecting the ball into the vacant corners.
World No. 107 Zakharova did not search for a Plan B and continued to go hard. She produced moments of brilliance at times but lacked the consistency to mount a comeback, eventually succumbing to Linette in an hour and 55 minutes.

Is the Alberta government engaging in American-style gerrymandering?
Take political parties out of electoral map-making, former Manitoba commissioner says
NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi has called the proposed redrawing of Alberta’s electoral boundaries a “Trump-style MAGA gerrymandered map.”
Premier Danielle Smith says rural-urban hybrid ridings are common, and serve communities well.
So which is it? Alberta’s electoral boundaries commission turned what is normally a routine process into a politically charged conversation this week. Political science experts told CBC’s West of Centre that Alberta’s map-making process should be reexamined to stave off American influences.
The new boundaries report comes on the heels of the U.S. midterm elections, where Republican efforts to redraw district lines weren’t enough to stop a blue wave of Democrat wins.
Greg Anderson, a political science professor at the University of Alberta who studies Canada-U.S. relations, says some U.S. states have commissions, but redistricting is generally understood to be driven by partisan efforts to gain advantage.
Here in Alberta, he sees echoes of that practice in the way the map lumps in some urban Lethbridge voters with those in surrounding counties.
“Just the way that the lines have been drawn as an effort to water down the impact of an urban area, it smells a lot like the gerrymandering that you see in the United States.”
Anderson said it’s common to see newly-drawn maps tied up in U.S. courts.
“That's sort of a sign that the stakes are really high.”
The Alberta NDP has already threatened to take the province to court on constitutional grounds, if the proposed map becomes law.
Per the usual process, Alberta had a bipartisan commission propose a new electoral map last spring.
But in an unprecedented move, the two UCP members on the commission submitted their own report and map in protest against the majority proposal.
Both maps were rejected by the government.
A UCP-majority committee struck a second commission, which created a third map — the one currently before the legislature.
A map showing a sole Lethbridge urban seat, as well as three hybrid electoral divisions combining parts of the city with vast surrounding rural regions. (Advisory panel on electoral boundaries)
Mount Royal political scientist Lori Williams says the first commission’s division and the subsequent re-do represent a breakdown in political norms.
“I think one of the strengths of Canada is the fact that we've got independent bodies — to some degree independent — even if they're multi-partisan bodies making decisions about these electoral boundaries.”
“It's the violation of that standard, that norm that's causing so much controversy here.”
Alberta’s Justice Minister Mickey Amery repeatedly told the legislature this week that the redistricting was non-partisan and independent.
There’s another way
Richard Sigurdson, a political science professor at the University of Calgary, said in an interview that there’s a way Alberta could avoid continuing down this road.
Sigurdson served on Manitoba’s 2008 electoral divisions boundaries commission and describes the process as completely non-partisan.
Manitoba’s commission is made up of its chief justice, chief electoral officer and three university presidents in the province. As dean of arts at the University of Manitoba, Sigurdson was brought on in the president’s place, as outlined in legislation.
He blames partisan appointments for the division that plagued Alberta’s first commission.
“Having any kind of partisanship in these commissions, in my view, is problematic and opens you up to criticism that you're not interacting above the board — that it's not really independent of government.”
A future without partisan appointments is Williams’ preferred outcome.
“If the rules aren't clear on this, there's going to be a temptation for some people to make it more to their advantage and to have more influence.”
