Taiwanese telco Chunghwa Telecom announced a slate of film and series investments at Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF), including police crime drama Gunshot, starring Kent Tsai, and Call Of Lobster, starring Choi Siwon and Chang Chen.
Chunghwa is one of three Taiwanese telcos that are investing in film and TV content through funds launched in partnership with the Taiwanese government.
The company’s previous content investments include feature films Arrested Memory, a Japan-Taiwan co-production directed by Sabu, and The Photo From 1977, directed by Frank Cheng and Sheng-Jung Tang. The two films have a combined 12 nominations in the upcoming Golden Horse Awards.
Gunshot, also starring Chan Tzu-Hsuan, Cheng Chih-Wei, Lu Hsiao-Fen and Mark Lee, follows three police officers with conflicting views of justice trying to navigate a system that rewards visibility over virtue. The eight-part series is produced by PTS Taigi TV with S11 Partners and Third Culture Content.
Watch on Deadline
Other drama series investments from Chunghwa include Yesterday’s Daughter, Tomorrow’s Mother, a family fantasy series created by award-winning producer Phoebe Ma and director Hung Tzu-peng; fantasy adventure series Guides To The World Below, adapted from a popular Taiwanese comic; and C’est La Vie, an urban drama blending cuisine and women’s personal growth, with actress Esther Liu serving as executive producer.
On the film front, Chunghwa is investing in Call Of Lobster, a cross-border action comedy loosely based on the true story of a Taiwanese lobster farmer who offered his services to the North Korean government. Chang Chen and Super Junior member Choi Siwon are set to star in the film, directed by Yin Chen-hao and produced by Calendar Studios.
Chunghwa boarded the project after it won the Chunghwa Telecom Award at TCCF in 2024. Taiwan’s Ministry of Culture is also backing the film.
Among other film investments, Chunghwa also announced its participation in Studio76’s Demon Of The East – Black Condo, part of a horror cinematic universe spanning four Asian countries. Outside of films and series, Chunghwa is also backing reality cooking show Next Z Chef and indie band Shallow Levée’s Speak in Silence Asian tour.
At the slate announcement event in TCCF, Taiwan’s Minister of Culture Li Yuan said: “Chunghwa Telecom is like a pyramid. I am grateful that, beyond building a strong foundation through its thriving core business, the company is also willing to invest at the very top of the pyramid, supporting film and television professionals as they continue moving forward and creating even better work.”
Chunghwa Telecom Senior Executive Vice President Lin Wen-chiyh said: “Chunghwa Telecom is more than just a platform operator; we are also a driving force behind the long-term development of the content industry. Moving forward, we will continue to connect funding, creative talent, and domestic and international partners, leveraging our group’s resources and industry partnerships to help Taiwanese content reach international markets.”

Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.
Amid an onslaught of AI vulnerability discovery and AI-assisted hacking, some of the most consequential critical infrastructure attacks this year may have little to do with the technology at all—instead providing a stark reminder that cybersecurity fundamentals are still key to digital defense.
Three sites in France that handle blood and plasma bags were briefly impacted this week by widespread attacks on vulnerable internet-connected refrigerators. On Wednesday, the Établissement Français du Sang (EFS) confirmed that cold rooms storing blood were “raised to very high temperatures” on November 2. The blood samples, thankfully, weren’t altered or damaged, the EFS said, because the organization’s alarm facilities and staff quickly detected the changes and implemented fail-safe measures.
The incident, however, comes amid a wave of cyberattacks in recent days affecting supermarket chains in at least 11 European countries that also drastically increased the temperatures of their refrigerators. Pictures from across the continent show huge volumes of food being trashed following the spikes. Similar fridge attacks in October affected hundreds of French stores that were forced to throw away food. And in August, roughly six commissaries and grocery stores on United States military bases suffered similar incidents resulting in spoiled food. The Pentagon is investigating the incidents and is collaborating with French law enforcement, Reuters reported last week.
“It's been true for more than a decade now that our dependence on connected technology is growing faster than our collective will to protect it, which has exposed us to accidents, adversaries, and now potentially agents,” says longtime critical infrastructure researcher Josh Corman, who is currently the executive in residence for public safety and resilience at the nonprofit Institute for Security and Technology. “These fragile cold-chain systems are too critical to fail, but we keep experiencing hard lessons.”
It is still unclear who is behind the incidents and whether the attacks are all connected or being carried out by multiple actors. The first recent wave of attacks against French supermarkets last month appears to have been caused by attackers exploiting unpatched refrigeration controllers exposed to the internet—including software versions that allegedly used weak passwords formulated based on the date.
Many of the hacks stem from attackers exploiting vulnerabilities in temperature controllers made by the Danish firm Danfoss, and researchers say the attacks would not have been particularly difficult to pull off. Danfoss did not return WIRED’s request for comment.
In other statements, Danfoss said impacted systems “were running outdated firmware” and urged customers to keep products updated. In an alert on Thursday addressing the rash of incidents, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said attacks could exploit flaws in cold storage systems via authentication bypasses, arbitrary code injections, and weak configurations. Experts have long warned about the dire threats to critical infrastructure posed by these types of weaknesses in so-called internet-of-things devices.
Russian hacktivists tried to claim responsibility for some of the attacks but did not provide credible evidence. Still, some researchers see signs that Russia-based actors may have been involved in at least some of the incidents. The Kremlin this week denied involvement. In other cases, researchers have found potential ties to Iran-linked actors. NextGov/FCW reported last week that unnamed US officials suspect Iran-linked attackers may have been behind the freezer attacks on US military bases, though they noted that the investigation is still ongoing.
This type of refrigerator/freezer attack is not new. Back in 2022, 16 supermarkets in Russia were targeted at the start of the country’s full-scale war with Ukraine. That year, 40 stores in Israel were similarly attacked, according to a 2025 report by Danfoss.
“Many businesses use older technology while the systems become increasingly connected,” Sweden’s National Cyber Security Center pointed out in a recent advisory about the freezer attacks, noting that companies should inventory which of their devices are connected to the internet, disconnect them whenever possible, and make sure they are kept access-controlled, patched, and monitored if they must be connected.

Indian stockbrokers’ combined total active user base shrunk by 0.5% to 4.59 Cr in October, dropping from 4.61 Cr users in September. Despite the broader market plateau, user consolidation accelerated in favour of newer players. Groww continued to cement its market-leading position with 1.38 Cr active users in October, commanding a 30% market share. Notably, it added 3.04 Lakh users in the month, more than any other competitor in the top 10. To note, Groww’s net active client additions in October were approximately 1.5X the combined additions of the next four largest brokers by active client base, Angel One, Zerodha, ICICI Securities and Upstox, which collectively added around 2.02 lakh active clients. But the positions below saw an intriguing shakeup. Zerodha, after losing clients in many months over the past year, slipped from second place. Angel One overtook Zerodha, adding around 2.4 Lakh users to take its active user count to 69.99 Lakh and its market share to 15.3%. It grew at a 3.3% rate over the past month to overtake Zerodha. “During the quarter, Angel One acquired nearly 15 lakh new clients, up 11.6% from the previous quarter, taking its client base to 3.99 Cr by September before it crossed 4 Cr in October. Its wealth management business continued to scale, with assets under management rising 19.1% quarter-on-quarter and 160.5% year-on-year to ₹16,000 Cr,” the company said in a statement. Meanwhile, more than 32K users or around 0.5% of Zerodha’s active user base turned inactive over the previous month. It ended the month with 67.59 Lakh users, compared to 67.92 Lakh users in the previous month, although its market share remained nearly unchanged at 14.7%. ICICI Securities held its fourth place with 21.64 Lakh active users, adding 3.7 Lakh users in October to take its market share to 4.7% market share. In fifth place, Upstox shed 0.6% of its user base as the startup saw 11.3 Lakh users leave to bring its active user count down to 18.43 Lakh with a market share of just 4%. Kotak Securities occupied sixth position with 14.05 Lakh active users while HDFC Securities finished seventh with 13.61 Lakh active users. The two bank-linked brokerages grew their user base by 0.9% and 0.5% respectively. Meanwhile, Dhan, in eighth place, added nearly 26K users over the past, as its user base increased 2.3% to 11.47 Lakh from 11.21 Lakh in September. It was able to match Groww in terms of growth rate to become the second fastest growing brokerage among the top 10 after Angel One. SBI Securities lost the most users after Zerodha, with an exodus of 17K users or 1.7% of its user base. The retail stockbroking subsidiary of SBI Capital Markets saw its active user count decline to 10.04 Lakh compared to 10.21 Lakh in September. Rounding off the top 10, Motilal Oswal’s active user count grew 0.8% to 9.16 Lakh from 9.09 Lakh. Beyond the top 10, Sahi added 34,372 active clients during October, adding to its bid to solidify its name in the discount brokerage space. Markets Recover In The Month Of October October marked a modest recovery for Indian equities after September’s sharp correction, although foreign investor selling remained elevated. The Nifty 50 rose 2.81% while Sensex gained over 3%. The gains ended the benchmarks’ two-month losing streak, but the recovery was not broad-based, with mid- and small-cap stocks continuing to face pressure. This teen boy set out to get people talking about periods. He's now a Diana honoree
Can a teenage boy change the way people think about menstruation?
At just 14, Aadvik Jain, studying in India's capital city, Delhi, set out to do exactly that. It all began when he had to watch a close friend struggle with debilitating menstrual pain that wasn't being taken seriously.
This year, he's among the 198 young people from 44 countries who were honored with the Diana Award, an international recognition for young changemakers working to improve lives in their communities. The awardees were announced on November 4 at a virtual ceremony streamed internationally.
Established in memory of Diana, Princess of Wales, the international award recognizes young people ages 16 to 25 for their social action and humanitarian efforts. This year, India accounted for nearly a quarter of the recipients, with 49 honorees.
Among them are Shiv Mandlik, who invented a bendable pole to help construction workers avoid working at dangerous heights and who developed an app to detect falls; Krish Aggarwal, who created an inexpensive filter that can be fitted onto ordinary fans to reduce indoor air pollution; and Kushal Sachdeva, who at age 11 began feeding a starving street dog. His organization, Protect Paws, has reportedly helped more than 1,500 stray dogs by arranging for medical treatment, vaccinations and reflective collars.
And then there's Jain. Now 18, he leads Team Period, an initiative he started in 2024 with three close friends. Together, they are challenging menstrual stigma through workshops, street performances, awareness campaigns and efforts to improve access to menstrual pads and products. He's also set to start studying medicine and public health at the University of Bologna in Italy in February.
NPR spoke to Jain through a video call about the experiences that inspired him, the challenge of persuading boys and men to join the conversation on periods and what he has learned about changing deeply entrenched attitudes.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
You were just 14 when you became concerned about menstrual health. What happened to make you realize that something needed to change?
It started with something that happened to a very close friend of mine in 2023, when we were in the tenth grade. We had been friends since the fifth grade. She used to call me her brother and would tie a rakhi every year [a sacred thread that girls tie around the wrist of a brother or brother-like figure, as a symbol of their bond, during the Indian festival of Raksha Bandhan].
During our midterm examinations, I noticed that she was struggling. She was in so much pain. I could not put a finger on it. What's happening? Does she have a fever? What's going on? So I checked in on her, and she said "I'm on my period, and I'm having really bad cramps." And then she just started crying. We took her to the medical room, where she was given a painkiller, and her parents were called to take her home. In India, menstruation is something that is very concealed. It's a very hush-hush topic. Not a lot of people talk about it openly in their families.
She had been experiencing severe cramps for six to eight months, and before that, her periods had been very irregular. But the next day, she was back in school, with the same pain. Her parents thought she was trying to get out of her examinations.
She is such a bright person, but for one or two weeks every month, she would become like a wilted rose. She couldn't concentrate in class or do well in her tests.
I went home and asked my mother what we could do. My mother spoke to our teacher, who contacted my friend's parents and encouraged them to take her to a doctor.
She was subsequently diagnosed with PCOS [now referred to as PMOS, or polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome], and doctors were also investigating the possibility of endometriosis. She received treatment, made changes to her lifestyle and gradually improved. She's so much better now, because of her own efforts, and because she got the help she needed at the right time.
That experience really stayed with me.
Why did her experience affect you so deeply?
I remember once breaking my little toe against the edge of my bed. My father left his office, which was two hours away, came home and took me to the emergency room. I had an X-ray, and my foot was bandaged.
I thought, what if we responded to menstrual pain with the same concern?
What if a girl could simply tell her father, "Dad, I'm having really bad cramps, and I can't go to school today," and he would say, "Okay, let me get you a heating pad"?
But because menstruation is such a hush-hush topic, especially around the men in a family, that kind of conversation often doesn't happen.
And sometimes, even the women in a family aren't able to support other women in the way they deserve.
I realized that this was something that needed attention.
How did that concern and empathy develop into Team Period?
I studied at Amity International School, and our school runs a program called Youth Power through its student newspaper, The Global Times. [the only registered school newspaper in India].
Schools form teams of four students, choose a social cause and spend several months working to create change in their communities. Then the schools compete with each other [to see who has the best ideas]. Our team consisted of me, Shivansh Arora, Aaratrika Jha Anand and Navya Manglik — so we're two boys and two girls.
Initially, Team Period began like any other school competition. We spent about six months working on the issue. But when the competition ended, I didn't want the work to end.
There is a certain feeling you get when you're talking to people, knowing that what you are saying matters, and maybe one day it could even change someone's life. But it wasn't just about that feeling. It was about the change we were creating at the grassroots level.
I have always been interested in public health, and I hope to work with an organization like the WHO or the United Nations one day. But as a 16- or 17-year-old, you can't just show up at the WHO and say you want to change things.
You have to start somewhere.
As a teenage boy, did you encounter resistance when you began talking about menstruation? Did girls ever accuse you of mansplaining?
Of course, people were surprised that a 15-year-old boy wanted to tackle menstrual shame.
But our friends were very supportive because we never approached the issue as experts. We approached it as learners. I never thought that I could explain what happens to a woman's body better than a woman herself.
At times, I was the face of the campaign. I was the spokesperson delivering speeches and talking to young women about menstruation. But it never came from a place of thinking that I knew more than they did. It came from a place of wanting to help solve a problem.
Everything we did was approached with empathy, sensitivity and respect. One girl might be completely comfortable talking about her periods in front of a classroom, while another might be deeply embarrassed.
Our goal is to end that shame, but we don't want to do it by shaming the person herself.
Were there moments when you realized that it might be harder than you thought to include boys in this conversation?
Yes. There was a workshop we organized at a school where the boys were asked to leave the room, so the girls could discuss these issues freely.
Initially, I was very upset because the whole point of our project was that boys should learn about menstruation, too.
But once the boys left, I saw girls who had been completely silent suddenly asking questions, laughing and speaking openly.
That was a learning experience for me.
Sometimes, girls need their own space to talk about these things. You can't force everyone to be comfortable immediately. We later held a separate session for the boys and eventually brought everyone together for a discussion. So at the end of the day, boys and girls were able to talk about it openly. I learned that creating an open environment is a process.
Can you describe an experience that convinced you your work was making a difference? Anything that really surprised you?
We once held an activity with middle-school students where we taught them to make simple heating pads using socks filled with lentils or chickpeas.
There was a boy, about 12 years old, who was very disruptive. He kept interrupting us and asking why he needed to learn about periods. His attitude was essentially that this had nothing to do with him. The teacher wanted to send him to another classroom, but we said no. We wanted him to stay and participate. About a year later, after I had finished school, I returned to visit my teachers and met that boy again.
He told me that his younger sister, who was barely 9 years old, had got her first period when they were alone at home. She was terrified. She had gone to the bathroom, seen the blood and started crying and screaming for help. But because of our workshop, he knew what was happening. He called his mother and asked where she kept the sanitary pads. He reassured his sister, helped her get cleaned up, made her a heating pad and even ordered chocolates for her.
By the time his mother returned, his sister was feeling much better.
He came up to me and thanked me. He said that when we first held the workshop, he couldn't understand why he needed to know any of this.
But when his sister needed help, he knew what to do. The fulfillment I felt in that moment was incomparable. To know that you've touched even one life is such a big honor.
You have used some unusual ways to get people talking about menstruation, including dance performances and flash mobs. How did those work?
We wanted to tackle menstrual shame from different directions, including through culture and performance.
One of our productions was a dance drama set during Durga Puja [a major Hindu festival honoring Goddess Durga's victory over a demon].
In the story, a young girl is performing the aarti [a Hindu ritual where a lamp is lit and prayers are offered] when her grandmother notices a menstrual stain on her clothes. The grandmother immediately excludes her from the prayers.
But Durga [the goddess] sees what has happened. She appears, comforts the girl and brings her back. I came up with the story, but the whole school helped put it together — the dance teachers, art teachers, costume designers, students and everyone involved in the production.
We performed it before an audience of more than 500 people in April 2025, and we've since performed or screened it at other events.
We also organized a flash mob at a mall and held activities at our school's winter carnival, where students, parents and grandparents participated in games about menstrual health.
One game involved picking colored chits containing questions about menstruation. People had only a short time to respond, which encouraged spontaneous answers instead of rehearsed ones. Sometimes a young boy would play, pick up a question and ask, all confused, "What is PCOS?"
We would stop the game and spend 10 minutes explaining it.
Our goal was to spark conversations.
You conducted surveys. Did this give you an insight into the way people think about menstruation?
We have been conducting surveys among students, parents and the wider community. At this point, we have collected around 4,000 responses.
One response that really struck us came from an eighth-grade girl.
She was angry that nobody cared if someone got a vegetable stain or ketchup on their clothes, but if a girl had a red menstrual stain on the back of her uniform, it became a huge issue.
Until then, our approach had been to teach boys to be sensitive — if a girl had a stain, you could quietly tell her or offer her your jacket.
But her response made us question that approach. Why should a menstrual stain be so embarrassing in the first place?
So we decided to normalize it.
We began wearing red stains on our uniforms. Some were stitched from red cloth, while others were stickers. At first, everyone laughed at us. Even the school objected because we were ruining the look of our uniforms with these big red patches.
But over the course of a week, more and more students joined in.
By the end, there was a sea of students wearing red stains. Some wore them on their backs, others on their shirts or identification cards.
When we conducted another survey months later, many students said they no longer felt that it was such a shame to spot or have a red stain.
We can't change attitudes across all of India immediately, but we were able to change something in our school.
In addition to changing attitudes and addressing stigma, what other aspects of menstrual care are you looking into?
There are several aspects to our work.
One is cultural — breaking down taboos and stigma. Another is logistical. How do you ensure that girls and women have access to menstrual products without feeling ashamed to ask for them? We installed a sanitary pad dispenser at our school.
Now we're talking to companies about how we could make dispensers available to other schools at a nominal cost. We are also exploring the possibility of developing our own design.
Disposal is another major issue. Used sanitary pads are often wrapped in newspaper and thrown into the garbage. But think about the people who sort that waste. How are they supposed to know what is inside the newspaper?
We're exploring a disposal system in which used pads can be sealed in specially designed bags, with clear warnings and illustrations in different languages. We want to think not just about the people using menstrual products but also those who handle the waste.
Your work has largely been concentrated in Delhi. Any plans to expand?
Until now, we've worked in government schools, orphanages, underserved neighborhoods and our own school in Delhi. We've also organized health camps.
But we were students, and our budgets were limited. We couldn't simply fly to Chennai or another city to replicate everything.
Now we want to decentralize Team Period and create local chapters.
Our team members are already spreading out to different cities and countries for their studies.
We'd like to bring in volunteers who speak different regional languages so that we can communicate more effectively with communities.
What does winning the Diana Award mean to you? Does it provide funding to help expand Team Period?
The Diana Award doesn't come with prize money.
But I think what it gives us is something equally valuable: recognition that our work matters.
When you're young and approaching potential sponsors or partners, people naturally have questions. They want to know whether you're legitimate and whether your work is making a difference. An international recognition like the Diana Award helps establish that credibility.
It gives us a platform to take our work to a larger audience.
For me, personally, it's deeply meaningful because we've faced moments when people questioned why boys were talking about menstruation. We've received strange looks from older people and even people of our own generation.
But this recognition tells us to keep showing up, even when things are difficult.

Your Mac's hard drive is full ... again. What's taking up all that space? Endless applications promise to answer this question and help you free up space, most with a subscription. I've tested many over the years, and few are easier to recommend than Purge.
This totally free, open source app gives you a quick breakdown of what's taking up space on your hard drive and offers a few specific ways to free it up. Even better: There are no ads or upsells. Purge can even delete Apple Intelligence's offline models from macOS 27, which could free up over 10 GB.
But even if you want to keep Apple's AI features, you can still clear up plenty of space. Your Mac, like any computer, tends to build up clutter over time. Sure, you might have forgotten about the games, images, and videos you downloaded, but caches also take up space. These are files downloaded and saved to speed things up, which can be useful. The problem is they can stick around longer than necessary and take up space. And then there are caches and settings left behind by apps you uninstalled ages ago—they're still there, eating up precious bytes.
Purge is designed to help you clean all that out, but it can do more. It's built around lists of files known to be safe to purge. There's also a list of things it will never touch, including crucial system files and your own documents. Finally, Purge sends files to the Trash instead of deleting them outright, so you can always recover them if something breaks.
To get started, download Purge and install it. Open the application, and it will show you what's taking up space on your Mac.
If you want, click the Clean Safe Items button, and the app will handle it, assuming you trust it. I recommend paying a bit more attention, though. First, delete some caches. You'll see a list of caches, all of which are safe to purge periodically.
You'll also see Apple's Aerial screen savers here. These videos are very cool, but take up a lot of space—delete them if you, like most 21st-century people, don't use a screen saver.
There's also a Dev Tools section, which isn't relevant for most people. If you use Homebrew, though, don't skip this—it's an easy way to delete cached installation files you don't need anymore.
The next tool shows you only the largest files on your computer, likely videos or other large media. I ended up moving a few things I'd forgotten about off my laptop—I bet you'll find something, too.
Up next is a tool for uninstalling apps. Note that this doesn't just remove the application—it also removes every file associated with it, including your settings, caches, and anything the application downloaded. Deleting applications in Finder doesn't do this, meaning you might leave all kinds of files behind.
Speaking of that, there's also a tool that shows leftover data from applications you've already deleted. In my case, it was several gigabytes, all basically wasted. I highly recommend checking this section and deleting anything large that you're confident you won't use again.
Finally, so long as we're talking about things you're not using, there's Apple Intelligence. Apple's most recent operating systems come preloaded with offline AI models, which power things like notification summaries, writing suggestions, and the new AI-powered Siri. You might like and use these features, but if not, Apple removed the toggle in macOS 27 that lets you disable them altogether.
That's why Purge has one final tool that can completely remove the Apple Intelligence models. Click it, and you'll see a list of installed models above a delete button. Click the button, and Purge will delete the models and prevent macOS from reinstalling them.
These features are why I plan on keeping Purge around. It's a great way to see what's taking up space on your drive and then do something about it.

WHO, the United Nations Foundation and Illumination have partnered to launch a Public Service Announcement (PSA) that reinforces safe and healthy practices during these challenging times, featuring Illumination’s globally beloved Gru and the Minions. The PSA focuses on lifesaving behaviors to help mitigate the impacts of COVID-19, including physical distancing, being active at home and remaining kind to each other —all aimed at making sure people of all ages stay safe and healthy during this pandemic.
“At this challenging time, we must find all ways possible to provide hope to people while sharing advice that can protect our health,” said Dr. Tedros Adhanom, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “WHO is excited to be working with Illumination and Steve Carell and the joys of the Minions and Gru to promote the importance of physical distancing, keeping active and connected, and being kind and compassionate to overcome COVID-19.”
The PSA is voiced by Academy Award® and Emmy Award® nominee Steve Carrell, who voices the character Gru in the Despicable Me franchise. The PSA will be localized into multiple languages including Spanish, French, Portuguese and Arabic, among others.
“Storytelling is a powerful tool to accelerate positive social change in the world. It is an honor to partner with the WHO and UN Foundation to remind people around the globe to protect themselves, each other and our communities during this pandemic. I am also appreciative to Participant for helping to organize the collaboration and to my partners at Comcast/NBCU for helping to amplify this important message,” said Illumination Founder and CEO Chris Meledandri.
Illumination is the first Hollywood Studio to partner with WHO, the UN Foundation and the COVID-19 Solidarity Response Fund to create an entertaining and educational PSA for global audiences. Participant helped facilitate the collaboration between Illumination to the United Nations Foundation and the World Health Organization.
"As the world continues to grapple with the challenges of COVID-19, one of our most powerful weapons is kindness," said Elizabeth Cousens, President & CEO of the United Nations Foundation. "We are delighted that the Despicable Me characters are letting their love show and showing ways to keep themselves and their communities safe during this unprecedented time."

Israel’s president has chosen Gadi Eisenkot, prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s strongest rival, to try to form a new government, after a deadlocked election that left neither man with a clear path to power.
Isaac Herzog’s office said he had informed Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party, on Saturday night “of his intention to task him with forming a government”.
It added that the formal appointment would take place in an official ceremony on Sunday at the president’s residence in Jerusalem.
“Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy,” Eisenkot wrote on X in his first reaction to the announcement of his designation.
Netanyahu is fighting to hold on to office after his religious-nationalist coalition lost its majority in an election on 27 October but still emerged as the largest bloc in parliament.
Should Eisenkot succeed in forming a coalition, he would take over as prime minister from Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving premier.
Eisenkot’s wide-ranging opposition bloc won 48 of the Israeli parliament’s 120 seats in October elections, while Netanyahu’s camp secured 53, leaving neither with a majority.
During party consultations with Herzog, 66-year-old Eisenkot received the endorsements of both Arab-majority lists, who could now play kingmakers after making unprecedented gains in the vote.
But it remains unclear if Eisenkot’s bloc would accept support from the Arab lists in forming a government.
Eisenkot, the military chief of staff from 2015 to 2019, has set out to unite Israelis after Netanyahu’s divisive tenure, under which the country moved sharply to the right.
He has vowed to crack down on extremist West Bank settlers who have attacked Palestinians with impunity, decrying recent incidents as “Jewish terror” abetted by Netanyahu’s government.
But the military man is no peacenik. He opposes the creation of a Palestinian state and vowed to end Hamas’s rule in Gaza and destroy the Islamist movement’s military wing.
Commanding the military during the 2006 war with Hezbollah, Eisenkot devised the so-called “Dahiya doctrine”. The idea, named after a Beirut suburb heavily damaged in that war, involves Israel vowing to use massive force against civilian infrastructure in areas controlled by Lebanese militant movement Hezbollah.

WASHINGTON — The Trump administration’s MAHA agenda has been derailed by corporate interests and the influence of money, a recently departed administration official told the podcaster Joe Rogan in a recording released Friday.
Calley Means, a key Make America Healthy Again leader who until recently worked in the White House and highest levels of the federal health agencies, said top White House officials were altering policies in response to industry influence and funding.
Means pointed to the fight over glyphosate, an herbicide many MAHA advocates argued causes grave health consequences. He recounted an “almost violent reaction” from industry groups that pressured agencies against researching or restricting the substance. He said a White House official later presented Means with a policy to boost its production — noting it was “not up for discussion.”

Some images of the Paris landmark shared on social media were authentic but miscaptioned. Others displayed evidence of AI generation. The Eiffel Tower has a well-documented history of being lit blue for various occasions, but there was no evidence that this happened in celebration of Democratic victories in the 2026 U.S. midterms.
A rumor that the Eiffel Tower was illuminated with blue lights to celebrate Democrats' victory in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections circulated in early November.
Following the election, people on social media shared purported images of the world-famous Paris landmark lit blue, with one post claiming this signified France stood "in solidarity with the new leadership in the House and Senate."
The claim gained popularity as the national conversation focused on the results of the midterms, in which Democrats, typically represented by the color blue, landed a decisive victory. The claim's popularity led Snopes readers to ask that we look into it.
There was no evidence France illuminated the Eiffel Tower blue to celebrate the results of the U.S. midterms.
Rather, some of the images shared in the posts were authentic, but taken during previous instances of the landmark being illuminated blue. Others displayed evidence of AI generation and were therefore fake. As such, we've rated this claim false.
For instance, one Facebook user shared a photo of the Eiffel Tower illuminated blue with the text, "They gave us the Statue of Liberty and now they lit up the Eiffel Tower in blue to celebrate with America." But that image shows the landmark illuminated blue with the 12 stars of the European Union, which was done in both 2008 and 2022 to celebrate French leadership of the EU. The Facebook user who shared the image also pointed out that some users were "attaching erroneous meaning to an unrelated photo."
Similar images to the one shared in the post from both 2008 and 2022 are available to view on the Getty Images repository, but our searches returned none from 2026.
Other images shared in some versions of the claim appeared to be generated using artificial intelligence.
The artificial intelligence detector Pangram said it was highly likely this particular image, used in the most-popular instances of the rumor, was generated with AI, though it should be noted that such platforms are not always reliable.
However, both OpenAI's Verify tool and Google's Gemini SynthID scan also confirmed the presence of a SynthID, which Google describes as "a technology developed by Google DeepMind that adds imperceptible digital watermarks to AI-generated content."
(OpenAI Verify)
(Pangram)
(Google)
A search of the Eiffel Tower's location tag on Instagram revealed dozens of posts that included photos of the landmark the week of the U.S. midterm elections, many of them at night, that clearly shows the landmark lit in its usual golden color.
Further, searches of Bing, Google, DuckDuckGo and Yahoo revealed no credible or relevant results about France illuminating the Eiffel Tower in blue as a result of the midterm elections, which would have been widely reported as international news. 
The official Eiffel Tower website has an entire page dedicated to the Eiffel Tower's blue illuminations, which states that "over the years, the monument has been bathed in blue to mark major events and support symbolic causes," naming "Europe, autism awareness, children's rights, tributes, or the colors of the French and Ukrainian flags," specifically.
According to the website, the first day the landmark was illuminated blue was May 9, 2006, in celebration of the 20th anniversary of Europe Day.
The site included other instances of the tower going fully blue in 2008, 2012, 2019 and 2021, as well as other instances of the blue lights being part of an overall display to convey the colors of the French and Ukrainian flags on the landmark.
There are other examples of the landmark's blue hue over the years available online. Photographer Peter Talke posted a photo of the Eiffel Tower illuminated in blue to his blog on Aug. 31, 2009. In September 2026, an Instagram user posted a blue-tinged Eiffel Tower among other photographs from Paris.
We reached out to the Eiffel Tower Operating Co. for further comment and will update this article if we hear back.
For further reading, we investigated a similar claim about Canada lighting Niagara Falls blue to celebrate Democrats' midterm wins.

Bank of Japan Gov. Kazuo Ueda said that while his nation’s inflation rate has reached policymakers’ target, it’s unclear how long it will stay there, and indicated it hasn’t yet become embedded among the broader Japanese public.
“Underlying inflation is 2% — our goal is to keep it there,” Ueda said in a question and answer session after delivering a speech at the International Monetary Fund in Washington on Friday. “I think we are in equilibrium,” he said. “Whether we could stay in that equilibrium for a very long time to come, we still don’t know.”
The remarks come a week after the BOJ marked a milestone by declaring that underlying inflation had reached the bank’s 2% target for the first time since the goal was introduced in 2013. Ueda didn’t offer any specific guidance on the central bank’s appetite to raise interest rates further, in an exchange with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva.

The Large Hadron Collider has been slamming protons together for years. But recently, a proton collision produced an improbable result that is the first step toward exploring the so-called “zeptoverse”—a scale of reality many, many times smaller than an atom. This would be the smallest scale of the physical world ever explored and may defy our expectations of how physics works.
While crashing protons together at nearly the speed of light, scientists at CERN found evidence of one of the most improbable decays of matter—so unlikely that it’s a phenomenon physicists have been hoping to observe for more than four decades. The collision produced numerous particles, including some known as neutral B mesons, and scientists found signals indicating that one of these had decayed into a muon and an antimuon.
Mesons decay all the time. These tiny particles, smaller than atoms, arise from collisions between other particles and exist only briefly before transforming into other particles. Muons, on the other hand, are similar to the electrons found in atoms, but about 200 times heavier. Scientists study these particles and their decays to test the predictions of current physics and search for clues to unknown particles.
The standard model—the sort of bible of particle physics—predicts that for every 10 billion decays of neutral B mesons, this transformation will occur once. In other words, even if scientists were to observe 10 billion of these particles decaying, they would expect to find, on average, only a single muon and antimuon. This discovery is the first time an experiment has obtained evidence of this phenomenon, the details of which the researchers have made available in a preprint on arXiv.
“Physicists have been chasing this decay for more than 40 years,” Marco Santimaria, who co-led the international analysis team, said in a press release from CERN. “Extreme precision is required to pick the muons out of the overwhelming background.”
The extraordinary rarity of this process explains why it’s taken decades of research to arrive at this discovery. But upgrades to the Large Hadron Collider in 2024 also made observing this phenomenon possible. The revamp enabled faster data collection, and new machine-learning techniques allowed researchers “to suppress the vast background of processes that would have otherwise swamped the signals from these rare beauty-particle decays,” as CERN described it in its statement.
This decay opens a new avenue for investigating the limits of what scientists have been able to observe. For now, the results are consistent with current physics predictions, but future measurements could reveal phenomena unique to the zeptoverse, which describes the scale where distances are measured in zeptometers (equivalent to one quadrillionth of a meter). To put this unit into perspective, a typical atom is about 100,000 million zeptometers in diameter. That’s also about the difference in size between you and one of your skin cells.
Beyond the zeptoverse lie even smaller scales, such as the Planck length, which is about 60 trillion times smaller than a zeptometer and the smallest theoretically possible unit in physics. Scientists still don’t know whether anything truly exists at that level, but it’s generally believed that physics as we know it completely breaks down on that scale. However, if scientists could gain access to this micro world, it could help us understand the first infinitesimal fraction of a second after the Big Bang, when the whole universe was such a size.
But, for now, much of what might happen there remains in the realm of speculation.

If anyone could find a connection between Elon Musk and Elizabeth Holmes, it's director Alex Gibney.
The Oscar-winning filmmaker has made movies on both polarizing figures. In 2019, he made the Elizabeth Holmes documentary "The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley." His latest doc is "Musk," a close-to-four-four examination of the richest man in the world.
In a recent interview with Business Insider, Gibney explained how Musk's rise reminded him of Holmes, who came to prominence in the 2010s as the founder of Theranos, a health technology company that boasted it could run hundreds of medical and diagnostic tests using only a few drops of blood. She's currently in prison for defrauding investors.
"I think there is a similarity with Elizabeth Holmes," Gibney told Business Insider. "What was rattling around in my head through this was 'confidence man.' Musk, like Holmes, was able, through force of confidence, to convince people of things that they knew not to be true. That became a superpower."

Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) has reportedly transferred about 695 engineers via an online lottery system anonymously. The move comes amid allegations of a cash-for-transfer scam against the civic body. Times of India reported the online system used for the transfers is called Employee Transfer System Based on Randomisation, which affected 152 junior engineers, 444 secondary engineers and 99 assistant engineers, including civil, mechanical and electrical cadres. Under the new system, reportedly all employees submitted up to five of their preferred posting locations out of which final selection was made. Talking about it, an official told the publication, “Eligible engineers were allowed to submit between one and five posting preferences and efforts were made to allot preferred postings. Transparency and impartiality were maintained in the transfer and posting process, which has once again shown that there is a positive attitude and satisfaction among the engineering cadre regarding the online process." Municipal commissioner (eastern suburbs) Avinash Dhakne assured that maximum engineers were given their preferred postings, calling it a fair and transparent process. Going forward, offline transfers would be restricted for exceptions only, such as mid-term transfers. Authorities are aiming to implement a similar online system for promotions as well. “This was a fair and transparent process. So now, offline transfers will be exceptions, in cases where there are mid-term transfers. All routine transfers will only take place through the online system. Even with bulk promotions, we will try to do it online only,” Dhakne was quoted by Times of India. The controversy around alleged cash-for-transfer surfaced last year. Diljit Dosanjh is set to perform in Indore on November 15 as part of his Aura India Tour. However, ahead of the concert, the district's child protection authorities reportedly directed the organisers to ensure that four of his popular songs are not played at the event, citing concerns over their lyrics and their possible influence on children.
The concert is scheduled to take place at C-21 Mall, where children above the age of five are permitted. A notice issued by the District Child Protection Officer asked the venue management to keep the four tracks out of the singer's setlist. Neither Diljit nor his team has issued a response to the directive so far.
Which Diljit Dosanjh songs have been banned in Indore?
According to a report in NDTV, the notice was issued on November 6 by the District Child Protection Officer under the Women and Child Development Department. It names four songs — Patiala Peg, 5 Taara, Jeeb Vicho Afeem (also known as Case) and Jatt Uthe Fire Karda.
The authorities raised concerns that the lyrics of these tracks could have “a wrong influence on young children.”
The notice also refers to a July 2019 order passed by the Punjab and Haryana High Court. While hearing cases largely related to noise pollution, the court had expressed concern over songs that glorified alcohol, drugs and violence. It observed that the “glorification of the liquor, wine, drugs and violence in the songs” across Punjab, Haryana, and Chandigarh “has increased in recent times.”
The court had further noted, "These songs affect the children of impressionable age." It had directed police chiefs to “ensure that no songs are played glorifying the liquor, wine, drugs and violence in any song even in live shows.”
What prompted the authorities to issue the notice?
The directive followed a complaint filed on November 1 by Chandigarh-based professor Panditrao Dharenavar, who was also a petitioner in the 2019 case. He approached the authorities seeking action against the four tracks and requested that Diljit not perform them “even with twisted lyrics.” He cited the High Court's directions and the Centre's anti-addiction initiatives.
Diljit Dosanjh confirms Indore concert will go ahead
Despite the restrictions, Diljit reportedly indicated that he will perform in Indore as scheduled. The singer, who recently kicked off his Aura Tour in Delhi, addressed the reports surrounding the concert and confirmed his November 15 visit.
“I will visit Indore on 15th of November. I will have poha first after visiting Indore. Anyone can say anything, but I will meet you in Indore on 15th November.” He also responded to reports of a possible security threat, saying, “I have heard in the news that there will be some ‘sankat’. But we know how to handle this. Do they know who we are?”
His remarks come after three private schools in Indore received emails threatening a bomb blast at the concert. The messages also warned the schools against sending children to the event. Bomb disposal teams searched the premises following the threats but did not find any explosives.
Additional Deputy Commissioner of Police Rajesh Dandotiya said the email appeared to be an attempt to spread panic and disrupt normal activities.
The Indore show is not the first Aura Tour concert to face security-related hurdles. On October 21, Delhi Police initially denied permission for Diljit's concert, citing security concerns, specific threat inputs and the arrangements required during the festive season.
The singer eventually performed at Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium in Delhi on October 30.

For three months, Suraj Kumar’s job was to feed discarded clothes into shredding machines in Panipat, an industrial city in the north Indian state of Haryana. Clothes discarded in the US, Canada and Europe arrive in the city to be torn back into fibres and spun into yarn, feeding a textile recycling industry that supplies markets across the world.
Suraj, 19, had travelled from West Bengal state to work in Panipat’s factories, following his cousins and friends who had already found jobs there. He hoped to earn enough to send money home to his parents. But in late August, an electrical short circuit in the machine propelled him into the shredding mechanism. The accident crushed both arms.
“I wish I had died rather than lost both my arms,” Suraj says. An only child, he had hoped his job in Panipat would support his parents. Instead, he fears he has become a financial burden on them. The work he had taken up to help his family has left him dependent on others, with no certainty about what his future will look like.
By some estimates, Panipat processes more than 1m tons of used clothing from across the world every year, making it one of the world’s largest textile recycling hubs. In the city’s 20,000 factories, employing about 300,000 people, discarded clothes are shredded into yarn and made into finished products, including home furnishings for brands such as H&M Home, Ikea, Primark, Tesco and Walmart.
But the fast-fashion industry, built on buying more and more clothes and wearing them less, carries a devastating cost for workers tackling its waste. Ramesh Chaudhary, an environmental activist who has worked in Panipat’s labour department, has been tracking reports of injuries and amputations across the city for the past five years. He estimates that at least one worker a day loses a limb, rising to as many as five on some days.
“Every day, we come across cases of workers injured inside factories, sometimes losing a hand or a leg, and sometimes even dying,” Chaudhary says. He gathers his information through a network of labour contractors who supply workers to factories across Panipat. But not all news of injuries reaches him, he says, suggesting the scale of the problem could be greater.
Between 17 and 24 August this year, the Guardian monitored reports from 11 private hospitals and two government hospitals in Panipat. In that period, six cases of textile workers with severe limb injuries were reported: two had lost an arm, another man lost both, one lost a hand, one lost a leg and the sixth their fingers.
Such injuries are common in Panipat’s factories, says Chaudhary, because machinery often lacks the necessary safety mechanisms. If a worker gets caught in a spinning machine, he says, cutting the power may not stop it immediately. By the time the machine comes to a halt, a worker may already have catastrophic injuries.
During numerous visits to spinning units and factories, the Guardian did not see anyone wearing any kind of safety gear. None of the workers interviewed reported having safety training.
India’s 1948 Factories Act places a duty on factory owners to protect workers’ health and safety. It requires serious workplace accidents to be reported to the authorities. But the effectiveness of safety oversight remains a concern, says Sandeep Sachdeva, co-founder of the Safe in India Foundation, which works to reduce industrial injuries.
“Factories are often audited by buyers, especially where quality and critical components are involved, and inspected by government industrial safety and health departments. Buyer audits tend to focus more on commercial requirements and product quality than on workplace safety or working conditions,” he says.
“Government inspections are selected through a central software system, but inspectors are now required to inform factories before visiting. Their role is now that of a facilitator-cum-inspector – a shift that undermines the effectiveness of inspections, particularly in factories with unsafe working conditions.”
For workers, losing a limb means losing their livelihood. Ramashankar Singh, who is in his fifties, from Chapra in Bihar, spent 18 years in Panipat’s factories before an accident last year led to him having a leg amputated.
It happened when a hot ball bearing fell on his foot. Ramashankar’s injury was first just wrapped in discarded cloth, before the factory owner sent him to a pharmacy.
The wound worsened as the infection spread. When Ramashankar approached his employer again, the owner agreed to arrange treatment and admitted him to a private hospital. By then, the infection had progressed so far that doctors had to amputate his leg above the knee.
“The factory owner said he would give me another job, possibly as a cook or a security guard at the factory,” Ramashankar says. “But that never happened.” The owner also said he would help him secure a government disability pension, but he has received no pension since the accident and relies on a prosthetic leg provided by a charitable organisation.
After so much of his life spent in a factory, Ramashankar says: “I have almost forgotten how to live without work. Much of my day now passes lying on my bed, staring at the ceiling fan.”
He also struggles with guilt that he has become a burden on his family.
India’s textile industry is the country’s second-largest source of employment after agriculture, directly employing more than 45 million people. An estimated 92% of its workforce is informally employed. In Panipat, more than 90% of workers are employed informally, says Ina Bahuguna, programme manager at the Estonia-based Reverse Resources, which monitors the city’s textile waste.
“Formal employment contracts and the social security benefits that accompany them, including pensions, are largely limited to workers in management, clerical roles and some specialised jobs, such as tailoring,” says Bahuguna.
Most workers on the factory floor lack these protections, leaving those who suffer serious injuries particularly vulnerable. Without formal employment or adequate social security coverage, they are left without employer-backed compensation, rehabilitation support or a source of income.
The Guardian asked several factory owners why they hired workers on a contractual or piece-rate basis rather than in permanent positions, and most cited the workers’ seasonal migration, saying some did not return to Panipat after travelling home.
For workers who sustain life-changing injuries, getting employers to pay for medical treatment can be a struggle. Indrapal Singh, who lost his arm in 2017, had worked in Panipat for 15 years, two and a half of those at the factory where he was injured. His hand was caught in a Chinese-made carding machine, which tore away the skin. He was given a painkilling injection but, as the infection worsened, his arm had to be amputated. The factory owner refused to pay his hospital bills.
Indrapal spent six years fighting his case through the courts, but says he received no compensation. The police told him that he had signed documents withdrawing his complaint, something Indrapal, who says he cannot read or write, disputes.
“I lost my arm, fought for six years, and in the end, all I got was a government pension of 5,700 rupees [£45]. The factory owner has faced no consequences, and the factory continues to operate as before,” he says.
Chaudhary says: “Workers have very little bargaining power when they are up against factory owners who are not only financially powerful but sometimes politically influential too. For many workers, taking them on in a legal fight is simply not an option.”
Arvind Kumar, the officer in charge at one of Panipat’s 12 police stations, says three workplace injury cases have been registered at his station so far this year. One involved the death of a worker. “Fewer than 1% of workplace injury cases reach the police and are formally registered,” he says.
Most cases, the officer says, are settled outside the formal legal system. Workers may receive a one-time payment towards medical bills, but then are generally left to manage the long-term consequences of their injuries on their own. The police rarely get involved.
For now, Suraj Kumar’’s family are grateful that the factory owner covered his hospital bills. They are not sure whether to register a police complaint.
“He [the owner] is like God to us. He is paying for our boy’s treatment,” says his mother, Sita.
Suraj struggles to imagine what comes next. “I thought that if I worked hard for two years, I could buy myself a motorcycle. I had so many things I wanted to do with my life. I never thought I would have to start by figuring out how to live without my arms.”

- Microsoft could soon consider selling Xbox following the Democrats' victory in the 2026 US midterm elections.
- Analyst Joost van Dreunen believes growing opposition to data centers could threaten Microsoft's AI expansion plans.
- He believes Microsoft's declining Xbox revenue could push the company to sell the division to fund its AI ambitions.
The Democrats have won control of both the House and Senate in the 2026 US midterm elections, marking a major political shift that could also affect Xbox. Gaming industry analyst Joost van Dreunen believes the US election results could push Microsoft to sell its gaming division, despite Xbox CEO Asha Sharma recently stating that Xbox is not for sale.
In the analyst’s November 5 Substack post, Van Dreunen points to growing voter opposition to data centers, with a recent Wall Street Journal report saying that more than 40 towns and counties discussed measures to limit data center construction, with at least 10 voting to restrict or ban new projects. For Microsoft, which is heavily invested in AI, this isn’t good news.
Microsoft’s growing focus on AI and data center expansion also played a part in the “XBOX Reset” in July 2026, which saw the company cut more than 3,000 jobs and make major changes across its gaming division. Furthermore, while PlayStation continues to grow its gaming revenue, Xbox is lagging behind Microsoft’s other business divisions.
Xbox generated $5.4 billion in revenue in the previous quarter of 2026, which includes Xbox Game Pass and other services, down 2% from the same period last year. Meanwhile, Microsoft’s Search and Advertising division grew from $5.9 billion to $6.6 billion, highlighting the gap between Xbox and the company’s other businesses.
Van Dreunen believes Microsoft could sell Xbox to free up resources and, mainly, revenue for its AI ambitions. He also argues that CEO Asha Sharma’s announcement of Xbox XP, a division focused on turning gaming IPs into films and TV shows, could make the brand more appealing to potential buyers, since it showcases Xbox as a more traditional entertainment company.
Asha Sharma also recently announced Xbox Labs, an experimental R&D unit exploring AI-powered game development. So, with Democrats now controlling both chambers of Congress, Van Dreunen believes Microsoft’s AI ambitions could make an Xbox sale a more serious possibility. That said, do you think Microsoft will sell Xbox after the US election results? Let us know.

What discs can a PlayStation 5 play?
Some of your old games and other media work on your PS5, turning it into a proper media hub.
With Sony's plans to stop making disc-based games come 2028, physical media enthusiasts may want to start stocking up soon. While some PlayStation 5 owners already veered in this direction by purchasing the disc-free console variant, many traditionalists can't stand the thought of this transition. While no new games released in 2028 and beyond will get physical copies, existing discs will still continue to work.
We're over a year away from this shift — one that could very well play into what the PlayStation 6 ends up being. In the meantime, if you have a stack of Blu-ray movies, your go-to show on DVD or some last-gen games sitting around, they should all work on the PS5. Let's go through which discs are compatible with Sony's current console.
Remember that if you own the Slim digital PS5 or a PS5 Pro, you can buy the detachable PS5 disc drive for $79. This isn't compatible with the original Digital Edition model.
Understanding game disc compatibility on PS5
Of course, all PS5 game discs will continue to work on the console, as will your old PS4 physical games. Barring a few titles, the PS5 is backward compatible with the "overwhelming majority" of PS4 titles, whether on disc or digital. From Bloodborne to Red Dead Redemption 2, plenty of iconic PS4 releases haven't received the next-gen treatment, but you're still able to enjoy them on the newer system.
Even better, the console's Game Boost tech delivers smoother frame rates for certain PS5 games including God of War, The Last of Us Part II and Days Gone. While this feature doesn't apply to every game, many of the ones that received patches upped performance to 60 fps on PS5 — an improvement from how those titles ran on a standard PS4.
According to Sony's PS5 backward compatibility page, a total of six PS4 games aren't playable. Apologies to fans of Hitman Go: Definitive Edition and some other obscure titles like We Sing or Just Deal With It! The company notes that other PS4 releases like demos and media apps might not be compatible, either.
Unfortunately, the PS5's backward compatibility doesn't go any further; the console won't play physical PS1, PS2 or PS3 games. Plenty of legendary titles from older generations are available to play digitally from the PlayStation Store, though many beloved games like LittleBigPlanet and Shadow Hearts: Covenant remain abandoned on their original consoles.
What media discs work with your PS5?
Many of the best streaming services like Netflix and Disney+ offer apps on PS5. If you're planning to treat the console like an all-in-one media hub, you'll be glad to know the PlayStation 5 supports both Ultra HD Blu-ray and standard Blu-ray discs, as well as DVDs. That means all those old movies and TV box sets you bought years ago still have some life in them. However, 3D Blu-rays are a no-go.
Home-burned video discs may work if you properly finalize them, but there are no guarantees. You can't drop raw video files onto a disc and play them on the PS5. The PS5 can't play audio CDs, which matches is predecessor (though the PS3 had this capability). If you want to listen to music while playing, Apple Music and Spotify offer apps for the console.
If this is something you want, a better option is connecting a USB drive with video or audio files, following Sony's instructions for folder naming and file types. That's a good workaround for files you'd otherwise play from homemade discs or CDs.
Finally, while it's probably obvious, Sony asserts that non-circular discs shaped like a "card, star or heart" will be rejected. Don't stick a small GameCube disc into the PS5, either.

Two attacks in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have killed 4 workers responding to the Ebola outbreak and injured 5 others.
The attacks occurred overnight on a shared living camp in Biakato Mines and an Ebola response coordination office in Mangina.
“We are heartbroken that people have died in the line of duty as they worked to save others,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, World Health Organization Director-General. “The world has lost brave professionals.”
The dead include a member of a vaccination team, two drivers and a police officer. No WHO staff are among those killed, one staff member was injured.
“My heart goes out to the family and friends of the first responders killed in these attacks,” said Dr Matshidiso Moeti, WHO Regional Director for Africa. “We are doing everything possible to bring the injured and front-line workers in the impacted areas to safety. These constant attacks must stop. We will continue to work with the DRC Government, partners and MONUSCO to ensure the security of our staff and other health workers.”
In the last week, there were 7 cases of Ebola, down from a peak of over 120 per week in April 2019.
“Ebola was retreating. These attacks will give it force again, and more people will die as a consequence,” said Dr Tedros. “It will be tragic to see more unnecessary suffering in communities that have already suffered so much. We call on everyone who has a role to play to end this cycle of violence.”
The situation is still evolving. WHO will provide updates as new information comes in.

A major California strawberry grower is cutting ties with six farms and laying off more than 500 workers as soaring water and labor costs squeeze the industry.
SoCal Berry Growers, a supplier for strawberry giant Driscoll’s, plans to permanently close its operations at six locations in Ventura County, according to a letter sent to Oxnard city officials Saturday. The closures, which will affect farms along California's Central Coast, and the resulting job cuts, are expected to take place between January 11 and January 25, 2027.
“As a result and based on currently available information, all the Company’s operations will cease and approximately 572 employees may suffer a permanent employment loss,” the letter states.
Driscoll’s, the world’s largest berry producer, sources its strawberries from independent family farms in growing regions including Florida, Mexico and Virginia, as well as other locations around the world, according to its website.
“We are deeply saddened by the news that SoCal Berry Growers plans to close its farms in Ventura County this January,” a Driscoll’s spokesperson told The Independent Saturday. “It’s a difficult day for California agriculture when a family farming business that has spent decades supporting livelihoods and contributing to the agricultural heritage of the Central Coast decides to close its farms.”
“These closures will affect far more than the farms themselves. Our thoughts are with the farmworkers whose livelihoods will be affected, their families, and the broader communities that have depended on these operations and taken pride in their contributions for generations,” the Driscoll’s spokesperson added.
The news comes as California farmers grapple with soaring production costs, including water, fuel, fertilizer and labor.
“Water quadrupled. Labor nearly doubled,” a recent study by the Farm Bureau of Ventura County titled "The $2.4 Billion Crisis,” states, pointing to how much more expensive it has become to keep farms running.
Strawberries were the county's top cash crop in 2025, generating approximately $807.8 million in revenue. But it cost farmers more than $815 million to produce them, according to Louise Lampara, CEO of the Farm Bureau of Ventura County.
“They didn’t make a penny and paid $8.1 million out of pocket,” Lampara told SFGATE.
Irrigation water prices jumped from $22.10 per acre-inch in 2007 to $88.83 in 2025, the report found. Meanwhile, hourly labor costs increased from $13 in 2020 to $25.16 in 2025. “It's an industry in crisis,” Lampara said.
The rising expenses are making it increasingly difficult for American growers to compete with imported produce, Lampara added. Farmers have little control over what grocery stores and other buyers pay for their crops, even as the cost of producing them continues to climb.
"We have such pressure right now from importers," she said, pointing to record volumes of imported strawberries, avocados and lemons.
Lampara said that overseas growers may operate under different regulatory requirements, making it harder for California farms to compete on price.
SoCal Berry Growers ceasing operations with the six farms comes months after the company’s employees voted to unionize with the United Farm Workers of America in July. The company challenged the unionization effort, alleging misconduct, but the California Agricultural Labor Relations Board upheld the election in August, ruling that it had not been conducted improperly.
"SoCal management is now saying it will shut down, in what we believe is a clear violation of the law to avoid their legal and moral obligations to the workers who pick the strawberries," United Farm Workers Vice President Roman Pinal said in a statement to the Ventura County Star this week.
The union said it plans to pursue legal options to protect its members.
The Independent has contacted SoCal Berry Growers and the United Farm Workers of America for comment.
