Earlier this week, people began sharing a rumor claiming the U.S. Space Force took over the Federal Aviation Administration, including air traffic control.
For example, on Nov. 5, a Facebook user posted (archived) the rumor, alleging President Donald Trump and tech entrepreneur Elon Musk were taking the U.S. into World War III. That post read in part:
LOOKS LIKE TRUMP AND MUSK ARE STILL TRYING TO KILL US ALL WITH WW3! Look what just happened LAST NIGHT WHILE WE WERE SLEEPING! WE ARE NOT OUT OF THE WOODS YET WITH THESE CRAZY PSYCHOS! SPACE FORCE JUST TOOK OVER THE FAA. AIR TRAFFIC IS NOW MILITARY.
From Lisa Derry (link at the end of this quote):
The Federal Aviation Administration's air traffic control system was transferred to the United States Space Force.
The corporate media is calling it a "temporary integration." A "national security precaution." A "seamless transition."
THEY ARE LYING TO YOU BECAUSE THE FAA WAS NEVER JUST ABOUT AIRPLANES.
What they are hiding in total panic: At exactly 01:00 AM Eastern this morning, the authority over every civilian air traffic control tower in the United States was transferred to Space Force Command. The transfer was signed at 11:47 PM the night before. It was not a budget decision. It was not a security review. It was a takeover.
No congressional hearing. No public announcement. No explanation.
THE SKIES ARE NOW MILITARY AIRSPACE.
Other users shared the same claim on Facebook (archived), Threads (archived) and X (archived).
Snopes readers also emailed to inquire about the rumor. For example, one person asked, "Is this true? The Federal Aviation Administration's air traffic control system was transferred to the United States Space Force."
Another reader sent, "This is going viral on the internet tonight. Is this true? The Federal Aviation Administration's air traffic control system was transferred to the United States Space Force."
In sum, Snopes' research, as well as our correspondence with Air Force and FAA officials, confirmed this rumor was false.
An FAA spokesperson told Snopes via email, "There is absolutely no truth to this rumor." A Space Force spokesperson also said, "These claims are false." (The government organizes Space Force under the Air Force, though both are still considered separate branches of the Armed Forces.)
Searches of Bing, DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo, as well as various social media platforms, found no news media outlets credibly reporting Space Force took over the FAA's air traffic control systems.
According to those same search engine queries, X user Mr. Pool, or @looP_rM_3117211, appeared to first post (archived) the fabricated story, minus the World War III mention, on Monday.
(Mr. Pool (@looP_rM_3117211) via X)
The same user, Mr. Pool, also recently shared other false- or unfounded-appearing stories also with the same writing structure resembling artificial intelligence-generated text, both on Telegram and X. For example, on Monday, the user falsely alleged a patent on a "suppressed" cancer cure from 1971 "just expired," adding that a "55-year cancer blockade" was "over."
We attempted to contact the X user, who is also on Telegram, to ask questions, including to confirm the user created the story and used AI to write it. We will update this article if we receive further details.
How we know it's written with AI
A scan of the post's full text with the Pangram AI detection tool returned a result reading, "100% of this text is AI," as well as, "We believe that this entire text is AI."
Snopes doesn't rely solely on AI detection tools to identify AI-produced content. Since some tools appear to vary in reliability, we consider the tools' results as one of several data points toward judging authenticity. For Pangram, we bear in mind the platform's strong performance in third-party and internal evaluations, as well as criticisms of the tool.
Outside of AI detection tools, visible signs of AI included the tricolon writing style — which reports have said can be an indicator of AI writing — with the words, "No congressional hearing. No public announcement. No explanation."
Other signs of AI we observed included the post's full text featuring three bullet points with emojis, as well as the following dramatic, forward-thinking conclusion for which we've found AI tools seem to commonly generate:
You don't transfer the FAA to Space Force unless you are ready to take control of the entire airspace above the United States.
They told you the FAA was civilian. They called you crazy for questioning the transfer. They laughed when you said the sky was being militarized.
Look at the flight boards tonight. The planes are still flying. But the system that guides them is no longer civilian. The sky is not falling. It is being claimed.
The airspace was never yours. It was always theirs. And now it is being taken back.
For further reading, we previously reported whether Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly, a retired astronaut, said Trump forming the Space Force military branch was a dumb idea.

What to know about the presidential wiretapping scandal rocking Indonesia
- Published
Authorities are investigating possible treason in Indonesia after a bombshell announcement this week that President Prabowo Subianto's phone conversations might have been spied on.
Several senior figures of Prabowo's administration have been embroiled in the wiretapping scandal, including his chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - who is not related to the president despite his name.
It is unfolding against what many have interpreted as a widening rift between Prabowo and his predecessor, Joko Widodo - otherwise know as Jokowi - who had thrown his support behind Prabowo's 2024 presidential campaign.
"Listyo's position, as we know, is actually very close to Jokowi," Made Supriatma, a visiting fellow at Singapore's ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, told BBC Indonesian.
"So now it's practically said that they're going their separate ways."
What happened?
Listyo Sigit Prabowo, the president's chief of staff, was arrested on Tuesday along with two senior police officers for allegedly wiretapping President Prabowo.
The three men are suspected of keying phone numbers, including Prabowo's, into the police's official electronic surveillance system - which allows authorities to intercept communications - without following proper procedures, such as obtaining an investigation warrant or case report.
Authorities say the operation was discovered last week after a tip-off from a police officer. But they believe the alleged wiretapping stretches back to 2025, when Listyo was serving as the national police chief.
This could amount to treason, as it involved "sensitive information" that could "endanger the interests and sovereignty of the nation", a spokesperson for the president told reporters on Wednesday.
In Indonesia, treason is punishable by life imprisonment or even the death penalty - though the country has not executed anyone in a decade.
The spokesperson said the motive behind the alleged wiretapping remained unclear.
It was not just President Prabowo who was targeted in the alleged wiretapping operation, either. Other targets included politicians, journalists, NGO representatives and businesspeople, authorities said.
On Thursday evening, police named a fourth suspect: Slamet Uliandi, from the national police criminal investigation unit. But he was not detained due to his ill health after suffering a stroke, according to authorities.
Listyo, who was appointed the president's chief of staff last month, was sacked from his new position shortly after his arrest.
This is not the first wiretapping scandal to have involved Indonesia's leaders. In 2014, several wiretapping devices were discovered at Jokowi's official residence when he was the governor of Jakarta. Former president Megawati Soekarnoputri claimed in 2024 that she had avoided using her personal mobile phone number because she was the target of wiretapping.
Indonesia's police chief Suyudi Ario Seto told reporters on Thursday that the probe into wiretapping was "purely law enforcement and has nothing to do with rivalries or anything else".
But many see it as the latest blow in a disintegrating alliance between President Prabowo and former president Jokowi, who led the country from 2014 to 2024.
Prabowo vs Jokowi
Jokowi had thrown his support behind Prabowo in the lead-up to the 2024 presidential election, as part of an alliance that ultimately propelled Prabowo to become Indonesia's next leader.
Riding to victory with him was Gibran Rakabuming Raka, Jokowi's eldest son, who became Indonesia's vice president.
Two years on, that alliance appears to be fracturing - even if neither party has confirmed the rift.
Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.
In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many of Jokowi's allies into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.
Meanwhile, uncertainty also looms over Gibran, Jokowi's son, who is mired in a growing controversy over the validity of his high school credentials, a pre-requisite to run for vice presidency. He now faces calls to be disqualified from his job, on the grounds that he should not have been eligible as a candidate.
The wiretapping scandal and subsequent arrest of Listyo - who rose to the top of the police force in Jokowi's administration, and is seen as one of the ex-president's longtime allies - is now adding to the tensions between Prabowo and Jokowi.
When asked about the wiretapping incident after the court session on Thursday, Jokowi told reporters that "we should all respect the ongoing legal process".
This latest scandal comes during a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. His flagship free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.
Experts, meanwhile, say all this has distracted from the more pressing challenges that Indonesians are facing on the ground - from economic uncertainties to environmental pollution.
In recent months, protesters have taken to the streets to pressure the government on a range of issues such as toxic wildfire haze, corruption, and cost-of-living woes.
"It's like we're living in a country on autopilot," Nicky Fahrizal, a researcher at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies in Indonesia, told BBC Indonesian.
"Because the way the government operates proves that it's not the people's interests that are being pursued, but rather the interests of individual groups."

Five European leaders have called for closer ties with Britain ahead of a crucial EU-UK summit.
In a letter to Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa, the leaders of Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Denmark, said stronger commitments from both on clean energy would be beneficial to both sides.
Andy Burnham will meet Von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, and Costa, who leads the European Council, on 20 November for the summit in Brussels.
The prime minister will use the summit to push for deals to cut costs and red tape for British farmers and businesses, support industry and boost growth.
In a letter seen by the Guardian, the leaders stated: “We call on you and the UK to agree during the summit on a path towards the conclusion of these negotiations.”
They described the UK as a “close partner in the energy transition,” adding that Britain’s integration into the EU’s internal electricity market was “necessary to unlock the full potential of the North Sea area and transform it into the largest clean energy hub in the world”.
Leaked draft documents prepared ahead of an upcoming summit in Brussels reveal that the EU is demanding financial contributions from the UK in exchange for access to its single market for electricity.
The paper, seen by Sky News, shows that the EU expects “appropriate level of financial contribution towards reducing economic and social disparities between the regions of the EU” from the UK in order to begin trading in the EU's single market for electricity.
It says both the UK and Brussels hope to “conclude these negotiations swiftly” so Britain can access the market “as soon as possible”.
The EU is also requesting that the UK scrap plans to deport European offenders under recent Home Office rules that permit foreign nationals to be removed once sentenced.
A British government source stated that the UK will not agree to the EU's demands regarding foreign criminal deportations, noting that member states have not yet approved the requirements.
It comes as the EU’s former Brexit negotiator warned the prime minister that he will not be able to rejoin its single market "à la carte", adding: “there is no cherry picking.”
The comment came after Mr Burnham said rejoining the EU's internal market is among options he could pursue when reworking the UK’s relationship with the bloc.
Speaking on BBC's Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg, Michael Barnier said: "There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms are clearly the four conditions to be inside a single market".

Katie Miller fervently lobbied for her husband, Stephen Miller, to become White House chief of staff, according to a new report.
After Republicans suffered crushing losses in Tuesday’s midterm elections, she called administration officials and allies, urging them to support her husband as Susie Wiles’ replacement if they considered him better suited to the job than other potential candidates, Politico reported.
By Friday, Stephen Miller had landed the top job. President Donald Trump announced that Wiles — his longest-serving chief of staff — would step down and be replaced by Miller, her deputy and the architect of Trump’s hardline immigration policies.
Trump’s frustration with Wiles had reportedly been building for months and her fate was sealed when Democrats romped to victory in the midterms, reclaiming both the House and the Senate.
“He started telling people he was done with Susie,” a source told Politico. “This is what happens when you get creamed.”
Katie Miller — a podcast host and former adviser to Elon Musk — did not push for Wiles’ ouster, sources told the outlet. She began making the case for her husband only after it became clear that Wiles was on her way out.
Miller made roughly six calls to people close to the president, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and people with ties to Vice President JD Vance. She argued that her husband should succeed Wiles if she departed. “I would appreciate if you could share that message,” Miller said, according to one source.
Miller declined to comment to Politico but she responded on X after the story was published.
“BREAKING: Wife supports husband,” she wrote. “If your wife doesn’t do this, find a new one.”
A mother-of-four, Katie Miller recently acknowledged she did not cast a ballot on Election Day. “You see that moms are too busy raising their children and taking care of them to go to the polls,” she told CBS News Wednesday. Vanity Fair reported last month that she is known to throw lavish parties for administration officials in her home on a military base.
When approached by Politico, the White House characterized Stephen Miller as a central figure in the Trump administration.
“Stephen Miller has been a key player in delivering on President Trump’s America First agenda since day one,” spokesperson Lauren Bis said. “He has spearheaded the administration’s crime crackdown including in D.C. and Memphis, record setting deregulation, unleashed American energy, dismantled drug cartels, and secured our border. Stephen Miller is widely seen as a more polarizing figure than Wiles, having helped shape some of the administration’s most controversial initiatives, including its deportation crackdown and push to end birthright citizenship.
A source close to the White House told Politico that the staffing change signaled to the president’s MAGA base that “the White House hears you.”
Meanwhile, Democrats on Capitol Hill widely condemned his promotion.
“Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries wrote on X. “His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today.”

Chilean film-maker Sebastián Lelio has died at the age of 52.
He was best known for the Oscar-winning trans drama A Fantastic Woman and his English-language films included Gloria Bell and The Wonder.
His partner Amalia Kassai announced his death on Instagram without specifying the cause of death but telling followers, in Spanish, that it was a painful time for his family. Chilean media reports that he died at his home in Las Condes, Santiago.
Lelio was born in Argentina but moved to Chile at the age of two. He studied journalism for one year before graduating from film school and then released 9/11 documentary Cero in 2003. His first narrative film The Sacred Family premiered at the San Sebastián film festival in 2005.
His follow-up, 2009’s Christmas, premiered at Cannes but it was 2013’s Gloria that provided him with a major international breakthrough. The drama, about a woman in her late 50s who starts dating again, premiered at Berlin and won its lead star Paulina García an acting award at the festival.
Lelio followed it up with A Fantastic Woman, a drama about the life of a trans woman, another breakout that became the first Chilean film to win the Oscar for best international feature. In a five-star review, the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw called it “a sublime study in the exalted ordeal of grief”.
“When we released it in 2017, a gender identity bill had been dormant in congress for seven years,” he said in a Guardian interview in 2018. “Somehow, the film’s release, and the year in which it became globally known, helped to reactivate the discussion in Chile.”
He made his English language debut with London-set drama Disobedience which told a queer love story between women played by Rachel Weisz and Rachel McAdams. It was nominated for five British independent film awards.
Lelio then remade Gloria as Gloria Bell, then set in America and starring Julianne Moore in the lead role. He followed it with a critically acclaimed adaptation of Emma Donoghue’s novel The Wonder starring Florence Pugh.
“I love working with actors, and need to know they trust me and can explore, get lost, be foolish or brave, and I’ll take care of them,” he said to the Guardian. “I love working on set – it is where the sparkle is.”
His final film was 2025’s The Wave, a musical protest drama that premiered at Cannes.
“Making a film is like a gift you leave somewhere – you then hide and see what happens,” he said.

Au's arrest last year was the first publicly known prosecution under Macao's national security law since it was enacted in 2009. A Macao court found him guilty of subverting state power, breaching confidentiality and establishing contact with organizations, groups or people outside Macao to commit acts endangering national security.
Critics said that his case reflected Beijing's emphasis on security and intolerance of dissent, even though Macao's pro-democracy movement has never been as influential as that in neighboring Hong Kong.
The 69-year-old assisted and cooperated with "hostile organizations" outside Macao for a long period of time in collecting and disseminating political views laden with ideas of subverting state power and false information, according to a court statement. They conspired to incite hatred among Macao residents against the central government, with an intent to overthrow and undermine the country's fundamental system, it said.
"Although the defendant is a first-time offender and admitted to a considerable portion of the criminal facts, he demonstrated a high degree of intent. The degree of unlawfulness and the potential consequences of his crimes are both very serious," the statement said.
Macao is a former Portuguese colony that has operated, like Hong Kong, as a special administrative region since its return to Chinese rule in 1999.
Au's wife says it's a groundless persecution
In a public letter, Au's wife, Virginia Cheang, wrote that she only hoped authorities would allow his family to exchange letters with Au and visit him regularly without conditions.
"From a closed-door trial to a public verdict, what kind of operation is this? It's a political trial and it's a groundless persecution to humiliate one's character," Cheang said.
Au's daughter in London, Au Hon I, told The Associated Press that her father is a peaceful family man who cares deeply about Macao, and the thought of him spending more time in prison without having done anything criminal was unbearable. She said that a lawyer earlier arranged by her family wasn't able to see him.
She felt that the ruling was setting boundaries of what citizens can do and what rights they have, saying "it's a very scary chapter that they're starting."
"It just doesn't feel like a safe space anymore being in Macao. And it's very heartbreaking," she said.
The court said that a lawyer approved by Au was appointed to act for him during the legal proceedings, and that he had exercised his right to a defense. The court also approved his family's request to visit him regularly.
Jorge Menezes, a Portuguese lawyer who practices in Macao, said that the trial was held in secret and that specific details — which organizations were involved and what information Au had provided to them — weren't revealed. Menezes noted that the statement said that Au had acknowledged some facts and it might have led people to believe that he had confessed to the crimes.
"From what I see, he did not plead guilty. Otherwise, they would have said. So this is misleading and unfortunate," he said. "It violates his dignity."
He said that Au's case was used to send a message to Macao residents that it was about anyone who challenges the authorities. The case could also carry a message for Hong Kong, because Macao is "a sort of laboratory" for the financial hub in situations like this.
Michael Polak, Au's international counsel, urged Portugal and the European Union to demand that Au, a Portuguese citizen, be allowed to leave Macao.
"A sentence like that for someone of that age is a sentence for life," he said. "If he was left in Macao, he could die in prison."
The court found Au colluded with multiple overseas groups
Macao has its own political and legal systems and Macao is the only Chinese city where casino gambling is legal. It has resorts run by affiliates of the American gaming companies MGM Resorts, Las Vegas Sands and Wynn Resorts.
The court found that Au helped overseas organizations spread false and distorted information between 2023 and 2024 to induce foreign countries to take hostile actions against China and Macao, incite hatred against the central government and undermine the smooth running of the 2024 city leader election.
As a lawmaker in 2021, Au leaked to overseas groups confidential information obtained during closed-door committee meetings over the renewal of gaming licenses, it said.
Au's trial was held behind closed doors in September.
The court earlier said that the judge decided against an open trial to ensure that national security interests wouldn't be undermined.
Au was seen as a mild pro-democracy activist
Au, a teacher-turned-lawmaker, served in the legislature dominated by Beijing loyalists for 20 years before stepping down in 2021. Au was also an organizer of Macao's commemoration of the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing.
Au said that he entered politics because he saw many social problems in daily life that required people to speak out. He said that the Tiananmen Square pro-democracy movement in 1989 brought him and his like-minded friends together, and he later felt Macao needed people to push forward an open and democratic society.
Before his arrest, Au was a rare voice in Macao who regularly criticized government measures and political developments on Facebook and in interviews, although many considered his critiques to be mild.
But the Macao government supported the ruling, urging all sectors to respect it. It said that the government would continue to strictly enforce the security law.
Beijing's Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office said that the ruling demonstrated Macao's firm resolve in safeguarding national security. It said that the ruling also reminded people to remain vigilant about the risks even in times of stability.
China's Foreign Ministry said that it firmly opposes any external forces using individual cases as a pretext to interfere in Macao's affairs.

The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has recommended a separate authorisation for satellite network providers and proposed permitting direct-to-device services using satellite and terrestrial mobile spectrum. The proposals can enable compatible smartphones to connect directly to satellites, potentially extending connectivity to areas without conventional mobile coverage. Under the proposed Satellite Communication Network (SCN) Provider Authorisation, companies can build and operate satellite networks and sell capacity to eligible telecom service providers. They cannot serve end users directly under this authorisation. The recommendations require government approval and do not immediately permit commercial D2D services. What Changes For Operators? The framework would give telecom operators a way to access satellite infrastructure through partnerships, while continuing to manage their customer relationships. For satcom companies, it would create a separate route to sell network capacity to telecom operators, without requiring them to build a consumer-facing service under the same authorisation. In effect, one company can operate the underlying satellite network while another sells connectivity to customers. This will support partnerships between satellite infrastructure providers and telecom operators seeking to extend their coverage. However, the SCN authorisation alone would not allow a satellite company to sell mobile or broadband services directly to consumers. It would require the relevant service licence or authorisation. The proposed nationwide authorisation would remain valid for up to 20 years, with renewal permitted for another period of up to 20 years. Connecting Phones To Satellites TRAI has proposed two routes for D2D connectivity – using spectrum earmarked for mobile satellite services or using spectrum already assigned to terrestrial mobile operators. For the first route, it has recommended that the government encourage handset manufacturers to include support for the relevant satellite bands in future smartphones sold in India. For the second, telecom operators can partner with satellite network providers to use their existing mobile spectrum for satellite connectivity. However, participating operators would collectively need to hold the relevant frequency channel across all 22 licensed service areas and agree to its use. TRAI has recommended permitting this arrangement without waiting for the World Radiocommunication Conference 2027. The satellite services would have to avoid interfering with existing authorised services and cannot claim protection from interference caused by them. TRAI has proposed an authorisation fee of 8% of adjusted gross revenue (AGR), without a minimum authorisation fee. Satellite network providers can obtain spectrum directly from the government or use spectrum held by eligible partner operators. In a partnership, spectrum rights would remain with the operator. Government-assigned satellite spectrum would be valid for up to five years, with a possible extension of up to two years. It would attract an annual minimum spectrum charge of ₹3,500 per MHz. For D2D services using a telecom operator’s existing mobile spectrum, TRAI has proposed no additional spectrum charges. Existing spectrum charges would continue. The proposals come amid efforts by Starlink, Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb, and Reliance Jio to tap India’s satellite connectivity market.

Kenyan doomsday cult leader given life sentence for murdering 191 people
- Published
A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to 200 years in prison for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.
Alongside 28 others, Mackenzie was found guilty of the murders for instructing members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".
Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie bore the "primary criminal culpability" for ordering his followers to fast to death, in one of the world's deadliest episodes of cult activity.
"The sentence is appropriate and just, to send an unmistakable message that such atrocities warrant the maximum penalties allowed by law," the judge added.
The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast. The sprawling investigation into the cases shocked Kenya and drew international attention.
The court sentenced Mackenzie to 100 years in prison for homicide and another 100 years for offences related to starvation.
The sentences within each category will run concurrently, but the two sets will run consecutively, bringing his total prison term to 200 years.
Mackenzie also faces separate manslaughter and terrorism charges, which he denies.
Prosecutors had sought the death penalty, arguing that the scale and circumstances of the killings warranted the harshest punishment.
However, Justice Mochache declined to impose the death penalty, despite ruling that the case met the threshold for its consideration.
"Nevertheless, the court declines the invitation to impose the death penalty on any of the victims," she said, adding that capital punishment would eliminate any prospect of rehabilitation and disengagement. The death sentence has not been carried out in Kenya since 1987.
Mackenzie was tried alongside 28 accomplices, including guards who enforced his fasting orders and gravediggers who helped conceal the victims' bodies in mass graves.
They received varying prison sentences of up to 160 years.
Justice Mochache described the killings as "cold and calculated", saying the perpetrators had shown no remorse and had even declared their willingness to fast to death themselves.
Before the hearing began on Friday morning, Francis Wanje, who lost eight relatives including two grandchildren in Shakahola forest, told the BBC's Newsday programme that he was "hoping for... a sentence which will match his [Mackenzie's] deeds in the forest".
Mackenzie and the co-accused had asked for leniency from the court.
Before their conviction on 19 October, they had all pleaded not guilty and repeatedly insisted that nobody was forced to die.
Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece", Justice Mochache said as she delivered her eight-hour judgement last month.
Those who opposed Mackenzie's teachings were beaten to death.
One of his co-accused said he had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows".
Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings" and those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus" the judge said.
The judge found that the deaths arose from an organised system, including religious teachings and directives that compelled followers to follow the deadly fasting.
Post-mortem results showed the cause of deaths to be starvation for most victims, while others died from suffocation, strangulation or head injuries.
The cause of death could not be determined for some, with their bodies having decomposed, while others died soon after their rescue as they were so emaciated.
The Shakahola deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.
The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.
Investigations by the state-funded Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) revealed that local administration and law enforcement officials had repeatedly turned a blind eye to the cult's activities.
"We expected at that time the police would take action immediately to go and rescue the other members there, but it didn't happen," said Wanje, who reported the case to the police in March 2023.
Wanje said a relative of his in the police force and a former cult participant had managed to save his grandson at the time. The child told the police what had happened and showed them the grave of his siblings.
"It was [supposed to be] his last day.. they [would have killed] my grandson."
The cult leader had previously been arrested and later released for lack of evidence.
Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003.
Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity, drawing thousands of followers in its branches across Kenya.
The church ran a television station called Times TV which would broadcast his sermons from his church in Malindi.
His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".
The main church shut down in 2019 and Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.
While the conclusion of the murder cases may bring a sense of justice for the victims and their families, the convictions only account for 191 victims, while more than 400 bodies were exhumed from the forest.

An Indian film that nobody would release is finally a hit - 18 awards later
- Published
A film about the tender love and quiet loneliness of an elderly couple, which took two years to reach cinemas after it was completed, is wowing critics and audiences across India.
The 111-minute Pyre, directed by television journalist-turned-filmmaker Vinod Kapri, also explores the pressing issue of outmigration which has left hundreds of picturesque Himalayan hamlets abandoned and turned them into ghost villages. It further reflects on the impact of climate change, which has made the region's weather increasingly harsh.
On social media, many Indians have shared videos showing audiences leaving theatres with tears in their eyes. Others have posted that they have not been so moved by a film in a long time.
The film's lead actors, ordinary villagers who had never faced a camera before, have also won praise from some of Bollywood's most respected figures, including Naseeruddin Shah and Anupam Kher.
Pyre's protagonists - Padam Singh (played by Kapri's uncle, Padam Singh) and Tulsi (played by Heera Devi) - are Bubu and Aama, local terms for grandfather and grandmother. The couple live in a small home in the mountains of the northern state of Uttarakhand .
It's a place where age is measured against momentous events. Singh was born two years before the outbreak of World War II. Tulsi was born in the year atomic bombs were dropped on Japan.
There are no roads and no electricity. Whenever the couple need help – which is often as Tulsi frequently has to be carried to hospital – Padam Singh uses a traditional long-horn instrument to summon neighbours. In return for their kindness, he pays them with goats.
"There's nothing here – just mountains," as one character puts it. So the young leave in search of greener pastures, and those who depart this beautiful, but blighted, land rarely return.
Kapri says his film remains focused on the "soulful love story of the ageing couple in their last days".
"They have shared a life together for 65 years and, for the last 28 years, they've been waiting for their son, Hariya, who's gone to Mumbai in search of work, to come back," Kapri tells the BBC. "It's a story of companionship, of loneliness and of waiting."
Their wait takes on a new urgency when suddenly, after all these years, a letter arrives from Hariya setting a date for his visit.
As Padam Singh and Tulsi count down the days, the handful of villagers around them leave one by one, until the couple find themselves alone in the vast mountain landscape.
"You and Tulsi should also leave as soon as possible. Otherwise, you won't even have four people to carry your body down the mountain to the funeral pyre when you or Tulsi die," one departing villager advises Padam Singh. "Or die before we leave," he adds in jest.
With no one left to call for help, Padam Singh builds two funeral pyres side by side right outside his door – one for his wife and one for himself.
"How will I carry you down the mountain if you die?" he tells Tulsi when she questions the decision.
Despite the bleak setting and the weight of the topics covered, Pyre is suffused with humour. The central couple are delightful. Like many long-married spouses, they seem to treat bickering as a love language.
Kapri, who is from Uttarakhand, got the idea for the film in 2018 after meeting an 84-year-old man in Munsiyari, a scenic hill town in the state.
"I visited him after seeing his photo in a Facebook post. The wrinkles on his face really fascinated me. His face was unique."
Kapri said he asked him and his wife what their biggest worry was.
"He said, 'My biggest worry is, if I die first, who is going to take care of her?' And she said, 'He doesn't know how to cook. So if I die first, I don't know who is going to cook food for him.' That was so heartwarming for me."
Kapri says he initially tried to make his film with "the real couple", but abandoned the idea after a week of shooting, when it became clear it was not working. He then approached actors Naseeruddin Shah and Ratna Pathak - a couple themselves - for the lead roles.
Shah loved the script, Kapri says, but felt that he and Pathak did not belong to the region and would struggle to do justice to the characters.
Kapri finally found his Padam Singh within his own family – his father's younger brother, a retired army soldier who expressed an interest in acting. He found his Tulsi in another village. Heera Devi, an elderly widow, had raised her children through years of farming, cutting grass and tending to her buffalo.
Over the years, Padam Singh and Heera Devi tell the BBC, they have watched stories of ghost villages, of children migrating for work, abandoning the elderly, play out all around them. They say today they are overwhelmed by the attention Pyre has got.
Since 2024, the film has been screened at some of the world's biggest festivals. It has won 18 awards, Kapri says, including three for best feature and 12 audience-choice best film prizes.
Despite its success at festivals, Kapri says, Pyre spent two years without a distributor. Even OTT platforms passed on the film and it finally reached cinemas only when a producer friend of his stepped in to fund a theatrical release.
But, he says, the modest 70-screen release on 30 October sparked favourable word-of-mouth reviews and with the demand for tickets going up, there was an increase in overall screenings too.
Meanwhile, the misgivings that both Padam Singh and Heera Devi say they initially had about stepping in front of the camera and forgetting their lines are gone now.
Heera Devi says she was even concerned about what her children would think - and what would society say?
Today she and Padam Singh are basking in the positive reviews of film critics and the affection of their audiences.
They have met teary-eyed people at multiple screenings - many wanting to touch their feet and hug them, many who said the film reminded them of their own parents and grandparents who are waiting in villages, towns and cities that they had come from.
"We felt immense joy and happiness. We've received so much love and inspiration - something we had never imagined," says Padam Singh.
But the best moment for him came when he met Naseeruddin Shah in Mumbai. "He watched the entire movie and had tears in his eyes. He hugged me. He said, 'Bubu, the role you have performed, I wouldn't be able to pull off even in seven lifetimes.'"
The film's appeal, Heera Devi says, is because "in reality, our village is just like this".
"Across villages in India, the elderly are left alone. No one's children stay at home anymore and it's the same situation for all parents. They keep waiting for their son and daughter-in-law, hoping that their grandchildren would visit and spend a few days with them. The loneliness is simply unbearable."
Padam Singh says he has a message for the younger generation in Uttarakhand and the rest of India.
"I want to tell them they must not abandon their motherland, the land where they were born," he says. "I also appeal to the government to bring education and employment to where people are - so that they don't have to wander away. When that happens, the parents who are being left behind will also be cared for."

US President Donald Trump on Saturday (local time) said that he has offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States to Dana White, the President and CEO of the Ultimate Fighting Championship. Trump, while describing White as a ‘violent Fighter and warrior ’, also requested the 57-year-old to “please take the job”.
The White House has been without a Press Secretary after Katie Zacharia was fired on October 16, after serving just five days in the role.
In a Truth Social post, Trump also said he has asked White to bring along some UFC fighters, including Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes, and Kayla Harris.
Quick answers to key questions
Dana White has not said whether he is seriously considering the position. He confirmed the offer and said he would meet Trump on Monday.
Trump described White as a “violent Fighter and warrior” and said the country needed people to defend it against what he called the “Lunatic Left.”
Trump named Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes and Kayla Harris.
The position was vacant after Katie Zacharia was fired on October 16, following five days in the role.
White confirmed that he would meet Trump on Monday. He did not say what they would discuss.
“We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other,” Trump said.
White, who has a decades-long association with Trump, confirmed the development and said that he will meet the US President on Monday.
The head of the largest mixed martial arts (MMA) organization didn't make it clear if he was seriously considering the position of becoming the primary spokesperson for the president of the United States.
White, who was in London on Saturday for a boxing event, declined to say what conversations he had with Trump but said, “I'm sure I'll have more to talk about after that.
The development comes as Trump is making some key changes in the administration, following the massive defeat of the Republican Party in the US midterm elections.
Trump on Friday announced he was replacing his longtime adviser Susie Wiles, who was seen as something of a tempering force on the president's impulses, with aide Stephen Miller to serve as the next chief of staff. Miller is known as the architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies and is among the most determined of Trump's inner circle.
Harmeet Dhillon, the Assistant Attorney General for the Civil Rights Division at the US Justice Department, was the first to announce her resignation. There are also growing speculations that more resignations or firings could follow in the coming days.
This includes Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth, who has been on the receiving end of criticism from Democrats and Republicans alike for the war in Iran. There are also reports that the Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, another Trump confidant, could announce his resignation in the coming days to announce his 2028 US presidential election bid.

Haitian gang reaches out to state disarmament group as gunfights persist
One of Haiti’s most powerful gangs says it has reached out to a state agency responsible for dismantling armed gangs in a push for “peace, stability and national reconciliation.”
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- One of Haiti’s most powerful gangs said Friday that it reached out to a government agency responsible for dismantling armed gangs in a push for “peace, stability and national reconciliation.”
The 400 Mawozo gang sent a three-page statement to The Associated Press stressing that “dialogue is not a capitulation,” but rather an “act of patriotic responsibility to preserve human lives.”
The United Nations and human rights groups have accused 400 Mawozo of raping, killing and kidnapping people, which it has denied. On Nov. 1, gang leader Wilson Joseph told the AP that he wrote to the U.N. secretary-general and requested that the organization send a delegation to Haiti for dialogue and mediation amid fears that the presence of Salvadoran troops could further escalate violence.
The gang, which refers to itself as a rebel group, said that it plans to participate in a peaceful demonstration later this month “in order to lay the groundwork for a national dialogue and peace negotiation process.”
“Haiti’s future cannot be built solely on confrontations and military operations," it said.
Haiti’s National Commission for Disarmament, Demobilization, and Reintegration told the AP that an individual contacted them on behalf of the armed group, but that the commission works alongside the prime minister's office. “For any dialogue with armed groups, we must follow the roadmap proposed by the government,” the commission said.
The letter was shared as Haitian police and foreign forces continue to battle gangs, with Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé announcing on X late Friday that one gang leader was killed. He did not identify the gang leader, but a local human rights group confirmed it was the leader of the Nan Boston gang known as Mathias. Nan Boston is one of the smaller armed groups based in Cité Soleil, a gang-controlled slum in Port-au-Prince.
“The gangs won’t be getting any sleep!” the prime minister wrote on X.
The AP reached out to a spokesperson for 400 Mawozo and asked if the gang is willing to lay down its weapons.
The person, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they don't want to be publicly identified to talk about these issues, responded that the gang is willing to engage in peace negotiations and that disarmament is a process.
When asked what 400 Mawozo seeks in exchange, the person said peace and the end of what they called “international interference.”
The gang’s announcement comes just weeks after El Salvador deployed more than 2,000 troops to Haiti following the disappearance of four Salvadoran aviation technicians who came under attack on Oct. 18 while deep in gang territory.
The United Nations has said that most of the Salvadoran personnel in Haiti are operating outside the framework of the U.N.-backed gang suppression force that is working with Haiti’s police and military as well as Vectus Global, the private security firm founded by former U.S. Navy SEAL and Blackwater founder Erik Prince.
The gang said it believes it would be “beneficial” if all “relevant military forces” suspend operations targeting certain areas pending the “effective opening of a dialogue on peace and stability.”
“This period should provide an opportunity for de-escalation, the protection of civilian populations, and the search for a lasting political solution,” it wrote.
In its letter, 400 Mawozo said it was worried about social media posts “targeting” the home of Joseph, best known as Lanmò Sanjou, especially comments attributed to El Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele.
On Friday, Bukele responded to a social media post in which he was tagged and allegedly showing Joseph's home. “Where is that house? Give us the exact address, and we’ll destroy it,” Bukele wrote on X.
In its letter, the gang described Joseph’s home as “a symbol of peace within the framework of its de-escalation process” and called on “all parties to respect international obligations relating to the protection of civilians and civilian property.”
The gang referenced certain articles within the Geneva Conventions as well as the Charter of the United Nations.
El Salvador's government declined to comment when reached by the AP on Friday night.

Sao Paulo GP Qualifying: Lando Norris claims rain-hit pole in wild conditions with Lewis Hamilton, Max Verstappen to start at back
Lando Norris tames awful wet conditions for his third Brazil pole in a row; Frustrated Russell drops down from second with grid penalty; Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen starting 20th and 21st; watch Sunday's Sao Paulo GP live at 5pm on Sky Sports F1, build-up from 3.30pm
Saturday 7 November 2026 22:31, UK
Lando Norris claimed pole position after a hugely-challenging Sao Paulo Grand Prix qualifying in treacherous wet conditions, for a race that will see Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen start at the back of the grid.
On a typically rain-hit day at ever-unpredictable Interlagos, qualifying was suspended for over an hour and 20 minutes after a torrential downpour hit the drivers' first laps of Q1.
The rain eventually eased - but never particularly stopped - to allow running take place and create a thrilling and unpredictable battle for pole.

In the end it was Norris who came out ahead as conditions worsened again in Q3 to seal a third successive Interlagos pole position for the outgoing world champion, on a weekend McLaren had already showed improved form in the dry following car upgrades.
Mercedes' George Russell was second fastest ahead of a race he already knew he carries a five-place grid penalty for an engine change, meaning he could not ultimately achieve pole position whatever he did.
He lapped 0.204s slower than Norris and from second will drop to seventh on Sunday's grid.
But the Mercedes driver was left frustrated not to have topped the qualifying timesheet outright, which he believes he would have done had he not been advised by his race engineer to back out of what turned out to be his final representative timed lap of Q3 when he came up behind Alex Albon's slower Williams.
Russell's engineer, Marcus Dudley, clearly hoped this would pay dividends by giving the Briton a clearer run on his next lap but the call coincided with the rain increasing again, meaning lap times quickly became slower.
Drivers swiftly headed back to the pit lane to mark an effective end to the Q3 battle as they all stayed in the garage as the clock ticked down to zero.
"I don't want to be P2. I want to be P1!" fumed Russell on team radio at the end of the session.
New world champion Kimi Antonelli qualified third but will move ahead of team-mate Russell to the front row alongside Norris.
Charles Leclerc was fourth for Ferrari but he has a 10-place penalty for an engine change to serve so will drop down into the midfield.
His team-mate Hamilton was also originally supposed to serve the same sanction but a problem with his fresh Ferrari engine in final practice triggered a complete power-unit change and locked him in to a back-of-the-grid start.
He will be joined on the back rows by old title rival Verstappen, who has also taken a new power unit in his Red Bull from Saturday's running.
Both drivers dropped out in Q2, Hamilton in 11th and Verstappen in 16th after opting not to run in the second phase at all in order to save wet tyres for the race, but neither result mattered given their overriding penalties.
Ferrari's heavier grid penalties increase Mercedes' chances of closing out the Constructors' Championship on Sunday. They will complete a title double for 2026 if they outscore their Italian rivals by three points or more.
Front-running penalties promote midfield runners up grid
The grid penalties for Russell, Verstappen and both Ferraris - which were all confirmed in the sessions ahead of qualifying - mean Sunday's grid has a different complexion to normal in a season dominated by the 'big four' teams.
Russell and Leclerc's demotions move Liam Lawson - whose future at Racing Bulls remain in huge doubt despite his impressive season - to a joint career-best third on the grid after the New Zealander already impressed in the wet to qualify fifth.
There were also strong performances in the rain from Audi's Nico Hulkenberg, who will start fourth, and Haas' Oliver Bearman, who will line up sixth. With Verstappen at the back, Isack Hadjar will be the lead Red Bull driver in fifth.
Fernando Alonso showed his old mastery of the rain to put under-powered Aston Martin into Q3 for the first time this season, while Williams' Alex Albon also made his first top-10 appearance of a difficult year.
Alonso and Albon will line up in eighth and ninth respectively.
That is just ahead of McLaren's Oscar Piastri - after he dropped out in Q2 - and Brazilian debutant Rafael Camara in 11th.
Haas' new signing hugely impressed on his F1 debut to make Q2 before blotting his copybook slightly by crashing into the barriers at the end of that second phase.
Arvid Lindblad will line up 12th after his Racing Bulls car was stopped by technical issues in Q2.
How Interlagos' unpredictable weather created thrilling qualifying
Rain has largely stayed away from the 2026 season but arrived with a vengeance at Interlagos on Saturday.
A big electrical storm following the end of final practice had already drenched the track, but conditions had started to improve, and the rain even briefly stopped, to allow qualifying to begin at its scheduled time.
But just as drivers were starting to queue at the end of the pit lane for the Q1 green light, the heavens opened again and as the cars were released onto the track conditions became treacherous almost immediately, forcing drivers to gingerly complete their out laps amid ever-worsening visibility and grip levels.
Race Control swiftly threw the red flag, which would eventually lead to a suspension of one hour and 23 minutes before the track was deemed suitable for F1 cars to return.
And while the rain did start to initially worsen again just as the session resumed, conditions steadily improved thereafter with a drier line eventually appearing around the lap and drivers able to switch to the shallower intermediate tyres from mid-way through Q2.
Impressively, while there were spins and off-track moments, only two drivers found the barriers. However, to the disappointment of the home crowd, they were both Brazilians. Gabriel Bortoleto slithered off the road in his Audi in Q1, although was able to return to the pits where he stayed due to car damage, while Camara hit the barriers at Turn 12 on the run up the hill.
In the end, despite Russell's feeling of what might have been, it was polesitter Norris who tamed the conditions the best.
"It was about getting two laps in at the beginning, not making any mistakes, and that's exactly what we did, so it's been a very good day," said the McLaren driver.

Justin Trudeau named distinguished fellow at Oxford's Blavatnik School of Government
Former prime minister will become member of school's World Leaders Circle
Former prime minister Justin Trudeau has joined England's Oxford University in a new role.
Trudeau, 54, joined the Blavatnik School of Government as a distinguished fellow and member of the World Leaders Circle, the school said in a news release on Friday.
The release says the former Liberal leader joins an international network of former heads of government, including former New Zealand prime minister Jacinda Ardern and former British prime minister Rishi Sunak.
From 2015 to 2025, Trudeau served as Canada's prime minister before stepping down.
The Blavatnik School, founded in 2010, says it is focused on public policy education and inspiring students to improve the "quality of government and public policy-making worldwide."
Trudeau says in the news release that he is looking forward to "contributing his experience" and working with other leaders to "consider how governments can respond to change and build a more hopeful, inclusive and prosperous future for everyone."
"In the decade that I was prime minister, the world went through profound change both geopolitically and technologically, which fundamentally reshaped our world," Trudeau said.
Ngaire Woods, dean of the Blavatnik School, said Trudeau brings "a wealth of experience, forged through a decade of public service" that will be beneficial to students.
"Our students are the public leaders of tomorrow, and the opportunity to learn directly from those who have navigated the complexities of government ... is invaluable," Woods said in the release.
Trudeau is expected to visit the school later this month.
Since stepping back from politics following his resignation as federal Liberal leader and prime minister last year, Trudeau has flitted in and out of the public eye, delivering speeches around the world and popping up at events with his popstar girlfriend Katy Perry.
Last month, Trudeau announced that he was venturing into the entertainment world with the launch of a new media and entertainment production company called Hope & Hard Work, a joint project with Katie Telford, his longtime chief of staff.

- Strauss Zelnick says piracy is a 'fact of life' for the entertainment industry.
- Zelnick believes video game piracy is less of a concern due to game file sizes, complexity, and server requirements.
- Take-Two plans to use legal and technical measures if piracy becomes a serious problem.
With GTA 6 just a few days away from its official launch, piracy is naturally becoming a talking point among gamers, but Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick doesn’t appear particularly alarmed. During a recent interview at the Wall Street Journal tech conference, Zelnick acknowledged that piracy is inevitable in entertainment but explained why it may be a lesser threat to video games than other media.
Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick Isn’t Worried About GTA 6 Piracy
When asked about piracy and how Take-Two plans to handle it, Zelnick offered a candid response. “I’m worried about everything all the time despite being very laid-back“, he said before explaining that piracy has been a constant throughout his career in entertainment. Zelnick stated:
Piracy is a fact of life.
He recalls his time in the movie business, where the company estimated that 10% to 20% of its business was pirated at any given time. The situation was even more difficult in the music industry, where he argued that piracy accounted for around 80% of the market in the mid-2000s.
However, Zelnick believes that interactive entertainment has a few advantages. “Piracy is less of an issue in interactive entertainment, but it’s not been a non-issue,” he explained, pointing to the enormous file sizes and complexity of some of the best video games.
That doesn’t mean that Take-Two plans to ignore the problem. Zelnick said if piracy becomes a significant issue, the company will respond with “legal and technical work.”
The CEO further noted that Rockstar’s games rely heavily on server connectivity for a good experience. As he put it, players would have to set up competitive servers themselves to replicate GTA 6, and “it won’t be a good experience.” This would make pirated copies less appealing to players.
In addition to that, reports surrounding PS5 jailbreaks have added another layer to the discussion. Recently, a PS5 firmware update just dropped, and some reports indicate that GTA 6 could require firmware version 14.22. This would naturally make it difficult for players with jailbroken consoles to access the game.
Ultimately, Zelnick’s comments suggest that Take-Two sees piracy as a manageable challenge rather than a threat capable of derailing GTA 6. While you wait for the GTA 6 release, have a look at our GTA 6 preload guide to learn about the requirements.

Alexis Ohanian wants to figure out the future of user-generated content. According to the Reddit cofounder, building social media apps is “not cool anymore” and so much of the internet has been compromised.
“I'm expecting some better version of the group chat to be that new version of UGC,” Ohanian told WIRED senior correspondent Lauren Goode at the inaugural WIRED World Fair.
Ohanian has a complicated relationship with the internet. He resigned from Reddit in 2020, following the killing of George Floyd, to make room for a Black board member and to pressure the company to reform its content moderation policies. The social site had been notorious for hosting violent and harmful rhetoric. Ohanian reflects on recently learning someone with a Reddit tattoo—once a sign of the site’s success to Ohanian—had since covered it up: “I don’t blame him.”
He now runs venture capital firm Seven Seven Six, which has over $1.3 billion in assets under management. He focuses on sports, where he finds real-life communities “in the age of AI slop” and a “manipulated” internet.
Ohanian is a proponent of the “Dead Internet Theory”—the idea that a lot of online activity and content is being generated by bots. Large language models have turbocharged this, with AI agents outrunning human users. “The internet that I grew up on … that was really built for humans first; user interfaces and experiences are going to go away,” said Ohanian, “because more of the internet is going to get created for these agents to use, [rather] than for people.”
In some ways, the advance in generative AI has been lucrative for sites like Reddit, which has licensed its vast archive of human conversations to companies including Google and OpenAI to train AI models. “Platforms like ours became very, very valuable to LLMs,” Ohanian said.
But the technology has also undermined the business. Reddit shares plunged 29 percent last week after the platform warned that Google’s AI-powered search was hurting referral traffic. Ohanian also worries the commercialisation of these conversations means they are full of “bullshit.” “The internet has gotten so manipulated because it is so incredibly valuable to do so,” he said.
Reddit recently said it would require users to sign in to fight third-party scraping and keep up user engagement. While Ohanian declined to say whether he agrees with the move, “there has to be provable humanity on the internet without being creepy.”
An early Anthropic investor, Ohanian is nonetheless optimistic about the potential benefits of AI. He is especially excited to see medical breakthroughs from the technology. “There is still a very real chance that this technology can cause a lot of harm for sure,” he said. “I think we have to be sober about how we're building and what we're doing, but I still can't help but see all of the things that can get so demonstrably better.”
