A new British startup believes that artificial intelligence is the key to speedrunning the slow and temperamental process of drug design.
Potential Sciences plans to build large-scale chemical datasets by using basic principles of physics to simulate interactions between atoms, then small molecules, then complex amino acids and proteins. With that data, it’s betting it can train AI models and prediction systems capable of identifying highly targeted drugs for specific diseases, bypassing costly and time-consuming lab experimentation.
“We want molecules that are never going to work in the clinic to fail fast,” Hatem Helal, Potential Sciences founder and CEO, tells WIRED. “That means having better predictors of how they will behave as they interact with human biology.”
The startup, which launched on November 5, says it has seed funding in the tens of millions of dollars from SovAI—the UK government’s AI venture capital fund—and Twin Path Ventures, among other investors. The founders declined to disclose the precise figure or valuation.
If things pan out as Potential Sciences hopes, it could pave the way for the accelerated development of new treatments for all sorts of diseases. By reducing the cost of experimentation, Helal says, the company’s approach could also make it economical for pharmaceutical companies to pursue drugs for rare conditions that have previously gone untreated.
“We want to make it possible to have more bespoke treatments for diseases—this idea that medicines can be one-off molecular combinations that are tailored to your unique human biology,” he says.
The question is whether Potential Sciences will be able to predict how well drug candidates will bind to disease-related proteins as accurately as it hopes, which would require a marked leap forward.
“I’m sure it will be an improvement,” says Peter Wolynes, a professor of chemistry at Rice University. But currently, “the engineering is at the level of the Romans, not of the Renaissance, in terms of how protein engineering is done,” he says.
Industry luminaries like Demis Hassabis, who won the Nobel Prize for Chemistry for his work at Google DeepMind, have long said that advances in AI will eventually lead to momentous scientific breakthroughs, in the same way the technology has recently carved up mathematics. The hope among startups like Potential Sciences is that drug discovery will be one of the first scientific frontiers to be transformed by the technology.
At the moment, a large proportion of AI drug discovery labs are developing models on top of a single public database of 3D atomic structures—the Protein Data Bank—which researchers have expanded over decades with the results of new experiments. The problem, according to Helal, is that the dataset remains too small to train AI models advanced enough to reliably accelerate the search for viable drug candidates.
“Of all the atoms in the universe, there’s around 1060 ways that you could assemble them into molecules that you could potentially give to a human,” says Helal. “Think of drug discovery as a search problem; it’s about how fast you can navigate and prune that space into promising molecules for a particular disease.”
To address that issue, Potential Sciences is trying to construct far larger datasets made up of synthetic data, produced by simulating interactions between different chemical compounds. From far larger pools of data, the theory goes, the startup will be able to train far more advanced AI models and prediction systems.
Academics see the potential in the simulation-based approach that Potential Sciences has adopted. “If we could calculate accurately the interactions between all molecules in the cell and the fluctuations in their structure we could predict where molecules would bind and that would indeed revolutionize drug development,” says Alan Fersht, an emeritus professor of chemistry at the University of Cambridge who specializes in protein engineering. “I am optimistic that this will eventually happen.”
In receiving investment from SovAI, Potential Sciences joins fellow AI drug discovery companies Basecamp Research and Isomorphic Labs, and materials discovery startup CuspAI.
The UK government established SovAI earlier this year with a mandate to invest in British startups capable of becoming indispensable components of the global AI supply chain, affording the country vital geopolitical leverage. The fund has at its disposal roughly $800 million and the ability to offer its portfolio companies access to the UK’s national AI supercomputer.
“Coming at drug discovery from a physics angle—the physics of chemistry—sets [Potential Sciences] apart from other companies,” says Joséphine Kant, head of ventures at SovAI, who has joined the startup’s board as part of the investment. “Giving them access to computing resources, they can do this work at a scale that would be very difficult otherwise for a small startup.”
However, AI drug discovery is a crowded market. Even with a leg up from the UK government, Potential Sciences will face steep competition from a multitude of entrepreneurs and academics racing to solve the same bottlenecks from varying angles of approach.
Nor does the ability to more quickly identify promising drug candidates eliminate the cost and time required to test their safety and efficacy, meaning new treatments will continue to take a long time to come to market, regardless of advances in AI. “The cost of designing a drug is nothing compared to figuring out what it will do to mice; to really sick patients; to normal people,” says Wolynes. “In some sense, it’s not the rate-limiting phenomenon.”
As the field progresses, startups like Potential Sciences will also have to contend with the prospect that technologies able to identify effective treatments could be abused to develop highly dangerous chemicals, too. “If we can design tools that perfectly minimize toxicity, it’s a bit flip to maximize it as well,” Helal says.
Potential Sciences doesn’t yet have all the answers. The startup hasn’t settled on a way to generate revenue from the various technologies it’s developing nor decided whether to make its models freely available, given the potential for misuse. But Helal is convinced that there are few more worthwhile problems to try to remedy with AI.
“There have been many waves of promising breakthroughs that don’t quite have an impact in drug discovery,” says Helal. “It’s a fundamental, high-impact problem for us to try and solve.”

In 1924, Dutch physician and physiologist Willem Einthoven was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine “for his discovery of the mechanism of the electrocardiogram (ECG)”.
His work made it possible to record the electrical activity of the heart with greater accuracy. By developing the string galvanometer and establishing a standard method for interpreting its recordings, Einthoven helped turn electrocardiography into an important tool for studying heart function. Today, the ECG is routinely used to investigate irregular heart rhythms, detect signs of reduced blood supply to the heart muscle and identify evidence of previous heart attacks.

The official handle of Indian Youth Congress also questioned the logic behind the retreat of the Delhi Police.
Administrative Indecision in The Past
This is, however, not the first time that the Delhi administration retracted its position during Diwali regarding firecrackers. Over the past two years, Delhi’s authorities and the courts have attempted to take a strong stance against firecrackers due to the city’s severe air pollution, but they have often backtracked on their decisions.
Ahead of Diwali 2024, the Delhi government imposed a complete ban on the manufacture, sale, storage and bursting of all firecrackers until January 1, 2025. The Supreme Court later criticised the poor enforcement of the ban and suggested that the government consider making it permanent. In December 2024, the Delhi government told the court that it had imposed a year-round ban on firecrackers.
However, the position changed soon. In April 2025, the Supreme Court refused to relax the ban, but in October it allowed green crackers to be sold and used in Delhi-NCR for a limited period during Diwali. The court said these crackers had to meet standards set by the National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI), and allowed their use only during specified hours. The Delhi government and the Centre supported the relaxation.
In effect, the authorities moved from a complete ban on firecrackers to allowing a limited category of green crackers, despite earlier court observations that even green crackers could not be considered a comprehensive solution to Delhi’s pollution problem.
Delhi Pays The Price
Delhi’s air quality worsened sharply during Diwali 2025, with the city’s AQI (Air Quality Index) reaching almost 500, falling under the hazardous category. Firecracker bursting was followed by a dramatic rise in PM2.5 and PM10 levels.
According to a Times of India report, between 9 pm and 10 pm on Diwali 2025, the PM 2.5 concentration of Delhi’s Nehru Nagar region saw a spike from 679 micrograms per cubic metre to 1,763µg/m³. The report also mentioned that the peak PM2.5 concentration was more than 29 times the national daily limit of 60 µg/m³ and around 118 times the World Health Organization’s recommended daily guideline.
Pollution Concerns Framed as Anti-Hindu
Following Diwali last year, Alt News had written about the Right-wing supporters in the country interpreting complaints on the detrimental environmental effects of bursting firecrackers as an “attack against Hindutva” itself.
YouTuber Dhruv Rathee had posted a video on his X page asking his audience to desist from burning firecrackers. Right-wing social media users immediately began sharing images of firecrackers that they had apparently hoarded. While some questioned Rathee’s stake in it, others indulged in whataboutery and asked whether he had shown environmental concerns on Bakrid. Certain users went to the extent of mockingly comparing the extreme pollution levels in India to the genocide in Gaza.
Similarly, when BJP leader Subramaniam Swamy wrote on X, “Exploding fire crackers after 10 pm today is a criminal offence. Police should crackdown on them”, Right-wing influencer Chandan Sharma (Hindutva Knight/@HPhobiaWatch) targeted Swamy’s daughter, The Hindu’s Diplomatic Editor, Suhasini Haidar, using obscene language for being married to a Muslim man.
Several Right-wing accounts, such as @NamitaBalyan, @AchAnkurArya, and @JaipurDialogues, posted photos showing the firecrackers and the knight sky shrouded in smog, ultimately dismissing grave environmental concerns under the garb of protecting Hindu festivals.

Chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting are among the most distressing side effects of cancer treatment in children. Preventing them is essential not only to improve quality of life, but also to help patients complete treatment. Yet the medicines used to prevent vomiting can themselves cause adverse effects, making the search for safe alternatives an important challenge in paediatric oncology.
An Indian multicentre clinical trial suggests that olanzapine may offer an alternative to dexamethasone, a corticosteroid routinely used to prevent chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting in children receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy — treatment with a high risk of inducing vomiting. The current regimen using dexamethasone is a guideline that is used regularly, but dexamethasone is a corticosteroid. The study was aimed at finding a comparable, non-corticosteroid option.

Susie Wiles knew about Vance’s post blaming GOP midterms disaster on Iran days before being axed by Trump
Vance blamed the Iran war for the Republicans’ humiliating performance at the midterm elections

During the final stretch of his campaign to protect Republican fortunes in the midterm elections, Vice President JD Vance adjusted his approach, speaking less about President Donald Trump and focusing more on the issues defining his own political identity.
Vance framed his argument for Republicans, who ultimately lost control of Congress in Tuesday’s vote, almost entirely through his own policy portfolio, according to a review of six speeches delivered since the Republican convention in September.
He bypassed signature White House policies, including deportations and the war in Iran, as public polling indicated that the president's declining popularity was dragging down Republican candidates.
Two sources familiar with the strategy described the pivot as intentional. Vance and his advisers viewed his primary themes—economic nationalism, foreign policy restraint, and public safety—as potent topics he could address with authority. While Trump integrated those concepts into his MAGA platform, Vance had positioned himself as their chief proponent, the sources noted.
This tactical change offers an early look at how the 42-year-old vice president could chart an independent course as Republicans begin to look beyond Trump.
Vance has not stated whether he intends to run for president in 2028, and Trump has offered no endorsements. Nevertheless, Vance is considered a premier potential contender who party officials say must inherit much of Trump’s coalition while distancing himself from his superior's political liabilities.
Vance moved more publicly on Wednesday to reinforce his personal political brand with a strikingly candid election postmortem. Writing on social media, he attributed the Republican defeat to the Iran war and laid out a strategy for a party recovery.
He called for a swift end to the conflict and urged Republicans to concentrate on affordability, reevaluate foreign relations, and reform the US relationship with Israel.
Trump, by contrast, has previously described voter concerns over affordability as a Democratic "hoax." He launched the military intervention in Iran following prolonged lobbying by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whom Trump later endorsed in the Israeli election.
The online post marked the first time Vance openly advocated for concluding the war.
Three individuals familiar with White House and vice-presidential communications said the vice president was not breaking with Trump, adding that White House chief of staff Susie Wiles had advance knowledge of Vance’s message.
On Friday, however, Trump restructured his senior White House team, replacing Wiles with Stephen Miller—a movement suggesting the administration intends to double down on several hardline positions.
While Trump acknowledged that high gas prices resulting from the Iran war contributed to the Republican defeat, he defended the conflict. "I would have done nothing different," he told reporters on Wednesday.
It could not be confirmed whether Trump was informed of Vance's statement beforehand.
Donald Trump Jr., the president's eldest son, publicly backed Vance's commentary on social media, alongside several conservative allies.
The exchange has further elevated Vance as a potential post-Trump conservative standard-bearer, according to Michael Ricci, a Republican strategist and former adviser to House Speakers John Boehner and Paul Ryan.
Ricci noted that Vance’s intervention pushed conservatives to debate the merits of the conflict and consider which core principles Republican presidential candidates should embrace in 2028.
"It’s simplistic to say this about him looking for ways to differentiate himself from Trump," Ricci said. "This is about him using his megaphone of the vice presidency to set the terms of debate."
Spokespeople for Vance declined to comment. White House representatives referred inquiries to Trump's Wednesday remarks, in which he expressed an understanding of Vance's view on the election results.
Democrats are preparing to link Vance—or any eventual Republican nominee—directly to Trump in 2028, particularly if the president remains central to vetting potential contenders.
"There’s a real challenge of how you position yourself to be viable in a general election while winning a primary that still requires you to bow down and kiss the ring," said Democratic strategist Igor Volsky.
Vance’s personal brand did not come through the midterms completely unblemished. Republicans suffered losses in states where he stumped, and some tactics he supported—including an ad from Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy casting doubt on sexual abuse reported by victorious Democratic candidate Amy Acton—may have turned voters away from Republicans.
Other prospective 2028 contenders have shared their own diagnoses of the defeat. US Senator Ted Cruz of Texas said Republicans had failed to do enough on affordability. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis argued that defeated candidates spent too much time on transgender issues while overlooking voter concerns regarding data centers and artificial intelligence. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has remained silent.
Vance's push to frame the conversation was evident throughout the campaign's final days.
In stump speeches, he told voters to back Republicans to ensure investigations into fraud within federal healthcare and antipoverty programs, connecting those topics to cost of living and the White House's immigration agenda. He largely ignored gas prices and the Iran war, and rarely mentioned Trump by name.
"I want my kids to raise a family in a country that is vibrant and thriving and free and prosperous. I want the simple things," Vance told one of his final rallies in North Carolina. "And because I want that for me, I want it for you too."

- The claim that the U.S. and Israel would carry out a nuclear strike on Iran after the 2026 midterm elections is unproven.
- The rumor stems from an X post by the conservative political commentator Tucker Carlson, who claimed on Nov. 1 that Trump could decide to carry out the alleged strike as early as next Nov. 7. Carlson claimed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was attempting to push Trump and his administration to use nuclear weaponry in the war in Iran.
- At the time of this writing, neither the Trump administration nor the Pentagon had confirmed whether the president was considering using nuclear force against Iran. Experts warned that doing so would have a devastating impact on the entire Middle East region and could start a global nuclear arms race.
- A White House spokesperson told Snopes that Carlson had "no insight into military planning or the Commander-in-Chief's thinking" but that Trump would "do what is right to keep the American people safe."
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We contacted the Department of Defense to ask whether Carlson's post was true. We also contacted Carlson to ask about the credibility of his anonymous source and any updates he had gotten on the situation since publishing his initial post on Sunday.
On Nov. 1, two days before the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, the conservative political commentator Tucker Carlson posted (archived) on X that "the Trump administration may be within days of launching a nuclear strike on Iran."
In a more than 700-word post, Carlson claimed that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was seeking to pressure U.S. President Donald Trump, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and U.S. Central Command head Brad Cooper to take out Iran's Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected key location in Iran's nuclear program, using a nuclear bomb.
According to Carlson's "informed observer," Trump could make a decision on whether to carry out a nuclear strike on Pickaxe Mountain as soon as Nov. 7.
Carlson's post also circulated on Facebook and Bluesky (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about Carlson's claim.
At the time of this writing, neither the Trump administration nor the Pentagon had confirmed that the president was considering using nuclear force against Iran.
The U.S. has not used nuclear power in warfare since dropping atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945, a move that forced a Japanese surrender and led to the end of World War II. Over the past month, Trump has given mixed signals in media interviews about his plans for ending the war in Iran, but has not suggested he was considering using nuclear force.
Experts warned that using nuclear force against Iran would have a devastating impact on the entire Middle East region, could inspire existing nuclear powers like Russia or China to use their arsenal in conflicts in Ukraine and elsewhere and would lead to a nuclear arms race.
A White House spokesperson said in an email to Snopes on Nov. 5:
President Trump has a wide range of options available regarding Iran, and he will do what is right to keep the American people safe. Tucker Carlson lost his way long ago due to a debilitating case of Trump Derangement Syndrome, and he has no insight into military planning or the Commander-in-Chief's thinking.
We contacted the Department of Defense to ask whether Carlson's post was true. We also contacted Carlson to ask about the credibility of his anonymous source and any updates he had gotten on the situation since publishing his initial post on Nov. 1. We await replies to our queries.
Why is Pickaxe Mountain important?
Though there was no proof that the Trump administration would use nuclear power to do so, Trump has been considering striking Pickaxe Mountain — the target Carlson claimed would require nuclear force — since at least July. For example, on July 21, Trump told reporters at the White House (time code 26:34), "We'll be hitting that area pretty soon and very heavily."
In September, the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a bipartisan think tank, wrote that Israeli intelligence reportedly indicated that Iranian authorities moved "uranium centrifuges and centrifuge parts," which are necessary to enrich uranium for commercial or combat use, to Pickaxe Mountain, which is near the Natanz nuclear facility.
At the time, the think tank wrote that Pickaxe Mountain would be "difficult" to destroy "even with the heaviest non-nuclear U.S. munitions." The facility is reportedly buried deep in a granite mountain and the U.S. does not have access to blueprints that would give away its size and shape, or whether it has weak points like the ventilation shafts the U.S. targeted at the Fordo nuclear facility during Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025.
Trump has repeatedly said since the start of the war in Iran that his and Netanyahu's primary goal is that Iran does not get access to enough enriched uranium to obtain a nuclear weapon. To achieve this aim, the U.S. and Israel would need to curtail Iran's nuclear material and capabilities like the site at Pickaxe Mountain through either force or diplomacy.
Carlson's post suggested without proof that the Trump administration was weighing up using its ultimate military power to achieve its aims in Iran.
Mixed signals about Trump's next steps in Iran
Trump has given mixed signals about how he wants to approach his and Netanyahu's goals in Iran. By October, Trump was still saying that he wanted to strike Pickaxe Mountain, though no reports suggested such a strike had taken place.
For example, Trump told Newsmax on Oct. 15, "We're looking at Pickaxe Mountain. We may have to go there. We'll take a shot at that one. We'll knock it out fast."
Starting after Oct. 20, several U.S. news outlets reported that the Trump administration was drawing up plans for strikes on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3. These reports did not say that Trump was considering using nuclear force.
In fact, Trump said on Oct. 15, in response to a question about whether he would use tactical nuclear weapons in Iran, "No, I wouldn't use nuclear. We don't have to."
This remark could suggest that the U.S. had non-nuclear ways of destroying Pickaxe Mountain or that Trump wanted to allow time for diplomatic negotiations to take place.
However, by the start of November, PBS reported that negotiations between Washington and Tehran on a deal to end the war were "tense." According to the report, Washington wanted early assurances that Iran would not develop a nuclear weapon, while Tehran wanted to defer the issue for later talks.
On Nov. 2, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi appeared to signal that the ball was in the U.S.'s court. He reportedly said:
We have put forward our conditions and proposal, and everything depends on Washington's political judgement. If it opts for sincere diplomacy, we are ready to engage. But if it intends to resort to deception or military action, it will face a response more bitter and more severe than before.
Carlson published his post alleging that the U.S. was considering a nuclear resolution to the war in Iran that same day.
By Nov. 3, despite the October reports that the U.S. was planning strikes on Iran after the midterm elections, Trump reportedly told the Financial Times that the U.S. seemed to be "getting everything we want" in diplomatic negotiations and had no plans for immediate strikes.
However, that same day, Trump also told Fox News (time code 13:57) the U.S. had to "do something large" in the war with Iran. He did not specify whether "something large" was in reference to diplomacy or military attacks, but did add, "A lot of people would like to do the heavy hitting."
Trump must balance input from Tel Aviv and Washington
It was unclear from Trump's Election Day interview with Fox News who "a lot of people" were, or who exactly the president was taking advice from on the war in Iran.
On Oct. 28, news broke that U.S. Vice President JD Vance reportedly sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran's top security body, in a bid to restart peace talks. The Wall Street Journal reported that Vance sent the letter at Trump's request, though Trump himself appeared to suggest it was Vance's idea. Either way, the letter suggested the U.S. had not given up on the idea of a diplomatic solution to the war in Iran.
On Nov. 1, Carlson claimed that Netanyahu had pressured both Trump and other officials, including Hegseth, to use nuclear power in Iran. PBS reported that there had been "growing fears" that Netanyahu could be pushing Trump to escalate the conflict in Iran.
Netanyahu, whose coalition failed to secure a majority in Israel's October elections, will lose his position as prime minister if he cannot form a 61-seat majority in the Knesset. PBS reported that Netanyahu could be, "pushing for new strikes against Iran in an effort to stay in power in an emergency government during renewed war." Snopes has not independently verified this claim.
Trump reportedly spoke to Netanyahu on Oct. 31, the day before Carlson's post, though the details of that call were unclear. However, the Telegraph newspaper reported it was unlikely Netanyahu would have pushed for a nuclear strike on Iran, writing that if Israel "were seen to be involved in any way in breaking the taboo on the use of nuclear weapons, it could rebound horribly. It would take only one strike on Israel to make it unliveable, given that it is such a tiny country."
Therefore, while Netanyahu might have reason to encourage refreshed strikes on Iran, it's unlikely he would push for those strikes to use nuclear weapons.
Ultimately, the mixed reporting throughout October and November and Araghchi's statement on Nov. 2 suggested the U.S. and Iran were preparing for both a diplomatic and a military resolution to the war, potentially developing at the same time. The available evidence did not suggest that the Trump administration, regardless of input from Netanyahu or anyone else, was planning a U.S. nuclear strike on Iran, something that could set off further strikes in the Middle East and Europe and lead to a nuclear arms race.
For further reading, follow Snopes' coverage of the war in Iran.

(Bloomberg) -- The gunman who killed six people in the historic Old Town district of Poland’s second largest city on Saturday is likely a domestic far-right extremist, according to Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski.
The alleged perpetrator, a 24-year-old Polish national whose name hasn’t been made public, was injured during an exchange of gunfire with police near the Main Market Square in Krakow and taken to the hospital, where he’s undergoing an operation, Kierwinski said.
The suspect drove onto the main Krakow square in a car and opened fire with an automatic rifle at what appeared to be random targets, according to government officials. Those killed included four women and two men, while a further 16 people were injured, the regional police said. 
Three police officers were injured in the shooting, including one with several wounds in critical condition in a Krakow hospital, Kierwinski said.
“Everything indicates he was fascinated by far-right ideology,” Kierwinski told reporters in Krakow. Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said Poland was dealing with an act of terrorism.
Video taken by a witness and showed by broadcaster TVN24 showed the suspected shooter apparently injured, laying on a sidewalk, dressed in military gear, a bullet proof vest and with a rifle. The defense minister said the suspect had no links to the Polish military.
Kierwinski said the suspect had a license for a firearm and that his car was full of ammunition and other guns that probably belong to his family. 
Prime Minister Donald Tusk said police are looking into “all the circumstances of the attack,” while President President Karol Nawrocki said he’s in contact with the relevant authorities and expects a full explanation of the circumstances. 
The district in Krakow, a city of some 800,000 located about 250 km (150 miles) south of Warsaw, is a Unesco World Heritage Site known for its medieval architecture. It’s a popular destination for tourists.

FIFA has joined forces with the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in supporting the #BeActive campaign launched on the UN International Day of Sport for Development and Peace to encourage people to be #HealthyAtHome as the world comes together in the fight against COVID-19, today and every day.
WHO recommends all healthy adults do at least 30 minutes a day of physical activity and children at least 60 minutes per day. As part of this, #BeActive and remain #HealthyAtHome include the following suggestions along with any other form of recreation to stay healthy at home:
- Taking some online exercise classes,
- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,
- Jumping rope, and
- Practising muscle strength and balance training.
“We are delighted that football is strongly supporting the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by asking everyone to #BeActive and to remain healthy at home during this difficult time,” said António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations. “FIFA has asked the football community, from member associations and clubs, to players and fans, to show their support, to put their rivalries aside and to show a new solidarity so we can overcome the coronavirus. This is an important lesson not only for today, but for every day.”
“More than ever, especially now, one thing must be clear to everyone, health comes first,” said FIFA President Gianni Infantino. “FIFA is delighted to support both the United Nations and the World Health Organization in amplifying the #BeActive campaign today, and we are encouraged that the football community is also playing an active role in ensuring the message understood globally. For the first time ever, we are all on the same team and together, with team spirit and positive energy, we will win.”
“WHO is proud to collaborate as part of the UN family with FIFA and football lovers worldwide to promote the importance of being active for both physical and mental health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “The #BeActive campaign supports WHO’s drive to help people be healthy at home.”
The campaign kicks off with Real Madrid CF, FC Barcelona, Liverpool FC and Manchester United FC asking football fans to set aside their rivalries and to come together to #BeActive in order to defeat the coronavirus. Other clubs, including Club América, CD Guadalajara, Beijing Guoan FC, Shanghai Shenhua FC, Mohun Bagan AC, East Bengal FC, Melbourne City FC, Sydney FC, Auckland City FC, Team Wellington FC, CA River Plate, Olympique de Marseille, TP Mazembe, CR Flamengo and SE Palmeiras will also join the initiative in the coming days.
As part of the campaign, world-famous players share the following message: “At this time, even rivals need to stick together. We have to keep our distance, but we do not lose our focus. We can show solidarity by being active, and active means following the guidelines from the WHO.”
The video campaign will be published on various FIFA digital channels, with regular subsequent updates from clubs and players across the world during subsequent days. #BeActive is also being supported with graphics toolkits for the 211 FIFA member associations and various media agencies to facilitate additional localisation and to further amplify the message.
WHO, the UN’s specialized health agency, and FIFA, football’s world governing body, collaborate closely to promote healthy lifestyles through football globally and launched the “ Pass the message to kick out coronavirus” campaign last month to share advice effective measures to protect people from COVID-19.

EXCLUSIVE: Heated Rivalry fans who have been eagerly awaiting Season 2 of Crave‘s hockey series are in for a great surprise. Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right politician who lost Brazil’s presidential election last month, has insisted his defeat is not “the end for Brazil” as he battles to maintain political relevance after fleeing to the US.
Bolsonaro absconded early last week shortly after losing the 25 October election to the leftwing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by more than 4m votes.
On Thursday night Bolsonaro made his first major public appearance since arriving in the US, speaking at a rightwing gathering at Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago property where he claimed “great things” were still to come.
“I know this wasn’t the end for Brazil and I know it wasn’t the end for America,” Bolsonaro, 45, told a gala dinner at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC)’s four-day “gathering of visionaries” event, where the former British prime minister Liz Truss is also due to speak.
“Even when what seems like the end isn’t what we’d hoped for, we must thank God and have even more faith that this isn’t yet the end,” he added. “No one shuts the door that he opens – and the door he shuts, no one opens.”
Earlier, in his first post-election interview, Bolsonaro made a series of unsubstantiated claims about election fraud and insisted he received “help from absolutely no one” to flee.
“It was all me,” Bolsonaro told the New York Times, contradicting reports that he was helped by the Trump adviser Jason Miller and Santiago Caputo, a close aide to Argentina’s rightwing president, Javier Milei.
He said he would “take to the grave” the full story of how he had fled Brazil, where he faces federal police investigations for money laundering and corruption. Bolsonaro is a member of congress who has held elected office for more than 20 years but he will lose parliamentary immunity early next year when his term ends, meaning he could then be prosecuted.
Brazilian analysts agree that by skipping the country after an election in which he received 59m votes, Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, abdicated leadership of the opposition and sabotaged his political future.
Thomas Traumann, an author and pundit for the TV network GloboNews, said: “Flávio was foolish enough to throw away the leadership of the opposition that he could have exercised had he stayed in Brazil. But the [Bolsonaro] family is still a player.”
Flávio Bolsonaro’s brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, also lives in self-imposed exile in the US and will have to serve a four-year sentence for coercion if he returns to Brazil. Four other members of the Bolsonaro family were elected to congress in last month’s election, including their brothers Carlos and Jair Renan and stepmother, Michelle Bolsonaro.
Traumann believed it was not inconceivable that Jair Bolsonaro would attempt a political comeback if he managed to negotiate his way out of his 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. However, as things stand, the 71-year-old is banned from running for office until 2060 and must live under house arrest.
Many doubt the Bolsonaro family can continue to control Bolsonarismo, the populist political movement that takes their name, with two key members in exile and one imprisoned.
“[The movement] is mortally wounded because of its mistakes and its crimes,” the political scientist Sérgio Abranches told the newspaper O Globo this week.
Abranches said democratic rightwing politicians now had a chance to “detach” themselves from the Bolsonaros’ anti-democratic movement and break off in a new direction before the next presidential election in 2030.
Flávio Bolsonaro told the New York Times he would “obviously” be a candidate in future elections but said his future lay in the US “at least for now”.
It is unclear where Flávio Bolsonaro, who has been granted a US visa by Trump, will live. His brother Eduardo set up home in Southlake, Texas, after leaving Brazil last year – although some expect him to move after the traditionally conservative state elected the Democrat Gina Hinojosa as governor in this week’s midterms.
In a video posted on CPAC’s social networks before Thursday’s event, Eduardo Bolsonaro played down the risk posed by the “blue tsunami” to their ability to stay in the US. “They [Democrats] will try [to make trouble for us] – but it’s not up to Congress … to revoke visas or citizenships,” he said.
Likening their plight to that of a female asylum seeker fleeing Iran for fear of being killed after refusing to wear a hijab, he added: “I am 100% legal – as is my brother and his family.”

Warning: this article contains discussion of eating disorders
"If you keep this up, you'll be in a wheelchair at 30."
That is what doctors told British long-distance runner Jake Smith four years ago.
From the outside looking in, his career was flying.
By the age of 23, he had signed a professional contract with Nike and represented Great Britain on the global stage.
But at the same time, his body was deteriorating - enduring a relentless pattern of race, illness, injury, repeat.
Balancing an intense training regime with disordered eating meant the 28-year-old returned from a running camp in Uganda weighing just eight stone (51kg) at 5ft 5in (1.7m). He had such brittle bones that he was told his career could be over.
After suffering two stress fractures in the space of four months, Smith sought professional help and was diagnosed with REDs – relative energy deficiency in sport.
It is a syndrome that can affect anyone and if left undiagnosed or untreated, can have an impact on performance and cause serious, long-lasting health problems.
The symptoms are slightly better documented in women - just last month, tennis player Emma Navarro revealed her diagnosis and subsequent decision to step away from competition until 2027.
But men are just as susceptible and due to stigma and lack of obvious warning signs, it can go undetected for longer and means many, like Smith, suffer in silence.
BBC Sport explains what the condition is, how it affects men and women and why, despite its prevalence and severity, REDs remains a relatively under-reported and overlooked area of sports science.
REDs can cause bone stress injuries, disrupted sleep, fatigue and low mood. Left untreated, the condition can lead to serious long-term health problems, including osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and fertility issues.
Dr Nicky Keay, an expert in hormone health, says many of these symptoms stem from hormonal disruption caused by insufficient energy intake.
"Hormones go to every single bit in your body. So, if your hormones are not working well for you, you're going to feel it in all sorts of different areas," she says.
"In order to have healthy hormones, they need to be fed regularly. If you're not doing that and there's an energy deficit, often some of those hormone systems will slow down or shut down completely."
Women have a monthly barometer of their hormone health with the menstrual cycle, described by Keay as a "free monthly medical check".
Put simply, she says, a woman suffering from REDs has her periods "switched off".
For men, it is more subtle – testosterone levels will drop, resulting in a reduced libido and fatigue.
The impact on a woman's period is why the condition was first referred to in the early 1990s as the "female athlete triad".
But it was renamed by the International Olympic Committee in 2014 to acknowledge the broader range of symptoms of energy deficiency and that it also harms male athletes.
"We realised we were ignoring the other half of the population," Keay says.
"It's a strange situation because normally it's women's health that is the one being ignored but, in this situation, it's the men who weren't being recognised or represented."
Twelve years later that decision appears to be vindicated, with recent research highlighting the prevalence in men.
Meta-analysis published in Australian journal Sports Medicine last year, following a study involving thousands of elite and amateur athletes around the world, indicated 44.2% of female athletes and 49.4% of male athletes had low energy availability.
So why is REDs so common?
One of the answers lies in the phrase 'lighter is faster'.
For decades, it had been an accepted wisdom in sports like endurance running, cycling, climbing, horse riding, dancing and aesthetic sports like diving and gymnastics.
And for athletes like Smith, it is how his problems started.
"I believed it for years. I thought that was the way forward," he says.
"I started thinking 'how do I improve my half marathon by 10 seconds? Is it a drop in weight?'. And that's when my head completely went."
Initially, the strategy can work.
When it comes to choosing energy to cover training demand or energy to stay healthy, the body has learned through evolution and threat of predators to always prioritise movement.
It means that athletes can drop weight and still train and exercise and achieve good results.
But eventually, the luck runs out.
Described by Keay as "fool's gold", the body will adjust to the energy deficit and cause a drop in performance and high risk of injuries.
Olympic and world champion Jonny Brownlee acknowledges under-fuelling mistakes he made in his triathlon career contributed to serious injuries.
"I didn't see the importance of it. Training came first and I think we weren't educated enough in how important fuelling was," he tells BBC Sport.
"You were seen, culturally, as a bit weak if you were fuelling on the bike. And the impact of that was definitely injuries - probably not recovering from my training quite as well as I should have done, stress responses, stress fractures. So there's that side of it and probably underperformance in races as well."
Brownlee, who recently announced his retirement, believes the culture of not fuelling on the bike has now changed but a stigma lingers around REDs and the perception that it is a "female issue".
"In females, there are more obvious signs but in males it can go under the radar a little bit and then it hits you by a really serious injury," he says.
"I think there's a stigma attached in there, or it's not looked at as the obvious answer to some of your problems, it's found later down the line. Men also don't like to talk about under-fuelling because it's just seen as 'you probably should feel better and you should be on top of that'."
It is those attitudes among male athletes that prompted Keay to conduct an experiment in 2019.
Assessing 50 male competitive cyclists, Keay found in her initial screenings that nearly half had poor bone health and 25% were suffering from REDs.
The cyclists were then split into two groups and across a six-month period, one half continued their training and fuelling habits as before while the others were tutored by Keay and offered nutrition and training advice.
"The group that I left to their own devices unfortunately went on the default and they lost even more bone mineral density, similar to an astronaut in space… And they performed OK, but relative to their functional threshold power, they didn't get the race results that you would have expected.
"For the group I took under my wing, there was an improvement in their bone health and really good race results.
"So, I had evidence that REDs definitely does exist quite extensively in my group of the male cyclists and you're going to underperform if you don't fuel sufficiently. The good news is that REDs is reversible. But if you don't take action, it's a decline."
As the syndrome and its symptoms are still not commonly known, it is often difficult to know where to find help.
After former GB runner Pippa Woolven's struggles with the condition, she set up a website called Project REDs which offers information and practical resources for athletes, coaches, parents and healthcare professionals.
Keay also helps people competing at all levels to recover from REDs. Most of her patients are women, but she is starting to see more men reach out for help who, she says, are often in "bad shape".
"I think the men are maybe more reluctant than the women, or maybe they don't realise they've got it. Sometimes they might use a different word for it, they say burnout," Keay says.
"I don't mind that though because there is definitely a psychological aspect to REDs. Why are you doing this? Why are you not eating the carbohydrates?"
Sometimes, it's hard to answer those questions because the under-fuelling is unintentional, either from not understanding or underestimating energy requirements or failing to match an increase in the intensity or duration of exercise with higher calorie or carbohydrate intake.
For others, former British cycling champion Brian Smith among them, the answer comes from intention.
Competing in the road race for Great Britain at the 1996 Olympics should have been the highlight of his career but, behind the scenes of the success, Smith was suffering with an eating disorder and serious mental health condition called bulimia – something he believes he developed from his sport's obsession with weight.
"I always felt like I was overweight. Everybody was under pressure regarding weight, but nobody really spoke about it," he says.
"I'm just under six foot and I've got large glutes and thigh muscles. As a road cyclist, I used to race at 68kg and for my height and build, that's quite skinny. I even got down to about 66kg and when I got down to that, I felt underpowered, I felt bad."
Smith, now 59, only discovered he had been suffering from REDs during his career when he started running eight years ago and developed three severe stress fractures, including one in his femur.
Such has been the toll on his body that Smith says he would now never encourage anyone to pursue a career as a professional cyclist.
"It really is not healthy," he says. "If you want to go to the highest levels of the sport, you will suffer later on in life. You're destroying your body.
"Sporting teams don't care - all they're worried about is performance. So they will nurture a rider, they will feed a rider, they'll get a rider to be a certain weight. They don't care about what happens to them later in life.
"I'm suffering now and I've so many regrets. I just wish I'd known more about this."
While Smith believes his sport has a long way to go in changing attitudes, British Cycling says a lot of progress has been made through education that starts at academy level and annual physical and psychological screenings.
"One of the big things we've done in the past 10 years is try and turn this into a performance-related conversation," Dr Nigel Jones, British Cycling chief medical officer, tells BBC Sport.
"Now, we couch the conversation with an athlete around 'if you under-fuel, you will not be able to perform at your best', whereas previously, conversations in power-to-weight ratio sports might have been 'you need to be lighter'.
"I think it would be naive to say REDs is never going to be an issue. But I would like to believe that its prevalence will reduce with the work that we're doing," he adds.
British Cycling is not alone in this approach, with World Climbing taking things a step further two years ago with the introduction of mandatory health checks on athletes.
Using a combination of pre-season questionnaires and 'random and targeted' screenings at competitions - similar to the way doping tests are enforced – climbers at World Championship or World Cup-level competitions are monitored for any indicators of low energy availability or REDs and could be prevented from competing if they are not deemed to be healthy.
The policy was drawn up by expert Professor Naama Constantini, who says she is "proud" of the move by World Climbing and believes other federations should follow suit.
"We are trying to educate and prevent. I'm not a policeman and we're not looking for cheaters. I'm a medical doctor and we want to make sure our athletes are healthy," she says.
"Prevention is the best medicine you can give. We want athletes and coaches to understand that it's not about weight. It's about strength, it's about performance and fuelling the body and you pay a price if you lose weight in an unhealthy way."
With more awareness and education, it is hoped the tide can be turned on REDs.
But many still suffer in ignorance, as well as silence. That is what motivates Jake Smith to keep sharing his recovery on social media, with hundreds of men and women messaging him for advice and support.
Smith has managed to reverse his condition and is now racing better than ever, recently completing the Berlin marathon in a personal-best time of two hours, nine minutes and 24 seconds.
The big goal is the 2028 Olympics, but he is adamant that the priority is making sure he stands on every start line as healthy as possible.
"I'd never want to see an athlete go through the years I've had. I'm 10-15 kilos heavier than I've ever been and the biggest thing I can say is I've never been so happy. You need a healthy body to do everything else.
"I'm heavier, I'm faster, I'm happier."

East Bengal and Chennaiyin’s season could not have been more different ahead of their Indian Super League clash. The reigning champion had a 100 per cent record with nine goals scored, while the host was winless in four games, finding the back of the net just once.
But at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium here on Saturday, anyone ignorant of these numbers would have struggled to tell which team was languishing in the bottom half of the table. The Diwali fireworks came early on a humid night in the city as Chennaiyin shocked East Bengal 5-3, powered by braces from Brison Fernandes and Irfan Yadwad.
The visitor, who was coming off a continental defeat in midweek, was given no time to gather their bearings by Chennaiyin, which opened the scoring in the fourth minute.
Loanee Ramon Tanque, who has faced criticism for his lack of output in front of goal so far in the tournament, somewhat redeemed himself after his deft one-touch pass released Yadwad into the right side of the box.
The rest was all too simple for the Indian forward, whose squared pass was astutely left in front of goal by Madil Talal, allowing Brison to come in behind and grab his first goal of the season.
Buoyed by the early advantage, Chennaiyin kept its foot on the pedal, with Talal often joining the forward line to stretch the East Bengal defence. The overload reaped rewards as Ramon and Yadwad sent warning shots, with Prabhsukhan Gill staying alert to deny them.
But the East Bengal custodian could only dive and watch helplessly for what came in the 18th minute.
Brimming with confidence, Brison took the ball from Talal on the left edge of the box and put his marker Lalchungnunga off balance before wrapping his foot around the ball, which struck the inside of the right post before going in.
ALSO READ | Project reset at Chennaiyin FC–Clifford Miranda looks to repay faith in ISL 2026-27
The action continued to be centred in East Bengal’s half, and the lead could have been extended if not for some sloppy finish from Yadwad. And when nothing seemed to be going right for the title holder, it was handed a way back on a platter.
A threat seemed to be neutralised when Ayush Dev Chhetri dispossessed Dani Ramirez near the Chennaiyin box in the 29th minute. But the 23-year-old took long to find a pass, allowing the Spaniard to wrestle back control and feed it through for Ake Loba. The Ivorian made full use of the chance and blasted the ball into the roof of the net to halve the deficit.
Matters deteriorated when Chennaiyin was forced to replace Talal with C. Lalhriatpuia (Hriata) after the Frenchman experienced some discomfort in his right leg. But despite the quick setbacks, Miranda’s men refused to let up and hand East Bengal a hold in the game.
With just five minutes of regulation time left, Brison once again found himself in the box, but this time was denied a shot by Jeakson Singh, who was found guilty of committing a late challenge by the referee.
Ramon stepped up to the spot and sent Gill the wrong way for his first goal in Chennaiyin’s blue, a moment wildly celebrated by Miranda, who ran all the way past the East Bengal dugout to get involved in the celebrations, while a few thousand Chennaiyin faithful in the stands brought out the Poznan.
East Bengal seemed to have been reminded that it is the champion by Antonio Lopez Habas during the break as it returned from the break with fresher intent and legs. Just 75 seconds after the restart, another avoidable opportunity fell into East Bengal’s lap after Muhammed Saheef handled the ball inside the area. Ramirez, who had a frustrating night until then, made no mistake in burying the ball into the top left corner.
But once again, Chennaiyin failed to taper off. The crosses were flowing; possession was controlled in midfield, and subsequently Chennaiyin’s lead grew.
And this time, it was Irfan’s moment to shine. His first of the game came on the stroke of the hour mark when Hriata’s attempt deflected off him to leave Gill wrong-footed. While that goal could be deemed lucky to an extent, nothing can be taken away from the 25-year-old’s second.
Hriata won the ball in the middle of the opposition’s half, played it to Ramon, who beautifully threaded it through for Irfan, who kept his head to beat an advancing Gill.
Both benches were utilised as the minutes ticked away, and East Bengal substitutes could muster only a consolation goal in the first minute of added time, with Hardik Bhatt’s long ball carefully brought down David Lalhlansanga before placing it past Mohammad Nawaz.
Now as the league heads into a break, East Bengal remains sixth in the standings, while Chennaiyin has climbed to eighth.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) held that laws penalising having more than two children have lost their relevance due to the falling fertility rate in India.
“We are of the strong opinion that laws that penalise having more than two children have lost their relevance. The foundation of such laws, that is, the fear of overpopulation, has crumbled due to demographic changes in the past few decades,” a Bench headed by Justice P.S. Narasimha observed in a 37-page judgment.
The court said its 2003 judgment (in Javed versus State of Haryana) which upheld such penal laws, needed a revisit by a larger Bench. India’s Total Fertility Rate (TFR) had fallen from 3.02 to 1.9. A TFR of 2.1, known as the replacement rate, would allow one generation to completely replace itself.
“Even though India’s population is not yet declining, the TFR falling below the replacement rate will soon result in a demographic transition towards an older population with a declining share of the working-age population. Therefore, laws aimed at limiting population growth have now lost their significance,” Justice Narasimha observed.
The 2003 judgment in the Javed case had referred to the situation that existed in China as of 2000 and drew inspiration from the measures that it had undertaken to control the population.
Justice Narasimha said the decades-old view that population explosion was an impediment for progress was outdated.
Healthy growth
“The earlier perception that population harms development does not hold water anymore. Rather than society and the courts being concerned about the negative consequences of high population, it should instead focus on the need to encourage a healthy growth of population,” the judgment, by a Bench comprising Justice Alok Aradhe, said.
The judgment pointed out that the share of persons aged 60 and above had already risen from about 8.3% in 2014 to 9.7% in 2024, and government projections place that share at nearly 15% by 2036.
India’s falling fertility rate, the court said, would necessarily mean a smaller proportion of younger persons in the future, and, correspondingly, a larger ageing population. It said the issue had been of significant concern in recent years.
The court said the failure to take notice of demographic changes would lead to only serious consequences for India. Failure to adapt not only produced injustice, but was also an abuse of power.
The judgment was based on a petition filed by Mangala Bhimrao Ingle, whose election as Sarpanch of the Kakoda gram panchayat in Maharashtra was set aside on the ground that she had more than two children. The lower courts and State authorities found that she had given birth to a third child in 2014, but still contested and won the panchayat elections in 2022. They had held that she acted in violation of Section 14(1)(j-1) of the Maharashtra Village Panchayats Act, 1959, which upheld the two-child norm.
Justice Narasimha found such laws linking motherhood to political representation a violation of Article 21 (right to life) under the Constitution.
“Allowing such laws to stand excludes an entire class of citizens from political representation on grounds bearing little rational connection to their capacity to hold public office. It compels an unconscionable choice between bearing children and democratic participation, impinging on the right to reproductive autonomy under Article 21,” Justice Narasimha observed.
Seeking an immediate re-visitation of the Javed judgment of 2003, the court permitted the appellant to continue in her elected position as Sarpanch of the Kakoda gram panchayat while staying any proceedings against her.

Trump's global health strategy is emerging. What will the Democratic Congress say?
By all appearances, it was a classic government ceremony. Officials in suits. Big black chairs around a wooden table. A cluster of microphones. It happened on October 8 in Lusaka, Zambia. Amid applause, U.S. and Zambian officials signed a global health agreement, called a Memorandum of Understanding or MOU.
But Mich Coker — the Chargé d'Affaires at the U.S. Embassy in Zambia — said this agreement was anything but classic.
"This MOU represents a fundamental shift," he said, speaking at the signing ceremony. He explained that the relationship between the two countries was moving "from a traditional donor-recipient model to a true partnership, one grounded in Zambian leadership, in Zambian ownership and in shared accountability."
Global health experts on all sides of the political spectrum and all over the world agree with Coker that there's been a fundamental shift in the U.S. approach to global health.
"The shift that's currently unfolding is very large and it's very rapid," says Janeen Madan Keller, acting co-director of the Global Health Program at the Center for Global Development.
The story of this fundamental shift starts at the beginning of the second Trump Administration with months of global health turmoil — Madan Keller and other experts say — but has given way to a clearer strategy. One with big goals, a short timeline and a lot less transparency than what came before.
Here is a look at where things stand now and how a Congress controlled by the Democratic Party might impact the new landscape.
First, the "chaos"
President Trump's second term started dramatically. When he dismantled USAID (the U.S. Agency for International Development), citing alleged "fraud, waste and abuse," everything changed overnight.
"It is a period that is best described as chaos," says Madan Keller. The repercussions were massive and immediate, she says, "for people and communities in some of the poorest countries of the world."
Clinics shut down suddenly. Patients ran out of HIV medications. In Zambia, as well as a number of other countries, many patients who relied on U.S.-supported clinics and programs faced tons of uncertainty and, often, dire health consequences.
"For the first half of 2025, there was a complete upheaval," says Jennifer Kates, senior vice president and director of global and public health policy at KFF.
A strategy emerged
Next came a new stage in the history of U.S. foreign aid. "Starting over the summer of 2025 and going into September, there actually was a sort of step back to develop an actual strategy and a plan," says Kates.
What emerged from the State Department was the America First Global Health Strategy with the stated goal of making "America safer, stronger, and more prosperous." The main way this strategy is being implemented is through agreements with individual countries. In the past, the U.S. had done more work through large international organizations or local non-governmental organizations.
Experts say one defining feature of these agreements is that they are transactional. For example, in Zambia "there was a massive scandal because activists were able to show that the agreement was planning to condition access to [U.S. global health] funding on access to [Zambia's] copper and rare earth minerals," says Asia Russell, executive director of the HIV/AIDS advocacy organization Health GAP. Her organization helped expose this situation.
While the part of the agreement about minerals was separated from the global health agreement after the public outcry in Zambia, many of the global health agreements do require the recipient country to share data such as pathogen information.
Big (but not new) goals
Speaking at the signing ceremony in Zambia, Coker ticked off some of the top priorities in the new strategy, including that recipient countries increase their financial contributions to health in the years ahead and that they are transitioned off aid in the near future.
He said in the Zambian MOU, the U.S. would pay $1.5 billion over five years "with Zambia simultaneously committing to increase its own domestic health expenditures by $975 million. We are charting a path toward a stronger, more self-reliant health system."
Another priority has been building up a country's own health infrastructure — and not a parallel system run by non-profits and NGOs.
"We are looking to have up to about 40,000 healthcare workers recruited through this support," said Zambian Health Minister Roma Chilengi at the same ceremony.
The priorities in the MOUs — such as recipient countries contributing more and being weaned off aid money — are not new ideas. In the world of global health they have long received bipartisan support. But, up until now, they've been hard to implement. "This approach really does kickstart them in a new way that had not occurred before," says Kates.
But in her view the chaos before this kickstart makes implementing these goals more challenging — as does the fact that everyone's now operating within a greatly diminished U.S. global health system.
The speed of the transition also troubles some. Madan Keller says that the strategy aims to achieve major changes in just a handful of years. "It's happening on a compressed timeline with arguably limited capacity to manage it, and that's where some of the risks and concerns are coming from," she says.
And Russell, for her part, is worried that the main goal of the Trump Administration has been hammering out MOUs rather than setting ambitious health-related goals, such as reducing HIV transmission. The Trump administration is focused on "process indicators — not impact indicators — as its first measure of success, which is basically a loser's gambit when it comes to pandemics," she says. "Rubio crowed about signing documents. That doesn't save lives."
The State Department declined an interview request but said in a statement that most African countries with MOUs now have drawn up implementation plans and "U.S. embassies globally are now focused on operationalizing these implementation plans [and] recipient country governments are also executing on the commitments they have made in the MOUs."
"Very hard to get the information"
Another major challenge in assessing the new strategy has been a lack of information provided to the public, says global health experts.
This represents a big break from past U.S. global health initiatives. For example, the U.S.'s flagship program for HIV/AIDS — called PEPFAR – "was a gold standard for collecting data on a regular basis and sharing it transparently — and then using that data to really inform decision making," Ramona Godbole, the former deputy director of policy, planning and programs at the now-defunct U.S. Agency for International Development, told NPR earlier this year.
"Now it's much more opaque and very hard to get the information. The agreements themselves have not been publicly released by the U.S. government," Kates says. Although, the text for some of the agreements have become available through litigation or Freedom of Information Act requests filed by advocacy groups.
There is even less information on the implementation plans, she says, which are supposed to contain detailed goals and metrics for how the money will be spent and what programs will be supported.
Kates says this is true despite the fact that U.S. taxpayers are underwriting the aid, which totals $16 billion committed across the 36 agreements that have been signed. That money comes from U.S. taxpayer dollars that Congress allocated to foreign aid. KFF has calculated that this represents a 34% drop in U.S. global health aid and it has left some countries without an agreement. For instance, Zimbabwe lost U.S. global health aid since the two governments were not able to agree to MOU terms.
In its statement, the State Department said: "Claims of a lack of accountability and transparency are unfounded….We have and will share every signed MOU with Congress."
A new blue Congress
In the wake of this week's midterms, there are new questions about how this fundamental shift in global health will play out. With the Democratic Party returning to the majority in Congress, many expect that lawmakers will demand more transparency.
"I think 100% they are going to demand: give us the MOUs, show us the implementation plans, come in and tell us more detail about what you're doing," Kates says.
Another question is whether the new Congress might try to resurrect what was dismantled. Kate says there are still a lot of unknowns about what the new Congress will do after it convenes on January 3 and how the Trump Administration will respond, but she expects lawmakers will first push for the public to get more information on what global health work the U.S. is and isn't currently supporting.
Russell says many global health activists are calling for more oversight — and she is one of them. "Congress needs to slam its feet, both feet, on the brakes unless and until it gets this information, gets this accountability," she says.

Do you know signs of a stroke? BE FAST are the words to remember
Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., suffered a stroke on Saturday. His prognosis is excellent, according to his office. His case illustrates the importance of knowing the warning signs of a stroke.
The American Stroke Association says following the six letters in the acronym BE FAST — can help save stroke victims and prevent permanent brain damage.
Murphy, 53, had the "A" for "arm weakness" — he felt numbness in his arm while he was at his son's hockey game, according to a statement from his staff. And they said he acted quickly to get care — that's the "T" for "time."
Being seen by medical professionals as soon as possible — be fast! — gives people the best shot at survival and full recovery.
Here are all six of the stroke-spotting signs in the BE FAST acronym, according to the American Stroke Association:
B – BALANCE loss
Dizzyness, trouble walking or a sudden loss of balance are all signs that a stroke may be occurring.
E – EYE changes
Is the person having trouble with their vision? Blurred vision, double vision or loss of sight in one eye are important symptoms.
F – FACE drooping
Ask the person to smile. Is their smile uneven? Numbness or drooping on one side of the face is a symptom.
A – ARM weakness
Numbness in one arm, as Murphy had, is a symptom. Weakness is too. Ask the person to raise both arms. Does one arm drift down?
S – SPEECH difficulty
Trouble talking is another common symptom. Can the person repeat a simple sentence? Is their speech slurred or hard to understand?
T – TIME to call 911
If you or someone you are with is experiencing these symptoms, call 911 as soon as you can. Getting care quickly is very important for survival and to minimize long-term effects.
A stroke happens when blood flow to or within the brain is interrupted. It can happen when an artery is blocked or when a blood vessel in the brain bursts. Brain tissue that is deprived of oxygen can be permanently damaged, resulting in long-term disability or death.
Other important symptoms of a stroke are a severe headache, confusion and numbness on one side of the body.
Stroke is the #4 leading cause of death in the U.S., killing more than 162,000 people in 2023, according to the American Heart Association.

The victim was identified as Paramjith Dhankhar, 43, who was employed by Vietnam-based FPT Software Company Limited at its Singapore office and was visiting his family for Diwali. He was previously a senior executive at Indian tech firm Tech Mahindra.
The suspect was identified as 42-year-old Mohan Sharma, a contractor and scrap-processing businessman. He was arrested from Ballabgarh on Saturday and his licensed handgun, with 59 live cartridges kept inside the bag used for storing the weapon, and two magazines—one of which was partially loaded—were recovered, police said.

The two men lived on different floors of four-storey building in Faridabad’s Sector 21C.
Relatives of the victim said that the two families had been embroiled in a dispute for the past three months over the Sharma’s German Shepherd pup defecating in the parking on the ground floor, following which Dhankhar’s family had filed a police complaint. “A week ago, Sharma had broken one of the three stilt entrance gates Dhankhar had constructed to avoid a dispute. The mortal remains of slain anti-drug activist Parvinder Singh Jhota, whose murder last month triggered protests and a political row, were brought to his native place here on Sunday for last rites.
Following a post-mortem at PGIMER in Chandigarh on Saturday (November 7, 2026), Jhota's body was taken to his native place, where last rites would be conducted.
Jhota was shot dead in broad daylight at a medical store in a busy marketplace in Mansa town on October 13. The store owner, who had fired at Jhota after the activist confronted him over the sale of addictive drugs to an elderly man, was subsequently arrested.
A large number of people turned up at his home to pay their last respects before the cremation was held.
On Saturday (November 7, 2026), a member of the joint action committee had said Jhota's cremation would take place at his native place in Mansa on Sunday.
The joint action committee (JAC), also known as the Parminder Singh Jhota Insaaf Action Committee, is a coalition of various social organisations and activists formed in Punjab after Jhota's murder.
The cremation will be held at Jhota's fields on Chakerian Road in Mansa. Jhota's father, Bhim Singh, on Saturday (November 7, 2026) called upon the youth of Punjab to pledge against drug abuse.
"We will take the body to our residence first and thereafter, between 12 and 1 pm, Jhota will be cremated on Diwali Day," said Singh while speaking to reporters in Chandigarh on Saturday (November 7, 2026).
Jhota's body was brought to PGIMER Chandigarh from the mortuary of Civil Hospital in Mansa in the early hours of Friday, after his family ended their 22-day agitation and agreed to a post-mortem following a meeting with Punjab government representatives.
On Friday (November 6, 2026), Jhota's father said he would go on a fast demanding the immediate transfer of Mansa Senior Superintendent of Police Vaibhav Chaudhary.
Jhota's family, along with the JAC, had been sitting on a protest in Mansa seeking justice for the slain activist. On October 28, two JAC members, Lakhvir Singh and Mohanjit Singh Sheron, were arrested during the protest.
On the evening of November 5, the JAC members were released from Nabha district jail after a meeting between the protesters and government representatives, including Assembly Speaker Kultar Singh Sandhwan and Agriculture Minister Gurmeet Singh Khudian, on November 4.
The murder incident, which took place while Jhota was hosting a Facebook Live session, triggered a political slugfest in Punjab, which goes to polls early next year.
Opposition parties in Punjab had stepped up their attack on the Mann government over the drug issue and law and order after Jhota's murder.
The JAC had been pressing for the resignations of Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann and Director General of Police Gaurav Yadav.
The Punjab government had earlier handed over the probe into Jhota's death to the CBI following his family's demand. The state government had suspended a station house officer, a deputy superintendent of police and a drug inspector in connection with the case.
The family has been demanding setting up a trauma centre in Jhota's name and compensation for each of the four injured persons in the incident, which were agreed to by the government.
Other demands the government agreed to include installation of Jhota's statue at either a park or a stadium.
